trackers.name: Kansas Land Trust
trackers.desc: Kansas Land Trust — a leading land trust/conservancy in Kansas. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Sierra Club Kansas Chapter — permit challenges and statehouse watchdog
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Kansas has no dedicated environmental public interest law firm, and the Sierra Club chapter is the state's main organised litigant and watchdog. It sued the Kansas Department of Health and Environment over permits for four swine CAFOs that had been split into separate LLCs to evade the statutory surface-water setback; a district judge called the agency's actions “unreasonable, arbitrary and capricious” and reversed the permits (later dismissed as moot on appeal). USE IT: chapter and executive committee meetings are open, and its five geographic groups are the way to find neighbours already fighting a permit near you.

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights (PDR) — Lexington-Fayette County

USE IT: farms of 20+ acres (or adjoining tracts totalling that) apply to the PDR office in the annual cycle; a Small Farm Program extends the same deal to smaller holdings.

USE IT: the clearest US template for a community that wants to BUY the working forest around it rather than watch it be subdivided — contact DLLT about how the community-forest purchase was financed and structured.

trackers.name: Georges River Land Trust — Knox & Waldo Counties

USE IT: the water-quality monitoring data is the useful part for a pollution dispute — an independent local record of river condition over time, held by a body with standing in the watershed.

trackers.name: Royal River Conservation Trust — Cumberland & Androscoggin Counties

USE IT: a trust with a track record of converting private parcels into permanently public land through the state LMF programme.

trackers.name: Frenchman Bay Conservancy — Hancock County

USE IT: it is running a USD 10 million campaign for urgent Union River acquisitions, so a threatened parcel there has a funded buyer to approach.

trackers.name: Blue Hill Heritage Trust — Blue Hill Peninsula, Hancock County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a community-based trust conserving land and water resources in perpetuity across the Blue Hill Peninsula — it owns conserved land, monitors conservation easements on privately owned property, maintains low-impact trails including one to the summit of Blue Hill Mountain, and runs a Farmland Forever programme specifically for protecting local farmland. USE IT: if peninsula farmland is under development pressure, Farmland Forever is the named local route; the trust also monitors existing easements, so it can tell you whether a parcel is already restricted.

trackers.name: Midcoast Conservancy — Lincoln, Knox & Waldo Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: an accredited trust covering 24 towns and 450 square miles across Lincoln, Knox and Waldo counties — the Damariscotta Lake, Medomak River and Sheepscot River watersheds — with 16,000+ acres conserved and 56 public preserves. USE IT: proof that river-barrier removal and invasive eradication are achievable locally — approach it for the project structure and funding path.

trackers.name: Kennebec Estuary Land Trust — Sagadahoc County

USE IT: its first easement covered more than 80 acres and 2 miles of shoreline, so shoreline and wetland protection is its established territory.

trackers.name: York Land Trust — York County

It recently protected 181 acres of forest along the Josias River in Cape Neddick in perpetuity, and won an L.L.Bean Maine Land Trust grant for accessibility work at Near Point Preserve. USE IT: it runs about 90 free public programmes a year, which is an easy way to reach the people who would turn out for a local land fight.

trackers.name: Three Rivers Land Trust — inland York County

USE IT: it states plainly that conservation means bringing people in rather than keeping them out, and works with towns as well as landowners.

trackers.name: Western Foothills Land Trust — Oxford County

USE IT: a trust used to assembling LMF-funded purchases of parcels adjacent to schools and village centres.

trackers.name: Moosehead Regional Land Trust — Piscataquis & Somerset Counties

USE IT: where a landowner change threatens traditional access, this is the body that treats that access itself as the thing to be conserved.

trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Northeast Region, Hadley MA — the federal wildlife authority covering Maryland. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Program Open Space (Maryland) — county-allocated land acquisition money
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: Maryland's land programme since 1969, funded by a 0.5% STATE REAL ESTATE TRANSFER TAX — so it is not a budget line that competes each year, it flows with property sales. Over 7,100 projects and 422,700 acres. Two arms: STATESIDE buys large tracts by fee simple and conservation easement for State Parks, Forests and wildlife management areas; POS LOCAL funds county and municipal acquisition and development. WHO IT SUITS: the local arm is the one most communities can actually reach. HOW IT DIFFERS, AND THIS IS THE POINT: POS Local funds are ALLOCATED ANNUALLY TO ALL 23 COUNTIES AND BALTIMORE CITY BY FORMULA. Money is already earmarked for your county — what it gets spent on is decided locally, entered in the county's POS Local Annual Program and then sent to the Board of Public Works. So lobby the county, not the state. Separately, the Rural Legacy Program covers 36 locally designated areas where land trusts acquire easements over working landscapes.

trackers.name: Maryland Program Open Space (DNR)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): Maryland's Program Open Space, funded by the state real-estate transfer tax since 1969, funds land acquisition and conservation easements — its Stateside component acquires large tracts and easements for state parks, forests and wildlife areas, and its Local component and Rural Legacy program give grants to county and municipal governments and to land trusts to plan, acquire and protect recreational and conservation land (422,700+ acres protected). USE IT: work through your county or municipality, or a Rural Legacy land trust, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Montgomery County Agricultural Land Preservation — Montgomery County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Montgomery County has preserved more than 70,000 acres — the highest share of farmland under easement of any county in the nation — through seven stacked programs anchored on the 93,000-acre Agricultural Reserve: the county Agricultural Easement Program buys development rights outright, while Transferable Development Rights and Building Lot Termination easements permanently cap or extinguish residential density on a property. USE IT: landowners facing development pressure can apply to the county Agricultural Easement Program (typically 6–12 months, no state approval needed); communities can cite Ag Reserve zoning and recorded TDR easements when opposing a subdivision.

trackers.name: Baltimore County Land Preservation — Baltimore County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: with nearly 70,000 acres already under easement, Baltimore County's Planning Department runs a county Agricultural Protection Program alongside the state MALPF and Rural Legacy programs, and funds easements and outright purchases itself within five designated Rural Legacy Areas — targeting farm and forest land, stream valleys and reservoir watersheds. USE IT: landowners inside a Rural Legacy Area apply through the land trust that sponsors it (Land Preservation Trust for Piney Run, The Manor Conservancy for Manor, the county itself for the Coastal area); easements can be sold or donated.

trackers.name: Harford County Agricultural Preservation — Harford County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a nationally recognised farmland preservation leader since 1977 with more than 64,000 acres preserved, Harford County runs its own Agricultural Land Preservation Program (HALPP) buying development rights under Chapter 60 of the county code, alongside the state MALPF programme, the Maryland Environmental Trust and the Deer Creek Rural Legacy Area (nearly 67,000 acres of watershed) which the county administers. USE IT: landowners with agricultural or forest land, at least one spare development right and qualifying soils apply competitively through Planning and Zoning; easements are perpetual.

trackers.name: Installment Purchase Program — Frederick County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: created in 2002 and funded by a dedicated share of the county's recordation tax, Frederick County's IPP buys permanent agricultural easements using installment purchase agreements — paying the farmer tax-free interest over 10 to 20 years with a lump-sum principal at the end, which for many families beats a single taxable payout. More than 24,000 acres preserved across 172 properties, alongside the county's MALPF and Critical Farms programmes. USE IT: apply through the Office of Agriculture; you need 50+ acres (or adjacency to protected land), qualifying soils and remaining development rights.

trackers.name: Agricultural & Woodland Preservation — Anne Arundel County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Anne Arundel runs a stack of easement programmes — its own local programme (from 1990, open to parcels of 50+ acres, 6,583 acres protected), the state MALPF programme (5,485 acres), and the Anne Arundel South Rural Legacy Area, a 37,381-acre corridor between the Patuxent and Rhode Rivers where the explicit goals include creating a greenway and extinguishing development rights. Recent easement offers have run $8,000–$10,000 per acre with cash at settlement. USE IT: deadlines differ by programme (MALPF 1 May; local 1 November and 1 April; Rural Legacy 1 December) — landowner interest drives the county's annual capital budget ask, so applying is itself the lobbying.

trackers.name: Rural Legacy Program — Maryland DNR
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): enacted in 1997 explicitly to discourage sprawl, Rural Legacy funds county governments and private land trusts — not the state directly — to buy conservation easements from willing owners inside locally designated Rural Legacy Areas, of which there is at least one in every Maryland county. Over 130,000 acres preserved, with annual awards recently running $15–35 million. USE IT: a local sponsor (your county or a land trust) applies each year to the Rural Legacy Board, and can also apply to expand an existing Rural Legacy Area or designate a brand-new one — so a community can get its landscape onto the map, not just individual parcels.

You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: Chesapeake Legal Alliance — pro bono environmental representation
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a coordinating body matching individuals and community organisations with pro bono attorneys — a network of over 300 lawyers and 95 firms across Maryland, Virginia, Delaware, Pennsylvania, New York, DC and West Virginia, handling nearly 100 legal projects a year. Work covers enforcement and compliance actions on water and land pollution, reviewing permit applications, and supporting participation in public processes — not only litigation. USE IT: bring them a permit application you want read before the comment deadline; that is the cheapest point at which a lawyer changes an outcome.

trackers.name: Great Lakes Environmental Law Center
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Detroit-based environmental-justice law nonprofit providing legal services to frontline communities — disproportionately communities of colour and low-income neighbourhoods — across Wayne County, all of Michigan, and the wider Great Lakes region. Record includes helping shut the Detroit incinerator and challenging air permits (e.g. Stellantis, asphalt plants) alongside residents. For activists in Michigan: a local litigator that practises community lawyering against polluters.

trackers.name: Little Traverse Conservancy
trackers.desc: Little Traverse Conservancy — a leading land trust/conservancy in Michigan. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Michigan Environmental Council

trackers.name: Environmental Law & Policy Center (ELPC)
trackers.desc: The Midwest’s leading public-interest environmental legal advocacy organization. WHO TO ENLIST against polluting facilities, pipelines, factory farms and dirty-energy projects across the region. You CAN: get legal and policy advocacy to challenge projects and permits. For activists: regional legal muscle and clean-energy expertise to fight harmful development. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: Michigan Dept. of Environment, Great Lakes & Energy (EGLE)
trackers.desc: Michigan’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Michigan. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Michigan Natural Resources Trust Fund — DNR acquisition grants
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): the Michigan Natural Resources Trust Fund, funded by state oil-and-gas mineral royalties, awards grants to local units of government (and the DNR) to acquire land for public recreation and for the protection of environmentally important or scenic land — by law at least 25% of annual funding goes to acquisition (over $1.3B granted since 1976). USE IT: work with your city, county or township to apply for an acquisition grant on a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Ottawa County Parks & Open Space — Ottawa County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Ottawa County Parks manages over 7,700 acres of parks, dunes, greenways and open space, bought and stewarded with a dedicated voter-approved Parks & Open Space millage renewed for ten years in 2026 — the money buys land and easements outright (the 353-acre Ottawa Sands dune purchase, ongoing Macatawa and Grand River Greenway acquisitions) and is routinely stacked with Michigan Natural Resources Trust Fund grants. USE IT: bring a threatened parcel adjoining an existing park or greenway to Park Planning staff; acquisitions go before the Parks and Recreation Commission in public.

trackers.name: Natural Areas Preservation Program (NAPP) — Washtenaw County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: established in 2000 by county ordinance and funded by a countywide quarter-mill NAPP millage (renewed by voters repeatedly), the programme buys natural areas outright for public nature preserves and, since 2010, also buys agricultural conservation easements — with 93% of millage revenue required by ordinance to go to land acquisition rather than overheads. It is run by the Washtenaw County Parks and Recreation Commission and has co-funded dozens of easements held by townships and land trusts. USE IT: landowners nominate their own land for purchase or for a purchase of development rights through the programme's application page.

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights (PDR) — Kent County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a voluntary county programme that pays farmland owners the difference between their land's unrestricted market value and its value as farmland, in exchange for a permanent deed restriction barring non-agricultural development — in one of Michigan's most agriculturally productive counties (over $231 million of annual output). Values are set by independent appraisal and negotiated farm by farm; the owner keeps title, can still sell the land as farmland, and can still borrow against it. USE IT: farmers facing development pressure apply to the county; the cash typically goes to debt reduction, expansion or generational transfer, which is what keeps the farm operating rather than selling out.

trackers.name: Greenbelt & Bluebelt Program — City of Ann Arbor
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Ann Arbor voters passed a 30-year, 0.5-mill Open Space and Parkland Preservation millage in 2003 to buy development rights on farmland and natural areas — mostly OUTSIDE the city limits — protecting nearly 8,000 acres with Washtenaw County and surrounding townships, and in 2024 adding a second 'Bluebelt' boundary covering the Huron River watershed upstream of the city's drinking water intake. USE IT: two features are worth copying. Removing development rights lowers land price, which the city uses deliberately to get beginning farmers onto land; and its buy-protect-sell initiative buys a farm, attaches an easement, then resells it cheaply to income-qualified small farmers who own no land, recycling the proceeds back into the fund.

trackers.name: Mississippi Outdoor Stewardship Trust Fund (MOSTF)

trackers.name: Mississippi Center for Justice
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a nonprofit public interest law centre working statewide on racial and economic justice, with environmental among its listed practice areas alongside civil rights, community development, disaster assistance and housing. USE IT: Mississippi has no dedicated environmental public interest firm, so this is the main route to free counsel for a community facing a polluting or unwanted facility.

trackers.name: County Soil & Water Conservation Districts — Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: under Mississippi's 1938 Soil and Water Conservation Law every county could organise a district, and today THERE IS ONE IN EVERY MISSISSIPPI COUNTY, overseen by the state Soil and Water Conservation Commission. Districts implement conservation practices on farm and forest land, work on erosion and water quality, and coordinate technical assistance from federal, state and local sources. USE IT: Mississippi has no dedicated environmental public interest law firm and few county land programmes, so the conservation district is often the only public body in the county with natural-resource expertise — use it for technical grounding, and pair it with the Mississippi Center for Justice for legal help.

trackers.name: Western Environmental Law Center (WELC)
trackers.desc: A nonprofit public-interest environmental law firm serving the interior West and Pacific Northwest — free to communities and grassroots groups. WHO TO ENLIST against drilling, mining, logging, grazing and development on Western lands. You CAN: get expert litigation and legal support to challenge projects and federal land decisions. For activists: dedicated Western environmental lawyers who take on extractive and development threats. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. trackers.name: Bold Nebraska — eminent domain and landowner defence

It organises landowners into collective bargaining blocs (the Nebraska Easement Action Team model), runs know-your-rights forums for landowners on carbon-pipeline routes across Nebraska, Iowa, the Dakotas, Minnesota, Kansas and Illinois, and points people to specialist condemnation counsel. USE IT honestly: Bold is an organiser, not a law firm, and it has at times negotiated community benefit agreements instead of opposing a project outright.

trackers.name: Natural Resources Districts (NRDs) — elected local resource government
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Nebraska is divided into 23 Natural Resources Districts — multi-purpose LOCAL UNITS OF GOVERNMENT, unique to Nebraska, established in 1972 with boundaries following major river basins rather than county lines, and governed by DIRECTLY ELECTED non-partisan boards. They conserve, protect, develop and manage natural resources, funded by a small share of local property tax (typically 1–2% of what a county collects), and partner with NRCS, state and federal agencies, municipalities and counties. USE IT: because the board is elected and the district follows your watershed, this is the most accessible and most watershed-relevant body of government in Nebraska — attend board meetings, stand for election, and raise land and water threats there.

trackers.name: Nebraska Attorney General
trackers.desc: Nebraska’s chief legal officer. WHO TO CONTACT for consumer fraud, environmental harm, charity and nonprofit abuse, antitrust and public corruption in Nebraska. You CAN: file complaints and tips the office can investigate and prosecute; most have dedicated consumer-protection, environmental and charities divisions. You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: often the most powerful and reachable ally against a local corporate or official target.

trackers.name: Nebraska Business Entity Search
trackers.desc: The official registry of companies, LLCs and corporations registered in Nebraska (Secretary of State / equivalent). You CAN get: an entity’s registered name, status, formation date, registered agent and often the officers or organizers behind it. You CAN’T get: the true beneficial owner if they hid behind a registered-agent service or nominee — follow the chain and cross-check with OpenCorporates. For activists: this is how you unmask the LLC behind a local development, rezoning or mass eviction — start here to find who really controls it and whom to hold accountable.

trackers.name: Nevada Land Trust
trackers.desc: Nevada Land Trust — a leading land trust/conservancy in Nevada. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Nevada Conservation League
trackers.desc: Nevada Conservation League — a leading citizen environmental watchdog for Nevada. WHO TO ENLIST against harmful development, extraction, sprawl and pollution. You CAN: tap their research, organizing, litigation and lobbying to fight a specific project, and plug into local coalitions. For activists: a statewide ally that already knows the players, agencies and law — often your best first call.

trackers.name: Western Environmental Law Center (WELC)
trackers.desc: A nonprofit public-interest environmental law firm serving the interior West and Pacific Northwest — free to communities and grassroots groups. WHO TO ENLIST against drilling, mining, logging, grazing and development on Western lands. You CAN: get expert litigation and legal support to challenge projects and federal land decisions. For activists: dedicated Western environmental lawyers who take on extractive and development threats. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: Nevada Div. of Environmental Protection (NDEP)
trackers.desc: Nevada’s state environmental regulator. WHO TO CONTACT for pollution complaints, permits, inspections and enforcement within Nevada. You CAN: report suspected violations, search permits and enforcement records, and pull state monitoring data — often the front-line regulator before the federal EPA. You CAN’T: reach interstate matters (escalate those to EPA). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE FEDERAL EPA (below): contact the STATE agency FIRST for anything inside state lines — routine permits, local pollution, inspections, state monitoring data; it is usually faster and more local. Go to the federal EPA regional office only to ESCALATE when the state won’t act, or when the matter crosses state lines or triggers federal law. For activists fighting a local polluter or a permit for an industrial site: this is your primary state contact and records source, frequently faster and more local than federal EPA.

trackers.name: Nevada Public-Records Law Guide (RCFP)
trackers.desc: Nevada’s public-records and open-meetings (‘sunshine’) law, explained by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. You CAN get: a plain-language, attorney-written guide to what records are public in Nevada, how to request them, what exemptions and fees apply, and how to appeal a denial. You CAN’T get: the records themselves — this tells you how to demand them. For activists: your practical playbook for prying documents out of Nevada and its local agencies — permits, emails, inspection reports — usually without needing a lawyer.

trackers.name: Nevada Dept. of Wildlife (NDOW)
trackers.desc: Nevada’s state fish & wildlife / natural-resources authority. WHO TO CONTACT on wildlife, habitat and state-protected species. You CAN: report habitat destruction, check state endangered-species and critical-habitat protections, and reach the agency that reviews a project’s impact on wildlife. You CAN’T: enforce the federal Endangered Species Act (that’s U.S. Fish & Wildlife). HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM FEDERAL USFWS (below): the STATE agency handles STATE-listed species, state habitat review and (in states like California) the wildlife review inside state environmental-review law; USFWS handles FEDERALLY-listed species and the federal ESA. Contact BOTH — a species may be listed under state law, federal law, or both, and each listing is a separate legal tool. For activists fighting a development: a protected species or critical habitat on-site can stop or reshape it — this is the state authority that confirms and can act on it, alongside federal USFWS.

trackers.name: EPA Region 9 (San Francisco)
trackers.desc: The EPA regional office — Region 9, San Francisco — the federal environmental regulator covering Nevada. WHO TO CONTACT: for federal enforcement, permits and cross-boundary pollution. You CAN: report violations to the federal EPA office that actually handles Nevada, and engage on federal environmental actions. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE REGULATOR: use the federal EPA when the state agency is captured, unresponsive or lacks jurisdiction — interstate pollution, federal permits (e.g. Clean Water Act §404 dredge-and-fill), federal facilities, or national environmental law. Don’t start here for a routine local permit; the state handles that faster. For activists: escalate a polluter or project to the EPA regional office with jurisdiction over your state when the state agency won’t act.

trackers.name: USFWS — Pacific Southwest Region
trackers.desc: The U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service regional office — Pacific Southwest Region, Sacramento CA — the federal wildlife authority covering Nevada. WHO TO CONTACT: the office that administers the Endangered Species Act in your region. You CAN: raise ESA-listed species and critical habitat (which can legally halt or reshape a development), and engage on Section 7 consultations. HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE STATE WILDLIFE AGENCY: USFWS is the ONLY body that enforces the federal Endangered Species Act and runs Section 7 consultations on federal actions and permits — the strongest wildlife tool of all. Use the state agency for state-listed species and state review; turn to USFWS the moment a FEDERALLY protected species or designated critical habitat is in play. For activists fighting a development: a federally protected species on-site, confirmed by USFWS, is one of the strongest tools to stop or shrink it.

trackers.name: Conservation and Resource Protection Grant Program (Question 1) — Nevada Division of State Lands
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or protect land): Nevada voters approved Question 1 in 2002, authorising up to $200 million in bonds for land conservation — water quality, lakes, rivers, wetlands, open space and wildlife habitat — administered by the Division of State Lands and ranked by staff and the programme administrator. The legislature followed with Assembly Bill 84 in 2019, authorising a further $217 million in bonds over ten years. Crucially the programme includes a dedicated category for NONPROFIT ACQUISITIONS OF LAND AND WATER, so a land trust or community organisation can apply directly rather than only through a government sponsor. USE IT: money is released in metered rounds rather than all at once, deliberately so smaller applicants have time to prepare — watch for the next round opening.

trackers.name: Conservation districts — Nevada DCNR Conservation Districts Program
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Nevada has 28 LOCALLY ELECTED conservation districts, governmental entities under NRS Chapter 548 described by the state as working 'much like school boards'. In a state where the federal government manages more than 85% of the land, the state's own strategic plan identifies their most distinctive power: districts can WORK ACROSS THE BOUNDARY BETWEEN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE LAND, and cooperate with neighbouring districts to address problems on a WATERSHED basis, which is why federal and state agencies route natural resource projects through them. USE IT: elected volunteer boards, so both winnable and open — and the cross-boundary role makes a district a rare local body that can engage on federal land decisions.

You CAN’T: force them to take your case. For activists: your state AG is often the most powerful — and most reachable — ally against a local corporate or official target, frequently more responsive than federal agencies.

trackers.name: New Hampshire LCHIP — Land & Community Heritage Investment Program
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): LCHIP, an independent New Hampshire state authority, awards matching grants to NH municipalities and nonprofits to conserve land and interests in land (and to preserve historic resources) — 290,000+ acres conserved, funded through state document-recording fees. USE IT: as a land trust or town, apply for a matching grant to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Land and Community Heritage Investment Program (LCHIP)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy the land): an independent state authority created by the legislature in 2000 (RSA 227-M) making matching grants directly to NEW HAMPSHIRE TOWNS, CONSERVATION COMMISSIONS AND NON-PROFITS — not only to state agencies — to conserve natural, cultural and historic resources. Over $68 million in 646 grants across 210 communities since 2001, conserving more than 247,000 acres of farmland, timberland and habitat. Each LCHIP dollar reportedly leverages several more in local, private and federal money, and grants are routinely stacked with the state's Drinking Water and Groundwater Trust Fund. USE IT: funded by a fee on real estate recordings, so its budget is fought over each biennium — in 2019 a fee increase passed the legislature and was vetoed. Watch the appropriation.

trackers.name: Town conservation commissions — NH Association of Conservation Commissions
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: under RSA 36-A a New Hampshire town or city may establish a conservation commission with power to ACQUIRE CONSERVATION LAND OR EASEMENTS, hold a municipal Conservation Fund fed by appropriations and tax-deductible donations, accept gifts of land, and comment on state wetlands permit applications. Under RSA 36-A:4-a, adopted by warrant article, a town can additionally authorise its commission to buy land OUTSIDE its own boundaries and to contribute Conservation Fund money to land trusts even where the town takes no property interest. USE IT: municipal ownership alone does not protect land in perpetuity — NHACC advises adding a deed restriction or an easement held by another conservation body, which also stops a future town board eyeing the parcel for a car park.

trackers.name: Monadnock Conservancy — Cheshire County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the only land trust dedicated to the Monadnock region of southwestern New Hampshire (est. 1989; the first NH land trust to be accredited), serving 39 towns and the City of Keene across Cheshire, Hillsborough and Sullivan counties — 24,000+ acres conserved, primarily through 250+ permanent conservation easements, plus land it owns outright. USE IT: call the land protection director (conversations are confidential and free) to discuss options for permanently conserving a threatened property.

trackers.name: Southeast Land Trust of New Hampshire (SELT) — Rockingham & Strafford Counties
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: SELT (est. 1980, formed by mergers of the Rockingham Land Trust, Seacoast Land Trust and Strafford Rivers Conservancy) serves all 52 communities of Rockingham and Strafford counties plus part of southern Carroll — nearly 30,000 acres conserved through easements and ownership, in the fastest-developing corner of the state. USE IT: approach SELT about holding an easement or acquiring land under sprawl pressure in the NH seacoast region; it routinely partners with towns and other trusts to assemble a deal.

trackers.name: Santa Fe County Open Space, Trails and Parks Program — Santa Fe County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the county buys land and accepts donations for open space under procedures set by Resolution 2009-206, managing roughly 9,400 acres — and recent purchases have been driven from below, including the 2,650-acre Bobcat Crossing Ranch in a wildlife corridor between the Sangre de Cristos and the Galisteo Basin. USE IT: anyone can file a Property Acquisition Application with the Open Space and Trails Planner; applications are scored partly on demonstrated community support, so letters, petitions and turnout at COLTPAC meetings materially change the outcome.

trackers.name: Open Space Program — Bernalillo County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: begun through a grassroots campaign that won a 1998 mill-levy referendum (renewed in 2000), Bernalillo County's Open Space Program bought and now manages 17 properties totalling roughly 1,150 acres from the Sandia Mountains to the Rio Grande valley — land the county says would very likely have been developed otherwise — and has partnered on the acquisition of about 780 acres more, including the Valle de Oro National Urban Wildlife Refuge, the first urban refuge in the Southwest. USE IT: the county is still buying (a South Valley acquisition was approved in 2026); acquisitions and open space master plans go to the County Commission in public.

trackers.name: Open Space Division — City of Albuquerque
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Albuquerque has been buying land for preservation since 1963 and now manages over 30,000 acres of Major Public Open Space — foothills, West Mesa volcanoes, Rio Grande bosque and five working farms bought to stop valley farmland disappearing. Voters approved a temporary quarter-cent tax in 1997 that raised about $36 million for acquisition, and the city recently raised the open space set-aside in its general obligation bond package from 2% to 3%, roughly $6 million every two years, with a stated goal of buying everything on the priority acquisition list by 2034. USE IT: the citizen Open Space Advisory Board sets acquisition priorities and also reviews any proposal to sell, lease or build on open space — so it is the body to petition both to protect land and to stop its disposal.

trackers.name: Triangle Land Conservancy
trackers.desc: Triangle Land Conservancy — a leading land trust/conservancy in North Carolina. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC)
trackers.desc: The Southeast’s leading nonprofit environmental law organization. WHO TO ENLIST when a development, highway, pipeline, landfill or polluting plant threatens your area. You CAN: get expert legal representation and advocacy to challenge permits and projects in court — SELC takes major regional cases at no charge to communities. For activists: proven legal firepower that has stopped and reshaped countless Southeastern projects. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. Get the service list wrong and the suit is vulnerable before it starts. The letter must set out the specific facts constituting violations. TWO BARS TO CHECK BEFORE SENDING: (1) wholly past violations — citizen groups lack jurisdiction where violations have ceased (Gwaltney v Chesapeake Bay Foundation, 484 U.S. 49 (1987)); the violation must be ongoing, though in the Ninth Circuit that burden is so minimised the bar is described as nearly meaningless — the position varies by circuit. (2) diligent prosecution — the suit is barred if by day 60 a State or EPA has commenced and is diligently prosecuting the same violation, and the Fourth Circuit in Naturaland Trust counted early enforcement processes. An agency stepping in can extinguish your suit. Standing must be shown — Friends of the Earth v Laidlaw, 528 U.S. 167 (2000). ASK FOR THE THING COMMUNITIES FORGET: settlements typically cover compliance, a supplemental environmental project, fee reimbursement — and periodic future site access for your group to monitor compliance, with the defendant paying for your consultant. That is the most durable term available and it is rarely requested. WATCH FOR CHANGE: EPA has proposed new notice requirements including a centralised electronic repository — check the current rule before serving.

trackers.name: Lands Legacy Program — Orange County
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: enacted in 2000 and backed by $10 million in bond money county voters have approved since 1997, Lands Legacy buys land outright for parks and nature preserves and buys or accepts donated conservation easements — over 3,000 acres protected, including 28 working farms and “Forever Wild” easements on stream corridors in the Jordan Lake watershed. Local money has pulled in over $5 million in state and federal grants, and projects run with Triangle Land Conservancy, the Eno River Association and the NC Land and Water Fund. USE IT: every two years the County Commissioners adopt an Action Plan setting acquisition priorities — that adoption is the public moment to get a threatened parcel named.

Crucially it sets its own eligibility criteria and can make offers within months of a flood using local fee money, instead of waiting years for FEMA. USE IT: it identifies high-risk properties before floods happen, so ask to be on the priority list early; leaseback arrangements are available case by case.

trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (bridge finance and the costs nobody funds): CTNC runs revolving loan funds holding several million dollars, lending at minimal interest to North Carolina land trusts so they can buy conservation land and easements in the mountains before their own fundraising closes — and as loans are repaid the money is lent again. USE IT: transaction costs are the usual reason a landowner's intended donation or bargain sale collapses — this is the fund that covers them.

Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. trackers.name: The Land Trust for Tennessee
trackers.desc: The Land Trust for Tennessee — a leading land trust/conservancy in Tennessee. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

(2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. You CAN: tap their research, organizing, litigation and lobbying to fight a specific project, and plug into local coalitions. For activists: a statewide ally that already knows the players, agencies and law — often your best first call.

trackers.name: Western Environmental Law Center (WELC)
trackers.desc: A nonprofit public-interest environmental law firm serving the interior West and Pacific Northwest — free to communities and grassroots groups. WHO TO ENLIST against drilling, mining, logging, grazing and development on Western lands. You CAN: get expert litigation and legal support to challenge projects and federal land decisions. For activists: dedicated Western environmental lawyers who take on extractive and development threats. HOW A NONPROFIT CAN AFFORD TO REPRESENT YOU: FEDERAL CITIZEN SUIT PROVISIONS. Each major federal environmental statute contains one — Clean Water Act §505 (33 U.S.C. §1365), Clean Air Act §304 (42 U.S.C. §7604), RCRA §7002, CERCLA §310, Safe Drinking Water Act §1449, TSCA §20 — letting individuals or groups sue for violations or challenge agency inaction, and seek injunctive relief, civil penalties, and reimbursement of legal costs and attorneys' fees. The fee provision is the structural reason these firms exist: costs may be recovered from the violator. THE 60-DAY NOTICE IS THE TRAP: no action may be commenced until 60 days' notice of intent to sue is given, and under 40 CFR Part 135 it must go by certified mail, return receipt requested to the alleged violator and to the EPA Administrator, the EPA Regional Administrator, the US Attorney General, the chief administrative officer of the responsible state agency and the State Attorney General. trackers.name: Utah LeRay McAllister Working Farm & Ranch Fund (UDAF)

trackers.name: Summit County Open Space & Agricultural Conservation — Summit County

USE IT: any landowner can file a Notice of Interest (no fee) to have a property evaluated against the criteria set by the county's open space advisory committees; the county never asks for payment during the process.

trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: since 2007 Salt Lake County has funded open space acquisition, and the holding of conservation easements on land owned by others, through an Open Space Trust Fund guided by a citizen advisory committee that sets the priority criteria and reviews every proposed acquisition before it reaches the County Mayor and Council. trackers.name: Environmental Advocacy Clinic — Vermont Law and Graduate School
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the environmental advocacy clinic at Vermont Law and Graduate School, which trains and supervises students on environmental and natural resource matters. trackers.name: Vermont Housing & Conservation Board (VHCB)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY (to buy or conserve land): an independent Vermont state funding agency that uses property-transfer-tax revenue to make grants and loans to nonprofits, land trusts, towns and state agencies to acquire and permanently conserve farmland, forestland, natural areas and recreational land (it has helped conserve 431,000+ acres, 746 farms). USE IT: apply, or partner with a land trust applying, to fund the purchase or easement of a threatened parcel.

trackers.name: Town conservation commissions — Association of Vermont Conservation Commissions
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Vermont towns can establish a conservation commission with real powers — managing municipally owned land and town forests, working with the planning commission on the town plan, PURCHASING LAND for the town's conservation needs, and establishing a local land conservation fund. USE IT: this is the route in a state with no county government — form or join your town's commission, get a conservation fund established at Town Meeting, then use it as the local match VHCB requires (33%, which can include in-kind services or donated land value).

trackers.name: Bennington County Conservation District — Bennington County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Bennington County's Natural Resources Conservation District — a non-regulatory local unit of government run by elected volunteer supervisors — gives free one-on-one technical assistance to landowners on forest and woodland stewardship, agroforestry, pasture and field-edge management, soil testing, and reducing flood and runoff damage, and connects landowners to state and federal conservation funding. USE IT: bring the district in early when you need a credible local technical read on what land is worth protecting and which programs will pay for it.

trackers.name: Rutland Natural Resources Conservation District — Rutland County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the conservation district for Rutland County — a non-regulatory local unit of government that provides agricultural and land-stewardship technical assistance to farmers and other landowners county-wide (in partnership with the Poultney-Mettowee district), runs an annual native tree, shrub and wildflower sale, and works with partners on water-quality improvement. USE IT: a low-barrier local starting point for landowners who want conservation advice and a route into state and federal programs.

trackers.name: Franklin County Natural Resources Conservation District — Franklin County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the conservation district for Franklin County and northwestern Vermont — a non-regulatory local unit of government that partners with land stewards and communities on water quality, soil health and the working landscape, and channels local fund-pool money into on-farm infrastructure critical to keeping farms viable rather than sold for development. USE IT: contact the district for technical assistance and for the funding routes available to Franklin County landowners.

trackers.name: Caledonia County Natural Resources Conservation District — Caledonia County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the conservation district for Caledonia County — an elected-supervisor local unit of government at 481 Summer Street, St. Johnsbury (802-424-3149) that runs stormwater master planning for towns, road erosion inventories, culvert and bridge work, and Passumpsic, Stevens and Wells River watershed restoration, and has commissioned dam-removal design work. USE IT: it publishes board agendas, minutes and requests for bids, so its meetings are a public place to raise a local land or water concern early.

trackers.name: Windham County Natural Resources Conservation District — Windham County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the conservation district for Windham County (Thomas Hall, Brattleboro; 802-689-3024) — it publishes its Natural Resources Assessment, Conservation Action Plan, budget, enabling state statute and strategic plan as public documents, and offers free consultations with a professional forester, river stewardship and introduced-species help, plus resources written for road and municipal officials. USE IT: the published assessment and action plan are usable evidence about what local natural resources matter and why, when you are contesting a proposal.

trackers.name: Orleans County Natural Resources Conservation District — Orleans County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the conservation district for Orleans County (est. 1946; 41 School Street, Newport) — a non-regulatory body led by local landowners offering lakeshore permitting assistance, lake watershed action plans, riparian planting, soil and manure testing, conservation planning and equipment rentals, and publishing a natural resources assessment and local fund pool. USE IT: the lakeshore permitting assistance and watershed action plans are the practical entry points for shoreline and water-quality disputes.

trackers.name: Lamoille County Natural Resources Conservation District — Lamoille County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Lamoille County's conservation district (est. 1945, Morrisville; 802-521-3006), which works with the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service and Farm Service Agency on watershed and stormwater work, sustainable forestry and agricultural outreach, and runs a nature center and forest school. USE IT: contact it for green stormwater infrastructure and watershed help, and for volunteer capacity on planting and installation work.

trackers.name: Grand Isle County Natural Resources Conservation District — Grand Isle County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the conservation district for the Lake Champlain islands (est. 1946; 3501 US Route 2, North Hero; 802-372-8400; info@grandislecountynrcd.org) — it gives hands-on technical assistance to farmers, landowners and communities, helps navigate programs and access funding, and manages project design and implementation for local natural-resource problems. USE IT: a small-county district that will help identify which funding program fits a specific parcel or water-quality problem.

trackers.name: Essex County Natural Resources Conservation District — Essex County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the conservation district for Essex County, in Vermont's Northeast Kingdom — it provides education, outreach and technical assistance to residents and municipalities, covering habitat restoration, farm and clean-water technical assistance, invasive species control, program navigation and grant management. NOTE: ECNRCD publishes through the state association's site rather than a domain of its own, so the page above is its canonical home. USE IT: ask it for program navigation and grant management help if a local project needs funding assembled.

trackers.name: Winooski Natural Resources Conservation District — Chittenden & Washington Counties

It offers one-on-one 'Kitchen Table Talk' consultations, writes Nutrient Management Plans free, runs Trees for Streams plantings, replaces failing culverts and rents skidder bridges (info@winooskinrcd.org). USE IT: it took on removal of the Hands Mill Dam — a significant-hazard structure a town lacked the capacity to deal with — so it is the body to approach when a local hazard is beyond a town's means.

trackers.name: Poultney Mettowee Natural Resources Conservation District — western Rutland County
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: created in 1940 as the first of Vermont's 14 districts, PMNRCD covers western Rutland County within the Poultney and Mettowee river watersheds — 309,000 acres and 17 Vermont and New York towns making up most of the South Lake watershed. It runs the Champlain Valley Native Plant Restoration Nursery, rents aerators and a no-till seeder to landowners, and is joint Clean Water Service Provider for Basin 2/4 under Act 76, allocating state clean-water funding. USE IT: as CWSP it helps identify and develop projects and prepare applications — a direct route to money for a phosphorus or erosion problem.

trackers.name: White River Natural Resources Conservation District — Orange & Windsor Counties

It runs a Local Funding Pool open to privately owned or leased agricultural or forest land in Orange and Windsor counties with no acreage limit (802-295-7942). USE IT: the Local Working Group report behind that pool is a public statement of local conservation priorities you can cite.

trackers.name: Otter Creek Natural Resources Conservation District — Addison County

USE IT: it maintains a list of contractors and helps enrol land in CREP, which pays rent for taking sensitive land out of production.

trackers.name: Ottauquechee Natural Resources Conservation District — Windsor County

NOTE: ONRCD publishes through the state association's site rather than a domain of its own. USE IT: an open monthly meeting is a low-barrier place to put a local water or land concern on a public record.

trackers.name: Loudoun County Conservation Easement Assistance Program — Loudoun County

trackers.name: Purchase of Development Rights (PDR) — Fauquier County

trackers.name: Conservation Easement Authority — Clarke County

trackers.name: Hawaiʻi Land Trust (HILT)
trackers.desc: Hawaiʻi Land Trust (HILT) — a leading land trust/conservancy in Hawaii. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land via purchase or conservation easement. You CAN: explore having a parcel conserved so it can’t be developed. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THIS IS FEDERAL: IRC § 170(h). A qualified conservation contribution is a qualified real property interest, to a qualified organization, exclusively for conservation purposes — every element must be satisfied. (A normal charitable deduction needs the full interest; an easement is a partial interest, deductible only by this exception.) THE FOUR QUALIFYING PURPOSES: outdoor recreation or education of the general public; protection of a relatively natural habitat; preservation of open space including farmland and forest land, either for scenic enjoyment or pursuant to a clearly delineated federal, state or local governmental conservation policy yielding significant public benefit; or a historically important land area. Note that third limb — an existing government conservation policy naming your area can carry the qualification. FOUR TRAPS THAT DEFEAT DEDUCTIONS: (1) PERPETUITY — temporary easements or ones permitting amendment that could adversely affect perpetuity fail §170(h)(2)(C) and (h)(5)(A). (2) MORTGAGE SUBORDINATION — if the land carries a mortgage when the easement is recorded, the contribution is not deductible unless the lender subordinates, and courts hold that subordination obtained after the donation date does not fix it — the entire deduction is disallowed. Coordinate with the lender before closing. (3) BASELINE DOCUMENTATION — Treas. Reg. 1.170A-14(g)(5)(i) requires a report on the property's condition at the time of donation, the reference point for all future monitoring: survey maps, scale maps, aerial and on-site photographs. (4) THE DONEE MUST QUALIFY — under §170(h)(3) a private foundation is not an eligible donee; every co-owner must join in granting; and the interest may not include land subject to a prior right to extract minerals by surface mining. CHECK THE ORGANISATION FIRST: the Land Trust Accreditation Commission assesses governance, finance, transaction practices and stewardship capacity, requiring at least two years incorporated and two completed acquisitions. Accreditation is not legally required, but a body that will not exist in thirty years cannot enforce an easement in thirty years. Ask what its monitoring programme is — qualified holders generally run annual inspections. AND KNOW THE BACKDROP: the IRS treats syndicated conservation easements as prohibited listed transactions under Notice 2017-10 where deductions significantly exceeded the amount invested — inflated appraisals draw scrutiny onto the whole field. State conservation easement statutes differ and are not covered here.

trackers.name: West Coast Environmental Law
trackers.desc: A pioneering environmental-law group serving British Columbia and beyond. WHO TO ENLIST / what to use: legal advocacy, an Environmental Dispute Resolution Fund, and guides to fighting harmful projects. For activists in western Canada: legal tools and support to take on a development. IT RUNS THE ONLY DEDICATED ENVIRONMENTAL LEGAL AID FUND RECORDED ANYWHERE IN THIS MAP. West Coast Environmental Law established the Environmental Dispute Resolution Fund in 1989, providing grants to individuals, community groups and environmental organisations who need to hire legal representation to resolve an environmental problem or dispute. Everywhere else in this file, environmental cases must squeeze into a general legal aid scheme not designed for them. HOW IT WORKS: grantees hire lawyers from the private bar at a legal aid rate — you are not assigned a lawyer, you engage one. Funding comes from the Law Foundation of British Columbia. THE FOUR KINDS OF WORK FUNDED: pursuing alternative dispute resolution; appearing before government tribunals; participating in environmental assessments; and challenging government decisions in court. NOTE THE THIRD — participation in an environmental assessment is funded, not only litigation. That is the stage at which most developments are actually shaped, and it is precisely what general schemes exclude: Ireland bars tribunal representation outright. AND COMMUNITY GROUPS ARE EXPRESSLY ELIGIBLE, which is the barrier that defeats applicants in Ireland, where being one of a group with the same interest is an express exclusion. Its origin is recorded as a deliberate attempt to get out of Vancouver and meet regional needs.

trackers.name: Nature Conservancy of Canada
trackers.desc: Canada’s leading national land conservancy. WHO TO CONTACT to permanently protect threatened land through purchase or easement. For activists fighting a development: a land trust can take the land off the table for good. THE MECHANISM THAT MAKES THIS WORK IS A FEDERAL TAX PROGRAMME: the ECOLOGICAL GIFTS PROGRAM, run by Environment and Climate Change Canada, which works with individual and corporate landowners who donate ecologically sensitive land, and with qualified recipient organizations which protect the land's biodiversity and environmental heritage in perpetuity. THREE THINGS FOLLOW: the land must be certified as ecologically sensitive — a determination under the programme, not a matter of opinion, so establish early whether your parcel qualifies; the recipient must hold qualified recipient status, and not every conservation body does — ask before structuring a gift; and the protection runs in perpetuity, which is the reason to use the programme rather than a private sale with promises attached. Corporate landowners are expressly included, which matters where the land is held by a company rather than a family. FOUR ROUTES ARE NAMED ON NCC'S OWN LANDOWNER PAGE: donating OR SELLING land, estate gifts, conservation agreements, and ecogifts. Sale sits on the list beside donation — a landowner who cannot afford to give land away is not outside this route. The conservation agreement protects land without transferring ownership, like the easements recorded elsewhere here (Costa Rica's servidumbre ecológica, Puerto Rico's Fideicomiso, Hong Kong's management agreements) — the instrument where a family will not sell but will accept restrictions. And an estate gift lets an owner keep full use and control during life. GO TO THE PROVINCIAL OFFICE, NOT THE NATIONAL ONE: founded 1962, NCC has offices in each province and works at a local level to secure parcels — the same pattern as Canada's legal aid plans, where the national body is not the contact point for a specific case. NOT TO BE CONFUSED with The Nature Conservancy (nature.org, Arlington, Virginia), a different organisation recorded separately in this map.
