It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Lawyers' Environmental Action Team (LEAT)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Tanzania's first public-interest environmental law organisation, founded in 1994 — legal and social-policy research, advocacy and selected public-interest litigation on mining and extractives, land, water, forests and wildlife. It supported Rufiji Delta residents in the constitutional petition that helped stop a 10,000-hectare prawn farm, and has acted for households facing demolition on utility way-leaves. A member of ELAW and of Friends of the Earth International. WHO IT SUITS: a Tanzanian community or residents' association fighting an extractive project, an eviction or a major land-use decision — LEAT litigates selectively, so expect a case-selection conversation rather than open legal aid.

trackers.name: Legal and Human Rights Centre (LHRC)
trackers.desc: Tanzania's largest human-rights NGO, running free legal-aid centres alongside public-interest litigation. WHO TO ENLIST: legal aid through the Kinondoni (Dar es Salaam), Arusha and Dodoma offices and the Haki Kiganjani mobile legal-aid service. You CAN: get free advice and representation, and draw on LHRC's annual human-rights reporting; it was a co-applicant in the 2026 East African Court of Justice judgment that struck down Tanzanian restrictions on who may bring public-interest litigation. For activists: the practical route to a lawyer when a land or environment dispute becomes a rights case.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: Open Data Tanzania
trackers.desc: National — official government open data / budget portal. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Tanzania.

trackers.name: BRELA
trackers.desc: Tanzania's Business Registrations and Licensing Agency. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Sikika (Public Finance Governance Programme)
trackers.desc: Tanzanian civil-society organisation whose Public Finance Governance programme researches budget transparency, public-expenditure management, auditing and oversight — including the Subnational Open Budget Survey and assessments of the Public Accounts and Local Authorities Accounts Committees — to drive accountability and policy change.

trackers.name: TanzLII
trackers.desc: Tanzania Legal Information Institute: free case law and legislation. · Find here: free Tanzanian judgments and legislation (TanzLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: Business Registrations and Licensing Agency (BRELA)
trackers.desc: Tanzania’s official company, business-name and intellectual-property register.

trackers.name: National Audit Office (Tanzania)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Tanzania — audits government accounts and the use of public money.

trackers.name: Prevention and Combating of Corruption Bureau (PCCB)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Tanzania — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: TANePS
trackers.desc: Tanzania's National e-Procurement System. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Tanzania, and for how much.

trackers.name: Tanzania Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (TEITI)
trackers.desc: National Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative body — discloses oil, gas and mining revenues, contracts and company ownership in Tanzania.

trackers.name: WAJIBU – Institute of Public Accountability
trackers.desc: Tanzanian public-accountability think tank (founded 2015 by a former Controller & Auditor General) that analyses CAG audit reports and the work of parliamentary oversight committees (PAC, LAAC, PIC), publishes simplified accountability reports on central, local and public-authority spending, and mobilises citizens and elected representatives around public financial accountability.

trackers.name: CCRO — collective tenure over village land, including as forest reserve
trackers.desc: HOW A TANZANIAN COMMUNITY SECURES THE LAND IT ALREADY OCCUPIES. The Village Land Act 1999 provides for both individual and collective rights (sections 12 and 13), and village land may be used by a community as pastoral grazing land, as a forest reserve, for a water dam and so on. Village Councils issue Certificates of Customary Right of Occupancy on application; a group on customarily held land over 250 hectares applies to its Village Council with the Commissioner of Lands' approval, and once granted the CCRO gives permanent tenure with all the attributes of a granted right of occupancy. THE COLLECTIVE FORM IS ITSELF THE PROTECTION: transactions and subdivisions require the consent of the entire group, so individual members cannot be picked off one at a time. THE SEQUENCE: the council must define and approve community by-laws; the village must obtain a Certificate of Village Land by having its outer boundaries surveyed, demarcated and registered; and boundaries and land use plans must be agreed through district-level demarcation and zoning. Issuance depends on regularisation of the village land, so the village-level work comes first.

trackers.name: Four limits on CCROs — and what tenure unlocked for the Hadza
trackers.desc: KNOW THESE BEFORE STARTING. 1. ELIGIBILITY IS RESTRICTED to Tanzanian citizens of African descent, or communities of such citizens, occupying under customary law. 2. TRANSFER OUTSIDE THE VILLAGE NEEDS COUNCIL APPROVAL — which protects village land from passing to outsiders, but seriously reduces collateral value, since rural banks prefer General Land titles; that undercuts one of the CCRO's own stated purposes. 3. IT IS SLOW — the International Land Coalition records long waits leaving people in limbo, inadequate implementation, difficulty understanding the legal texts and overlapping roles between land institutions. 4. CUSTOMARY ARRANGEMENTS THE ACT ENCOURAGES CAN DISCRIMINATE AGAINST WOMEN — worth naming, because a community drafting its by-laws under this process can address that deliberately rather than inherit it. WHAT TENURE UNLOCKED: after the Hadza obtained their CCRO, recognised ownership let them enter conservation programmes paying community members from certified carbon offset credit revenue for managing forest conservation — part paid to local scouts enforcing the community's own land use plans — plus eco-tourism work. Tenure first, revenue second. AND THE ROUTE BY WHICH LAND LEAVES COMMUNITY CONTROL: village land can be converted to General Land, requiring survey, registration, gazetting with local and presidential approval, valuation and compensation — watch for it.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Rainforest Trust — will fund a local organisation to buy the land outright, as it did at Magombera, and warns you never to pay an intermediary to apply
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a funder that pays in-country organisations, Indigenous Peoples and communities to create or expand legally recognised protected areas — and that has financed outright land purchase in Tanzania: its chief executive is on record supporting the purchase and management of Magombera, the forest secured in 2018 and subsequently declared a nature reserve. It offers two grant types: Feasibility Awards, for working out whether protection is possible, and Protected or Conserved Area Creation Awards for doing it — which means a community that does not yet know what the route or the price would be can be funded to find out. Its stated targets are sites facing immediate and direct threats, typically from loggers, miners or ranchers, so an active development threat strengthens rather than weakens the application. One criterion is worth quoting in a proposal: substantial management authority over the area is to be led by Indigenous Peoples or local communities. THE WARNING IT PUBLISHES ITSELF, WHICH SAYS SOMETHING ABOUT WHO PREYS ON THESE APPLICATIONS: you never need to pay a consultant or an intermediary to apply, only applications submitted directly by eligible organisations are reviewed, and the funder will work with you to refine a proposal that fits. WHO IT SUITS: a registered local non-profit, or a community working through one, with a specific parcel and a conservation case — not an individual landowner and not a campaign without a legal vehicle. CAVEATS: it counts Biosphere Reserve, World Heritage and Ramsar status as NOT amounting to protection on their own, so a site already carrying one of those labels still qualifies as unprotected; its focus is the tropics and subtropics; and it is recorded here for Tanzania because Tanzania is where a source names a purchase it funded — it works in dozens of countries and its presence in yours has to be checked, not assumed.

trackers.name: Tanzania Forest Conservation Group — they do the legal work of turning your village forest into a reserve in the village's name
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an organisation with 37 years in Tanzania that walks villages through legally establishing a Village Land Forest Reserve — the step that converts forest anyone can be allocated into forest the village has reserved and manages, and keeps the revenue from. THE NUMBER THAT EXPLAINS THE URGENCY: more than 17.6 million hectares, about 80 per cent of the forest standing on village land in Tanzania, is not legally reserved at all, and roughly 469,000 hectares are cleared a year. Unreserved village forest is the cheapest thing in the country for an outsider to acquire. WHAT THEY ACTUALLY DELIVER, not what they advocate for: 8 villages helped to establish new reserves covering 19,000 hectares in a single year; 61 communities supported through community-based forest management and participatory village land use planning over five years; a coastal programme creating ten new reserves in Lindi region with the villages themselves deciding where the reserve boundaries fall; and 24 villages earning roughly US$200,000 in a year from forest enterprises — the income that makes conserving the forest survivable rather than merely virtuous. They also set up village savings and loan associations, and through their Forest Justice programme they support villages to take forest crimes through the legal system and back local community-based organisations across a hundred villages to run their own advocacy. WHO IT SUITS: a registered village with forest on village land and a village assembly willing to act — this is a route for communities that still hold the land, not for recovering land already taken. THE WARNING THEY PUBLISH THEMSELVES: a 2019 government notice recentralised approval of harvesting plans and of buyers of forest products from village reserves, which cuts the revenue that makes reserving worthwhile and, in their own assessment, disincentivises communities from reserving more forest. Reserve the forest anyway, but do not budget on the revenue arriving unimpeded.

trackers.name: UCRT — has obtained communal title deeds over more than a million hectares for pastoralists and hunter-gatherers, using group land certificates
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a registered Tanzanian NGO working since the 1990s with roughly 40 to 60 pastoralist, agro-pastoralist and hunter-gatherer communities in the northern rangelands, to secure their rights to land and natural resources. THE INSTRUMENT, WHICH IS THE CLOSEST THING TO BUYING YOUR LAND THAT TANZANIAN LAW OFFERS: a Certificate of Customary Right of Occupancy (CCRO) formally allocates a parcel of village land — and UCRT piloted the stronger version, a group or communal CCRO granting customary group title over a defined communal area, which on approval provides permanent tenure to the holder. Under the Village Land Act an individual or group living on customarily held land over 250 hectares may apply to their Village Council with the Commissioner of Lands' approval. THE PREPARATION IS THE WORK, and it is the same list everywhere: the council must define and approve community by-laws, hold a certificate of village land, and agree boundaries and land use plans through a district demarcation and zoning process. UCRT does exactly those steps with communities — demarcation and boundary reconciliation, mapping, village registration, land use planning, by-laws. WHAT IT HAS PRODUCED: reported figures range from 1.1 million hectares secured in one account to 1.7 million hectares covering more than 400,000 people in 120 communities in a later one; for the Hadzabe specifically it obtained title deeds for customary rights of occupancy over 20,000 hectares, and over 46,320 hectares by another account, and helped secure Mongo wa Mono, the only Hadzabe-majority village in Tanzania. WHY THIS BEATS A CONSERVATION AGREEMENT: a communal CCRO is title, not a contract with an NGO or a promise from a district — it is the answer to the question of what stops the land being allocated to an investor. UCRT also runs a Hadzabe cultural mapping project to demonstrate the relationship to land, and works with women's rights and land forums in the region. WHO IT SUITS: pastoralist, hunter-gatherer and agro-pastoralist communities in northern Tanzania holding land customarily and facing agricultural expansion, investor allocation or exclusion. CAVEATS: the process runs through the Village Council, the district and the Commissioner of Lands, so it needs functioning village institutions and takes time; UCRT's own area is the northern rangelands, not the whole country; reported hectare and community figures differ between sources and years, so treat them as orders of magnitude; and no intake route or fee information was published.

trackers.name: HakiArdhi — trains Land Rights Monitors who live in the village: 600 volunteers across 300 villages, there before any lawyer is
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Land Rights Research & Resources Institute (LARRRI/HAKIARDHI), founded 1994 in Dar es Salaam, working on the land rights of rural and peri-urban small producers. THE INSTRUMENT, AND IT IS THE CHEAPEST STANDING DEFENCE IN THIS FILE: since 2012 it has built and trained a network of about 600 male and female “Land Rights Monitors” operating in some 300 villages — volunteers ELECTED BY THEIR OWN COMMUNITIES after village-wide capacity-building, trained in the land law, with deliberate gender balance. What they do: train neighbours on their land rights, advise village leaders, facilitate negotiation and mediation in disputes, and report serious violations back to HakiArdhi for further action. Reported reach: around 15,000 villagers supported over three years. A trained monitor lives in the village; a lawyer arrives after the damage. That is why this class of resource matters most where large-scale land-based investments arrive with little warning — the monitors were built specifically around the impact of those investments. HakiArdhi also researches, publishes and runs national land rights advocacy jointly with other Tanzanian civil society, and the model has been documented in detail by legal-empowerment practitioners precisely so others can copy the process: community capacity-building first, then election, then training, then reporting lines back to a national body that can escalate. WHO IT SUITS: Tanzanian villages and small producers facing investor acquisitions, boundary disputes or pressure on village land, and organisations elsewhere wanting a replicable village-monitor model. CAVEATS: monitors are trained volunteers, not lawyers — they mediate and refer rather than litigate; for public interest environmental litigation Tanzania's LEAT entry is the route, and for group certificates of customary right of occupancy, UCRT. A second HakiArdhi domain exists as a development mirror; the .or.tz site is the current one.

trackers.name: Simanjiro voluntary land easements — 23,000 hectares kept open by paid agreement, with the village keeping the land and the grazing
trackers.desc: WHAT TO SIGN INSTEAD OF SELLING: on the Simanjiro plains east of Tarangire National Park, a consortium of tourism companies began working with Terrat village in 2005 and Sukuro village in 2009 to protect wet-season grazing through two VOLUNTARY LAND EASEMENTS totalling 23,000 hectares. THE TERMS ARE THE INSTRUMENT, and they are simple enough to copy: under the agreement livestock AND wildlife may graze the land, while FARMING, PERMANENT SETTLEMENTS, CHARCOAL PRODUCTION AND ILLEGAL HUNTING ARE NOT PERMITTED — and the communities earn an income for maintaining the land-use practices they were already following, while the tourism companies get sustained wildlife on land they do not own. An easement is the middle instrument this file has been missing: you do not sell, you do not lease the parcel out, you keep using it — you are paid to accept written limits on what may be done to it. That makes it available to a village that would never sell and could not afford to buy, and it is enforceable because the restrictions are written rather than customary. It sits between the two Tanzanian routes already recorded here — certificates of customary right of occupancy, which document who holds the land, and Wildlife Management Areas, where villages set aside communal land and transfer management authority to a registered Authorized Association. ASK WHICH OF THE THREE YOU ARE BEING OFFERED, because they give away very different things. Reported as a cost-effective model that has held; related work in the same landscape has cut crop damage on farms next to conservation areas by up to 70 per cent through village game scouts and community volunteers. WHO IT SUITS: northern Tanzanian pastoralist villages under pressure to convert grazing land to farming or settlement, and communities seeking income without transferring rights. CAVEATS: the payer is the TOURISM INDUSTRY, so the money depends on visitors and on companies that benefit from your restraint — read the term, the renewal and the exit clauses, and check who enforces the restrictions against outsiders. This is not a title; for CCROs and group certificates see Tanzania's UCRT entry, and for village-level monitors, HakiArdhi.

trackers.name: Tanzania's Register of Legal Aid Providers — paralegals are recognised in national law, and the Registrar keeps the list you can ask for
trackers.desc: WHAT THE LAW GIVES YOU: the Legal Aid Act, signed and gazetted on 3 March 2017, which OFFICIALLY RECOGNISES PARALEGALS NATIONALLY for the first time, replaces the old criminal-proceedings-only statute and extends legal aid to CIVIL proceedings — which is what a land case is. It applies to Mainland Tanzania. THE LIST TO ASK FOR: the Act establishes a REGISTER OF LEGAL AID PROVIDERS kept by a REGISTRAR, with ASSISTANT REGISTRARS at REGION AND DISTRICT level — the public officers who register community-based organisations are eligible to serve as them. Every institution intending to provide legal aid must apply to the Registrar for registration, and registration certificates are issued WITHOUT COST (renewal attracts a fee). So there is a district-level official whose job is to know which organisations near you are lawfully providing free legal aid — ask the Assistant Registrar for the register rather than hunting organisation by organisation. WHAT AN “INDIGENT PERSON” MEANS HERE, since eligibility turns on it: a person whose means are insufficient to engage a private legal practitioner, AND other categories of persons where the interests of justice so require — the second limb is broader than a pure means test. Legal aid services expressly include legal education and information, legal advice and assistance. The Registrar also investigates complaints of malpractice, negligence or misconduct against legal aid providers and can suspend or cancel a registration, and inspects providers' offices to check the quality of what they offer. If a paralegal or provider mistreats you, there is a named official to complain to. The national board includes a High Court judge as chair and a representative from the paralegal umbrella body. WHO IT SUITS: Tanzanians on Mainland who need free legal help with a land, boundary or civil matter, and communities wanting to verify that whoever is advising them is lawfully registered. CAVEATS: A STATUTORY FRAMEWORK, NOT AN ORGANISATION — it tells you who is authorised, not who has capacity; paralegals may NOT do work reserved for advocates; and it does not apply in Zanzibar. For village-level Land Rights Monitors, Tanzania's HakiArdhi entry; for public interest environmental litigation, LEAT; for group certificates of customary right of occupancy, UCRT.

trackers.name: TNRF — a member-driven forum of more than 3,800 people and organisations with a steering committee elected from the membership, a community film unit, and a land trust that bought a ranch
trackers.desc: THE 3,800-MEMBER FORUM AND ITS FILM UNIT — the largest membership body this file has found in Africa: the TANZANIA NATURAL RESOURCE FORUM (TNRF, tnrf.org) IS A MEMBER-DRIVEN NGO WITH A GROWING MEMBERSHIP OF MORE THAN 3,800 PEOPLE AND ORGANISATIONS, DRAWN FROM COMMUNITY-BASED ORGANISATIONS, NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATIONS, THE PRIVATE SECTOR AND INDIVIDUAL MEMBERS — WITH A STEERING COMMITTEE DRAWN FROM THE MEMBERSHIP THAT MEETS QUARTERLY to review and guide the secretariat. Community-based organisations AND individual members can join, and the governing committee comes out of the membership and sits four times a year. A Tanzanian village association can become a member of the body that speaks on natural resource policy — and an individual can too. That is the cheapest standing in this file. ITS PURPOSE, IN ITS OWN WORDS: TO BRIDGE THE GAP BETWEEN PEOPLE'S LOCAL NATURAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT NEEDS AND PRACTICES, AND NATIONAL NATURAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT PRIORITIES, POLICIES, LAWS AND PROGRAMS — supporting members by IMPROVING COMMUNICATION, SHARING INFORMATION, PROMOTING COLLABORATION AND STRENGTHENING COLLECTIVE ACTION, and engaging SECTOR MINISTRIES AND PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEES. WHERE IT CAME FROM: TNRF WAS FORMED IN 2001 AS THE WILDLIFE WORKING GROUP BY A SMALL INFORMAL GROUP OF PEOPLE WISHING TO PROMOTE A NEW RIGHTS-BASED APPROACH — holding that resource management challenges SHOULD NOT BE SIMPLY APPROACHED AS TECHNICAL AND OFTEN ISOLATED CONSERVATION ISSUES — became TNRF in October 2005, and BECAME AN INDEPENDENTLY REGISTERED NGO WITH ITS OWN MEMBERSHIP AND GOVERNING STEERING COMMITTEE IN FEBRUARY 2006. A small informal group became a 3,800-member national forum in five years. It began as a working group, not as an NGO — which is the cheaper way to start, and the registration followed once there were members to govern it. THE TOOL WORTH ASKING FOR BY NAME: TNRF RUNS A FILM UNIT WHOSE STATED AIM IS TO PRODUCE FILMS THAT HELP COMMUNITIES SHARE THEIR VOICES AND OPINIONS ON ISSUES REGARDING GOVERNANCE OF NATURAL RESOURCES. A film made in your own language, of your own people speaking, is evidence that travels where a written objection does not. Ask the film unit what it takes to be filmed — and note it exists to carry community voices, not to publicise the organisation. ITS STRUCTURES AND ITS REACH: TNRF has run THE WILDLIFE WORKING GROUP, THE TANZANIA FOREST WORKING GROUP AND THE PASTORALIST LIVELIHOOD TASK FORCE, promotes COMMUNITY BASED NATURAL RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AS THE FOCUS FOR STRENGTHENING CITIZENS' VOICE IN FORESTRY, RANGELANDS, WILDLIFE AND FISHERIES, produces a BIANNUAL NEWSLETTER, and COORDINATES 13 PARTNERS WITH RESPECTIVE PROJECTS UNDER AN INDIGENOUS COMMUNITY CONSERVED AREAS GLOBAL SUPPORT INITIATIVE — one member of which produced a book on USING INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE IN THE CONSERVATION OF THE ENVIRONMENT, WATER SOURCES AND FORESTS, LAUNCHED BY A GOVERNMENT MINISTER. A minister launching a book on indigenous knowledge is an endorsement you can cite. If your case rests on customary practice, that book and that launch are Tanzanian precedent that the state has accepted the argument in principle. AND THE LAND PURCHASE: A STEERING COMMITTEE MEMBER IS RECORDED AS HAVING PLAYED A PIVOTAL ROLE IN ESTABLISHING THE TANZANIA LAND CONSERVATION TRUST'S FIRST LAND ASSET, A NAMED RANCH. A Tanzanian land conservation trust exists and holds land. If buying is the answer for your ground, that is the domestic vehicle to ask about. WHO IT SUITS: Tanzanian village associations, pastoralists, and anyone wanting membership standing, a film, or a land-holding trust. CAVEATS: A FORUM AND CONVENOR, not a litigator or a funder. For public interest environmental litigation, Tanzania's LEAT entry; for communal title over more than a million hectares, UCRT; for Land Rights Monitors who live in the villages, HakiArdhi; for the village assembly consent that cannot be bypassed, the village land transfer entry.

trackers.name: Maliasili and its Conservation Fund — unrestricted multi-year money for local African conservation organisations, with published selection criteria and an Expression of Interest route (16 countries, filed here because the file has no regional key)
trackers.desc: UNRESTRICTED MONEY, AND A FORM YOU CAN ACTUALLY SUBMIT — and a note first, so nobody is misled: THIS IS A CONTINENTAL RESOURCE COVERING 16 COUNTRIES, FILED UNDER TANZANIA ONLY BECAUSE THIS FILE HAS NO REGIONAL KEY AND ITS NAMED TANZANIAN PARTNERS AND RANGELANDS PORTFOLIO SIT HERE. If you are reading this from anywhere else in Africa, it applies to you too. MALIASILI SELECTS HIGH-POTENTIAL LOCAL ORGANISATIONS AND PROVIDES THEM WITH CUSTOMISED, MULTI-YEAR SUPPORT IN ORGANISATIONAL STRENGTHENING AND LEADERSHIP DEVELOPMENT, AND INCREASED ACCESS TO FUNDING — AND IS STRENGTHENING AND SUPPORTING NEARLY 60 LOCAL ORGANISATIONS WORKING IN COMMUNITY-BASED CONSERVATION ACROSS 16 COUNTRIES. SINCE ITS INCEPTION 15 YEARS AGO IT HAS SUPPORTED 75 ORGANISATIONAL STRATEGIC PLANS, TRAINED 237 CONSERVATION LEADERS, AND RAISED AND LEVERAGED OVER USD 27 MILLION FOR ITS PARTNERS. Twenty-seven million dollars raised FOR other organisations rather than for itself. That is what an intermediary is for, and it is the opposite of the conduit organisations this file has warned about elsewhere — the money ends up with the local body, and the strategic plan and the leadership training come with it. THE FUND, AND WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT: THE MALIASILI CONSERVATION FUND IS A POOLED FUNDING INITIATIVE PROVIDING MULTI-YEAR, UNRESTRICTED SUPPORT TO A PORTFOLIO OF AFRICAN CONSERVATION ORGANISATIONS, AND HAS RAISED USD 12.3 MILLION OF A REVISED FOUR-YEAR TARGET OF USD 16 MILLION. UNRESTRICTED is the word that matters and it is rare. Almost every funder in this file pays for a project; unrestricted money pays for the organisation — the salaries, the vehicle, the accountant, the years between projects. A partner states the problem exactly: THE FUNDING WE RECEIVE IS PROJECT-BASED, SO A LOT OF IMPORTANT WORK IS LEFT BEHIND. If you are choosing between two offers, the unrestricted one is worth more than a larger restricted one. THE CRITERIA ARE PUBLISHED, WHICH MEANS YOU CAN TEST YOURSELF AGAINST THEM BEFORE APPLYING: AN ORGANISATION MUST BE COMMITTED TO ITS MISSION AND TO IMPROVING ITS ORGANISATIONAL PERFORMANCE; MUST HAVE CAPABLE AND MOTIVATED LEADERSHIP WITH A COMPELLING VISION AND THE DESIRE TO WORK COLLABORATIVELY; AND MUST ADDRESS AT LEAST ONE OF — STRENGTHENING LOCAL RIGHTS OVER LAND AND NATURAL RESOURCES; BUILDING STRONGER LOCAL MANAGEMENT AND DECISION-MAKING INSTITUTIONS; OR DELIVERING ECONOMIC INCENTIVES FOR COMMUNITIES TO INVEST IN CONSERVATION. Read the third criterion again: STRENGTHENING LOCAL RIGHTS OVER LAND is the first thing listed. This is a conservation funder whose own criteria put land rights ahead of species. An organisation fighting a land taking qualifies on its face. AND THE ROUTE IN IS NAMED: THE PROCESS BEGINS WITH AN EXPRESSION OF INTEREST FROM ORGANISATIONS THAT WANT SUPPORT, FOLLOWED BY INITIAL DISCUSSIONS AND REFERENCES AND DUE DILIGENCE. An Expression of Interest is a document you can write this week. Most funding in this file arrives through somebody else's project; this one has a front door. WHAT THE SUPPORT ACTUALLY COVERS: STRATEGIC PLANNING; MONITORING, EVALUATION AND LEARNING SYSTEMS; COMMUNICATION STRATEGIES AND PRODUCTS; BOARD GOVERNANCE, TEAM PERFORMANCE AND DEVELOPMENT; FUNDRAISING; WORK PLANNING; AND MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS — plus PEER-BASED LEADERSHIP PROGRAMMES THAT BUILD THE ABILITY TO GENERATE COLLABORATION AND COLLECTIVE ACTION AMONGST DIFFERENT ORGANISATIONS. Board governance and fundraising are the two things that fail first in the small organisations throughout this file, and both are on the list. So is a peer programme that puts leaders of different organisations in the same room — which is how a national coalition starts. WHERE IT CONCENTRATES: EAST AFRICA'S SAVANNAH LANDSCAPES; THE KAVANGO-ZAMBEZI TRANSFRONTIER CONSERVATION AREA SPANNING NAMIBIA, ANGOLA, ZAMBIA, BOTSWANA AND ZIMBABWE; AND MADAGASCAR, WITH ITS NEW AND RISING MALAGASY CONSERVATION LEADERS. Named partners include a Kenyan wildlife conservancies association acting as an umbrella across one landscape, a Tanzanian organisation securing land and resource rights for indigenous and local communities that COMBINES LEGAL ADVOCACY WITH PRACTICAL SUPPORT, a Ugandan organisation building effective local institutions for natural resource management, a Tanzanian community forest conservation network, and ACADIR in Angola. CAVEATS: THIS IS A FUNDER AND CAPACITY BUILDER THAT SELECTS ITS PORTFOLIO — not an open grant window, and not a litigator. For communal title over more than a million hectares, Tanzania's UCRT entry; for a 3,800-member forum with a community film unit, TNRF; for public interest environmental litigation, LEAT; for Land Rights Monitors living in the villages, HakiArdhi; for the Angolan partner, Angola's ACADIR entry.

trackers.name: The four funders behind Tanzania's communal titling, Carbon Tanzania paying the same communities afterwards, the Hadzabe certificates over 23,000 hectares, and the village committees that enforce the plan — with a court ruling as caution
trackers.desc: FOUR FUNDERS, ONE TITLE, AND WHO PAYS AFTERWARDS — this file already holds the Tanzanian organisation that gets communal title; this is the money and the machinery around it: THE CERTIFICATES WERE OBTAINED WITH FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL SUPPORT FROM THE DOROBO FUND FOR TANZANIA, THE NATURE CONSERVANCY, THE WILDLIFE CONSERVATION SOCIETY, AND MALIASILI. Four named funders behind one titling programme. That is the answer to how a community affords to title its land: not one donor, but a stack — a domestic fund, two international conservation organisations, and a capacity builder. Approach them as a set, and ask each which part it covers. AND THE INCOME AFTERWARDS, WHICH IS THE PART MOST TITLING PROJECTS LACK: UCRT HAS TEAMED UP WITH CARBON TANZANIA, WHICH IS PAYING THESE SAME HUNTER-GATHERERS TO EFFECTIVELY REINFORCE THEIR EXISTING CONSERVATION REGULATIONS. Paid to enforce the rules they already had. That is the sequence to aim for — title first, then a payment stream attached to the rules the title lets you make. A certificate with no income behind it is a document; a certificate with a buyer for the conservation outcome is a livelihood. THE CERTIFICATES THEMSELVES, AND THE WORDING TO ASK FOR: AFTER SEVERAL YEARS OF NEGOTIATIONS THE ASSISTANT COMMISSIONER AND DISTRICT GOVERNMENT GRANTED THE COMMUNITY A CUSTOMARY RIGHT OF OCCUPANCY FOR AS LONG AS THEY CONTINUE TO EXIST — THREE CERTIFICATES ISSUED FOR AN AREA OF 23,000 HECTARES COVERING TWO NAMED VILLAGES, ALLOWING PEOPLE FROM BOTH VILLAGES TO USE ANY OF THE AREAS, WITH RESTRICTIONS BASED ON ZONING PREVIOUSLY DETERMINED BY UCRT, THE COMMUNITY AND THE VILLAGE COUNCIL: CERTAIN AREAS ZONED FOR SETTLEMENT AND GRAZING, WHILE A LARGE PORTION IS RETAINED PURELY FOR HUNTING AND GATHERING. For as long as they continue to exist is the term of the grant. And note the cross-village clause: people from either village may use any of the three areas, so the certificates do not cut the land into blocks that separate families from ground they have always used. If you are negotiating zoning, that clause is the one to insist on. THE SAFEGUARD BUILT INTO A COLLECTIVE TITLE, AND THIS IS WHY COLLECTIVE BEATS INDIVIDUAL: THE COLLECTIVE NATURE OF THE TITLE MEANS THAT TRANSACTIONS AND SUBDIVISIONS CAN ONLY TAKE PLACE WITH THE CONSENT OF THE ENTIRE GROUP, THUS PROVIDING GREATER TENURE SECURITY TO AT-RISK COMMUNITIES AND MINORITIES. No one household can be bought out. That single clause is the difference between a community that holds together under pressure and one that is picked apart parcel by parcel — which this file has recorded happening across the continent. If you are choosing a tenure form, choose the one that requires the whole group to agree before anything moves. THE BODY THAT MAKES IT WORK ON THE GROUND: VILLAGE RANGELAND MANAGEMENT COMMITTEES ARE INSTRUMENTAL IN IMPLEMENTING RANGELAND MANAGEMENT PRACTICES, ENSURING THAT GRAZING PLANS ARE ADHERED TO AND RESOLVING LAND USE CONFLICTS. Resolving land use conflicts is in the committee's job, not the court's. A village committee that settles grazing disputes is cheaper and faster than anything else in this file — constitute one and give it that mandate in writing. WHY THE TITLE MATTERS AT ALL, STATED PLAINLY: IF COMMUNITIES LACK TITLE OVER THEIR LANDS, THEY ARE UNABLE TO ENFORCE LAND USE PLANS THAT DEFINE THE KIND OF ACTIVITIES PERMITTED IN WHICH ZONES. No title, no enforceable plan. That is the shortest statement of the problem this whole file addresses. AND THE CAUTION, RECORDED BECAUSE IT BELONGS BESIDE THE CARBON INCOME: A RESEARCH REPORT ON SOIL CARBON CREDITS IN NORTHERN TANZANIA NOTES THAT A COURT CASE HAS RECENTLY RULED THAT AT LEAST ONE OF THE CONSERVANCIES INVOLVED WAS ESTABLISHED ILLEGALLY ON COMMUNAL LANDS, and describes carbon projects targeting areas measured in the millions of hectares across the Tanzania-Kenya border. A conservancy ruled illegal on communal land, and carbon projects covering 1.5 million hectares next door. Carbon money is real and so is the risk: before signing a carbon agreement, ask who holds the title, what happens to your rights for the length of the contract, and whether any court has ruled on the scheme. The same organisations appear on both sides of this record — read the caution and the opportunity together. WHO IT SUITS: Tanzanian pastoralist and hunter-gatherer communities, anyone titling communal land, and communities offered a carbon deal. CAVEATS: CARBON AGREEMENTS ARE LONG CONTRACTS — take independent advice. For communal title over more than a million hectares, Tanzania's UCRT entry; for 23,000 hectares kept open by paid easements, the Simanjiro entry; for a 3,800-member forum with a community film unit, TNRF; for public interest environmental litigation, LEAT; for unrestricted multi-year money, the Maliasili entry.

trackers.name: How the Tanzanian communal title was actually won — the lawyer, the Commissioner of Lands, the re-survey — and what the 40-year carbon contracts 59 villages signed actually say
trackers.desc: WHO WON THE TITLE, AND WHAT THE CONTRACTS SAY — the sequence first, because it is the most reusable thing in this file's Tanzanian record: A UCRT LAWYER SCRUTINISED LAND LAW AND POLICY, AND HE AND SOME COMMUNITY REPRESENTATIVES MET WITH THE COMMISSIONER OF LANDS WITH A PROPOSAL TO ISSUE A COMMUNAL TITLE. A NAMED COMMUNITY MEMBER WAS A CRITICAL VOICE ADVOCATING TO THE COMMISSIONER FOR LAND RIGHTS. THE COMMISSIONER AGREED — WHICH THEN NECESSITATED AGREEMENT BY LOCAL VILLAGES, WARD AND DISTRICT, A RE-SURVEY OF THE AREAS, AND EVENTUAL ISSUANCE OF COMMUNAL TITLE IN OCTOBER 2011. Lawyer reads the law, lawyer AND community members go to the Commissioner together with a written proposal, Commissioner agrees, then villages, ward and district sign off, then a re-survey, then the certificate. Six steps, in order, and the community was in the room at the top of it — not represented, present. Budget for the re-survey: it is the step nobody costs and everybody needs. AND WHO ENFORCES IT AFTERWARDS, STATED PLAINLY: ENFORCEMENT IS PRIMARILY THE RESPONSIBILITY OF THE VILLAGE GOVERNMENT TO ENFORCE BY-LAWS FOR THE DIFFERENT AREAS, USUALLY ENTAILING A FINE BEING LEVIED. The village government enforces, by by-law, with a fine. Not the police, not the park service. So the by-laws have to exist and the fine has to be set before the title is worth anything — draft them while the certificate is being processed, not after. THE BUFFER TACTIC WORTH COPYING: ADDITIONAL GRAZING TITLES WERE FACILITATED FOR NEIGHBOURING PASTORALISTS, WHICH SERVE AS BUFFER ZONES TO THE FIRST COMMUNITY'S LAND, AND IN WHICH THAT COMMUNITY RETAINS FORAGING ACCESS. Title your neighbours' land too. A titled neighbour is a buffer; an untitled one is the gap a project comes through. And the reciprocal access clause — each retaining use of the other's zone — is what stops the two titles becoming a fence between allies. AND THE PART THAT PAID FOR IT TO LAST: the communal title PROVIDED THE FOUNDATION FOR A CARBON PROJECT — REVENUE LINKED TO FOREST AND WOODLAND PROTECTION, DESCRIBED AS A CRITICAL COMPONENT FOR LAND TITLE SUSTAINABILITY. NOW THE WARNING, IN DETAIL, BECAUSE COMMUNITIES ARE BEING ASKED TO SIGN THESE NOW AND THIS FILE OWES YOU THE TERMS: MOST VILLAGERS DON'T UNDERSTAND HOW CARBON MARKETS WORK. MANY SIGN 30 TO 40 YEAR CONTRACTS WITHOUT KNOWING WHAT RIGHTS THEY'RE GIVING UP OR WHAT THEY'LL GET IN RETURN. VILLAGES USUALLY GET A ONE-TIME SIGNING FEE — SOMETIMES CALLED DOWRY MONEY — THAT CRITICS SAY LEADS TO RUSHED, SECRETIVE AGREEMENTS. THE CONTRACTS ARE IN ENGLISH, NOT SWAHILI, AND OFTEN EXCLUDE WOMEN AND YOUTH FROM DECISION-MAKING. A contract in a language your assembly does not read, a lump sum on signature, and forty years of obligations. Three demands before anyone signs: the full text in your own language, no signing fee until the assembly has had the text for a stated number of weeks, and women and young people in the meeting that decides. THE NAMED SCHEME, WITH ITS NUMBERS, SO YOU CAN COMPARE WHAT YOU ARE OFFERED: A RANGELANDS CARBON PROJECT SPANNING 970,000 HECTARES, MANAGED BY A NAMED CONSERVATION GROUP ON BEHALF OF A EUROPEAN CORPORATE CLIMATE ARM, PAYS 59 VILLAGES BETWEEN 40 AND 130 MILLION TANZANIAN SHILLINGS — ABOUT USD 15,000 TO 50,000 — OVER A 40-YEAR PERIOD FROM JANUARY 2024 TO DECEMBER 2063, IN EXCHANGE FOR CARBON CREDITS. IN RETURN, COMMUNITIES MUST LIMIT ACTIVITIES SUCH AS GRAZING AND BURNING GRASSLANDS. Do the division before you sign: USD 15,000 to 50,000 per village across FORTY YEARS is a few hundred to just over a thousand dollars a year, against a permanent limit on grazing and burning. Burning matters more than it sounds — controlled burning is how rangeland is managed, and giving it up changes the grass. Ask what the payment is per year, per household, and what happens in year 41. AND THE LEGAL GAP THAT MAKES ALL OF THIS RISKY: TANZANIA'S LAND LAWS RECOGNISE BOTH STATUTORY AND CUSTOMARY OWNERSHIP, BUT THERE ARE NO CLEAR RULES FOR CARBON TRADING — LEAVING RURAL COMMUNITIES EXPOSED TO EXPLOITATION. No rules for carbon trading means the contract IS the law between you and the buyer. Everything you fail to write in, you do not have. Get a lawyer of your own — not the project's — and note this file's separate record that a court has already ruled one conservancy in these landscapes was established illegally on communal land. ALSO NAMED: THE DOROBO FUND SUPPORTS AND FUNDS MANY GRASSROOTS EFFORTS PROMOTING SOCIAL, ECOLOGICAL AND ECONOMIC SUSTAINABLE GROWTH IN TANZANIA, INITIATED BY A LOCAL SAFARI OPERATOR, and A TANZANIA CARBON CREDIT FOUNDATION, ARUSHA, A REGISTERED NON-PROFIT WHICH SAYS IT EXISTS TO BRIDGE THE GAP BETWEEN GRASSROOTS ENVIRONMENTAL EFFORTS AND INTERNATIONAL CARBON MARKETS AND TO SUPPORT COMMUNITIES TO PARTICIPATE. A fund started by a safari operator is a reminder that domestic private money exists: the tourism business nearest you has a commercial interest in the landscape staying intact. Ask it. WHO IT SUITS: Tanzanian communities pursuing communal title, and any community anywhere being offered a carbon contract. CAVEATS: THIS ENTRY DELIBERATELY CARRIES BOTH SIDES — carbon revenue sustained one title and carbon contracts are being signed badly elsewhere. For communal title over more than a million hectares, Tanzania's UCRT entry; for the four funders and the collective-title safeguard, the titling funders entry; for 23,000 hectares kept open by paid easements, Simanjiro; for public interest environmental litigation, LEAT.

trackers.name: The Whakatane Mechanism — a community can request a field assessment of a protected area (or a proposed one) that is harming it, and a team including the government conservation agencies is constituted to come and look
trackers.desc: YOU ASK FOR THE ASSESSMENT; THE AGENCIES HAVE TO COME — placement note first: THE MECHANISM IS GLOBAL, FILED UNDER TANZANIA BECAUSE THE EAST AFRICAN COMMUNITY CALL RECORDED BELOW CAME FROM HERE AND THIS BUCKET HELD NO CONSERVATION-DIALOGUE ROUTE; THE PILOT WAS KENYAN. HOW IT STARTS, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE FIND: AT THE REQUEST OF AN INDIGENOUS PEOPLE, A TEAM — INCLUDING A GLOBAL CONSERVATION UNION, INDIGENOUS PEOPLES' ORGANIZATIONS, GOVERNMENT OFFICIALS AND OTHERS — IS CONSTITUTED TO CONDUCT A FIELD ASSESSMENT. The community asks, and the team is assembled. Everywhere else in this file the assessment is commissioned by the developer or the ministry and the community is a subject of it. Here the community is the requesting party and the conservation agencies sit on the team as participants. That inversion is the reason to know the mechanism's name. WHEN YOU CAN USE IT: THE ASSESSMENTS IDENTIFY AND ADDRESS PROBLEMATIC AREAS WHERE PEOPLE ARE STILL NEGATIVELY IMPACTED BY PROTECTED AREAS OR PROPOSED PROTECTED AREAS, AND WHERE PEOPLES' RIGHTS ARE BEING VIOLATED — THEY PROPOSE SOLUTIONS AND DEVELOP TRANSPARENT AND ACCOUNTABLE PROCESSES TO IMPLEMENT THEM, AND SPECIFY RECOMMENDATIONS TO ADDRESS GAPS BETWEEN ACTUAL OBSERVED PRACTICE AND RIGHTS-BASED CONSERVATION. OR PROPOSED PROTECTED AREAS. You do not have to wait until the park exists. If a reserve is being planned over your land, that is the moment the assessment is worth requesting — before boundaries are gazetted and rangers are posted. WHO IMPLEMENTS IT: JOINTLY, IN EACH PROTECTED AREA, BY THE RESPONSIBLE GOVERNMENT INSTITUTIONS, THE CONSERVATION UNION, A FOREST PEOPLES ORGANISATION, LOCAL INDIGENOUS PEOPLES ORGANISATIONS AND LOCAL COMMUNITY ORGANISATIONS. The government agencies are inside the process rather than opposite it. That is what makes the findings hard for them to dismiss afterwards. THE PILOT SHOWS THE EXACT SEQUENCE, AND IT IS WORTH COPYING STEP BY STEP: HAVING BEEN UNABLE TO PERSUADE THE FOREST SERVICE AND THE WILDLIFE SERVICE TO ENTER INTO DIALOGUE WITH THEM, THE COMMUNITY REQUESTED A PILOT ASSESSMENT. THEN CAME CONSULTATIONS AND DIALOGUE SEPARATELY WITH HIGH-LEVEL DECISION-MAKERS AND WITH COMMUNITY LEADERS, TO DEVELOP UNDERSTANDING AND SECURE BUY-IN FOR THE PROCESS; A FIRST ROUNDTABLE AT THE REGIONAL OFFICES; A SCOPING STUDY VISIT TO THE SITE TO CONSULT THE COMMUNITY AND ASSESS THE SITUATION; AND A SECOND ROUNDTABLE ATTENDED BY ALL THE PREVIOUS PARTICIPANTS PLUS THE OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT AND THE MINISTRY OF FORESTS AND WILDLIFE. Separate meetings with each side first, then a roundtable, then a field visit, then a bigger roundtable. The separate meetings are the part groups skip — nobody agrees to sit down until they have been spoken to alone. And note the escalation: by the second roundtable the Office of the President was in the room. AND THE DETAIL WORTH REMEMBERING: A DEVELOPMENT BANK DID NOT ATTEND BUT ASKED TO BE INFORMED OF THE OUTCOME. A financier watching from outside and asking for the result. Make sure it gets one — this file has recorded elsewhere that the bank behind a project is reachable in ways the agency is not. WHAT THE ASSESSMENT FOUND: THE SCOPING STUDY FOUND THE COMMUNITY HAS A POSITIVE RELATIONSHIP WITH THEIR NATURAL ENVIRONMENT, AND INDICATED THAT COMMUNITY STRUCTURES, PRESENCE AND LIVELIHOOD PRACTICES CONTRIBUTE TO PROTECTING THE FOREST, MOORLAND AND FAUNA — SO THERE IS AN OPPORTUNITY FOR DECISION-MAKERS TO REVERSE THEIR EARLIER ATTEMPTS TO EVICT, AND INSTEAD SUPPORT THEIR CONTINUED CONSERVATION OF THEIR LANDS. AND THE DECISIONS TAKEN DURING THE ASSESSMENT ARE NOW BEING IMPLEMENTED. An official finding that the community's presence protects the forest is the document that turns an eviction case around. If you believe your practices sustain the land, this is the process that can put that on the record in a form the agencies signed. THE CHEAPER ALTERNATIVE, WHERE NO MECHANISM IS AVAILABLE: A CAMEROONIAN NATIONAL PLATFORM OF FOREST INDIGENOUS PEOPLES INVITED CONSERVATION ACTORS TO A LISTENING EVENT, TO HEAR TESTIMONIES DIRECTLY FROM THE PEOPLE AFFECTED BY THEIR DECISIONS — AND IN THE SHORT TERM THE EVENT LED TO IMPROVED COMMUNICATION. The community convened it and invited the conservationists to listen. That costs a hall and some travel, and it reverses who is hosting whom — which is most of the point. AND THE TANZANIAN VOICE ON RECORD, from a community representative at a continental protected areas congress: THIS IS WHY OUR LANDS ARE SO ATTRACTIVE FOR THE CONSERVATIONISTS TO COME AND EVICT US. THEY SAY WE ARE DESTROYING OUR LAND — IF WE HAVE DONE THAT THEN WHY IS OUR LAND ATTRACTING THEM? That question is the argument in one line, and it was put to the conservation union at its own congress. Use it. WHO IT SUITS: African communities harmed by an existing or proposed protected area, especially where the agencies refuse to meet. CAVEATS: AN ASSESSMENT PRODUCES RECOMMENDATIONS AND A DIALOGUE, NOT AN ORDER — and it depends on the co-convenors having capacity when you ask. For the rapid legal support centre and the judgment still unimplemented, Kenya's Strategic Legal Response Centre entry; for the collective title safeguard and the carbon contract warnings, Tanzania's titling entries; for the community-run assessment of 34 protected areas, DR Congo's MappingForRights entry.

trackers.name: PINGO's Forum, Arusha — Tanzania's pastoralist and hunter-gatherer coalition, six organisations in 1994 and 53 now, with its P.O. Box, phone and email — and the regional pastoralist networks with named focal points in four countries
trackers.desc: SIX ORGANISATIONS IN 1994; FIFTY-THREE NOW: THE PASTORALISTS INDIGENOUS NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANIZATIONS' FORUM IS AN ADVOCACY COALITION OF INDIGENOUS PEOPLES' ORGANIZATIONS, CURRENTLY 53, WORKING IN TANZANIA FOR THE RIGHTS OF THE MARGINALIZED INDIGENOUS PASTORALISTS AND HUNTER-GATHERER COMMUNITIES — ESTABLISHED IN 1994 BY SIX PASTORALISTS AND HUNTER-GATHERER ORGANIZATIONS IN THEIR STRUGGLE FOR LAND RIGHT AND DEVELOPMENT AGENDA, AND FORMALLY REGISTERED IN 1996. Six to fifty-three over thirty years, and the founding purpose was land. Note also the two-year gap between forming in 1994 and registering in 1996: a coalition can exist and work before it is legally registered, and the registration follows the work rather than preceding it. AND PASTORALISTS AND HUNTER-GATHERERS IN THE SAME COALITION FROM THE START. This file has recorded those two groups being set against each other over the same ground almost everywhere; in Tanzania they founded a national body together. THE CONTACTS ARE PUBLISHED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE ENTRY: P.O. BOX 14437, AT A NAMED STREET LOCATION AND GARDEN ENTRANCE IN ARUSHA, TANZANIA — WITH A TELEPHONE NUMBER AND AN EMAIL ADDRESS. WHAT IT DOES FOR MEMBERS: LOBBYING AND ADVOCATING FOR CHANGE ON GOOD GOVERNANCE AND HUMAN RIGHTS — SOCIAL, ECONOMIC, POLITICAL AND CULTURAL; CAPACITY BUILDING OF MEMBER CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS AND OTHER KEY STAKEHOLDERS; AND NETWORKING WITH LIKE-MINDED ORGANISATIONS. ITS NAMED RESULT AREAS ARE WORTH READING AS A CHECKLIST: THE RIGHTS OF PASTORALISTS AND HUNTER-GATHERERS AS REFLECTED IN GOVERNANCE PRINCIPLES, POLICIES, LAWS AND STRATEGIES; THE SOCIO-ECONOMIC AND POLITICAL RIGHTS OF WOMEN AND YOUTH AS PROMOTED AND PROTECTED BY THOSE COMMUNITIES; PASTORALISTS AND HUNTER-GATHERERS ENGAGED IN CLIMATE CHANGE POLICY PROCESSES AND LESS AFFECTED BY THE IMPACT OF CLIMATE CHANGE; AND ADEQUATELY AVAILABLE, ACCESSIBLE AND CREDIBLE INFORMATION FOR DECISION MAKING BY STAKEHOLDERS. Women's and youth rights framed as PROMOTED AND PROTECTED BY the communities themselves, not for them. That wording matters when an outside body arrives arguing that a community's customs are the obstacle — here the community is named as the protector. THE INTERNATIONAL SEAT IT HOLDS: THROUGH A NETWORK THAT BRINGS TOGETHER COUNTRIES, ORGANIZATIONS AND EXPERTS TO PROVIDE TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE FOR ADDRESSING LOSS AND DAMAGE CAUSED BY CLIMATE CHANGE, IT HELPS ENSURE THAT INDIGENOUS PERSPECTIVES FROM TANZANIA ARE INCLUDED IN SHAPING GLOBAL CLIMATE SOLUTIONS. LOSS AND DAMAGE is a specific funding stream with a technical assistance network attached, and a Tanzanian pastoralist coalition has a place in it. If your community has already lost land, water or herds to climate impacts, that is the channel where compensation is being designed — and there is a national body already inside it. THE DEFINITION IT ADOPTS, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE HERE FOR ANY COMMUNITY ARGUING ABOUT WHO COUNTS: AN INDIGENOUS PERSON IS A MEMBER OF A COMMUNITY RETAINING MEMORIES OF LIFE LIVED SUSTAINABLY ON A LAND-BASE, AS PART OF THAT LAND-BASE — AND INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE IS ANY APPLICATION OF THOSE MEMORIES AS LIVING KNOWLEDGE TO IMPROVE PRESENT AND FUTURE CIRCUMSTANCES. A definition built on memory and land rather than on ethnicity or official lists. It also makes indigenous knowledge a present-tense practice, not a heritage item — which is the framing that lets a community claim it is managing the land now, rather than having managed it once. THE REGIONAL BODIES IT SITS ALONGSIDE, EACH WITH NAMED HOLDERS: A EUROPEAN FOCAL POINT AND AN EASTERN AFRICAN FOCAL POINT HELD BY A KENYAN ORGANISATION, WITH A CORE GROUP INCLUDING EASTERN AFRICAN PARTNERS IN UGANDA, ETHIOPIA, THE SOMALI REGION AND KENYA — AND SEPARATELY AN EASTERN AND SOUTHERN AFRICA PASTORALIST NETWORK WITH A PUBLISHED MEMBERS LIST. Named focal points in four East African countries and a published members list for the wider network. A pastoralist organisation anywhere in the region can find its nearest peer from those two pages — and a focal point is a person whose job is answering. AND THE WORK IT PUBLISHES: it has posted on a continuing human rights situation in a named division and district, on a monitoring mission by a heritage body, on a delegation of community representatives touring several countries, and on a UN Special Rapporteur on the rights of Indigenous Peoples COLLECTING INFORMATION. A Special Rapporteur collecting information is a window that opens and closes. If it is open when your case is live, submissions are usually accepted from communities directly — ask the coalition how and by when. WHO IT SUITS: Tanzanian pastoralist and hunter-gatherer organisations, and pastoralist groups across East and Southern Africa looking for their regional network. CAVEATS: AN ADVOCACY COALITION — it lobbies and builds capacity rather than litigating or funding land purchase. For the assessment a community can request of a protected area, Tanzania's Whakatane entry; for the collective title safeguard and the carbon contract warnings, the Tanzanian titling entries; for the continental indigenous network with 135 member organisations, South Africa's IPACC entry.

trackers.name: Adam Teva V'Din — Israel Union for Environmental Defense
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Israel's first public-interest environmental law organisation, founded in 1990 — a combined staff of lawyers, scientists, urban planners and an environmental economist, which is what lets it fight at the planning-committee stage rather than only in court. It petitions the High Court against coastal privatisation, oil-shale projects and ministerial inaction; its legal action has forced the Ministry of Environmental Protection to publish new conditions on businesses, won a ruling that Dead Sea Works must pay for the water it uses, and helped save the Bat Yam cliff. WHO IT SUITS: residents and local environmental groups facing a planning decision or a polluting facility. It is membership-based and picks strategic cases, and its planning team is often more use early than its litigators are late. ASK FOR THE HEAD OF PLANNING BY NAME. Adam Teva V'Din publishes its team: Yael Dori, urban planner, is Head of Planning, and describes her own work as helping people understand planning procedures and interventions in order to prevent unnecessary development — for a land-defence campaign she is the correct first call, not the litigation desk. Adv. Amit Bracha is Executive Director, Tamar Gannot attorney and Deputy Director, Eli Ben Ari legal advisor, Dr Arye Vanger chief scientist. Contact contact@adamteva.org.il, 9 Carlebach Street, Tel Aviv 6713213. THE TACTIC WORTH COPYING, FROM THE BAT YAM CLIFF RESULT: the site was saved and the planning committee will evaluate transferring the building rights inland instead. Framing an objection as relocate the rights rather than cancel the scheme gives a committee a route that does not strip the landowner of value, and is often the only version a committee will adopt. THE TIMELINE, IN THEIR OWN WORDS: Eli Ben Ari describes land-use cases running over a decade of hearings to reach the Supreme Court. Treat litigation here as a long instrument and the planning objection as the fast one.THE PRECEDENT TO CARRY INTO ANY PLANNING FIGHT HERE IS A COASTAL HOUSING PLAN THAT WAS CANCELLED. AFTER A PROLONGED LEGAL BATTLE, ON A HIGH COURT PETITION BROUGHT BY THIS ORGANISATION TOGETHER WITH LOCAL RESIDENTS AND THE MUNICIPALITY, THE COURT IN MAY 2021 CANCELLED THE DEPOSIT OF THE PLAN AND RETURNED IT FOR RE-PLANNING — CRITICISING THE STATE AND THE NATIONAL PLANNING COMMITTEE FOR NOT HAVING CARRIED OUT A LAND SURVEY AT THE SITE. TWO THINGS IN THAT ARE USABLE BY ANYONE. FIRST, THE GROUND: A PLAN ADVANCED WITHOUT THE SURVEY THAT SHOULD HAVE PRECEDED IT IS VULNERABLE, AND THE FAILURE IS THE AUTHORITY'S RATHER THAN YOURS TO PROVE. SECOND, THE FORM: RESIDENTS WERE CO-PETITIONERS ALONGSIDE THE ORGANISATION AND THEIR OWN MUNICIPALITY — so the question to ask is not only whether this body will take a case, but whether it will take one WITH you and with your local authority. IT ALSO TAKES ON ENFORCEMENT, WHICH IS RARER AND MORE USEFUL THAN LITIGATION. A COURT APPROVED AN AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE STATE AND THE ORGANISATION UNDER WHICH IT WILL HANDLE THE TREATMENT OF SOIL CONTAMINATION AT A SITE WHERE ABOUT TWELVE THOUSAND APARTMENTS ARE PLANNED — on plans approved almost a decade earlier, under which some building permits had already been issued. THE ORGANISATION CALLED IT A MILESTONE IN TRANSPARENCY TOWARDS THE PUBLIC. Where permits have already issued, contamination is one of the few things that can still reopen a site. IT LITIGATES OVER PUBLIC MONEY FROM NATURAL RESOURCES TOO: in December 2025 the High Court held, on petitions including this organisation's, that water produced by a mineral-works company within its concession area is NOT part of the concession it pays royalties for, and that it must pay separately for that water. AND IT DEFENDS THE RIGHT TO BRING SUCH CASES AT ALL. It has campaigned against narrowing the STANDING of environmental and human rights organisations, warning that doing so silences the public's voice, and naming what the legal tools actually deliver: clean air, ACCESS TO BEACHES, NATURE AND PARKS, supervision of polluting plants, environmental transparency, drinkable water and the protection of natural resources for future generations. IF STANDING IS BEING RESTRICTED WHERE YOU ARE, THAT FIGHT IS UPSTREAM OF EVERY OTHER ONE IN THIS MAP. PRACTICAL NOTE: it publishes an annual activity report, which is the fastest way to see what it is currently working on and whether your subject is among its live files before you write.

trackers.name: EcoPeace Middle East
trackers.desc: Founded in 1994 as Friends of the Earth Middle East and still a member of Friends of the Earth International, EcoPeace is staffed and directed jointly by Jordanians, Palestinians and Israelis, with its own offices in Amman, Ramallah and Tel Aviv and a national director in each. WHO TO ENLIST: the office in your own country. Its Good Water Neighbors programme works with communities on either side of a shared water problem, pairing them across the border rather than treating each in isolation. You CAN get community-level organising support and technical and advocacy weight on water, sewage and Jordan Valley development. You CAN'T get a litigator — EcoPeace works by cross-border cooperation, research and advocacy, not by suing proponents, so a community that needs a permit or an approval challenged in court should look elsewhere. For activists: in Jordan and Palestine this was the only substantial environmental organisation with an office and a named national director that could be verified on its own domain.

trackers.name: State Comptroller and Ombudsman
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Israel, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: The Knesset
trackers.desc: Official Israeli Parliament site with comprehensive legislative information, committee records, and voting data. — Holds to account: lobbyists & influence-seekers — find who is lobbying whom, and meetings held.

trackers.name: Government Procurement Admin.
trackers.desc: National public-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Israel, and for how much.

trackers.name: Supreme Court of Israel
trackers.desc: Official Supreme Court verdicts and decisions database. · Find here: judgments and case information of the Supreme Court of Israel.

trackers.name: Central Bureau of Statistics
trackers.desc: Israel's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Israel.

trackers.name: Corporations Authority
trackers.desc: Israel's Registrar of Companies. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Israel — Governmental Freedom of Information Unit
trackers.desc: Accountability source (FOI oversight body); Israel — Governmental Freedom of Information Unit — the national authority overseeing citizens’ right of access to public information (ICIC member).

trackers.name: Israel Corporations Authority
trackers.desc: Israel's registrar of companies. Here you can trace companies, their directors and filings registered in Israel.

trackers.name: Israeli Corporations Authority — Companies Registrar (company register)
trackers.desc: Accountability source (official company register); Israeli Corporations Authority — Companies Registrar (company register) — Israel’s official Companies Registrar (Rasham HaChavarot) under the Ministry of Justice — free public company status search.

trackers.name: The Privacy Protection Authority (PPA)
trackers.desc: The Privacy Protection Authority (PPA) — Israel’s national data-protection / information authority, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Israeli registrar of companies
trackers.desc: official company register in Israel

trackers.name: Israel — State Comptroller & Ombudsman
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution; constitutional external auditor of all state bodies and the central public-complaints ombudsman, Israel.

trackers.name: SPNI — founded over a lost fight, and what came of it
trackers.desc: ISRAEL'S OLDEST AND LARGEST INDEPENDENT ENVIRONMENTAL NON-PROFIT, working to preserve species by protecting the lands and waters needed for their survival. ITS HISTORY IS THE REASON TO RECORD IT HONESTLY: SPNI was founded in 1953 by Azaria Alon and Amotz Zahavi in response to plans to drain the Hula Valley — and it lost that fight: the government and the JNF drained the majority of the wetlands. But after 40 years of campaigning, roughly 10 percent of the Hula wetlands were re-flooded in the early 1990s. Losing the immediate fight, building an institution, and recovering a fraction four decades later is a truer picture of this work than most success stories. WHAT IT DOES NOW: biodiversity protection, environmental education, bird protection, sustainable ecotourism, and work with policy makers, schools and communities — including producing an agricultural management plan for the Hula Valley, so it does technical planning, not only advocacy. It has a branch structure and is an IUCN member; it received the Israel Prize in 1980. THE STANDING CONTEXT it names for any Israeli land fight: a small country with a growing population whose remaining open spaces are increasingly under threat of development.

trackers.name: Nature Israel — the diaspora funding channel for Israeli conservation
trackers.desc: HOW THIS WORK GETS PAID FOR. Nature Israel — formerly the Canadian Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel, founded in 2011 — exists to raise awareness and funds supporting SPNI's activities in Israel. It is a diaspora fundraising channel rather than a grant-making body, so the route for a local group is partnering with or working through SPNI rather than applying to Nature Israel directly. HONEST GAP, STATED SO IT IS NOT MISTAKEN FOR COVERAGE: what could be verified for this entry is an organisation and a fundraising channel, not a standing Israeli grant programme with published eligibility for local community groups. If such a programme exists it should be added alongside this rather than inferred from it.

trackers.name: SPNI — the body that will carry your objection, and the one that files them by the thousand
trackers.desc: THE PRACTICAL POINT IS NOT THAT SPNI OBJECTS TO PLANS — IT IS THAT IT COLLECTS AND SUBMITS OTHER PEOPLE'S OBJECTIONS AT SCALE. When the government moved in 2026 to dilute environmental impact assessment requirements for large projects, around 1,300 individuals lodged their opposition through SPNI, alongside appeals from SPNI itself, Adam Teva V'Din, Zalul, Green Course, 15 Minutes and the Israel Association of Public Health Physicians. In 2024 it published the Hebrew legal memorandum on the Gaza-border reconstruction bill and told the public how to register objections to the proposed planning committee. If you have a local plan and no organisation, this is the route that turns one letter into a filed mass objection. WHO TO ASK FOR: Iris Han leads its open-landscape and planning work — irish@spni.org.il; Dan Alon runs the Israeli Ornithological Center; Yoav Perlman is the BirdLife contact at yoavp@spni.org.il. Head office Ha Negev 2, Tel Aviv. THE LOCAL LAYER MATTERS AND IS OFTEN MISSED: SPNI runs locally managed community branches in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Haifa, Beer Sheva and Modiin, each focused on its own city's fights, plus more than ten field schools — approach the branch for an urban plan rather than head office. Founded 1953 in direct response to the draining of the Hula Valley, roughly 800 employees, Israel Prize 1980, and the organisation behind the 2004 Coastal Law that bars new development within 300 metres of the shoreline — which means for any coastal site the first question is whether that 300-metre bar applies before anything else is argued. Pair it with Adam Teva V'Din, already in this file, which litigates; SPNI's strength is planning objections and open-space advocacy rather than the courtroom. VERIFICATION CAVEAT: the canonical domain spni.org.il is established from BirdLife International's partner record and from staff addresses published in conference proceedings; the specific landing page was not fetched during verification, and the organisation's main site is Hebrew-language.

trackers.name: Zalul — the campaign that succeeded moved the discharge instead of treating it; read that before you frame yours
trackers.desc: THE MOST USEFUL THING ZALUL'S RECORD TEACHES IS HOW A WIN CAN GO WRONG. Five factories had been permitted since 2001 to release some 10,000 cubic metres of dangerous sewage a day into the Kishon at Haifa; Zalul's campaign got local and national leaders to treat it as a priority — and the ministry's answer was an alternative plan to pipe the untreated sewage to the sea about two kilometres from a popular bathing area. The pollution was relocated, not removed, and Zalul had to start again on the demand that the factories treat their waste before releasing it anywhere. If your objection asks for a discharge or a nuisance to stop at a place, expect a proposal to move it, and decide in advance what you will accept. WHAT IT DOES: founded 1999 in Ramat Gan to protect Israel's seas and rivers; it reports environmental neglect, commissions studies, drafts and proposes legislation, runs an Environmental Economics Outreach Center as an economic advocacy and advisory body, and works with a legal consultant on environmental lawsuits — note the wording, because it means the litigation capacity is a consultant rather than an in-house practice, and for a case you want run rather than supported, Adam Teva V'Din is already in this file. Its team is described as spanning advocacy, academia, environmental specialists, lawyers, public relations and lobbying. Contact office@zalul.org.il. Documented outcomes attributed to its campaigns include the closure of the hazardous ammonia tank in Haifa, an end to the sludge from the Shafdan treatment plant being tipped into the sea, and recognition of navy personnel who developed cancer after diving in the Kishon during service as victims of pollution — that last one is worth knowing because it shows a route through personal-injury recognition rather than environmental law. A petition against the ALA pipeline discharging into the Gulf of Acco drew over 10,000 signatures from Acco residents. SCOPE LIMIT, AND IT IS SHARP: this is a water body. Seas, rivers, streams, beaches, discharge and marine ecosystems, with polluting industry and gas and oil companies as its usual targets. If your fight is a land development with no water dimension, this is the wrong door — use SPNI for planning objections and Adam Teva V'Din for litigation. SOURCING CAVEAT: zalul.org.il is confirmed as the canonical domain, but the campaign outcomes and the Kishon figures above come from a charity registry filing and third-party pages rather than from Zalul's own site, which this session did not read directly. Treat them as the shape of its record, and take exact figures from Zalul before quoting them.

trackers.name: Green Course — the organisation that beat a power station through a mayoral election after the objection process had already failed
trackers.desc: THE REASON TO CALL THEM IS THE ASHKELON PRECEDENT, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING ANY ISRAELI CAMPAIGN CAN LEARN. A third coal-fired power station at Ashkelon was approved in 2001. Green Course activists did not fight it only through the planning process — they used the 2003 local elections to put it on the agenda, initiating debates on environmental issues between the candidates for mayor, and a mayor who opposed the station was elected. The scheme was fought on the municipal electoral calendar, not just in the objection file. If your project needs a municipality's cooperation and there is an election inside your timeline, that is the lever, and this is the organisation that has actually pulled it. THE COMPANION LESSON IS WHAT HAPPENED IN JERUSALEM, BECAUSE IT SHOWS THE OBJECTION ROUTE FAILING ON ITS OWN: a committee of the Ministry of the Interior heard the objectors in August 2005 and then decided to keep promoting the plan anyway. What changed it was sustained public pressure at the National Council for Planning and Construction — a protest tent outside the ministry, a staged funeral for the hills of Jerusalem, and a demonstration of over 800 people on the morning of the decision. Being heard is not the same as being answered. WHAT THEY WILL DO FOR YOU: Open Spaces is one of their named campaign areas, and their Environmental Leadership Program exists to train community leaders to organise and run a campaign, teaching strategic planning, mobilisation, influencing decision makers and working with media. That is the offer — they will teach and staff a community campaign, with several hundred activists and volunteers behind it. Founded 1997, based in Tel Aviv; contact through megama@green.org.il. WHAT THEY ARE NOT: lawyers, a fund, or a landholder. They describe themselves as an activist field organisation working to influence decision makers. For litigation this file carries Adam Teva V'Din, for planning objections SPNI, for discharge and marine matters Zalul. Note also that directory listings give two different Tel Aviv addresses for this organisation; take the address from green.org.il rather than from a profile site.

trackers.name: Bimkom — planners who will draft your objection and represent you at the hearing, and the appeal is not as of right
trackers.desc: THE TRAP THAT CATCHES OBJECTORS IN ISRAEL IS AT THE APPEAL STAGE, AND BIMKOM STATES IT PLAINLY FROM ITS OWN EXPERIENCE: objections filed by the public are often rejected or only partly accepted, and an objector may then appeal to a higher planning body — but Bimkom has frequently had to REQUEST PERMISSION to appeal, and in some instances the only way to obtain that permission has been to petition the courts. The appeal is not automatic. Budget for a permission stage, and for the possibility that unlocking it means going to court over the right to be heard rather than over the plan itself. WHAT THIS ORGANISATION ACTUALLY DOES, IN ITS OWN WORDS: provides professional planning advice to communities, objects to harmful plans, and represents communities in planning and legal proceedings. That combination is rare — a planner who will both write the technical case and stand up with you at the committee. It was founded in April 1999 by professional planners and architects, and has submitted objections to hundreds of plans, most of them jointly with communities. THE TACTIC WORTH COPYING IS NOT OBJECTING BUT COUNTER-PLANNING: Bimkom works with communities to produce alternative, community-led planning principles and planning documents that then serve as the basis for negotiation with the planning authorities, and it reports that this has in some cases changed state-led plans. A committee that must choose between approving a scheme and rejecting it will usually approve; a committee handed a worked alternative has a third option. If you can afford one piece of professional work, make it the alternative plan rather than the objection letter. It also works on market-driven urban regeneration specifically — pressing for social considerations in those plans, for regulation of developers' activity, and for the rights of residents in affected neighbourhoods — which is the relevant expertise where redevelopment threatens to displace people rather than where a project threatens open land. WHERE TO WRITE: 43 Emek Refaim Street, Jerusalem, P.O.B 8376, 9108301; +972-2-5669655; bimkom@bimkom.org. It works with both Jewish and Arab communities, and separately runs a team on planning in Area C of the West Bank, where it files objections and petitions on behalf of Palestinian localities. THE LIMITS: it is not a conservation body and not a general law firm. Its frame is planning rights, housing and infrastructure for disadvantaged communities rather than habitat or landscape, so a purely environmental objection may sit outside what it takes on — for that this file carries SPNI for planning objections on open space and Adam Teva V'Din for litigation. And it works alongside legal organisations rather than replacing them: a documented objection to a district rail master plan was filed jointly with a legal centre on behalf of 130 residents, rejected by the subcommittee, and followed by a request for permission to appeal — the sequence this entry opens with.

trackers.name: Life and Environment — the environmental umbrella holds a seat on the National Council for Planning and Construction, with full rights
trackers.desc: THIS IS THE MOST STRUCTURALLY POWERFUL THING THIS FILE HAS FOUND ANYWHERE IN THE REGION, AND IT DATES FROM 1975: Life and Environment proposed an amendment to the Planning and Building Law which was approved that year, and under it the organisation has the right to nominate a permanent representative as a member of the National Council for Planning and Construction WITH FULL RIGHTS. The environmental movement does not merely petition the national planning body; it sits on it. For a local group facing a plan, that means the umbrella it can join has a voting presence in the forum where national planning policy is set — a channel no single community organisation could construct for itself. Ask what the current representative's position is on your plan, and ask early, because a seat is only useful to those who know it exists. WHAT IT IS: the umbrella body for the Israeli environmental movement, by its own account covering more than 150 national and local organisations, founded in 1975 by a former member of the Knesset who had chaired the Internal Affairs and Environment Committee, together with a co-founder of the Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel and the then head of the Nature Reserves Authority. In the same year it established the first Knesset Environmental Lobby. Its early record includes halting the import of aluminium slag from a German plant that was to be buried at the Timna mines, and it set up environmental committees inside sixteen civil organisations and public institutions including the Federation of Local Authorities. WHAT IT OFFERS A SMALL GROUP NOW: it runs an accelerator for grassroots environmental organisations and works through local authorities and coalitions specifically to strengthen local implementation and empower grassroots bodies, and it convenes the Israeli Presidential Climate Forum. If your organisation is too small to be heard, the realistic path is to join the umbrella rather than to grow first. THE LIMITS: it is a coordinating and policy body, not a litigator, a funder of your case, or a landholder.
