The practical instruction is to find the current version before writing anything, and to quote its own language back in the application. What this entry does not establish. This research did not verify the current grant ceilings, the application deadlines, or whether a particular round is open, because those change with each cycle and the document consulted was one round's guidelines. Treat the foundation as a confirmed route to money for environmental and community work in this country, and confirm the terms of the open round directly. Read this with the national conservation trust fund, the nature society, the land mapping organisations and the pro bono lawyer entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The valuers' board register — check the valuer behind a compensation figure, and where to complain about one
trackers.desc: A compensation figure is a valuer's opinion, and the valuer is on a public register. The board keeps and maintains the register of valuers, appraisers, estate agents, property managers, probationary valuers and probationary estate agents, together with the register of firms of valuers, appraisers and estate agents, and its site carries a search listing for those registers. When a number is put in front of a household — for an acquisition, a settlement or a buy-out — the first questions are who signed it and whether that person appears on this register, and both are answerable in a few minutes without asking the party that produced the figure. The board is statutory, and it disciplines. It was established in 1981 under the finance ministry and operates under the valuers, appraisers, estate agents and property managers legislation of the same year; its published functions include approving and rejecting applications for registration, conducting the professional examinations, regulating the professional conduct and ethics of valuers, appraisers, estate agents and property managers, and taking disciplinary action. A valuation that misdescribes a property therefore has a forum to be complained to, not merely an argument to be had. Instructing a registered valuer of your own is the practical counter. Valuers and appraisers are described as the professionals who advise on the valuation of property including houses, factories and shops. A report from a valuer the community instructs is what converts a belief that land is worth more into a document the other side has to answer, and it is the single most useful expense a group facing acquisition can make. Check the registration before instructing, and make sure the registration number appears on the report. Contact and identity are published, and the search route can move. The board publishes a named office address in the capital with telephone numbers and an email address, and issues numbered notifications about its information system and portal migrations — so if the register search page changes, go to the board's own site and look for the register or search listing rather than assuming the service has gone. Read this with the land acquisition, the national conservation trust fund, the pro bono legal scheme and the community mapping entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: SUHAKAM — a representative may file for the community, it can summon witnesses, and it stops if the matter goes to court
trackers.desc: Someone can file on the community's behalf. Under the commission's establishing legislation it may inquire into an alleged infringement of human rights on its own motion, or on a complaint made by an aggrieved person or group of persons, or by a person acting on behalf of an aggrieved person or group. Documented practice includes customary landowners lodging a formal complaint through an environmental organisation about encroachment on their land, with the commission's state office undertaking to engage with the affected landowners, visit the areas to verify, and report in the section of its annual report devoted to the two Borneo states. A representative complaint is the practical form for a village where no single person wants to be named first. It can summon witnesses. Its inquiry powers include the power to summon a witness, which published analysis records as carrying an implied power to enforce the summons and a duty on the person summoned to comply. That is a power a community cannot exercise itself and cannot buy, and it is the main practical reason to use this route rather than write more letters. It stops if the matter goes to court, and it does not enforce. The commission may not inquire into allegations that are the subject of proceedings pending in any court or that a court has finally decided, and must cease an inquiry if the matter is afterwards brought before a court; it will not normally inquire into matters within another agency's jurisdiction or duplicate another body's work; and it is not an enforcement agency — where an inquiry discloses a violation it refers the matter with its recommendations to the relevant authority and informs the complainant of the outcome. Sequence therefore matters: this route is used before litigation, not alongside it. National inquiries are its heaviest instrument, and land has been one. It has conducted a national inquiry into the land rights of indigenous peoples covering both the peninsula and the Borneo states, assessing laws, procedures and administrative practice against customary concepts of ancestral land, and publishing the findings — a body of material a community can cite rather than argue from scratch. Offices are published in the capital and in both Borneo states. Read this with the customary rights entries, the community land mapping organisations, the pro bono hub and the whistleblower protection entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Consumers' Association of Penang — a legal section that represents communities, and a complaints desk taking thousands a year
trackers.desc: There is a legal section whose stated job is representing communities. The association's published description of its own sections records a legal section that handles public interest cases and represents communities in need of legal assistance, working closely with the complaints section to provide legal advice and to monitor laws that affect consumers. For a village that cannot afford counsel and does not qualify for state legal aid, an organisation whose own account of itself includes representing communities is a different proposition from one that will merely write a letter of support. The complaints desk takes three to four thousand a year, by post, telephone and in person. Its complaints section is described as handling around three to four thousand complaints annually on all kinds of issues, received through the mail, by phone and by personal visits. A body already handling that volume knows which agency actually acts and which merely acknowledges — and the fact that people can simply walk in matters where writing a formal submission is itself the barrier. It publishes in four languages. Its news magazine appears in English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil editions, published bimonthly, alongside a magazine for schoolchildren. A case carried in four languages reaches the whole of an affected population rather than the part of it that reads the national press in one language, which in this country is the difference between a local grievance and a public one. The record is public, and one item is a template. Published statements include demands for action on two decades of pollution in a named river said to have cut the monthly income of more than a hundred small fishers, on coastal erosion and marine pollution at a named beach, and on illegal dumping across several states; and the association was part of a coalition of sixty-one organisations of farmers, consumers and environmental interests that submitted feedback to the biosafety department objecting to an application for a genetically modified rice field trial. That coalition objection is the template worth copying: many named organisations, one submission, to the department holding the application. Read this with the community land mapping organisations, the bar's pro bono hub, the environment department's assessment entries and the valuers' board register already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: National Heritage Act — any person may nominate, and a neighbouring site can be designated to protect the one beside it
trackers.desc: Any person may nominate. The heritage legislation of 2005 provides that any person may nominate to the Minister any natural heritage, any tangible or intangible cultural heritage, any living person or any underwater cultural heritage to be declared as National Heritage. The right is stated in those terms and is not confined to owners, councils or societies, which makes the nomination the single most direct step available to a community here. A neighbouring site can be designated to protect the one beside it. Where a site has no natural or cultural heritage significance of its own, but the Commissioner is satisfied that it should be designated because of its proximity to, and for the protection and enhancement of, another site already designated as a heritage site, the Commissioner may designate that site too — with the designation falling away if the designation of the other site is revoked. That is the provision for the field, the frontage or the slope next to a protected place, and it does not require the neighbouring land itself to be historic. Sixty days before designation, seven before entry, and an interim order in between. At least sixty days before making a designation the Commissioner must give the owner written notice of the intention to register, in the prescribed form; objections are dealt with and the decision served on both the objecting party and the owner. The Commissioner may enter a site at any time to inspect, survey, investigate or carry out work necessary to determine whether to designate it, on not less than seven days' written notice to the owner or occupier, and entry is not to be effected where a person objects on conscientious or religious grounds. An Interim Protection Order may be made, and contravening one is an offence, as is contravening a Monument Preservation Order made pending approval of a registration. Contractors must report what they find, and the register is a public list. An agent, contractor or executor of the federal government, a state government or an owner of alienated land who discovers an object having cultural heritage significance must report it to the Commissioner. The Commissioner establishes and maintains the national heritage register, which began in 2007 with fifty inaugural entries and has grown across categories covering buildings and monuments, archaeological sites, natural sites, tangible and intangible objects and living persons; gazettal as National Heritage is made by the Minister against nine statutory criteria including historical importance and rarity or uniqueness, and ownership of land or property so declared remains with its original owner. Read this with the nature society, the community land mapping organisations, the assessment exhibition dates and the valuers' board register entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Land acquisition — your own valuer's fees can be reimbursed by the government, and the objection is Form N within six weeks
trackers.desc: You may engage your own valuer, and the cost can be reimbursed by the government. The valuation and property services department, which advises the land administrator on compensation in acquisition cases, states in its own published account of the process that all persons interested can engage a private valuer and that the costs can be reimbursed by the government. For a household or a village facing an official figure produced by the state valuer, that single sentence changes the economics of disputing it: an independent valuation is not a cost that has to be found before the argument can be made. A person interested is defined as anyone who has an interest in the compensation, which is wider than the registered proprietor. The sequence, and the two forms that matter. A gazette notification declares that land is to be acquired; persons interested attend an enquiry conducted by the land administrator, at which all of them may make a claim for compensation within the prescribed time; the valuation department carries out a detailed study of the losses that can be compensated and advises the administrator; and the administrator then prepares a written award in the prescribed form. A person interested who is dissatisfied with the award may make a written objection in the objection form, and an appeal must be filed with the land administrator within six weeks from the date of the award. The award date and the six weeks are the two things to write down when the award arrives. What the award covers, and what the department will defend. The award deals with the measurement of the land, the amount of the compensation, the person to whom it is payable and the apportionment of the compensation, and compensation is assessed on the basis set out in the schedule to the acquisition legislation. The department states that it will defend its valuation if the landowner or any person interested refers the objection to the High Court — which is a useful thing to know in advance: the objection is not answered by an official reconsidering a file, but by a valuer defending a figure in court. How to use it. Obtain the award, note its date, identify which of the four heads is being disputed, engage a private valuer on the footing that the fees may be reimbursed, and file the objection within the six weeks. Read this with the valuers' board register for checking the valuer behind the official figure, the legal aid department's eligibility calculator, the land title search and the pro bono hub entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Forest Conservation Certificate — corporate money for keeping forest standing, on public land too, with results counted in hectares
trackers.desc: A national fund that channels company money into keeping forest standing. The forest fund is an agency under the natural resources ministry, set up to develop and run financing instruments for forests. Its first instrument, launched in 2024, is the forest conservation certificate: a non-market mechanism through which private-sector money supports conservation projects, with results denominated in hectares of forest conserved, mandatory indicators reported by every participant, third-party audits and a public registry. Participation is voluntary and can be at site level or across a whole forest complex. It is expressly not a carbon instrument — the fund states that it is not intended to generate carbon credits and cannot be used to support offsetting, a separate carbon offset programme being developed for that. Community-facing bodies can hold a certificate on public land. The protocol allows participation by landowners or entities with clear legal title, and — the provision that matters for a group with no title — by non-government or private entities holding written approval from the state government to apply for and hold a certificate for conservation activities on a specified area of public land. The written state approval is therefore the document to obtain first; the certificate follows it. All proponents and donors must become parties to a conservation agreement setting out the commitments. What the money can be spent on. Eligible activities cover conservation and sustainable forest management broadly, including increasing the area of permanent reserved forest, protected areas and totally protected areas; restoring the ecological integrity and function of degraded forest; and protecting endangered, threatened and endemic species. For a community fighting a clearance, the first of those is the useful one: the instrument exists to pay for enlarging protected forest, which is the opposite of the transaction a developer is proposing. Why a company would sign, and how big the pipeline is. Donors receive an income tax deduction of up to ten per cent of aggregate income, the certificates can be used in corporate sustainability reporting on the biodiversity topic, and companies may donate in respect of their own land provided it goes through the fund. Published reporting records eighty sites identified nationally as conservation locations with sixteen fully assessed for projects, and named corporate agreements covering large forest areas with village participation. Approaching a company with a specific site, a state approval and a tax deduction attached is a different proposition from asking for a donation. Read this with the national conservation trust fund, the nature society, the community land mapping organisations and the environment department's exhibition dates entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Macaranga — a newsroom whose whole beat is the environment here, and which trains other newsrooms to cover it
trackers.desc: A journalism portal whose only subject is this country's environment. Macaranga describes itself as a journalism portal covering the environment and sustainability in Malaysia, aiming to provide in-depth journalistic features on issues and to build knowledge about ecosystems. It is small and independent — run by its two co-founders, one a science journalist who has written for international science publications and holds a rainforest investigations fellowship — and it works with a local, regional and international content-producing and publishing network. For a community whose case depends on a slow, technical story that a daily paper will not carry, that focus is the point: the outlet exists to do the long version. Its work reaches beyond its own readership. Published accounts record that key stories have been supported by grants from international journalism funds, that dissemination of some stories has been supported by an established national news outlet, and that its stories have been quoted and used in reports, at conferences, and by government agencies, researchers and business groups. It also runs a monthly environmental news segment with a national radio station. A story placed here can therefore travel into the places where a project's approvals are argued about. It trains and mentors other newsrooms, which multiplies the routes in. Macaranga has run workshops and mentorship programmes for reporters from multiple newsrooms and for university students, with grants to produce stories and months of mentoring, on subjects including climate disinformation and indigenous peoples, just energy transition, and poaching and over-extraction of natural resources; mentee stories have appeared in mainstream outlets. A community that does not get a response from the portal itself may still find that a reporter who trained through it is now covering the beat at a larger paper. How to approach it, and what it needs. This is a features operation, not a wire service: what it can use is documents, a timeline, named people willing to be quoted, and a specific, checkable claim rather than a general grievance. It is funded by grants and by reader contributions and states that it is seeking funds to cover editorial and operational costs, so expect capacity limits and plan for a story that takes weeks. Read this with the community land mapping organisations, the forest conservation financing entry, the environment department's exhibition dates and the human rights commission entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Court judgment search — the government service that reaches published grounds of judgment, and the separate east Malaysian portal
trackers.desc: There is a listed government service for finding judgments. The national digital services catalogue lists a court case judgment search that, in its own description, enables users to search, review and access court judgments and written grounds of judgment published by the Federal Court, the Court of Appeal, the High Court and other courts. That is the entry point worth starting from, because it is maintained as a public service rather than as a practitioners' subscription. East Malaysia has its own judgment portal. The judiciary operates a separate electronic portal for Sabah and Sarawak carrying a judgment section with its own listings and update dates. A community in those states should search there as well as on the federal service, since the court structures and registries differ — the courts in east Malaysia falling under a separate high court, as do the courts of the peninsula under theirs. Written grounds are the document to look for, not the order. An order records what was decided; the written grounds record why, and it is the reasoning that tells a community whether its own facts fit. The chief registrar's office also maintains an electronic judgment management system among its services, and the judiciary's library compiles and binds grounds of judgment for the use of judges — an indication of how central those documents are to how the courts themselves work. Know what is free and what is not. The judiciary's library subscribes to commercial legal databases for the use of members of the judiciary, and those services are not open to the public; a third-party site republishes several thousand decisions drawn from the judiciary's electronic judgment system, categorised by subject including administrative law and land. Use the government service first, use republished collections to find a case quickly, and go back to the official text before relying on anything. Read this with the land acquisition entry, the valuers' board register, the pro bono hub and the environmental journalism entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Land purchase funding through an international conservation funder working with local partners
trackers.desc: An international funder that pays for land purchase, working through a local partner. The funder's own project page records that it and a local partner are working to purchase land to expand an existing national park in this country, with the local partner proposing that the new protected area — stated at 248,927 acres — be constituted as a state park. The site is described as lying within a globally important tiger conservation landscape and forming a critical wildlife corridor within the national forest linkages master plan, holding lowland and foothill dipterocarp forest with at least 43 mammal species, eighteen of them highly threatened, and six of the country's eight wild cat species. For a community whose land adjoins or forms part of a corridor like that, this is the model to understand: the money for acquisition comes from outside, but the proposal, the partner and the biodiversity case are local. What makes a site fundable. Read the stated grounds and they are a checklist: a named landscape of international importance, a corridor function already recognised in a government plan, documented species richness, and a specific proposal for what the land becomes afterwards. A community assembling a case for outside acquisition funding should be able to answer each of those in the same terms, and the government plan reference is the one most often overlooked. The same funder supports the analysis stage, not only purchase. Another of its projects in this country works with a regional rainforest research partnership to produce high-resolution maps integrating land use and biodiversity, to help a state government identify where to create new protected areas in pursuit of its own stated target of raising protected coverage from twenty-three to thirty per cent of land area, with boundaries then marked according to the forestry department's standard procedures. Where a state has a stated coverage target, a community's site can be argued as a contribution to it. Read this against what can go wrong. Reported cases in this country include a forest management unit of over 101,000 hectares where conservation groups had worked for three years toward a conservation economy before logging and plantation rights were acquired by a timber company, and a cancelled internationally funded conservation project covering 283,500 hectares. Acquisition funding takes time, and a competing commercial transaction can close first. Read this with the forest conservation certificate, the environmental journalism portal, the pro bono hub and the land acquisition entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Mining leases and quarry approvals — the three-year documents a tenement holder must produce, and the official search at the state land office
trackers.desc: A mineral tenement is granted first and the impact work comes after — and the holder may not operate until it is done. A state assembly's published answer on quarry approval procedure records that impact assessment is generally carried out only after the state authority has approved the mineral tenement in principle, and that the tenement holder is not permitted to carry out any development or mining work until named documents are approved within three years of the tenement being issued: an environmental impact assessment report from the environment department, and an operational mining scheme approval from the minerals and geoscience department. The gap between grant and permission to work is therefore a documented state, and the two documents are specific things to ask for by name. Monitoring is against the approved scheme, not against a general standard. The same answer records that the holder must comply with all tenement conditions and with the conditions set by the relevant departments, and that the minerals department conducts periodic monitoring to ensure the holder operates according to the approved operational mining scheme letter. A complaint framed as a departure from the approved scheme is therefore addressed to a document the regulator itself holds. Quarries operate under state quarry rules, with a renewal form. A further answer records a quarry operating under a permission form issued in a stated year on the basis of comments from technical departments including minerals and environment supporting the renewal of the quarry permit; records the environment department's finding that the operator had implemented control measures under state guidelines and complied with the environmental quality legislation and with state quarry rules enforced by the minerals department; and records the department's view that dust and noise problems followed housing built later without a buffer zone between the quarry and the houses. The buffer point cuts both ways and is worth knowing before an argument about who came first. Where to look the tenement up. A state land and mines office's published answers record that information about a mining licence is obtained through an official search document at the state director of lands and mines office, that the state minerals and geoscience department keeps mining records, and that applications for quarry operation approval go to that department on a named form. The federal department records that it administers and enforces the mineral development legislation of 1994, the quarry rules and related regulations, and assists in enforcing state mineral enactments, with mining rights issued only to genuine miners for an area and period matched to the deposit's life. Read this with the forest conservation certificate, the land acquisition entry, the pro bono hub and the judgment search entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Kebenaran merancang — neighbouring owners get a served notice and twenty-one days to object with reasons, plus the local plan publicity and hearing
trackers.desc: An adjoining landowner is served with notice and has twenty-one days to object. The planning control rules made under the town and country planning legislation contain the prescribed notice to a neighbouring owner, which states that it is to inform you of your right, as the owner of land adjoining the land to which the application relates, to object to that application within twenty-one days of the date the notice is served, and that the objection must be accompanied by a statement of the grounds for it. A state planning department records among the matters the local planning authority weighs the objections of neighbouring landowners made under the relevant section, applications requiring the advice of the national physical planning council, and comments from the relevant technical departments. Grounds in writing, inside three weeks, from the neighbour: that is the most direct entry point in this country's planning system. Development without planning permission is prohibited outright. The same department records that planning permission means permission granted with or without conditions to carry out development; that no person other than the local authority may commence, undertake or carry out any development unless planning permission has been granted or extended under the named sections; and that offences are stated in the Act, including developing land contrary to the zoned land use gazetted by the local plan or modifying an approved planning permission. Ask which zone the local plan gazettes for the site. The Act's own structure tells you where the openings are. The published Act lists publicity in connection with draft structure plans, preparation of draft local plans, publicity in connection with a draft local plan, inquiry and hearing in respect of a draft local plan, approval or rejection of the draft, alteration, revocation and replacement of local plans, special area plans, a duty to consult, the development proposal report, the layout plan, preparation of plans by a qualified person, treatment of applications, appeal against the local planning authority's decision, lapse of planning permission, and revocation and modification of planning permission and building plan approval. Each of those is a document or a stage a community can ask about by name. Know which planning law applies to you. The department records that this Act was made under a named constitutional article and is in force only in the peninsular states, applying in each state from a date fixed by the state authority with the minister's agreement, while two other states and the federal territory use their own planning laws. Read this with the environment department's exhibition dates, the land acquisition entry, the pro bono hub and the title search entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Perintah pemeliharaan pokok — a tree preservation order under the planning Act, the 0.8 metre rule that applies without one, and replacement on conviction
trackers.desc: Cutting a tree whose girth exceeds 0.8 metres without the local authority's written permission is an offence in itself. The planning legislation contains a section prohibiting the cutting and similar treatment of a tree whose girth exceeds 0.8 metres, and a city council records prosecuting six people in the magistrates' court for felling two named trees with girths above that threshold without its written permission, all of whom pleaded guilty and were fined a stated total. That number is measurable with a tape before any argument about ownership. The preservation order is the stronger instrument, and damaging a tree is defined broadly. A district council's explanation records that the Act's tree part gives special protection to mature trees so they are not felled and the area's ecological system is maintained, and that damaging or destroying a tree includes scratching, peeling, nailing, painting, poisoning, burning, boring, patching, chipping, notching, binding with wire and cutting around the girth, along with other acts that injure or disfigure it. It records that breaching a preservation order is an offence carrying a fine of up to a stated maximum or imprisonment up to six months, and that a person convicted of felling a tree under such an order may be required to replace it by planting another of suitable size and species. Those listed acts are what a photograph of a ring-barked or poisoned tree can be matched against. What the order can cover, and where it cannot reach. A state planning department's practice note on preservation orders records that the local planning authority may from time to time propose additions to an order; that the order does not extend to trees already defined under other written law or located in areas declared as forest reserve, water catchment or hill conservation areas; that grounds for permitting work include a tree that is dead or nearly dead, and prevention of imminent danger; and that the environmental quality legislation is relevant alongside. Establish which regime the tree sits under before writing. There is an appeal, and it is named. The Act's arrangement of sections includes appeal against a tree preservation order, revocation of such an order, the prohibition on cutting a tree of more than 0.8 metres girth, and the appeal board itself. Read this with the planning permission entry, the forest conservation certificate, the heritage nomination route and the mining lease entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: State water authority — fifty-metre river reserves gazetted as protection zones, written permission for altering a water source, and directive letters and water protection orders against a polluting premises
trackers.desc: A state water authority can gazette the river reserve itself as a protection zone. Answers tabled in a state assembly record that the water management board gazetted a named mukim as a protection zone under a stated subsection of its 1999 enactment in July 2009, to control activities in the river reserve, the buffer zone and the surrounding environment, including firefly habitat along a particular reach; and that the board has been gazetting fifty metres of river reserve on each bank of three named rivers as protection zones, with survey work under way on further tributaries for the same purpose. Ask whether the stretch beside a project is already gazetted, and if not, that it be surveyed for gazetting. Two licence types cover activities at the water's edge. The same answers record periodic monitoring of compliance with conditions at premises licensed by the board under a written permission for water source alteration activity and a licence for the entry or release of pollutants; and record a mapping and inventory study of land use activities within the fifty-metre river reserve, carried out by aerial surveillance using drones and maintained in a geographic information system, with monthly monitoring of the risky activities it identifies. That inventory is a document to ask for by name. The director can order works, and do them at the operator's cost. The answers record that the board's director may issue an order by written notice — a directive letter — to any person or public authority carrying on a water source alteration activity under a named section; that if the order is not complied with the board or a person authorised by it may enter the work site, carry out the works ordered and take any other action to give effect to the order, with costs recoverable as a debt due to the board; and that where demolition of a building or construction within a river reserve is required, the board refers the matter to the state government. They also record directive letters and water protection orders issued under two named sections to polluting or at-risk premises, requiring pollution control at source and immediate cleaning works. Penalties and the emergency committee are stated. The answers record that breach of a named section carries a fine up to a stated maximum, imprisonment up to three years, or both, with a further daily fine while the offence continues after a compliance notice; that the enactment was amended in 2020 to raise fines, compounds and imprisonment; and that a state water pollution emergency committee, with the board as its secretariat, investigates the source of a river pollution incident and takes immediate cleaning and legal action. Read this with the planning permission entry, the environment department exhibition dates, the tree preservation order and the quarry approval entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Fisheries Act 1985 and the fishing zones — Zone A reserved to traditional coastal fishers, the marine park written permission, and the licence-condition offence used against trawlers
trackers.desc: The zoning system puts the first five nautical miles in the hands of coastal fishers. The state fisheries department records that the national fisheries waters zoning system has five zones — Zone A from nought to five nautical miles, Zone B from five to twelve, Zone C from twelve to thirty, and two outer zones — and that the Act is enforced to prevent conflict between coastal fishers in Zone A using traditional gear and commercial fishers in Zone B using high-capacity gear; it records that trawler intrusion from Zone B into Zone A harms the coastal ecosystem, changing the seabed in shallow water and destroying natural habitat for fish fry and other marine life. Where a vessel is working close inshore, the zone it is licensed for is the first fact to establish. Breaching a licence condition is itself the charge. A state assembly answer records that a Zone A vessel licensed for traditional gear such as drift nets, but actually using a trawl net, is dealt with as breaching a licence condition under a named section of the Act; records a named trap gear listed among prohibited fishing methods nationally; and records the state fisheries department running focused operations against illegal trawlers, with vessels seized and stated values, and a table of arrests across several years. That is a complaint route with a documented enforcement record behind it. Marine parks and reserves need written permission to enter. The Act provides that any person in a marine park or marine reserve in these waters without written permission commits an offence under the relevant part; that the minister may make different regulations for different marine parks and reserves, including dividing a park or reserve into zones and prescribing the conditions applying to each; and that the minister may establish a national advisory council for marine parks and marine reserves. What the Act covers, and where the discretion sits. Published description records the Act as covering conservation, management and development of maritime and estuarine fishing and fisheries in these waters, protection of aquatic mammals and turtles, riverine fishing, and the establishment of marine parks and reserves; and records that the Director General of Fisheries is the management authority with wide power over permit conditions, with a person aggrieved by a refusal given a route of appeal. Read this with the river reserve gazetting, the planning permission entry, the tree preservation order and the quarry approval entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Wildlife Conservation Act 2010 — destroying the nest or eggs of a protected animal is its own offence, hunting within four hundred metres of a salt lick is another, and offences are arrestable
trackers.desc: Destroying a nest or eggs is a separate, named offence, with a heavier penalty for the fully protected species. The 2010 wildlife conservation legislation provides that any person who damages or destroys the nest or eggs of protected wildlife commits an offence, punishable on conviction by a fine up to a stated amount or imprisonment up to one year or both, and that the same act against fully protected wildlife carries a higher fine and up to two years. Where clearing would take a nesting tree or a nesting bank, that is the provision to name, and it does not require any animal to be killed. The offence list reads as a checklist of what a site operator may not do. The Act's part on offences includes hunting wildlife in a wildlife reserve or wildlife protected area; hunting at prohibited times; hunting protected wildlife in the closed season; hunting with poison, bait, poisoned bait, bird lime or nets; hunting with weapons or traps other than those prescribed; hunting within four hundred metres of a salt lick; hunting from a vehicle; disturbing a salt lick or its surroundings; cruelty to wildlife; and provoking wildlife. The poison provision carries a fine up to fifty thousand ringgit or two years or both, and applies to a licensed hunter and to anyone else alike, with an exception only for a public officer destroying crop pests under the director's supervision. Entry to a reserve needs the director's permission, and enforcement is immediate. The Act contains provisions on permission to enter a wildlife reserve and protected area, and its enforcement part provides that offences under the Act are arrestable offences, with authorisation of public officers following. The three schedules decide which rule applies. The Act defines protected wildlife as the species listed in the First Schedule, fully protected wildlife as those in the Second Schedule, and immature wildlife by the maturity standards in the Third Schedule, with wildlife covering any wild animal or bird, vertebrate or invertebrate, live or dead, mature or immature. A national biodiversity information system publishes the Act with the species it lists, and the department publishes the regulations made under it. A 2021 amendment raised the imprisonment term for a stated offence from two years to three and tightened marking and labelling duties on licence holders. Read this with the fisheries zones, the river reserve gazetting, the tree preservation order and the planning permission entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Standing in environmental judicial review — the "real and genuine interest" test the Federal Court settled, the case that stopped a retrospective exclusion, and the appeal provisions inside the Act
trackers.desc: The standing test was settled in a 2014 case, and it is lower than proving a private right. Published reporting of a senior lawyer's account records that the biggest hurdle in public interest cases is locus standi — whether the party has a real and genuine interest and is adversely affected; that courts historically struck out cases where standing failed but have taken a much more robust approach in recent public interest litigation; and that in a 2014 Federal Court case, brought by a trade union congress challenging the government's refusal to disclose water privatisation concession agreements and audit reports, the court found the union had standing, ruling that it only needed to demonstrate a real and genuine interest in the subject matter and that it was adversely affected. Published analysis quotes the judgment directly: to pass the adversely affected test the applicant has at least to show a real and genuine interest, and it is not necessary to establish infringement of a private right. That sentence is what a community's lawyer needs when standing is challenged. An earlier case shows what participation rights are worth in court. Published case material records an action in which plaintiffs sought a declaration that a company had to comply with the assessment section of the environmental quality legislation and the guidelines under it; records the court holding that a valid assessment cannot be made without some form of public participation, that this is a right vested in the plaintiffs, and that the minister's order amounted to removing their entire right to participate and give views before approval; and records that the order excluding one state from the assessment regime, gazetted on the very day the summons was filed and applied retrospectively, was held wholly invalid because the Act does not authorise retrospective orders. The appellate history is recorded too, and is mixed. The Act's own machinery names the approval conditions and an appeal board. The legislation provides that a person intending a prescribed activity must submit an assessment report to the director general before any approval is granted by the relevant approving authority, and that where the report is adequate he shall approve it, with or without conditions attached, informing the proponent and the approving authorities; and its contents list an appeal section and an appeal board, alongside an environmental fund with its committee, contributions and application. Read this with the environment department's exhibition dates, the pro bono hub, the human rights commission and the environmental newsroom entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: MyEQMS — the department's public monitoring portal, the air pollutant index by station with its six pollutants and colour bands, and the parallel river and marine water quality index systems
trackers.desc: One public portal carries the department's environmental monitoring, and it is filterable by state. The environment department runs a public portal under its environmental quality monitoring programme, with the air pollutant index management system giving the latest reading for each area with the time the reading was taken; guidance published for the public describes filtering by state to generate the readings for a chosen place, and a departmental mobile application carrying the same data. The department's own front page lists alongside it the marine water quality index management system and the river water quality index management system, plus a regional hotspot information feed. A community can therefore check air, river and coastal indices from the same source. The index is built from six pollutants, on twenty-four hour readings, with published bands. Published material records the index reported by time as calculated from the sub-indices of six pollutants — sulphur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, ground-level ozone, carbon monoxide, and particulates below ten and below two and a half microns; records the bands as 0 to 50 good, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy, above 300 hazardous; and records that the index is computed on a twenty-four hour reading, not a one-minute reading — the point to make when a proponent quotes an instantaneous figure. It records the fine particulate parameter taken into the index calculation following a station upgrade programme, with the national haze action plan's alert levels revised accordingly. The station network's size shows in routine reporting. National reporting of a single morning records readings taken from the portal at a stated time, with sixty-three of sixty-eight monitoring stations nationwide at moderate level and named towns listed with their numbers; other reporting records a later morning with seventeen areas across six states and two federal territories at unhealthy levels, the highest named with its reading. Open burning has its own reporting line. Published material records the public asked to report open burning or fires to the fire and rescue service on the emergency number and to the environment department on its toll-free line, with the number given. Read this with the environment department's exhibition dates, the accredited laboratory, the river reserve entry and the environmental newsroom entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Ecological Fiscal Transfers — federal money paid to states for gazetting and funding protected areas, the guideline setting allocation criteria, and the reporting that found most of it untraceable
trackers.desc: Federal money is transferred to states specifically for conservation, and the purposes are stated. Published material records the transfer as a mechanism moving national funds to subnational governments based on conservation objectives and performance, its purpose being to encourage states to prioritise biodiversity conservation through terrestrial and marine protected areas, gazette new protected areas, fund protected areas, and compensate for lost economic opportunities; and records that from 2022 it was revised as a special allocation, with the finance ministry allocating funds to the natural resources ministry, which implements the scheme with the states, that ministry having developed a guideline explaining allocation criteria and monitoring and evaluation procedures. Because states control land while the federal government carries the international commitments, this is the money a state can be asked what it did with. The reporting found most of the money untraceable, and says so. An environmental newsroom's investigation records little transparency on most of the money disbursed, despite some state-level data from two named states; records that its reporter asked the ministry and two state authorities for case studies of how funds were used and did not get any answer, and that seven major conservation groups in the peninsula were asked about their experience with these funds and none had received any. A webinar summary records that the ministry did not disburse funds in certain years, that most states provided little detail, one being most transparent but only from a stated year, and that there is currently no penalty for states that reduce forest cover, and little compensation for states that already maintain high forest coverage. Asking a state for its allocation and its spending is a question with a documented history of going unanswered — which is itself the finding to cite. Other conservation finance routes are named alongside it. Published material records the federal conservation trust fund as having channelled a stated sum to 112 conservation projects since 2015; records a payment for ecosystem services charge raising a stated sum in one state imposed on developers or project proponents building telecommunications towers and transmission lines within permanent forests; and records a federal forest fund supporting private investment through forest carbon certificates. A state foundation records a 2017 agreement with the state forestry department and a state environmental trust forming a dedicated patrol team to enforce regulations and monitor a named rainforest landscape. Read this with the conservation trust fund, the forest conservation certificate, the environmental newsroom and the state water authority entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The indigenous peoples' network and the rivers network — an umbrella of community organisations with three secretariats, community mapping training that has won legal cases, and the dam network beside it
trackers.desc: An umbrella network of community organisations exists, with published addresses in three states. Published description records the network as the umbrella for indigenous community-based organisations and communities, supported by associated members drawn from indigenous and indigenous-focused organisations, giving one figure of 83 organisations and communities and earlier accounts giving twenty-one; records it established as a national network in the 1990s at a first indigenous national workshop and legally registered in 2009, with its national secretariat in a named town and mini secretariats in two other states; and records it as the focal point for indigenous rights and advocacy, providing assistance and a platform for indigenous communities nationally, regionally and internationally. Published contact material gives its post box, telephone and email. Members support each other through named joint activities, including mapping. The same description records members and organisations supporting each other through exchange and joint activities such as training, conferences, exhibitions, mapping, and joint memoranda to the government; records a general assembly electing the main committee every three years, responsible for carrying out its resolutions and reporting back; and records a media release announcing the network's work to map indigenous traditional lands and territories with a named secretary general as contact. Mapping training has produced legal results, and the trainer says so. A partner organisation records that since the early 1990s it has trained dozens of indigenous activists in community mapping, enabling communities to map areas of ancestral land claims and win legal cases and negotiations. That is the clearest statement in this bucket of what a map is worth in court. A rivers network works the dam cases with contact details published. Published material records a Sarawak rivers network building broad-based support to mobilise the public against state plans for more dams destructive to people and ecosystems, partnering with organisations, community-based organisations and communities in dam-affected areas; records it supporting and empowering communities to protect their land, rivers and watersheds through capacity building, networking, research, education and advocacy, and promoting village-scale renewable energy systems with a named partner that trains rural indigenous technicians in micro-hydro; and gives its secretariat address, telephone and email. Read this with the indigenous trust in Sabah, the customary rights entry, the environmental society and the environmental newsroom entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: TRCRC — a restoration organisation that buys seedlings back from communities, trains indigenous ground teams to collect and germinate seed, and holds living collections of threatened tree species
trackers.desc: A community can be paid for the seedlings it grows, under a stated model. The organisation records developing a seedling programme with an indigenous community in a named state park, teaching communities to identify key plant species, collect the seeds and germinate them in communal nurseries, with the planting stock they create then going through a sustainable finance model whereby they are able to sell the matured saplings to support restoration works in that region. Its own listings record a seedling buyback programme and a seed-to-tree initiative with indigenous peoples and local communities, and record a site ground team made up of members of two named indigenous communities. For a community holding degraded land, that is income attached to restoration rather than to clearance. It holds the plant material, which is what restoration actually needs. The organisation records itself established in 2012 with a two-fold mission — to preserve tropical rainforest plant species and lead landscape-wide protection and reforestation projects — and aims to establish multiple ex-situ living collections and plant nurseries throughout the country, germinating, propagating and eventually reintroducing rare and endangered plant species back into their native habitats, reconnecting forest fragments using native trees from nurseries and seedlings from rescued threatened plants. It names its three collection sites, and records that a large percentage of tropical seeds are recalcitrant and difficult to store for long periods — which is why living collections exist rather than seed banks alone. Its site arrangements show what a community can ask a forestry department for. It records one site prioritising collection of seeds outside protected areas, sitting inside a certified sustainable forest management project, and records that with support from the state forestry department it created a ten-year forest management plan for the site, including measures for long-term sustainability. Published material records restoration species selection depending on land conditions, existing species and availability of tree stocks, with a preliminary study of the site carried out to create a planting plan, and replanting involving government agencies, other organisations, companies and local communities. Read this with the forest fund, the nature society, the indigenous trust and the ecological fiscal transfers entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: EPSM and the environmental organisations directory — a volunteer-run society that campaigned for the assessment law itself, its named campaign record, and a published list of organisations with phone numbers
trackers.desc: The oldest environmental society here helped bring in the assessment law that communities now use. Published description records it set up in 1974 by a group of concerned individuals as the first environmental organisation in the country focusing on the adverse impacts of human activities on the environment, remaining a non-profit run by volunteers, active in highlighting pressing environmental issues, undertaking studies and proposing solutions based on research, with early focus on air, water and noise pollution, deforestation, waste and public transport; and records it involved in protecting a named national park and advocating for the introduction of the proactive environmental impact assessment legislation. The assessment window recorded elsewhere in this bucket exists partly because this society pushed for it. Its methods and campaigns are listed by name. The society records having highlighted environmental problems through the mass media, made representation to government agencies, campaigned against polluters, undertaken surveys and studies, and contributed to environmental education through talks, forums, seminars and its publication; and records a campaign list including named forest and cave sites, a national park, a named radioactive waste site, a named dam, the societies legislation amendments and the environmental impact assessment, alongside monitoring the environmental quality legislation and its subsequent regulations. That list tells a community which fights this body has actually joined. A directory of the country's environmental organisations gives the contacts. A published list records named organisations with street addresses or post boxes, telephone and fax numbers and email addresses — including an environmental management and research association, this society, a global environment centre, the nature society, a marine sciences society and a Sabah community organisation partner, several of them already recorded in this bucket. A professional association records itself as a non-profit association of organisations, professionals, students and people with an interest in learning and promoting effective ways to manage the impacts of human activities on the environment, with its own street address published. Read this with the nature society, the friends of the earth affiliate, the consumers' association and the assessment exhibition entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: BRIMAS and community-based mapping in Sarawak — an indigenous organisation that trains longhouses to map their own customary land, and the international project that funds village-level work
trackers.desc: Communities here are trained to map their own land, and the organisation that started it is named. Published material records that in 1996 the organisation organised a training session on community-based mapping for non-governmental and community-based organisations in the state, with support from mapping trainers from an international project, so that the communities could produce their own maps; and records that from 1997 onwards it has been in the forefront of community-based mapping in the state, receiving overwhelming requests from communities to map their customary land and to train the community to map their own land. Where the state is slow to delineate boundaries, a community that can map its own is not waiting. The organisation is indigenous-led and its remit is broader than mapping. Published description records it as an indigenous non-profit organisation working at grassroots level in the state, formally established in July 1993, whose purposes are to educate indigenous communities about their rights, to promote community-based sustainable resource management and conservation, to empower their initiatives toward self-reliant and resilient communities, to assist in their pursuit of self-sufficiency, and to ensure the survival of their traditional knowledge, arts and culture. The funder beside it states a rule worth quoting. An international project records that its goal is providing international support for indigenous and locally-led campaigns to protect rights and to advocate internationally for mechanisms supporting community-led forest conservation; that it has a range of local partners in the state and across the country; and that it does not initiate its own campaigns, but responds to the needs of its local partners and provides whatever support best suits their programmatic and campaign needs, having over the years provided small grants for village-level projects, workshops on community mapping and street protests, on the stated belief that it is there to support, rather than lead, campaigns. That is the test to apply to any outside body offering help. Published commentary records other bodies a community can approach for mapping support, naming a state Dayak association and a community information and communications centre, and advises documenting oral histories and physical markers such as old longhouses, burial sites and fruit trees alongside the maps. Read this with the indigenous network, the rivers network, the customary rights entries and the environmental society entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The National River Care Fund and the river care programme — a small grant a community group can apply to for its own river work, plus ranger training and a community network
trackers.desc: There is a small grant fund for a community's own river work, and its purpose is stated. The organisation records the national river care fund as a small grant programme established to support local communities, community-based organisations and non-profit organisations to pursue their own river conservation initiatives, with the goal of establishing and encouraging a river care civil society that has the capability to contribute. A grant framed around their own initiatives is different from being enrolled in someone else's project. The programme behind it works at river basin scale with community participation written in. The organisation records the river care programme's aim as promoting and supporting integrated management of river basins and water resources with particular focus on stakeholder engagement, community participation, waste management, biodiversity and wetland conservation, nature-based solutions and citizen science approaches, and its mission as promoting the protection, restoration and sustainable use of rivers by enhancing multi-stakeholder participation and knowledge to stimulate local action. It records a restoration project on a named tributary focused on biodiversity enhancement through community participation, and a catchment project that aims to conserve the upper catchment of a named river basin serving as water supply to indigenous and local communities. It records the blunt background figure: more than 90 per cent of the country's water resources come from rivers, yet only 47 per cent of rivers remain clean. It trains people and connects them. Its milestones record developing a river ranger programme to educate people on every aspect of the freshwater ecosystem and a solid waste ranger programme; forming a friends-of-the-river-basin group; launching a community network uniting existing and future community partners; and running a river open classroom teaching why waterways matter. Published description records it as a Malaysian non-profit established in 1998 with four programmes — forest and coastal, river care, peatland, and outreach and partnership — and gives its floor, building and street address. Read this with the environmental society and directory, the nature society, the indigenous network and the restoration organisation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Penang Forum and the state fishermen's associations — a state-level coalition focused on one state's own governance, the official fishermen's associations that challenged an approval, and the court ruling on planning permission
trackers.desc: A coalition exists whose stated focus is one state's own governance, not the country's. It records itself as a broad coalition of non-governmental organisations working towards local democracy and sustainable development in that state, and states that while we may be concerned about many social and environmental issues at the national level, our focus is on improving policies, governance and public participation in the state itself. It records having initiated a project in 2009 to promote public transport, producing a transport master plan as a willing collaboration between the state government and civil society, which the state then changed to a version requiring massive hill cutting and land acquisition. A coalition that once co-wrote a state plan, and then opposed its replacement, is a specific kind of ally. The fishermen's own associations are named and they went to the appeals board. Published material records objections raised by fishermen including the official fishermen's association, a named southern area fishermen's association, and all the units of the fishermen's villages; and records that the fishermen challenged the approval of the environmental impact assessment report before the appeals board set up under the environmental quality legislation, with no hearing date fixed at that time. Village-level fishermen's units, an area association and the official association are three separate doors. The litigation reached the appellate court, and the ground was procedural. Published material records a court of appeal decision concerning the reclamation, and records an environmental organisation stating that the ruling leaves the project without valid planning permission and requires an immediate halt; it records the case as challenging planning permission given by the state director of town and country planning upon the approval of the state planning committee, on concerns including the failure by the state planning committee to consult the national physical planning council before permission was granted. Published reporting records a memorandum to the national human rights commission from a coalition of the forum and the fishermen's association, supported by 38 organisations, and a national anti-reclamation movement described as a coalition of 32 environmental organisations. Read this with the river care fund, the environmental society and directory, the indigenous mapping organisation and the assessment exhibition entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Sabah's Native Courts — a village headman's court, a chief's court and a district court that hear customary land disputes, with the assessors, the appeal ladder and the judicial review that checks them
trackers.desc: Customary land disputes have their own courts, and the first one sits in the village. Published description records the state's native courts as established under a named 1992 enactment and as a crucial institution for administering justice within the native communities of the state, whose jurisdiction is designed to uphold and administer native customary law with authority to adjudicate breach of customary law, land disputes, inheritance, marital issues and adoption. For a community whose claim rests on custom rather than a title deed, that is a forum built for exactly that evidence. The tiers are published, and so is who sits on each. Published material records the headmen's court presided over by a headman with two assessors; the chief's court by a native chief with two assessors; the chief's superior court by senior chiefs with assessors; the district native court by a magistrate with two assessors; the resident's native court by a resident with two or four assessors; and the native court of appeal by a judge with one or more assessors. Published research records that the first two levels of the native court do not permit advocates — so the earliest hearings are conducted by the parties themselves. The officers are named by rank, and the scale of one training event shows how many there are. Published research records customary law experts at district level as native chiefs, with the highest grade titled district chief, and records the duty of district chiefs and native chiefs as maintaining social harmony and upholding customary law among the indigenous peoples in the district. Reporting records a single leadership course attended by 258 customary chiefs — three district chiefs, 20 native chiefs, 40 native chief representatives, 194 village heads and one kapitan from four named areas. The check on these courts is judicial review, and it has been used. Published material records that the decisions of the native courts are subject to judicial review, and that decisions have been quashed by the civil court on the ground of jurisdictional error, citing a named case in which an order was set aside because the court had acted without or in excess of jurisdiction. Read this with the Sarawak mapping organisation, the indigenous network, the state coalition and the fishermen's associations entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Local authority one-stop centres — the council department that receives every development application, a committee chaired by the mayor meeting at least twice a month, and the site objection notice on the checklist
trackers.desc: Every development application passes through one department in the council, and it says what it does. A municipal council records its one-stop centre department as responsible for three main activities — standardising application procedures and processes, simplifying the application process, and coordinating and speeding up approval of land development applications — covering planning permission applications among others. A second council publishes the department's email, the name of the department head and the head's email, and records the centre as having begun as a small unit in October 2003 under the council secretary. For a resident who wants to see what has been applied for next door, that department is the counter, and it has a named head. The committee that decides is chaired by the mayor and meets on a published cadence. A published manual records three categories of local authority — city council, municipal council and district council — and records that the one-stop centre committee is chaired by the mayor or council president, holds powers delegated by the full council, and meets at least twice a month, with pre-committee meetings encouraged. Knowing the decision body meets fortnightly, under a named chair, is what lets an objection arrive before the decision rather than after. The checklists show what a developer must file, including an objection notice on site. One city council's planning permission checklist lists required items including the approval documents of existing and previous development plans, layout planning permission forms with approved stamps, and a site objection notice, and separately requires a social impact assessment report for development under a named subsection of the planning legislation. Another council's checklist requires the latest assessment tax and land tax copies, title or sale and purchase documents with the land office approval letter, and a power of attorney. A third records that plans and technical documents must be signed by a registered professional town planner, and that checklists cover building plans, engineering and infrastructure plans, landscape plans, the start-work notification and the certificate of fitness site inspections. Read this with the state coalition and fishermen's associations, the native courts, the river care fund and the environmental society entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: District land offices and the land administrator's inquiry — the hearing where compensation is fixed and objections recorded, who must attend, the six-week window for Form N, and the four things a court can be asked to change
trackers.desc: The land administrator holds an inquiry, and its purpose includes hearing objections. A district land office records the administrator's role as processing acquisition under the 1960 legislation, conducting the inquiry to determine the amount of compensation payable to interested persons, taking possession of the land, and managing issue of title for the area taken and continuation title for the remainder; and records the inquiry's purposes as to hear; to determine the valuation of the land to be taken; to determine the amount of compensation; to determine the interest of each person making a claim; and to hear objections, if any, by interested parties regarding the area of land to be taken. For a household facing acquisition, that hearing is where the number is set. Who must attend, and what an interested person may do, are listed. The same office records those who should attend as the registered landowner or representative, registered interested parties or representatives, and the agency applying for the acquisition or its representative, provided a representative is appointed in writing; and records the rights and responsibilities of an interested person as attending the inquiry, making a compensation claim, objecting to the area of land to be taken, and objecting to the court. It records compensation as based on market value at the date of the gazette notification under a named section, applying the valuation principles in the First Schedule. Four things can be put to a court, and the clock is six weeks. The office lists the matters that may be objected to in court as the area taken; the amount of compensation paid; the person to whom compensation is paid; and the apportionment of compensation, with the procedure being to submit the objection on Form N to the land administrator and pay a deposit. A state land office records that Form N must be submitted within six weeks of receiving the award form. Where notices appear is published too. The state office records that after approval the administrator issues public notices and displays them at the land office, on public notice boards in the sub-district or town where the land is located, and on or near the land itself, with specific notices served on the registered owner and interested persons. Read this with the local authority one-stop centres, the native courts, the state coalition and the environmental society entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Village development and security committees — a thirteen-member committee in every village, a headman who chairs it, monthly meetings with attendance allowances, and the district panel that screens who gets appointed
trackers.desc: Every village has a committee, and its size and officers are fixed. A state assembly record describes the body as individuals appointed by the state government for a set period as facilitators and links between government and the local community, and as intermediaries at the grassroots who channel any problem or complaint to the relevant party, and records membership as thirteen people — a chairperson, a secretary and eleven committee members. Published description records the committee as a grassroots organisation for administering and managing a village, headed by the village head, or by the traditional headman in indigenous communities, who automatically becomes chairperson. For a village with a problem to raise, that committee is the standing body whose stated job is to carry it upward. Meetings are monthly and attendance is paid. The same description records that meetings are held once a month, and that the chairperson, secretary and committee members receive a meeting attendance allowance, with the sub-district headman, a permanent state government officer, also taking part, and records that a sub-district has a headman's office. A published procedure records that the chairperson and secretary are responsible for financial performance reports on what the committee implements. Who gets appointed is screened at district level. The ministry records that the bodies were renamed twice — to community management councils in 2018 and to development and security committees in 2020 — and records that a committee is established at district or parliamentary level to screen candidates for membership, with appointment conditions improved to ensure that those appointed are qualified and capable of administering the village. A state's guidelines record the chairperson's conditions as including residence in the village or its administrative area for at least five years before appointment, passing security screening by the police, the state religious department, the insolvency department and the national anti-drugs agency, and being a registered voter in the state constituency. Read this with the local authority one-stop centres, the district land offices, the native courts and the state coalition entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Sarawak's native courts — a five-tier ladder from the longhouse headman upward, jurisdiction defined by the area a headman actually covers, and a chief overseeing 21 longhouses and 2,815 families
trackers.desc: The court's territory is defined as the area the headman actually covers. The state's native courts ordinance defines the local area of jurisdiction as, for the headman's court, the area in which the village head or longhouse head exercises jurisdiction; for the chief's court, the area in which the chief exercises jurisdiction; for the chief's superior court, the area in which the senior chiefs exercise jurisdiction; and for the district and residency native courts, the district or division. It defines customary law as a custom or body of customs to which the law of the state gives effect, and a headman as any person holding, with the approval of a lawful authority, an appointment, rank or position specified in the schedule. A court whose boundary is the community's own is a different proposition from a court whose boundary is an administrative line. Land disputes start at the longhouse and rise if unsettled. Published research records that a boundary or customary land dispute is first taken to the customary leader or longhouse head, and if it is not resolved the case is referred to the headman's court, and records that customary land has its legitimacy because the native court recognises the customary land ownership of the owner, with the prosecuting party and the party being prosecuted required to submit evidence to prove claims against the land. It records disputes as arising from different interpretations of customary land definitions, complicated where those involved in development lack knowledge and clear understanding of the status, existence, validity and actual land area. The scale one chief covers is published, and so is a proposed restructuring.
