It initiates the comprehensive multi-sectoral development plan that the local legislature approves, assists in setting the direction of economic and social development and coordinating development efforts in the area, and carries out monitoring and evaluation of the use of public resources; an executive committee acts on the council's behalf between sessions and includes a representative of the non-governmental organisations on the council; and sectoral or functional committees may be formed with community coordinators and volunteers. Meetings, minutes, and the practical hook. The barangay development council is to meet at least once every six months, with a majority of all members as the quorum, and its secretariat prepares the minutes for signature by the chairman. Getting a proposal into the minutes of a council whose composition your own organisation helped fill is a different proposition from writing to an office. Read this with the citizen participatory audit, the agrarian legal assistance, the human rights commission and the investigative newsroom entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: LRC-KsK — direct legal services, paralegal training, and cases filed inside the community's own campaign
trackers.desc: Three programmes, and one of them is direct legal services. The centre describes itself as maintaining three programmes: research and policy development; direct legal services; and advocacy and campaigns support. A community facing a mine, a plantation or a dam therefore gets representation, research and campaign support from a single organisation rather than assembling three, which matters most when the same facts have to serve a court filing, a policy submission and a public argument at the same time. Its stated method is translation. The centre says it seeks to bridge the gap between the informal articulation of the aspirations of marginalised communities on one side and the formal, technical, bureaucratic and legal language used by the state on the other. That is precisely the gap in which most community objections die: the grievance is real, the wording is wrong, and the office replies that no valid ground was raised. An organisation whose stated purpose is that translation is worth approaching before a deadline rather than after one. What the assistance looks like in practice. Its published account of its work with indigenous peoples and upland rural communities records paralegal training, community field visits and briefings, the provision of documentary research resources, and the filing of legal cases in courts in the context of the communities' own campaigns and struggles. That last phrase is the one to hold it to: the case is filed inside the community's campaign rather than replacing it. Track record, and how to approach. Established in December 1987 by four lawyers and operating from early 1988, registered as a non-stock, non-profit, non-partisan cultural, scientific and research organisation, and the national member of a global environmental federation since the early 1990s, the centre was instrumental in the crafting and the defence of the constitutionality of the indigenous peoples' rights legislation of 1997, has acted as legal counsel for marginalised and poor communities, campaigned on the mining legislation of 1995, and continues to pursue an alternative minerals management bill and petitions questioning the shares of proceeds under that legislation. Its office address and telephone numbers are published. Approach it with the community's own campaign already defined, since that is the frame it works inside. Read this with the reserved seats on local development councils, the agrarian legal assistance, the human rights commission and the investigative newsroom entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Right-of-way compensation — what must be deposited before possession, sixty days for the court, and the 2025 Act that changed the numbers
trackers.desc: Money goes into court before possession is taken. Under the right-of-way legislation of 2016, on filing an expropriation complaint or at any time afterwards and after due notice to the owner, the implementing agency must immediately deposit with the court, in favour of the owner, the sum of three amounts: one hundred per cent of the value of the land based on the current relevant zonal valuation of the revenue bureau issued not more than three years before the complaint; the replacement cost at current market value of the improvements and structures; and the current market value of the crops and trees on the property, as determined by a government financial institution or an independent property appraiser. Only on compliance does the court issue the order to take possession. The three-year limit on the zonal valuation is the detail most worth checking: a deposit resting on an older valuation does not meet the statute. Sixty days for the court, and the difference is paid afterwards. The court must determine just compensation within sixty days from the filing of the expropriation case, and once the decision is final the agency must pay the owner the difference between what was already paid and the amount the court determines. Separately, where an area has no land classification, the city or municipal assessor is required to produce the classification and the corresponding declaration of real property within sixty days of filing — so an absent classification is a duty on the assessor rather than a reason for delay. Negotiation comes first, and refusing has a thirty-day consequence. The implementing rules record that expropriation follows where, within thirty days, the owner refuses or fails to accept the agency's price offer for a negotiated sale, or fails or refuses to submit the documents needed for payment, or where negotiation is not feasible; the case is then filed through the solicitor general for national agencies or the government corporate counsel for state corporations. Knowing that the thirty days converts a negotiation into a court case is what makes the negotiation stage worth taking seriously. The costs split, and the Act that has since changed the numbers. On transfer of title through expropriation the agency pays the documentary stamp tax, the transfer tax and the registration fees, while the owner pays the capital gains tax and any unpaid real property tax. Note also that a further right-of-way statute was published in September 2025 and took effect the following month, reforming these rules — published summaries record it as providing for one hundred per cent of replacement cost taking depreciation into account, and fifteen per cent of the market value of crops and trees, with amounts based on the approved schedule of market values under the 2024 real property valuation legislation and, in its absence, on zonal valuation and assessed value. Check which statute governs the project in front of you before relying on any figure here. Read this with the environmental legal assistance centre, the agrarian legal assistance, the certified true copies of land titles and the public attorney's office entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The EIS system — a written request from any stakeholder can trigger a hearing, and the scoping agreement you can sign
trackers.desc: The bureau publishes the notices, the reports and the summaries in Filipino. The assessment division maintains running lists of notices of public scoping and of public hearings and consultations, each entry naming the proposed project, the proponent and the location, and linking the notice together with the impact statement or review report, its annexes, and an environmental summary in English and in Filipino — for some projects in Bisaya as well. That is where a community finds out that a project near it has reached the hearing stage, and where the report it will have to answer can be downloaded before the meeting. A written request from any stakeholder is one of the triggers for a public hearing. Under the impact statement system, public meetings and hearings are generally held at the department's discretion in three situations, as set out in a structured summary of the rules by an environmental law organisation: where the project will affect a great number of people; where there is mounting public opposition to the proposed project; or where a written request for a hearing has been submitted by any stakeholder. For certain environmentally critical projects a public hearing is mandatory rather than discretionary. The third trigger is the one a community controls: a letter, filed and acknowledged, is a documented request that the discretion has to be exercised against. The scoping session produces an agreement participants can sign. Public participation runs at four points — scoping, the terms of reference, public meetings or hearings, and review of the final assessment — and the rules provide that participants in the scoping session can sign the scoping agreement. Scoping decides what the assessment will study, which is the stage at which an issue is included or quietly left out; a signature on the agreement puts a community's presence and its issues on the record before any report is written. For environmentally critical projects the proponent must conduct scoping and prepare a formal scoping report that serves as the basis for the statement. The certificate is a permission with conditions, not a clearance in the abstract. The governing decree provides that no person, partnership or corporation may undertake or operate a declared environmentally critical project, or a project located in an environmentally critical area, without first securing the compliance certificate; a separate proclamation defines which projects and areas those are. The decision takes the form of a certificate or a denial letter, and the certificate itself states the scope and limitations of the approved activities together with conditions ensuring compliance with the environmental management plan. Those conditions are the text to read: breach of a condition is a different and more tractable complaint than opposition to the project as a whole. The certificate expires, and a changed baseline forces a new application. Published summaries of the rules record that the certificate automatically expires if the project has not been implemented within five years of issuance, or if no extension was requested within three months of its validity ending; and that where baseline characteristics have significantly changed, so that the assessment embodied in the environmental management plan is no longer appropriate, the bureau shall require a new application, the report on which focuses on the component that changed. For a project approved years ago and revived, those two provisions are the first things to check. Check who wrote the assessment. Preparers of the statement must be accredited by the environmental bureau and sign a sworn statement of eligibility. Accreditation and that sworn statement are documents that exist and can be asked for. Read this with the technical and scientific support organisation, the environmental legal assistance centre, the recognised laboratories and the local development council entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Solicitation permit — required before asking the public for anything, including online, with the mayor's permit alongside it
trackers.desc: Any person or group wanting to solicit or receive contributions for charitable or public welfare purposes must get a permit first. The solicitation permit legislation of 1978 gives the social welfare department exclusive authority to regulate the solicitation of donations and receiving of contributions for charitable or public welfare purposes, with permits secured from its regional offices; a departmental order of 1994 governs the conduct of solicitation and fundraising at regional level; and a 2001 executive order gives the department's secretary final authority over national fundraising campaigns. A benefit show, a raffle, a bingo social or a street collection is inside this. Online appeals are covered too. A departmental circular of 2021 provides that permits may be granted for activities conducted online, on digital platforms or on social media, with applications accepted by email, mail or courier as well as in person. Validity is based on the submitted project proposal, not exceeding one year for a regular permit and six months for a temporary one, and processing fees are waived during a state of emergency or calamity. Published guidance records that a permit is used within the specified city, municipality, region or area, does not extend outside the country even where donors or beneficiaries are citizens, and may run up to two years for an organisation with a good track record. Registration comes before the permit. The department's standards bureau states that foundations, non-governmental organisations and other institutions must be registered and licensed with the department before they can apply for a solicitation permit, with processing through an electronic licence and permit system that also issues certificates of registration, licences to operate and accreditation. Build that sequence into the timetable: registration, then licence, then permit. The local government permit is separate. The local government code gives city and municipal mayors authority to regulate charitable and welfare activities in their jurisdiction, and published guidance records that many cities and municipalities require a mayor's permit and a barangay clearance for a fundraising activity in addition to the national permit. Penalties, and the reporting channel. Violation carries imprisonment of not more than one year or a fine, or both, with officials of a corporate offender penalised personally; permits may be revoked for breach of conditions and not renewed for failure to submit post-activity reports. The department publishes an address for reporting unauthorised solicitation, which is also how a community checks a collector claiming to act for a project. Read this with the assessment system, the environmental legal assistance centre, the island purchase and the e-library entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Mining tenement lists — permit type by name, the five-hectare line between governor and department, and the quarry conditions to check
trackers.desc: The bureau's own programme description names every permit class, which is how you ask about the one next to you. It records issuance of mining permits and contracts under the mining legislation of 1995, including exploration permits, mineral agreements, financial or technical assistance agreements, mineral processing permits, industrial sand and gravel permits, and related permits such as ore transport permits, mineral ore export permits, accreditation of traders and dealers, declarations of mining project feasibility and certificates of environmental management and community relations record. It also records the small-scale mining programme under separate legislation, operating through declared people's small-scale mining areas and provincial or city mining regulatory boards. Name the permit class when you write; the file is kept by class. Regional offices publish tenement lists with the barangay named. Regional listings published by the bureau set out, for approved permits and pending applications, the tenement identifier, the applicant, the address, the date filed, the area in hectares, the location down to barangay, the commodity, the status and a contact person and number. A regional office page likewise lists holders by permit class, including industrial sand and gravel permits and government seabed quarry permit applications. Practitioner material records that the bureau publishes details of existing exploration permits, mineral agreements, assistance agreements and processing permits, pending applications, and pending cases before the mining adjudication board and panel of arbitrators. Five hectares is the line that decides who issues the permit. Press reporting of a provincial review records that under the mining legislation, permits for sand and gravel extraction over an area of five hectares and below are issued by the governor through the provincial mining regulatory board, while for areas above five hectares the environment department issues the permit. Establish which side of that line a quarry falls on before deciding whom to petition. The conditions on a quarry permit are checkable in the field. The same reporting records that an environmental compliance certificate is among the requirements before issuance and sets the conditions of operation — including limiting extraction to a uniform depth of one metre from the original riverbed, prohibiting washing of quarry materials within the riverbed to avoid siltation and turbidity, and prohibiting stockpiles left in the riverbed during extraction to avoid obstructing water flow. Depth, washing and stockpiles are three things a resident can photograph. And the freedom of information route works on this bureau. Published request records show members of the public asking the bureau for tenement information, including one request stating that the requester owns a lot in the area and needs the information to investigate illegal quarrying, with reports of permit holders quarrying beyond their boundaries into adjacent private lots and some with expired permits; the request is recorded as partially successful. Read this with the assessment system, the environmental legal assistance centre, the solicitation permit and the e-library entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: National Cultural Heritage Act — discovery halts the earthmoving, the five-day report, and the archaeological impact assessment inside the clearance
trackers.desc: A discovery stops the work, and only a written authority restarts it. The 2009 heritage legislation, published in the official gazette, provides that when the presence of any cultural or historical property is discovered, the national museum or the historical institute shall immediately suspend all activities that will affect the site and immediately notify the local government unit with jurisdiction; that the local government shall promptly adopt measures to protect and safeguard the integrity of the property and, within five days of the discovery, report it to the appropriate agency; and that the suspension is lifted only on the written authority of that agency and only after systematic recovery of the archaeological materials. Implementing rules put it plainly: where an archaeological site is discovered on a project that already holds a clearance, all earthmoving activities shall cease immediately, subject to assessment by the national museum. A clearance already granted is therefore not the end of the matter. Assessment of archaeological impact sits inside the environmental clearance. The implementing rules record that prior to issuance of an environmental clearance certificate an archaeological impact assessment is required in areas declared as heritage zones and in known or newly discovered archaeological sites; and the Act provides that any government or non-government infrastructure project or architectural site development shall include anthropological, archaeological, historical and heritage site conservation concerns in the environmental impact assessment system. Ask whether that assessment was done, and by whom. Named prohibitions, and a buffer zone measured in metres. The Act makes it an offence to destroy, demolish, mutilate or damage a world heritage site, national cultural treasure, important cultural property or archaeological and anthropological site; to modify, alter or destroy the original features of, or undertake construction or real estate development in, any declared national shrine, monument, landmark or historic structure without prior written permission — including within the designated security or buffer zone extending five metres from the visible perimeter; and to explore, excavate or dig for materials of cultural or historical value without prior written authority from the national museum, with no excavation permitted except under the supervision of a certified archaeologist. Reporting an unknown site is rewarded, and the local ordinance does not override this. The Act provides for incentives for persons who discover and report previously unknown archaeological sites, and states that its provisions on exploration and excavation supersede local, municipal, regional and autonomous regional resolutions and ordinances; treasure hunting permits are issued only by the national museum. Read this with the tenement lists, the assessment system, the environmental legal assistance centre and the e-library entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases — no docket fees, deferred filing fees for a citizen suit, the SLAPP defence and the protection order
trackers.desc: The rules remove the first barrier: money. The supreme court's rules of procedure for environmental cases, published in full by the judiciary, provide that a petitioner for the special writs is exempt from payment of docket fees; and that for an ordinary environmental case the payment of filing and other legal fees by the plaintiff is deferred until after judgment unless the plaintiff litigates as an indigent, constituting a first lien on any award, with the same deferral applied for a citizen suit. A community can therefore start a case it cannot yet pay for. Three remedies, and where each is filed. The rules provide a citizen suit, a writ of continuing mandamus for unlawful neglect of a duty under environmental law — filed with the regional trial court, the court of appeals or the supreme court — and the writ for violation of the constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology, filed directly with the supreme court or any station of the court of appeals. Published guidance records that the latter is available to a natural or juridical person, people's organisation, non-governmental organisation or public interest group on behalf of others, where the damage is of a magnitude affecting inhabitants of two or more cities or provinces; that the petition must state the act or omission, the environmental laws violated, the extent of damage and the reliefs sought; and that reliefs sought can include inspection, production of documents, rehabilitation, monitoring and periodic reporting. The clocks are short. The rules provide that within three days of filing, if the petition is sufficient in form and substance, the court shall issue the writ and the clerk shall issue it including a cease and desist order and other temporary reliefs effective until further order; that the respondent must comment within ten days; that the case is submitted for decision with memoranda within thirty days; that judgment follows within sixty days from submission; and that appeal to the supreme court lies within fifteen days and may raise questions of fact. A protection order may issue where the matter is of extreme urgency and the applicant would suffer grave injustice and irreparable injury, with a seventy-two hour form, and judges must report any such order to the supreme court within ten days. The harassment suit has its own answer. The rules define a strategic lawsuit against public participation as an action intended to harass or stifle enforcement of environmental laws, allow a defendant to raise it as a defence and counterclaim for damages, and require resolution within thirty days after a summary hearing. If the developer sues the neighbours, that is the rule to read first. Read this with the environmental legal assistance centre, the assessment system, the public attorney's office and the mining tenement entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Water permits and the protest — thirty days after posting to file, sixty days for resolution, and the one bar on who may protest
trackers.desc: A water permit application is posted, and a person adversely affected has thirty days to protest. The water code's implementing rules provide that any person who may be adversely affected by the proposed appropriation may file a verified protest with the board within thirty days after the last day of posting of notice; that interested parties including the concerned water district, private water company or franchisee, or registered irrigators association, company or cooperative are required to comment on the application within fifteen working days of receiving a copy; that where no protest or comment is filed the board decides within sixty days; and that protests, unless restrained by a court, are resolved within sixty days from submission. Watch for the posted notice; the clock runs from the last day of posting, not from the day you hear about it. The published procedure names the steps and the fee. The board's own application page records that after thirty days of posting, another thirty days is allotted for an affected party to file formal opposition; that the protestant submits an opposition letter with a stated protest fee; that the protest is docketed and assigned to a hearing officer who conducts the hearing, with resolution recommended to the executive director; and that notices are posted through named national and provincial offices, with a water rights investigator conducting an ocular site inspection and reporting back. Those are the offices that hold the file. One restriction decides whether your protest is heard. The board's rules of pleadings, practice and procedure provide that a protest filed solely on the ground of adverse effects on the privilege to use water from any source may not be entertained unless the protestant is a water permittee. A community relying on a spring or a well should therefore consider registering or permitting its own use before the fight, not during it. The rules record that households using a source for single household purposes shall register with the board. What the board weighs, and what it now requires. The board records that permits may be granted for domestic, irrigation, power, fisheries, industrial, livestock, recreational and commercial purposes; that a 2025 resolution adopts standard per capita consumption values for evaluating domestic and municipal applications, at stated litres per capita per day for rural areas and for the capital region and highly urbanised cities; and that another 2025 resolution requires an applicant to construct a monitoring well in water deficit, fully appropriated and water constrained areas to determine the groundwater table and water quality. Ask whether the area has been declared water deficit or fully appropriated, because that changes what the applicant must build. Read this with the environmental case rules, the assessment system, the ancestral domain certification and the tenement list entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Municipal waters and the fisherfolk registry — fifteen kilometres reserved by preference, the registry that decides who may fish, and the council whose consultation conditions any exception
trackers.desc: The first fifteen kilometres from the coastline are municipal waters, and resident fisherfolk have preference in them. Published summaries of the fisheries code record that resident municipal fisherfolk and their cooperatives and organisations are given preferential fishing privileges in municipal waters, which include streams, lakes and rivers within the municipality or city and marine waters within the fifteen kilometre zone from the coastline; that use of municipal waters is restricted mainly to municipal fisherfolk with limited commercial fishing under strict conditions; and that duly registered fisherfolk organisations and cooperatives have preference in the grant of fishery rights by the municipal or city council under the local government legislation. Practitioner commentary records the constitutional duty to protect the rights of subsistence fishermen to preferential use of communal marine and fishing resources. The registry is the document that decides who may fish, and it is posted. The Code provides that the local government shall maintain a registry of municipal fisherfolk who are fishing or may desire to fish in municipal waters, for determining priorities among them, limiting entry into municipal waters and monitoring fishing activities, with the resource management council submitting the list of priorities for consideration; and that the registry shall be updated annually or as necessary and shall be posted. Get on the registry, and read the posted one. A review records a parallel registry of municipal fishing vessels by gear type, and that the local government, in consultation with the council, determines licence fees for fishing in municipal waters. An exception for commercial vessels exists, and it is conditional. The Code allows the local government, by an appropriate ordinance, to permit small and medium commercial fishing vessels to operate in the ten point one to fifteen kilometre band, provided among other conditions that there is no commercial fishing in municipal waters less than seven fathoms deep; practitioner commentary records that this requires the council's approval as well. Ask for the ordinance, the depth and the council's minutes. Sanctuaries, reserves and assessments sit in the same Code. Published summaries record that fish refuges and sanctuaries are established to preserve habitat with restricted commercial fishing and that local governments can establish sanctuaries in municipal waters in consultation with the council; that the department may designate fishery reserves beyond fifteen kilometres; that protection measures apply to rare, threatened and endangered species; and that an environmental impact statement and compliance certificate are mandatory before projects affecting the environment. Read this with the environmental case rules, the assessment system, the water permit protest and the ancestral domain certification entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Wildlife Act critical habitats — mining, logging, quarrying, burning and dumping made illegal acts inside them, and free and prior informed consent where wildlife sits in ancestral domain
trackers.desc: Inside a critical habitat, the ordinary activities of a project are themselves illegal acts. Published material on the wildlife legislation records that effecting any of the following in a critical habitat is an illegal act: dumping of waste products detrimental to wildlife; squatting or otherwise occupying any portion of the critical habitat; mineral exploration or extraction; burning; logging; and quarrying. It records further illegal acts including trading, collecting, hunting or possessing wildlife, gathering or destroying active nests, nest trees and host plants, maltreatment, and transporting wildlife, with imprisonment and fines scaled to whether the species is critically endangered, endangered, vulnerable, threatened or other. Establishing that a site is a critical habitat therefore converts a planning argument into a list of prohibitions. Critical habitats are designated outside protected areas, and land can be acquired for them. Published summaries record that under the Act's critical habitat section the government designates critical habitats outside protected areas to safeguard threatened species, which are protected from exploitation, with possible land acquisitions to ensure their conservation. That is a route where the site sits outside the protected area system. Free and prior informed consent applies where wildlife is used in ancestral domain. The joint implementing rules provide that utilisation of wildlife resources found within ancestral domains or ancestral lands is subject to the issuance of a free and prior informed consent under the indigenous peoples legislation; that wildlife in protected areas is governed by the protected areas legislation, with aquatic and marine resources there governed by this Act and the fisheries code as the case may be; and that wildlife species in coastal areas are managed by the agriculture and environment departments, or the provincial council in one province, in coordination with local government units. Who holds jurisdiction decides who you write to. The Act gives the environment department jurisdiction over terrestrial plants and animals, all turtles and tortoises and wetland species including crocodiles, waterbirds, amphibians and dugong, and the agriculture department jurisdiction over declared aquatic critical habitats and aquatic resources including marine mammals other than dugong, with the lists revised and regularly updated by joint administrative order, and internationally listed species mapped onto the domestic categories for penalty purposes. Read this with the municipal waters registry, the environmental case rules, the ancestral domain certification and the assessment system entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Protected Area Management Board — the board a community sits on, its clearance as a precondition to the environmental compliance certificate, and the power to stop and demolish a persistent violator
trackers.desc: Board clearance comes before the environmental compliance certificate. Published summaries of the expanded 2018 protected areas legislation record that development projects in protected areas with potential significant impact require an environmental compliance certificate, and that the management board's clearance is a prerequisite to its issuance; that the protected area superintendent handles day-to-day management, plan preparation, law enforcement and permit issuance, provides the board's secretariat and operates a data management system; and that the board also regulates special use permits inside protected areas. Where a project sits inside a protected area, the board is therefore the body to address before the assessment agency. The board has seats for barangays, indigenous peoples and accredited organisations. The law as amended provides for a board including the chairpersons of the barangays where the protected area is located; regional directors of named national agencies; three representatives from either a non-governmental organisation or a people's organisation, accredited by both the environment department and the provincial government, in existence at least five years and with a track record in protected area management; and at least one but not more than three representatives from all the indigenous peoples present in the area and recognised by the indigenous peoples commission. Getting a community organisation accredited is therefore a route onto the body that clears projects. Persistent violation can end in closure or demolition at the owner's cost. The Act provides that for every continuing violation, or where a violation continues for thirty days and the total fine reaches a stated amount, the board through the superintendent and other deputised entities shall cause the cessation of operation and either forfeit the facility to the protected area office or demolish it at the cost of its owner; that government-owned facilities must instead submit a plan for a compliant substitute and execute the management plan within a year; and that administrative fines run between stated floors and ceilings. Occupation, plans and buffer zones are all provided for. The Act provides that the occupation of local governments and communities within the protected area shall be respected, with the board assessing that physical occupation within ninety days of its creation and recommending measures to protect their wellbeing; that the secretary may designate buffer zones through the board; that every protected area must have a management plan within one year of establishment, covering zoning, habitat conservation, community development, research, climate adaptation and disaster risk; and that permit and contract holders must submit a rehabilitation plan to the board, with a bond remitted on renewal, released only after satisfactory rehabilitation attested by the board. Read this with the wildlife critical habitats, the assessment system, the ancestral domain certification and the environmental case rules entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Airshed governing boards and the Clean Air Act — seats for people's organisations and NGOs on the board for your airshed, the multi-sectoral monitoring team for each local government, and the citizen suit provision
trackers.desc: Every airshed has a governing board with seats reserved for people's organisations and non-government organisations. The 1999 clean air legislation provides that airsheds are designated on the basis of areas with similar climate, meteorology and topology affecting pollutant interchange and diffusion, or sharing common interest or facing similar development programmes; that a governing board is created for each, chaired by the environment secretary; and that board membership includes the provincial governors and city and municipal mayors of the airshed, a representative from each concerned government agency, and representatives from people's organisations, from non-government organisations, and from the private sector. Published material records the board formulating a policies and strategic plan for the airshed, coordinating its members' functions and preparing an annual air quality status report. Find out which airshed a site is in, then find out who holds those seats. A multi-sectoral monitoring team is convened for each local government. The Act provides that the department must convene, for each local government unit, a multi-sectoral monitoring team with broad public representation for periodic inspections of pollution sources, to assess compliance with the emission limitations in permits. That is a named inspection body a community can ask to join or to act. Any citizen may sue, and an administrative complaint can be filed by anyone. The Act provides that for purposes of enforcing the Act or its implementing rules, any citizen may file an appropriate civil, criminal or administrative action in the proper courts against the persons it lists; that the department shall, on its own instance or upon verified complaint by any person, institute administrative proceedings, without prejudice to any affected person's own action; and that filing one action does not preclude another. Published material records the adjudication board able to impose daily fines until compliance and to issue cease and desist orders shutting facilities that pose an immediate threat to public health. Non-attainment status changes what may be built. Published description records areas classified as attainment or non-attainment; that in non-attainment areas programmes prohibit new sources of the pollutant concerned, with local governments preparing further measures, and a surcharge on annual emission fees; and records the air quality management fund financing containment, clean-up, restoration of ecosystems and rehabilitation of areas affected by violators, sourced from fines, damages, permit proceeds and emission fees, allocable per airshed. Read this with the environmental case rules, the recognised laboratories, the assessment system and the protected area board entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The national geoportal and the mapping agency's downloads — basemaps and thematic layers with metadata naming the data owner, the twelve-class land cover map, and topographic and hazard sheets by grid
trackers.desc: The geoportal serves the national basemaps and other agencies' thematic layers in one viewer. The mapping agency records the geoportal project as intended to hold and serve all the base maps the agency produces and eventually the fundamental and thematic datasets of the other data-producing agencies, promoting participation by other data producers, and records the portal as used to find and access geospatial data and services and to advocate standard multiscale basemaps for strategic planning, decision making and situational analysis. The viewer's own terms record that a user shall acknowledge and cite the agency or data owner as the source; that the currency of each dataset is in the metadata provided by the data owner, viewable by right-clicking the loaded layer; and that only layers appearing in the download window's dropdown are downloadable, with the data owner to be contacted for restricted layers. Checking the currency in the metadata is what stops an out-of-date layer being quoted at a hearing. A positional caution is published, and it matters for boundary arguments. The viewer records observed discrepancies of as much as ten metres when using basemaps other than the agency's own basemaps and named ortho imagery. Where a claim turns on whether a structure sits inside a boundary, that is the warning to read first. Land cover is published in twelve named classes, downloadable in several formats. The agency's land cover project records a mandate to generate and continuously update the nationwide land cover map using the latest satellite imagery complemented by ground and image validation, giving the spatial location, extent and distribution of twelve types — closed forest, open forest, mangrove forest, brush and shrubs, grassland, perennial crop, annual crop, open or barren, built-up, marshland or swamp, fishpond and inland water — with download in spreadsheet, mapping and image formats and service links for map services. Topographic and hazard sheets are downloadable by grid. The agency's downloads page records map files in document, image and archive formats, including high resolution topographic maps at fifty-thousand scale and hazard maps, and a national topographic series at two-hundred-fifty-thousand scale presenting terrain with hundred-metre contour intervals, road and river networks, settlement areas, vegetation cover and selected man-made structures, downloadable sheet by sheet from an index map. Read this with the ancestral domain certification, the assessment system, the mining tenement lists and the protected area board entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Foundation for the Philippine Environment — an endowment created out of a debt-for-nature swap, the three purposes its investment income is bound to, and the national conservation organisation beside it
trackers.desc: A permanent endowment exists to fund non-government environmental work, and its founding terms are published. The foundation records itself as registered in January 1992 and considered the largest grant-making institution outside government for the environment and sustainable development, organised to help reverse the rapid destruction of the natural resource base through a strategic and integrated conservation programme, and records its uniqueness as lying in the endowment fund itself. It publishes the founding agreement's binding terms: the investment income from the endowment is to be used for conservation of biological diversity including terrestrial and aquatic flora and fauna; technical skills and capability building to develop the organisational and technical competence of project proponents to become more responsive to the need for, and take the initiative for, environmental protection and management; and community-based resource management projects designed to protect and use natural resources sustainably, including training programmes, community organising and extension. Those three clauses are the test a community's proposal has to meet. The money came from a debt-for-nature swap, and that history is recorded. A national conservation organisation records that a delegation including its then president negotiated a second debt-for-nature swap, resulting in the establishment of the foundation, providing a permanent endowment to fund environmental initiatives; published material records the swap programme as the first partnership between government and non-governmental organisations, leading to a stated endowment under a natural resources management programme, and records tables of the foundation's grants to named local organisations by year. The same organisation works on the ground and reports numbers. That organisation records restoring forests with local communities to sustain the supply of water, clean air and other natural resources, its restoration method having community partners propagate native trees to restore degraded portions of protected areas, with a native tree and fruit nursery established with the community at each site, income from seedlings produced and maintenance income for safeguarding the new forests, and community ecological sanctuaries established at village level. It records over 460 hectares rainforested with over 800,000 native tree seedlings, and a municipal resolution giving local protection to an endemic plant. Read this with the forest foundation grants, the environmental legal assistance centre, the community forest agreement and the protected area board entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Alyansa Tigil Mina — an alliance of mining-affected communities with named convenor organisations, a published office address and coordinator contacts, and the provincial moratorium it helped win
trackers.desc: An alliance exists whose members are the affected communities themselves. The alliance records itself as a coalition of organisations and groups who have decided to collectively challenge the aggressive promotion of large-scale mining, composed of non-governmental organisations, people's organisations, church groups and academic institutions, and describes itself as both an advocacy group and a people's movement working to protect communities and natural resources threatened by large-scale mining. Published description records it as a coalition of mining-affected communities and their support groups, with human rights as the central basis of its work, particularly defending community and individual rights, and records its aim as shifting the policy framework from extracting and profiting from minerals to mineral management. Another account records its lobbying as relying on the actions of twenty-five sites of struggle — the communities opposing large-scale mining projects. It tells you exactly how to reach it and what help it wants. Its site publishes an office unit and street address, and its releases give the national coordinator's name, email and mobile number, and a policy and advocacy officer's name, email and number; it invites people to share skills in research, community organising, fundraising and photography and to contact the named convenor organisations to find out how to work together. Naming its convenors — including bodies already recorded in this bucket — is what lets a community pick the nearest door. Its record includes a provincial moratorium and named campaigns. The alliance records a provincial board approving a fifty-year moratorium on endorsement of new mining applications, crediting communities, indigenous peoples, church and youth groups and stating the moratorium would not have happened without their persistent lobby and protest actions, with a legal centre's director calling the ordinance a step toward protecting remaining forests; records picketing an international mining conference; and records its standing demands as a moratorium on mining, repeal of the 1995 mining legislation and passage of an alternative minerals management bill, that bill described by a legislator as crafted with the help of advocates including the alliance, anchored on land and natural resources management and a human rights-based approach. It also records around eight hundred closed-down mines awaiting rehabilitation. Read this with the environmental legal assistance centre, the mining tenement lists, the mine rehabilitation fund and the indigenous certification entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: PAFID — participatory three-dimensional mapping for ancestral domain claims, work taken only on a community's written request, and a map that was carried into a mining consultation
trackers.desc: An organisation exists that maps a community's territory with the community, and it works only when asked in writing. Published description records it as a social development organisation assisting indigenous communities to secure or recover traditional lands and waters since 1967, forming partnerships to secure legal ownership over ancestral domains and to shape government policy, and records that it works exclusively with the indigenous peoples' sector, specifically upon written or signed requests for assistance from indigenous communities or their representatives. That written-request rule is the safeguard a community should look for in anyone offering to map its land. The mapping method is described step by step, and it is the community's own record. Published material records a mapping process beginning with consultations in which elders and leaders provide information about the territory and discuss needs and obligations, then members producing rough sketch maps identifying boundaries and important features such as mountains and water bodies, whose dimensions and coordinates are verified by GPS ground surveys before the sketches are refined and a relief model built up in cardboard layers. It records the resulting maps as used to create a record of the territory, to engage other stakeholders, and as a planning tool during community assemblies. The maps have been used at the moment of decision. Published reporting records a mapping facilitator and local indigenous people producing a three-dimensional map of a valley and watersheds targeted for mining, brought to the public plaza on the morning of a public consultation and unveiled after the company's experts had presented, with the facilitator saying it was the people's map and that they did not invent it. Published material records digitised maps helping document formal claim dossiers and allowing communities to demand their right to free, prior and informed consent, while the process itself increases communities' capacities to engage in land-related decision-making. Its current services are listed. The organisation records work to secure ancestral domain titles and defend territories, support agroforestry and economic resilience, provide specialist training in geographic information systems, carbon measurement and participatory research, and deliver potable water systems; and records a project to map, document and register a named community conserved area with a global registry, and a forest resource assessment conducted with community forest guards. Read this with the indigenous certification entry, the mining alliance, the legal centre and the environmental studies entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Tanggol Kalikasan and the Alternative Law Groups — a public interest environmental law office with a national and an area office, and the coalition of developmental law organisations it belongs to
trackers.desc: There is a law office whose only client base is the environment and the communities in it. The office records itself as a non-stock, non-profit public interest environmental law office, operating since 1987, initially as the legal defence arm of a named conservation foundation until it registered as a separate entity in 2001 — that foundation already recorded in this bucket — with a national coordinating office in one named city and a fully staffed area office in another. It records its mission as facilitating the empowerment of communities and institutions to manage their ecosystem through law and other creative mechanisms, and records its programmes as aimed at encouraging greater citizen participation in environmental law enforcement and in policy-making on resource allocation. A community that wants enforcement of an existing rule, rather than a new case, is the client this office is built for. Its outreach runs through broadcast and local government training. It records producing a radio and television programme to increase awareness of environmental management and protection and provide current events and up-to-date issues, and records an environmental governance institute programme as the strategic response to increasing demand for capacity building of local government units, running at two levels — one for barangay officials, one for municipal, city and provincial officials. Training the officials who will decide a permit is a route most communities never consider. The coalition behind it names the other offices a community can approach. A coalition of non-government organisations with legal programme components adhering to the principles of alternative or developmental law lists its members, including this office, an indigenous peoples' international centre for policy research and education and an alternative legal advocates organisation for a named island group. Published description records a lawyer's path through that world — an internship at a university human rights centre assigned to the legal assistance centre already recorded here and to an indigenous rights organisation, then direct legal services to community clients — fisherfolk, farmers, upland dwellers, urban poor and indigenous peoples — with community paralegal training and environmental legal education for communities, law enforcers, government agency and local government officials, lawyers, judges and prosecutors. Read this with the legal assistance centre, the mining alliance, the mapping organisation and the environment foundation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Kalikasan PNE and the Manila Bay coalition — a national campaign network with named member organisations, independent fact-finding missions, and a People's Plan drafted against a reclamation masterplan
trackers.desc: A national campaign network exists, and its member organisations are listed by name. Published description records it as a network of non-governmental organisations, grassroots organisations and environmental advocates, founded in 1997 to coordinate and synchronise grassroots-based campaigns on environmental concerns, and describes itself as believing that the struggle for the environment is the struggle for the people's welfare. A coalition site lists its member organisations by name, including a fisherfolk federation, a metro environmental network, a health workers' association, a climate change network for community-based initiatives, a bay-specific alliance, a science and technology advocacy group and a centre of environmental concern — so a community can approach the member closest to its own issue rather than the network in the abstract. It runs independent fact-finding when the state's account is doubted. A published release records the network joining an independent civil society fact-finding mission to locate two missing environmental activists, and records what the mission established: that witnesses in a named town confirmed a violent abduction, contradicting police claims that no such incident occurred; that closed-circuit cameras police cited had been out of operation for weeks; that officers declined to file a blotter report when a mother approached them, in violation of the law; and that they refused to sign the required form for cases of enforced disappearance under the named statute. It records the network as convenor of an environmental defenders congress formed in 2018. Against a reclamation masterplan it is drafting an alternative. A partner organisation records the bay as a crucial site for biodiversity and home to over 23 million people, with an estimate that more than 11 million people are threatened with displacement due to land reclamations and related disaster risks under a large-scale top-down masterplan, and records that as an alternative the network is developing a People's Plan. It also records concern at a planned raid on the headquarters of an environmental organisation — the risk that comes with this work. Read this with the mining alliance, the environmental law office, the mapping organisation and the legal assistance centre entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: NGOs for Fisheries Reform and the coastal coalitions — a members' coalition for fisherfolk organisations, a just transition framework written for coastal communities, and the 15-kilometre municipal zone they defend
trackers.desc: Coastal communities have a coalition whose members are their own organisations. Published description records it as a coalition of non-government organisations focused on fisheries policy reform and advocacy, established in 1994, which played a significant role in the development and amendment of the fisheries legislation, aiming to empower small fisherfolk communities through coordinated campaigns, projects and activities that promote sustainable development and community-based coastal resource management, with fisherfolk organisations and coastal communities named as those it serves. Its own site is served over plain http, so treat the address with the usual care. It writes frameworks with its members rather than for them. That site records that, through consultations with member and partner organisations and people's organisations, it developed a just energy transition framework for fisheries and coastal communities, to serve as a guide for coastal communities and fisherfolk organisations; and records a case story of a member's disaster rehabilitation and recovery programme on a named island through a self-help group. It records a further network of fisherfolk and non-government organisations supporting the strict and full implementation of the fisheries statute. The zone they defend is defined in law, and the threat to it is named. A partner organisation records the fisheries code as containing the provisions that protected the 15-kilometre zone for municipal fishers, which formed the basis of early campaigns to safeguard small-scale fishers' access to near-shore marine resources, and records partnering with coastal communities, fisherfolk associations and enforcement agencies to strengthen monitoring systems, raise awareness of illegal commercial intrusions, promote community-led patrols and support vessel monitoring mechanisms for commercial boats. Reporting records a manifesto signed by more than 1,100 fisherfolk groups nationwide opposing a bill to legalise commercial fishing in municipal waters, arguing coexistence is impossible with subsistence fishers ending up on the losing end; and records a coalition director citing gains in the cancellation of foreshore lease agreements and land tenure security for fishing households. Read this with the municipal waters entry, the fisherfolk registry, the coastal legal centre and the environmental network entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The provincial NGO network and its para-enforcers — 39 member organisations in one province, community patrol training, administrative cases filed on what patrols catch, and free legal advisory
trackers.desc: A provincial network files the cases that community patrols generate. Its programme pages record that it will file administrative cases against illegal activities identified and apprehended by para-enforcers and community members, and offer technical guidance to community members on patrolling and handling illegal activities. Patrol, apprehension and case-filing in one provincial organisation is the chain most communities cannot assemble alone. Its membership is provincial and counted. It records itself as organised in November 1991 by mainstream non-governmental organisations and people's organisations in the province, with the motivation of presenting a broader consensus that would carry more weight in the policy making process in various local government units in the province, and records that it is currently composed of 39 provincial organisations, its general assembly meeting yearly as the highest policy-making body. It publishes a road, barangay, city and postcode address. Its stated targets are named developments, not general principles. It records collaborating with local and national partners on advocating for a total mining ban, opposing the division of the province, and preventing forest-encroaching development and plantations; and records its diagnosis that reports to enforcement agencies often go unaddressed, leaving violations unresolved and response efforts ineffective amid illegal logging, illegal fishing, land grabbing and other unlawful activities, compounded by a culture of impunity. Naming the province's division and specific plantation expansion as targets tells a community whether this network is already in its fight. It also carries livelihood and free legal services. It records improving the livelihoods of member organisations' communities through micro-financing, market access, and free-of-charge legal advisory, and a youth programme. A published profile records its purpose as enabling poor and marginalised sectors to sustainably manage the natural resources of the province while actively participating in local governance, stating that any development measure that will not promote sustainable development will not be tolerated and that access will be democratised in favour of small-scale fisherfolk, indigenous peoples, small farmers, the urban poor and women. Read this with the environmental legal assistance centre, the mining alliance, the environmental network and the mapping organisation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: City and provincial environment offices — a devolved city office that issues quarry and sand-and-gravel permits, provincial and community field offices with published directories, and the hectare thresholds that decide who signs
trackers.desc: A city can have its own environment office, created by its own ordinance, that issues the permits communities most often fight. One city records its local environment and natural resources office as created by a numbered city ordinance and renamed by a later one, with duties including establishing, maintaining, protecting and preserving communal forests, watersheds, tree parks, mangroves, greenbelts and similar forest projects, performing devolved functions from the national department and assisting in implementing laws, and ending illegal exploitation of forest and mineral products and the city's pollutive and destructive activities. It lists among its services issuance of commercial sand and gravel permits, industrial sand and gravel permits and mountain quarry permits, new and renewal, and publishes an office email. For a barangay facing a quarry, the permit counter is inside city hall. Provincial and community field offices are published with directories. A regional department site lists its field offices — provincial environment and natural resources offices and community environment and natural resources offices — by name; a provincial office publishes a directory; and a provincial government's own environment office publishes named section chiefs for its regulating and permitting section and its monitoring and enforcement section. A named official for permitting and another for enforcement is the difference between writing to an institution and writing to a person. The hectare thresholds decide which office signs. Published administrative rules record that for community forest management agreements the community office reviews applications within ten working days and approves those covering 500 hectares and below, endorsing larger ones upward; that the provincial office reviews within five working days and approves more than 500 up to 5,000 hectares; and that the regional director approves more than 5,000 up to 20,000 hectares. The same rules record that field offices shall maintain and continuously update control maps and associated registries indicating the various projects and tenure instruments over forestlands in their jurisdiction. Read this with the community forest agreement entry, the provincial NGO network, the mapping organisation and the environmental legal assistance centre entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Lupong Tagapamayapa — a conciliation body of ten to twenty residents in every barangay, a three-member panel the parties themselves choose, and the certificate without which most cases cannot be filed
trackers.desc: Every barangay has a standing conciliation body of its own residents. The published law records that there is created in each barangay a conciliation body composed of the village head as chairman and ten to twenty members, constituted every three years, with the village secretary concurrently serving as its secretary, keeping a record book of all complaints filed, recording the results of mediation proceedings before the village head and submitting a report to the proper city or municipal courts. Published rules record their purpose as assisting disputants to obtain a just, speedy and inexpensive amicable settlement of disputes at the barangay level. For neighbours in a boundary or nuisance dispute, the first forum is a body of their own neighbours, and its records go to the courts. The parties choose the three people who hear them. The law records that for each dispute a conciliation panel of three members shall be constituted, chosen by the parties to the dispute from the list of members; and published description records that the village head mediates or arbitrates as directed by the parties, and if unable to achieve settlement refers the case to that panel, which can conciliate, mediate or arbitrate, with the law also providing for resolution of disputes through the indigenous system of dispute resolution. Choosing your own panel from a published list of residents is a rare degree of control over who hears a case. The certificate is the gate to court, and the timetable is published. Published description records that if neither the village head nor the panel achieves settlement, the secretary issues a certificate to file action in court, and that disputes covered by the system must pass through barangay conciliation as a condition precedent before a case may be filed in court or with many government offices, unless an exception applies — the exceptions including where one party is the government or a public officer sued in relation to official duties, or where the parties live in different cities or municipalities. It records the conciliation stage as 15 days, extendable by another 15, with roughly 30 to 45 days before a certificate issues, and records a settlement as enforceable through barangay mechanisms and, where necessary, through the courts, subject to repudiation on limited grounds. Read this with the local development councils, the city and provincial environment offices, the provincial NGO network and the fisheries coalition entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Municipal, city and provincial assessors' offices — certified tax maps and adjoining-lot ownership certificates over the counter, the honest limit of a tax declaration as proof, and a records copy held at province level
trackers.desc: An assessor's counter issues certified tax maps and a certificate naming who owns the adjoining lots. A city assessor's published service charter lists, by counter number, issuance of a certified copy of tax maps; a certificate of adjoining lot ownership; and issuance of a certified copy of tax declaration, with priority given to senior citizens and persons with disability, and records that requests may also be made by formal communication, with receipt and release through the records section, giving processing times that rise with the number of copies. For a community mapping who surrounds a threatened parcel, a certificate of adjoining lot ownership is the document that names the neighbours. A provincial office lists the wider record set. A provincial assessor publishes issuance of a computer-generated copy of the tax declaration; photocopies of property record forms, field assessment and appraisal sheets and supporting documents; photocopies of the tax map and the tax map control roll; and certifications of total landholdings, non-encumbrance, non-improvements and no real property. Published description records that for property in a municipality the record starts at the municipal assessor's office but a copy is usually also maintained at the provincial assessor's office, so a lost municipal file is not the end of the trail. What a tax declaration proves — and does not — is stated. Published description records the tax declaration as a formal assessment document used by provincial, city or municipal assessors to show market and assessed property values as the basis for collecting real property tax; records tax declarations and receipts as prima facie proofs of ownership or possession of the property for which such taxes have been paid, usable as a basis for a claim of ownership if accompanied by actual proof of possession; and warns that they are not conclusive evidence of ownership. It records the requirements for a certified true copy as a letter of request to the assessor, valid identification, a notarised special power of attorney where the requester is not the registered owner, and the latest tax receipt, with release within the day or up to three working days. Read this with the barangay conciliation body, the city and provincial environment offices, the local development councils and the provincial NGO network entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The municipal and city council's own rules — a published session day and hour, the difference between a closed committee meeting and a public hearing, and the posting rule that fixes when an ordinance takes effect
trackers.desc: A council publishes the day and hour it sits, and where. One municipality's internal rules record that the regular session shall be every Tuesday of the week, held at the council session hall from nine to twelve in the morning and one to five in the afternoon, except when there is an invitation from the barangays or issues that need to be tackled during regular session; record that a special session may be called by the presiding officer or by the majority; and record Mondays as used for committee meetings and hearings. Knowing the standing session day is the difference between arriving with a delegation and reading about a decision afterwards. A committee meeting is closed; a public hearing is not. The same rules record that as a general rule a committee meeting shall be attended only by the committee members, unless a majority decides to allow other persons to be present, especially invited resource persons or consultants, and distinguish that from a committee hearing. A city's published system records a committee hearing as composed of the chairperson, vice-chairperson and one member with the sponsor of the ordinance or resolution, and a public hearing as conducted by the committee concerned with representatives of the public covering the areas concerned in the ordinance or resolution, with a lead committee scheduling where two or more committees are involved. The rules also record that no tax ordinance or revenue measure shall be enacted in the absence of a public hearing duly conducted. Posting fixes the date an ordinance bites. Published description records that unless otherwise stated, an ordinance or resolution approving the local development plan and public investment programme takes effect ten days after a copy is posted on a bulletin board at the entrance of the provincial capitol or the city, municipal or barangay hall and in at least two other conspicuous places; that the secretary shall cause that posting not later than five days after approval; and that the text shall be disseminated and posted in Filipino or English and in the language or dialect understood by the majority. A city records that a council failing to act on barangay ordinances within thirty days of receipt means they are deemed approved. Read this with the barangay conciliation body, the local development councils, the assessors' offices and the city and provincial environment offices entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Datalex
trackers.desc: Official Armenian judicial information system: case search, schedules and court decisions. · Find here: free Armenian legislation and court decisions (Datalex).

trackers.name: EcoLur Informational NGO
trackers.desc: Armenia's environmental information organisation, built around a repeatable model rather than a single campaign: it runs named S.O.S. campaigns site by site — Amulsar, Teghout, Akhtala, Qajaran, Kapan, Agarak, Sotq, Ararat and others — acting as the information coordinator for residents living beside a mine or a polluter. WHO TO ENLIST when what you need is the evidence and the timetable rather than a lawyer. You CAN: use its independent-experts library, which collects geologists' and geomorphologists' opinions, social-impact surveys of affected communities and reports on new circumstances in an ESIA — the material that turns an objection into an argument. It also publishes notices of scheduled public hearings on exploration and mining permits and reports the council votes on them, which is the single hardest thing for a rural community to learn in time. For activists: it works with CEE Bankwatch and other Armenian groups on complaints to development-bank accountability mechanisms, so it is a route to the financing side as well as the permit.

trackers.name: FPWC — Caucasus Wildlife Refuge (Foundation for the Preservation of Wildlife and Cultural Assets)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: gives a community an alternative buyer for its own land. FPWC built the Caucasus Wildlife Refuge from 2011 by taking on land from more than a dozen communities across Ararat and Vayots Dzor — mostly by lease, with the payments going back to the villages for their own improvements — and it now covers around 30,000 hectares buffering the Khosrov Forest State Reserve, the first privately protected area in the South Caucasus. It employs local rangers and funds part of the work through ecotourism rather than donations alone. USE IT: this is the counterparty when someone else wants your community's land. Gnishik gave its land to the refuge under pressure to lease it as a hunting ground instead; another community turned down a company's cash offer and ceded the land for conservation. If a concession, a hunting lease or a mine is being dangled at your council, FPWC is the competing offer that keeps the ground intact and still pays. Note it is lease-based, so the community keeps title. THE TRAP — A LEASE IS NOT A MINING VETO. In 2016 FPWC leased 5,000 hectares from the Vayots Dzor village of Vardahovit for 25 years to build a wildlife migration corridor; the area overlaps the Vardenis mining site, where Mendia Resources LLC applied for an exploratory permit, and FPWC's own environmental programmes coordinator told Hetq the mining posed a threat to the project. Surface tenure and subsoil rights are granted separately in Armenia, so a council that leases its pasture to a conservation body has not thereby stopped a licence being issued underneath it — put the subsoil question on the table during the negotiation, not after signature. WHO TO CONTACT: Khanjyan street 47/1 apt. 14, Yerevan 0001; +374 10585884 / +374 11585884; info@fpwc.org; the refuge's own pages are at cwr.fpwc.org, which names the rangers and lists Urtsadzor Community among its partners. HONEST GAP: FPWC's own domain describes the refuge and names the partner community but does not publish lease terms or payment figures — the lease-and-pay arrangement is documented by World Land Trust, which funds FPWC, and the Vardahovit case by Hetq, so treat the amounts as a question to ask rather than a figure established.

trackers.name: ARMEPS
trackers.desc: Armenia's electronic procurement system. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Armenia, and for how much.

trackers.name: Audit Chamber
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Armenia, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Statistical Committee of Armenia (ArmStat)
trackers.desc: Armenia's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Armenia.

trackers.name: Corruption Prevention Commission
trackers.desc: Armenia's independent commission overseeing asset declarations and integrity.

trackers.name: Hetq
trackers.desc: Armenian investigative outlet reporting on corruption and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: Union of Informed Citizens (UIC)
trackers.desc: Armenian NGO (since 2014) working to consolidate democracy through multi-component election observation, state-procurement monitoring, and advocacy for electoral, constitutional and anti-corruption reform. Runs the Fact Investigation Platform (FIP.am) fact-checking outlet and the Reforms.am tracker.

trackers.name: State Register of Legal Entities
trackers.desc: National company / corporate registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Armenia Multi-Sector Register
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Publicly searchable.

trackers.name: Court of Cassation of Armenia
trackers.desc: Court of Cassation of Armenia — appellate court in Armenia (Wikidata record).

trackers.name: SLAPP suits against Armenian defenders — take advice before you post
trackers.desc: READ THIS BEFORE CAMPAIGNING PUBLICLY. International groups issued a solidarity statement over Armenian environmental and human rights defenders facing defamation and criminalization. Around one mining project the recorded pattern was: dozens of activists sued for social media posts or for comments made during meetings; 2 media outlets sued for publishing news stories about the project; and 2 members of parliament sued for their speeches during parliamentary meetings. That last fact is the measure of the exposure — if parliamentary speech draws a suit, an ordinary resident's comment certainly can. Anyone campaigning on an Armenian extractive project should assume defamation exposure for ordinary public comment, keep records of the factual basis for every claim made, and take legal advice before posting rather than after being served. This is recorded plainly because listing funding opportunities alone would understate what this work costs here.

trackers.name: Caucasus Nature Fund — it matches the state budget, so that is the lever
