trackers.desc: Legislator / public-official financial interest & asset declarations.

trackers.name: Stats NZ
trackers.desc: New Zealand's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in New Zealand.

trackers.name: Nature Heritage Fund — government money to buy the land
trackers.desc: A GOVERNMENT FUND WHOSE PURPOSE IS BUYING LAND of significant ecological or landscape value — set up in 1990 as the Forest Heritage Fund, renamed in 1998 to cover wetlands, tussocklands and shrublands too. As policy, the Committee recommends acquisition proposals as scenic reserves and covenant proposals as conservation covenants under the Reserves Act 1977, with exceptions considered if justified; all funded covenants carry the fund's standard covenant conditions. THE POINT THAT MATTERS WHEN APPROACHING A VENDOR: where land purchase is involved, the information you provide is treated as commercially sensitive and confidential between you and the fund — so an approach need not become public. MECHANICS: use the official form, check it against the application checklist first, and quote the project number you are given in all correspondence through the Funds Advisor. Rounds are not continuous — email NHF-Admin@doc.govt.nz with subject 'subscribe' to hear when the next opens. BE REALISTIC ABOUT SCALE: the fund ran at about $10m a year in the early 2000s but had fallen to roughly $2m a year by 2016.

trackers.name: Lottery Environment and Heritage — and how to skip the match-funding rule
trackers.desc: GRANTS FOR PLANS, REPORTS AND ONE-OFF PROJECTS, administered through CommunityMatters. Natural heritage projects protect native flora and fauna including the ongoing costs of pest and predator control — running costs, not just capital. The committee funds small projects under $250,000, expressly including feasibility studies, conservation plans, condition reports, maintenance plans, ecological restoration plans and specialist reports. THE MATCH-FUNDING RULE, AND ITS EXEMPTIONS — THIS DECIDES WHETHER YOU CAN APPLY: projects must normally have secured at least one third of total costs as partnership funding before submitting. But partnership funding is not required for natural heritage projects under $150,000 that do not involve capital works, nor for feasibility studies, conservation plans and specialist reports. A group with no match money should aim squarely at those categories. OTHER ROUTES: Ngā Whenua Rāhui negotiates voluntary protection of indigenous ecosystems on Māori-owned land through kawenata, Māori reservations or management agreements; the Community Environment Fund sits with the Ministry for the Environment; and the Stephenson Fund gives $2,000–$20,000 for pest and weed control, revegetation and fencing.

trackers.name: Te Awa Tupua — the governance framework, not the headline
trackers.desc: IT IS NOT A RIVER SUING POLLUTERS — and getting that wrong is why the precedent is so often cited badly. Section 14 of the Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act 2017 makes Te Awa Tupua a legal person with all the rights, powers, duties and liabilities of a legal person — but a 2024 study drawn from more than thirty interviews in the region found day-to-day governance has drifted away from the abstract question of status toward Māori kawa and a dense set of new institutions, with authority devolved to hapū and communities. Personhood resolved the ownership question without deciding how competing uses are weighed. THE STRUCTURE IS THE REPLICABLE PART: Te Pou Tupua (s.18) exercises the rights on behalf of and in the name of Te Awa Tupua and is two people — one appointed by Whanganui iwi, one by the Crown — acting jointly as the human face of the river. Te Karewao advises, and where Te Pou Tupua acts on a discrete part of the river it must include a person appointed by the iwi and hapū with interests in that part. AND TE KŌPUKA IS THE PROVISION TO COPY: the strategy group comprises iwi, relevant local authorities, departments of State, commercial and recreational users, AND environmental groups, with the statutory purpose of acting collaboratively to advance the health and well-being of the river — environmental groups hold a statutory seat alongside commercial users, on a body whose purpose is the river's health rather than balance between interests. THE PRACTICAL HOOK IS SECTION 38, providing for review of RMA planning documents — the framework reaches into ordinary resource-management planning rather than sitting beside it. The unit of protection is an indivisible and living whole from the mountains to the sea, incorporating all physical and metaphysical elements — the whole catchment, not a reach. Settlement quantum NZ$80 million; Deed signed 5 August 2014. THE WARNING THAT BELONGS WITH IT: claims were first put to Parliament in 1873 and the Act came 144 years later — and in 1903 the Coal-mines Act Amendment Act declared the beds of all navigable rivers ‘shall remain and shall be deemed to have always been vested in the Crown’, passed directly in response to Whanganui River Māori claims. A legislature faced with a successful Indigenous claim legislated it away, retrospectively. This map records the same lesson from El Salvador's repealed mining ban: the instrument is only as durable as the politics around it — which argues for the Te Kōpuka model, with other interests inside the tent, over statutory language alone.

trackers.name: Native Forest Restoration Trust — buys on the open market (New Zealand)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a charitable trust formed in 1980 out of the protest against the felling of giant totara in Pureora Forest, which buys native forest and wetland outright and holds it permanently. Its own pages give over 8,500 hectares owned and managed and well over 9,000 hectares secured since it began — the gap being between what it still holds and what it has ever bought; older third-party figures of around 7,000 hectares are out of date. USE IT: it states plainly that it competes on the open market, which almost nothing else in this file does — it bids against other buyers and says it could not do so without public donations. That makes it the body to approach when a block is actually for sale rather than merely at risk. Three routes it publishes and communities miss. The bequest: it asks for unrestricted gifts so its successors can send them where the need is greatest at the time, and one reserve was bought with a legacy from an estate combined with a single large donation. The appeal: 113 hectares of coastal flats on the Kaipara Harbour were added with NZ$60,000 raised from supporters plus two major gifts. And the Memorial Forest Scheme, under which two private individuals bought a 242-hectare block through the Trust in 1991 to commemorate someone — a route nobody raises with a grieving family. THE TRAP: that same block had been inspected by the Wildlife Service in 1984 and recommended for addition to the conservation estate, and it never happened; the owner meanwhile turned down repeated offers from pine-planting companies. A government recommendation is not protection. The Trust also notes that bequests which establish an endowment for ongoing management are what keeps a reserve alive, so land offered without one is the harder ask.

trackers.name: DOC Community Fund — the live route now the Nature Heritage Fund has closed (New Zealand)
trackers.desc: WHAT IS LIVE: the DOC Community Fund supports community-led conservation projects on public and private land. That is the general-purpose route for a New Zealand community group, and the Department's funding page is where the current rounds and the other government funds are listed together. READ THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE, BECAUSE IT CHANGES THE OPTIONS: the Nature Heritage Fund has permanently closed. Established 1990 to stop indigenous forest on private land being logged, it was the contestable fund that protected ecosystems on private land by direct purchase or covenant, and across 35 years it protected hundreds of thousands of hectares — 341,881 hectares in its first 25 years, about 1.3 per cent of the country. Its closure was announced in the 2025 budget. Any guidance that still tells a New Zealand community to apply to it is out of date, and the direct-purchase route it represented no longer exists in that form. WHAT REMAINS FOR MāORI LAND: Ngā Whenua Rāhui is a contestable ministerial fund, established 1991, for voluntary protection of indigenous biodiversity on Māori-owned land. Protection is by kawenata — a reviewable 25-year formal agreement tailored to the whenua, under which landowners retain full ownership and management and keep their tikanga and tino rangatiratanga. A Kaitakawaenga meets applicants, visits the land, and may arrange an indigenous biodiversity or cultural assessment at no cost to the applicant — which is a free ecological survey, and one of the few in this file. Land under a Ngā Whenua Rāhui kawenata became non-rateable from July 2021. Applicants must be Māori land authorities, trusts, incorporations, organisations representing whānau, hapū or iwi, or Māori owners of General land, and must hold the legal right to enter the agreement. THE OTHER PLACES THE DEPARTMENT POINTS TO: Lottery Environment and Heritage grants for protecting natural, cultural and physical heritage, and the Lottery Significant Projects Fund, which gives capital grants to purchase, create or improve community assets of regional or national significance where total project cost is $3 million or more.

trackers.name: Open space covenants — what they cover, and the SECOND instrument for restoration sites
trackers.desc: WHAT A COVENANT IS: a LEGAL AGREEMENT between the trust and a landowner to protect a special open space feature IN PERPETUITY — entered into VOLUNTARILY by the landowner. The area for protection is spatially defined and a covenant is REGISTERED AGAINST THE TITLE of the property, specifying the values to be protected and A SET OF ACTIONS WHICH ARE PROHIBITED. A registered title restriction with a named list of prohibited actions is stronger than any planning designation a council can later revise. AND WHY IT REACHES WHAT PARKS CANNOT: approximately 70 PER CENT of New Zealand — 19 MILLION HECTARES — IS PRIVATELY OWNED, with just over 16 million hectares farmland; a particular strength is the ability to protect ecosystems or species which occur IN THE LOWLANDS or on specific geology, WHICH MAY NOT BE WELL REPRESENTED IN PUBLIC CONSERVATION LAND. Since 1977, more than 187,202 HECTARES has been protected by private landowners registering covenants, covering forest remnants, wetlands, lakes, PEAT LAKES, coastline, tussock grasslands, rural landscapes, ARCHAEOLOGICAL SITES, geological formations and areas of high scenic value. AND THE SECOND INSTRUMENT, for ground not yet good enough to qualify: a RESTORATION AGREEMENT was developed for projects that DO NOT HAVE STRONG ENOUGH EXISTING BIODIVERSITY VALUES to meet the covenant criteria — more suitable for NATIVE REVEGETATION OR WETLAND RESTORATION.

trackers.name: The Nature Heritage Fund — 341,881 hectares bought in 25 years, AND NOW CLOSED
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DID: in its first 25 years the fund PURCHASED AND PROTECTED 341,881 HECTARES of land, representing 1.3 PER CENT OF NEW ZEALAND'S LAND AREA. It supported projects that protect areas of high ecological value ON PRIVATE LAND EITHER BY DIRECT PURCHASE, OR COVENANT, and was an independent, contestable fund available to ALL privately owned land with high biodiversity or ecological value. AND WHAT HAS HAPPENED TO IT, which is why this is filed as a warning rather than a door: in its 2025 budget the government announced THE CLOSURE OF THE NATURE HERITAGE FUND, despite increasing revenue from the international visitor levy for the conservation department. The single largest land-purchase fund in the country was closed by a budget line — so a community relying on a public acquisition fund should check it still exists before building a plan on it, and should say plainly what its closure costs. AND WHAT IT USED TO OFFER, worth recording because these are the terms to ask any successor for: a system of ACCORDS AND EXCHANGES where agreements can be reached AND LAND EXCHANGED in order to achieve both the goals of protection AND ECONOMIC SURVIVAL FOR THE LANDOWNER; and assistance to private owners or organisations WITH MANAGEMENT COSTS. Applications were encouraged from MULTIPLE ORGANISATIONS wishing to form funding or future management partnerships.

trackers.name: Joining someone else's appeal — a $100 form instead of a $600 one
trackers.desc: THE CHEAP WAY IN, and it is the most useful cost comparison in the New Zealand file: if someone else has appealed, a submitter can join as a SECTION 274 PARTY — the filing fee is $100, against a $600 FILING FEE for lodging an appeal of your own. Six hundred dollars to start a case, one hundred to join one — so a community that cannot fund its own appeal should watch for anyone else's and join it. WHO QUALIFIES: those with an interest greater than the public generally will NORMALLY INCLUDE NEIGHBOURS, DOWNSTREAM RESOURCE USERS, IWI AUTHORITIES AND ENVIRONMENTAL INTEREST GROUPS — excluding trade competitors acting to block competition. AND THE MECHANICS, published in full: prepare the notice in accordance with FORM 33 of the Resource Management (Forms, Fees, and Procedure) Regulations 2003, and lodge the original and one copy WITHIN 15 WORKING DAYS after the period for lodging a notice of appeal ends, at the correct regional office — Christchurch for the South Island, Wellington for the lower North Island, Auckland for the upper North Island. Documents go by hand, courier, post, or email, and if your notice is lodged after the closing date, you can apply for A WAIVER OF THE TIME LIMIT.

trackers.name: The Environment Court's own legal assistance page — THREE places to find a lawyer, and legal aid covers RMA cases
trackers.desc: WHERE TO FIND THE LAWYER, named by the court itself: you can find AN ENVIRONMENT LAWYER through the NEW ZEALAND LAW SOCIETY, the RESOURCE MANAGEMENT LAW ASSOCIATION, or YOUR LOCAL COMMUNITY LAW CENTRE. Three named routes to a specialist, one of them free and local, published by the court a community will appear in front of. AND THE FUNDING POINT THAT MOST PEOPLE ASSUME IS UNAVAILABLE: legal aid is government funding to pay for legal help for people who cannot afford a lawyer, and under a named section of the Legal Services Act 2011, LEGAL AID MAY BE GRANTED IN RELATION TO ALL APPLICATIONS, SUBMISSIONS, AND APPEALS UNDER THE RESOURCE MANAGEMENT ACT 1991, or to the Environment Court under any other Act. Legal aid covers planning submissions, not just courtroom appeals — which puts a lawyer within reach at the stage where objections actually work. The court states its purpose plainly: legal aid helps people to resolve legal problems that may go to court and MAKES SURE THAT PEOPLE ARE NOT DENIED JUSTICE BECAUSE THEY CAN'T AFFORD A LAWYER. AND THE LIMIT ON WHAT THE COURT ITSELF WILL DO: court staff can advise you on the court processes, BUT THEY CANNOT PROVIDE YOU WITH LEGAL ADVICE.

trackers.name: The Centre for Social Impact funding guide — the EIGHT kinds of funder in New Zealand
trackers.desc: WHAT IT MAPS, and it is the answer to 'where would the money even come from': funding available to community organisations in New Zealand generally comes from EIGHT MAIN TYPES OF SOURCES: COMMUNITY TRUSTS, ENERGY TRUSTS, GOVERNMENT AND COUNCIL FUNDS, COMMUNITY FOUNDATIONS, GAMING TRUSTS, FAMILY AND INDIVIDUAL TRUSTS AND FOUNDATIONS, LICENSING TRUSTS, AND CORPORATE FOUNDATIONS, each with its own criteria, priorities and processes. New Zealand's four filed funding entries were all government conservation money. Seven of those eight are not government at all, which is what a group discovers only after the state fund it was counting on closes — as the national land-purchase fund did. AND HOW TO FIND YOURS: the guide lists THE COMMUNITY TRUST FOR EACH LOCAL AREA, points to a national body holding information about the COMMUNITY FOUNDATIONS around the country, gives a full list of the GAMING TRUSTS, and advises visiting your REGIONAL COUNCIL'S website and typing 'community grants' into the search box — each council usually providing several grant options. AND THE ADVICE ON APPROACH: a funder interested in RESTORING NATURAL ENVIRONMENTS will look to fund organisations doing work on this issue, and to BUILD RELATIONSHIPS with them THAT MAY RESULT IN LONG-TERM FUNDING PARTNERSHIPS. It also lists the documents and information to have ready before applying anywhere.

trackers.name: Rātā Foundation small grants — NO CLOSING DATES, you choose when to apply
trackers.desc: THE TERM THAT MATTERS WHEN A PROJECT APPEARS SUDDENLY: this programme is for organisations requesting $20,000 OR LESS, and WE DON'T HAVE CLOSING DATES — YOU CHOOSE WHEN TO APPLY. A fund with no closing dates is the only kind that can respond to a development application lodged without warning — every other fund in this file runs on annual rounds a community may have missed by months. AND THE TIMEFRAME, published honestly: generally the time-frame for a funding decision will be TEN WEEKS, once we have received a complete application and all the required information. AND THE LIMITS: you can only receive ONE GRANT IN OUR FINANCIAL YEAR, and you can apply to only ONE FUNDING PROGRAMME AT A TIME. The application focuses on THE DIFFERENCE YOUR PROJECT MAKES, or the needs of your organisation. AND WHAT THE FOUNDATION FUNDS, which puts environment work squarely inside its remit: it describes itself as THE SOUTH ISLAND'S MOST SIGNIFICANT COMMUNITY INVESTMENT FUND, and says its funding makes more of a difference in communities which face barriers... AND WHERE PEOPLE ACT FOR THE BENEFIT OF OUR ENVIRONMENT.

trackers.name: A regional guide to the legal protection of land — every route, including GIFTING IT OUTRIGHT
trackers.desc: WHAT THE GUIDE SETS OUT, and it is the route-map New Zealand's bucket was missing: creating a CONSERVATION COVENANT on your land is one of the best ways to ensure biodiversity values are LEGALLY PROTECTED, REGARDLESS OF WHO OWNS IT IN THE FUTURE, and there are a number of VOLUNTARY AND GOVERNMENT-INITIATED covenants available — not only the one national trust's. AND THE ROUTE THAT COSTS A COMMUNITY NOTHING AT ALL: you can GIFT LAND to a public agency or NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATION DURING YOUR LIFETIME OR LEAVE IT VIA YOUR WILL. Gifting land is an amazing legacy that can ensure biodiversity values are protected BEYOND ONE'S OWN LIFE. Gifting during your lifetime, not only by will, is the faster half of that sentence — an owner under pressure to sell can hand the land over now rather than leaving it to an estate. AND WHAT ELSE THE LIBRARY POINTS TO: advice on leaving a GIFT OF PROPERTY to the national trust, and A TRUST THAT OWNS AND MANAGES OVER 7,000 HECTARES of now protected reserves, which PURCHASES SIGNIFICANT ECOLOGICAL AREAS to ensure they are protected into the future. A second national body that actually buys land, alongside the covenanting trust, is the buyer a New Zealand community should know exists.

trackers.name: Community Law — 24 centres, free one-on-one legal help, and OUTREACH CLINICS IN SMALL COMMUNITIES
trackers.desc: THE FREE LEGAL SERVICE THE ENVIRONMENT COURT ITSELF POINTS PEOPLE TO: there are 24 COMMUNITY LAW CENTRES throughout New Zealand, and MOST COMMUNITY LAW CENTRES OPERATE OUTREACH SERVICES OR CLINICS IN SMALL COMMUNITIES. You can CONTACT YOUR LOCAL CENTRE DIRECTLY to make an enquiry or arrange an appointment. Outreach clinics in small communities are the difference between a service that exists and one a rural objector can actually reach — and the centres run from KAITAIA TO REKOHU (THE CHATHAMS). AND WHAT THEY OFFER, in their own description: WE'RE LAWYERS AND WE'RE ALSO COMMUNITY WORKERS, providing ALL SORTS OF FREE LEGAL HELP, FROM EASY-TO-READ INFORMATION, TO COMMUNITY WORKSHOPS, TO ONE-ON-ONE LEGAL HELP, plus the COMMUNITY LAW MANUAL online and LEGAL LETTERS a person can FIND AND ADAPT to SOLVE YOUR PROBLEM YOURSELF. A bookable legal-education workshop is a thing a residents' group can request as a group, not merely an individual appointment. THE HONEST LIMIT, which they state themselves: online resources and workshops are FOR ALL NEW ZEALANDERS, but they AIM TO GIVE FREE ONE-ON-ONE LEGAL HELP TO PEOPLE WHO DON'T HAVE MUCH MONEY — so the individual casework is means-directed even where the workshops are not.

trackers.name: Lawyers for Climate Action NZ — a charity of legal experts that litigates against polluters
trackers.desc: A STANDING BODY OF LAWYERS ORGANISED TO ACT, not a referral list: it describes itself as LEGAL EXPERTS DRIVING EFFECTIVE ACTION IN NEW ZEALAND AGAINST CLIMATE CHANGE, holding that THE LAW IS ONE OF THE MOST POWERFUL TOOLS FOR RESPONDING TO THE CLIMATE CRISIS. WE USE THE LAW TO ACCELERATE CLIMATE ACTION, HOLD GOVERNMENTS AND POLLUTING COMPANIES TO ACCOUNT, AND ULTIMATELY CREATE SYSTEMIC CHANGE. An organisation whose stated purpose is holding polluting companies to account through the courts is one a community facing an emitting project can approach directly — and it already has the practitioners assembled. AND WHAT IT IS, formally, which matters for whether it can act: LAWYERS FOR CLIMATE ACTION NZ INC. IS A NEW ZEALAND REGISTERED CHARITY AND IS NOT FOR PROFIT, with a membership of NEARLY 400 MEMBERS who receive MONTHLY UPDATES ON OUR WORK, THE OPPORTUNITY TO CONTRIBUTE, AND CONNECT WITH OTHER MEMBERS. Four hundred lawyers who can be contacted as one body is a resource no single community could assemble, and membership is open rather than closed to the profession's own.

trackers.name: Protecting your whenua — the covenant route, step by step, with the TRUST paying the survey
trackers.desc: THE PROCESS SET OUT FOR A LANDOWNER RATHER THAN FOR A LAWYER, which is rare in this file: once all landowners agree the proposal and deed, it goes to the trust for approval; BEFORE YOU CAN FINALISE THE COVENANT, YOU'LL WORK WITH YOUR LOCAL REP TO FENCE THE AREA OF LAND YOU WANT TO PROTECT. YOUR REP WILL INSPECT THE FENCING ONCE IT'S DONE. THEY'LL ALSO ORGANISE AND PAY TO GET A SURVEY OF THE COVENANT BOUNDARIES DONE. The trust organises and pays for the boundary survey — the professional cost that most often stops a smallholder, carried by the body asking for the protection. AND WHAT HAPPENS AT THE END: the trust WILL REGISTER THE COVENANT WITH the land titles authority TO GET IT ADDED TO THE LAND TITLE. AT THIS POINT, YOUR WHENUA IS LEGALLY PROTECTED FOR THE FUTURE. AND THE MONEY AFTERWARDS, which answers the running-cost problem this file keeps meeting: ONCE THE COVENANT IS IN PLACE, LANDOWNERS CAN APPLY TO THE TRUST'S CONTESTABLE FUND FOR FUNDING TO DO FURTHER WORK TO IMPROVE THE COVENANTED land. AND THE WARNING GIVEN HONESTLY TO THE OWNER: A COVENANT LASTS FOREVER. MAKE SURE YOU UNDERSTAND THE IMPACT OF PUTTING A COVENANT ON YOUR land — BOTH FOR YOUR FAMILY TODAY AND FOR FUTURE GENERATIONS. A body that warns the owner about permanence before signing is one a community can introduce without risking the relationship.

trackers.name: The leverage figure — every government dollar drew $6 to $7 from landowners
trackers.desc: THE ARGUMENT THAT WINS PUBLIC MONEY FOR PRIVATE-LAND PROTECTION, quoted in a funding debate: a university study FOUND EVERY DOLLAR OF trust MONEY HAD SEEN FARMERS AND OTHER LANDOWNERS INVESTED 6 TO 7 DOLLARS FOR HABITAT PROTECTION. A leverage ratio is the number that gets a conservation body funded — and any community arguing for a public contribution can compute the same figure for its own site. AND WHY THE MODEL IS DEFENSIBLE POLITICALLY, in the responsible minister's words: WE BACK FARMERS TO KNOW WHAT IS BEST FOR THEIR LAND, THEY CHOOSE TO PROTECT IMPORTANT CONSERVATION AREAS, RATHER THAN HAVING RULES FORCED ON THEM. Voluntary protection is defended as the opposite of imposed rules, which is how it survives changes of government — the same ground as the Danish voluntary-agreement rule in batch591. AND THE SCALE AND THE CONSTRAINT: the covenants PROTECT MORE THAN 5000 POCKETS OF LAND COVERING 180,000 HECTARES, protections continue EVEN IF THE LAND IS SOLD, and the bottleneck is capacity, not willingness: MORE AND MORE LANDOWNERS WANT TO COVENANT SPECIAL AREAS ON THEIR PROPERTIES, BUT the trust SIMPLY HASN'T HAD THE RESOURCES TO KEEP PACE.

trackers.name: Banks Peninsula Conservation Trust
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: a community-driven trust set up by peninsula landowners in 2001 — notably, following a mediated settlement of landowner appeals to the Environment Court — that protects biodiversity on private land by voluntary rather than statutory means. THE KEY POINT: it holds COVENANTING AUTHORITY STATUS, so it can itself place a legally protective covenant in perpetuity over areas of high biodiversity and landscape value. Most regional groups can only refer you elsewhere; this one can do the protecting. USE IT: for Banks Peninsula and wider Canterbury land, it is a local alternative to a national covenant, run by people who live there. It also works at landscape scale through the Wildside project alongside Christchurch City Council, DOC and Environment Canterbury, and runs practical workshops on weed control, biodiversity and fire-risk mitigation.

trackers.name: Tiaki Tāmaki Makaurau — guide to the legal protection of land (Auckland)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Auckland's conservation portal, with a practical guide to every route for legally protecting biodiversity on land in the region — a conservation covenant, which binds the land REGARDLESS OF WHO OWNS IT IN FUTURE, or a binding land management agreement with Auckland Council or the Department of Conservation, alongside the national QEII option. USE IT: two Auckland-specific things are worth knowing. The council route is a genuine alternative to a national covenant and may move faster for a local site. And single trees can be protected — the portal carries the guidelines and nomination form for the region's NOTABLE TREE SCHEDULE, which is a real lever when a development turns on removing mature trees rather than clearing a whole site. The portal also lists conservation projects by area if you are looking for people already active near you.

trackers.name: Conflict of Interest Commission
trackers.desc: Croatia's commission resolving public officials' conflicts of interest. — Holds to account: lobbyists & influence-seekers, top officials & cabinet, officials handling public money & power — find who is lobbying whom, and meetings held; their assets, interests and integrity declarations; corruption cases, sanctions and integrity data.

trackers.name: Supreme Court of Croatia
trackers.desc: Official site of the Vrhovni sud with published case law (sudska praksa). · Find here: the judgments and information of the Supreme Court of Croatia.

trackers.name: Povjerenik za informiranje (Information Commissioner, Croatia)
trackers.desc: Croatia's independent Information Commissioner oversees the Right of Access to Information Act (NN 25/2013): deciding appeals against denied access, conducting inspection supervision of proactive disclosure, running an open-data portal on access-to-information compliance, and reporting to the Croatian Parliament (Sabor). USE IT: appeal a refusal here, and check the portal for the body's own compliance record before you do.

trackers.name: Imamo pravo znati — FOI requests (HRV)
trackers.desc: Accountability source (FOI request platform); Imamo pravo znati — civic Freedom-of-Information request platform (Alaveteli/mySociety network) — lets citizens file public-records requests and publishes the requests and the authorities’ responses in a public archive.

trackers.name: Zelena akcija / FoE Croatia — prostorno planiranje guide
trackers.desc: Croatia's oldest environmental association, active since 1990 and running on campaigns, nonviolent direct action and public participation. WHO TO ENLIST when a spatial plan, incinerator or waste facility is being pushed through against a neighbourhood — they have fought exactly these, from the Rebro medical-waste incinerator to Sisak landfill expansion. You CAN: use their free Priručnik on spatial planning and why public participation matters, and draw on an organisation that shares expertise with other groups, individuals and communities. For activists: the practical route into Croatia's planning consultation process, plus a partner with SLAPP experience.

trackers.name: Justice and Environment — European green-law network
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the European network of environmental-law NGOs, whose national member here is Zelena akcija. Its fifteen members act as the environmental-law service point in their own countries, taking cases and intervening in legislative processes, while the network defends communities and nature in court and lodges infringement complaints against member-state governments. Its standing themes are access to justice under the Aarhus Convention, environmental assessment and pollution control. WHO IT SUITS: anyone who does not yet know which lawyer to call — knock on Zelena akcija's door first, and use the network only if your problem crosses a border. The network itself does not take individual cases; its members do. YOUR NATIONAL MEMBER IS Zelena Akcija (zelena-akcija.hr) — go to them, not to the network. J&E members serve as environmental law ‘service points’ in their countries, handling cases, participating in legislative processes and sometimes providing legal analyses and consultations for national governments. The network has 11 full and 4 associate members, and can launch infringement proceedings against faulty governments — a route a national body alone does not have. CURRENT SCOPE: access to justice under the Aarhus Convention, climate, environmental assessments, and the Environmental Liability Directive. It previously worked on waste, transport, health and Natura 2000, so an older document may overstate what it covers today.

trackers.name: State Audit Office
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Croatia, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: data.gov.hr
trackers.desc: National — Croatian government open data portal. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Croatia.

trackers.name: EOJN
trackers.desc: Croatia's electronic public-procurement notices system. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Croatia, and for how much.

trackers.name: Croatia Register of Beneficial Owners
trackers.desc: National beneficial-ownership register: official database of the natural persons who ultimately own or control companies and legal entities. Access restricted to authorities/obliged entities.

trackers.name: Sudski registar
trackers.desc: National company / corporate registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS)
trackers.desc: Croatia's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Croatia.

trackers.name: Oštro
trackers.desc: Croatian investigative center reporting on corruption, power and public money.

trackers.name: FZOEU udruge calls — the numbers, and a second call in autumn
trackers.desc: CROATIA'S ENVIRONMENTAL FUND RUNS A DEDICATED CALL FOR CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS. Eligible: associations registered under the Zakon o udrugama whose activity is directed at environmental protection, energy efficiency and renewables. REAL NUMBERS, SO YOU CAN JUDGE THE EFFORT: at one signing 69 contracts were awarded across EUR 6.89 million of project value, of which 66 were civil society projects — EUR 900,000 for 58 environmental protection projects and EUR 100,000 for 8 energy efficiency ones. So a typical environmental grant is on the order of EUR 15,000, not a transformative sum but reachable. Since 2013 the Fund has co-financed 392 projects worth EUR 5.5 million. MISSING A ROUND NEED NOT COST A YEAR: the Fund's director stated that high interest meant a new call was planned for the autumn. Funded work includes waste prevention, re-use, nature and biodiversity protection, climate education and energy poverty. EU-FUNDED PROJECTS MAY STILL APPLY — but only for the portion not co-financed from European funds, a partial rather than absolute bar.

trackers.name: The larger Croatian money is municipal — and needs a warden's decision first
trackers.desc: WHERE THE BIGGER SUMS SIT, AND THE PRECONDITION. FZOEU is a legal person with public authority whose statutory purpose includes preserving natural communities and realising citizens' right to a healthy environment — language worth quoting back in correspondence. Its direct-subsidy track for removing waste dumped in the environment made EUR 6 million available to towns, municipalities and public institutions managing protected parts of nature: local self-government gets up to 50 percent of justified remediation costs and institutions managing protected areas up to 80 percent, both capped at EUR 200,000 per project. THE PRECONDITION: the location must be one for which a communal warden (komunalni redar) has issued a decision under the waste management law — so getting that decision issued is the first step, before any funding conversation. AND NOT EVERY ROUTE IS A CALL: the Fund will not issue a public competition where it acts as a contracting party directly co-financing and participating in a programme, so direct co-financing can be negotiated rather than competed for.

trackers.name: Industrial Emissions Portal — what the facility actually releases
trackers.desc: IT ANSWERS ‘WHAT IS THIS FACILITY RELEASING, AND HOW MUCH’ — with named sites and quantities, not a description of a regulator. The Industrial Emissions Portal gives public access to environmental data from industrial facilities across EU Member States, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, Serbia and the UK. The Industrial Emissions Portal Regulation (IEPR) replaces the earlier E-PRTR Regulation and implements the Kyiv Protocol on Pollutant Release and Transfer Registers — binding since 8 October 2009, the only legally binding international instrument on PRTRs, and a protocol to the Aarhus Convention. THE MECHANISM IS REPUTATIONAL, AND THE UNECE SAYS SO OPENLY: though it regulates information about pollution rather than pollution directly, it is expected to exert downward pressure ‘as no company will want to be identified as among the biggest polluters’. That is the campaign use — the register produces a ranked, official, quotable list. THE MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT, AND IT PREVENTS A FALSE CONCLUSION: an installation not shown on a PRTR is either not an industrial activity covered by it, OR has not reached the stated pollutant-specific thresholds. Absence from the register is NOT evidence of no pollution — check the activity list and thresholds before relying on an absence. TWO DEFINITIONS THAT HELP: ‘the public’ includes natural or legal persons and their associations, organizations or groups, so an unincorporated community group qualifies; and a ‘facility’ is installations on the same site OR ON ADJOINING SITES under one operator — which matters where a plant has been split across parcels. As a scale example the UK register covers 91 pollutants back to 2007. IF YOU NEED ANOTHER COUNTRY: prtr.unece.org keeps a PRTR Global list of national registers, maintained by the OECD Working Party on PRTRs with UNECE, alongside CEC Taking Stock for North America and the NGO-built Blue Map Database in China — where a government has not built a register, that is the precedent for one built anyway.

trackers.name: Aarhus Compliance Committee — one person may bring the State itself
trackers.desc: THE ONLY ROUTE IN THIS MAP BY WHICH ONE PERSON CAN BRING A STATE ITSELF BEFORE AN INTERNATIONAL BODY over environmental decision-making. Under Decision I/7 (2002), paragraphs 18–24, communications may be brought by one or more members of the public concerning any Party's compliance — no organisation, no accreditation, no minimum number. The ACCC is a quasi-judicial body reporting to the Meeting of the Parties. THE MOST MISUNDERSTOOD PART: YOU DO NOT HAVE TO EXHAUST DOMESTIC REMEDIES. Paragraph 21 says the Committee takes account of any available domestic remedy unless its application is unreasonably prolonged or obviously ineffective. What you must do is state whether steps have been taken and, if not, why not — a section of the form, not a bar to entry. WHAT MAKES IT INADMISSIBLE: anonymity, abuse of the right, being manifestly unreasonable including de minimis, incompatibility, or concerning a non-Party or a State that opted out — and no State has opted out. The only one most people risk is ‘de minimis’: frame it as a systemic failure of information, participation or access to justice, not a complaint about one permit. PRACTICALITIES THAT DECIDE WHETHER IT LANDS: there is a required format, and cut-off dates tied to meetings — as a worked example, communications received by 4 May 2026 were for the 15 and 18 June 2026 meeting, provided they were complete, in format, and needed no translation. Check the current cut-off; missing it costs a cycle. Submit in English, French or Russian — the secretariat translates, but needing translation can push you past a cut-off. Send copies, not originals. AND KNOW THIS BEFORE YOU FILE: once preliminary admissibility is determined the case gets a number and BECOMES PUBLIC — there is a confidentiality section on the form. The process runs receipt → admissibility → response by the Party → draft findings → public hearing → final findings and recommendations. Address: Aarhus Convention Secretariat, UNECE, Palais des Nations, Geneva. CONFIRM YOUR STATE IS A PARTY before relying on this — this entry is recorded here on the basis that the state is bound by the Kyiv Protocol to the Convention, which implies but does not prove Party status.

trackers.name: EIA Directive — ask for the screening determination
trackers.desc: IF A PROJECT NEAR YOU IS PROCEEDING WITHOUT AN EIA, THERE IS A PUBLISHED, REASONED DOCUMENT EXPLAINING WHY — AND ALMOST NOBODY ASKS FOR IT. Annex I projects get mandatory EIA; Annex II projects — the far larger category — go through a screening procedure using the Annex III criteria. Under Directive 2014/52/EU the developer supplies specified Annex IIA information, and that determination SHALL be made available to the public and must be duly motivated. Ask for the screening determination: it is the most useful document in the procedure and the one people do not know exists. TIMING: determinations must be made within 90 days of complete information, unless the authority extends the period giving reasons in exceptional cases and informs the developer. BUT BE REALISTIC ABOUT THE LIMIT: proposals to require public participation during screening were dropped from the 2014 text as impractical — you have a right to the determination, not a right to be heard before it is made. THREE MORE THINGS THE 2014 AMENDMENT GIVES YOU: reports must be more understandable to the public, especially on the current state of the environment and alternatives; competent authorities must prove their objectivity to avoid conflicts of interest — making a conflict a ground of challenge, not a complaint; and the grounds for consent decisions must be clear and transparent. ASK ALSO WHETHER A SCOPING OPINION HAS BEEN REQUESTED — it fixes what the assessment is required to look at. Reports must carry a non-technical summary (Annex IV), and information must be provided as early as possible, electronically, by public notice or bill posting, or in local newspapers. THE DIRECTIVE IS A FLOOR, NOT A CEILING: Member States may lay down more stringent conditions and fix penalties — check the national transposition before assuming the EU minimum applies. The regime is Directive 2011/92/EU (applying since 17 February 2012) as amended by 2014/52/EU, codifying rules in force since 1988 and aligned to the Espoo and Aarhus Conventions. ONE PATTERN TO WATCH: the legislative history records concern that formal screening could become a ‘mini-EIA’ before the full EIA — an unusually detailed screening determination is itself an argument that full assessment was warranted.

trackers.name: Espoo points of contact — a named official, and ‘were you notified?’
trackers.desc: A NAMED OFFICIAL, A DIRECT EMAIL, AND A QUESTION WITH A DOCUMENTARY ANSWER. The UNECE publishes the points of contact regarding notification under article 3 of the Espoo Convention on EIA in a transboundary context: notifications of activities likely to cause significant adverse transboundary impact shall be transmitted to the relevant points of contact. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR AN ORDINARY LAND CASE: if a project sits near a border, the affected country's point of contact should have been notified — so ask both points of contact whether notification was given. It is a cheap, precise question, and failure to notify is a procedural defect in the consent. The list gives each Party's named official, department, postal address, telephone and email: Czechia's sits in the Department of EIA and Integrated Prevention at the Ministry of the Environment; Denmark's is the Agency for Green Transition and Aquatic Environment using the functional address espoo@sgav.dk; Croatia's is a Director at the Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development; Canada's is the President of the Impact Assessment Agency. PREFER A FUNCTIONAL ADDRESS WHERE ONE IS LISTED — named officials move. AND NOTE A ROUTING PATTERN: some Parties route notification through their Ministry for Foreign Affairs c/o their Permanent Mission in Geneva rather than an environment ministry — where that is so, the environment ministry may not hold the file and the foreign-ministry route is the correct one. A SECOND DIRECTORY, AND A SECOND ROUTE TO THE SAME DOCUMENT: the EEA publishes a list of Eionet national focal points covering 32 member countries and 8 cooperating countries (Albania, Bosnia, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Moldova, Montenegro, Serbia, Ukraine). Data are reported upwards — from stakeholder, to competent authority, to the EEA, to the Commission — so if your national authority has reported something, the EEA holds it too. Where a national body is unresponsive or its figures look wrong, the same data sits one level up in a body with no stake in the local decision. CONFIRM YOUR COUNTRY APPEARS ON THE LIST before relying on it. SCOPE: Espoo governs transboundary notification and Eionet governs data reporting — for the domestic EIA procedure itself, see the EIA Directive entry recorded separately.

trackers.name: Eurosite / ELCN — who already holds land near you, and the easement route
trackers.desc: A DIRECTORY OF THE PEOPLE WHO ALREADY HOLD AND MANAGE LAND IN YOUR COUNTRY — which is who you need when the answer to a development is getting the land into protective hands. Eurosite, established 1989, is one of the largest pan-European organisations bringing together NGOs, governmental organisations and private bodies, with members from the Atlantic islands to the Black Sea and from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean. ITS ELCN STRAND IS ABOUT PRIVATE LAND SPECIFICALLY: the European Land Conservation Network was built to support private landowners — non-public bodies or individuals — willing to engage in conservation ON AT LEAST PART OF THEIR LAND. That last phrase is the opening: a landowner who will not sell may still protect a portion, and there is a European network built to make that happen. The three tools it promotes are conservation easements, privately protected areas, and land stewardship agreements. AND A FUNDING ROUTE IS ATTACHED: ELCN and the ILCN have run sessions on using EU LIFE funding for private land conservation, aimed at landowners and conservationists preparing a LIFE project proposal; in November 2025 Eurosite-ELCN launched a working group on nature finance and land stewardship focused on finance mechanisms that mobilise private investment, co-chaired by the former head of the EU LIFE Programme. IF YOUR FIGHT IS A QUARRY, ASK FOR THIS BY NAME: Eurosite and partners published work on project selection criteria for conservation easements to protect nature in European quarries — a published European method for putting an easement over one. The network also co-hosts meetings of the Commission's Expert Group on the Nature Directives (NADEG) on tools and incentives for private land conservation — the most important working-level platform between the Commission, member states and interest groups. IF EUROSITE DOES NOT REACH YOUR COUNTRY, the International Land Conservation Network (founded 2014, the first global network of private land conservation practitioners) is the wider net, active from Canada to Australia to Latin America. BE PRECISE ABOUT WHAT THESE ARE: networks of practitioners — they connect you to the organisation that can act; they do not buy land themselves. Ask the network who operates in your country; membership is not asserted here.

trackers.name: Zelena Istra — gets the regulator to rule against the county (Croatia)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a Croatian environmental association based in Istria which runs a standing programme on public participation in environmental decisions and takes consultation practice apart case by case. It documents that the Information Commissioner warned the county a second time for breaching the access-to-information law in how it ran the consultation on the county spatial plan — and its own assessment is that most towns and municipalities in Istria would fail the same test. That is a finding by the national regulator, obtained and publicised by an association a community can ring, and it is reusable by anyone in the county facing the same practice. WHY IT IS USEFUL EVEN IF YOUR CASE IS NOT IN ISTRIA: its president has put the underlying problem publicly and precisely — that in Croatian impact-assessment procedures the legitimacy of a decision rests on observing the minimum prescribed procedure rather than on meaningfully including the local public and absorbing what it says. A community that understands that is aiming at the right target: not whether the consultation felt inadequate, but whether the prescribed steps were actually completed. WHAT IT IS NOT: not a land buyer and not a law firm. Croatia has no conservation land buyer that I could find across three separate searches, which is recorded in the batch 01, 02 and 25 notes. This is a regional watchdog with a documented record of getting an authority ruled against, and it complements Zelena akcija, which the file already holds at national level.

trackers.name: Rewilding Velebit — a resident team holding 23,000 hectares of hunting concession (Croatia)
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: the local Rewilding Europe team working the 145-kilometre Velebit massif on Croatia's Adriatic coast, between two national parks. Croatia is the country where three separate searches in this file found no conservation land buyer at all; this is the closest thing to one. WHAT THEY HAVE ACTUALLY SECURED: a 23,000-hectare Velebit Wildlife Reserve hunting concession in the heart of the rewilding area, including three offshore islands, with a hunting cessation inside it and 44 red deer released to build the population; a temporary ban on hunting red deer and Balkan chamois approved by the Croatian hunting authorities; and a natural grazing pilot on the 53,000-hectare Ličko Polje Natura 2000 site secured through an agreement on grazing rights, now running around 220 large grazers. THE INSTRUMENT TO NOTICE: a hunting concession, not a purchase. In a country where conservation bodies do not buy land, control was obtained by taking the concession and then ceasing to hunt, and by agreeing grazing rights rather than acquiring the pasture. A Croatian community should ask what rights over its threatened site are separately held and separately transferable — hunting, grazing, forestry — because that is how this team got control of 23,000 hectares. ALSO WORTH KNOWING: the team works with the University of Zagreb's Faculty of Forestry to have the Ramino Korito old-growth beech forest designated a special woodland reserve, so there is an existing academic partnership for getting a Croatian site formally recognised. Three Rewilding Europe Capital loans have gone to enterprises in this area, making it the model case for that financing route.

trackers.name: Udruga Biom — and the delegated management route (Croatia)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: one of Croatia's leading nature conservation organisations, active since 2006, at Čazmanska 2, Zagreb, +385 1 5515324, the country's BirdLife partner since 2013 and full partner from 2018, an IUCN partner since 2011, with over 400 paying members and around 8,000 volunteer hours a year. THE ROUTE IT OPENS THAT NOBODY ELSE IN CROATIA DOES: it promotes delegated management of protected areas — that is, a civil society organisation taking on the management of a protected site rather than the state doing it. In a country where three separate searches in this file found no conservation body that buys land, delegated management is the nearest equivalent: control and responsibility without purchase, in the same family as the Velebit hunting concession filed in batch 61. Ask what it takes to have a site managed this way. WHAT IT CAN ACTUALLY DO ON THE GROUND: it leads Croatia's largest nature restoration initiative to date, aiming to restore at least 560 hectares of grassland and improve management across a further 1,020 hectares in the Krka, Cetina, Svilaja and Dinara regions. It runs habitat restoration and ornithological volunteer camps in Učka Nature Park, citizen science, and a bird identification programme through which more than 500 people have trained. It also works against poaching and other wildlife crime. AND IT WORKS WITH THE PEOPLE A PROJECT AFFECTS: its own description names stakeholders affected by projects among the groups it works with, alongside the public, partner NGOs and government bodies, to push for higher conservation standards. WHAT IT IS NOT, CHECKED SPECIFICALLY: not a land buyer. Croatia remains without one after four searches. Its other entries here are the Istrian watchdog that obtained regulator findings against a county, the national spatial-planning guide body, and the Velebit rewilding team.

trackers.name: Nacionalna zaklada za razvoj civilnoga društva — institutional support, not project money
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: Croatia's national foundation for civil society development, described as the leading public institution for cooperation, networking and financing of civil society organisations in Croatia. Its stated aim includes building the capacity of civil society to take part in social development, through grant programmes, co-financing of EU projects and international programmes. Croatia had no funder in this file. THE PRODUCT THAT MATTERS MOST, AND CROATIA HAS AN ENVIRONMENTAL STRAND OF IT: it runs rounds of institucionalna podrška — institutional support for the stabilisation and/or development of associations, rather than project grants. Successive rounds have included calls for associations working on democratisation and social development, for associations that have not previously received institutional support from the foundation, and — in at least one round — for associations for the protection of the environment, nature and ecological sustainability. Reported award levels for the democratisation strands have run up to €39,000. WHY THAT IS THE RIGHT SHAPE: this file has now found core funding in four other places and each time it has been the most valuable thing on offer, because a Croatian association that can pay for itself between fights is still there when the next permit is issued. Watch specifically for the environmental strand and for the first-time-applicant strand, which exists precisely for organisations that have never had this support. TWO OTHER MECHANISMS WORTH KNOWING: it co-finances EU projects, and it operates a scheme providing the compulsory co-financing share that an organisation lacks after winning support elsewhere — in the documented case, 20% of the approved amount for projects funded under a Euro-Mediterranean programme. A community that has won a grant it cannot match has somewhere to go. And it can accept ad hoc requests outside its published calls, in order to respond to current needs of civil society development beyond what the competitions foresee. USE IT WITH CROATIA'S OTHER ENTRIES: the Istrian watchdog, the national spatial-planning guide body, the Velebit rewilding team and the delegated-management conservation organisation. Croatia still has no land buyer.

trackers.name: Mreža Zelenih telefona — one number, 072 123 456, routed to the nearest of eleven groups
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the Network of Green Phones, a national environmental helpline for Croatia. Any citizen can report an environmental problem or ask for information on 072 123 456, and calls from anywhere in Croatia are redirected at the price of a local call to the nearest member association. By mutual agreement each association covers the county where it has its seat, and some cover neighbouring counties too. WHAT THEY ACTUALLY DO WITH YOUR CALL: activists and volunteers approach solving the problem together with citizens, in cooperation with the competent institutions, and then supervise the resolution. Their work includes helping or mediating for citizens in reported cases and acquainting them with the remit and workings of the responsible institutions. That is casework plus follow-up, on a free phone number. THE RECORD: around 35,000 cases reported to the network, with roughly 1,399 citizen reports in just six months of 2020, and the network's own research finding 49 per cent of cases successfully resolved. A published, unflattering-if-it-were-worse success figure. WHO IS ON IT, which doubles as a county-by-county directory of Croatia's environmental associations: Zelena akcija (Zagreb), Eko Pan (Karlovac), Žmergo (Opatija), Zelena Istra (Pula), Sunce (Split), Eko Zadar, Nobilis, Zeleni Osijek, Ekološka udruga Krka (Knin), Franjo Koščec, and others. The first Green Phone was set up in 1992 at Zelena akcija; the network itself was founded in September 1999 by seven environmental associations with USAID support, and grew from there. AND THERE IS AN APP: Pametni Zeleni telefon, a free application making it simpler for citizens to report problems they notice in the city or in nature, built with the Berlin organisation UfU — already in this file as Germany's environmental law institute — and funded by the German environment agency.

trackers.name: Zeleni forum — the Croatian environmental network, and its rotating secretariat
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the network of Croatian non-governmental environmental organisations, active since 1998, aiming to influence the creation and implementation of environmental protection and nature conservation policy and to create a permanent platform for cooperation among citizens' associations and other actors of environmental civil society. Croatia had Zelena akcija, Biom and Zelena Istra filed individually but no network — and this file has found across eighteen countries that the membership list is the most useful free artefact. WHAT THE SECRETARIAT ACTUALLY DOES FOR YOU: informing and coordinating, MAINTAINING THE DATABASE OF MEMBER CONTACTS, organising the annual assembly and smaller coordination meetings, and coordinating fundraising activities. Ask the secretariat for the contact database — that is its stated job. AND THE HISTORY THAT TELLS YOU WHO THE MAJOR PLAYERS ARE: the forum was led by Zelena akcija of Zagreb (1998–2001), Zelena Istra of Pula (2001–2006), Udruga Sunce of Split (2006–2009), Zelena akcija again (2009–2019) and Udruga Biom of Zagreb since 2019. The rotation of the secretariat is a ranked list of the country's strongest environmental organisations, and Sunce of Split is the one not yet filed here. ITS METHODS, stated: launching and coordinating joint campaigns, actions and projects; informing and encouraging public participation in decision-making; and strengthening the capacity of citizens' associations — their skills, human resources and technical infrastructure.

trackers.name: Croatian land consolidation for nature — and the gap in the law it exposes
trackers.desc: THE HONEST FINDING FIRST, because it governs everything else a Croatian community tries: a public nature institution states plainly that Croatian laws NEITHER RECOGNISE NOR DEFINE private protected areas. That is why this file could find only one Croatian land acquirer. AND THE QUESTION IT PUTS INSTEAD: in the absence of state or other publicly owned land for declaring effective new protected areas, does the future of nature protection lie in private reserves — or in privately owned land managed according to the principles of the land ethic, the care of a good steward, and the needs of the wild life that inhabits it? THE MECHANISM IT PROPOSES, which is ordinary agrarian policy turned to conservation: komasacija — consolidation — the grouping of agricultural AND OTHER LAND into larger and more regular cadastral parcels. The institution's point is that 'other land', from a nature conservation standpoint, would be land that should be put to work as habitat for wild plants and animals, and that deliberate consolidation with neighbouring parcels could assemble a future nature reserve. THE OBSTACLE, RECORDED PLAINLY: the fragmentation of thousands of land parcels in the zone around any protected area in Croatia is today's reality, and habitats in some counties are almost completely fragmented. Meanwhile private capital is quietly and continuously consolidating land — the same tool, used by the other side.

trackers.name: Sunce, Split — it has an Odjel okolišnog prava, and it writes the boundary-change studies
trackers.desc: WHY THIS ONE CLOSES A REAL GAP: Sunce ran the Croatian environmental network's secretariat 2006–2009 and is described as one of the leading Croatian civil society organisations advocating, educating and informing on environmentally responsible solutions grounded in expert and research work. It works through four arms — a nature protection programme, an environment and sustainable development programme, an education and information department, and an ODJEL OKOLIŠNOG PRAVA, an environmental law department. AND THE SERVICE THAT MATTERS MOST TO A THREATENED SITE: its nature protection department lists, as a current project and service, preparation of an expert study for the purpose of producing the technical basis FOR CHANGING THE BOUNDARIES of a designated significant landscape — the Pakleni islands. An organisation that writes boundary-change studies for protected areas is one that can write the case for extending protection over your ground. This file has recorded that document as the bottleneck in eleven countries. ITS OWN STRATEGIC GOAL, worth quoting back: increased influence of Sunce on public policy AND ON JUDICIAL PRACTICE in the field of nature, environment and sustainable development, alongside increasing the area of protected marine areas and establishing zones of strict protection. PRACTICAL: Obala hrvatskog narodnog preporoda 7, 21000 Split; +385 21 360779; green phone 072 123 456.

trackers.name: The Mreža zelenih telefona counties — one number, and the associations that answer it
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: Croatia's green phone network runs regular operation in the Karlovac, Split-Dalmatia, Dubrovnik-Neretva, Šibenik-Knin, Međimurje, Varaždin, Lika-Senj and Primorje-Gorski kotar counties — and the project that funded it names the associations that run it, county by county: Eko Pan of Karlovac, Sunce of Split, Udruga Žmergo of Opatija, Ekološka udruga 'Krka' of Knin, Eko udruga Franjo Koščec, and Zaštitarsko-ekološka organizacija Nobilis, with Eko Zadar, Zeleni Osijek and Zelena Istra as collaborators. That is a county-by-county map of who answers the phone in Croatia — the local organisation a resident actually reaches, rather than a national office in Zagreb. WHAT THE PROJECT ALSO BUILT, which tells you what these groups can do: collecting data on the structure, methods, procedures and resources of local and state authorities and identifying problems and obstacles in the effectiveness of their fieldwork; and capacity-building programmes both for civil society organisations AND for local and state authorities on environmental and nature protection. Budget 225,661.87 euro over 24 months, 90 per cent EU funded. Ask your county's green phone association — it has been trained on how your own authority works.

trackers.name: WWF Adria — a regional office covering eight countries, and it sues
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: WWF's regional representation in Zagreb, operating in eight countries of the region, from Slovenia to Albania, as part of a network with more than a hundred offices worldwide. A single office a community can reach that works across the whole Western Balkans — useful where a river or a species crosses a border. AND IT LITIGATES, WITH NAMED PARTNERS: WWF Adria, Zelena akcija, Udruga BIOM and the Hrvatsko društvo za zaštitu ptica i prirode filed a claim in the Administrative Court in Osijek against the ministry over a decision permitting the extraction of 460,000 m³ of sediment from the Drava WITHOUT ANY OBLIGATION TO PRODUCE AN ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT STUDY OR AN ECOLOGICAL NETWORK ASSESSMENT. THE TWO MOVES WORTH COPYING: because the excavation works had ALREADY BEGUN, the organisations asked the court not only to annul the decision but ALSO TO ISSUE AN INTERIM MEASURE HALTING THE WORKS; and they attacked the underlying document, arguing the decision rested on a deficient elaborat based on flawed and outdated data. AND THE ARGUMENT THAT EXPOSED THE PURPOSE: a county announcement stating the extracted sand could be used for the needs of motorway construction on a named corridor confirmed, the organisations said, that the aim was to satisfy construction needs rather than flood defence. Find what the spoil is for — it may prove the stated purpose false. A CROSS-BORDER LEVER RECORDED WITH IT: neighbouring Hungary banned sediment extraction from the Drava and declared a national park on its own side, and the open letter argued Croatia as an EU member should stop a practice applied in non-member states.

trackers.name: Hrvatsko društvo za zaštitu ptica i prirode — the Osijek river science behind the cases
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: a membership organisation founded in 2001 and registered in Zagreb, working the Drava and Danube, and one of the four claimants in the sediment case. Croatia's bucket had Zelena akcija, Biom, Zelena Istra and Sunce — this is the river and bird science organisation of the eastern rivers. THE TECHNICAL CASE ITS SPOKESMAN PUT, which is the shape of the argument anywhere sediment or gravel is taken: extraction in such large quantities will result in further incision of the river bed and a worsening of the overall condition of surface AND GROUNDWATER, and of all the plants and animals dependent on that water. AND WHAT ITS PARTNERS ADD ON THE PROCEDURE: the environmental impact assessment system is what ensures the consequences of a work such as gravel and sand extraction do not do more harm than good, while contributing to balanced economic development alongside conservation of an area's fundamental natural values. The organisations had warned on several occasions about the inconsistency of procedures and breaches of the law, particularly regarding the production of environmental impact and ecological network studies. IT ALSO ACTS ON HUNTING AND DAMS: with Biom and WWF Adria it opposed the content of a new hunting law, and it has spoken against hydropower on the Sava, where 582 hydroelectric plants are foreseen in the whole Sava basin, twenty of them on the Sava itself.

trackers.name: Pravo na grad — its stated job is giving EXPERT HELP TO LOCAL FIGHTS
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS FOR, in its own words: an association acting against the privatisation and excessive economic exploitation of public and common goods and spaces, with particular emphasis on the participation of citizens and organised civil society IN THE MANAGEMENT OF PUBLIC GOODS. AND ITS FOUR PARALLEL ACTIVITIES, the second of which is the reason to call it: (a) co-organising campaigns; (b) PROVIDING EXPERT HELP TO LOCAL FIGHTS in developing and carrying out their campaigns, ORIENTING THEM IN THE LEGISLATIVE AND SPATIAL-REGULATORY FRAMEWORK, and CONNECTING THEM WITH OTHER SOCIAL ACTORS WHO CAN HELP; (c) networking local and national initiatives in the struggle for SPATIAL JUSTICE and building partnerships inside and outside the civil society field; (d) gathering and disseminating expert knowledge and practical experience about processes of socio-economic transformation concerning public goods, public services and public infrastructure. Orientation in the regulatory framework plus introductions to allies is exactly what a new local group lacks, and here it is a standing service rather than a favour. WHERE IT CAME FROM, which tells you it works: the association grew out of a multi-year campaign started by independent culture and youth organisations together with Zelena akcija, against the devastation of public space in Zagreb — above all the construction of a shopping centre and public garage inside a city block. Its coordinator and deputy are named publicly and its statute is available through the national register of associations.

trackers.name: Stop megafarmama — a national initiative that pools twelve local citizens' groups
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: an initiative gathering an animal protection organisation, Zelena akcija AND TWELVE LOCAL CITIZENS' INITIATIVES, which has fought for over a year against more than 20 projects for rearing, slaughtering and processing chickens planned right beside protected areas and in the very heart of communities, with a capacity of over 200 MILLION CHICKENS A YEAR. Twelve village initiatives inside one national campaign is the structure that turns twelve separate losing fights into one winnable one — and a community facing an intensive livestock unit has somewhere to join rather than start. THE HARMS IT LISTS, which double as an objection checklist: such plants consume enormous quantities of drinking water and land, while leaving communities MANURE DEPOSITS, WASTE WATER, AMMONIA AND HARMFUL GAS EMISSIONS, HEALTH RISKS, STENCH, NOISE, INTENSIVE LORRY TRAFFIC and other consequences the locations cannot bear. AND THE ARGUMENT THAT CARRIES BEYOND ONE VILLAGE: Croatia must not become a space where someone else's waste is dumped, whether literally or through projects that other states and communities no longer want to accept. The consequences of water, soil and air pollution do not stay in the project studies — they are lived by generations of citizens WHO HAVE THE RIGHT TO SAY NO TO HARMFUL PROJECTS. With megafarms, they note, we still have the chance to stop the damage before it happens.

trackers.name: Ured za udruge — the state office that publishes every open call, and trains you to apply
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES FOR AN ASSOCIATION, and all of it is free: the government's Office for Associations provides information about CURRENT CALLS for financing associations FROM THE STATE BUDGET AND FROM EUROPEAN UNION FUNDS; acts as National Contact Point for the EU citizens, equality, rights and values programme; provides TECHNICAL SUPPORT TO APPLICANTS and to those implementing contracted projects; and runs informative and educational activities about the programme FOR USERS THROUGHOUT CROATIA. A state office whose job is telling associations where the money is, and helping them apply for it, is the first call before any grant round — and this file has recorded the same shape in Slovenia's CNVOS and Moldova's civic portal. AND WHAT ELSE THE PAGE POINTS TO: it sets out what support associations can get from state bodies and public institutions, AND WHERE THEY CAN OBTAIN FREE SERVICES OF INFORMATION, ADVICE AND TRAINING, and it helps in finding answers to other questions about cooperation between the state and associations. Alongside it sits a Council for Civil Society Development. It is also where the environmental fund's own calls for associations are announced — so one page covers both the money and the help to reach it.

trackers.name: The ministry's list of COUNTY nature-protection institutions — one per county, with address and phone
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the ministry's own directory of PUBLIC INSTITUTIONS FOR MANAGING THE PROTECTED NATURAL VALUES OF THE COUNTIES — and it publishes, for each one, the full institution name, A STREET ADDRESS, POSTAL CODE AND TOWN, A TELEPHONE NUMBER, often a fax, AN EMAIL ADDRESS AND A WEBSITE. Croatia had 31 filed entries; this is the sheet that reaches every county. Croatia has a separate nature-protection institution for each county, and the ministry publishes all their addresses on one page — so a community never has to write to the capital about a local site. WHO IS ON IT, from the entries visible: institutions for a coastal county, a mountain-and-coast county, a northern county with its own name, a Danube-plain county agency, a Slavonian county, an Istrian institution with its own brand name, a Karlovac institution with another, TWO further branded institutions, and a separate PUBLIC INSTITUTION FOR MANAGING THE NATURAL VALUES OF THE CITY OF ZAGREB at a named park address. Even the capital city has its own institution, run out of a park — the list makes no exceptions. Several counties operate under working names rather than the formal title, which is why the ministry list matters: it maps the brand to the county.

trackers.name: JU Priroda Varaždinske županije — every member of staff, by name, role and mobile
trackers.desc: WHAT ONE COUNTY INSTITUTION PUBLISHES, and it is the most complete staff list in this file: the DIRECTOR, an EXPERT ADVISER, an EXPERT ASSOCIATE ON PROJECTS, an EXPERT ASSOCIATE, A NATURE WARDEN (čuvar prirode), and a projects associate — each with their own name, qualification, DIRECT TELEPHONE OR MOBILE NUMBER AND PERSONAL EMAIL. A named nature warden with a mobile number is the person who goes and looks at the site, and this file has looked for that role across forty countries. THE INSTITUTION: established with the aim of MANAGING THE PROTECTED AREAS of its county, with its OIB, third-floor street address, two landlines and a fax published. Within its remit it publishes data on the protected parts of nature, and explains that the ecological network is a system of mutually connected areas, and that nature and parts of nature are of interest to the Republic of Croatia and enjoy its particular protection. AND WHAT IT HOLDS, useful as precedent: the first proclaimed REGIONAL PARK in Croatia, which extends through FIVE Croatian counties, and the only preserved fossil volcano in Croatia, a site of the semi-precious stone agate. A designation that crosses five counties shows a site does not have to sit inside one administrative boundary to be protected.

trackers.name: Pravo prvokupa in protected areas — the state gets first refusal, and can SUE to void a sale
trackers.desc: THE RULE: owners who hold property in NATIONAL PARKS AND NATURE PARKS AND IN STRICT AND SPECIAL RESERVES, and decide to sell them, WILL HAVE TO OFFER THEM TO THE STATE FIRST. For other protected areas — regional parks among them — the right of first refusal goes to the counties or the City of Zagreb. AND HOW IT RUNS: an owner deciding to sell must set out their offer WITH THE PRICE AND THE CONDITIONS OF SALE. The state and the counties must respond WITHIN 90 DAYS of receiving the written offer; if they do not accept within that period, the owner may sell UNDER THE TERMS OF THE OFFER. AND THE ENFORCEMENT, which is the part that matters to a community watching a sale go through: if owners BYPASS the right of first refusal, the state or the counties CAN SUE THEM AND SEEK ANNULMENT OF THE PURCHASE CONTRACT — within 90 days of learning that the contract was concluded, and at the latest WITHIN FIVE YEARS of its conclusion. A sale inside a protected area that skipped the state's first refusal can be undone up to five years later, so a community that discovers one has a body to report it to rather than a fait accompli.

trackers.name: The prvokup order and the 30-day noticeboard — how a Croatian sale must be announced
trackers.desc: WHERE FARMLAND SALES SURFACE: the agricultural land act prescribes a STRICT ORDER of persons with the right of first refusal on the sale of ARABLE LAND, VINEYARDS, ORCHARDS, OLIVE GROVES AND PASTURES. The procedure runs THROUGH THE LOCAL SELF-GOVERNMENT UNIT, WHICH PUBLISHES THE OFFER ON ITS NOTICEBOARD FOR 30 DAYS. Thirty days on a municipal noticeboard is the window in which a community learns that fields around it are for sale. AND THE TIE-BREAK: if several persons of the same rank accept the offer, priority goes to the one with THE LARGER AREA OF ADJOINING LAND. AND THE FORMALITIES THAT DECIDE WHETHER A SALE STANDS: the written notice is the foundation of the whole procedure. It must be delivered BY REGISTERED POST WITH RETURN RECEIPT or handed over personally against signature, so that the start of the 30-day period is precisely established, and must carry the exact description with cadastral parcel number. The holder answers in writing — SILENCE COUNTS AS REFUSAL; if they accept, the contract is concluded on the same terms, and the owner cannot afterwards raise the price or change the payment conditions. For registered cultural property the state's own deadline is 60 DAYS, and FAILURE TO NOTIFY THE STATE RENDERS THE CONTRACT NULL.

trackers.name: What the Croatian fund gives associations — and the SLIDING SCALE by where you are
trackers.desc: WHO CAN APPLY, and the bar is far lower than Slovenia's: the tender is intended for civil society organisations, that is ASSOCIATIONS, WHICH ARE ENTERED IN THE REGISTER OF ASSOCIATIONS AND HAVE OPERATED FOR AT LEAST ONE YEAR in the Republic of Croatia, and which are directed at work in one of the fields: ECOLOGY, ENVIRONMENTAL AND NATURE PROTECTION, PROTECTION OF THE SEA AND THE MARINE ENVIRONMENT, CLIMATE CHANGE, SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT AND SPELEOLOGY. One year of existence, against two in Slovenia — so a group registered at the first sign of a threat can be eligible by the time the next round opens. AND THE AMOUNTS, from the fund's own tender documents: one round put 6 MILLION KUNA to civil society; another set total available funds of 1,200,000 KUNA with a maximum of 200,000 KUNA per project; an earlier one approved donations of 10,000 to 80,000 KUNA per project; and a recent call caps an applicant at 30,000 EURO. AND THE SLIDING SCALE THAT DECIDES YOUR SHARE: the fund pays UP TO 80% of justified costs for projects in AREAS OF SPECIAL STATE CONCERN and the first group of islands, 60% in MOUNTAINOUS AREAS and the second island group, and 40% in the remaining areas — and the 80% rate also applies to projects carried out for the PROTECTION, MAINTENANCE, CONSERVATION AND MANAGEMENT OF PROTECTED PARTS OF NATURE. Work inside a protected area is funded at the highest rate wherever it is.

trackers.name: Federal Data Protection & Information Commissioner (FDPIC)
trackers.desc: Federal Data Protection & Information Commissioner (FDPIC) — Switzerland’s independent data-protection / information commissioner, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Swiss Federal Supreme Court
trackers.desc: Official published decisions of Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court. · Find here: the leading decisions and judgments of the Swiss Federal Supreme Court.

trackers.name: Entscheidsuche.ch
trackers.desc: Free open-data portal searching all published decisions of Swiss courts at every instance — federal and cantonal. · Find here: a free aggregator of Swiss federal and cantonal court decisions (Entscheidsuche).

trackers.name: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)
trackers.desc: Switzerland's independent FOI authority — arbitration board for access to official documents under the Freedom of Information Act; mediates and issues recommendations on refused requests.

trackers.name: Pro Natura — Verbandsbeschwerderecht
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: Switzerland's oldest nature-protection organisation, holder of the Verbandsbeschwerderecht and steward of over 700 nature reserves. Under article 12 NHG and article 55 USG a closed list of about thirty organisations, designated by the Federal Council, can challenge permits for projects affecting nature — and their appeals succeed three to four times more often than private parties'. WHO IT SUITS: you, only through them. The right was deliberately built NOT to be a popular action: it is restricted to bodies active across the whole of Switzerland, purely non-commercial in purpose, and working in that legal field for at least ten years, which excludes any committee formed for a single case. So take your project to a listed organisation early. Two traps: in several cantons an Einsprache during the permit procedure is a precondition for appealing later, and since 2024 the right no longer reaches small residential projects inside the building zone. CHECK A 2024 RESTRICTION BEFORE RELYING ON THE APPEAL RIGHT: for building projects under 400 square metres of FLOOR area inside the building zone, nature and landscape organisations can no longer insist on compliance with environmental law. Pro Natura records this as part of increasing efforts to weaken protection, previously aimed at building outside the zone. The threshold is floor area, not site area — a small building on a large plot may still fall below it, so check the current position before relying on this route. AND SIX ORGANISATIONS HOLD THE RIGHT, NOT ONE: WWF Schweiz, Pro Natura, Greenpeace, BirdLife Schweiz, VCS and SES, with the Stiftung für Landschaftsschutz and Schweizer Heimatschutz alongside — if one declines your case the others exist, and VCS covers transport projects, which is the right door for a road or terminal.

trackers.name: Federal Patent Court of Switzerland
