The movement records having formed program committees on different environmental issues, comprised of experts and activists, which study the issue and organise campaigns in the form of seminars, conferences, public rallies, deputations, memoranda, press conferences and publications; records three strategic issues as rivers, energy, and ethnic minorities and the environment of their habitat; and records that it builds connections with local pro-environment organisations that already exist and helps such organisations develop in areas where they do not exist now. For a community with no organisation behind it, that last sentence is the offer. Its structure and its membership discipline are documented. Published material records the movement launched in 2000, converted from an earlier community-based group formed in the capital in 1997, with a central committee, an executive committee, eighteen program committees and fourteen sub-committees, and about five hundred members after removing some three hundred and fifty inactive ones; and records that it has to fend off membership requests from officials who want to use its name for personal benefit. It records financial support coming from its members, and charity from citizens and national organisations, and gives its street address, telephone numbers and email. That funding base is what keeps it independent of the projects it opposes. District committees and named local conveners exist, and they can be found. A waterkeeper network's member list records individuals by river, each with their other roles — one recorded as convener of the movement's district committee, a former elected sub-district vice chairman, and a member of a district river saving committee; another as the movement's general secretary in a named city and member secretary of a swamp forest protection committee. What it actually does is on the record, case by case. Its activities pages record a press conference demanding a stop to encroachment and construction of a multi-storey building on a named river, recommendations sent to a deputy commissioner on the demarcation of four rivers around the capital, a team visiting a road development project where a stated number of trees were at issue, and joint actions with named local committees. Read this with the environmental lawyers' legal cell, the land rights organisation, the landless people's organisation and the ecologically critical areas entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Kapaeeng Foundation — five named programmes including legal aid and fact-finding, published on-site inquiry reports, and a running record of eviction and land acquisition cases with numbers
trackers.desc: A human rights organisation for indigenous peoples publishes its programmes, and legal aid is one of them. The organisation lists five programmes — capacity building; documentation and information sharing; fact-finding and media advocacy; human rights; and legal aid and support — and records its human rights work as including publication of a human rights report on indigenous peoples, networking with indigenous peoples' and human rights organisations at local, national, regional and international level, and capacity building of indigenous organisations and communities. Fact-finding and legal aid in the same organisation is what a community facing eviction needs. It publishes the record, which is how individual cases stop being invisible. Its own listings record specific matters with numbers: a government move to acquire 9,145 acres of land in a named area; obstruction of shifting cultivation threatening the livelihood of 80 indigenous families; a boundary agreement threatening 90 families; 6,000 tea workers facing eviction threat due to establishment of a special economic zone; 100 families living in fear of eviction with a village head arrested; a food crisis affecting at least 500 families in 45 villages; and a World Bank-funded project starting without meaningful consultation with the region's institutions and indigenous peoples. It records a civic rights team denied access for an on-site inquiry into alleged land grabbing and eviction, and publishes on-site inquiry reports and a watch bulletin among its outputs. Its published demands name the instruments a community can invoke. Its report launch records demands to develop legal mechanisms against illegal land dispossession, form a separate land commission for plain-land indigenous peoples for restoration of dispossessed land, give constitutional recognition to indigenous peoples per ratified international instruments, and have the national human rights commission investigate violations regularly; and its documentation records posters published in Bangla on free, prior and informed consent under the international declaration. Its address, telephone and email are published. Read this with the land rights organisation, the landless people's organisation, the acquisition compensation and the legal cell entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: BLAST — free legal aid in land and constitutional matters through district unit offices, a panel of about 2,600 pro bono lawyers, and published email addresses for each district office
trackers.desc: Land cases are inside its remit, and the offices are in the districts. The trust records providing legal advice and representation at all levels of the justice system, in particular to those living in poverty or facing disadvantage or discrimination, with services including mediation, litigation and legal rights training delivered through its head office, nineteen unit offices and two project offices across the country; other published accounts give twenty and twenty-one district offices, four university law clinics, fifteen community-based hubs and a law clinic in slum areas. It records itself as the only legal services group to provide advice and assistance in criminal, family, civil, land and constitutional law matters. For a household facing acquisition or eviction, land and constitutional work in the same free service is the combination that matters. The pro bono panel and the mediation numbers show the capacity behind it. Published description records a network of more than 2,600 lawyers, an enlisted panel providing services on a pro bono basis with a nominal honorarium alongside its own staff lawyers, paralegals and researchers at headquarters and each district unit; another account gives the panel as about 2,300. It records facilitating alternative dispute resolution through mediation for family, land, financial, petty criminal and labour matters, and having settled 62,263 disputes across the country to June 2023, noting that mediation allows individuals and families to quickly recover land, assets, maintenance, dower or arrears of wages. Its structure puts local bar leaders in charge locally, and its contacts are published. Its own history records it designed to ensure local involvement and decentralised leadership, with elected leaders of each district bar association heading district management committees, and civil society members in its advisory committees, established in 1993 with a board of trustees including eminent jurists, lawyers, professionals and former judges of the Supreme Court. A published listing gives separate email addresses for named district and project offices, and its head office address, email and telephone numbers are published. It records having conducted over 175 investigations of human rights violations used to support litigation. Read this with the environmental lawyers' legal cell, the land rights organisation, the indigenous rights foundation and the acquisition entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Ain o Salish Kendra — an investigation unit that produces evidence for litigation, seventeen named units including mediation, litigation and outreach, and fact-finding training for grassroots activists
trackers.desc: The evidence unit is separate from the litigation unit, and it says what its output is for. The organisation records establishing its investigation unit in May 1994, considering the importance of verified information, data, documents or reports, and records that unit as investigating and reporting on human rights violations; it states that its investigations of violations are a very useful source for litigation, advocacy, campaign or any other remedial purpose. It records the unit as also engaged in community mobilisation against any human rights violation and as providing fact-finding training for human rights activists working at grassroots level. For a community whose complaint will stand or fall on documentation, a unit that trains villagers to do the fact-finding is the resource behind every later step. Its units are named, which tells a caller which desk to ask for. Published description records seventeen units and one component, listing investigation; documentation; publication and communications; legal advocacy and policy reform; media and international advocacy; mediation and rapid response; litigation; outreach; a halfway home; psycho-social and counselling; human rights awareness; gender and social justice; training; child rights; administration; finance and accounts; and planning, monitoring and evaluation. Its registration and standing are on record, and so is its position on eviction. The organisation records itself as a national legal aid and human rights organisation providing legal and social support to the disempowered, registered with the registrar of joint stock companies under the societies registration legislation in 1986 and with the NGO affairs bureau under the foreign donation regulation ordinance in 1993, and accorded special consultative status with the United Nations economic and social council in 1998. Its shelter pages record that repeated evictions without ensuring alternative resettlement plans, and failure to protect public and private lands from illegal encroachments by land developers and grabbers, show the country falling far behind its commitments, that the concerned authorities have not complied with existing laws and rules, and that human rights organisations and citizens' groups have taken legal initiatives to prevent forcible eviction and land grabbing, with the judiciary responding positively. Its street address, mobile, telephone and email are published. Read this with the legal aid trust, the environmental lawyers' legal cell, the indigenous rights foundation and the land rights organisation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Committees of Concerned Citizens — local volunteer watchdog groups with published membership rules and a land remit, the youth groups attached, and the information-desk campaigns they run
trackers.desc: Local volunteer watchdog committees exist with a published constitution, and land is inside their remit. The chapter records the committees as groups of citizens with high credibility, integrity, social acceptability and leadership capacity to inform, motivate and mobilise citizens in challenging corruption and promoting integrity in service delivery at local levels, working voluntarily and non-partisan to promote social accountability in key public service delivery institutions such as education, health, local government and land. A community whose problem is a land office rather than a developer has a structure aimed at exactly that. The rules are specific, which is what makes them copyable. It records committee membership as ranging from 9 to 21 members from diverse professional groups including a representation of women; a president elected from the members for a two-year term subject to yearly review, with two vice-presidents, one of whom must be a woman; and issue-based sub-committees of 7 to 11 members, whose president sits on the main committee while other sub-committee members can be from outside it. It records eligibility as a person of high integrity free from any allegation of corruption, politically non-partisan with no direct or formal involvement in partisan political activity, and a permanent citizen and resident of the committee's area. The support arrangement is stated, and so is who decides. It records that once a committee is formed it takes over all responsibilities and determines its programmatic priorities, with the chapter providing only technical and financial support — the committee itself devising strategies, preparing plans, budgeting and implementing programmes. Published material records a network of 45 committees across eight divisions, with earlier accounts giving 36 committees in 34 of the country's 64 districts, and a volunteer base of more than 5,000. Youth groups run the information-request side. The chapter records 61 youth groups, 45 working under the committees, for people aged 15 to 25, whose activities include information disclosure services aimed at enforcement of the right to information legislation, including information fairs and training for information seeking, alongside study circles and campaigns. Read this with the information commission, the environment movement, the land rights organisation and the legal aid trust entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Sundarbans district society and the Deputy Commissioner's NGO portal — a Khulna-based organisation working at village and union level, and the district register that lists who works where
trackers.desc: A district-based society works at village scale in the mangrove belt, and its address is published. It records itself as a community-based non-profit, non-government and development organisation committed to maintaining ecological balance and creating harmony between humans and nature, registered as an NGO from the government's NGO affairs bureau, established to address the adverse impacts of global warming, unsustainable use of natural resources, drinking water crisis, mangrove ecosystem and biodiversity destruction, increasing use of dirty energy, gender inequity and human rights violation. Published description records work since 2010 across environment and ecosystem, disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation, clean and solar energy, livelihoods, water and sanitation, wildlife conservation and protection, and women and child rights, with more than 40 projects completed, and records it working hand in hand with local communities, respecting indigenous knowledge, culture and ecological wisdom. It publishes its house, road, area, city and postcode with telephone and email. The district administration keeps a register of who works where. A district portal published from the Deputy Commissioner's office of that district, with a contact email, profiles organisations and gives their project addresses down to village, union, sub-district and district, along with the networks and forums each belongs to and links to its projects; that portal is served over plain http, so treat the address with care. For a community that wants to know which organisations already operate in its own union rather than nationally, a district register kept by the district administration is the shortest route. Its site-level projects and its awards are both recorded. The portal records a solar village project at a named village, union and sub-district as a model case of renewable energy and environment-friendly sustainable development near the mangrove forest; and published listings record a divisional environmental award in five consecutive years, a national environment award, an energy globe national award, a top-twenty district development award and an international prize. Read this with the committees of concerned citizens, the legal aid trust, the environment movement and the land rights organisation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Waterkeepers Bangladesh and its local coordinators — named river waterkeepers, coordinators listed by upazila and district, and a coastal keeper who was also an elected upazila vice chairman
trackers.desc: Local coordinators are listed by name against their own sub-district and district. The organisation's local coordinators page lists people against places including a coastal upazila in one district, three separate coastal upazilas in another district, and named upazilas in two further coastal districts. A named person in your own sub-district is the shortest possible route into a national water network. The river keepers are named by river, not by region. Published material records the organisation conducting operations to protect rivers through four named river keepers — for a capital river, two regional rivers and a river bordering the mangrove forest — and records it as administered by a named non-governmental, not-for-profit organisation. Its members' page records one keeper as convener of the national environment movement's district committee, a former elected vice chairman of an upazila council, and general secretary of a citizens' good governance body — a single contact who sits in the district environmental movement, the elected sub-district council and a governance watchdog at once. The organisation invites exactly the contact a community needs to make. Its contact page states that it wants to hear from people who have questions about our work, or want to find out how to join our growing alliance of citizens working to protect our water bodies, or want to voice your concern about pollution and/or illegal activities into the rivers and surrounding watershed, and publishes a house, road, block and housing society address in the capital, two telephone numbers and an email address, alongside a named coordinator. Its team page names a coordinator, a head of finance, administration and human resources, a head of research and implementation, a finance and accounts officer and a programme officer. Read this with the environment movement, the district NGO portal, the committees of concerned citizens and the legal aid trust entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: District legal aid offices and the upazila and union committees beneath them — an office inside every district judge court, a named officer with a published room location, and village-level committees that collect applications
trackers.desc: Every district has a legal aid office inside the district judge's court, and one publishes its room. A district judiciary site records the office of the district legal aid officer at the district judge court, publishes an official email, and gives its location as the west side of the third floor of the chief judicial magistrate court building, second button of the elevator, with a social media page for its activities. A floor and a lift button is the level of detail that gets someone through the door. Committees exist below the district, and their job is collecting applications. Published description records the state programme as run under a 2000 legal aid statute through the national organisation, with 64 district legal aid committees maintaining the legal aid fund allocated by government, spent for poor litigants upon their applications; and records that upazila and union legal aid committees were formed under a 2011 regulation, with the main function of collecting and receiving applications for legal aid and sending them to the district committees. It records the organisation having printed posters, pamphlets and leaflets and distributed them at district, upazila and union levels. A union committee that takes the form and forwards it removes the journey to the district town. Where else to go is listed, and so is the staffing gap. Published reporting records access points as district legal aid offices housed within district judge court buildings across the country, a supreme court legal aid office, labour law legal aid cells at labour court buildings in two named cities, and union legal aid committees at grassroots level, alongside named non-governmental providers. A justice data service records that each district office is run by a district legal aid officer, that at one date only 27 districts had a full-time officer, and that government mediations can only be conducted by offices with a full-time officer. Eligibility is by category as well as income. Published description records entitlement for any poor person, and specifically for people receiving old age allowance, women holding a named support card, victims of trafficking and acid attacks, insolvent widows, abandoned or distressed women, disabled people and poor detainees. Read this with the riverkeepers and coordinators, the district NGO portal, the committees of concerned citizens and the legal aid trust entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Union village courts — a five-member bench each side helps pick, filing fees of two and four taka, no lawyer needed, and the union councils where every one of them sits
trackers.desc: Each side names two of the five people who will decide, and one of them must be a council member. A union council's own page records that the court is constituted with five members — a chairman and two members nominated by each party — one of the two nominated by each party being a member of the union council concerned, with the council chairman as the court's chairman. Another union council records that if the chairman cannot act or his impartiality is questioned, the sub-district executive officer nominates another council member who has not been nominated by any party, and that where a party cannot nominate a council member because of partisanship, another person may be nominated with the chairman's permission. For a household in a village quarrel, choosing two of the five deciders — and having a route when the chairman is not neutral — is the practical core. Filing costs a few taka and no lawyer is needed. The same page records that people across the union's jurisdiction can file by paying two taka in a criminal case and four taka in a civil case, that there is no need for a lawyer, and that no other court can accept a matter falling wholly within the village court's jurisdiction. It records the compensation ceiling as raised from 5,000 to 25,000 taka by the 2006 legislation, with formation, management, scrutiny of cases, issuance of decrees and preservation of records all identified as council activities. What these courts actually hear includes property and crops. Published description records the subject matter as including stolen property, recovery of movable property, compensation for destroyed property and loss of crops due to livestock, and lists criminal matters including criminal trespass, harmful acts and damage up to a stated ceiling. Published material records the courts as existing in every union under the 2006 legislation, and records a scaling programme covering 1,080 unions across 154 sub-districts in 30 districts, with a recommendation that each council building have a separate designated space for the village court, allowing a court bench and case records. Read this with the district legal aid offices, the riverkeepers and coordinators, the district NGO portal and the committees of concerned citizens entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Union and upazila standing committees — thirteen or more committees of five to seven members that ordinary residents can sit on, seventeen at sub-district level, and the candid record of how few actually meet
trackers.desc: Every union council is required to form standing committees, and residents can be on them. Published analysis records that under the 2009 local government legislation there is a provision of 13 standing committees in the union council to support the council in ensuring transparency, accountability and people's participation in planning and implementing, and that each council is supposed to form at least 13 standing committees on different issues, including education, health, family planning, social welfare and disaster management, and agriculture, fisheries and livestock. Other published description records that every union council must form 13 or more committees of five to seven members, covering areas including finance and establishment, audit and accounts, and taxation and collection. A committee of five to seven people, on subjects including audit and taxation, is a seat a resident can occupy. The sub-district tier has seventeen, under a named section. Published commentary records that under the sub-district council legislation standing committees serve as a crucial tool for preserving the openness and accountability of the sub-district council, with a numbered section providing for their creation, and records that the law gives clear instructions for the creation of 17 committees. Another account records the sub-district council as responsible for local development planning and implementation, health services, environment management, training local leaders, and coordinating offices within the sub-district area. Why they matter is that they can discuss anything. Published commentary records that as the committees are not bound to obey any formal law, they can discuss anything and submit the report to the council, and that they have the full potential to inspect the overall functions of the union council and the sub-district council. The candid failure rate is on record. The same analysis records that these committees are not active in about 90 per cent of the councils, because elected chairmen and members are not properly aware of or interested in their functions; and commentary records that the government did not allocate the money necessary for the committees to function, with meeting costs met from a small contingency line. Read this with the ward assembly and open budget session, the union village courts, the district legal aid offices and the committees of concerned citizens entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Mouza headmen, para karbaris and the hill district councils — a customary justice tier with no court fee, a council that supervises the land staff, and a land commission whose 23,000 pending cases have produced no decisions
trackers.desc: The customary tier hears disputes with no court fee, and the appeal route is named. Published research records that under the 1900 manual the headman of a mouza can give a decision in a dispute among the residents of the mouza, may fine up to a stated small amount, and may retain stolen property until further order of the deputy commissioner; that the circle chief has the same power and sits above the headman in the hierarchy; that they conduct dispute resolution according to social norms; and that from their decision an appeal lies to the deputy commissioner, with no court fee required. It records mouzas as demarcated between one and twenty square miles, each with a headman, and records that the post is not hereditary though a headman's son gets preference. It records that the country's largest legal aid organisation covers 61 districts but excludes this region — which is why the customary tier matters here more than anywhere else in this file. The named office-holders are counted. Published reporting records seven headmen and 340 para heads under one circle chief, three headmen and 165 under another, and four headmen and 12 under a third, and records those office-holders mobilising people from their own administrative units to submit petitions to the land commission after a 2016 amendment. The council supervises the land staff, and the commission has stalled. The 1997 accord records that the council can supervise and control the functions of the headman, chainman, amin, surveyor, kanungo and assistant commissioner for land. Published description records that the 2016 amendment recognised customary rights and confirmed that land disputes would be resolved in consonance with the law, custom and practice in force in the region, and that an earlier change replaced the chairperson's unilateral decision power with a quorum of the chairperson and three other members. It records the commission as unable to work for want of rules, with 23,000 cases pending and no decisions given. Read this with the indigenous rights foundation, the land rights association, the district legal aid offices and the union village courts entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Cross Cultural Foundation (CrCF)
trackers.desc: Founded in 2002, The Cross Cultural Foundation (CrCF) is a Thailand-based nonprofit foundation working to ensure equal access to justice for all people in Thailand by monitoring and investigating human rights abuses; advocating for and promoting a vision of justice that empowers people to understand and realize their rights; and the direct protection of human rights through legal strategies. Within this integrated purview, CrCF has focused on initiatives that enhance access to justice for Thai citizens as well as indigenous and minority populations, including migrant workers, refugees or defenders in exile, stateless persons, and victims of conflict; the prevention of torture of human rights defenders; and providing free legal aid and tangible assistance to vulnerable groups in Thailand’s southern border provinces. We work closely with international human rights networks to empower and include indigenous and minority populations.

trackers.name: National Statistical Office of Thailand
trackers.desc: Thailand's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Thailand.

trackers.name: พ.ร.บ.ป่าชุมชน 2562 — community forests, after a 26-year campaign
trackers.desc: THAILAND'S COMMUNITY FOREST ACT, published in the Royal Gazette on 29 May 2019 — 8 chapters, 104 sections. Its purpose is to promote communities acting together with the state in conserving, restoring, managing, maintaining and taking benefit from natural resources, environment and biodiversity. CHECK WHICH PARTS WERE IN FORCE WHEN: most of the Act applied the day after publication, but chapters 4–8 and sections 97–103 took effect 180 days later — so older commentary may describe a different legal position. The Forest Department publishes the Act and its subordinate instruments with English versions available for download. CIVIL SOCIETY PUSHED FOR THIS LAW FOR MORE THAN 26 YEARS — worth knowing both as the honest timescale of statutory change and because it means the movement infrastructure around community forestry in Thailand is deep and long-established. A national policy committee chaired at Deputy Prime Minister level now drives establishment of community forests, builds the countrywide community forest network as the supporting mechanism, and promotes community forests as carbon dioxide sinks under Thailand's greenhouse gas targets.

trackers.name: Check the subordinate law exists — and the no-permission planting route
trackers.desc: THE ACT ALONE MAY NOT REACH YOUR FOREST. Subordinate legislation is what makes it operable, and some was still incomplete: a ministerial regulation designating valuable trees (ไม้ทรงคุณค่า) was issued in 2564, but the royal decree on establishing community forests in other state areas was still being procured for study and drafting, and the ministerial regulation designating conservation forest areas was still in coordination between the national parks and forestry departments over land being prepared as national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. So if your forest sits in a conservation area or on ‘other state land’, check whether the enabling instrument yet exists before building a plan around the Act. AND A ROUTE THAT AVOIDS PERMISSION ENTIRELY: a Thai forest-law briefing records that where a project is carried out jointly with the Royal Forest Department — planting for the state and sharing carbon, with the private party controlling and maintaining — permission is not required, and the law was being amended so planting inside reserved forests would not require permission either. Check the current position before assuming you need a permit for restoration planting.

trackers.name: กองทุนสิ่งแวดล้อม — a village committee can be the applicant
trackers.desc: THAILAND'S ENVIRONMENTAL FUND, established in the Ministry of Finance under the 1992 National Environmental Quality Act as a financial mechanism on the polluter pays principle. TWO INSTRUMENTS, AND THE SPLIT DECIDES WHICH IS YOURS: loans go to the private sector, state enterprises and local administrative organisations; grants (เงินอุดหนุน) go to government agencies, local administrative organisations, public organisations and environmental NGOs. Civil society is on the grant side. THE ELIGIBLE LIST IS UNUSUALLY BROAD: alongside registered environmental NGOs it names the village volunteer network for protection of natural resources and environment (ทสม.), tambon community organisation councils, village committees (คณะกรรมการหมู่บ้าน), state educational institutions and local natural environment and arts conservation units. A community body that is not a registered NGO can therefore be the applicant — rare in this map, where most funds demand a registered legal person. Support follows 6 framework directions under section 23(4), published for the 2566–2570 budget period, with a guidance manual on developing proposals.

trackers.name: Get into the provincial plan first — the condition on Thai grants
trackers.desc: THE STEP THAT COMES BEFORE THE APPLICATION. A project seeking a grant must be included in the provincial-level action plan for environmental quality management under section 39 of the 1992 Act — and a local administrative organisation applying must already have allocated matching revenue in the proportion set by National Environment Board announcement. So the first move is getting your project into the provincial plan, not drafting a proposal. That is a months-ahead, relationship-based task at provincial level, and a strong proposal outside the plan will not be funded. WHAT HAS BEEN FUNDED: forest fire management, and an organic agriculture network project to protect natural resources in a watershed headwater area in Chiang Mai — so headwater and fire work are both established categories. Separate approval procedures exist for promotion projects, private-sector loans and wastewater or waste facility construction. CONTACT BY SUBJECT: natural resources 02-265-6593, environment and pollution 02-265-6591, climate change 02-265-6598, email envifund@onep.go.th. An English section exists.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: EnLAW มูลนิธินิติธรรมสิ่งแวดล้อม — legal help for communities a project has not hit yet
trackers.desc: Its stated purpose is legal assistance to people and communities affected, or who may be affected, by pollution, environmental, natural-resource and health problems — the 'may be' is the part worth reading twice, because it means you do not have to wait for damage before approaching. Founded in 2544 BE (2001), it litigates and also trains communities to use their own participation rights, under the framing of building environmental justice in Thai society through legal and human-rights mechanisms. Manager and co-founder: สุภาภรณ์ มาลัยลอย. It is one office in Bangkok, not a branch network — 7 Soi Lat Phrao Wang Hin 32 Yaek 6, Lat Phrao Wang Hin Road, Lat Phrao, Bangkok 10230 — so a community in the provinces is dealing with a small team at a distance, and the Thai-language pages are substantially fuller than anything in English. The more useful part may be the network it names, which multiplies the doors available in Thailand: ศูนย์พิทักษ์และฟื้นฟูสิทธิชุมชนท้องถิ่น, มูลนิธิศูนย์ข้อมูลชุมชน (Community Resource Centre Foundation), มูลนิธิบูรณะนิเวศ (EARTH), สมาคมนักกฎหมายคุ้มครองสิทธิ์และสิ่งแวดล้อม, สมาคมนักกฎหมายสิทธิมนุษยชน and ศูนย์ทนายความเพื่อสิทธิมนุษยชน. If EnLAW cannot take the case, ask which of those can.

trackers.name: มูลนิธิสืบนาคะเสถียร Seub Nakhasathien Foundation — stopped a dam by supplying the alternative
trackers.desc: The thing that worked was not the objection. By April 2012 the foundation had written to government, run academic forums and produced media against the Mae Wong dam for years, and the project kept advancing. What changed it was a walk from the forest to Bangkok led by Sasin Chalermlarp and joined by tens of thousands, which forced the expert committee to suspend its consideration of the EHIA, and the appointment of a technical committee on engineering, economics and wildlife that concluded the EHIA was defective and the scheme should be stopped. The part to copy is what came after. Alongside opposing the dam, the foundation and its network put forward an alternative water management proposal for the same catchment — and local agencies subsequently took that proposal up and carried it out, which is what dissolved the argument that there was no other way to hold the water. The Royal Irrigation Department withdrew the EHIA from the Office of Natural Resources and Environmental Policy and Planning on 3 October 2017. The honest lesson is that none of it ended the matter. The EHIA had gone back before the water resources expert committee on 1 September 2017 after an earlier rejection, and the foundation describes its own position since as a watch without an end rather than a victory, because a shelved scheme here returns. Plan for years of monitoring after you win, and tell your own people that at the start rather than at the end. Its allies matter as much as its methods: the 2014 round of objections was joined by a student network and by the Engineering Institute of Thailand, whose statement that the water should be managed differently carried weight an environmental group's could not. Find the professional body whose own members would have to build the thing. The site is in Thai.

trackers.name: MRC prior consultation (PNPCA) — the six-month window on any Mekong mainstream project
trackers.desc: Any project proposed for the Mekong mainstream triggers a six-month prior consultation across all four member countries, and there are regional and national stakeholder forums inside it. Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam are the members. The process begins when the proposing country's National Mekong Committee submits to the Commission, and the clock starts on the day the last Joint Committee member receives the submission forwarded by the Secretariat. Xayaburi started on 22 October 2010 and ran six months to a decision; Pak Beng's six-month milestone was marked in June 2017. Your entry point is your own National Mekong Committee, not the Secretariat in Vientiane. Each member country has one, it is the body that submits and receives, and it is the route by which a riverside community's evidence reaches the process. Inside the six months the Secretariat produces a Technical Review Report, external expert groups on fisheries and on sediments contribute analysis, the project is compared against the Commission's Preliminary Design Guidance, and regional and national stakeholder forums are held whose outcomes the Joint Committee considers alongside the technical review. Know the difference between the mainstream and a tributary, because it decides which process applies. A tributary hydropower project requires notification to the Joint Committee only; a mainstream project requires the full prior consultation with consensus sought among the four members. Twenty-eight tributary notifications had been received by June 2009, before any mainstream submission existed. And know what prior consultation is not. It is an inter-governmental process aimed at consensus on whether a project should proceed and under what conditions. It is not a veto and it has not stopped a mainstream dam. What Pak Beng produced was a Joint Committee statement calling on the Government of Lao PDR to make all reasonable efforts to address potential adverse transboundary impacts, and a Joint Action Plan for the period after the six months. Treat the six months as the window in which independent evidence enters an official record that outlives the decision, and plan the rest of the campaign around what that record enables. PNPCA is one of five sets of Commission procedural rules made under the 1995 Mekong Agreement, alongside those on water quality, data sharing, water use monitoring and water flow maintenance.

trackers.name: EARTH มูลนิธิบูรณะนิเวศ — community sampling with laboratory results, and a public pollution map
trackers.desc: This fills the category most communities discover they need too late: somebody who will take a sample and get it analysed. Working with Greenpeace Southeast Asia and residents of Map Ta Phut, the foundation set up a Thailand Bucket Brigade — a community air-sampling unit whose members collected samples in the industrial estate and sent them to a laboratory in the United States, with support from Global Community Monitor. The results identified volatile organic compounds including benzene, toluene and styrene, along with sulphide compounds. An independent number from an accredited laboratory is what turns a community's account of smells and illness into something a regulator and a court have to answer. That programme is a precedent rather than a standing service. It belongs to the early 2000s campaign at Map Ta Phut, so ask the foundation what sampling support it can offer now instead of assuming the brigade still runs. The method itself — community members collecting samples to a documented protocol and sending them for independent analysis — is reproducible anywhere and is the part to copy. Its standing public resource is the pollution map. The foundation publishes a map of industrial pollution sources alongside an archive of its own investigations, which is where to begin when establishing what is already on record about a site before commissioning anything new. It is one of the organisations EnLAW names in its network, and the two fit together: the foundation supplies the evidence, EnLAW takes the case. For a Thai community the sequence is to establish what the map already shows, get independent sampling done, then take the results to counsel. Nonthaburi office: 211/2 Soi Ngamwongwan 31 Yaek 12, Ngamwongwan Road, Mueang, Nonthaburi 11000, 02 952 5061, earth@earththailand.org. The site is Thai-first.

trackers.name: Smart EIA Plus — search the report, the monitoring returns, and the licence of whoever wrote it
trackers.desc: Three registers, and the second and third are the ones nobody thinks to open. The environment policy office's information centre lets anyone search initial examinations, full assessments and health-impact assessments and check the status of a report in the system; search the monitoring reports filed after approval; and search the register of licensed report preparers, including checking a preparer's licence. It also lists the reports currently submitted for consideration and the projects that have received approval. Monitoring returns being public answers the question most countries here leave open. The recurring gap elsewhere in this file is that nobody is obliged to check whether approval conditions are kept, or that the record is not reachable. Here the post-approval reports are searchable, so whether an operator has filed and what it filed are questions with published answers — which turns a condition into something arguable rather than something that exists only on paper. The person who wrote the report holds a licence, and you can verify it. Report preparers must be licensed and that register is searchable too. An assessment written by somebody whose licence is not in order is a different problem from an assessment whose conclusions you dispute, and it is a far quicker one to establish. You can also see who will decide. The division publishes the rosters of the expert review committees organised by sector — land and air infrastructure, water infrastructure, water resource development, industry and supporting utilities, petroleum, petrochemicals and chemicals, and others — so the committee that will consider a given project, and its membership, are knowable before the meeting rather than after it. The division also publishes the assessment legislation, the guidance on preparing reports and on reviewing them, and its material on public participation and on health impact assessment.

trackers.name: พอช. CODI — low-interest loans to a community cooperative to buy the land, not to individuals
trackers.desc: It lends to buy land, and it lends to the cooperative rather than to people. The community organisations development institute, a public body, supports communities financially by lending for land purchase and house construction at low interest over long repayment terms, alongside grants toward construction and shared infrastructure — and it approves the money through the housing cooperative the community itself establishes, not to individuals, with the cooperative's committee managing the project and the building work. That structure is the entry point rather than a detail: form the cooperative first, because there is nothing for the institute to approve until one exists. The community does the work, and that is the design. Residents form a committee, survey their own situation, problems and needs, form a savings group to provide their own capital, design the houses and the layout, and manage construction, with the institute supporting rather than delivering. A community that has already organised itself against a project has done a great deal of this, which makes the distance from campaign to application shorter than it looks. It negotiates with the landowner on the community's behalf. The institute describes itself as an intermediary supporting negotiations with landowning agencies of every type. Where the obstacle is who owns the ground rather than what it costs — which is the position most communities in this file find themselves in — that is the more valuable half of what is on offer. Terms, scale and an honest limit. Reported measures include suspension of principal and interest for six to twelve months for housing loan organisations in defined circumstances, and development lending at one per cent over three to five years, allocated by cooperative size, to repair a cooperative's finances and support members' livelihoods; the programme reports more than three thousand projects and hundreds of thousands of households over two decades. This is a housing security instrument rather than a conservation one, and the entry should say so — but where a community's answer to a development is to secure ownership of the ground it already lives on, it is the largest fund of its kind recorded in this research.

trackers.name: The pollution complaint system — and the four national lines it points you to instead of itself
trackers.desc: The system's own advice is to go to the body with direct authority. The pollution control department runs an online complaint reception system, and it tells complainants that in order to have the problem resolved quickly they may report directly to the agency that holds the power to act, then lists those agencies. That is unusual and useful: most complaint systems draw everything toward themselves. Here the instruction is that routing beats escalating, and a complaint sent to the body that can actually act moves faster than one sent upward. It publishes four national lines and two tiers of local office. Alongside the department's own hotline on 1650 and its switchboard numbers, the page lists the ministry's line on 1310, the interior ministry's line on 1567 and the government's line on 1111, together with the provincial offices of natural resources and environment and the sixteen regional environment and pollution control offices. Choose by who holds the power over the thing complained of rather than by who is nearest or best known. The online form has four steps, and the third is where complaints are won or lost. It asks for the complainant's details, the details of the problem being complained about, the location of the pollution problem, and then confirmation that the complaint has been received. Give the location as precisely as the form allows — coordinates, or a landmark and a distance — because the same instruction has now been recorded for every reporting channel in this file, and because a confirmation of receipt is worth keeping. Use it against the record the operator has already filed. The assessment monitoring system recorded elsewhere in this file shows what an operator reported about its own emissions and discharges; this system is where a discrepancy between that record and what people can see goes; and the provincial and regional offices are the bodies that hold both. A complaint that names the monitoring return it contradicts is a different document from one that reports a smell.

trackers.name: กองทุนยุติธรรม Justice Fund — pays the lawyer, the court fees and the travel, and stands surety for bail
trackers.desc: It pays the costs that quietly stop people attending their own case. The justice fund, established by the ministry of justice under its own 2015 act, assists people in conducting litigation by covering the lawyer's fee, the court fees, and other expenses including accommodation and travel. Those last two are named in the fund's own description of what it covers, and they matter: across this research the obstacle for a rural community is rarely the lawyer alone, it is the four hundred kilometres to the court and the night before the hearing. For bail, the fund office itself stands as surety. Where temporary release of an accused person or defendant is sought, the office acts as the guarantor and carries out the bail itself rather than reimbursing somebody else for doing so. Where a confrontation over land has produced charges — the turn this file records again and again — that is the difference between a village losing its people to remand and not. Apply at the provincial office, not the capital. Requests go to the provincial justice office in every province, or to the ministry's joint service centre in Bangkok, with a ministry hotline and an electronic service as further routes, and litigation assistance is applied for on a named form of which one original is required. Published guidance records that the committee or its chair considers the request and notifies the applicant of the result within seven days of consideration. The lawyer is on a contract the fund enforces. Where an engaged lawyer wilfully fails to appear or abandons the case, the fund office must terminate the engagement and demand return of the fees already paid within fifteen days, and the lawyer must reimburse the court fees where the loss resulted from that default. A community whose assigned lawyer goes quiet is therefore complaining to a body that holds the contract and the money, not asking a favour of the profession. Read this with the environmental law foundation and community cooperative lending entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: LandsMaps and the land office — check the parcel yourself, then book the counter
trackers.desc: You can look up the parcel yourself, for nothing. The lands department's parcel search returns, on a search by province, district and title deed number, the shape and position of the parcel, its area, the state of the ground as visible from satellite imagery and street view, the coordinates of the responsible land office and the appraised value for that parcel. For a community that has been told a plot is smaller, emptier or further from the river than it is, that check costs nothing and can be done before anybody is asked for anything. And the counter can be booked in advance. The department's own list of public tools includes queue booking for registration and survey applications, downloadable forms and a public service manual. A visit to request a certified copy or a survey is therefore something to arrange rather than something to queue for, which matters when the person going has to take a day off work to do it. The online view is preliminary, and this entry says so. Published guidance records that what the system shows is for initial checking only, that it cannot stand in place of the title document or of an actual survey, that the boundary drawn on a screen can deviate from the markers on the ground, and that appraised values change with the valuation cycle. Use the map to find a discrepancy, not to prove one: for proof, ask the land office for the copy, and where the boundary itself is disputed, for a survey. Allocation projects have their own record. The same set of tools includes a search system for land allocation projects and condominium developments, alongside the office of the private surveyors' commission. Where the development a community is facing is a registered allocation project, that registration exists as a separate record and is worth pulling in parallel with the parcel itself. Read this with the community forest registration and pollution complaint entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Official Information Act — an information centre you may inspect, and a board that must answer in thirty days
trackers.desc: Every agency keeps an information centre, and inspection is the right. Under the 1997 official information act state agencies must make specified categories of information available for public inspection at an official information centre, among them the decisions and rulings that have direct effect on private persons — permits, approvals, determinations and the outcomes of appeals arising from an agency's exercise of its powers — together with work manuals, the criteria and steps of public services, basic and statistical data and procurement records. A community does not have to begin by asking for a copy: it can go and look at what the agency is required to hold open. A complaint reaches a board with a thirty day clock. Anyone who considers that an agency has failed to publish the information the act requires, has not made information available for inspection, has refused disclosure, has delayed, or has not afforded reasonable convenience, may complain to the official information board, which must complete its consideration within thirty days of receiving the complaint, with any extension requiring reasons to be shown. Refusals go to a tribunal rather than back to the agency. An appeal against an order refusing disclosure, against an order refusing to hear the objection of an interested person, or against a refusal to correct personal information, is lodged through the chair of the board for decision by an information disclosure tribunal, with a fifteen day limit on the objection appeal. The act also provides that where other laws, rules or regulations conflict with it, this act applies instead. Nothing is released while an appeal runs, and there is a template for the document that supposedly does not exist. Where an appeal has been lodged the official may not disclose the information until the appeal period has passed, which protects an objecting party and delays a requester in equal measure. The board's office publishes model letters for exercising these rights, including one for complaining in order to have checked information which an agency has said does not exist. A published template for challenging a claim that no such document exists is rare, and it is the letter most often needed. Read this with the assessment records, the land parcel search, the justice fund and the community forest entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Prachatai — a national outlet whose stated beat is local communities, publishing in Thai and English
trackers.desc: Its stated beat is exactly the subject of this file. The outlet's published aims include providing reliable news relevant to Thai civil society, focusing news coverage on the problems, concerns, activities and accomplishments of local communities and of civil society movements and organisations, striving for the freedom and independence of Thai news media, and promoting active public participation in it. A dispute over a dam, a mine or a village's land is therefore on-beat here rather than a favour being asked, which is not true of most national newsrooms in any country in this file. It publishes in Thai and in English. The English edition carries underreported stories for readers outside the country, so a local case can reach the domestic audience and reach funders, buyers, lawyers and researchers abroad in the same week. Where the money or the customers behind a project are foreign, that second audience is the lever, and it costs a community nothing to ask for the story to run in both. The record shows it covers these cases. Recent reporting includes Indigenous communities and environmental defenders demanding action over water contamination in a river system fed by mining across the border, and public forums on Indigenous and forest policy. Before approaching, find whether a comparable case has already been covered and take that piece with you: a newsroom that has run the story once has a reporter who already understands the subject. What it is, and what it is not. It is an independent non-profit daily web newspaper founded in June 2004 by a group that included a senior member of the press council, a journalism lecturer, two senators, senior journalists and civil society leaders, registered since 2006 as a Thai foundation and supported by donations and reader subscriptions, with internships offered. It is a newsroom, not an advocate: it decides what to publish and when, and a published story is a pressure, not a remedy. Read this with the environmental law foundation, the community sampling organisation, the justice fund and the official information act entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: ธนาคารที่ดิน — a state body that buys the land first and lets you repay at three per cent, and registers people before they lose it
trackers.desc: It buys the land, and the household repays afterwards. Officials of the land bank institute describe the process from the start: people who need land but lack the money register with the institute, which pays to buy the land from a private owner up front; the applicants then repay it in instalments at three per cent a year, and are afterwards trained in mixed sufficiency farming, with monoculture excluded. For a household or a community about to lose the ground it lives on, an institution that fronts the purchase price is the rarest resource recorded anywhere in this file — most of the acquisition entries here describe organisations that buy land for conservation, not ones that buy it for the people already on it. Registration is open, by group or individually. The institute publishes registration forms for assistance with farmland under its sustainable land management project and its project on preventing and remedying the loss of land rights of farmers and the poor, including for those seeking land by lease or by hire purchase, in both group and individual categories. The group category matters: a village association can register as one applicant. Its stated first priority is stopping the loss before it happens. Its programme on preventing loss of rights assists low-income people and farmers who have pledged their farmland as security for a loan, operating as a fund that takes such land into its own hands, and it states that priority goes to assistance given before the sale-with-right-of-redemption process has been entered. Officials name the urgent categories as farmers in dispute with the state, who would otherwise face prosecution, and those whose mortgaged land is about to be sold at auction. The record, and the limits. Reported cases include the purchase of two hundred rai for farmers affected by a railway project and a forest reclamation policy, the purchase of a former palm plantation allocated to a named community, and assistance over three years to some two thousand six hundred farmers across roughly three thousand rai. Eligibility centres on farmers and low-income people and the mission is stated as reducing inequality in landholding and preventing the loss of rights, so this is a route for agricultural land and livelihoods rather than for buying land purely to conserve it; the institute's own structure has also been under review, so confirm its current form before applying. Read this with the community organisations development institute loans, the community forest registration, the justice fund and the land office entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: กสม. — a commission that can take the case to court in your place, and the complaint routes it publishes
trackers.desc: It can go to court on your behalf. The commission's published functions and powers include submitting a matter together with its opinion to the administrative court where a rule, an order or any other administrative act is found to affect human rights and raises a question of conformity with the constitution or the law; and filing a case in the courts of justice in place of an injured person, upon that person's request, where it considers this appropriate in order to remedy a human rights violation affecting the public as a whole. A commission that can litigate on request is a materially different resource from one that only investigates and reports, and that power is the reason to approach it early rather than as a last gesture. The complaint routes are published, and a signature is required. Its guidance records that a complaint may be made orally, sent by post, or submitted through the website form, with a complaint record form available for download; and that the complaint must bear the signature of the complainant or of a representative authorised in writing by a person entitled to file. For a village committee that means deciding who signs, or who holds the written authority, before anything is drafted. It publishes what it cannot take. Alongside the complaint guidance the commission publishes the categories of complaint it cannot accept for investigation, a chart of the examination process a complaint goes through, and statistics on complaints and on use of its online service. Reading the exclusions first is what saves the months that a misfiled complaint costs. There are regional offices, and a registration service for organisations. Regional office pages carry their own complaint instructions and forms, and the commission operates a registration service for private human rights organisations and professional councils. Registering a community organisation with the commission gives it a status that can be cited afterwards, which is worth more than it appears when a group is later described as an outside agitator. Read this with the environmental law foundation, the justice fund, the community sampling organisation and the land bank entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: สภาองค์กรชุมชนตำบล — a statutory community council a village registers itself, and its route to cabinet
trackers.desc: A village can register its own statutory council. Community organisation councils are established under the community organisations council legislation of 2008 at tambon, municipal and district level, and published accounts record 7,795 of them across the country at the sixteen-year mark. Registration runs on a published application form for notifying the establishment of a community organisation council under section five of the Act, with the criteria, methods and forms announced by the national community organisations development institute, which also publishes the form for dissolving a council. Registration is therefore a form and a set of criteria rather than a favour to be requested. Their published remit includes forests, water and land. The roles recorded for these councils vary with local conditions but include the care and conservation of the environment, forests, water sources and food sources; the promotion of occupations, local wisdom, arts and culture; and the resolution of problems of farmland, housing and public utilities — all carried out by coordinating with partner bodies locally, including state agencies and the elected local administrative organisation. A council formed before a project arrives is a standing body with those subjects already in its remit. The national assembly of councils reaches the cabinet. Under section 32 of the Act the national meeting of tambon community organisation councils gives opinions and recommendations on the setting of policy and of economic and social development plans and laws, and on the public services of state agencies or local administrative organisations that affect an area larger than one province, covering the economy, society, quality of life and the environment; and it summarises the problems faced by people in the various provinces together with proposed solutions, for submission to the cabinet for consideration and direction. A problem crossing provincial boundaries therefore has an upward route that does not depend on a minister happening to take an interest. What it is, and what it is not. The council sits alongside the elected local administrative organisation rather than inside it, and its powers are to give opinions, to coordinate and to propose rather than to decide. Register early: a council that already exists when a project appears is a body with standing to be consulted, while one formed in response to the project is easier to dismiss. Read this with the community forest registration, the environment fund, the justice fund and the state land bank entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: โบราณสถาน — nothing may be built inside a monument precinct without the Director-General's written permission
trackers.desc: Inside the precinct of an ancient monument, building requires written permission. The monuments legislation of 1961, as amended in 1992, prohibits any person from repairing, altering, changing, demolishing, extending, destroying or moving an ancient monument or any part of it, from excavating anything, or from constructing a building within the precinct of an ancient monument, except in accordance with an order of the director-general of the fine arts department or with that director-general's written permission — and where the written permission sets conditions, those conditions must also be complied with. The permission is a document with a date and conditions attached: asking to see it, and asking whether its conditions are being met, is a more useful question than asking whether the work is allowed. The department may register a monument, or define an area of land as one. Published legal commentary records that the Act empowers the fine arts department to announce the registration of any ancient monument and to define any area of land as an ancient monument, and that this is framed as a discretionary power the department may exercise as it sees fit. The power to define an area of land, rather than only a structure, is the one worth invoking when asking the department to act: a community with a ruin, a mound or an old settlement site is asking for a boundary, not a building listing. Registered movable items carry their own permission rule. Registered antiques and objects of art may not be repaired, altered or changed except with the written permission of the director-general, again subject to any conditions the permission sets; officials may examine such items between sunrise and sunset or during working hours for the purposes of the register; and where an antique or object of art is seen to have special artistic, historical or archaeological value the director-general has power to proceed to register it. Commercial use inside a registered precinct is licensed and charged. For the promotion of education and the dissemination of art and culture, the director-general may give written permission for a person to carry on business for profit within the precinct of a registered ancient monument which has no lawful owner or possessor, with the permit holder bearing all the costs of the undertaking and paying royalties, remuneration and other fees. Where a business is trading inside a monument precinct, the questions are under what written permission, on what conditions, and what it pays. Read this with the assessment report search, the community forest registration, the justice fund and the official information act entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: เวนคืน — the preliminary price committee, the heads of compensation beyond the land, and the 2025 change to the deadlines
trackers.desc: One central statute, and a committee that fixes the first figure. The expropriation and acquisition of immovable property legislation of 2019 is the general law laying down the criteria and method for expropriation, which the state and its officials must follow. Under it, a committee determines the preliminary price of the property and the compensation, and the criteria for that preliminary price are set by the statute together with a ministerial regulation made in 2021 which prescribes how the preliminary price of expropriated land is arrived at, using among other things the median of the data gathered. Asking which regulation and which data set produced the preliminary figure is therefore a concrete question with a documentary answer, rather than an argument about whether the figure feels low. Compensation reaches well past the value of the land. Published legal accounts of the statute record that the criteria and methods set by ministerial regulation cover the cost of demolition, the cost of moving, the value of buildings, structures and other immovables attached to the land, the cost of constructing new buildings and other attached immovables, the loss of rights arising from the use of the immovable property, and other damage arising from the owner having to leave the expropriated land. A claim confined to the land itself leaves most of those heads unclaimed, and each of them has its own basis in the regulation. How the sequence runs. Where the state needs land for a public purpose, a royal decree fixes the area within which land is to be expropriated so that officials may enter and survey the property; the compensation is then determined and the person whose property is to be taken is invited to enter into a sale contract; if agreement is reached the owner signs, receives the compensation and the title is transferred to the state; where agreement cannot be reached and there is an urgent necessity to take possession or use the property, the state proceeds by the other route the Act provides. Two changes approved in 2025, both of which matter to a claimant. Cabinet approval was given to amendments extending the period for which the minister may allow the preliminary price committee more time — as necessary but not exceeding one hundred and eighty days, where the previous limit was ninety — and providing that an owner whose property has been demolished, or a person entitled to compensation, keeps the right to claim the money arising from the expropriation even after the statutory period for claiming it has expired, so that the entitlement is no longer lost by delay. Check whether those amendments are in force before relying on either. Read this with the environmental law foundation, the justice fund, the land office parcel check and the land bank entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: ระบบสืบค้นคำพิพากษาศาลฎีกา — the judgment search system the courts say is for the general public, not only lawyers
trackers.desc: The courts state in their own announcement that this is for the public. The judiciary's public information office announces a search system for supreme court judgments, orders on petitions and rulings, and says in terms that it is for school and university students and members of the general public as well as practising lawyers, giving the address of the search site. That framing matters: a community using it is doing what the courts publish it for, not borrowing a practitioners' tool. What it holds, and what it does not. The system covers the supreme court's judgments, orders on petitions and rulings. The supreme court sits at the top of the ordinary courts and its decisions are final, but it operates separately from the administrative court and the constitutional court. Most disputes about a permit, an assessment decision or an official's refusal belong to the administrative jurisdiction, so a community should search this system for the private-law side of a dispute — damages, nuisance, contract, land title — and go to the administrative court's own published decisions for the rest. Knowing which court decides your kind of complaint is the first thing to establish, because it decides which body of decisions is relevant at all. How to use it alongside the file's other Thai entries. The environmental law foundation and the justice fund recorded elsewhere in this country's entries are the routes to representation and to costs; a handful of judgment references found here is what makes the first conversation with either of them concrete. The pollution complaint system and the assessment document search give the administrative record; judgments give the treatment of that record by a court. Practical notes. Search by the legal concept and the statute name rather than by the project type, since judgments are indexed by law rather than by industry; note the case number and year of anything useful; and where a judgment will be relied on, obtain the official text rather than a summary. Read this with the environmental law foundation, the justice fund, the expropriation entry and the assessment document search entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: การเรี่ยไร — the solicitation licence, the documents the district office asks for, and what counts as soliciting
trackers.desc: Asking the public for money is licensed, and a district office issues the licence. A district office's own service description records the issue of licences to organise a solicitation and to carry one out under a named section of the solicitation control legislation of 1944. Among the documents it lists as required are a copy of the bank passbook of the account in which the solicited money will be held, a certificate of good conduct from the applicant's parent organisation or a credible person, and the project together with a site plan showing where the solicitation will be held and photographs. Assemble those before applying: the bank account and the site plan are the two that take time. Selling things counts as soliciting. Published summaries of the statute record that solicitation extends to buying, selling, exchanging, compensating or providing services where it is expressly or impliedly indicated that the transaction is not ordinary but is intended to gather property, in whole or part, for some undertaking. A benefit sale, a charity auction or a sponsored service is therefore inside the licensing regime, not outside it — a point communities routinely get wrong. Two routes, and a committee. Academic analysis of the statute records two cases: solicitation claimed to be for the benefit of the government service, a municipality or the public interest, which may be held only with the permission of the solicitation control committee; and solicitation on public roads or in public places, and solicitation advertised through printed matter, which the statute deals with separately in another section. The same analysis records that the committee decides so that permission criteria are applied to a common standard, and notes that the statute does not clearly prescribe methods of solicitation beyond that section. Ask the district office which of the two routes your appeal falls into before filing. There are penalties. Published summaries record imprisonment and fine ranges for breaches, with the amounts fixed in 1944 terms and now nominal — the real consequence is that an unlicensed appeal can be stopped and discredited at the moment it matters. Read this with the community organisations development institute loans, the environmental law foundation, the justice fund and the judgment search entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: ผังเมืองรวม — the ninety-day posting, the right to petition for amendment, and the two committees that read the petitions
trackers.desc: A comprehensive plan is posted for ninety days, and interested persons may petition against it. Reporting on the planning procedure under the 2019 planning legislation records that after the public hearing stage the draft comprehensive plan is posted publicly for ninety days, during which interested persons may submit a petition asking that a provision of the plan be amended, changed or revoked. The petitions are then collected and an accompanying opinion prepared, considered by the metropolitan comprehensive plan advisory committee, and considered again by the provincial planning committee.
