A coalition that wants to take a block of production forest out of the logging and conversion pipeline cannot do it as an association; it has to constitute a company to hold the licence. Peer-reviewed work on the scheme records permit terms of sixty to a hundred years during which logging is not allowed until timber stocks recover, with holders permitted instead to develop non-timber forest products, environmental services and forest area utilisation, and around 600,000 hectares under the scheme across sixteen permit holders. The boundary is where the years go. The project's own record shows the closed-traverse boundary demarcation report for Jambi ratified in January 2016 and submitted for formal determination in February 2016 and again in September 2019, with South Sumatra's ratified in April 2016 and likewise submitted. A permit is not the same as a settled boundary, and the gap between them is measured in years. People already live there, and this entry would be dishonest without saying so. Around three hundred Batin Sembilan families live in and range across the forest, taking rattan, jerenang, sialang honey, jelutung latex, damar and medicinal plants. The area holds at least 374 recorded vertebrate species, of which about 29 per cent are endemic or legally protected, and it has faced sustained encroachment for oil palm. A restoration licence does not settle who lives on the land; it settles what may be cut.

trackers.name: AMDAL public participation — ten working days, and a seat on the appraisal commission
trackers.desc: A representative of the affected community sits on the commission that assesses the document. Affected communities must be involved, through their representatives, in the appraisal of the environmental analysis and its management and monitoring plans, and a representative of the affected community is a member of the appraisal commission itself. That is a seat at the table rather than a comment on a notice board, and establishing who holds it for your project is the single most useful question in the Indonesian process. The written route is ten working days from the announcement. Any member of the public giving clear personal identification may submit suggestions, opinions and responses in writing or recorded form within ten working days of the announcement, in Indonesian or in the local language, and they go both to the proponent and to the authority assessing the document — the minister through the central commission secretariat, or the governor, or the regent or mayor, according to which level is appraising it. What counts as useful content is defined, and it is not technical. Submissions may consist of descriptive information about the state of the environment around the proposed activity, local values connected to it, and the community's aspirations regarding it. A community does not need a consultant to supply the first of those, and local values are expressly admissible — which is unusual and worth using. The announcement comes before the terms of reference are written. The proponent must announce the plan before drafting the scoping document, the announcement must reach everyone affected by any decision in the process, and community input is required to be a consideration in scoping — so the ten days fall at the point where the study's boundaries and depth are still open. Announcements are published on the national environmental documents system, where the public submits its response through the system itself, and where the site and monitoring maps are uploaded and viewable. An environmental approval can later be revoked where the management and monitoring plans are not carried out or the document proves false or misleading.

trackers.name: Accredited legal aid organisations — a locator, and the one document you must bring
trackers.desc: Free legal aid is delivered through accredited organisations, and the ministry publishes where the nearest one is. Bodies that pass verification and accreditation are obliged to provide legal aid to the public and particularly to those who cannot afford it, funded from the annual state budget, and the obligation covers non-litigation work as well as litigation. That second half matters most before a case exists: negotiation, mediation, drafting and community legal education are within what an accredited organisation is required to do, not favours to be asked for. One document decides whether the door opens. An application may be made orally or in writing and must contain at least the applicant's identity and a short account of the matter, with the case documents handed over — and it must attach a certificate of indigence issued by the lurah, the village head or an official of equivalent rank where the applicant lives. Obtain that certificate first; it comes from the same village office a community is usually already dealing with, and without it the file is incomplete however strong the case. More than half the country has no accredited provider, and the ministry says so. The accreditation round covering 2019 to 2021 produced 524 accredited organisations spread across Indonesia, but only about 42 per cent of the country's 514 regencies and cities had one at all. A community outside that 42 per cent should expect the nearest accredited organisation to sit in another regency and should plan for distance from the start rather than discovering it late. Check the cycle, and know what this register is not. Verification and accreditation are run every three years and cover re-accreditation of existing organisations as well as new applicants, so a body listed in an old cycle may no longer be accredited. This register is far wider than the eighteen-office legal aid network recorded elsewhere in this file but shallower; for structural cases and for customary territory, read it alongside those entries rather than instead of them.

trackers.name: BPDLH — the state environmental fund, its community small grant, and the published criticism of its reach
trackers.desc: A state fund whose stated purpose includes small grants to communities. The environmental fund management agency is a public service body under the finance ministry, formed in October 2019 under the regulations on environmental economic instruments and on environmental fund management and taking over from the earlier forest development financing agency. It systematically collects environmental protection funding from domestic and foreign, public and private sources, including bilateral support, international institutions, the private sector and philanthropy — and its published distribution orientation covers small grants, green investment and capacity building for communities as well as for officials. The community small grant is the door, and the window can be very short. The forestry ministry together with the fund has launched a community fund service for the environment as a small grant to communities, groups or environmental organisations carrying out inclusive conservation-based activities, channelling billions of rupiah in a round. In one such round proposals were open for five days. Watch for the announcement rather than planning around a season, and have the proposal drafted before the window opens. Where the money comes from, and how it is grouped. Sources include the state and regional budgets, cash surplus, donations, corporate social responsibility, revenue sharing from carbon trading, loans and other government environmental programme funds, grouped at least into funds for tackling pollution or environmental damage and trust or conservation assistance funds. Reported disbursements include cocoa cultivation, mangrove rehabilitation in a river basin and research funding, alongside an announced fund for the welfare and sustainable economy of indigenous peoples and local communities. The criticism is published in parliament, and it is the practical warning. A member of the relevant parliamentary commission has argued that the environmental funds under management must be made accessible to the communities on the front line of caring for nature rather than only to large institutions with established administrative capacity, and that the scale of funds managed has not been matched by disbursement on the ground. Treat the administrative burden as the real barrier: read this with the accredited legal aid and customary territory entries recorded here, because a registered body with someone able to write a proposal is the unit this fund can actually pay.

trackers.name: Environmental complaints — a statutory right, and a definition that reaches the planning stage
trackers.desc: The right to complain is in the statute, and the procedure is in a regulation. The 2009 environmental protection and management law provides that every person has the right to take part in environmental protection and management and to make a complaint arising from alleged pollution or damage to the environment. The ministerial regulation of 2017 on the procedure for managing complaints of alleged pollution, environmental damage and forest destruction sets out how those complaints are handled. A complaint can be made at the planning stage. The regulation defines a complaint as the delivery of information, orally or in writing, from any complainant to the responsible agency, about an alleged violation, a potential effect or an impact in the environmental or forestry field arising from a business or activity at the planning stage, the implementation stage, or after implementation. A community therefore does not have to wait for the damage: potential impact and the planning stage are inside the definition itself. No other complaint channel recorded in this file opens before the work starts. The local environment agency has a published service standard. Provincial environmental agencies publish service standards for handling environmental complaints that cite the same regulation alongside the wastewater quality and continuous online effluent monitoring rules. Ask the agency for its service standard for complaint handling, because it states what the agency has undertaken to do rather than what a complainant hopes it will. Behind the agency sits the enforcement directorate. The ministry's law enforcement directorate general operates regional offices whose investigators build cases and hand suspects to public prosecutors, with reported examples including a sawmill operator and illegal logging suspects. Where a complaint goes nowhere with the local agency, the regional enforcement office is the next address rather than the end of the road. Read this with the accredited legal aid, customary territory and environmental fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Cek Berkas, Bhumi and Sentuh Tanahku — check the parcel, the file and the certificate without needing a name
trackers.desc: Three public checks, run by the land ministry itself. The ministry publishes a file checking service, where entering the land office, the file number and the year returns the status of an application; an interactive land map carrying the geospatial data of the ministry's work units, with a parcel search; and a mobile application through which a certificate can be looked up, a parcel located on the map and the progress of an application followed. Applications for land services can also be lodged online with any land office in the country, with their status followed in the same application. The parcel search returns the right, the area and the map — but not the owner's name. Published guidance records that a search shows the type of land right, the area and the parcel map, and that the result does not display the owner. That combination is unusually useful: a community can establish what right exists over the ground beside it and how large the parcel is without ever asking for anybody's identity, which is the objection that most often blocks a request of this kind. If the parcel is not on the map, the application invites you to plot it. The same application carries a participation feature for plotting a parcel where the certificate has not yet been mapped, alongside published requirements and a cost simulation for land procedures. Being absent from the map is therefore a fixable state rather than a verdict, and the cost simulation tells a household what the fix will cost before it starts. Read it against the community's own map. This file already records the customary territory mapping work carried out by communities in this country; that map records what a community holds, and these records show what the state believes is there. Where the two disagree, the disagreement is the case — and both documents are obtainable before anybody is asked to sign anything. Read this also with the environmental complaint and accredited legal aid entries recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Komisi Informasi — mediation that becomes a binding decision, and failure to publish is itself a dispute
trackers.desc: Failure to publish is itself a ground of objection. A public body must respond to an information request within ten working days. The grounds on which an applicant may then object in writing include refusal of the request, information supplied incomplete, no response at all, information supplied outside the statutory period — and the non-provision of the periodic information that a public body is obliged to announce under the openness of public information law and the commission's service standard. For a community, an unpublished mandatory disclosure is therefore a dispute that can be brought, not merely an absence to be complained about. The ladder, in working days. The written objection goes to the superior of the body's information management officer within thirty working days of the response or refusal. Where that superior does not answer within thirty working days, or the answer does not satisfy, the applicant may bring a dispute to the information commission within fourteen working days. After registration the commission begins within fourteen working days by summoning both parties to the preliminary examination stage, and it must resolve the dispute within a maximum of one hundred working days. Mediation produces a binding decision. Where mediation reaches agreement, that agreement is set down in a decision of the commission which is final and binding; where mediation fails or a party withdraws, the commission continues through non-litigation adjudication. A settlement reached here is an enforceable instrument rather than an understanding between the parties, which is unusual among the routes recorded in this file. And there is an execution route if the body ignores it. Where a public body does not carry out the commission's decision, the applicant may go to the administrative court to have the decision executed. Disputes may be lodged in person at the commission or online through its dispute management system, and central and regional commissions divide the work by jurisdiction. Read this with the parcel and file checks, the environmental complaint route and the accredited legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Nusantara Atlas — clearance alerts tied to the concession, the mill and the village boundary
trackers.desc: The alert is tied to the concession, so it names a company. The platform's dashboard links deforestation and fire alerts to the land-use layers that matter — palm oil, pulpwood and mining concessions, palm oil mills, protected areas and administrative boundaries all the way down to village level — and its own description is that this lets anyone quickly pinpoint the companies involved in forest clearance. Turning a cleared patch of ground into an identified operator is the step communities most often cannot take for themselves, and it is the step that makes every later approach — to a regulator, a buyer, a lender or a court — possible. Time lapse imagery can be generated and saved. Users can produce satellite time lapse animations on the fly from named imagery sources and save them as a file, and can analyse deforestation and fire trends both historically and in near real time, with fire hotspots tracked daily and the expansion of roads and its effect on forests followed as well. A dated before-and-after animation of a particular block of forest is evidence a village can hand to a journalist, an agency or a lawyer without owning a single instrument. It is open access, and republishable with attribution. The platform's terms state that its own materials may be downloaded, copied, reproduced, republished, modified, transmitted, distributed and made available to the public, provided the work and the identified source are clearly attributed. Evidence that can lawfully be reused, quoted and circulated is worth considerably more to a campaign than evidence locked behind a licence. What it is built for, and where it stops. The operator describes itself as a geospatial organisation working with satellites, cloud computing, field investigations and governance data, helping non-governmental organisations, academics and governments verify the activities of agribusiness, and helping indigenous forest communities put the boundaries of their ancestral lands on the map; coverage extends beyond this country to Malaysia, Brunei, Papua New Guinea and Colombia, and the platform has been used to verify no-deforestation pledges inside concessions and the performance of protected areas, village forests and restoration projects. It supplies data and maps: it does not litigate or represent, and an alert is a prompt to verify on the ground rather than proof of illegality in itself. Read this with the customary territory mapping, the parcel and certificate checks, the legal aid organisations and the environmental complaint entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Investigasi Bersama Tempo — a fellowship pairing local journalists with a national investigative desk, and a free manual
trackers.desc: The programme pairs a local journalist with a national investigative desk. Published descriptions record a fellowship in which journalists from a range of media carry out an investigation jointly with the magazine's editorial team, receiving guidance and mentoring from reporters experienced in investigative work, with the stated aims of producing investigations, spreading investigative practice to other outlets and raising the capacity of journalists in the regions. A community's evidence almost always reaches a local reporter first; this is the route by which that reporter reaches national capacity, rather than the community having to persuade a national newsroom from a standing start. Civil society is inside the model, not outside it. Later editions of the programme were described as involving more non-governmental organisations, with collaboration between journalists and civil society coalitions presented as a necessity for reporting grounded in data and fact. An organisation already assisting a community — a legal aid office, an environmental group, a land network — can therefore be the way in, which matters where villagers have no direct contact with any newsroom. The desk's beat already includes environmental corruption and mining. A journalist on the magazine's investigative desk is described as focusing on environmental corruption, food and mining, holding fellowships from international rainforest reporting programmes, and the magazine's environmental investigations have covered illegal nickel mining and the destruction of small islands by mining. A desk that has already worked those subjects will recognise what a village's documents show. There is a free published manual, and there are dates to check. An investigative journalism training manual in Indonesian was produced jointly with an international environmental justice organisation and the media group's training institute, which focuses on building journalistic, media and communication capacity across the country. The programme descriptions relied on here date from 2018 and 2019, and this research did not verify the current edition, call or contact point: confirm before relying on it. Read this with the environmental forum's regional offices, the legal aid offices, the clearance alert platform and the assessment participation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Badan Bank Tanah — at least thirty per cent for redistribution, ten-year use rights, and the route displaced communities have used
trackers.desc: A state land body must set aside at least thirty per cent for redistribution. Established under a 2021 government regulation as a special status legal body created by central government with particular authority to manage land, it allocates a minimum of thirty per cent of the state land assigned to it for agrarian reform, with the allocation determined by the minister. Published figures for early 2026 record an inventory of about thirty-four thousand eight hundred hectares, of which eleven thousand eight hundred and twenty-three hectares — just under thirty-four per cent — were allocated to agrarian reform, with around twenty thousand hectares held as land reserve. A stated, measurable proportion is something a community can quote when asking what is available near it. What a recipient gets is a time-limited use right first. The body's own account records the grant of a time-limited use right over its management right to agrarian reform subjects, for a period of at least ten years. Published accounts add that recipients sign an agreement before a notary undertaking not to transfer or sell the land for ten years, to use it productively for its designated purpose and not to abandon it; that the body monitors use and provides support on access to financing and market links with local government; and that where those obligations are met and the recipient is judged economically independent, it recommends upgrading the status of the land to freehold ownership. Communities displaced by a megaproject have used this route. Reported cases include residents affected by the construction of an airport and a toll road section for the new capital receiving land under the scheme, with an allocation of one thousand eight hundred and seventy-three hectares in the district concerned and a first stage covering four hundred hectares, carried out with the land ministry and an agrarian reform task force. Where a project takes land, this is one of very few named routes by which the same state hands some back. The limits are real and should be established first. Eligibility runs through agrarian reform subjects determined administratively; the first grant is a use right rather than ownership, with a ten-year restraint on sale attached; and the same body also supplies land for government projects and for investment, which is part of its stated purpose rather than a contradiction of it. Establish which category a particular parcel sits in before assuming the thirty per cent applies to it. Read this with the customary forest recognition, the parcel and certificate check, the legal aid offices and the clearance alert entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: LPSK — statutory protection for a reporter or witness, and the one document the application turns on
trackers.desc: A reporter, not only a witness, may apply. Under the witness and victim protection law of 2006 as amended in 2014, the agency may extend protection and other rights to witnesses, victims, reporters, cooperating suspects and experts, and its published answers record that an application may be lodged by the person concerned, by family, by a companion or legal counsel, by law enforcement officers, or by a competent official or guardian where the application concerns a child. The agency publishes several channels through which an application can be submitted. For a villager who has reported illegal clearing, dumping or a permit breach and is then threatened, being a reporter is itself a recognised status rather than an informal one. The application turns on one document. Among the formal requirements are a written application, a copy of identity or family card, an original power of attorney where a lawyer or companion applies, and — the decisive item — a letter or document from the competent agency stating the applicant's status as witness, victim, reporter, cooperating witness or expert in the criminal case. Get the acknowledgment or receipt of the original report first: without a document establishing that status, a protection application has nothing to stand on. The supporting material it may ask for is a list of things to keep from day one. Published accounts of the procedure record that the agency may request the police examination record, an account of the importance of the testimony, summonses from the police, the prosecutor or the court, and the report or information lodged with the police, a state commission or a government body relating to the person's status as a reporter. Every one of those is a piece of paper a community should be filing from the day its first complaint is made, not assembling after a threat arrives. Emergency protection exists, and so does a stated weakness. The agency's 2024 service standard lists proactive services and emergency protection alongside ordinary applications. But published legal scholarship notes plainly that protection is not automatic: the witness or victim must apply and must satisfy the requirements, and public awareness of the agency remains low. Apply early, keep the paperwork, and do not assume anyone else will initiate it. Read this with the legal aid offices, the environmental forum's regional offices, the clearance alert platform and the satellite monitoring entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Registered environmental laboratories — the published list, and why an unregistered lab's result cannot be used
trackers.desc: Two things make a laboratory count here: accreditation and registration. The ministry's standards body defines an environmental laboratory as one holding an accreditation certificate for testing environmental quality parameters and for taking samples, together with a registration identity, and describes registration as the process of recording and recognising an already-accredited laboratory as an environmental laboratory. A laboratory that holds international testing accreditation but has not been registered is therefore not an environmental laboratory for these purposes, and that distinction is invisible on a letterhead. The list of registered laboratories is published. The ministry unit responsible maintains and publishes the register of environmental laboratories, with the current list available from that page. Check a laboratory against the list before sending a sample anywhere, and write down its registration number: it is the number that will be asked for later. The legal consequence is the reason this matters. Published guidance records that the reporting of environmental test results must be done through laboratories that are both accredited and registered with the ministry, and that without both, analysis results cannot be used as valid evidence in legal proceedings, in public complaints, or in the evaluation of environmental documents such as the impact assessment or the environmental management and monitoring undertakings. A community that pays for testing at an unregistered laboratory has bought a number it cannot use — which is the most expensive mistake available in this whole area. Registration is supervised, and renewed by reporting. Applications are made through the ministry's one-stop portal with the accreditation certificate and its scope annex and a recommendation letter, and must be completed within thirty days of a complete file; registered laboratories must report their continued compliance with the registration requirements to the ministry unit at least once a year; and supervision is carried out regularly by the accreditation committee and otherwise by ministry units. Two questions follow: when the laboratory last reported, and what its registered scope covers — because scope decides whether it may test the parameter in question at all. Read this with the clearance alert platform, the assessment participation route, the legal aid offices and the witness protection agency entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Dana Desa — the village's own budget, with environmental conservation named, and the meeting where it is decided
trackers.desc: Environmental conservation is a named use of the village's own money. Published summaries of the 2026 focus areas for the village fund include strengthening climate-resilient and disaster-resilient villages, with activities expressly covering waste management, environmental conservation, and the prevention of flooding and drought, alongside adaptation to floods, landslides, tidal flooding, coastal abrasion and forest fires, and education and preparedness for disaster risk. A village that wants to protect a spring, a mangrove belt, a slope or a water catchment is therefore asking for something already on the national list rather than proposing an exception. The decision is made in a meeting anyone in the village can attend. Planning runs through the village development planning deliberation, which produces the annual village work plan as the yearly expression of the medium-term plan, and the rules preserve room for other priority programmes decided through the village deliberation according to local conditions, urgent needs and the village's own authority. Published guidance urges residents to attend and to speak if proposed programmes do not match the stated priorities. That meeting is the moment the money is allocated, and a proposal recorded in its minutes is worth more than any letter written afterwards. The village must publish how the money will be used. The ministerial regulation directs village governments to publish the focus of village fund use, through the village information system or other publication media. Where that has not happened, the question has a regulation behind it rather than only a grievance. The scale, and the squeeze. The national allocation for 2026 is reported at around sixty trillion rupiah, but a substantial share is directed to a new village cooperative programme, with village government operational costs capped at three per cent of the allocation, and village commentaries describe the room for other uses narrowing sharply against the previous year. Ask the village office for the current allocation and for the published statement of focus before assuming there is space. Read this with the customary territory mapping, the biodiversity grant fund, the state environmental fund and the environmental complaint entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Cagar Budaya registration — free to register, and protection attaches while the assessment is still running
trackers.desc: Registration is free, and protection begins before any decision. Under the cultural heritage legislation and the implementing regulation of 2022, every person who owns or controls an object suspected of being cultural heritage must register it with the regent or mayor without charge, and anyone who finds such an object must report the find to the authority responsible for culture, to the police, or to the relevant agency in the area where it was found. The provision that matters most for a community is the next one: during the assessment process, the object, building, structure or location that has been found or registered is protected and treated as cultural heritage. Protection therefore attaches at registration rather than at designation, which makes this the fastest protective step recorded anywhere in this file. Thirty days after the expert team reports. The regent or mayor must issue the determination of cultural heritage status within at most thirty days of receiving the recommendation of the cultural heritage expert team stating that the registered object, building, structure, location or geographical unit is eligible. Those expert teams are constituted by ministerial decision at national level, gubernatorial decision at provincial level and regent or mayoral decision at district level, and may be assisted in their assessment by the technical implementing unit or the local agency responsible for cultural heritage; registered museum collections are assessed first by a curator and then passed to the team. Customary communities are the exception on area ownership. A cultural heritage area may only be owned or controlled by the State, except for areas owned hereditarily by customary law communities, and the transfer of ownership of cultural heritage ranked at national, provincial or district level is restricted. For a community whose claim rests on inheritance rather than title, that exception is the sentence to read alongside its customary territory mapping. What the register brings, and where the machinery is set out. Once recorded in the national register, the owner of cultural heritage is entitled to legal guarantees, and the finder of an object, building or structure determined to be cultural heritage has entitlements of their own. The implementing regulation of 2022 governs registration, preservation, area management, incentives and compensation, supervision and funding, and requires the minister, governor or regent and mayor to determine ranking on the basis of assessment and the expert team's recommendation, to classify and record in the national register, and to issue status certificates. Register first and argue afterwards. Read this with the customary territory mapping organisation, the assessment participation window, the accredited legal aid organisations and the information commission entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Pengadaan tanah — five forms of compensation, fourteen working days to object, and the remnant plot you can force them to take whole
trackers.desc: Compensation is not only money. The land acquisition legislation of 2012 provides that compensation may be given in the form of money, replacement land, resettlement, share ownership, or another form agreed by both parties. A household that wants land rather than cash, or a community that wants resettlement together rather than individual payments, is therefore asking for something the statute already lists, and the form is negotiated at the same meeting as the amount. Thirty working days to the meeting, fourteen to object. The land agency holds the deliberation with the entitled parties within at most thirty working days from the appraiser's valuation being delivered to it, in order to set the form or the amount of compensation on the basis of that valuation, and the agreement reached is recorded in minutes which become the basis for payment. Where no agreement is reached on the form or the amount, the entitled party may lodge an objection with the local district court within at most fourteen working days after the deliberation; and a party dissatisfied with that court's decision may bring a cassation appeal to the supreme court within fourteen working days. Practitioner analysis of the court procedure records that the district court must decide within thirty working days of registration, that the examination proceeds without mediation, exceptions, counterclaims, replies or rejoinders, that the cassation memorandum is due within seven working days of the statement of appeal and the counter-memorandum within seven working days of notification, and that the supreme court decision is final with no further review available. The remnant plot. Where a plot affected by the acquisition is left with a remainder that can no longer function according to its designation and use, the entitled party may demand replacement of the whole plot. That is the provision for a farm cut in two by a road, and it is a demand rather than a request. Challenging the location, not the money, is a different route with a different clock. Where objections raised in the repeat public consultation are rejected and the governor determines the project location, an entitled party may bring a claim in the administrative court against that determination within thirty working days of its issue — subject to a supreme court circular requiring administrative remedies to be exhausted first. Deciding at the outset whether the fight is about the location or about the compensation therefore decides which court, which clock and which preliminary step applies. Read this with the assessment participation window, the customary territory mapping, the accredited legal aid organisations and the parcel and file check entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Kitabisa — public donation platform open to communities, 5 per cent fee, verification required, and no politics
trackers.desc: A community can open a public fundraising page here without being an organisation. The platform states that it facilitates anyone wishing to raise funds online and has been used by global non-governmental organisations, local foundations, communities, alumni associations, students and individuals. Creating a campaign page is free; the platform charges a five per cent administration fee on online donations collected, with exceptions recorded for religious alms and for natural disaster campaigns initiated by official institutions or non-governmental organisations, where the fee is nil. It states plainly that it provides only the facility and holds no funds to disburse itself, and that success depends on the quality of the content, the breadth of the network and the effort of the campaigner. Verification is what makes it credible, and it is a documentary process. The platform requires account verification and category-specific verification with supporting documents and identity checks before donations can be withdrawn, and states that the five per cent covers that verification, identity and document checking, platform security and the screening of campaigns that breach its terms. Published guidance records that funds can be withdrawn even if the stated target is not reached, provided verification is complete and withdrawal conditions are met — which matters for a community raising toward a purchase price it may not reach in one campaign. The legal footing is stated, and it is checkable. The operator records that its foundation is registered with the law and human rights ministry, that it holds a permit for the collection of money and goods from the social affairs ministry under a numbered ministerial decision of 2018, and that it is audited by a public accounting firm with an unqualified opinion published. A community asking donors for money can point to that rather than to its own assurances. One limit to plan around. The platform's community guidance states that it does not facilitate fundraising for practical political purposes, or campaigns carrying political identity or promoting a party. A campaign against a project should therefore be framed around the land, the livelihood or the legal costs, not around a political contest. Read this with the accredited legal aid organisations, the customary territory mapping, the judgments directory and the compensation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: MODI and MOMI — the national mining licence database and the concession map, searchable by commodity, location and licence status
trackers.desc: Every mining licence holder must be registered in one national database. Published descriptions record that the mineral and coal directorate general's data system holds company data for mineral and coal operators including non-metallic minerals and rock, and that business entities and individuals holding the various classes of mining permit are required to be registered in it, with changes of shareholders, directors and commissioners also recorded through it. The system is described as covering company data, licensing data, investment, workforce, mining accidents and commodity development, and as managing royalty and state revenue data from mineral and coal sales. A community can therefore ask a short question about the operator next to it: is it in the register, and under what permit. What the database will tell you. Guidance records that a search can be run by type of permit, commodity, location and permit status, and that entries show the essential details including the licence validity period, the area of the concession and the commodity mined — with the observation that where a company's name is not found in the database its legal status is questionable. It also records the practical caveat: operators complain that a licence lawfully extended on paper may not yet show as extended in the database, so a stale status is not by itself proof of illegality. The map shows the boundaries, and the overlaps. The companion geographic system, built under a 2011 ministerial regulation, is described as a web-based information system covering all mining areas in the country, integrating provincial, district and city data and accessible from anywhere; it shows the distribution of mining business permit areas, people's mining areas and state reserve areas together with the licence status of a concession, and integrates data from other sectors including electricity, ports, oil and gas, forest areas, administrative boundaries, taxation and trade. Descriptions note it is used to check concession boundaries precisely because disputes arise between mining companies and other sectors such as plantations and forestry — the same overlap a community is often standing on. The legal footing, and why that matters. The mining areas regulation of 2010 obliges regional governments to manage data and information on mining activities within their authority, and the 2011 ministerial regulation provides that the mining areas information system is managed nationally to standardise coordinates and base maps when permit areas are issued, and must be accessible to provincial and district governments. That is the basis on which a local official can be asked to produce the coordinates of a permit area. Read this with the judgments directory, the accredited legal aid organisations, the customary territory mapping and the public donation platform entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Posbakum and fee waiver — a legal help desk in every first-instance court, hearings held outside the court building, and the state paying the case costs
trackers.desc: Three services exist for people who cannot afford to litigate, and they are set out in one supreme court regulation. Court pages explaining the 2014 supreme court regulation on legal services for people without means record three services across the general, religious and administrative court systems: a case cost waiver, under which the state bears the cost of the proceedings so that a person or group without economic means can litigate free of charge; hearings held outside the court building, whether fixed, periodic or occasional, at a place within the court's jurisdiction, as circuit hearings or at a permanent external hearing place; and a legal aid post established at every first-instance court. For a rural community, the hearing outside the building is the one that removes the travel barrier, and it can be requested by parties without means. What the help desk actually gives. The post provides information, consultation and legal advice and prepares the legal documents a person needs, staffed by personnel from a provider institution working with the court under a cooperation agreement with agreed service hours. Court pages record that where a user cannot pay the case costs the post gives them the fee waiver application form to submit to the court president, and that where a user needs representation in the hearing itself the post supplies information on the procedure and the list of legal aid organisations under the 2011 legal aid legislation, or other organisations or advocates able to act free of charge. The post is therefore the doorway to the accredited organisations already recorded in this file. The fee waiver route was simplified, and the proof required is named. Reporting on the change records that an applicant still brings a certificate of inability to pay issued by the village or sub-district head, or a social assistance card or other document proving inability to pay the case costs, and registers the claim — but no longer has to attend a hearing and wait for an interlocutory ruling to learn whether the waiver is granted. The application goes to the court president through the registry; the registrar checks eligibility and budget availability and passes the result to the president, who grants or refuses, issuing a fee waiver service decision letter if granted. Court pages also record that where a case has been declared cost-free at first instance, an appeal, cassation or review application must be accompanied by that first-instance decision letter. Keep the letter. Read this with the accredited legal aid organisations, the legal aid federation, the judgments directory and the customary territory mapping entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Perhutanan sosial — five schemes for legal community management of state forest, thirty-five year approvals, and what the application must contain
trackers.desc: There are five named schemes, and picking the right one is the whole task. A government press release records the five: village forest, state forest whose management rights are given to a village institution for the welfare of the village; community forest, state forest whose main use is to empower local people; people's plantation forest on production forest built by a community group; customary forest, forest inside the territory of a customary forest community; and forestry partnership, cooperation between local people and a forest manager or the holder of a forest utilisation permit, forest services permit, forest area borrow-and-use permit or primary forest industry permit. Published summaries record the corresponding tenure documents for each scheme, and record an allocation target of over twelve million hectares for the programme. A community whose forest is threatened by a concession should establish which scheme fits its situation before it applies. What the approval is, and what it is not. Published legal material records that a social forestry management approval gives legal access to forest utilisation for village forest, community forest, people's plantation forest, forestry partnership and customary forest, in protection forest, production forest or conservation forest according to function; that approval may be given to individuals, forest farmer groups or cooperatives; and, in terms, that the approval is not a right of ownership over the forest area. Read that sentence before promising anyone a title. The application has a stated contents list. A published application guide records that the request goes to the minister signed by the group head, the head of a federation of farmer groups or the head of a cooperative, accompanied by a list of applicants' names with copies of identity cards acknowledged by the village head, a general description of the area covering physical and socio-economic conditions and its potential, and a proposal map at a stated scale according to the area. It records that community forest management means working the land as a group, a federation of groups or a cooperative, with agroforestry mixing perennial forest species and seasonal crops. Published analysis records a minimum group size and that individuals must join or form a group. Timing, and the working group that is supposed to help. Provincial forestry material records community forest permits issued for thirty-five years, with the province recording an early programme history and its own facilitation work: preparing village forest documents, forming village forest management institutions and running technical training for participants. A provincial social forestry working group established by the governor is tasked with outreach to local communities and related parties. Ask the provincial forestry service for that working group. Read this with the mining licence database, the court legal aid posts, the customary territory mapping and the donation platform entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: KKPR and the spatial plan — the conformity document every licensed activity needs, the two-year assessment, and the grounds for cancelling or revoking it
trackers.desc: Every licensed activity must conform to the spatial plan, and the conformity itself is a document. The 2021 government regulation on spatial planning defines conformity of a space utilisation activity as the conformity between the planned activity and the spatial plan, and covers planning, utilisation and control — control including assessment of the implementation of that conformity, assessment of the realisation of the plan, incentives and disincentives, sanctions and dispute settlement. Provincial explanatory material records that all activities with a business licence must conform to the general or detailed spatial plan in force, with the conformity system applied digitally and integrated into the national single submission platform. Ask for the conformity document and the plan it was measured against. The assessment happens within two years, and mismatch must be corrected. Published summaries of the regulation record that assessment of the implementation of the conformity document is carried out no later than two years from its issue, and that where non-conformity is found the activity must be adjusted; that control is exercised to make everyone comply with the plan and with the conditions in the conformity document; and that sanctions and dispute settlement follow a spatial audit. A community that believes an operation has drifted from what was approved is asking for that audit. Cancellation and revocation have stated grounds. The land ministry's directorate general records that a conformity document may be cancelled where it was obtained through an unlawful procedure such as falsified applicant data or a location mismatch, and — under the regulation and a named ministerial regulation — where it causes social, security or environmental impacts or disturbance to national vital objects; and that revocation applies where the activity being carried out does not match what the document set, revocation being part of the administrative sanctions an authorised official may impose. It also records officials discussing the need for a formal mechanism of public complaint to the minister. Those grounds are the wording to use in a complaint. Participation and information are provided for. Provincial material records that the public has the right to access spatial plan information openly, including through the national geospatial information system, and that regional governments must provide a spatial data portal and facilitate public participation in oversight; published summaries record that control of space utilisation may involve community groups, spatial planning forums and professional associations, and may use online complaint channels. Read this with the assessment participation entry, the customary territory mapping, the parcel checking services and the mining licence database entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Coastal and small islands law — the right to propose the zoning plan, permits required of anyone using coastal resources, and customary law communities exempted from the permit
trackers.desc: Communities have a statutory right to propose the plans that govern the coast. Published summaries of the coastal and small islands legislation record that it covers granting the community the right to propose the drafting of the strategic plan, the zoning plan, the management plan and the action plan for coastal and small islands management; the regulation of location permits and management permits for every person and for customary law communities, local communities and traditional communities using coastal and small island resources; the use of small islands and the waters around them; and the allocation of authority between the minister, governors and district heads. The zoning plan is the document that decides what may happen where on a coast, and the right to propose its drafting is the way in. The 2014 amendment replaced the tenure right with permits, and exempted customary communities. Published analysis records that the earlier coastal waters business right was replaced by a permit system; that customary law communities are released from the obligation to hold a permit; and that use without a permit where one is required carries criminal sanctions up to a stated maximum term and fine under a named article. Establishing that a community is a customary law community therefore changes what it must hold. The recognition condition is the practical obstacle, and it is documented. The same analysis records that the article recognising customary law community rights makes recognition conditional on the village legislation's requirements, which often makes it difficult for customary communities that are not formally registered; and records the revised law being the legal basis on which a bay reclamation permit was cancelled and a project on a named small island halted. The history is worth knowing before relying on the plan. Published commentary records that the constitutional court struck down the coastal waters business right, and struck down the provision limiting who could take part in drafting coastal management planning, with the revision then accommodating community involvement in proposing plans and adding a mandate to have regard to coastal waters space according to local wisdom; and records civil society arguing that coastal and small island resources are open access and common property, so that permits parcel them out. It also records that many local governments still lacked an adopted zoning plan. Read this with the spatial conformity entry, the customary territory mapping, the social forestry schemes and the assessment participation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The 2024 conservation law — a new preservation-area category for important ecosystems outside protected areas, conservation as a duty of government and the public, and heavier penalties with ecosystem restoration
trackers.desc: Important ecosystems outside the protected area system now have their own legal category. The 2024 law amending the 1990 conservation legislation defines a preservation area as an area outside nature reserve areas, nature conservation areas and the conservation areas in waters, coastal areas and small islands, whose ecological condition is maintained to support the life-support function or the survival of biological natural resources and their ecosystems. Official explanations record that this was formulated to guarantee application of conservation principles outside those areas, so that important ecosystems including wild plants and animals outside them gain legal certainty in their management. Where a site matters ecologically but sits outside every protected boundary, that category is the one to name. Conservation is stated as a duty of government and of the public, with funding attached. The law provides that conservation of biological natural resources and their ecosystems is the responsibility and obligation of the government, regional governments and the community, and that the government and regional governments, according to their authority, are responsible for providing adequate and sustainable funding for conservation activities. It records strengthening of the role and involvement of the community, including customary law communities, in conservation. That funding duty is a thing to ask about when a conservation obligation is said to be unaffordable. The three pillars, and the two area types, are defined. Official material records the three pillars as protection of life-support systems; preservation of the diversity of plant and animal species and their ecosystems; and sustainable use of biological natural resources and their ecosystems; and the law defines a nature reserve area as one whose principal function is preserving that diversity while also serving as a life-support buffer system, and a nature conservation area as one combining life-support protection, species preservation and sustainable use. Penalties now reach restoration and release. Published legal commentary records that the amendment strengthens prohibitions, sanctions and criminal provisions to protect the integrity of those areas, tightens and increases criminal and corporate sanctions, and adds additional penalties in the form of compensation, ecosystem restoration, rehabilitation, translocation and release of animals, and strengthens the authority of the civil service investigators. Read this with the coastal and small islands law, the spatial conformity approval, the customary territory mapping and the social forestry entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Supreme Court's environmental case guidelines — the decision that recognises class actions, organisation standing and citizen lawsuits, and the statutory articles each rests on
trackers.desc: The Supreme Court issued guidelines for handling environmental cases, and they set out three routes side by side. The 2013 decision of the chief justice bringing into force the guidelines on handling environmental cases, published in the court's own legal documentation system, sets out the class action procedure and the citizen lawsuit or actio popularis, defining the latter and grounding it in the judicial power legislation, in the judge's duty to explore, follow and understand the values living in society, and in the constitutional provision read together with the environmental protection legislation. Where a community is choosing how to bring a case, that document is the court's own map of the options. Three articles carry the three routes. Published legal material records that the environmental legislation gives the public the right to bring a group representative action for its own interest or the interest of the community where it suffers loss from pollution or environmental damage; that another article provides that the public has the right to bring an action against a planned business or activity that already holds an environmental permit, in the administrative court; and that a further article provides that an environmental organisation has the right to bring an action in the interest of preserving environmental functions. The forestry legislation carries its own representative action right. Organisation standing was won in court before it was written into statute. Published legal reporting records that the first shift came in an action by a national environmental organisation — the same one already recorded as this bucket's first entry — against a pulp company and five ministers and a governor, in which the district court recognised the organisation's legal standing although no regulation then provided for it; that the concept was afterwards adopted into the 1997 environmental statute and confirmed in the 2009 replacement. A precedent won without a rule is worth knowing when a court says a community has no standing. The honest limits are recorded too. Published analysis records that the citizen lawsuit has no clear statutory rule of its own in a civil law system, resting on the representative action provisions and the court's guidelines; and records its value as forcing government and corporations to be more accountable and transparent, beyond winning or losing. Read this with the legal aid offices, the decision directory, the environmental complaints entry and the assessment participation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: PROPER — the annual public rating of company environmental compliance, the five colour bands, and the black rating that follows deliberate pollution or refusal to obey an administrative sanction
trackers.desc: Every rated company is placed in one of five public colour bands, and the ministry publishes the result. The environment ministry records that, to make company performance easy for the public to understand, compliance is grouped into five colour ratings — black for a company whose activities cause serious environmental impact but which does not carry out environmental management; red for one that has made efforts but is still not compliant; blue for one that is compliant; green for one going beyond compliance through energy and water efficiency, hazardous and non-hazardous waste reduction, biodiversity conservation, community empowerment and disaster response; and gold for environmental and social innovation. Published material records the criteria as split between compliance — completeness of environmental documents including the assessment, control of water, air and soil pollution, hazardous waste management and periodic reporting — and beyond compliance. Looking up a company's colour is a five-second check before any meeting with it. The black rating has a stated legal trigger. A directorate's account records black as the rating for a company that deliberately acts, or is negligent, so as to cause pollution or environmental damage, and violates the applicable legislation, or does not carry out an administrative sanction; published material records that a company rated black is automatically placed on a government and public watch list, may be threatened with refusal of a permit extension, and that banks may refuse credit to a company rated non-compliant. That is a lever a community can point at when the company is seeking finance or renewal. The numbers show how many sit in the failing bands. Published analysis records participation rising from around three thousand two hundred companies in one recent cycle — with stated counts of gold, green, blue, eight hundred and eighty-seven red and two black — to more than five thousand four hundred in a later year; the ministry's own release records over five thousand assessed. Reporting records one year in which no company was rated black while six hundred and forty-five remained red, and asks whether that non-compliance carries no pollution risk. The programme is explicitly a disclosure instrument, not a substitute for enforcement. Published commentary records the ministry describing it as a public disclosure programme for environmental compliance, and stating that it does not replace conventional enforcement instruments such as civil or criminal environmental law enforcement; and records the electronic reporting system that replaced manual collection and analysis of the underlying data. Read this with the environmental complaints entry, the registered laboratories, the assessment participation and the clearance conformity entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: HuMa and the People's Legal Companions — a network of trained non-lawyer legal companions working with communities on land and natural resources, its field school, and its conflict database
trackers.desc: The organisation's central instrument is a network of trained companions who work with communities, not a litigation department. Its own pages record that it was founded to help build a just social order through arrangements for managing natural resources that place the people as the main actor, and that this is carried out through people's legal companions — people who work within social movements to empower the people's own legal resources and to reform state law toward social and ecological justice. It records five basic characteristics required of them: asserting the rights of customary and local communities to land and natural resources as the main focus; asserting the need for autonomous space to exercise those rights; fighting for local law as the sufficient condition for exercising them; taking customary and local communities as the subject of the work; and using a rights-based approach and participatory methods. Where a community needs someone to work alongside it rather than appear for it, that is the described role. The companions are trained, and the training method is stated. The organisation records the abilities a companion must have, including social and legal analysis using tools such as legal pluralism and critical legal studies, human rights values, and practical skills for returning law to the people; and records a field school built on the premise that participants already hold knowledge and experience and are not empty when they arrive, providing a forum to construct or deconstruct that knowledge in dialogue. Published material records its aims as increasing the quality and quantity of those companions and mainstreaming people's law in natural resource reform. It keeps a conflict database, and the figures are cited by others. The organisation records collecting primary conflict data obtained from its companions and network partners across various regions. Published academic work cites its record that 91,968 people from 315 customary communities have been victims in natural resource and land conflicts. A community wanting its own case counted in a national series has a place to report it. Its stated priorities name the projects communities face. Press reporting quotes its director naming the outstanding work as mining permits, cement plants, and revisions or draft laws concerning the people's rights to manage their living space, conflict and criminalisation. It maintains a public library of its own publications. Read this with the legal aid offices, the customary territory mapping, the accredited legal aid organisations and the environmental case guidelines entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: ICEL and its landmark decisions portal — a searchable analysis of environmental judgments, an anti-SLAPP book aimed at the courts, and community empowerment as one of its three stated approaches
trackers.desc: There is a portal of analysed environmental judgments, run by a law organisation rather than a court. The portal invites users to search analysis of environmental law decisions in the country, which is a different thing from the raw judgment database already recorded in this bucket: a community can read what a decision was held to mean, not only what it said. The organisation behind it records itself as an independent non-governmental organisation for environmental law, engaged in advocacy and community empowerment, established in 1993 as a foundation, and records its founding trigger as development focused on economic growth that affected the environment with destruction and pollution and neglected the needs of people whose lives depended on natural resources. Community empowerment is one of three stated approaches, and the others are named. Published description records the organisation working through legal reform and policy advocacy, capacity building, and community empowerment, empowering communities on climate justice issues and helping them develop the tools they need to voice their rights within environmental protection systems; it records staff describing the work as providing a bridge between policymakers and civil society and the grassroots, and as ensuring the voices of people whose rights will be impacted are heard and integrated into policy recommendations. It records the organisation working with local civil society organisations to identify common goals and shared challenges and running public consultations for civil society groups. It produces material aimed squarely at the courts. The organisation records launching a book on anti-SLAPP policy and environmental management, hosted with the Supreme Court's public relations channel — SLAPP being the retaliatory suit a community campaigner is most exposed to; and records a workshop for law lecturers on climate change law, noting that such courses are not yet developed in the country's legal education. Historical material records its earlier programme of environmental advocacy training and moot court competitions for law faculty students, and compilations published as books, including a compilation of environmental cases covering enforcement through the courts, administrative enforcement and other routes. Read this with the judgment directory, the accredited legal aid organisations, the environmental case guidelines and the legal companions entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: JATAM — a mining advocacy network of village, island and core nodes, provincial bodies with their own addresses, and its stated services from accompaniment to litigation
trackers.desc: A network exists specifically for people living beside mines, and it is structured by node rather than by headquarters. The network records itself as a network of non-governmental and community organisations concerned with human rights, gender, environment, indigenous peoples and social justice issues in the mining and oil and gas industry, working with victim communities in many regions damaged by mining and oil and gas activity. It records its own structure as village nodes, island nodes and a core node, and states that the movement is not centralised in any one node but is a joint movement of its constituents and supporting public. A community can therefore approach the nearest node instead of the capital. Its services are listed, and they run past advocacy into court. The same profile records the network's work as accompaniment of victim communities, research, education, public awareness campaigning, policy advocacy and litigation processes, and records that any individual or group working for fairer and wiser management of mining and energy, and supporting the network's position, can be involved and support its work. A directory records its founding year as 1995, its legal form as a network, its fields of activity as advocacy, legal aid, accompaniment and research, and gives its secretariat's building, floor, unit and postcode. Provincial bodies are separately constituted, with their own founding records. A provincial node records itself as established in November 2000 by seven non-governmental networks and two people's organisations in that province, working to spread information and advocacy on the negative impacts of the mining industry, and records that because the network is a forum of organisations it has only articles of association legitimised by its members, all of which hold legal personality; it publishes its own contact page. Its published research names actors and mechanisms. Reporting records a network report on a nickel region documenting administrative changes between two villages and boundary documents appearing without public socialisation, used to expand concessions into customary territory, and naming village officials who also held company or organisational roles. A survey report records communities near operating mines estimating they could feed themselves three to six months, against a year where mining had stopped. Read this with the mining licence database, the legal companions, the customary mapping and the environmental organisations entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: KIARA and the coastal advocacy team — a fisherfolk coalition founded by nine named organisations, its published Jakarta address, and the joint litigation team that sued a reclamation approval
trackers.desc: Coastal and fishing communities have their own coalition, and its founders are named. The coalition records itself as a non-governmental organisation founded in 2002, initiated by nine civil society institutions focused on marine and fisheries issues, and lists those nine by name — a maritime association, a coastal development network, named foundations, a coast and sea network, a fishers' advocacy network and a natural resource management group — recording that they made the coalition a supporting and reference network and a joint campaign vehicle. Another account records it as initiated by named environmental, rural and fisher federations, committed to strengthening fisher groups and communities living in coastal areas and small islands so that they obtain protection and a decent livelihood from the government. A directory publishes its street address, sub-district and postcode in the capital. Its stated position is that coastal space belongs to the people who live there. The coalition records that management of space in coastal and marine areas is the sovereignty of coastal communities, present from long ago and passed down, that those communities hold strong knowledge and traditions in guarding the coast and sea, and that massive evictions, reclamation, mining, tourism and industry threaten the loss of traditional space management practices. It names the actors it works for as fishers, women fishers, fish and shrimp cultivators, salt farmers and coastal customary communities. The litigation is done through a joint team, which is the part worth copying. Published reporting records the coalition and the environmental forum — already recorded in this bucket — acting through a coastal and small islands rescue advocacy team to sue a central government marine spatial approval for a 90-hectare business and tourism reclamation at the state administrative court, in an area covering five named urban villages containing 469 fishery households and 29 fisher groups; records a legal aid institute previously winning an information disclosure case over the same project; and records the coalition's secretary general arguing that hardship for coastal communities, traditional fishers' sea access, coral reef ecosystems and flood risk were enough grounds to refuse the approval. Read this with the environmental forum, the legal aid institutes, the coastal law and the mining network entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: BRWA — the body where a community registers its mapped customary territory, why it was created, and the participatory mapping partners behind it
trackers.desc: A mapped customary territory can be registered with a named body, and that body exists precisely because nobody else was keeping the record. The registration body records itself as the institution where customary territories are registered, formed in 2010 on the initiative of the indigenous peoples' alliance, a participatory mapping network, a forest watch organisation and a plantation watch organisation — the alliance already recorded in this bucket. It records the reason for its creation plainly: data and information on the existence of indigenous communities and their territories produced by participatory mapping were not well documented, and the government did not have maps or social data on the existence of indigenous peoples and their customary territories, which was a problem both for government and for communities when efforts were made to push for recognition and protection of indigenous peoples' rights. For a community whose map exists only on its own wall, a national register is what turns it into evidence. Its legal basis and its early structure are recorded. It records its first legal standing as resting on a numbered decision of the alliance's secretary general in 2011, which made it an autonomous body of the alliance with a head appointed as daily manager on the proposal of its board of patrons; and records that in its early period it had two regional offices, in a named western province and a named central province, as a model for developing territory registration service offices in those two regions. The mapping itself is a described process with published scale. Published material records the alliance and the registration body carrying out participatory mapping of customary territories, with 7.4 million hectares mapped participatively by member communities by a stated year, and records the alliance as also providing legal services and case handling for customary communities in relation to their rights. It records the registration body's head describing three processes usually followed in participatory mapping, and records advice from a provincial spatial planning official that mapping should be coordinated with neighbouring villages over coastal and forest boundaries, so that boundary decisions are certain and later problems are avoided. Read this with the indigenous alliance, the legal companions, the mining network and the customary forest entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Auriga Nusantara — deforestation figures verified against satellite imagery and field visits, concession-level breakdowns naming who cleared what, and training for journalists and activists in the tracking tools
trackers.desc: Deforestation here is counted by a civic foundation, concession by concession. Published reporting records its annual status report finding 261,575 hectares of natural forest lost in 2024, up 4,191 hectares on the previous year, and records that about 58.7 per cent — roughly 153,498 hectares — was inside company concessions, broken down as 36,068 hectares in logging concessions, 41,332 in wood plantation concessions, 38,615 in mining concessions and about 37,483 in oil palm concessions. A community facing a concession can therefore cite a national figure attributing clearance to that class of permit. The method is stated, and it includes going to look. The same reporting records researchers collecting secondary data, then classifying and verifying indicated deforestation areas against satellite imagery, working from tree cover loss alerts, and records field monitoring by the foundation's team verifying deforestation inside a named coal concession, with the date the photograph was taken. It records field investigation of nickel mining at a named archipelago finding destroyed and bleached coral as well as deforestation, from vessel traffic and sediment cover, and records that 381 mining permits across 289 small islands, totalling 921,000 hectares, threaten coastal ecosystems and local livelihoods. It works the supply chain end too. Reporting records the foundation and a foreign investigative organisation analysing around 10,000 industry raw material fulfilment filings to the forestry ministry's data system and identifying 65 mills receiving and processing timber from natural forest clearance, then combining that with trade data to show the top five users of deforestation timber in 2024 all sold products to Europe; and records its mapping finding 2.9 million hectares of natural forest converted directly to oil palm to 2019. It teaches the tools rather than keeping them. Reporting records the foundation running training for journalists and non-governmental activists in named land-cover and supply-chain tracking platforms, with staff explaining that the data can be used as comparison data to analyse what actually happened in a place and whether the government has correctly assigned the status of an area. Read this with the customary territory register, the mining network, the environmental forum and the legal companions entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The provincial accredited legal aid offices — the regional ministry list of every accredited office with its head and address, the poverty letter from the village head that opens the door, and the three-day answer rule
