Amendments enacted alongside the Authority's creation allow the cabinet or the minister to designate a project as priority and bypass minimum review timelines and public consultation, with a companion amendment removing the EIA requirement altogether for road construction, major housing, large-scale tree removal and certain resort structures; both carry a 42-month sunset clause expiring in November 2028. A separate 2022 tree regulation still requires the Authority's approval and local council witnessing for public tree removal and prohibits taking beach trees, trees within 20 metres inland, trees in protected areas and any tree over 50 years old. That one is a live complaint route: the Authority acted on it in October 2025 over more than 500 palms removed from Lhaimagu in Shaviyani Atoll for resort landscaping, and fined the island council.

trackers.name: Maldives Green Fund — permitted uses, a monthly published ledger by island, and the balance that answers 'there is no money'
trackers.desc: Its permitted uses include addressing environmental issues faced by communities, which is unusually direct wording for a national fund. Governed by a trust statement issued by the finance minister in 2019, the fund exists to manage protected areas under the environment protection law, to assist environmental and social programmes in those areas, to facilitate protection of environmentally significant areas, and to address environmental issues faced by communities. It takes the green tax levied on tourists, and also accepts contributions and donations from the private sector and from international organisations, and allocations from revenue generated by managing protected areas. The ledger is published monthly, and that is what makes it usable. The finance ministry issues a Green Fund Report as a statistical release carrying the month's receipts and expenditures together with a monthly series spreadsheet, and the reports name individual projects and the islands they sit on — coastal protection at a named island, water systems at named islands. A community can therefore establish what the fund has spent on its own island, what it has spent elsewhere, and what remains, without asking anyone for permission. The balance is the argument. Collections have run far ahead of spending: the December 2025 report put the fund's balance at about 3.59 billion rufiyaa against project outflows for the year of about 275 million, on inflows exceeding 2.25 billion. Where an island is told there is no money for coastal protection, a water system or waste management, the published balance is the answer, and it is the ministry's own figure. Two changes to check. The rate doubled from 1 January 2025, to twelve US dollars a day at resorts, safari vessels and larger hotels and guesthouses and six dollars at smaller ones, with children under two exempt, so inflow figures in older reports understate what now arrives. And a decision was taken to allocate waste management money from the green tax to island councils directly, so that islands manage their own waste rather than depending on the centre; whether your council has received an allocation, and what it did with it, is a council-level question. The reports come from the finance ministry; the fund's purposes are set out by the environment ministry. Two further points from the finance ministry's own release. The statistical release explains its own figures — outflows represent expenditure on projects earmarked for the fund, and the balance is the difference between inflows and outflows for the year — and the underlying data is collected from the revenue authority with a monthly series available as a spreadsheet. The published expenditure list is in practice a list of which islands received something: island waste management centres, water and sewerage systems and coastal protection works, alongside larger regional schemes. Before writing to anyone, look through the series for your own island and for the amount, because a council asking for a waste facility is asking for a category the fund already funds elsewhere. The monthly report is published by the finance ministry at its statistical releases page under the title Green Fund Report.

trackers.name: Bar Council of the Maldives — the registers that tell you who is actually licensed
trackers.desc: Four public registers, and the one most people miss is higher rights of audience. The council, established under the 2019 legal profession law as the country's first unified, self-regulating bar, publishes registers of law firms, of legal practices, of public notaries and of higher rights of audience. The last of those tells you which lawyers may appear in the higher courts — a different question from whether someone is licensed at all, and the one that matters if a matter is going up rather than staying put. Check the registers before instructing anyone. The registers are current rather than historical, which makes an absence meaningful. Legal practices that do not pay the annual fee by 31 March each year are removed from the register. A name on the register is therefore a practitioner in current standing, and a name that is not there is itself a fact worth knowing before money changes hands. Know how practice is structured, because it tells you who you are contracting with. A lawyer practising alone must do so through a sole proprietorship registered under the sole proprietorship law and then registered with the council as a legal practice; lawyers practising together must do so through a partnership. Licensing itself requires completion of a licensing training programme and passing the bar examination administered by the council, held once each calendar year. There is a foreign counsel route, and it needs a sponsor. Maldivian reporting of the council's rules records that a foreign lawyer may be authorised to represent clients in Maldivian courts for a limited period of up to one year under a single permit, that the request must be made through the Attorney General's Office, the Prosecutor General's Office or a registered law firm, that the council must decide within seven days of the request and supporting documents, and that an interpreter must be present unless the presiding judge does not object to the lawyer's language. In a jurisdiction this small, where local counsel may be conflicted or unwilling, that is a real alternative — but it requires a registered firm or a state office willing to make the request.

trackers.name: EIA data collection guideline and the wastewater monthly returns — what must be sampled, and who holds the results
trackers.desc: The regulator publishes the sampling design an assessment is supposed to follow. Its data collection guideline specifies, among other things, taking three control water samples away from the project site, three water samples from the project site and a representative number of further samples, and sets out how coastal change is to be measured — cross-shore beach profiles, bathymetric data presented on a map, the extent of sediment plumes with the sites affected by high sedimentation and turbidity identified, and the wave, current and tidal parameters that govern how effluent disperses. A community can therefore check an assessment against the regulator's own stated method rather than against an opinion, and can copy that method when taking its own samples. The control samples away from the site are the part most often missing. Without them there is no baseline against which the project site readings mean anything, and the guideline requires them. If an assessment has no controls, that is a specific and checkable defect to put in writing during the comment window recorded in the other entry for this country. On the wastewater side there is a monthly return, and somebody already holds it. The national wastewater quality guidelines set maximum allowable concentrations for discharge and require all analytical data from all sample points to be submitted to the utility regulator monthly in electronic format; any non-compliance must be notified immediately with the components and concentrations concerned, together with a plan of action naming who is responsible and the expected date of compliance, and a maintenance plan annually. A community living beside an outfall should ask the utility regulator for those monthly returns rather than commissioning its own testing first. Two further checks. The assessment must be carried out using accredited assessors approved by the environment regulator, so whether the named assessor is on that approved list is a question with a documentary answer. And the utility regulator issues site-specific guidelines for the discharge of waste waters based on the assessment's recommendations — that site-specific guideline, not the general standard, is the document the operator beside you is actually held to, and it is worth asking for by name.

trackers.name: ERA complaints — confidential, acknowledged in three working days, and an authority that values the damage
trackers.desc: Three channels, and an acknowledgement you can hold them to. A person reporting an environmental violation or non-compliance may call the authority's compliance hotline during office hours, email a written complaint describing the incident, its location and any supporting evidence, or deliver or post a signed letter addressed to the chief executive. The authority states that all complaints are treated confidentially and are acknowledged within three working days. Ask for that acknowledgement, keep it, and quote its date when following up — it is the only fixed point most complaints in this file ever get. The authority values the damage, and that is its own job. Its published mandate includes studying damage to the environment of the country, imposing penalties on offenders, and assessing and valuing the compensation related to environmental damage before taking further action. Where a community wants a figure attached to what was destroyed — the reef, the trees, the lagoon — that valuation sits on the regulator's own list of functions rather than being something the community must commission and then defend. It is a scientific body as well as an enforcement one. The same mandate covers researching and investigating pollution in the local environment and giving technical information, advice and guidance to the relevant authorities; regulating protected areas and species under the environmental protection statute; setting the standards and procedures for the assessment reports that any significantly impacting project must produce; and maintaining a knowledge base and making that information available to the public, with an assessment repository and a laws page published on its site. And the information right is printed on the regulator's own pages. The authority's site records that the right to information act gives every citizen the right to access information from state institutions. Where an acknowledged complaint then goes quiet, the information request is the next document to send, and it is the regulator itself that has told you so. Read this with the assessment data collection guideline and the green fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Maldives Land and Survey Authority — approves council land requests, and regulates the surveyors
trackers.desc: An island council's land decision is not the last word. The authority's land section assesses the land approval requests submitted by local councils and grants the approvals, collects and maintains the land management data gathered from island councils, and is charged with ensuring that local councils and other relevant departments follow the guidelines and regulations enforced by the responsible ministry. For a community objecting to what its own island council has done with a piece of land, that is a second address — and one whose stated job includes checking whether the council followed the rules. It gives legal opinions on land conflicts, and it sets valuation floors. The same section assesses and provides legal opinion on land conflicts referred to it, prepares land handover documents for ministries, and runs a land valuation committee which sets minimum rates for residential land and for commercial land. Where the argument has become one about compensation rather than permission, a nationally set minimum rate exists and can be asked for. Surveys are registered and surveyors are regulated. The authority's survey standards and regulation function covers the registration of surveys, the setting of standards, the regulation of surveyors and the approval of surveys, and it has published guidelines for the land registration survey of islands. A survey relied on by a project can therefore be checked — whether it was registered and approved, and whether the surveyor is regulated — which is the same instrument this file records for Taiwan's register of licensed testing laboratories. And the map is the national one. The mapping section creates and maintains the country's base maps and the official registry of islands, the survey section travels to every island to measure and collect the geographic data, and the national map is published as the authoritative source under the authority's mandate to maintain the national land registry. Read this with the environmental complaints, green fund and assessment comment window entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Resilience Maldives — petitions against dredging, a halted reclamation, and a public record of the coverage
trackers.desc: A petition that preceded a halt. The organisation ran petitions calling for dredging operations to be suspended and for a proposed land reclamation beside a biosphere reserve to be stopped, on the ground that dredging could disrupt water flow, damage coral reefs and threaten marine biodiversity, with long-term consequences for the livelihoods and tourism that depend on the ecosystem. Its own record then notes that the government announced it would halt that reclamation following public opposition. For a community weighing whether a petition is worth the effort in this country, that sequence is the evidence. The win is recorded with its limit attached. The same record welcomes the decision and states plainly that the pause is temporary and does not address the broader environmental threats facing the atoll, urging all parties towards practices that protect the marine ecosystems there. Recording a victory together with what it did not achieve is how a campaign keeps its credibility for the next project — and it is the opposite of the practice that makes a community distrust its own advocates. They keep a public record of the coverage, with dates and sources. The organisation maintains a media and public record page, collecting the reporting on each campaign with the outlet, the publication date and an excerpt of what was said. That is a practice any community can copy at no cost: a dated list of what was reported, and by whom, is the cheapest archive there is, and it is what makes a later account of events hard to dispute. Read it beside the campaign already recorded here. This file already holds the citizen-led campaign that went for an injunction and works through island councils; this is a second organisation working the same ground by petition and documentation. Between them a community facing reclamation has two doors rather than one, and they use different instruments. Read this also with the environmental complaints, green fund and comment window entries recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Gazette's announcements — island leases tendered in public, with the map attached
trackers.desc: Uninhabited island leases are tendered publicly, and the map is attached. The government gazette carries the announcements through which the tourism ministry puts out to public tender the lease, development, operation and management of tourist resorts on named uninhabited islands, or on plots of land within them, with the number of beds specified, a map of the islands annexed to the announcement, and a minimum lease acquisition cost that the winning bidder must pay within a stated period of the letter of award. For a community whose nearest uninhabited island is being leased, the announcement and its map are public before anything is signed, and they name what is intended for the island. Bid openings are open to anyone who attends. Announcements state that bids will be publicly opened in the presence of the bidders' designated representatives and anyone who chooses to attend, at the address, date and time given; late bids are rejected and in some tenders electronic bidding is not permitted. An opening that anybody may attend is a fixed, public moment in a process that otherwise happens on paper. Amendments, re-announcements and cancellations are published too. Where a bidding document is amended, the amendment is published as its own gazette page referring back to the original announcement number; where an announcement is cancelled, the replacement says so and supersedes it by number. The history of a tender is therefore traceable through the gazette rather than existing only in the procuring agency's file. Two checkable lists sit behind the process. International competitive bidding is conducted under the public finance regulation, bidders register with the finance ministry and pay the registration fee through the government's online payment portal, and for construction work only members of the national contractors registry holding the relevant grade are eligible to participate. Whether the contractor on a site is registered, and at what grade, is therefore a question with an answer. Read this with the land and survey authority, the environmental complaints route and the green fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Auditor General's Office — state companies auditable, private audit licences issued here, and asset statements filed here
trackers.desc: The auditor general reports to the public, not only to the state. The office describes itself as established under the audit act to enable the auditor general to discharge a legal mandate, and states that the auditor general reports directly to the parliament, to the president and to the public, auditing all the offices, departments and institutions operating under the legislative, executive and judicial powers of the state. A duty owed to the public is the sentence to quote when asking for a report. A project run through a state company is still inside the audit scope. Published descriptions of the office's powers record a discretion to conduct performance audits of ministries, departments, government offices and other government institutions, of state-owned enterprises and business entities in which the government holds a controlling interest, and of government trusts, alongside financial statement audits and compliance and special audits. In a country where infrastructure, utilities and land development are frequently carried out through state-owned companies rather than ministries, that scope is the point. The office licenses private auditors and can cancel a licence. The same descriptions record that the audit act empowers the auditor general to issue and cancel the audit licences of private auditors and to set the rules governing their issue and cancellation. Where a developer's accounts are signed by a private auditor, the body that licenses that auditor is therefore named — the second such lever recorded in this file, after the accountancy supervision recorded for Myanmar. Asset statements are filed with this office. Under the constitution the president and each cabinet member, and members of certain independent commissions, submit statements of all property and monies owned by them, their business interests and their assets and liabilities to the auditor general. One caution: the detail on licensing, on performance audit scope and on asset statements comes from a published profile of the office rather than from its own pages, so ask the office to confirm the current position before relying on it. Read this with the gazette tender announcements, the land and survey authority, the environmental complaints route and the green fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: National Health Laboratory — a published price list for water chemistry, sample acceptance criteria, and two other laboratories
trackers.desc: The price list is published, test by test. The national health laboratory's information sheet sets out the tests available and their prices for the analysis of water chemistry, the acceptance criteria for water chemistry samples, the sampling methods it follows for physicochemical analysis, the container types required for each group of parameters and the minimum quantity of sample needed for each test. A community can therefore price a water test and prepare the sample correctly before it goes anywhere near a counter, which is the step at which most attempts at independent evidence fail. Payment runs through the government portal against a requisition number. The sheet directs that payment for sample testing be made through the state payment portal, quoting the requisition form number as the reference and the requisition total as the amount, with a payment link issued once the request is approved. That makes the transaction traceable: a receipt carrying a requisition number is itself evidence that a particular sample was submitted on a particular day. The laboratory is accredited, and it is the state's own checker. It is a division of the food and drug authority with a mandate covering the safety, quality control and hygiene verification of food and pharmaceuticals, has held accreditation to the international testing laboratory standard since December 2008, is divided into chemistry and microbiology sections, and tests water, food and swabs brought from food establishments, factories and resorts. The water utility's own published answers record that the environmental agency checks water quality through this same laboratory — so a result from it is not a second opinion, it is the opinion the regulator already relies on. Two other laboratories exist, and one will collect the sample. The water utility runs its own laboratory accredited to the same standard since 2013, offering water quality assurance packages that include sampling materials — cooler box, sampling bottles and bags — with training in correct sample collection, and a sample collection service from any point in the capital; and a private life sciences laboratory offers food and water testing with a dedicated microbiology facility. Where the state laboratory is slow, or a result needs checking against another, there are two further doors. Read this with the assessment data collection guideline, the regulator's comment window, the green fund and the land and survey authority entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Island land use plans and the Local Government Authority — the plan that decides what gets built, and the direction of travel
trackers.desc: The island's land use plan is the document that decides what gets built where. Under the decentralisation law the island council must prepare the island's development plan and land use plan within three months of the elected members taking office, with technical assistance from the atoll council, and the plan is then submitted to the planning ministry for approval. The first request a community should make is for the current plan and its approval status: published reporting recorded sixty-eight councils having submitted land use plans at one point with nineteen approved, and funds released to those whose plans were approved, which means whether your island has an approved plan at all is a live question rather than an assumption. The authority above the council is where complaints about a council go. The local government authority is a state institution established under the same law to regulate, oversee and develop the system of local governance; its published mandate covers monitoring that councils act in accordance with the Constitution and the decentralisation law, coordinating councils nationally, and harmonising the standards, procedures and regulations that different councils make. It runs an electronic platform through which it deals with councils, and published accounts record that it may suspend councillors for negligence, for abuse of council powers or resources or for breach of the code of conduct. The direction of travel is against council control of land, and a community should know it before relying on a council's refusal. Published accounts record amendments allowing central government to proceed where council approval is not given within an adequate time and requiring councils to report their activities to central government; and a bill under review that would allow the cabinet to remove land or property from a council's jurisdiction for government development projects, with the authority notifying the council and the property reverting to state control, would require councils to transfer land even before the island's physical development plan is approved, and would classify obstructing a government project without reasonable grounds as prohibited conduct for a councillor. A council that says no may not be the end of the matter. Two things survive the change, and both should be obtained in writing. Such a decision is required to be made public, and existing legislation requires compensation for investments made on reclaimed land. Get the plan, its approval date and any jurisdiction decision on paper. Read this with the gazette's island lease announcements, the regulator's comment window, the green fund and the land and survey authority entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Baa Atoll Conservation Fund — small grants to the community, financed from tourism, inside a biosphere reserve
trackers.desc: Small grants go to the community, and the money comes from tourism. Published accounts record an independent trust fund into which income generated from the atoll's natural assets and ecosystem services is channelled, supporting conservation, research, education and community sustainable development, with small grants provided to the community through the fund and support for the biosphere reserve office, all managed by an independent fund board. For a community in this atoll, that is a named local fund with an application route — not a national window in the capital and not a foreign donor's call. Its stated purpose is co-financing. The fund describes itself as existing to co-finance activities that ensure the atoll is a world-class model of atoll ecosystem conservation in accordance with its designation as a biosphere reserve. Co-financing means an applicant is expected to bring something to the table — a council contribution, community labour, a resort partner — and knowing that before drafting is the difference between an application that fits the fund and one that does not. The protection arrived with the money. Published accounts of the project behind the designation record that eight new protected areas were declared in the atoll and the boundaries of two existing ones extended, giving ten protected areas by its close, with core areas in which extraction of any kind is prohibited, across an atoll of more than a hundred and thirty-nine thousand hectares. Designation and finance came together, and that pairing is the argument to make in any other atoll: protection that funds the community is easier to agree than protection that only restricts it. The launch figures and the office are on record. The reserve and the fund were launched in June 2012, with a quarter of a million United States dollars handed over by an international environment facility through a United Nations agency and a first instalment of fifty thousand dollars from the government against an agreed quarter million; the biosphere reserve office in the atoll's capital island is funded by government while its work plan is funded by the fund; and contact details and a donation route are published. Read this with the national green fund, the regulator's comment window, the island land use plans and the gazette lease announcement entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Protected area designation — the evidence the ministry itself cites, and one island, one reef, one mangrove per atoll
trackers.desc: The stated policy is one island, one reef and one mangrove in every atoll. Government announcements record sites being designated as protected under section four of the environmental protection and preservation act on the recommendation of cabinet, and state the administration's plan to designate at least one island, one reef and one mangrove in each atoll, with batches of sites declared across several atolls. A community asking for its mangrove, its reef or its uninhabited island to be protected is therefore asking for something the government has already said it intends to do everywhere — which is a different conversation from asking for an exception. The reasons the ministry gives are the specification for a community submission. In recommending a group of sites for protection, the environment ministry's paper cited research reports; first-hand reports from craftsmen of the area, specifically fishermen and farmers; non-governmental organisations, associations and experts from the environmental field; and traditional knowledge passed down through generations. That list names the evidence the decision-maker has itself relied on, and it expressly includes the knowledge of the people who use the place. Assemble a submission in those four categories and it matches what has already persuaded. Designation has stopped a project before. Published accounts record one northern island designated under the act in 2018 which had previously been considered for the development of an airport intended to boost tourism infrastructure in the atoll, and record around ninety-three sites designated in recent years with management effort lagging well behind designation. Designation is a status rather than a management plan, so the question that follows a successful request is who has been assigned to manage the area. A regulation governs the detail. A protected areas regulation issued by the environment ministry in 2018 sets out the framework, including provision for an agency to be designated as the party assigned to manage a protected area. Read this with the island land use plans and the local government authority, the regulator's comment window, the atoll conservation fund and the gazette's island lease announcement entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Cultural heritage protection — losing a historic site is a criminal act, and there is a named centre to notify
trackers.desc: Destroying a historic site is a criminal act under the 2019 legislation. The heritage legislation ratified in September 2019, which repealed the 1979 law on historical and cultural properties, was described on enactment as ascertaining the procedures and jurisdictions of the state and of individuals and as stipulating that acts resulting in the loss of items or sites of historical significance are criminal acts, its stated purpose being to safeguard the perpetuation of items and sites of historical significance for future generations and to ensure the documentation, preservation and protection of cultural heritage. Where a project would remove an old mosque, a coral stone structure, a bath tank, a cemetery or a similar site, the exposure is therefore criminal rather than merely administrative, and saying so in writing at the outset changes what a contractor is willing to do. There is a named national body under the Act. A national centre for cultural heritage was established under that legislation, and the president subsequently renamed the former heritage department to it under the section of the Act providing for this; the centre operates under the culture ministry and conserves and protects both tangible and intangible heritage. That centre is the office to notify in writing the moment a site is threatened, and a dated letter to it becomes part of the record whatever happens next. The constitution places the duty on every citizen. The constitution makes it the responsibility of every citizen to preserve and protect the culture, language and heritage of the country. A resident writing to the centre about a threatened site is therefore discharging a constitutional responsibility rather than making a request as an interested party — and that framing belongs in the first line of the letter. A civil society body works alongside the state one. A heritage association promotes the country's history and culture, works on protecting and developing historical sites, and states that it works with government and private organisations. Two letters are better than one: the statutory centre, which can act, and the association, which can speak publicly. Read this with the protected area designation route, the island land use plans and the local government authority, the environmental regulator's comment window and the atoll conservation fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The business registry portal — a free lookup by name or number, and the permanent number that crosses government systems
trackers.desc: A free public lookup, by name or by registration number. The business registry is maintained by the economic development and trade ministry, and the ministry announced that all services related to the business registry would be processed online through its business portal from the first of January 2022. Published guidance on using it records that basic company lookups by name or registration number are free, that no account and no local identity document are required, that the interface is in English, and that results are returned immediately, with no bulk access. For a community trying to name the operator behind a reclamation, a resort lease or a harbour project, that is a first step that costs nothing and takes minutes. The permanent number is the key that crosses systems. Every business entity is assigned a registration number and a unique permanent number at the time of registration, and that permanent number serves as the primary identifier across government systems. Recording it once makes every later request — to the regulator, the council, the audit office or the information commissioner — precise rather than approximate, and it survives a change of trading name. Three registration tracks, not one. The legal framework rests on the companies legislation of 1996 and its amendments together with separate regulations for sole proprietorships and for foreign companies. An operator may therefore be registered on a track other than the company register, which is worth knowing before concluding from a blank search that an entity does not exist; foreign-owned project vehicles in particular sit under their own regulations. Names can be reserved before they are registered. The name search and reservation step allows a name to be reserved for a period before registration, or registered immediately. A name appearing in a project announcement may therefore be reserved rather than incorporated, and the difference is visible on the portal. Read this with the gazette's island lease announcements, the environmental regulator's comment window and complaints route, the auditor general's office and the information commissioner entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Bandaara goathi — island plot allocation, the land use plan that must exist first, and the council point policy that decides who gets one
trackers.desc: No plot can be allocated until the island has an approved land use plan. The government service for approval and amendment of land use plans states the rule plainly: an approved land use plan is required before land allocation in the islands and cities, under the amendment to the decentralisation legislation. That single requirement is the leverage point for a community that wants a stretch of island kept as it is — the plan is approved before allocations follow, amendments to it go through the same service, and both are decisions made on paper that can be asked for. Residential plots on the islands are the ordinary route to land. Policy analysis records that around nine in ten inhabited islands allocate residential plots — bandaara goathi — rather than built housing, with plots averaging roughly two to three thousand square feet, and that many allocated plots remain unbuilt. The land and survey authority's valuation committee sets minimum rates for residential and commercial land and the authority is charged with ensuring councils follow the ministry's guidelines and regulations, so a council decision that departs from them has somewhere to be raised. The council's own point policy decides who qualifies. Island councils run point-based allocation policies and amend them; reporting on one island with high land values records a requirement that an applicant own no land, or no land above six hundred square feet, anywhere in the country. Anyone intending to apply should obtain the current point policy for their own island rather than assume the national criteria apply, because it is the council's document that governs. The national schemes run on different rules again. Reporting on the current capital-region programmes records allocations of fifteen thousand plots of one thousand two hundred and fifty square feet alongside some seven thousand nine hundred flats, with eligibility rules revised so that a spouse's property counts against an applicant only where it exceeds four hundred square feet in the capital region rather than any property anywhere, and a separate track for applicants whose spouse already holds housing. Where a family has been displaced or is being asked to give up land, which scheme they fall under decides the criteria entirely. Read this with the land and survey authority, the island land use plans and local government authority entry, the gazette's tendered island leases and the protected area designation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Maldives Independent — relaunched in 2025, staff-owned, with an air quality monitor and a stated pitch address
trackers.desc: A twenty-year-old independent newsroom, relaunched and owned by its own journalists. The outlet describes itself as an award-winning Maldivian publication with a twenty-year history, relaunched in February 2025 and entirely owned and operated by its Maldivian staff, some of whom have been with it for well over a decade. Founded in 2004 under an earlier name and rebranded in 2015, it publishes feature articles, investigative journalism, a daily news roundup, timelines, a podcast and social content, with coverage spanning politics and corruption through to climate change, and it has added a Dhivehi edition, a weekly newsletter and a live air quality monitor. Staff ownership is the structural fact that matters here: there is no proprietor whose other interests a story might touch. It publishes the address to pitch to, and how it is funded. The outlet invites opinion pitches to a stated editorial address, and sets out its funding: a membership programme of direct reader support, institutional newsletters sold to the diplomatic and business community, and recognition or support from international media development bodies including the organised crime and corruption reporting network, a global media development forum, an international press institute and a regional journalism organisation. Its stated position is that media is most accountable when supported directly by its audience rather than by politicians or oligarchs. The history is part of the resource, and it is not comfortable reading. Published accounts record that the newsroom suspended operations in January 2020 after fifteen years, that in the period before this one of its journalists was disappeared and a contributor was killed, that a presidential commission into those cases did not resolve them, and that police entered the outlet's headquarters in 2016. The relaunched newsroom's own stated aim, in its chief executive's words reported by a journalism institute, is to survive long term and to get nobody killed. Anyone bringing a sensitive story should read that history as information about risk on both sides of the exchange, and discuss protection before sending documents. The practical shape of it. A lean full-time editorial team of an editor-in-chief and two senior journalists with a chief executive, working with freelancers, and a membership programme launched in late 2025. Expect capacity limits, and note that a second independent outlet describing itself as editorially separate from party, government and sponsor also maintains a newsroom in the capital with contributors across the atolls. Read this with the island land use plans, the environmental regulator's comment window, the information commissioner and the auditor general entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: State legal aid — criminal cases only, the constitutional right to counsel, and the documented reasons islanders cannot use it
trackers.desc: State legal aid here is criminal, not civil, and that boundary decides everything. Published country profiles record a constitutional right to counsel and that the attorney general's office provides legal aid to indigent criminal defendants; descriptions of the office's functions likewise put the provision of legal aid to the needy in criminal cases inside its mandate, alongside representing the state in all civil matters. A community fighting a reclamation, a lease or an eviction is in civil or administrative territory, where no equivalent state service is recorded — so the realistic plan is a private lawyer, an organisation with in-house counsel, or the complaint routes that do not require representation. Knowing that before spending weeks seeking free civil representation is the point of this entry. The obstacles are documented, not guessed. A development-agency working paper prepared with the attorney general's office records that guidelines and income verification for determining the state's responsibility to provide a defence are too complicated and do not reflect people's actual ability to hire a lawyer; that because the lawyers are resident in the capital, people living on the islands struggle to reach counsel at all; and that a pilot placing at least one lawyer in each major atoll, or mobile lawyers, could address it. Those three findings are the ones to cite when asking why a case on an outer island has no representation. The profession has one regulator, and it is the place to start. There is a single bar, established under the legal profession legislation of 2019, which regulates the profession and its conduct and discipline — the register entry already recorded for this country. Since most lawyers are based in the capital, the practical sequence is: identify practitioners through the register, ask directly about island-based or remote representation, and establish fees before travel is arranged. Where representation is not available, use the routes that do not need it. The information commissioner, the environmental regulator's complaints channel and the auditor general's office recorded elsewhere in this country's entries all accept complaints from individuals without counsel. Read this with those entries and with the bar council register and the island land use plan entries already recorded here.

trackers.name: The judicial administration department — where court orders and rulings are published, and the two branches outside the capital
trackers.desc: Rulings that bind lower courts are published by the judiciary's administrative department. The department mandated to organise and oversee the administration of the judiciary, functioning under the supreme court, publishes the court system, court orders and rulings and related material on its site — including procedural rulings of the supreme court set out in full with case number and date. For a community, the value is that the rulings which govern how cases are handled are readable in advance rather than discovered at a hearing. Each court is bound by the rulings of the courts above it, and the department states so. Its account of the system records a three-tier structure — supreme court, high court and lower courts, the latter divided into superior and magistrate courts — that every court may overturn decisions of courts below it, and that each court is bound by the rulings of the courts above under a named constitutional provision. That is the point that makes a superior ruling worth finding: unlike the civil law systems elsewhere in this file, a higher court's ruling here binds the court hearing your case. The high court sits in three places, not only the capital. The same account records that the high court consists of three separate branches, located in the capital, in the southern city and in a northern atoll capital, and that it has original jurisdiction in cases named by the judicature legislation as well as hearing appeals from lower courts. For an island community, the existence of branches outside the capital is a practical fact about whether a case can be conducted at all, and it sits directly against the finding recorded earlier here that lawyers are concentrated in the capital. The case system is electronic across all tiers. The department describes an electronic court case management system in use by all tiers of the judiciary, covering filing, processing, approvals, appeals and reproduction of case documents according to court regulations, with case records entered and updated electronically. Where a case number is known, ask the registry what that system can produce. Read this with the state legal aid entry, the bar council register, the island land use plan and the information commissioner entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Associations Act 2022 and the 2024 regulation — two people can register, the Registrar has thirty days, and fundraising rules go in your own basic rules
trackers.desc: The statute that governs forming a body to hold money was replaced in 2022. The presidency's announcement records that the associations legislation ratified in May 2022 governs the exercise of the constitutional right to form associations — incorporation, registration and regulation, the general rights and obligations of such entities, and the duties of the Registrar of Associations — and that it specifies terms for fundraising, financial liabilities and dissolution. It required a Registrar to be appointed within thirty days, with the Registrar to make the rules under the law, and gave the Registrar discretion to dissolve inactive associations that fail to pay annual fees and miss a six-month deadline to settle fines. It came into force six months after ratification and repealed the 2003 Act. Two applicants is the threshold, and the decision has a clock. Published legal commentary records that an association can be registered by two or more applicants, that the new regime allows both natural and legal persons to apply so that two or more companies may jointly register one, and that the Registrar must decide on registration within thirty days of the application documents being submitted, with consequences where no decision is taken in time. It also records categories outside the regime, including associations formed under an Act of Parliament, international associations operating under ratified agreements, and student, teacher or guardian associations of educational institutions. Your own basic rules must set out how you fundraise. Commentary on the 2024 regulation made under the Act records that organisations must have well-defined basic rules covering membership fees, fundraising procedures and other operational details; that the regulation covers budgeting, bank accounts, business operations, loans and auditing; that annual reports including financial statements must be submitted to the Registrar; and that reports must go to the Registrar within thirty days of the general meeting. Drafting the fundraising procedure into the constitution at formation is therefore not optional. What is permitted, and who carries the risk. The regulation is recorded as defining permitted activities ranging from business activities to promoting ideologies — expressly excluding political movements — advocating for legal changes and engaging in rural development; organisations are private entities owning their own assets, but executive committee members can be held personally liable for rule violations. Advocating legal change is inside the permitted range; party politics is not. Read this with the island land use plan, the bar council register, the state legal aid limits and the judicial administration entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Where to get water tested — an accredited utility laboratory with a test requisition form, a private food and water laboratory, and the state verification chain
trackers.desc: There is an accredited laboratory that sells testing, and it publishes a requisition form. The water and sewerage company's water quality assurance service describes a laboratory certified to the international testing standard, offering a package with daily, monthly, biannual and annual testing parameters, sampling materials including cooler box, sampling bottles and bags with training on the correct sampling method, sample collection from any point in the capital, no waiting at the collection counter for verification and payment, and an annual water quality certification. Its laboratory pages publish a water quality assurance test requisition form. A community that suspects contamination can therefore buy an accredited test rather than argue from smell and colour — and the sampling training matters, because a badly taken sample is the usual reason a result is dismissed. The tests are framed against the regulator's own standards. Reporting on the service records that the package lets clients verify that water quality meets the standards specified by the environmental protection agency, and that tests are run to the parameters required under those regulations. Ask for the test set that matches the agency's parameters, so the result speaks directly to the standard. The state verification chain is published, and it names three more bodies. The company's own answers record that its water quality is maintained by hourly monitoring of production parameters on site and daily monitoring by its own laboratory, verified by independent tests carried out by the food and drug authority, and also checked by the environmental protection agency through the national health laboratory, with dedicated sampling points assigned on each island where it produces drinking water. Those are three separate institutions that already hold results for your island. There is a private alternative. A clinic's life sciences laboratory describes itself as a provider of food and water testing, operating a modular clean room laboratory for microbiological testing with controlled environments and cross-contamination prevention, established to close the gap in food and water testing in the country. A second laboratory matters when the first is the utility whose water is in question. Read this with the assessment comment window, the island land use plan, the bar council register and the associations regulation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Petition Committee and the e-petition portal — a standing committee that takes citizens' petitions, with land and lease objections among the ones already filed
trackers.desc: Parliament has a standing committee whose subject is petitions. The parliament's own pages list a petition committee among the standing committees of the current parliament, record that standing committees are permanent bodies whose formation is set in the standing orders, and record that they meet to study in detail the bills, issues, petitions and motions referred to them; petitions also appear as their own category of chamber document alongside bills, resolutions, emergency motions and parliamentary questions. A community whose objection has been refused by an authority has a second forum, and it keeps a public record. Land and lease objections are already among the petitions it has taken. The committee's published listing includes a petition objecting to a council's decision to give an island's north coast for building a guest house, and a petition seeking not to cancel a gazetted list of flat owners under a named housing scheme. That first example is precisely the kind of decision this file exists for: a local council allocating coastline for a tourism development. Read the committee's own listings to see how such petitions were worded. The route was digitised in 2025, and the thresholds changed. A development agency's announcement records that the parliament launched the country's first electronic petition system in February 2025, allowing citizens to submit and track petitions online with signatures and submissions verified through the national digital identity mechanism; that it minimises the need for member sponsorship, expands access for people living on remote islands, and introduces different thresholds with legal triggers in the legislative process; and that its objectives include introducing timelines for petition responses and enabling special petitions to be debated in the chamber. Commentary records that petitions traditionally required wet signatures and physical delivery to the parliament, and that any number of citizens may sign a petition which then had to be sponsored by a sitting member before reaching the committee. Check the current threshold before collecting signatures, because the number decides what happens next. Related channels sit on the same site. The parliament publishes its standing orders and regulations, a whistleblowing page, an information officer contact and a civil society parliamentary network. Read this with the island land use plans, the environmental regulator's comment window, the campaign organisations and the information commissioner entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The utility regulator — complaints about water, sewerage, electricity and waste in one place, a public register of licensed designers, and the island deadline
trackers.desc: One authority now regulates water, sewerage, electricity and waste, and takes complaints on all of them. The utility regulator records that it was established in December 2020 under its own Act to regulate public utility services under one roof; that the functions previously carried out by individual agencies were transferred to it, the energy authority being abolished and the environment agency's regulatory responsibilities for water, sewerage and waste management devolved to it; and that its services include investigating and taking action on complaints regarding public utility services. An island whose supply is failing, or whose waste is being handled badly, now has one addressee rather than three. The mandate is a list of duties a complaint can be framed against. The published mandate includes examining whether water and sewerage systems are designed to the standards prescribed by the ministry and approving those designs; assessing the quality of water supply and of system designers, issuing licences to engineers and designers and compiling and making public a register of such persons; ensuring services are provided to prescribed standards and charged in accordance with the regulations; ensuring the quality of water supplied for public use in collaboration with local councils and the service provider; determining standards for equipment and for water produced for commercial and public use; taking action against those who violate the Act; and collecting information and statistics on water and sewerage services. Check the designer against the public register before accepting that a system is properly built. The regulations reach the village watershed. A summary of the 2021 general regulations, made under the water and sewerage Act and the regulator's own Act, records that they cover the stages of establishing a water and sewerage system including preparation of an environmental impact report, standards for systems, damage caused by natural causes, safety and quality measures, registration and licensing of systems, licences to provide services, and the supply of water in villages with prohibition of discharge into any village watershed. That prohibition is the sentence to quote where waste is being put into an island's own water. There is a deadline, and it has moved. Government records show the Act was ratified in 2020, and that a second amendment ratified in August 2025 aims to ensure every inhabited island has timely access to an adequate water supply by 2027, providing for technical advice and guidance to local councils, licensing requirements for technical professionals, criteria for water testing laboratories established in the country, and penalties for misuse of systems. Read this with the water testing entry, the environmental regulator's comment window, the island land use plans and the green fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: General Fisheries Regulation — the lagoon boundary measured from the vegetation line, the net rules for personal consumption, and the nationwide gear prohibitions
trackers.desc: The lagoon boundary of an inhabited island is set by a measured rule, not by custom. The 2020 general fisheries regulation, made under the 2019 fisheries legislation and published in the government gazette, contains a chapter on determination of lagoon area, providing that for islands other than resorts the lagoon area is determined by reference to the distance between the vegetation line and the reef as the regulation sets out, with a separate boundary regulation governing islands leased for tourist resort development. Where a project claims an area of lagoon, that measurement is the thing to check. The regulation's chapters also cover fishing using a net for personal consumption, fishing from lagoon waters, best practice guidelines, scuba diving for fishery, prohibited species for harvesting and for export and import, fish aggregating devices, information sharing, fisheries observers and rangers, the fisheries registry and penalties. Five kinds of fishing are prohibited outright in these waters. The 2019 Act provides that the following are prohibited in the maritime zones: purse seine fishing; gillnet fishing; trawl net fishing; fishing using a net, with the exception of bait fishing and fishing for personal consumption; and fishing using an explosive, poison or other such chemical. Those five are checkable from a boat or a photograph. Even the personal consumption exception carries conditions. The regulation sets a policy for the use and requirements of nets used for personal consumption within the maritime zones, including that a net shall not be left in use for longer than two hours, and provides that no person may be sent diving for bait fishing, fishing or related activities without ensuring the stated safeguards. Those are the conditions to quote when a commercial operation claims the personal exception. Licences can be suspended or revoked, and observers are appointed publicly. The Act provides that a fishing licence may be revoked or temporarily suspended where revocation is important to manage a specific type of fishery, where a licensed vessel is used in contravention of the Act or a licence condition, or where the vessel's registration is affected; and that a licence may not be transferred to a third party without the ministry's approval. It provides that the ministry shall determine, by public announcement in the government gazette, the parties who will act as observers on licensed vessels. Published reporting records that a shark fishing ban across the exclusive economic zone, first imposed in 2010 with compensation to the fishermen affected, has been continued under this Act. Read this with the environmental regulator's comment window, the atoll conservation fund, the protected area designation and the island land use plan entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Protected species and the rules that come with a protected area — the ministry's own regulation, the acts banned inside a designated area, and the trade bans notified by date
trackers.desc: The protected species regulation is published by the ministry itself, alongside the protected areas regulation. The ministry's publications page carries the protected species regulation of 2021 as a downloadable instrument under environmental protection. Published legal material records the framework around it: the 1993 environment protection and preservation Act, under which the ministry is responsible for identifying protected areas and natural reserves and making the rules for their protection, for requiring an impact assessment before any development project that may affect the environment, and with authority to terminate any project that has an undesirable impact on the environment; the 2018 protected areas regulation; the 2021 endangered species protection regulation; the plants protection Act; and the 2022 regulation for protection and preservation of island vegetation and flora. Naming the instrument is what makes a request specific. Inside a protected area, five acts are banned and the permitted uses are listed. National reporting of three designations records that fishing, sand mining, removal of stones, collecting shells and littering are banned in protected areas, while bait fishing and shallow trolling outside the core zones are allowed, as are swimming, snorkelling, diving and picnics; and records two islands designated as protected areas with sustainable use, one for coral reef and mangrove ecosystems providing breeding and nesting grounds, the other for a wetland described as nationally significant to neighbouring island communities. It records that two of the protected islands had previously been considered for airports, with one airport plan scrapped after the environment agency raised alarms based on the impact assessment — the sequence a community can point to. The species bans are dated and numbered. Published listings record marine species prohibited from killing, catching, collection or extraction, each with the notice number and date of the ban — dolphins, whales, giant clams, triton shells and berried or undersized lobsters from 1993; black coral from 1995; the Napoleon wrasse and whale shark later that year — and record a broader list including turtles, skates and rays, all corals other than one named type, parrot fish, eels, pearl oysters, puffer fish and bait fish. A trade notification records import and export bans on turtles, all ray species and locally endangered birds under the 1993 Act, gazetted by public announcement with offences punishable under the environment liability regulation. Read this with the protected area designation entry, the regulator's comment window, the fisheries regulation and the green fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The other environmental organisations — a research-based advocacy body campaigning against a named reclamation, a coral institute that works on policy with parliament, and the joint statement listing what has been rolled back
trackers.desc: One organisation's stated work is halting a named reclamation project in a biosphere reserve. Its own pages record that it was established in November 2019 and has grown through action, research-based advocacy and community-driven sustainability efforts, shaping environmental dialogue, supporting policy discussions and mobilising public engagement; that its initiatives aim to halt a thirteen-hectare land reclamation project and safeguard a named bay inside a biosphere reserve, a habitat for manta rays, whale sharks and coral reefs; and that it won a climate justice award in 2019 for a stewardship programme, recognising research-informed climate justice action and science-based advocacy. A community facing a reclamation has an organisation here that has run exactly that fight. A coral institute works the policy side with named counterparts. Its advocacy page records that it works to protect reefs in danger of being damaged or destroyed from infrastructure development and other human-driven threats, working with non-governmental organisations, construction companies, government officials, members of parliament and the community to highlight the dangers and encourage more robust policy and implementation; and records a schools programme teaching children to grow and transplant corals to their home reef. A marine conservation body states a measurable target. Published material records a Maldivian reef organisation, registered here in 2020 after working since 2016 as a foreign charity's project because it felt it necessary to have Maldivian organisations and people at the centre of conservation efforts, working to support well-managed and effectively enforced marine reserves covering thirty per cent of the country's waters and locally tailored small-scale fisheries. Another long-running island group is recorded conserving the beaches and reefs of one island, its volunteers observing the changes caused by reclamation and by jetty and harbour works, and lobbying for protection. A joint statement names what has been rolled back. A statement by two organisations, endorsed by civil society bodies across the country, records their objection to the abolishment of the semi-autonomous environmental protection agency, the legalisation of destructive activities in protected areas, the reopening of the shark fishery, and the fast-tracking of opaque mega-development and reclamation projects, and cites international findings that reclamation and coastal structures harm the reefs and mangroves that protect island communities. Read this with the citizen campaign entry, the protected area designation, the dredging entry and the green fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Dredging and reclamation conditions — the distances the 2013 rules set, the amendments that opened protected areas to permitted works, and the mitigation terms a permit must carry
trackers.desc: The original distances are the baseline to measure a project against. Published reporting records that under the 1993 environmental protection legislation and regulations introduced in April 2013 there were clear prohibitions on sand borrowing and dredging in sensitive zones, listing them: a hundred-metre perimeter from the edge of a lagoon to an island's shore; the outer five hundred metres of any lagoon measured in from the outer wall; fifty metres inside the lagoon from an island's shoreline; and within two hundred metres of areas deemed protected or sensitive under the law. Those four numbers are measurable on a chart. The amendments are what a community has to check for, because they moved the line. The same reporting records that a year after the original rules, amendments allowed such activities with an agency permit provided stringent conditions were met — comprehensive marine life research, arrangements for the protection and management of the area, evaluation and mitigation of impacts on groundwater aquifers, and drainage adequate to address flooding; and separate reporting records later gazetted amendments allowing reclamation, sand borrowing and dredging in protected and environmentally sensitive areas where the project is approved by the cabinet or a cabinet committee, with commentary arguing successive amendments have weakened the safeguards. Establish which version of the regulation governs the permit in front of you. The permit conditions themselves are the enforceable part. Reporting of the regulator's own statement records that assessments for such projects require strict mitigation: maintaining at least five hundred metres from house reefs, extracting sand only from designated borrow areas, closing overflow control valves, using designated routes away from sensitive lagoons, monitoring turbidity, and suspending operations during weather warnings issued by the meteorological service. It records the regulator receiving a surge of complaints alleging work continuing without adequate safeguards, failure to install bund walls and silt screens before reclamation begins, and sand extraction outside approved areas, and warning it will take legal action against operators who breach permit conditions. Suspension has been ordered before. Reporting records the agency ordering suspension of dredging, reclamation and sand pumping for a stated month to reduce anthropogenic stress on reefs during a bleaching event, a special permit granted for one resort project despite it, and the agency looking into reported non-compliance with the order. Read this with the regulatory authority's comment window, the complaints entry, the assessment data guideline and the protected area designation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The statistical yearbook — every table downloadable as a spreadsheet, an environment chapter counting protected areas, sewerage and waste, and population by island back to the censuses
trackers.desc: Each table in the yearbook is published separately, in document and spreadsheet form. The statistics bureau publishes the yearbook as a comprehensive and systematic compendium of statistical information demonstrating social and economic developments and demographic transitions, with successive annual editions on the same path; every table is listed by number and title with both a document and a spreadsheet download beside it. Taking a single table as a spreadsheet, rather than a whole report as a document, is what makes the numbers usable in a submission. The environment chapter counts the things a project affects. Its tables include the number of islands that have a sewerage system across stated years; the number of protected areas and species by type across stated years; monthly waste collected by type; and waste transported to the named waste island in tonnes. Where a designation or a waste figure is disputed, that is the published series to cite. Population is published island by island, and back through the censuses. The same chapter set includes total population by island for the census and the registered population; the number of inhabited islands by size of population across six census years; population by age and sex for four censuses; and sex ratio by locality — with later editions carrying projected mid-year population of non-administrative islands by age and sex to 2030, buildings authorised for construction and completed by number and floor area in the capital, and reported cases of selected diseases by locality. The census and the bureau's own releases sit alongside. The census site records the population and housing census and the economic census carried out on stated dates, and states that a census provides information at national, atoll and island level to plan and provide a wide range of public services; its statistical releases page carries the provisional results with population by demographic characteristics at republic, capital and atoll level. The bureau's site publishes a dataset category with dated releases and headline indicators. Read this with the island land use plans, the green fund ledger, the protected area designation and the regulatory authority entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The NGO federation and the NGO directory — a national network of island and atoll associations with named officers, its stated objects including advocacy, and a public directory of registered organisations
trackers.desc: A national federation of associations exists, registered and with named officers from island societies. The federation records itself as registered in 2006, a network of civil society organisations, and lists its office holders by name with the association each comes from — island development societies, youth societies, a care society and a women's development society from named atolls and islands. It records a membership structure categorised into national member associations, regional member associations and affiliate members, and provides that a regular member of a member association becomes an individual member of the federation by virtue of that membership. For an island association wanting weight beyond its own island, that is the existing structure. Its stated objects include advocacy and getting issues into national policy. The federation records its objects as promoting and supporting social development at island, atoll and national levels; supporting and guiding development of the non-governmental sector; training the personnel of non-governmental and community-based organisations in techniques of community mobilisation; identifying pressing and emerging issues that need to be incorporated in national policy directives and development strategies; and undertaking advocacy activities to get those issues incorporated — resting on its stated belief that providing space for seeking opinions from various levels and segments of society is essential to an enabling environment for equitable distribution of resources and development benefits. A public directory of organisations exists, and so does the registration route. A national portal describes itself as an online directory and resource centre for the country's non-governmental organisations; separate published directories list environment and climate organisations working in the country, with stated result counts by category. Published procedural material records registration of a non-governmental organisation, self-help group or community group as handled by the ministry responsible for youth, sports and community empowerment, giving its street address, floor, telephone and email, and records the common requirements — a non-profit purpose, a governing body, and minimum membership. Read this with the associations Act entry, the campaign organisations, the green fund and the island council entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Transparency Maldives and its advice centre — free confidential legal advice for reporting corruption, a published office address, and demands on climate project documents a community can borrow
trackers.desc: A free, confidential advice centre exists for reporting corruption. Published material records that an advocacy and legal advice centre in the country can be contacted to report corruption, and that such centres provide free and confidential legal advice and allow people to safely report corruption. The organisation running it records itself as committed to eliminating corruption and promoting good governance through advocacy, research and public engagement, describes itself as non-political, and publishes its building, floor and street address in the capital. For someone who suspects a lease or a contract on their island was bought rather than won, that is a route that does not require going to the authorities first. Its published demands are usable as a checklist by a community facing a project. A press statement calls for timely and accessible publication online of all documents and information regarding project implementation and monitoring — monitoring and evaluation reports, audits, finance reports and project documents — kept up to date, and for climate projects to be monitored by a third party or an independent monitoring body. Those are the documents to ask for by name. It further calls for strengthened citizen engagement, meaningful consultation and inclusive participation when changes to laws and policies directly affect people's lives, and for the principles of decentralisation in the constitution to be upheld to empower local councils — the councils already recorded in this bucket. It also names the practical measures and the risks. The same statement calls for disaster response drills and training for local communities, clear coordination between government agencies, local councils and emergency responders, and nature-based solutions such as mangrove restoration and artificial reefs to reduce erosion and storm impact, and says local knowledge should supplement technical knowledge in preparedness planning. It calls for protection of civic space, media freedom and access to information, and for oversight institutions to have sufficient funds, resources and independence to perform their duties, free from intimidation and political influence, having expressed concern at deterioration of civic space. Read this with the information commissioner, the anti-corruption route, the island councils and the green fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The marine research institute — the body that officially monitors reef condition, a national monitoring programme running since 1998, and published status reports with long-term coral cover figures
trackers.desc: Reef condition here is officially monitored by a named state institute, and its record goes back decades. Published description records the institute as responsible for officially monitoring the condition of the country's coral reefs, with two main programmes — a national coral reef monitoring programme dating from 1998 and a national coral reef restoration and rehabilitation programme launched in 2019 — and records it cooperating with the environmental agency and international bodies in reef monitoring and research. It records the institute founded in 1984 as the research arm of the fisheries ministry and restructured under its present name in August 2019, and publishes a contact form, telephone and named research officer. For a community facing dredging or reclamation, that is the domestic body whose data the decision is supposed to rest on. The long-term figures are published and they are stark. Its own status report records the monitoring programme established after the first reported mass coral bleaching event of 1998, to collect long-term nationwide data, and records that live coral cover after that bleaching dropped to as low as 1 per cent, against previous records of close to 50 per cent mean live cover. It records that increased frequency and intensity of bleaching events reduces the potential for reefs to recover between disturbances, and states the country depends entirely on the functions of healthy reef systems for its sustenance and economy. It records work toward a more holistic set of protocols with reef composition integrated into long-term monitoring, and refers to a coral database as a repository of reef health information. Its published outputs and events are usable material. The institute records a biennial marine science symposium series described as the nation's leading platform for the communication of marine research conducted in the country, publishes reviews including one on marine turtle status based on data gathered from a citizen-science programme, and records pre-bleaching baseline surveys completed in a named atoll and work assessing coral spawning times and locations.
