Read this with the environment protection fund and designated laboratories, the public interest litigators, the accredited laboratory and the local level planning cycle entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: जग्गा प्राप्ति ऐन — the fifteen-day notice, the compensation determination committee, and the comparables it is allowed to use
trackers.desc: Two notices, and the second one carries fifteen days. The land acquisition legislation of 2034 in the local calendar runs through published notices before compensation is fixed. A Supreme Court judgment applying the Act records the sequence in a real case: the initial officer published the notice required for the purposes of the section on preliminary action, and the chief district officer then published a fifteen-day notice for the purposes of the sections dealing with the compensation stage, with notices also published around the land being acquired. A community should therefore expect two separate publications, and the fifteen-day one is the one attached to compensation. The Act itself is published by the law commission and mirrored by the ministries and the roads department, so the text is easy to obtain in the original. A committee fixes the compensation, and the statute lists what it must consider. Compensation is determined not by the acquiring agency but by a compensation determination committee, which must have regard to the matters set out in the Act's own section on the point. Where an owner disputes the figure, the argument is therefore about whether those listed matters were considered — a narrower and more answerable question than whether the sum feels low. What the committee may use as comparables. In the case recorded, the committee fixed compensation having regard to the statutory factors, to the compensation paid the previous year for land acquired for the same project, and to the valuation held by the land revenue office; and it paid compensation for the trees and bamboo standing on the land as well as for the land itself. Two practical points follow: the previous year's payments for the same project are legitimate comparables that an owner can ask for and cite, and standing trees and bamboo are compensable items that should appear separately in the award. Where the court drew the line. The same judgment rejected a challenge that the statutory periods under the earlier sections had not been completed, holding that the publications made were sufficient, and found no legal right of the petitioner to have been taken away. A challenge built only on the length of the notice periods therefore starts from a weak position; a challenge built on what the committee did or did not take into account is on the ground the statute itself marks out. Read this with the land revenue and survey offices, the district legal aid committees, the public interest litigators and the land rights organisation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The twenty-four hour rule — information touching a person's life and safety must be released within a day
trackers.desc: Where a request concerns the safety of a person's life, the clock is twenty-four hours. The information commission publishes the right to information legislation, and among its provisions is one that matters when a dispute has turned dangerous: notwithstanding the ordinary timeframes for responding, where an applicant has requested information related to the protection of a person's life, the information officer must make that information available to the applicant within twenty-four hours of the request. Ordinary requests run on the standard timetable; a request framed on this ground does not. For a household facing threats connected to a land dispute, or seeking to establish what an authority knows about a risk to someone, that provision converts an information request into an urgent one. Frame the request on its face. The provision turns on what the request is about, so the application should state plainly that the information sought relates to the protection of a person's life and should identify what is sought with enough precision that it can be produced in a day. A general request that happens to touch on safety will be treated as a general request. Keep the receipt and the time of submission: the twenty-four hours run from the request. Form matters too. The same legislation provides that the information officer shall, so far as possible, make the requested information available in the form in which it was requested — which is worth invoking where a summary would be offered instead of the document, or a reading instead of a copy. Where this sits. The Act's stated purpose is to make state activity open and transparent in accordance with democratic practice, to make public bodies accountable and responsible to citizens, to simplify citizens' access to information of public importance held by public bodies, to protect sensitive information whose disclosure would adversely affect the interests of the state and citizens, and to protect and enforce the citizen's right to be informed. Read this with the national information commission appeal ladder, the district legal aid committees, the public interest litigators and the land records offices entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: चन्दा ऐन — donations need prior permission from the local administration, and foreign grants need council approval first
trackers.desc: Collecting donations without prior government permission is unlawful. The donation legislation of 2030 is published by the law commission, and reporting on it records the rule plainly: no person, government or non-government office or organisation may collect or take donations from anyone without prior approval, the exception being voluntary giving at no fixed rate for religious, philanthropic or other public purposes with prior permission obtained. The same reporting records that the Act clearly provides that donations may be collected only with permission from the local administration, and that responsible officials state that collecting without government permission is unlawful. A community planning a public appeal starts at the district administration office, not at a bank. Foreign money runs through a separate approval. Model constitutions issued for organisations registering with district administration offices provide that where grant money is to be taken from a foreign association or organisation, the prior approval of the social welfare council must be obtained before any assistance or grant is received, and that audit reports and work progress statements are to be sent to the district or area administration office and to the council. The council itself is described as established under the social welfare legislation of 2049 with responsibilities for affiliation and renewal of non-governmental organisations, approval and coordination of foreign grants, project approval, monitoring and evaluation. Bank arrangements are prescribed in the model rules. The same model constitution provides that money received by an organisation is to be deposited in a local bank and the account operated on the signatures of any two of the chairperson, secretary and treasurer, the treasurer being mandatory. Setting the account up that way from the start avoids a later dispute about who controls the appeal's money. Expect more than one permission. Published commentary records a multi-agency permission system in which a single project can involve the relevant ministry, the finance ministry, the home ministry, the social welfare council and local government. Ask at the outset which of those your appeal needs, and in what order. Read this with the twenty-four hour information rule, the national trust, the district legal aid committees and the environment protection fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Mining permits — the fifty-metre exclusion around named places, the annual renewal notice, and the measuring device on extracted volumes
trackers.desc: The mining regulations set a fifty-metre exclusion, and the list of protected places is long and specific. The mines and minerals regulations published by the law commission set out the conditions a permit holder must observe when extracting: to work so as to make maximum proper use of the mineral and conserve mineral resources; to adopt measures causing the least possible adverse effect on the environment, giving due attention to environmental protection; and not to carry out extraction within at least fifty metres of places set aside for national and public interest and safety, or of ancient monuments, towns, graveyards, cremation grounds, public roads, ghats, dams, canals, pipelines, forts, garrisons, cantonments, temples, mosques, churches, houses and factories — nor to build a house, factory or godown in such an area. That list is a checklist a community can walk with a tape measure. The permit application itself records who the technician is, and the exact boundaries. The prescribed application form requires the applicant's name, occupation and contact details, particulars of the technical person — professional qualification, training and experience, whether the applicant's own or another's, with that person's name and address — and the four boundaries of the area applied for, by zone and district. The permit itself is issued for a named mineral within a described area between stated dates. Ask for the permit and compare its boundaries and dates against what is happening. The department publishes notices that matter to neighbours. Its notice list includes annual notices on renewal of mineral permits for the fiscal year, notices on fixing and amending prohibited areas, notices requiring installation of a device to measure the quantity of mineral extracted, notices that mineral extraction and sale must not be carried out on the basis of a prospecting licence alone, notices suspending mineral work, and notices of intent regarding specific minerals. A prospecting licence being used as cover for extraction is a named wrong the department has publicly warned about. Conditions are set at permit stage. Press reporting records the department stating that when granting mining permits it sets conditions so that the environmental impact assessment is not undermined, revenue is collected in proportion to registration and production, and local people benefit. Those three are the headings under which to frame a request for conditions on a permit near you. Read this with the twenty-four hour information rule, the national trust, the environment protection fund and the district legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Leasehold forestry — degraded national forest handed to a group of poor households for forty years, renewable, with a lease certificate from the district forest officer
trackers.desc: A group of households can hold forest land for forty years without buying it. Published material on the leasehold forestry approach records that patches of degraded national forest are handed over to small groups of households below the poverty line under a lease agreement of up to forty years, giving the group exclusive user rights on the basis of a management plan, with the possibility of extension for a further forty years based on performance. The land remains government land; the group manages and uses it, the district forest officer approves the operational plan and issues the lease certificate, and the group operates under its own constitution. For a community whose land is threatened by degradation or informal use, this is a route to a documented, exclusive, long-term holding. The eligibility test is specific, and worth checking against. Published studies record identification of member households through participatory well-being ranking, with criteria of holding less than half a hectare of land and an annual income below a stated ceiling, households with up to one hectare of arable land included as exceptions where below the poverty line; groups average around ten households, with each household allocated roughly half to one hectare. Pro-poor leasehold forest is recorded as free of lease fee, while industrial leasehold forest pays a fixed amount, and the rules require identification of potential leasehold forests with open bidding for applications. The recorded results are ecological as well as economic. Assessments record rapid natural regeneration at most sites, increases in biodiversity, and vegetation cover rising from around a third at new sites to around nine tenths after seven years, with fodder and forest products harvested where little or none were produced before. Programme figures record tens of thousands of households in several thousand groups holding tens of thousands of hectares, with average group and plot sizes published. Those figures are the argument for asking a district forest office to hand over a specific degraded patch. Know how it differs from community forestry. Published comparison records that community forestry targets whole communities and concentrates on protecting well-stocked forest, while leasehold forestry redistributes assets by leasing degraded areas to specifically targeted resource-poor households — and records the friction between the two approaches, and criticism that exclusion by small groups can disadvantage the poorest. Choose the instrument that matches who is to hold the land. Read this with the mining permit exclusion list, the national trust, the district legal aid and the donation permission entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: नेपाल कानून पत्रिका and the court's full-text decisions — the law journal online, cause lists, and the orders the court itself highlights
trackers.desc: The law journal is online in full text, free. The judiciary publishes the national law journal as a searchable site of full decisions, with each case given a detail page carrying the judges, the procedural history — for example an appeal from a named appellate court decision under a stated section of the judicial administration legislation — and the reasoning in full. For a community whose lawyer says a point has been decided before, this is where the decision itself can be read rather than taken on trust. The supreme court's own site carries the orders it wants known. The court publishes recent important judgments and orders on its front page with case numbers and dates in the national calendar, including public interest matters — one recorded order concerning use of a public exhibition ground and route where educational and health institutions are located, restricting its hire for assemblies other than social, professional, educational, intellectual, cultural and archaeological gatherings. Read those entries: they show what kinds of public-space and public-interest arguments this court has recently accepted. The judicial framework is published beside them. The court's general information pages record the statutes and rules in force for judicial administration — the constitution, the judicial administration legislation of 2073, the supreme court legislation of 2048, and the supreme court, high court and district court rules — together with the judiciary's strategic plans, listings by district and high court and by judge, the law journal, and full-text decisions and orders. They also publish a toll-free number and the registrar's office contacts. Daily and weekly cause lists are published, and a bar body highlights key decisions. The supreme court bar association's site offers selection of a court and publishes daily and weekly cause lists alongside an archive of important judgments, orders and decisions, and a channel for court users' complaints and suggestions. A cause list tells you when a case is being heard, which is how a community attends the hearing on a project affecting it. Read this with the public interest litigators, the district legal aid committees, the environment regulations schedules and the land acquisition entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: जलस्रोत ऐन — the statutory order of priority that puts drinking water first, water user associations, and the transfer of a completed project to them
trackers.desc: The Act sets an order of priority for water use, and drinking water is first. The water resources legislation, published by the law commission, sets out the order in which water resources are to be used: drinking water and domestic use first, then irrigation, then agricultural uses such as livestock and fisheries, followed by the further uses listed in the same provision. Where an industrial or hydro project is drawing the source a village drinks from, that ranking is the sentence to quote — it is the statute's own hierarchy, not an argument about fairness. Water user associations are recognised bodies, and a completed project can be handed to them. The Act provides for user associations and records that where the government has developed a water resources project under the named provisions, it may on completion transfer the project to a user association on prescribed conditions; that ownership of a transferred project belongs to that association; and that the association operates it, subject to the Act, as if it held the licence itself. A community that maintains a canal or a supply system therefore has a statutory vehicle that can end up owning the works. Provincial and local governments can legislate within notified thresholds. The Act provides that provinces and local levels may make their own law and use or develop water resources under it, in respect of drinking water, hydropower, irrigation and other water resources of the standards, capacities or quantities specified by the federal government by notice published in the gazette. Ask the palika which local law applies before assuming the federal one is the only rule. Unlicensed extraction has been litigated. The law journal already recorded in this bucket carries a decision on groundwater in the capital valley, recording that associations, industries, hotels and housing developers had extracted groundwater for industrial and commercial purposes without legal licence, irregularly and beyond capacity, with consequences for the valley's geological structure, for buildings, and for residents' fundamental right to live in a safe environment. Extraction without a licence is therefore a matter the courts have already engaged with. Read this with the accredited laboratory, the environment protection regulations, the twenty-four hour information rule and the local planning cycle entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Crusher and riverbed extraction standard — the two-kilometre and other distances a crusher must keep, what the amendment removed, and the writ filed against it
trackers.desc: The standard fixes distances a crusher must keep from named places, and they are measurable. National reporting of the 2077 standard on excavation, sale and management of stone, aggregate and sand records that a crusher industry may not operate within two kilometres of dense settlement, forest, national park, reserve, international border, educational institution, religious, historical or archaeological site, or the offices of security agencies; that it may operate only two hundred metres from a transmission line and fifteen hundred metres from the foot of the Chure hills; and that industries not complying were required to relocate to a new site by a stated date. Measure from the boundary of the settlement or the school before arguing about dust. Extraction from the river has its own distances. Reporting of the standard as adopted records that river-derived material may not be taken within two kilometres of dense settlement and forest areas, within five hundred metres of a highway, or within one kilometre downstream and five hundred metres upstream of a road, bridge or suspension bridge; and records that the cabinet made provision for large, national pride, transformative and priority projects not to face shortages of construction material. Those numbers are what a complaint about a riverbed operation is measured against. Know which version is in force, because the amendment moved the lines. Reporting records that the standard was later amended, with the effect that crusher industries came closer to settlements and the environment; and separate reporting records that the provision barring excavation and collection within two kilometres of dense settlement and forest and within five hundred metres of a highway was removed outright in the amended standard. Ask which version the operator's approval was issued under. The amendment has been challenged in the Supreme Court. Reporting records that three named advocates, described as environmental lawyers, filed a writ at the Supreme Court seeking annulment of the amended standard, arguing it was amended to make extraction by crushers easier, with the petitioners asking for an order quashing the decision. A community facing a crusher can therefore ask what became of that petition. Read this with the mining permit entry, the environment regulations schedules, the law journal and the district legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Aquatic Animal Protection Act — closing or demolishing a fish ladder or dyke is an offence, poison and explosives in water bodies are restricted, and local authorities carry powers
trackers.desc: Interfering with a fish ladder is named as an offence in its own right. The aquatic animal protection legislation, in force since 1961, provides for the protection and conservation of aquatic animals; prohibits the killing and trapping of aquatic life; prohibits the closing or demolishing of the doors of a fish ladder, a dyke or any kind of structure placed in the water to protect aquatic animals; and restricts the introduction of poison and explosive substances into water bodies for any use. Where a dam, weir or diversion is proposed, the fish ladder is not just a design feature but a structure the law protects — and shutting its doors is the conduct the Act names. The prohibition covers destroying a dam or water system to catch fish. A published country report records that under this Act any party is punishable for introducing poisonous or explosive materials into a water source, or destroying any dam, bridge or water system with the intent of catching or killing aquatic life, and describes it as one of the oldest statutes here to recognise the value of wetlands and aquatic animals. Local authorities hold powers under it, and appeals lie to the court. Published summaries record that the Act further provides for penalties, appeals to the appellate court, powers of local authorities and rule-making powers of the government. That local power is the practical route: the body to approach about a blocked ladder or a poisoned pool is close at hand rather than central. The enforcement record shows what it is used for. Published case material records prosecutions for using explosives to catch fish in a named river, where the method killed large numbers of fish and damaged river habitat, with imprisonment imposed and the explosives confiscated and destroyed, charged under this Act alongside the explosives control legislation; records penalties for fishing during a prohibited period in a protected area, sometimes combined with community service in environmental conservation; and records that electro-fishing, explosives, poison and prohibited netting are all barred, with fines, confiscation of gear and possible imprisonment. Read this with the crusher standard, the water resources act, the environment regulations and the district legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Buffer zone user committees — the two-kilometre belt around a park, the thirty to fifty per cent revenue share written into the Act, and the current dispute over whether it is still being paid
trackers.desc: A belt around each park has elected committees with a statutory claim on park revenue. Published review records that the fourth amendment to the 1973 national parks and wildlife conservation legislation added sections on establishment of buffer zones, provisions of compensation, formation of users committees for management of forest resources inside the buffer zone, and a provision to allocate thirty to fifty per cent of revenue generated from protected areas to local communities for community development; and that the 1995 buffer zone regulation stipulates formation of a people's council for management of the buffer zone, constituted from members elected from the buffer zone users committees. Other published work records the buffer zone as a belt of roughly two kilometres around a park or reserve, and records buffer zone community forest user groups and conservation area management committees managing forests for local use, monitoring wildlife, controlling wildlife crime and running small community development projects. Where a community lives beside a park, those are the bodies to join or form. The share is disputed now, which is the live fact. National reporting records the department's director general stating that earlier thirty to fifty per cent of revenue generated from natural resources in national parks went to the buffer zone committees, used for roads, education and other local needs, but that after federalisation in 2015 the share was reduced to twenty per cent; and separate reporting records buffer zone stakeholders saying the committees have not received their share since last year, demanding the funds be provided in accordance with the law. Establishing what has actually been transferred, and when, is therefore the question to put to the department. The restrictions that come with the belt are documented too. The same reporting records residents arrested for cutting trees they had planted on their own land inside the buffer zone and for thatching a cowshed roof, a ward chair stating that many buffer zone residents settled there before the zone was declared and live on private land whose ownership rights are not fully recognised, and named fishing communities being barred from fishing. The scale is on record. Published material records buffer zones demarcated around twelve protected areas over roughly fifteen years, covering thousands of square kilometres across dozens of village units in twenty-seven districts, with a benefiting population near a million, and records compensation figures set for human death and injury caused by named species. Read this with the aquatic animal protection Act, the community forest entry, the crusher standard and the district legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Supreme Court's compiled environmental judgments — the court's own collection of decided cases, the constitutional right and compensation clause they rest on, and the anyone-may-complain provision in the 2019 Act
trackers.desc: The court publishes a compilation of its own environmental judgments, with the ratio of each set out. The supreme court's site carries a compiled collection of environment cases, summarising decisions and their reasoning — including that the fundamental rights guaranteed in the constitution are for the protection of the interests of citizens and it is the responsibility of the state to create an environment where citizens can enjoy them; that since living in a polluted environment is bound to affect health, living in a pollution-free environment is inextricably linked with the right to live, and to preserve that cleanliness it is important to protect forests, lakes, ponds, rivers, clean air and water and maintain environmental balance; and, in one case, that a named area should be declared a protected forest under the forest legislation. It also records the court observing that the state has a constitutional duty to compensate for damage, while noting the lack of laws and policies providing compensation for such damage. Reading how the court has already reasoned is cheaper than arguing it afresh. The constitutional right has two limbs, and the second is the compensation clause. Published material records the constitution providing that each person shall have the right to live in a healthy and clean environment, and that the victim of environmental pollution and degradation shall have the right to be compensated by the polluter as provided for by law, with a proviso preserving legal provisions balancing environment and development in national development works. The 2019 Act opens the complaint to anyone, and sets an appeal clock. A law firm's summary of the Act records that, unlike the 1997 Act, it envisages an elaborate complaint mechanism under which anyone may complain to the regulating authorities about a person who is violating or may violate the Act, and on investigation a person found guilty must pay reasonable compensation to the aggrieved person; and that anyone aggrieved by a decision on a fine may appeal within thirty-five days, to the district court where the decision was taken by a local authority. It records the Act prescribing an environmental fund, audited by the auditor general, funded from federal, provincial and local government, nationals and institutions, and foreign governments or international institutions. Read this with the law journal entry, the environment regulations schedules, the public interest litigators and the district legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The national air quality monitoring network — thirty stations and a real-time portal, the standard the readings are judged against, and the government's own account of what the network still cannot measure
trackers.desc: There is a national network and a public portal, and a government document states its size. A ministry framework document records that ambient air quality monitoring began in the early 1990s, expanded in 2002 with foreign development support, and was re-established following the 2012 national ambient air quality standards, resulting in thirty monitoring stations and an online portal providing real-time data on particulate matter and select gases. Published network listings record the department's monitoring as a named real-time sensor network of thirty stations, with station-level readings for fine and coarse particulates carried through to public aggregators, each attributed to the department's own portal. A community can therefore cite both the reading and the standard it is measured against. The government states the gaps itself, which is the more useful half. The same document records that further upgrades are needed to monitor all the standard's parameters, particularly lead and benzene, and to expand gaseous pollutant monitoring for effective public health and environmental response. Where a project's assessment claims no exceedance, the absence of monitoring for a parameter is a documented fact rather than an accusation. The pollution's origin is quantified, and part of it is not local. The same document records the country among those with the world's worst air pollution, with more than ninety per cent of the population regularly exposed to hazardous levels; and records that in the capital's valley about a quarter of the air pollution comes from outside the valley, more than half of that from outside the country, and in the southern plains two-thirds — a figure worth having before a proponent attributes everything to transboundary haze. It records key domestic sources as boilers and furnaces in food and beverage, textiles and hospitality, largely burning biomass such as firewood and rice husk. An expansion is documented, with what it is meant to deliver. A contractor's project record describes a national network measuring fine and coarse particulates, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, ozone and carbon monoxide continuously, with a central calibration tower, intended to compare urban and rural air, support health research linking readings to respiratory illness and hospital admissions, and underpin public index dashboards and advisories. Read this with the accredited laboratory, the crusher standard, the environment regulations schedules and the compiled judgments entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Conservation area management councils and committees — a locally elected council running one conservation area, the committee structure used in the others, and the entry-fee revenue ploughed back locally
trackers.desc: One conservation area is managed by a locally elected institution, and that is on record. A published analysis of conservation under the federal constitution records that management of conservation areas previously lay with the central government which reserved the power to delegate management to a third party; that in three named conservation areas management responsibilities were delegated to a national non-governmental trust; and that one conservation area has been managed by a locally elected management council. It records that the constitution now accords management responsibility for conservation areas differently, leaving the future roles of both bodies uncertain, and discusses the sources of funds for operating conservation areas and agencies. A community asking who should run the protected area beside it has a precedent for the elected-council answer. The committee structure the trust builds is named. The trust's own pages record that it helps establish and strengthen community-based institutions — a conservation area management committee, a buffer zone user committee and a community-based anti-poaching unit — and records this arrangement as having reduced poaching, forest encroachment and illegal grazing. It records the first conservation area as the only financially self-sustaining protected area in the country, its model subsequently followed as a key management model. The financing is a fee retained locally, which is the transferable part. Published material records the trust receiving no government support for operating that area but granted the right to collect entry fees from visiting trekkers, the revenue ploughed back to implement conservation and development activities in the area, with additional funds raised from national and international donors; it records the trust's stated belief that such areas will ultimately have to be managed by the local people themselves in perpetuity, with the focus on building local capacity. The scale and the mandates are documented. The trust records the first area at a stated size with over a hundred thousand residents across five districts and fifteen rural municipalities, a further area entrusted to it by a dated gazette notice for twenty years, and a management mandate renewed for a further ten years in another case; published material records it as having undertaken over three hundred projects and managing over a third of the country's protected area coverage. Read this with the trust entry, the buffer zone user committees, the forest users' federation and the leasehold forestry entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: LAHURNIP — indigenous lawyers offering legal aid and strategic litigation, the 2024 Supreme Court ruling requiring consent before measures affecting indigenous communities, and its published consent protocol manual
trackers.desc: An organisation of indigenous lawyers offers legal aid to communities hit by projects. The organisation records itself as established in 1995 by professional indigenous lawyers, registered under the institution registration legislation, non-profit and non-political; and records that it empowers, mobilises and provides technical support for advocacy, and legal aid to those indigenous peoples whose lands, territories, resources and livelihoods are disproportionately affected by, or struggling to defend rights violated mainly by, the state, development aggression and business or economic activities, working to hold the state, development finance institutions and companies accountable. It records its work as strategic litigation, documentation and reporting nationally and internationally, research and policy advocacy, and capacity building together with indigenous peoples' organisations and others, and lists legal and technical support to rights holders among its services. A Supreme Court ruling it brought sets a consent requirement, and local governments have begun acting on it. A published award citation records the 2024 Supreme Court ruling, made public in 2025, in the organisation's case against the prime minister's office and others, where the court directed all levels of government to align laws and policies with international standards on indigenous peoples' rights and required government bodies to seek free, prior and informed consent from indigenous communities before taking measures that affect them; and records that following the ruling some local governments began enacting laws and policies to implement the relevant standards. That is the citation a community puts in front of a municipality. It also wrote the protocol a community uses to exercise that consent. Published material records a consent protocol manual developed by the organisation, and records an investigation finding that a development bank must take urgent steps to uphold consent rights in its funding of the hydropower sector, the communities' concerns including violation of consent rights, lack of compensation for loss of land, and insufficient environmental and social impact studies. The award citation records its contribution to the national action plan on business and human rights adopted in 2023, including commitments on consent, community participation in environmental assessments, and protection of indigenous peoples. Read this with the public interest litigators, the buffer zone committees, the district legal aid committees and the compiled environmental judgments entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: A directory of the country's environmental organisations — profiles by theme, an open registration route for groups not yet listed, and the named bodies a community can approach
trackers.desc: There is a public directory of organisations working on environment and climate here, and it is open to new entries. The directory records the listed bodies as dedicated to advancing climate education, advocacy, policy and resilience across the country, and invites anyone working for a climate organisation not already listed to register a profile to be added. For a community group that has just formed, being findable is worth as much as finding others. The listings carry what each organisation actually does, with themes attached. Profiles record a student-led non-profit on forest and environment; a youth-led coalition of young people and youth groups; a research and advocacy organisation committed to promoting ecological sustainability; a women-led organisation focused on solving local environmental issues; a not-for-profit established in 2019 by young people in the capital; and a centre for indigenous peoples' research and development, established in 2011, aiming at policy research. Entries carry theme tags including wildlife and biodiversity, ecosystem conservation, water and conservation, policy advocacy, disaster risk reduction, agriculture and renewable energy, so a community can search by the thing it is facing. One profiled organisation shows what these bodies offer beyond campaigning. The directory records a water conservation foundation as a leading civil society organisation committed to promoting interdisciplinary action research, policy advocacy and building the climate and disaster risk resilience capacity of communities, and records it engaging with civil society organisations, universities and volunteer groups to help build their capacities across climate, disaster risk, agriculture, food systems and renewable energy, and contributing report and proposal writing. Proposal-writing capacity in a partner organisation is often what turns a village's problem into a funded project. Read this with the forest users' federation, the public interest litigators, the land rights organisation and the indigenous lawyers entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: A published list of lawyers and firms with their specialisations — named contacts, telephone numbers and which firms take cases outside the valley, plus the bar's own legal aid units
trackers.desc: There is a published, numbered list of lawyers and firms in this country, and it says what each one does. A foreign mission's legal assistance page lists firms and organisations with a named contact person, street address, telephone and mobile numbers, email and website for each, states each one's fields of specialisation, notes which firms accept cases outside the capital valley, and records the languages spoken. For a community outside the capital, that last line — whether a firm travels — is often the whole question. The list includes free providers: it records a legal aid and consultancy centre with a named contact and its own website, and records another organisation as providing free legal consultation and free legal assistance for helpless people. The oldest free provider describes its own machinery. That centre records itself as established in 1987 and registered in 1993 under the association registration legislation, providing free legal aid, psychosocial counselling, mediation, paralegal services and court representation, alongside policy advocacy, legislative drafting and human rights training, with mobile legal camps and grassroots awareness drives as outreach and a team of senior legal aid officers, legal aid officers, paralegals and young lawyers. It records its litigation producing Supreme Court orders directing the government to legislate, in named and numbered cases. The state and bar routes are mapped, with their weaknesses stated. Published material records four sources of legal aid: court-appointed remunerated lawyers at the district, appellate and supreme courts; district legal aid committees formed where the legal aid legislation has been implemented, each with a single-room office and one government staff member; the bar association, providing aid through units — with units in the supreme and appellate courts and district units in most district courts, and women lawyer centres under those units having three or more women lawyers; and domestic and international organisations. It records the committees' weakness as having no lawyers of their own, depending on the bar, whose assigned lawyers are paid very low, and the bar's as having no funding of its own for legal aid. Read this with the district legal aid committees, the public interest litigators, the indigenous lawyers and the organisations directory entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Digo Bikas Institute — a sustainability watch tracking whether environmental rules are actually enforced, community vulnerability assessments run with municipalities, and the water foundation beside it
trackers.desc: Someone is tracking whether the environmental rules are being enforced, which is different from knowing what they say. The institute records that as the country entered a new federal governance system a number of environmental regulatory provisions are being revised or amended, and that in that context its sustainability watch work is to monitor and track the enforcement of the environmental regulatory regime and the progress, or the lack, of policies and plans related to sustainable development. It records its climate justice work as policy analysis, advocacy, outreach and networking, and states that the vision of modernization and development propagated and implemented by the political, bureaucratic and technocratic establishment impacts people's livelihood and environment. For a community told a rule protects it, an organisation that checks enforcement is the one to ask. Its assessments are run jointly with local government. Its own notices record a two-day climate change vulnerability and risk assessment from a right to food perspective completed in a named municipality, jointly organised with the institute; record an orientation on solid waste management conducted with a volunteer cohort and the chief officer of a waste management and cleanliness branch; and record a workshop organised with a national indigenous disabled women's association on the national climate commitment process from a climate justice lens. It records community electrification with solar mini-grids as a way to power rural areas, with reliable electrification in hundreds of suitable villages — the alternative proposal a community can put beside a large scheme. The water foundation beside it is the research body for river disputes. That foundation records itself as non-governmental, non-political and not-for-profit, conducting interdisciplinary research on interrelated issues affecting the use and management of water with specific focus on the Himalaya-Ganga region, founded in 1999 and reincorporated with a district administration office in 2000, generating and disseminating knowledge through research, publications and engagement in public dialogues, and working with local communities as well as with organisations at local, national, regional and international levels. Read this with the organisations directory, the public interest litigators, the indigenous lawyers and the environment fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: NEFIN — an indigenous umbrella with councils in seven provinces, seventy-two districts and more than 3,000 villages, affiliated federations including one of lawyers, and its climate programme
trackers.desc: The structure reaches the village, and the counts are published. The federation records itself as the umbrella organisation of all the indigenous peoples of the country, established in 1991, whose main objective is safeguarding indigenous peoples' rights, with chapters comprising province coordination councils in all seven provinces, district coordination councils in 72 districts, more than 3,000 village coordination councils, 13 affiliated federations — of indigenous journalists, youth, students, film makers and lawyers among others — and chapters in more than 25 countries. Other accounts give district councils in more than 71 districts and 12 affiliated federations, and record membership as 55 or 56 indigenous peoples' organisations distributed through the plains, hills and mountains, representing 59 recognised indigenous nationalities. An affiliated federation of indigenous lawyers, reachable through a village council, is a shorter route to counsel than a national search. Its stated work is capacity, not only advocacy. Published description records it as autonomous and politically non-partisan, supporting member organisations in leadership development, strengthening decision-making capabilities, networking and enabling them to fight for securing indigenous peoples' rights, including rights to self-determination, and as committed to promoting and protecting the rights, identities, cultures, languages and traditional knowledge systems of indigenous communities. It records a climate change partnership programme begun in 2009 to get recognition and optimisation of indigenous peoples' contribution in climate actions, undertaking advocacy, information dissemination, awareness raising and capacity building, with a programme coordinator quoted that indigenous peoples' voices have been undermined in climate change projects and programmes procured by the government. The standards its lawyers cite are named. Published reporting records an indigenous lawyer — from the association already recorded in this bucket — urging alignment of the national biodiversity plan with the international declaration, the labour convention and the global biodiversity framework, and with a numbered constitutional provision and the current five-year plan; and records activists insisting that free, prior and informed consent must be mandatory to protect indigenous rights to own, use and control ancestral lands, territories and resources. Read this with the indigenous lawyers, the forest users' federation, the land rights organisation and the organisations directory entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Community forest user groups and the division forest office — the seven-step handover, the group's own constitution and operational plan, the 33 per cent women rule, and the permit its committee issues
trackers.desc: A user group is a legal body in its own right, and the source says so plainly. Published material records that under the forest legislation user groups are legal, autonomous and corporate bodies having full power, authority and responsibility to protect, manage and utilise forest and other resources as per the decisions taken by their assemblies and according to their self-prepared constitutions and operational plans, with minimal scope for interference from the state forestry agency, while the land legally remains part of the state. That combination — local control of use, state ownership of land — is the exact shape of the protection available. The handover route runs through the district or division office, step by step. Published material sets out the process: with technical and other support from the district forest office, formation of the group and preparation of its constitution by the forest users; preparation of the operational plan including survey, demarcation of the forest area, forest inventory and calculation of annual increment; submission of the plan to the office; approval and issuance of the handover certificate; and records that the office needs to conduct a field verification of the plan before approving and handing over. It records one group's five-year plan prepared with technical support from the forest technician of the district forest office. The group's internal rules include a quota, and the committee issues its own permits. Published material records that a group includes a general assembly of all members and an executive committee that by law must include 33 per cent female members, and that the assembly defines and recognises use rights and makes decisions on protection, harvesting, benefit sharing and mobilisation of group funds; and records that to transport forest products a committee or person designated by the group shall issue a permit and stamp the timber. The scale shows how common this is. Published material records 22,415 groups organising about 14 million people and 2.9 million households, protecting more than 2.3 million hectares, with earlier counts of about 13,000 and more than 14,000 groups; records group sizes ranging from 10 to 850 households with forest areas from less than one hectare to 750; and records 74 district forest offices whose activities include supporting groups with technical skills in field activities like forest inventory. Read this with the forest users' federation, the indigenous federation, the land rights organisation and the lawyer list entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The municipal judicial committee — a three-member body in every one of 753 local governments that decides boundary, water, pasture and crop-damage disputes, with ward mediation centres and appeal to the district court
trackers.desc: Every municipality and rural municipality has a three-member committee that decides neighbourhood land disputes. Published description records that under a named constitutional article a three-member judicial committee coordinated by the vice-chairperson or deputy mayor settles disputes within its jurisdiction, with powers set out in the local government operations legislation, divided into disputes it settles itself and disputes it may settle only through mediation. It records the first category as including boundaries of land, dams, ditches, or the distribution and use of water; damage to crops; and pastureland, green fodder and fuelwood. For neighbours in a boundary or irrigation dispute, the first forum is in the municipal building, not a court. The two lists and the appeal are published. Published material records the committee as empowered to settle disputes in 13 specific matters and to refer 11 others for mediation, and records the mediation-only list as including land encroachment, unauthorised construction and physical assault. It records that decisions can be appealed to the district court and onward, that in adjudication and arbitration the opinion of the majority is the decision of the committee, and that in mediation the committee keeps a roster of mediators and refers the parties to mediation centres at the ward level. Other published description adds jurisdiction over unpaid wages, house rent up to a stated ceiling, building setback violations and obstruction of public roads. Who chairs these committees is the striking fact. Published reporting records that the constitution requires mandatory election of a male and a female as either mayor or deputy mayor, and that as a result women won 91 per cent of the deputy positions — deputy mayors and vice-chairpersons — so the committees are overwhelmingly led by elected women. The stated weakness is the ward layer. Published material records that although the constitution and the legislation envision mediation centres at ward level, they have not been established in about 80 per cent of all locations due to lack of resources, and records that fear of breaching laws prevents judicial committees from deciding cases. Read this with the community forest user groups, the district legal aid committees, the lawyer list and the indigenous federation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Ward offices — 6,743 of them, a five-member committee including two women, the chairperson who certifies land and house documents, and the duty to act against building without permission
trackers.desc: The ward chairperson certifies land and house documents, and is required to act against unpermitted building. Published reporting on a 2017 government order records that the ward chairperson shall prepare the budget and plan of the concerned ward; collect and maintain data of households; maintain records of public property; conduct child and environment-friendly programmes; carry out market monitoring; initiate action against anyone who builds a house without obtaining permission of the local level; and prepare a monthly progress report; and that the chairperson shall issue letters of recommendation and certify various documents related to personal incidents, land, house, citizenship, reconciliation and relationship, in both Nepali and English. For a household documenting long use of a plot, the ward office issues the paper — and the same office is the one meant to stop a building going up without permission. There are thousands of these offices, and most local civil servants work in them. Published research records 6,743 wards across 753 local governments, each local government divided into between five and 35 wards; records wards as the constituent units of local governments and the units closest to the people for delivering local-level services, with most of the country's local-level civil servants working in ward offices; and records 77 district coordination committees at the intermediary level, noting they do not have the same revenue rights as their predecessors. The committee's composition guarantees women's seats. Published description records each ward as governed by a committee of a directly elected ward chairperson and four ward members, two of whom must be women, serving five-year terms, with ward chairpersons sitting automatically on the municipal executive and assembly; and records committees as formulating annual and periodic ward development plans through participatory processes involving community assemblies and neighbourhood meetings, prioritising infrastructure such as local roads, bridges, irrigation systems and small-scale hydropower. The candid assessment is published too. Published commentary records that the committees' institutional and organisational capacity is poor and has remained more or less neglected despite their enormous roles and responsibilities, while noting they have been instrumental in collecting resources through taxation and non-taxation means. Read this with the municipal judicial committee, the community forest user groups, the district legal aid and the indigenous federation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: District land revenue and survey offices — two separate offices holding ownership and boundary records, the encumbrance search that reveals court orders, and re-measurement when a map is old or disputed
trackers.desc: Ownership and boundaries live in two different district offices, and a claim needs both. Published legal description records that the ownership certificate is issued by the land revenue office showing ownership details, while the survey map is the graphical representation of land boundaries prepared by the survey department, and that both are essential and must be consistent. It records that the process provides multiple administrative channels — the survey department for measurement verification, the land revenue office for record corrections, and local government for community mediation — which are faster and less expensive than court proceedings. For a household in a boundary dispute, that is three named routes before any court. Re-measurement can be ordered, and only licensed surveyors count. The same description records that if the existing map is old or disputed, the land revenue office will order a survey to ensure accuracy, and that for new property divisions or boundary disputes, survey is mandatory. It records that only licensed surveyors recognised by the survey department, or official department staff, may conduct legally valid surveys; private survey companies must hold valid licences; and unauthorised surveys have no legal standing. It records required documents as the citizenship certificate, the original ownership certificate, tax clearance receipts and any existing survey maps, with court orders or mutual agreements where a dispute is being resolved, and records that where a survey determines encroachment, the survey department documents the violation. The encumbrance search is the check most likely to be skipped. Published guidance records that verification means going to the district land revenue office for the area, presenting the parcel number and asking staff to verify the current ownership record against their register; requesting an encumbrance search to confirm no loans, mortgages, court orders or restrictions are registered against the parcel; and cross-referencing against the survey department's field book to confirm boundaries and area. It records the certificate as containing the owner's name and citizenship number, the parcel number, the district, municipality and ward, the area in local units, the land classification and the date of last registration, and warns never to rely on a photocopy. Read this with the ward offices, the municipal judicial committee, the community forest user groups and the district legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The municipal recommendation letter in the assessment procedure — every affected local body must sign off before a report goes forward, plus the complaint route anyone can use and the fines for proceeding without approval
trackers.desc: An assessment report cannot move forward without letters from every affected local body. A published government presentation on assessment procedure lists, among the steps, collection of recommendation letters from all concerned village and municipal bodies, before submission of the report by the proponent to the concerned ministry and its forwarding onward along with comments and suggestions. For a community whose municipality is sympathetic, that letter is a point of leverage that sits at the start of the process rather than at the end. Anyone may complain, and compensation can follow. Published legal description records that, unlike the earlier legislation, the 2019 environment legislation envisages an elaborate complaint mechanism, under which anyone can make a complaint to the regulating authorities about someone who is in violation or may violate the provisions, and that upon investigation, if the person is found guilty, they must pay reasonable compensation to the aggrieved person; it records that a person aggrieved by a decision on a fine may appeal. The penalties for proceeding without approval are stated in figures. The same description records fines up to five lakh rupees where a proposal is implemented without a brief environmental study report or contrary to an approved one, and up to ten lakh rupees where it is implemented without an initial environmental examination report or contrary to one; and records that where a study report does not meet the criteria, the developer may be barred from submitting a report for up to five years. Published description adds that proceeding without required approval can bring project suspension and restoration orders, and that an environmental clearance decision can be challenged through administrative appeal or judicial review where proper procedures were not followed or the decision was arbitrary, illegal or in bad faith. Read this with the environment rules schedules, the municipal judicial committee, the ward offices and the public interest litigators entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: District courts — one in each of 77 districts with 287 judges, original jurisdiction over land disputes, appeals from the local judicial committees, and a 35-day civil appeal window
trackers.desc: The court that hears a land case sits in the district, and appeals from the local committee land there too. Published legal description records 77 district courts, one per district, as the base tier with original jurisdiction for most civil and criminal cases, and records the local-level forum as a judicial committee at each rural municipality or municipality, limited to civil disputes only. Another account records the district courts as exercising original jurisdiction over the vast majority of civil and criminal cases, hearing appeals from local-level judicial committees, and serving as the entry point for property disputes, with 287 judges serving across all 77 courts. For a community whose case has outgrown the municipal committee already recorded here, this is where it goes next. What the court takes at first instance includes land disputes and decree execution. Published description records the district court's jurisdiction as covering original civil claims subject to the pecuniary thresholds for tribunals and the high court, original criminal trials for most offences, family matters, land disputes, debt recovery below tribunal thresholds, and execution of decrees; and records the civil sequence as the plaint, the summons, the written statement, mediation referral under the mediation legislation, framing of issues, evidence, judgment, decree and execution, and the appellate route. The appeal clock and the province-level bench are published. The same descriptions record seven high courts, one per province, with eleven additional benches established for geographic convenience covering all 77 districts; record high court jurisdiction as appellate over district court judgments, original writ jurisdiction to issue habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition and quo warranto within the province, and original jurisdiction over specified serious offences; and record that appeals from district court decisions are filed at the high court of the concerned province, with a deadline of 35 days for civil cases and 70 days for criminal cases from the date of judgment, further appeal to the supreme court requiring leave. Read this with the municipal judicial committee, the district legal aid committees, the public interest litigator and the law journal entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Mother Nature Cambodia
trackers.desc: A youth-led Cambodian environmental rights movement, active since 2012, which stopped a Chinese-led hydroelectric dam threatening an Indigenous community in the Areng Valley and helped end the sand-export trade that was destroying the Koh Kong estuaries. Right Livelihood Award, 2023. It was deregistered as an NGO by the Ministry of Interior in 2017 and has continued without legal registration. CHECK YOU HAVE THE RIGHT ONE: a separate, government-aligned organisation using the same name was launched in 2025 — this entry is the original movement, at mothernaturecambodia.org. For activists: association carries real risk. Five members have been imprisoned since July 2024 on plotting and lese-majeste charges, bail refused by both the Appeal and Supreme Courts, and dozens more have been arrested since 2015.

trackers.name: National Audit Authority
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Cambodia, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: MoC Business Registration
trackers.desc: National — Ministry of Commerce business / company register of Cambodia. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Constitutional Council (Cambodia)
trackers.desc: Constitutional Council (Cambodia) — supreme court (Cambodia).

trackers.name: Cambodia — Ministry of Economy & Finance (MEF)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; administers financial & economic policy and the distribution & allocation of the national budget, Kingdom of Cambodia. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Cambodia.

trackers.name: Community Forest agreement — a written request starts it, 15 years runs it
trackers.desc: ESTABLISH WHICH MINISTRY HOLDS YOUR FOREST FIRST — Cambodian forest is state owned and split between the Forestry Administration under MAFF and the Ministry of Environment for protected areas, and a March 2016 reshuffle moved protected areas and nature preserves to the Environment ministry, so older guidance may name the wrong body. ON FA LAND: Sub-decree 79 (2003) under the 2002 Forestry Law gives any Cambodian community the right to establish a Community Forest on state public property. IT STARTS WITH A WRITTEN REQUEST from the local communities to the Forestry Administration, which then assesses their requirements and problems with the involvement of local authorities. The management committee is formed with help from the Commune Council and elected by secret ballot with at least two-thirds of members present at a public meeting. TWO DOCUMENTS GIVE YOU HARVESTING RIGHTS: a Community Forestry Agreement and a Community Forest Management Plan, both approved by the FA Cantonment. TERM: not more than 15 years from approval, extendable on monitoring and evaluation reports. KNOW YOUR secondary users — non-members who may still access the forest consistent with the plan — and note that royalties and premiums should be set after consultation with the community.

trackers.name: Community Protected Areas — you get management rights but not exclusion rights
trackers.desc: THE GAP THAT DECIDES WHETHER THIS ROUTE SOLVES YOUR PROBLEM. Inside Ministry of Environment protected areas, communities may agree to manage part of the area — but legal analysis finds CPA communities hold only partial land tenure: they can generally exercise access, use, withdrawal and management rights, but lack exclusion rights, the ability to keep outsiders from entering or using CPA land. So a CPA can manage a forest but cannot keep others out of it — if your threat is incursion by outsiders rather than your own community's use, this route does not by itself solve it. WATCH THE DROP-OFF: of 182 CPAs established across 31 protected areas, 141 hold a Prakas of recognition, only 39 have a signed management agreement and just 48 a completed management plan — recognition is common, real management authority is not. AND A 15-DAY DEADLINE: within 15 days of being elected the CPA committee must obtain a warrant of recognition from the Commune/Sangkat Chief to legitimise its leadership. OTHER VARIANTS EXIST: Community-Based Production Forest, Partnership Forestry where the commune council is the management body rather than a community committee, and Community Conservation Forestry with more limited use rights.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants — a concept paper, and only shortlists get a reply
trackers.desc: MONEY THAT GOES DIRECTLY TO COMMUNITY ORGANISATIONS. GEF SGP has financed projects in Cambodia since 2005 through the UNDP country office, supporting nearly 218 grant projects, with grants up to USD 50,000 awarded competitively to local NGOs and community-based organisations. WHAT YOU SUBMIT FIRST IS A CONCEPT PAPER, not a full proposal — and only shortlisted proposals are contacted, so the concept paper is your entire first impression and silence is the normal outcome otherwise. THE ENTRY POINT IS A PERSON: contact the GEF SGP National Coordinator at UNDP Cambodia, Corner Sothearos & Sihanouk Blvd, Tonle Bassac, Phnom Penh, for guidelines — verify the current post-holder on UNDP's page rather than relying on a name recorded here, since individual officials move. BUDGET FOR A MATCH: SGP expects applicants to match funding with equivalent contributions, so this is not full cost recovery. WHAT SATISFIES THE MATCH — AND IT IS NOT ONLY CASH: UNDP's own wording is that the remaining funding may come from the organisation, community contribution and/or other donors, either monetary or in kind and services. Labour and in-kind contribution count, so budget them deliberately rather than assuming the match must be found in money — for a community group with no cash this is the difference between eligible and not. AND THE CEILING MOVES BY PHASE: recorded calls show USD 20,000 in an earlier round and up to USD 75,000 under Operational Phase 8, so verify the live call rather than relying on a fixed figure. Note too that Indigenous Peoples' community groups are named as eligible applicants in their own right alongside NGOs and CBOs — which matters given that the Community Protected Area route leaves communities without exclusion rights.

trackers.name: Check which landscape the call names — and the sub-grant route
trackers.desc: GEOGRAPHY IS THE FILTER THAT DECIDES ELIGIBILITY. Cambodian SGP calls target specific landscapes rather than the whole country — recorded examples include villages and districts inside and nearby the Central Cardamom Mountain National Park and biodiversity hotspots; the Stung Siem Reap Watershed in Siem Reap province; and Mekong River, Tonle Sap and coastal provinces under a blue economy stream running since July 2019 on community-based use of ocean and coastal resources. A strong project outside the named landscape does not qualify, so check the live call before investing time — the same trap this map records for Sri Lanka. A DEDICATED INDIGENOUS PEOPLES STREAM EXISTS: since June 2023, under the UNDP Climate Promise initiative, IPOs, local NGOs and CBOs working directly with indigenous communities in the forest and land use sector may apply — including for indigenous community-based ecotourism as an option that does not rely heavily on forest and land resources. AND IF YOU CANNOT WIN A DIRECT GRANT: REDD+ programmes in Cambodia support organisations which in turn sub-contract grants and further funds to local NGOs and small local initiatives — so being a sub-grantee of a larger programme holder is a real route for a group too small to apply directly.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: CLEC — 254 community paralegals in 18 provinces, and lawyers for when they charge you
trackers.desc: Its strategic litigation runs in two directions at once: civil land-and-natural-resource claims for communities, and criminal cases brought against community representatives, land activists and human rights defenders. The second half is the one to remember — when opposing a project turns into a prosecution of the people opposing it, this is an organisation whose lawyers already do that work. The nearest door is usually not the head office: 254 community-based paralegals, 69 of them women, are spread across 18 provinces and the capital, drawn from community representatives, land and labour activists and well-regarded local figures, and they live in the communities rather than visiting them. They cover legal training, consultation, local mediation and community advocacy. Alongside the courts CLEC runs the 'Peace Table' — non-judicial multilateral mediation, and mobile mediation, putting community members, government authorities and the private sector in one room. A December 2023 sitting at Kaoh Nheaek in Mondulkiri was chaired by the deputy district governor with the provincial land department and the Council for Local Dispute Resolution present, and settled a farmland claim in one session; a second sitting the next day took up ten hectares of indigenous community reserve land occupied by outsiders. The limit of that format is built into it: it works when the local authority is willing to convene and the other side turns up, and it produces an agreement rather than an enforceable order. The access-to-justice programme is explicitly framed around resolution and compensation where development projects affect community land tenure. Created in 1996, localised in 2001 and recognised by the Ministry of Interior. The domain is cleccambodia.org — clec.org.kh is the address people guess, and it is not where the organisation is.

trackers.name: LICADHO — free representation in land-grabbing cases, and a medical team that documents the injuries
trackers.desc: The eligibility list is explicit, which is rare and saves a wasted approach. The Human Rights Legal Office provides free legal representation in land grabbing and eviction cases, in cases involving human rights defenders, and in gender-based violence cases; torture by police or prison officials and illegal arrest are taken case by case. Anything outside that list gets legal advice from the paralegal team or a referral to another organisation offering free legal services, not representation. LICADHO gives its own reason for existing in this form: Cambodia lacks legal aid lawyers, so victims go unrepresented and are exposed to judicial corruption and to grossly unfair out-of-court settlements — the settlement, not the trial, is where these cases are usually lost. The medical team is the part nobody thinks to ask for. The Medical Office treats communities affected by land grabbing, at eviction and relocation sites, during protests and in prison, and runs a clinic at the Phnom Penh office; its staff accompany the monitors to events specifically to document the health impacts of violence as well as to treat them. Contemporaneous medical documentation by an independent body is evidence, and it is far harder to obtain after the fact. Reach is a monitor in Phnom Penh and in each of 12 provincial offices, with street addresses and telephone numbers published on the contact page, and the monitors do not stop at documentation — they request intervention from local authorities, negotiate with the parties, or take the matter public. Established in 1992 to monitor the UN-organised election, it puts forced evictions since 2003 at an estimated 300,000 people. Its site carries a searchable record of land concessions with the companies' countries of origin and their crops. Its joint research with Equitable Cambodia on microloan debt in Kampong Speu, surveying 717 households, documents coerced land sales as a consequence of over-indebtedness — where a community is losing land to debt rather than to a concession, that is the work to cite. Cambodia is dangerous ground for land activists; approach through a provincial office rather than announcing anything first.

trackers.name: MRC prior consultation (PNPCA) — the six-month window on any Mekong mainstream project
trackers.desc: Any project proposed for the Mekong mainstream triggers a six-month prior consultation across all four member countries, and there are regional and national stakeholder forums inside it. Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam are the members. The process begins when the proposing country's National Mekong Committee submits to the Commission, and the clock starts on the day the last Joint Committee member receives the submission forwarded by the Secretariat. Xayaburi started on 22 October 2010 and ran six months to a decision; Pak Beng's six-month milestone was marked in June 2017. Your entry point is your own National Mekong Committee, not the Secretariat in Vientiane. Each member country has one, it is the body that submits and receives, and it is the route by which a riverside community's evidence reaches the process.
