Inside the six months the Secretariat produces a Technical Review Report, external expert groups on fisheries and on sediments contribute analysis, the project is compared against the Commission's Preliminary Design Guidance, and regional and national stakeholder forums are held whose outcomes the Joint Committee considers alongside the technical review. Know the difference between the mainstream and a tributary, because it decides which process applies. A tributary hydropower project requires notification to the Joint Committee only; a mainstream project requires the full prior consultation with consensus sought among the four members. Twenty-eight tributary notifications had been received by June 2009, before any mainstream submission existed. And know what prior consultation is not. It is an inter-governmental process aimed at consensus on whether a project should proceed and under what conditions. It is not a veto and it has not stopped a mainstream dam. What Pak Beng produced was a Joint Committee statement calling on the Government of Lao PDR to make all reasonable efforts to address potential adverse transboundary impacts, and a Joint Action Plan for the period after the six months. Treat the six months as the window in which independent evidence enters an official record that outlives the decision, and plan the rest of the campaign around what that record enables. PNPCA is one of five sets of Commission procedural rules made under the 1995 Mekong Agreement, alongside those on water quality, data sharing, water use monitoring and water flow maintenance.

trackers.name: WCS Cambodia — helped five villages get their forests declared Community Protected Areas
trackers.desc: This is the body that does the paperwork with you. Working with the provincial Department of Environment, it consulted village representatives, helped them assemble the series of documents submitted to the Ministry of Environment requesting that their forests be declared Community Protected Areas, and trained them in resource management, patrolling, and how to report forest and wildlife crime to the authorities. The Ministry issued five proclamations on 9 December 2016 establishing five areas totalling more than 8,400 hectares. External funders paid for the work, so the community was not asked to finance the application. Understand what a Community Protected Area gives and what it withholds. Legal analysis of the framework records that these communities hold access, use, extraction and management rights over the area — and do not hold exclusion rights. They cannot keep outsiders from entering or using the land. That single gap is why a designation can be granted and the forest still be cleared, and it is the first thing to establish before treating recognition as protection. Community forestry is a different category with a harder guarantee. Community forests sit under the agriculture ministry's forestry administration rather than the environment ministry, they are on state public property, and they cannot be granted an economic land concession. Over three hundred exist. Whether your ground falls under one ministry or the other decides which of the two you should be pursuing, and that question is worth settling before any application is drafted. Two cautions, on the numbers and on the body. Published counts of Community Protected Areas and their total area do not reconcile with the stated size range, so take current figures from the ministry rather than from any summary. And this is the Cambodia programme of an international conservation organisation rather than a Cambodian membership body — for legal defence and paralegals, read it alongside the entries for CLEC and LICADHO.

trackers.name: Environment Endowment Fund and the sustainable development council's grant windows
trackers.desc: There is a statutory fund, and asking what is in it is a budget question with a documentary answer. The environmental protection law establishes an environment endowment fund administered by the environment ministry for environmental protection and natural resource conservation in the Kingdom, drawing on contributions from the Royal Government, grants from international organisations, donations from charitable individuals and from non-governmental organisations and other lawful sums, and held in a special account within the national budget. A fund constituted by statute and carried in the national budget leaves a paper trail, which is what makes the question worth putting. The council inside the ministry runs grant windows with published guidelines. The national council for sustainable development, a policy body established in 2015 and sitting within the environment ministry, has published grant application guidelines organised by numbered window and round on its own site. Windows and rounds mean written eligibility criteria and dated deadlines, so ask for the current window's guidelines rather than making a general approach and hoping. What has already been funded shows what fits. A programme run through the council together with the environment ministry, the sub-national democratic development secretariat and the mines and energy ministry, financed by a foreign embassy and a development agency, set out to promote community-based natural resource management and payment for ecosystem services alongside circular-economy waste management and solar energy. A proposal framed as community-based natural resource management is written in the council's own vocabulary rather than against it. The agreement is the thing to aim at, and money follows it. Reporting records twelve communities, covering 44,139 hectares of forest land and nearly thirteen thousand people across three wildlife sanctuaries in one province, signing an agreement with the environment ministry on the sustainable management of natural resources. Read this with the community protected area and community forestry entries recorded here: recognition of the community as manager comes first, and the funding conversation is much shorter afterwards.

trackers.name: Cadastral Commission and the cadastral administration — decisions between possessors, and a duty to tell you a parcel's status
trackers.desc: The cadastral administration has a duty to tell people what a parcel is. Under the land law the cadastral administration, supervised by the land ministry, is competent to identify properties, establish cadastral index maps, issue ownership titles, register land, and inform all persons as to the status of a parcel — its nature, its size, its owner and any encumbrances over it. That last function is the one communities overlook. Before objecting to a project, ask the provincial cadastral office what the parcel actually is, who is recorded as holding it and what encumbrances sit on it, because that answer shapes every argument that follows. A Cadastral Commission decides disputes between possessors, and its decision is final. The land law provides that the commission decides disputes over immovable property between possessors and that its decision is deemed final. That matters because it is a route for people holding land by possession rather than by title — the position of most rural communities in this country — and it does not begin with a court. The procedure is published, and it is worth citing by number. The ministry publishes the prakas setting out the guidelines and procedures of the cadastral commission, a supplementary instruction on implementing that prakas, an instruction on the procedure for resolving land disputes by the administrative commission and the cadastral commission in adjudication areas under systematic land registration, and the sub-decrees appointing the composition of the national commission. Work out from those which commission has your case before filing anything, because the wrong commission is a lost season. A concession can never arise from occupation on the ground. Land concessions create rights only for the period fixed by the concession contract and must rest on a specific legal document issued by the competent authority before the land was occupied. Where a company is already clearing, asking for that document and its date is a fair and answerable question. Read this with the community forestry and community legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: RDIC laboratory — water testing for individuals as well as organisations, and the contaminants it works on
trackers.desc: It tests for individuals, not only for organisations. The laboratory states its purpose as making water quality testing services available to organisations, companies and individuals, so that drinking water is safe and the environment protected. Across this research the recurring limitation on state laboratories has been that they serve agencies and companies rather than households — the position recorded for Malaysia, and the reason two earlier attempts to find a testing route in this country were written up as dead ends. Here a household or a village group can be the client. The contaminants it works on are named. Alongside testing, the laboratory describes research into emerging environmental and public health issues, giving groundwater arsenic and pesticides in vegetables as its examples. A community worried about either is approaching people who already work on the question rather than asking for something novel, and that shortens every conversation that follows. Its capacity is described, which means its method can be questioned. The laboratory records capacity built up since 2004 through new instruments and the adoption of new standards and protocols, collaboration on dozens of research projects on environmental and public health topics, and the training of Cambodian science students, some of whom went on to graduate study. A laboratory that trains and publishes is one whose methods can be examined and defended, which matters on the day a result is challenged by the party it embarrasses. Ask what it is accredited or recognised for. This country has a standards law under which laboratories can be recognised, and at least one utility laboratory has been assessed against the international testing standard under that framework. The standing instruction recorded throughout this file applies here as everywhere: ask which specific tests fall inside an accreditation or recognition, and ask for the measurement uncertainty to be given with the figure. Read this with the community paralegal network, the land-grabbing litigators and the community forestry entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: General Department of Public Procurement — bidding announcements listed by agency and year
trackers.desc: There is one national list of bidding announcements. The finance ministry's general department of public procurement publishes notices that a procurement subject has been put out to tender, each identified by the procuring agency and the year — among them provincial departments of public works and transport, the capital's own public works department, provincial administrations and authorities such as the body responsible for the great lake. The list runs to many pages and is browsable rather than searchable by keyword, so a community looking for its own province works through the pages for the relevant year. What the announcement gives is the agency, the year and the procurement subject. Oversight is central, delivery is local. The ministry is the authority for procurement policy and oversight, while the procurement itself is carried out by line ministries, provincial administrations and public institutions under that oversight. That means the complaint about a local procurement has an addressee above the body that ran it, which is the pattern this file records for procurement regulators across the region. The honest limit: the announcement is the invitation, not the outcome. Published assessments describe the system as still largely manual and paper based, with no mandatory national electronic procurement requirement and procurement data not consolidated or published to an open contracting standard. Award information, in particular, is not reliably published. Ask the procuring agency directly for the award decision, and treat the published list as the record that a tender existed rather than as a record of who won it. A new law is in force with its regulations still settling. A new law on public procurement was promulgated in 2023, replacing the 2012 law and introducing more severe penalties along with a contract template set by ministerial regulation; reporting at the time recorded that the implementing regulations remained in draft and that existing regulations continued to apply until they were finalised. Read this with the cadastral administration, the business registration search and the community forestry entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Anti-Corruption Unit — street complaint boxes, bank secrecy that does not hold, and protection still in draft
trackers.desc: Bank secrecy is not a sufficient reason to withhold evidence. The anti-corruption law empowers the head of the unit to order public authorities, government officials, people holding public office through election and units in the private sector, financial institutions among them, to cooperate with the unit's officials in an investigation, and to ask national and international institutions to cooperate in forensic examination; unit officials hold judicial police powers and seizure follows the criminal procedure code. Published accounts of the law record that bank secrecy is not sufficient justification for failing to provide evidence relating to corruption offences. Where the money behind a project runs through a bank, the statute has already answered the objection that is usually raised. The channels include boxes on the street. Accounts written by the unit's own officers record complaints accepted in person at the headquarters or at branch offices in the provinces, through complaint boxes placed on public streets, by post to a numbered box, and through the unit's website, with guidelines on reporting corruption downloadable in Khmer. For someone who cannot travel and will not write, a box on a street is a channel that costs nothing and identifies nobody. Anonymous information is acted on, but the protection laws are still drafts. The state's own report to a United Nations treaty body records that whenever the unit receives information about corruption, even anonymously, it acts as an independent judicial police force, and that it treats the safety of witnesses and informants as a non-negotiable condition — while also recording that a law on the protection of witnesses and a law on the protection of informants were still being prepared. Protection here rests on practice rather than on statute, which is the difference between this entry and the Timorese and Bruneian ones, where it is written into law. It has monitored resource auctions. The same state submission records the unit's investigation officers monitoring timber bidding across nine provinces and following up irregularities in bidding sessions. A body that has attended auctions of a natural resource is one a community can ask to attend the next one. Read this with the cadastral administration, the community paralegals, the land-grabbing litigators and the procurement announcement entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: National Audit Authority — the twenty-eight day comment window, and 'audit as special requirement'
trackers.desc: There is a draft stage, and it lasts twenty-eight days. The audit law requires the auditor-general to send a copy of a proposed report to the head of the institution being audited; if that head provides written comments within twenty-eight days of receiving it, the auditor-general must consider those comments before preparing the final report, and if no reply comes within that period the proposed report stands. For anyone following an audit, that is a known month in which the audited body is composing its answer — and the answer becomes part of the record rather than a private conversation. Special-requirement audits are a named category. Published accounts of the law's scope record that the authority may audit government institutions and also non-profit organisations, associations and political parties, certain private sector entities identified in the law, and may carry out audits as special requirements. A request that a particular matter be audited is therefore asking for something the statute already provides for by name, which is a better position than asking for a favour. The reports go to both chambers. The authority was established as an independent body to execute the external audit function of government and has operated since 2002; it must certify the statements put to it and issue its audit reports to the National Assembly and the Senate, covering accounting records, financial reports, management systems, operational controls and programmes of government institutions. The honest limit is the lag. Published accounts record long delays in practice — an audit covering one financial year released more than five years after that year closed, and described at the time as only the third such audit since the authority opened. A community should plan around that: the audit is a slow instrument in this country, and for a project that is happening now the faster routes already recorded here — the anti-corruption unit's complaint channels and the published procurement announcements — will matter more. Read this with the anti-corruption unit, the cadastral administration, the community paralegals and the procurement entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Investment registration — the conditional certificate that lists every licence a project needs, and the complaint that can trigger an inspection
trackers.desc: A project's own certificate names the licences it must hold. The published account of the investment approval scheme records that the development council acts as a one-stop shop and obtains the necessary licences from the relevant ministries and entities listed in the conditional registration certificate on the applicant's behalf, and that where the documents are complete and the activity is not on the negative list a registration certificate is issued within twenty working days. That gives a community a concrete first question: which ministries appear on this project's conditional certificate, and has each of them actually issued its licence. It converts a general objection into a list of named authorities, each of which can be asked separately. The approval attaches to the project, not to the company. The scheme states that an investment approval is issued not to an investor or an investing enterprise but to a project, and the law distinguishes export, supporting industry, domestically oriented and expanded projects. A change in ownership therefore does not restart the permissions, and an expansion may require its own registration — so establishing which category and which phase is in front of you matters before anything else is argued. A complaint from an affected person can trigger an on-site inspection. Published summaries of the investment law record that submitting the report on implementation of an investment project does not exempt that project from on-site inspection where the council considers it necessary, or where there is a complaint from persons claiming to be affected by the implementation of the project. That is a named route from people on the ground into an inspection of the project itself, rather than into a general grievance system. Read the law, and note what is not published. The council publishes the investment law and its sub-decree, including the negative list and the incentive annexes, so the categories, conditions and timelines can be checked directly. But the published material concerns procedure and incentives rather than a public register of approved projects, so certificate details ordinarily have to be obtained from the operator or from the individual ministries rather than downloaded. Read this with the business registration search, the community forestry agreements, the procurement records and the anti-corruption unit entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: NatureLife Cambodia — the organisation that has got sites formally designated, and trains the community patrols
trackers.desc: It has had land formally protected, repeatedly, and the sites are named. The organisation's own published account records that it advocated for and facilitated the designation of a Ramsar site on one river system, of multiple community protected areas, of two protected landscapes and of a wildlife sanctuary. For a community whose ground has no legal status at all, the practical question is not what designation exists on paper but who has actually obtained one before — and this is an organisation that has done it more than once, in named places, with the environment ministry. The community-side work is patrols and enterprises rather than seminars. Published accounts record community scouts and a youth team trained in basic forest patrolling, the formation and training of a women's patrol team at a named community protected area which then carried out its first patrol, support for saving groups and sustainable agriculture, and community-based enterprises — one on the great lake reporting income of about three and a half thousand United States dollars over four months, with a share contributed back to the conservation activities of the community protected area. Those are the components a community actually needs: people trained to walk the boundary, and an income that makes the walking sustainable. It works with the ministry, and it has moved national policy. Working since 2004 as the country programme of an international bird conservation body and becoming the national partner organisation in December 2020, founded by twelve people of whom ten came from that earlier programme, it collaborates with the environment ministry and other organisations across several protected areas, maintains national conservation working groups, has drafted species action plans, and secured a national ban on a veterinary drug lethal to vultures. An organisation that has changed a national rule is one whose letter carries weight locally. What that means for approaching it, and the limits. This is a conservation organisation with a species and habitat mandate, not a legal aid body and not a land rights campaigner: it can help build the case for protecting a site with demonstrable biodiversity value, and it will not litigate a land dispute or represent anyone in one. Approach it with wildlife and bird records, a map, and a clear account of the threat, rather than with a grievance. Read this with the cadastral commission, the community forestry agreements, the legal aid organisations and the investment registration entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Equitable Cambodia — training, community mapping and money behind community-led advocacy on land
trackers.desc: It funds and equips community-led advocacy rather than only speaking about it. The organisation's community empowerment and legal awareness programme lists its main activities as curriculum development, training-of-trainer workshops, direct community training, monitoring of the trainings its grassroots facilitators run, youth training and legal internships, and — the part that matters most — supporting community-led advocacy around land and natural resource rights by providing financial and technical support and helping build community capacity. A community that needs both a trainer and a small budget has one address for both, which is rare anywhere in this file. The organising programme teaches mapping, enumeration and personal security. Its community organising programme for housing rights, launched in 2013 and working across twenty communities in the capital with more than a dozen trained organisers, trains participatory leadership and facilitation, land law and the relevant government regulations, housing rights, advocacy and negotiation skills, participatory community mapping and enumerations, and personal security. Mapping and enumeration are how a community documents itself before somebody else counts it, and personal security appearing on a training list is an honest signal about the environment this work happens in. There is a published community guide, and facilitators trained to teach it. A guide to defending land and housing rights was developed with international partners for communities threatened with displacement, with grassroots facilitators trained since 2009 to run workshops using it around the country, and a further volume covering skills for challenging displacement: community organising, engaging existing grassroots networks, evidence-based media and political advocacy, negotiation, organising non-violent direct actions, and pursuing international grievance mechanisms. What it is, and the frame it works in. It is a Cambodian organisation established in 2012 with roots in an earlier programme dating from 2003, working on the housing, land and natural resource rights of poor and vulnerable communities through policy research, evidence-based advocacy, coalition building and community organising, with a separate programme tracking the operations of foreign companies and development actors. Its own account records that nearly fourteen per cent of the country's land was transferred from small-scale food producers and indigenous peoples to agro-industrial firms. It organises, trains and documents; it is not a law firm. Read this with the cadastral commission, the community forestry agreements, the legal aid organisations and the investment registration entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: CamboJA and its news arm — story grants, legal support for reporters, and published monitoring of what happens to them
trackers.desc: One association carries the reporting, the training and the legal support. Founded in 2019 by journalists including former staff of two closed or sold newspapers, the alliance describes itself as the country's only independent network of professional journalists, representing more than a hundred members. Its programmes cover research and advocacy that monitors the situation of journalism and documents attacks on press freedom while connecting at-risk journalists with support services; training in ethical journalism; and a news arm publishing in-depth and investigative reporting in both English and Khmer. Published assessments describe it as the only organisation left providing independent news, capacity building and legal support to journalists facing court allegations, and its news arm as the last remaining independent local newsroom after another outlet was closed in February 2023. It funds reporters to take stories on. Its published description records that the news programme supports independent journalists with story grants so that they can report important stories free from self-censorship and institutional pressure, and the outlet received an international journalism prize in May 2025 for investigative reporting and daily coverage of issues undermining the rule of law. A community with documents is therefore approaching a place that can pay a reporter to travel, which is often the actual obstacle. Its monitoring tells you what covering your case may cost the reporter. Its 2025 report documented sixty-one cases of violence and rights violations affecting fifty-seven journalists; its first-quarter 2026 report recorded eleven violations, with topics linked to violations including environmental issues, land disputes and human rights, and noted authorities resorting to criminal charges including incitement rather than the civil remedies in the press legislation. A survey of seventy-four journalists across the capital and twenty-two provinces found that sixty-two per cent felt unsafe reporting on environmental issues and only five per cent felt safe, citing intimidation, restricted access to information and to sites, legal threats, online harassment and physical violence. The funding position is fragile, and worth knowing. Its executive director has said publicly that the organisation relied on foreign aid grants for more than half its operating costs, and that cuts to that funding destabilised operations and forced it and similar groups to look for other donors. Approach with a complete file and a realistic sense of capacity. Read this with the land rights training and organising body, the cadastral commission, the community forestry agreements and the protected area designation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Cultural heritage law — it covers privately owned property and natural features, and an excavation permit can be withdrawn without compensation
trackers.desc: The law reaches privately owned property, and natural features as well as buildings. The cultural heritage law of January 1996 applies to movable and immovable cultural property whether publicly or privately owned, where its protection is in the public interest, and defines cultural property as any work produced by human agency and any natural phenomenon of a scientific, historic, artistic or religious nature which bears witness to a certain stage in the development of a civilisation or of the natural world and whose protection is in the public interest. A spring, a cave, a hill or a stand of trees with religious significance can therefore be argued under the same statute as a temple, and private ownership is not an answer to it. Excavation and survey need prior authorisation, and it can be taken away. Carrying out excavations or surveys, on land or under water, without the prior authorisation of the competent authority is prohibited. Where an authorised excavator fails to respect any one of its obligations, the authority may withdraw the authorisation or the scientific rights or both, and excavations are suspended from the day the holder is notified of the withdrawal; once withdrawn, the party concerned may not claim any compensation for eviction from the site or for expenses already incurred. That is a sharper consequence than most permit regimes in this file carry, and it is worth citing in any complaint about how a licensed dig is being conducted. Classification, protected sites, and the state's power to expropriate. Protected sites containing archaeological reserves are to be established; classification of public or private cultural property already inventoried, whose protection is in the public interest from a scientific, historical, artistic or religious point of view, is made by the competent authority; and in the event of the discovery of cultural immovables whose protection is in the public interest, the competent authority may exercise its right of expropriation under the expropriation legislation. Where a declaration is made, the authority must announce its decision within three months. A royal decree of 1994 separately defines the protection perimeter of the main temple region and four further national categories of protected site with their management rules. The documented failure, and what it tells you to do. Reporting from December 2022 records the demolition of three buildings of the 1930s which had been added to the provincial culture department's national heritage list in 2017, with the pagoda's monk council stating that it had been unaware that national heritage registration certificates for the buildings existed and that the ministry had not produced copies of them. The lesson is concrete: obtain the registration certificate itself, with its number and date, and put a copy in the hands of whoever occupies or manages the site, because a listing nobody can produce on the day the machinery arrives protects nothing. Read this with the community paralegal network, the free legal representation organisation, the cadastral commission and the site designation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Expropriation Law — compensation paid in advance at market value stripped of the project's effect, and complaining after payment is still allowed
trackers.desc: Compensation is to be fair, just and paid in advance. The expropriation legislation of 2010 applies to expropriations for public physical infrastructure projects serving the public and national interest, and sets out to define the principles, mechanisms and procedures of expropriation together with fair and just compensation. Published accounts of it record that compensation must be fair and just and paid in advance of the taking, and that it is assessed on the fair market value of the property. Payment in advance is the sequence to hold an authority to: a demand to vacate before compensation has been paid departs from the law's own order. The project's own effect on value is stripped out. The assessment excludes changes in value occurring after the declaration, and therefore the effect of the project itself. That cuts both ways and is worth understanding before arguing: an owner cannot claim the uplift a new road brings, but neither can an authority pay less because the announcement itself depressed local prices — and the date of the declaration is the pivot for both. A related provision denies compensation for new construction put up after that point. Complaining after payment is expressly preserved. The law provides that an owner or holder of a real right who has already received compensation from the expropriation committee still has the right to file a complaint under the complaint and resolution procedures the law sets out, with complaints going to a complaint resolution committee and the formalities fixed by sub-decree. Owners may also complain to contest the validity of the expropriation or to seek its relocation. Accepting payment here does not close the door, which is the opposite of the position in some neighbouring systems — but the same provision records that the expropriation may still be carried out despite an unresolved dispute, so the complaint does not stop the works. What the process involves, and where the law stops. Published accounts describe a lengthy sequence: a project proposal for government review, a survey detailing the rights of property owners, meetings with local authorities, and notice to owners by declaration in several forums, all under an expropriation committee. Where owners refuse to leave, the committee may ask the competent authorities to act. The law does not govern expropriation dealt with in an agreement or memorandum between the government and a partner country — so for a foreign-financed project the first question is whether such an agreement exists and what it says. Read this with the community paralegal network, the organisation providing free representation in land-grabbing cases, the cadastral commission and the community mapping and advocacy entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Indigenous communal land title — three ministries, an internal rule and a map, and the gap in protection while you wait
trackers.desc: Three stages, three ministries. Collective title for an indigenous community was introduced by the land legislation of 2001 and given a procedure by a sub-decree of 2009 together with a rural development ministry circular. The stages are: the rural development ministry issues a letter recognising the group as an indigenous community; the interior ministry registers the community as a legal entity; and the land management ministry registers the communal land and issues the title. Each stage is a separate application to a separate ministry, and a community that has completed two of them has not yet got a title — a distinction worth being precise about when talking to officials or to a company. Two further documents decide whether the application can be filed at all. Before the title application goes in, the community must have adopted internal rules on collective land use and management, and must have mapped its land — in practice with a local organisation providing the survey and the GPS work — designating the areas used for homes, for rotational farmland, for ancestral burial grounds and for spirit forests and mountains. The ministry then confirms the area, checks that it does not overlap other land users, and issues the title, which comes with a condition to protect a portion of forest, usually the burial and spiritual areas. The internal rule and the map are therefore the two pieces of work a community can start on its own account before any ministry has acted. The gap while you wait is documented, and it is the danger. Published analysis records that during the lengthy process communities have no protection against an economic land concession being granted over their land until the first two steps are complete, that communities overlapping or near concessions face greater difficulty obtaining title, and that a separate national private titling drive was reported to have cut across the collective process. The environment ministry can also reject an application that overlaps a protected area, and has done so for a number of communities. A community starting this process should assume the first two steps are the urgent ones. The numbers, and what they imply about timing. Of roughly 455 indigenous communities, published counts record recognition by the rural development ministry rising from around 155 in mid-2021 to over 190 later, legal entity registration by the interior ministry at around 150, and communal titles issued to 33 communities by 2021 — covering some 33,900 hectares and around 3,200 families — 36 by mid-2022 and 43 by 2024. This is a multi-year route, not an emergency remedy, which is why it is worth starting before a project appears rather than after. Read this with the community paralegal network, the free representation organisation, the cadastral commission and the community mapping and advocacy entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Finding a licensed valuer — the association's list of full-licence appraisal companies, and the one-year licence to check
trackers.desc: There is a published list of valuation companies holding full licences. The national valuers and estate agents association publishes its members by category, including a list of full-licence appraisal companies with their addresses and contact details. For a household or community facing a compensation figure, that list is the practical starting point: it names firms that can be commissioned to produce an independent valuation, in a country where the alternative is taking the acquiring body's number on trust. Valuation is a licensed activity, and the licence lasts a year. Real estate service businesses — property management, valuation and appraisal, and agency — are regulated by a real estate and pawnshop regulator sitting under the non-banking financial services authority within the finance ministry. Under the governing instrument of December 2022, a licence is issued to a legal entity and a professional certificate to a qualified individual, with separate licences for management, valuation and agency work, and no such business may operate without one. Published legal analysis records that the same instrument reduced the validity of licences and certificates from three years to one. That short validity is what makes the check worth doing: ask for the current licence, not a certificate issued at some point in the past. The regulator, and how licences are now obtained. An earlier instrument of November 2022 requires a valuation company or valuation specialist to hold the valuation services licence or the valuation professional certificate before seeking accreditation, and reporting records that from August 2024 applications for professional certificates and licences are made through the regulator's online portal. Knowing which body licenses the valuer also tells a community where a complaint about a valuation would go. What to ask for when commissioning. The purpose and basis of the valuation, the comparables relied on, and whether the firm has acted for the developer or the acquiring institution on the same land — the association list gives names, but the conflict question has to be asked directly. Read this with the community paralegal network, the free representation organisation, the expropriation law and the cadastral commission entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Court judgments are not published here — what is published instead, and what that means for building a case
trackers.desc: Start from the fact rather than discovering it after weeks of searching: court judgments are not publicly published in this country. University legal research guides state this plainly, with two exceptions — the decisions of the Arbitration Council, a tribunal conducting mandatory but non-binding arbitration of collective labour disputes, published on its site since June 2003; and selected decisions of the Constitutional Council, available from 2003 onwards. A further guide notes a French-language collection carrying selected decisions of the Constitutional Council and the Supreme Court. There is no general judgments database to search, and no amount of looking will produce one. Precedent works differently here, which changes what a case needs. The same guides record that this is primarily a civil law country, that court decisions do not have precedential value and are not often referred to in other cases outside the arbitration and international tribunals, and that they are nonetheless recognised as a secondary source of law. They also record that in civil cases, where no written law applies or the law is unclear, judges may consider other secondary sources including customs, traditions, conscience and equity, under the courts organisation legislation. That last provision is the practical opening: a community's customary use of land is not merely background, it is a source a judge is permitted to consider where the written law does not answer the question. Build the case on the written law and the record instead. Since precedent will not carry the argument, the weight falls on the statute, the sub-decree, the licence conditions and the documents recorded elsewhere in this country's entries — the cadastral records, the environmental assessment file, the complaint receipts. The Constitutional Council's decisions are the one class that binds: guides record that its decisions are final and binding with supremacy in the legal system, so that all legal instruments must conform to them. Where the gazette matters. In civil law systems the official journal is often the sole authoritative source of legal texts until codes are updated, so verify the version of any law relied on. Read this with the indigenous communal land title, the licensed valuers, the legal aid organisations and the cadastral commission entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: LANGO — registration before activity, banking details filed with the interior ministry, and the political neutrality clause
trackers.desc: Registration comes before activity, and unregistered activity is penalised. Civil society monitoring records that the 2015 associations and non-governmental organisations law is the primary legal framework for civil society here; that domestic organisations must register with the interior ministry and, before submitting the required documents, obtain approval from local authorities; and that applicants often cannot complete registration without ministry assistance and repeated revisions. Published analysis of the law records that activity by an unregistered domestic association or organisation attracts a fine of up to ten million riel, that the ministry examines the documents and the legality of the statute and decides whether to accept or reject, and that the law does not specify precise grounds for rejection. A community group planning to hold and spend money must therefore start with the local authority approval, not with the bank. Banking details are filed with the ministry. Reporting records the ministry requiring domestic organisations to submit banking details, with enforcement stepped up around tax requirements, and notes that only a small fraction of several thousand registered domestic organisations had done so at the time. Expect the account to be part of the compliance file, not a private arrangement. Annual reports and audits are standing obligations. Domestic and foreign organisations must submit annual activity and financial reports and are subject to government audits; a foreign organisation operates under a memorandum of understanding with the government, which can be terminated for breach of the financial reporting or neutrality provisions. The neutrality clause is the risk to understand before campaigning. Article 24 requires both domestic and foreign associations and organisations to maintain neutrality towards political parties, and monitoring records that this vague clause has been invoked to threaten suspension or closure of organisations accused of political involvement, with separate election legislation prohibiting civil society organisations from engaging in the electoral process. A land campaign should be documented as being about the land, the law and the licence — never about a party. Read this with the indigenous communal land title, the licensed valuers, the legal aid organisations and the entry recording that judgments are not published, already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Mineral licences — six categories with size and depth limits, the heritage prohibition, and the forestry pre-study
trackers.desc: Six licence categories, and the smallest one carries hard physical limits. The mineral resources legislation of 2001 makes six categories available: artisan mining, pits and quarries mining, gem mining, mineral or gemstone cutting, mineral exploration and industrial mining. An artisan licence may be issued only to nationals, for exploration and exploitation using locally available common instruments and the holder's own labour or family help of no more than seven persons, limited to minerals found in loose state in silt, gravel, sand and rock, within a demarcated area no larger than one hectare and to a maximum depth of five metres. Excavators working a pit deeper than five metres or wider than a hectare are outside the artisan category whatever the operator says. Pits and quarries licences are what most local extraction runs on. That category covers construction and industrial minerals mined from pits and quarries for construction, chemical and secondary industry. Published material records it as valid for two years, applied for at the ministry's one window service office with the fee paid at the mineral resources revenue management office, and sets out published service fees by material — one figure for construction sand, gravel, laterite and clay, a higher one for construction stone, dimension stone, gypsum and similar material — alongside fees for small and large-scale industrial licences, renewal and transfer. Fees and validity are checkable facts to hold a quarry against. Two prohibitions worth knowing before anything else. Published analysis records that the mining law prohibits all mining in national cultural, historical and heritage sites, and permits mining in protected, reserved or restricted areas only with the written permission of the responsible authority; and that while the forestry legislation of 2002 allows mining within the permanent forest estate, any proposed operation must first be the subject of a prior study and evaluation by the agriculture, forestry and fisheries ministry. Ask for the written permission, or for the prior study, by name. Scale, and where the decisions are made. Published figures record active industrial mining licences, mineral exploration licences and several hundred construction mining licences as at one count, with gold mining permits granted to seven companies across five provinces in 2021. A ministerial proclamation authorises provincial and capital departments of mines and energy to review, decide and issue mining licences to citizens, and a separate decision governs exploitation of all types of sand to protect the freshwater and marine environment, with the ministry running public competitions to select sand mining companies at named locations. Read this with the indigenous communal land title, the licensed valuers, the legal aid organisations and the entry recording that judgments are not published, already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Bar Association legal aid — the court certifies you as poor first, then the president has fifteen days to assign a lawyer
trackers.desc: The route runs through the court before it reaches the bar. Published accounts of the bar association's legal aid work record that it accepts low-income clients after they have been determined sufficiently impoverished by the chief judge of the courts and the chiefs of the court clerks, that once approved a person may submit the accepted request for legal assistance to the bar association president, and that the president then has fifteen days to designate a legal aid department attorney to the case. That is the sequence to follow, and the fifteen-day clock is the point at which to follow up. Who may petition, and to what standard the lawyer must work. The same accounts record that the law on the bar obliges the association to provide legal assistance to the impoverished in certain circumstances; that a named article states people with no property, no income, or income insufficient to support their living may petition for free legal aid to the chief judge and the chiefs of the court clerks; and that another article requires all lawyers to defend legal aid clients with the same procedures and standards as paying clients. Quote that standard if the service is thin. Know the limits before relying on it. Published analysis records that the department's pro bono aid is available only after a successful petition to the chief of the court, that its assistance is generally limited to criminal defence cases, and that misdemeanours fall outside the service; and that where the court does not authorise legal aid, individuals turn to legal aid organisations, which receive more inquiries than their resources allow. A land dispute is unlikely to be taken by this route, so read it alongside the organisations already recorded in this bucket. What exists in practice, and where. Reporting records the association recruiting several hundred volunteer lawyers across the country, with volunteers offering free consultation and others free advice and defence for the poor, reachable during regular business hours; a policy calling on members to give advice, counselling and legal services free at their own offices; free representation figures in the thousands of cases and clients at municipal and provincial courts; funding from a bar fund of mandatory contributions from all member attorneys plus a government contribution, with a stated increase; and a legal office established in each of the twenty-five municipal and provincial prisons for confidential lawyer-client consultation. It also records the association acknowledging irregularities by some volunteers and having mechanisms to review lawyers' conduct. Read this with the community paralegals, the free representation in land grabbing cases, the mineral licence categories and the associations law entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Sub-decree 72 on environmental impact assessment — the annex that decides whether a project is caught, public participation in the purposes, and the thirty-day silence rule
trackers.desc: Public participation is written into the sub-decree's own purposes. The 1999 sub-decree, published by the development council, states its purposes as requiring an assessment on every project and activity, private or public, reviewed by the environment ministry before submission to the government for decision; determining the nature and size of proposed and existing activities subject to assessment; and fostering public participation in the assessment process in recognition that people's concerns should be considered in project decision-making. Quote that third purpose when a proponent treats consultation as optional. It applies to proposed, existing and in-process private, joint-venture and public projects listed in its annex, except projects responding to a declared state of emergency. The annex is the document that decides whether a project is caught, and it uses thresholds. Published training material reproducing the annex records physical thresholds for listed categories — for example buildings above a stated height or floor area. Establish whether the project crosses the annex threshold before arguing about the report's quality, because that is what determines whether a report is required at all. Guidance records that all projects go through an initial assessment to determine whether a full assessment is required; that a later ministerial proclamation of 2020 on classification of assessment for development projects updates the sub-decree; and that an annex to that proclamation distinguishes the initial assessment, based mainly on existing available data, from the full report, based on primary data gathered in and around the project site. The full report must contain the consultation results. The same analysis records that a full report must contain the project overview, methodology and scope, a summary of the relevant framework, a full description and action plan, a description of existing physical, ecological and socio-environmental resources, detailed information on the results of public consultation, and mitigation measures. Ask for that section by name and check whether your meeting appears in it. The thirty-day silence rule is the weakness to know about. The sub-decree requires the ministry to review and submit findings and recommendations to the project sponsor and approval institution within thirty working days of receiving the initial report and pre-feasibility study, and the same period for a full report. Published analysis records that if the ministry fails to respond within thirty days the approval institution may assume the report complies and proceed, and that where findings are given the approval institution is only required to consider them. Watch the thirty-day mark, because silence favours the project. Read this with the community forestry agreements, the paralegal network, the expropriation law and the mineral licence entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Law on Water Resources Management — the licence, the consultation with local authorities before it is granted, farmers' water user communities, and the water law implementation area
trackers.desc: Local authorities must be consulted before a water use licence is granted. The 2007 water resources legislation, published in full by the development council, provides that before granting a water use licence to any person the ministry shall consult with the other agencies and the local authorities concerned on the water utilisation and the construction of waterworks proposed; that all water and water resources are owned by the State; and that a licence is the permit document conferring the right to use water. Ask the commune and district whether they were consulted, because the consultation is a condition of the grant, not a courtesy. Licences can be modified, suspended or cancelled, and the grounds are listed. The Act provides that the ministry may modify, suspend or cancel a water use licence for violation of the conditions imposed in it or of the law's provisions; that it may amend or cancel a licence at the holder's request; and that the government may amend a licence in the public interest, with proper compensation to the licensee in that case. A licence is therefore not fixed once issued, and a community's evidence of breached conditions goes to a named power. Farmers using one irrigation system may form a recognised community. The Act provides that to ensure effective and sustainable management and operation of the irrigation system the ministry shall initiate the creation of farmers' water user communities; that all farmers using water from the same irrigation system or part of it may form one; and that its statutes are registered with the provincial or municipal directorate, after which it is fully entitled to carry out its statutes and formally recognised. Published policy material records a circular recognising these communities as legal entities in charge of everyday management of irrigation schemes, with the provision that irrigation systems will be developed only with the community's approval, while noting observers' view that the system has not worked effectively. A troubled basin can be declared an implementation area. The Act provides that a basin, sub-basin or aquifer may be declared a water law implementation area where there are likely to be conflicts among water users, problems of water pollution or watershed degradation; that the ministry keeps a centralised inventory of water resources showing location, quantity and quality, with data from other institutions submitted to it; and published material records that the data collected must be freely available to the public. Anyone drilling or digging wells professionally or commercially must supply the ministry with a detailed report on the operation and its technical specifications. Read this with the assessment sub-decree, the community forestry agreements, the mineral licence categories and the paralegal network entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Community fisheries — the committee that alone may apply for the fishing area agreement, the by-laws and membership rules, and the right of appeal when an agreement is not renewed
trackers.desc: Only the community fisheries committee may apply for the area agreement, and it can ask for technical help to draft it. The sub-decree on community fisheries management provides that only the community fisheries committee has the right to apply to the fisheries department for approval of a community fishing area agreement, and that it may request technical assistance from the provincial or municipal fisheries office, or from an individual skilled in community fisheries management, to draft it. It also provides that the committee may appeal if the agreement is not renewed. That appeal right is the answer when a community's agreement is allowed to lapse. The area is state public property with boundaries fixed by proclamation. The sub-decree provides that community fishing areas are state public property, with the boundaries of each defined by proclamation of the agriculture, forestry and fisheries minister; that commune and sangkat councils shall cooperate in establishing community fisheries; that the by-laws must state the listed matters; that a member must be at least eighteen and may be a member of only one community fisheries, in the place where they live; and that community fisheries property may not be sold, exchanged, rented, donated, shared, divided, borrowed, pawned or transferred. The fisheries law defines a community fishing area as state fishery domain handed over to the community under an agreement between the head of the fisheries administration cantonment and the citizens living in or around it, who depend mainly on fisheries and use traditional gear. What the area protects, and what is banned inside it. Published country material records that the 2006 law encourages creation and maintenance of conservation zones and secures local community rights to use fishery resources for traditional, religious and livelihood purposes through community fisheries; that only small-scale fishing gear may be used in them; and that the persistent illegal activities include electrofishing, prohibited nets, and cutting of flooded forest within community fisheries and state fishery domains. It records fisheries administration officers acting as judicial fisheries police, able to investigate and compile documents for the courts, with penalties applying to government officers too, and records inundated forest area having fallen from several hundred thousand hectares to a small fraction. Read this with the water resources law, the environmental assessment sub-decree, the community forestry sub-decree and the paralegal network entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Protected Areas Law zoning — clearing for infrastructure barred outright in the core and conservation zones, community zones reserved to local and indigenous use, and the fifteen-year community protected area agreement
trackers.desc: Clearing and bulldozing for public infrastructure is strictly prohibited in the two strictest zones. The 2008 protected areas law provides that all clearance and bulldozing of open land or forest land in protected areas for building any type of public infrastructure through the core zone and the conservation zone is strictly prohibited, and that such activities may be carried out only in the sustainable use zone and the community zone, with the government's approval at the environment ministry's request. Establishing which zone a route crosses therefore decides whether the project is barred or merely conditional. The same law bars military exercises, training and camping in those two zones except for national security needs, and prohibits swidden agriculture there. Four zones, and the community zone is reserved to local and indigenous use. Published material records each protected area divided into core, conservation, sustainable use and community zones; that the core zone holds threatened and critically endangered species and fragile ecosystems with access generally prohibited except for named officials and researchers; that entry to the conservation zone requires advance permission from the conservation administration on site, with use of forest by-products for livelihood by local communities and indigenous minorities allowed where it causes no harm; and that the community zone is managed for the socio-economic development of local communities and indigenous peoples holding residential land, paddy, gardens or swidden, with management for non-local use not allowed. A community can hold part of the sustainable use zone under agreement. The law provides that the environment ministry may allocate part of the sustainable use zone to communities residing within or adjacent to a protected area as a community protected area, which enters into an agreement with the conservation administration valid for up to fifteen years; that the administration may suspend operations for review where the agreement or management plan is not followed; and that the ministry may revoke the agreement for contravention. Land title inside a protected area runs through the ministry. Published material records that issuing land title or permission to use land in these zones requires prior agreement from the environment ministry; that development and investment in the relevant zone may be permitted only after consulting relevant ministries, local authorities and local communities; that a national zoning guideline was issued under the law; and that a sub-decree marked a stated large area as community zones, with observers noting it may ease communal land titling for indigenous groups. Read this with the community fisheries, the community forestry sub-decree, the assessment sub-decree and the water law entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The 2023 Environment and Natural Resources Code — twelve books with public participation among its stated principles, community protected area agreements extended to twenty-five years, and the criticism recorded beside it
trackers.desc: The Code replaces the patchwork, and public participation is named among its principles. A published legal summary records the Code's first book as containing general provisions including the roles and duties of the environment ministry, policy development, and principles such as polluter pays, public participation and the precautionary principle; records book three covering waste obligations, pollution control, hazardous substances, water and marine pollution, air pollution and ozone-depleting substances; records book four on establishment and management of natural protected areas including national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and natural heritage sites, and on watershed, water resources, river basins, forests, wild plant habitats and wildlife, fisheries, minerals and coastal and marine resources; and records book five on strategic environmental assessment, environmental impact assessment, the environmental management plan and environmental audit. It records that during the Code's application only the incompatible parts of other laws in force cease to have effect, and that the Code applies where no separate rule is provided by a special law — which is how to work out whether an older instrument already recorded in this bucket still applies. The community protected area agreement was lengthened, and that is concrete. A legal organisation's account records a national consultant stating that the Code improves public participation and access to environmental information, has the potential to strengthen the rights of communities dependent on natural resources and forests, and that one of its key components increases the duration of a community protected area agreement from fifteen up to twenty-five years, with decision-making power transferred toward the local level. The fifteen-year figure is the one already recorded in this bucket under the protected areas law. The criticism is recorded beside it. Published commentary records indigenous communities' concern that the adopted Code excludes indigenous peoples' inputs and fails to recognise their rights in forest and natural resource management, and argues that participation must be conducted in good faith, be just and transparent, and engage from the initial process to the final stage in shared decision-making. An access assessment records that right-to-information provisions in environmental laws are subject to broad confidentiality exceptions, that proactive disclosure is not required, and that the country scored lowest on participation while the law recognises broad legal standing in most environmental cases. Read this with the protected areas zoning, the community fisheries, the assessment sub-decree and the water law entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The assessment report profile page — draft reports published in full and free, searchable by province, sector and keyword, with a summary attached to each and the legal framework alongside
trackers.desc: Draft assessment reports are published in full, without restriction, on a non-government platform. The open data organisation records that its assessment profile page provides public access to assessment reports and related environmental information; that users can search and filter reports by province, sector and keyword, for communities, researchers, journalists, civil society organisations and students; that each profile includes summarised project information to convey the key aspects quickly, while also providing free access to full draft reports without restrictions; and that the site hosted a stated number of reports across sectors and investment projects at the time of writing. Where the ministry's own copy is not obtainable, that is where to look. The page also carries the process and the legal framework. The same account records that the page offers an overview of the country's assessment process and legal framework to support public understanding of environmental governance and assessment procedures. A community reading a report can therefore check, on the same site, which step the project should be at. Why the platform exists is stated plainly. Published material records that the law requires assessment reports for most large development projects but that the general public's access to these reports is limited; that at the platform's launch its director said it would let the public, academics, environmentalists and locals access information and summaries of reports in digital format, so they can monitor ministry-approved development projects to see whether these have any negative impact on their livelihood and the environment; and that the page displays draft versions of reports shared by the government with related non-governmental organisations. The page carries tabular information, digitised reports and map visualisation. The underlying data is downloadable and licensed for reuse. The organisation's data hub lists datasets built from assessment reports, tagged to economic land concessions and plantations, environmental impact assessments and mining, in spreadsheet format; and the profile page records the organisation's own materials as published under an open licence, while stating it is a private non-profit open data group, not a government or intergovernmental domain, and cannot guarantee third-party accuracy in every instance. Read this with the assessment sub-decree, the environmental code, the protected areas zoning and the community fisheries entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The indigenous peoples' organisations — a registered national body with its registration number, the alliance and youth and advocacy networks beside it, and what they do for a community seeking collective title
trackers.desc: There is a registered national indigenous organisation, and its registration is public. The organisation records itself as a local, non-governmental, not-for-profit organisation officially registered at the interior ministry on 30 June 2014, giving its registration number, and publishes its background, mission and organisational chart. It records producing a national report on the demographic and socio-economic situation of indigenous peoples, running dissemination and consultation workshops on measures and legal norms related to collective ownership rights of indigenous communities in a named province, and holding a signed one-year project agreement with a foreign development agency. For a community starting a collective title claim, that is a registered body with published governance. An alliance and two networks sit alongside it, with stated functions. Published material records an alliance of indigenous communities and peoples' organisations, associations and networks, serving as a platform for solidarity, cooperation and coordination of actions for the promotion and assertion of collective rights; records an advocacy network supporting communities in fifteen provinces, providing legal awareness, facilitating community organisation, training community members, and submitting complaints and petitions to relevant authorities; and records a youth organisation building capacity of indigenous youth in relevant international and national laws, human rights documentation and advocacy, accountability and transparency, with members in eight provinces and a stated membership figure, active in struggles against agri-business companies and hydropower projects. The numbers show why the assistance matters. Published material records that by 2024 collective land titles had been issued to 43 of 455 communities, another account giving 40 of 580 communities, about seven per cent; records the alliance's coordinator stating the process takes at least three years; and records a statement that it may take a hundred years for all indigenous peoples to receive collective title at that rate, the procedures being exceptionally complicated, lengthy and costly. It records recognition figures by two ministries at an earlier date, and records that granting economic and social land concessions over the same land hinders the communal titling process. Read this with the indigenous communal title entry, the paralegal organisation, the community protected areas and the cadastral commission entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Community forest patrol networks — grassroots patrols that document logging with counts and species, a youth network that publishes patrol findings, and the recorded risks of doing it
trackers.desc: Communities here patrol and document their own forests, and the reporting names how it works. Published reporting records community members patrolling their forests to document the losses and push the government to stop the cutting, records a named community protected forest representative for one sanctuary working with the agriculture ministry in an unpaid capacity, and quotes him that they should be working together with authorities, rangers and police but often are not — rangers sometimes having connections with illegal loggers, and outsiders with the village police. It records resin tappers who once worked more than 400 trees each and now each have just over 100, and records national tree cover loss of more than 7 million acres since the 2000s. That resin-tapper figure is the kind of before-and-after count a community can gather itself. A youth network turns a patrol into a published record. Reporting records a youth network conducting a 55-kilometre patrol of a named wildlife sanctuary across three districts over three days and recording at least 100 cases of illegal logging, mostly of rare timber, with cross-sections ranging from 45 centimetres to 1.5 metres and the species listed by name; and records the network calling on the environment ministry to end restrictions on local communities, forest activists, associations, civil society organisations and the public participating in patrolling, protecting and conserving the forest, in accordance with the constitutional rights and duties of citizens and the nature protection legislation. Distance, days, case count, sizes and species is a template. The risks are recorded plainly, and belong in any decision to do this. Published reporting records a member of a grassroots forest network attacked with a machete while sleeping in a hammock after patrolling for illegal loggers; records defenders facing mounting intimidation and legal threats, including the arrest of a journalist and threats of legal action against an activist who shared evidence of logging; and records a prominent rights organisation — already in this bucket — providing legal support to detained environmental activists. Read this with the community forestry agreements, the protected areas zoning, the paralegal network and the legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The NGO Forum's land and livelihoods programme — four named projects covering resettlement, indigenous land, forestry and tenure, about a hundred member organisations, and a membership fee scaled from ten dollars
trackers.desc: The projects are named separately, so a community can ask for the one that matches its problem. The forum records a resettlement and housing rights project supporting organisations to encourage authorities and developers to provide sufficient information on new projects to affected communities, and to consult with them before development starts, to minimise the negative impact of new developments, land grabs and resettlement; an indigenous peoples' land rights project supporting organisations to secure indigenous land and protect communities by preventing or mitigating the negative impacts of development projects and economic land concessions; a forestry rights project supporting organisations working together to prevent or mitigate negative impacts of concessions on forest-dependent communities and promoting alternative livelihood options; and a land security project supporting organisations advocating improved land tenure security and better land dispute resolution mechanisms. Membership is open and the fee is small. The forum records itself as a membership organisation of approximately 100 local and international non-governmental organisations, records that organisations committed to its mission may apply for membership, with applications considered by a management committee elected from among the member organisations and eligibility criteria set out in its by-laws, and records a membership fee ranging from ten to three hundred dollars based on the organisation's overall budget. A village association can therefore join a national advocacy body for the price of a bus fare. It runs an evidence centre and reports what its members thought of it. Published material records a land information centre established in 2006 to provide evidence-based advocacy for the programme, renamed a research and information centre in 2011 and later extended to support the environment programme as well; and records network members rating the programme as important in influencing and promoting land rights, particularly land tenure security, the protection of rural property rights and community access to land registration, with government participation in its conferences enabling government and affected communities to discuss issues directly with each other. Its street address, post box, telephone and email are published. Read this with the indigenous organisations, the paralegal network, the community forestry and the legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The NGO database and the housing rights task force — a searchable directory of registered organisations with profiles, and a registered local body organising communities in the capital
trackers.desc: There is a searchable database of the country's non-governmental organisations, with a profile page for each. A cooperation committee runs the database, whose entries record an organisation's stated vision, objectives, values and registration details. That is how a community checks whether the body offering to help it is registered, and finds others working on the same issue. One profile shows what a housing rights organisation states it does. The database records a housing rights task force as registered as a local non-governmental organisation under the interior ministry on 8 January 2010, whose stated goal is a capital where all communities know their rights, know how to exercise them, have the political will and internal organisation for collective action, and consistently demand transparency, accountability and sustainability in all local development policies; whose objective is building relationships with government to bring about improvements in the protection of housing rights; and whose activities are geared towards working with the strengths communities already have and empowering them in areas where they need support, under stated values including solidarity and cooperation, transparency, social justice and accountability, gender equality and equity. The organising skills taught to communities are listed, and they are the practical curriculum.
