Published material from a land and housing rights organisation — already recorded in this bucket — records its community organisers, a team of more than a dozen individuals from neighbourhoods throughout the capital, training communities in participatory leadership and facilitation skills, land law and relevant government regulations, housing rights, advocacy skills, negotiation skills, participatory community mapping and enumerations, and personal security, working in 20 communities across the city. It records a separate programme that has, since 2009, trained a new group of 30 facilitators each year on a community guide to defending land and housing rights, through four to five day training-of-trainer workshops, with those facilitators then supported and given financial support to organise community education workshops for at-risk communities in their own regions. Read this with the land rights organisation, the indigenous bodies, the paralegal network and the NGO forum entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Sithi human rights portal and its land rights modules — a documentation platform for cases, and Khmer-language explainers on how ownership is actually acquired
trackers.desc: There is a documentation portal for rights cases, and land is one of its subjects. The organisation records the portal project — its name meaning rights in Khmer — as begun to develop and implement collaborative and decentralised approaches to human rights advocacy, striving to facilitate more detailed research and analysis, and more sophisticated evidence-based dialogue and advocacy, and to progress tactics for monitoring, documentation and information sharing. For a community whose case would otherwise exist only in its own memory, a national documentation platform is where it becomes citable. The land explainers are in Khmer and cover the transactions people actually face. The portal records a land rights module on acquisition of ownership, explaining possession, ownership and the procedures to become an owner of immovable property through sale, exchange, succession and gifting, with content based on the country's land law and delivered as a short video, infographics and quizzes in Khmer — the second module in a series. Material in the language people speak, on how title is actually acquired, is what stops a family signing away a claim it did not know it had. The organisation behind it runs named projects, including one on land and one on business. Published description records six main projects — protecting fundamental freedoms, business and human rights, the rights portal, land reform, sexual orientation and gender identity, and judicial reform — and records the freedoms project as working for people reporting on or working to address violations, including union leaders, community activists and peaceful protestors, by mitigating circumstances in which legal instruments are used to violate fundamental freedoms. It records the business project as concerned with the overall impact of business and investment on the human rights landscape, and records that large swathes of the country have been leased for commercial exploitation through opaque economic land concessions. Its reach includes radio. A defenders organisation records the centre as having organised at least 165 radio shows, covering land rights, business and human rights, digital rights and fair trial rights, and as the first non-governmental organisation to organise public forums in the country. Read this with the indigenous organisations, the NGO forum's land programme, the paralegal network and the forest patrol entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Provincial indigenous organisations — a Ratanakiri association working with 94 communities in 18 communes on collective land titles, and a north-east organisation covering three provinces
trackers.desc: One provincial association works with 94 communities in 18 communes, and its registration is dated. Published description records the association as founded by an indigenous peoples' elder group from early 1999 through comprehensive consultation with indigenous communities and organisations in the province and country, whose objective is to give priority and power to indigenous communities so they can protect their land, natural resources, identity and rights; records it officially registered with the interior ministry on 15 October 2007; and records that its main priority target is one named province where it works with 94 communities in 18 communes, naming eight indigenous peoples among them, and that it spreads its work to other provinces through cooperation with indigenous peoples' organisations. A community in that province can therefore approach a body that already works in its own commune. Its practical service is getting collective title, and the effect is recorded by villagers. Published material records the association as helping communities obtain collective land titles — legal documents that authenticate their collective ownership of their villages and the hills, fields and forests that surround them — with four communities well on their way to finalising the cumbersome and lengthy process, titles that once in hand can serve as deterrents to land grabbing. Reporting records a former head of one village's land committee saying the community first rallied around collective title to protect their community from a company seeking to mine the land for gems and minerals, and that if it was not for the title the land would be with them. It also records the strain: 32 families left that village's title after it was gained in 2014, preferring individual titles. A second organisation covers three north-eastern provinces. A national NGO database records it as a Cambodian non-profit non-governmental organisation founded in November 2006 and registered with the interior ministry on 25 January 2007, operating in three named north-east provinces, recognised as a local NGO working for indigenous peoples' rights, which encourages ownership and participation of indigenous peoples as its approach to protect their land and natural resources. Read this with the indigenous organisations, the NGO forum's land programme, the rights portal and the paralegal network entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The commune and district land dispute bodies — the commune authority that conciliates but cannot decide, the district cadastral commission that opens a file, and the elders it may co-opt
trackers.desc: The first stop is the commune authority, and its limit is stated plainly. Published description records that registered land disputes go to court, while unregistered land disputes are resolved by several levels of authority, beginning with the commune or sangkat authority, which only reconciles opinions but does not make decisions, with cases usually heard before the commune officers before being sent to a higher level. Knowing that the commune can conciliate but not decide stops a community mistaking a commune meeting for a resolution. The next two bodies are named and their roles distinguished. The same description records administrative commissions established in all areas undergoing systematic land registration, which receive complaints and resolve disputes by mediation, referring cases to the cadastral commission where mediation is not possible; and records the cadastral commission as responsible for disputes over unregistered land and those that cannot be resolved at lower levels. Published material records the commissions as sitting at district, provincial and national levels, generally acting as mediator or conciliator outside the court system, with the provincial and national levels holding full jurisdiction to decide who is the lawful possessor or owner, and a party disagreeing with a national written decision able to seek judicial review. The district commission must open a file, and it can bring in local elders. Published regulation records that the district commission has the duty to conciliate conflicts arising outside adjudication areas, that conciliation shall follow customary rules alongside cadastral rules, that the ministry determines the complaint form, and that the commission shall register and open a file for all disputes submitted to it. It records that the chief of the commission may invite the concerned representatives of district, commune and village authorities and local elder trustees to join as ad hoc members, with district land office staff assisting. The caseload problem is recorded too. Published analysis records the commissions as overloaded with cases and often dismissing cases that concern powerful elite and private companies. Read this with the rights portal's land modules, the provincial indigenous organisations, the NGO forum's land programme and the paralegal network entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Provincial environment departments and the commune councils beside them — the hands-on provincial body defined by its own ministerial proclamation, the commune council that writes the development plan, and the honest verdict on complaining upward
trackers.desc: The provincial environment department is described as the hands-on body, and its remit is set by a published proclamation. An analysis records that provincial departments of environment play a more active, hands-on role related to management of the environment and natural resources than provincial administrations, which integrate national policies into provincial plans; that municipal, district and commune administrations typically cooperate more actively with the provincial departments relevant to their jurisdictions to implement policies, legal instruments, strategic plans, guidelines and programmes, while with provincial administrations they may execute duties like reporting; and that the roles and responsibilities of each provincial department are defined in a proclamation, the ministry having issued a proclamation on the organisation and functioning of provincial departments of environment applicable to all of them, usable as a template tailored to each province. A community can therefore ask for the proclamation that governs its own province's department. The commune council's job includes writing the plan the project will be measured against. Published description of the commune administration legislation records that each commune shall have a council; that the commune is a body representing citizens in its commune with missions to serve the general interests of its commune; and that commune councils shall prepare, adopt and implement commune development plans. Getting a hazard into the commune development plan is cheaper than fighting the project after approval. The honest verdict on complaining upward is recorded. A published legal analysis of community protected areas records that the local practice of communities filing complaints with the provincial authorities has been ineffective, and that clear boundary demarcation, for both economic land concessions and community protected areas, is important for conflict prevention as well as conflict resolution, noting that stakeholders often have inadequate knowledge of where boundaries lie. That is the reason a community's own map matters more than its next letter. Read this with the commune and district land dispute bodies, the rights portal's land modules, the provincial indigenous organisations and the NGO forum's land programme entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: District cadastral offices and the commune chief as the filing route — 197 district and 25 provincial offices, an adjudication panel that seats two respected elders, and the honest cost gap between the two registration systems
trackers.desc: An application for individual registration is filed through the commune chief, not directly at the district. Published legal description records that the land possessor must file a land registration application to the district, khan or municipal cadastral office via the commune chief or sangkat chief, and records that to obtain full ownership that is legally recognised and cannot be infringed upon, and that can be used to defend against any third party, land must be registered with the cadastral administration office. Published research adds that an occupant can request authorities to register their land at state cadastral offices and submit an application form at the office of the commune or sangkat where the property is. Knowing the commune office is the doorway saves a wasted journey to the district town. The adjudication panel seats two elders from the area. The same description lists panel membership as including a responsible officer from the provincial or capital department of land management, urban planning, construction and cadastral affairs; the district or municipality governor or their representative; the commune or sangkat chief or their representative; and two respected elders from the area under adjudication. Two elders from the locality sitting on the body that decides a claim is the closest thing here to community representation inside the process. The office network is counted. Published description records that 197 district and 25 provincial or municipal offices of the land ministry carry out actual implementation of land registration and administration of land transactions, with the land registry kept and maintained at three levels — national, provincial and district — and the smallest unit being the land parcel, situated within a single commune or sangkat. The cost difference between the two routes is stated plainly. Published description records systematic registration, done commune by commune, as low cost but time consuming, and sporadic registration as the route for those who do not wish to wait, but which is typically more expensive and, in another account, much less accessible to the majority. Read this with the provincial environment departments, the commune and district land dispute bodies, the provincial indigenous organisations and the rights portal entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Commune/Sangkat Fund and the annual investment programme — money allocated to all 1,621 communes by formula, a plan villagers help write, and the conservation projects that lose out to roads
trackers.desc: Every commune gets a transfer, and villagers help decide what it buys. Published description records commune planning as consisting of two tasks — developing the complete five-year commune development plan, and reviewing and updating the annual commune investment plan — with councils considering strategies for physical infrastructure and non-infrastructure meant to address the needs of citizens. It records that the planning process marks a certain level of participation from citizens and partnership between stakeholders, that a district integration workshop shows the importance of participation by non-governmental organisations, line departments and councils in sharing information to respond to commune priorities, and that councils can request and call for external support to their area. For a village that wants a culvert, a water point or a protected pond, that annual plan is the document to get into. The scale is national and the formula is published. Published research records the fund as scaled up nationwide from 2002 with a 2001 law lending political legitimacy to decentralisation at the lowest rung — communes and villages; records a funding allocation formula defined in part by the commune's existing population and poverty headcount; and records that the law gave recipients latitude to determine the types of investment projects to finance and to manage them. Other research records that by 2010 the government had assumed full financial and operational responsibility, with nearly three per cent of the central budget contributed each year, allocated by a transparent formula across all 1,621 communes and sangkats, producing more than 40,000 local infrastructure projects across 14,073 villages, mostly rural roads, water supply systems, irrigation dams and canals. The bias against conservation is recorded plainly. A conservation organisation records that because of the lack of essential infrastructure in rural communities, commune council members and district authorities almost always prioritise this type of work, and that using the investment programme for natural resource management requires changing the prevailing perceptions and attitudes toward the process. Read this with the commune and district land dispute bodies, the provincial environment departments, the community fisheries and the NGO forum's land programme entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Provincial and municipal courts of first instance — a court in the capital and in every province, a published list of them, and a small-claims procedure that can be started orally
trackers.desc: There is a court in the capital and in every province, and they are listed by name. A judicial council's pages publish the list of courts of first instance — the capital's municipal court and each provincial court, named one by one, twenty-four in all. Published description records that there is a court of first instance in the capital and in each province, comprising a president, vice-presidents, judges, clerks, administrative officials and other legal experts; and records that these courts have jurisdiction to adjudicate all general cases except those falling under the jurisdiction of a special or extraordinary court. For a community, the court that hears a land case sits in its own province. A small claim can be filed orally. Published legal description records that the code of civil procedure provides special procedures for small claim matters of a value not more than one million riel, and records that a civil action shall be filed through a written complaint to a competent court, except for a small claim, which can be filed orally. It records the first-instance procedure as comprising filing of a lawsuit, preparatory proceedings for oral argument, and oral argument. Being able to start a case by speaking rather than filing a drafted complaint matters where a household cannot afford counsel. The court's internal divisions and the practical constraint are recorded. Published description records that the court is in principle composed of civil and criminal departments, but that in practice, as the number of judges is very limited, there is still no clear separation between the departments, and a judge may handle both civil and criminal cases. Other description records specialised civil and criminal courts as established within the first instance structure, with the civil court taking cases related to labour, commercial and administrative disputes. Published advice notes that a litigant needs a lawyer certified to appear in the court, and that many are not. Read this with the commune and district land dispute bodies, the bar association legal aid, the community paralegals and the district cadastral offices entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Timor-Leste — SERVE, I.P. (Serviço de Registo e Verificação Empresarial)
trackers.desc: National company registry; the one-stop SERVE maintains the Companies Register, issues unique company numbers & commercial-registration certificates and licenses business activity, Timor-Leste. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Timor-Leste — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares the state budget and publishes budget transparency & execution data, Timor-Leste. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Timor-Leste.

trackers.name: Ombudsman for Human Rights and Justice (Provedor) of Timor-Leste
trackers.desc: National institution of Timor-Leste that provides free legal representation and defends access to justice, fair-trial and due-process rights for people who cannot afford counsel.

trackers.name: Tara bandu — a customary law named in the statute's own definitions
trackers.desc: A CUSTOMARY PRACTICE DEFINED BY NAME IN NATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL LEGISLATION IS RARE. The Environmental Basic Law (Decree-Law No. 26/2012 of 4 July) defines tara bandu in Article 1 as ‘a custom that is part of the culture of Timor-Leste that regulates the relationship between humans and the environment’, recognising it as applicable under rituals-based local common law, intended to conserve and promote the environment. So a tara bandu is not an informal arrangement the state may choose to respect — it is an instrument the environmental law itself names. It is a ceremony enshrining customary law with state recognition, generally at the scale of the suco, the smallest administrative division, over several years, focused on forests and on relations among people — and it anchors participatory land use plans, including agreements on property boundaries, rules of engagement, and interdictions and sanctions. One ceremony can settle a boundary, set a rule and attach a sanction — three things most jurisdictions need three separate processes for. AND IT NOW REACHES THE SEA: coastal communities have applied tara bandu, traditionally terrestrial, to marine resource management, creating MPAs that often give seagrass and dugongs special protection.

trackers.name: Vila Maumeta — temporary closure by ceremony, and the statute that backs it
trackers.desc: A WORKED, DATED TEMPLATE. At Vila Maumeta on Ataúro Island, the community with the NGO Roman Luan and the government demarcated a Marine Protected Area by applying tara bandu rules for closures; the MPA was launched in September 2017. Communities set temporary closures of a marine or terrestrial area through a tara bandu ceremony — a periodic instrument renewed by ceremony, which is a different and often easier proposition than permanent designation. The same Ataúro communities went on to water conservation and permaculture. THE STATUTE THAT BACKS IT: Decree-Law No. 5/2016 establishing the National System of Protected Areas provides that classification of a protected area should take into account the uses and customs of Timor-Leste which do not contravene the Constitution — naming lisuk, ofatin lulik, lisane and tarabandu — with community leaders, traditional leaders and local communities in the involved and adjacent area engaged. Named customs, named participants. It also provides for communities participating actively in environmental impact evaluation carried out in or near the area and for programmes offering alternative income. Decree-Law No. 6/2020 adds the biodiversity framework, covering protection, rehabilitation and ex situ restoration and requiring active participation of all sectors of society. Regulation 2000/19 focuses on forests, coral reefs and mangroves.

trackers.name: GEF Small Grants Programme — up to US$50,000 direct to communities
trackers.desc: THE COMMUNITY-SCALE ROUTE. The GEF Small Grants Programme, running since 1992 and implemented by UNDP, reached 135 countries of 144 eligible in GEF-8, which secured US$135 million for the core programme with nearly US$1 million allocated to each participating country — a per-country floor, so the money is not competed for across borders. Grants of up to US$50,000 go directly to local communities, community-based organisations and other non-governmental groups. Focal areas: biodiversity, climate change, land degradation and sustainable forest management, international waters and chemicals. READ THE COUNTRY PROGRAMME STRATEGY FIRST — each country writes its own, emphasising particular themes and geographies, so global eligibility does not mean your region or theme is in scope. Under SGP 2.0 the implementing agency may be FAO or Conservation International rather than UNDP, and the host may be a national host institution rather than the UNDP country office — confirm which applies before addressing an application.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Rede ba Rai — the national land network, and the legal-aid members inside it
trackers.desc: This is the body that already knows your land problem, because monitoring and advocacy on land and housing is the whole of what it does. Rede ba Rai is a long-standing national civil society network on land rights, and its members, working with community representatives, contributed to the development of Timor-Leste's 2017 Land Law. The reason to approach the network rather than any single organisation is who is inside it. Its partners include women's rights organisations and — as Oxfam records of the joint land programme — Juristas Advocasia, a legal aid and paralegal organisation that trains communities on legal issues, so the network is the route to a paralegal or a lawyer as well as to a campaign. The specific risk it has documented is the cadastre. Its own research, including a 2013 study with the Haburas Foundation on land registration and land justice and later work on the National Cadastre System, recorded poor and inaccurate public information given to participants and illegal requisites imposed on them. That matters because registration is where a household loses a claim it believed was safe, and it happens quietly at a desk rather than at a public hearing — so the moment to make contact is when the cadastre team arrives, not after a title issues. Expect Tetun. The site publishes press releases and research launches in Tetun with little English, so anyone without the language should ask for a named contact rather than trying to read it. The office is in Vera Cruz, Díli.

trackers.name: La'o Hamutuk — hundreds of submissions, and it files into the other country's regulator too
trackers.desc: Its own count is the reason to start here: a dozen submissions to government agencies in Australia, and hundreds to Timor-Leste's government and its international development partners. Independent, non-partisan and Timorese, founded in 2000 and publishing in Tetum and English, it monitors the country's large development projects and keeps the primary documents somewhere a person can actually reach them — the strategic environmental impact assessment for the Tasi Mane refinery and LNG complex sits on its own site. Before commissioning or writing anything, check whether the assessment you need is already there. The move worth copying is the cross-border submission. In June 2023 it filed with the Northern Territory Environment Protection Authority on the Darwin Pipeline Duplication Project, arguing from a Timor-Leste perspective into an Australian assessment process. Where a proponent is domiciled elsewhere, or connected infrastructure sits in another jurisdiction, that jurisdiction's regulator may accept a submission from people it will affect abroad — and almost nobody tries. Its licensing investigation is the model for finding out what a regulator has actually done. Joining a technical assistance process in 2014 it asked how many environmental licences had been issued; the list that came back showed eleven granted and five in process, of which only two were large projects in the highest impact category, and the regulator's own list recorded one of those as issued with political interference. Its conclusion, in its own bulletin, was that the licensing law was violated more often than obeyed and that the official gazette had never published an environmental licence at all. Ask for the register, not the file. That is the transferable step: asking how many permissions have been granted, and in what categories, produces a picture no single file can, and it is a question a regulator finds harder to refuse than one about a particular project. Based in Dili.

trackers.name: Lei das Terras first registration — free survey, informal rights recognised, and the litigation you must declare
trackers.desc: A household that never held papers is not outside this law; it is the reason for it. The special regime recognises rights acquired before independence, both the formal titles granted under the Portuguese and Indonesian administrations and informal customary rights and rights arising from long possession, and it creates an informal property right expressly to correct the injustice of never having been able to formalise. Someone who never obtained documents can invoke that right on the same terms as someone whose rights were formalised, and possession is treated as a basis both for attributing ownership and for compensation where two rights overlap. The systematic survey costs nothing, and staying out is the risk. The law provides that systematic cadastral survey is free and that incentives are to be given for declaring ownership. Cost is therefore not a reason to remain outside the national first registration, and the earlier warning recorded here about the cadastre stands: the moment another party writes down a boundary is the moment a claim is lost, and the answer is to be inside the process rather than outside it. The trap is in the implementing decree, and it is severe. Parties to judicial proceedings in which the ownership of an immovable is in issue are obliged to inform the Ministry of Justice that the litigation exists, before the deadline for submitting ownership declarations — failing which the registration is made in favour of the party that declared. A family already in court over its land can therefore lose the registration by winning nothing and saying nothing. Corruption, falsification of documents and false declarations under the decree are punishable under the penal code. Two further provisions worth knowing. The regime provides for community protection zones and communal immovable property, and requires special attention to vulnerable groups with notifications in both official languages. Ownership of immovable property is confined to Timorese citizens, and to legal persons of Timorese law whose capital is wholly and exclusively held by nationals — which matters when identifying who is actually behind an acquisition.

trackers.name: Defensoria Pública — free representation in any court, and it is a breach if you are charged
trackers.desc: Representation in any court, whatever the nature of the case and whichever side you are on. The public defender service is a public body responsible for providing comprehensive and free legal assistance, judicial and extrajudicial, to those with insufficient economic resources, and its statutory competence is to represent people who come to it in any court of Timor-Leste, whatever the nature of the proceedings and whatever the procedural position of the parties, as well as in any mediation. Claimant or defendant, civil or criminal, and including work outside court — advice and drafting before proceedings exist is inside its remit, not a favour. The constitutional provision is the one to cite. The constitution guarantees access to the courts to defend rights and interests protected by law and provides that no one may be denied justice for lack of financial means; the service's first statute followed in 2008. An applicant turned away should quote that guarantee rather than argue about resources. If you are asked to pay, that is a breach — and there is somewhere to report it. Reporting in Timor-Leste records citizens alleging that public defenders charged for their services and neglected cases, and the ombudsman responding that their obligation is to provide free support because the State guarantees their salaries, that charging violates the service's statute and its code of ethics, and that he had asked the Ministry of Justice to attend to the irregularities. A community asked for money should record the date, the person and the amount, and take it to the ombudsman. Two structural facts worth knowing. The service has technical and functional independence but sits under the tutelage of the Ministry of Justice, and the ombudsman has argued publicly that this should change to avoid conflicts of interest — which is worth weighing when the opposing party is itself a state body. And its governing council may select, by curricular competition, non-Timorese judges, prosecutors, public defenders or lawyers with at least five years of experience from civil law systems to serve as public defenders, so foreign-qualified defenders may be available. Read this with the land law entry recorded here, where the deadline for declaring litigation is the trap.

trackers.name: PNDS — a grant the suku itself chooses, plans and spends, with a public accountability meeting
trackers.desc: The community holds the money and does the building. The national suku development programme, run by the state administration and finance ministries with others, provides a subsidy directly to the community so that it can choose, plan, design and implement small-scale infrastructure in its own suku. The governing decree draws the line by value and by builder: this programme covers infrastructure worth less than seventy thousand United States dollars, approved at suku level and implemented by the local community, as against the district programme covering works up to half a million dollars, approved at district level and built under contract by civil construction firms. Where a community wants the work done by its own people rather than by a contractor, that threshold is the dividing line. There are two budgets, and the operational one is the quietly important half. The grant is made up of an infrastructure budget covering construction, materials and workers, and an operational budget covering training, meetings, incentives and administration. The operational budget pays for the meetings — which is the cost that most often stops a community organising at all, and it is rare to find it funded openly rather than treated as overhead. The scale is small and concrete. Reported from one suku: an infrastructure subsidy of 44,250 dollars spread across three works — two multi-purpose community centres at roughly nineteen thousand dollars each and a public sanitation construction at 5,729 dollars — all completed and awaiting handover. Plan proposals at that order of magnitude rather than at project-finance scale. Accountability is a public meeting with itemised figures. At the final accountability meeting the suku management team presents each of its roles to the community, together with a description of how the infrastructure budget was spent and a report on the operational budget, with village chiefs attending. Ask when the next such meeting is and read the two reports. The honest limit is the national budget: in one year the technical secretariat could allocate to only 202 suku, so ask which phase and cycle your suku sits in and when it comes round.

trackers.name: Provedoria dos Direitos Humanos e Justiça — an ombudsman whose reach includes majority state-owned companies
trackers.desc: Its reach includes companies the State owns. The ombudsman is an independent constitutional authority acting as both a national human rights institution and a traditional ombudsman, and it works on human rights and good governance violations arising from acts or omissions by public authorities. Those authorities are defined broadly: public hospitals and schools, the police and military, central and local government, anybody employed by the State, private individuals serving in a public capacity, and companies which are majority government owned. Where a development is being driven by a state-owned company, that last category is the door, and it is not one most communities know is there. It can investigate and recommend, independently. Its statute gives it competence to consider complaints, carry out investigations, and direct to the competent bodies the recommendations it judges appropriate to prevent or repair an illegality or an injustice, with the stated purposes of combating corruption and influence peddling, preventing maladministration and protecting human rights throughout the territory. It exercises those functions independently of the government, the other organs of sovereignty, political parties and all other entities and powers, and may establish delegations anywhere in the country; reported offices include Dili, Baucau, Maliana, Same and Oé-Cusse. Know the limit before filing. The functional activities of the national parliament and of the courts fall outside its investigative powers, with the exception of their administrative activity and acts done in superintending the administration. A complaint about a judicial decision will go nowhere; a complaint about how an administration behaved will not be turned away on that ground. Its own reported figures tell you what to expect, and the instruction they give is to bring proof. In a recent half year the office reported registering 127 complaints, split between human rights and good governance, with a minority taken into investigation, a handful referred to the public prosecutor, some sent to mediation, and a majority of concluded inquiries archived for lack of evidence or because no violation was found. A published survey also found that most citizens do not know the institution exists — which is much of the reason for recording it here. Read this with the public defender and land registration entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Haburas Foundation — the oldest environmental group, the tactic that held up a dam, and how to approach it
trackers.desc: A domestic organisation with a network, not a single office. The foundation was formed by Timorese students in 1998, during the occupation, and describes itself as the oldest and most active national environmental group in the country. It works through a wide network of local community groups and draws on Timorese custom to promote environmental management that answers local development needs, and it is a core member of the country's land network coalition. A community approaching it is therefore reaching a coalition rather than one organisation. The recorded tactic is to demand the study before the decision. Where a culturally significant lake was threatened by a proposed hydropower station and by plans to pump it to irrigate sugarcane plantations, the foundation pushed for further environmental studies of the ecosystem and of the impact on local communities before any development moved forward. That is the move this research has recorded working in several countries: contest the evidence base rather than only the outcome, because a project that cannot show its studies cannot proceed cleanly. Tara bandu is the instrument they revive. The customary framework lets communities apply ancestral ecological knowledge to present-day stewardship, and is brought into force through a ceremony attended by local and traditional authorities; it has been used to establish marine protected and locally managed marine areas as well as inland rules on what may be harvested, with what methods and equipment. A community rule carrying customary force is a different object from a petition, and it is enforced by the people who made it. And they attach an income to keeping the place intact. Alongside community reforestation and watershed management work, the foundation specialises in community-run tourism and hosts study tours, which is an argument a community can put beside the one the developer is making. Read this with the public defender, ombudsman and land registration entries already recorded for this country. Approach it by naming the project and asking for advocacy. What the foundation's public pages foreground is environmental education, community-run tourism, international study tours and the cafe at its headquarters, with the advocacy work stated but not detailed. That does not mean the advocacy has stopped — it has published research with the land network on land registration and land justice, and has run donor-supported work on civil society approaches to resolving land title and tenure — but a first approach should name the project and ask for the advocacy side rather than sending a general enquiry through a tourism-facing contact form. Its strength is a combination nobody else in the country has: environmental standing built over twenty-five years, a customary practice frame, and a seat in the land network. Its weakness is speed and legal firepower, for which the network's legal aid members are the better door — go to both at once rather than in sequence.

trackers.name: AIFAESA and the national reference laboratory — who checks water from a spring, and who now runs the test
trackers.desc: Its remit covers springs and reservoirs that communities actually drink from. The inspection and enforcement authority created in 2016 has the mission of ensuring control of the quality of foodstuffs, their transport conditions, and the sanitary conditions of the places where they are produced and sold, together with establishments and places of public use. Its competences expressly include verifying the conformity of the quality of water for public consumption — bottled water, water from the public network, and water from reservoirs and springs used by the population. That last phrase is the one that matters here: the water a village actually drinks is inside the mandate, not outside it. It can open proceedings and impose fines. The authority was created to concentrate the inspection and enforcement of economic activity, sanitary conditions and food quality in one body with the powers to institute administrative offence proceedings and to apply fines and sanctions where the law provides for them. An inspection body that can fine is a different proposition from one that can only report, and the distinction decides how a complaint should be framed. Since 2024 the laboratory work sits with a different institute. Following the creation of the national public health institute as the country's national reference laboratory, a legislative amendment approved in April 2024 clarified that the collection of samples and the carrying out of laboratory tests relating to public and food health belong to that institute, while the authority retains the remaining inspection and enforcement competences. So the inspection request goes to the authority and the sample and the test go to the reference laboratory: an earlier round of this research failed to find a laboratory in this country precisely because it was looking at the wrong body. And there is a municipal tier that sees licensing. Municipal sanitary surveillance authorities collaborate in inspecting the production and circulation of food and the hygiene and salubrity of establishments and places of public use, and give opinions on licensing processes for activities, establishments or works which require the ministry's opinion. A licensing opinion is a document, and a community that knows it exists can ask for it. Read this with the ombudsman, public defender, environmental organisation and land registration entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Comissão Anti-Corrupção — anonymous complaints in the law, and powers to sample and to seal
trackers.desc: Anonymous complaints are provided for by the law itself. The 2020 law on measures for preventing and combating corruption, published in August 2020 and in force after a hundred-and-eighty day period, provides for the acceptance of anonymous complaints by the police and judicial authorities, for protection of the identity of those who report, and for protection against reprisals. Reporting without giving a name is therefore a statutory option here rather than a practice that depends on an official's discretion. Its investigative powers reach the site itself. Under the law creating it, the commission is a specialised and independent criminal police body, and in criminal investigation it may examine books, documents, records, archives and other relevant material held by the entities under investigation, conduct surveillance, intercept communications with judicial authorisation, carry out expert examinations, measurements and the collection of samples for laboratory testing, and seal premises; it may also propose to the public prosecutor precautionary measures including the freezing of assets. A body that can take samples, measure and seal is a different instrument from one that writes letters. It can be asked to advise a public body. Among its prevention competences are collecting and analysing information on the causes and prevention of corruption, running awareness work, and advising any public institution or entity on ways to prevent and combat corrupt conduct. Where a council or a department keeps producing approvals that look wrong, an advisory request about its procedures is available as an alternative to an accusation against a named person. The 2020 law also aims at procurement. It requires publicity and transparency in procurement and public contracting, that acquisitions of goods and services be made on economic criteria and on the principle of optimising the relationship between cost and benefit, and that administrative procedures be simplified so as to reduce the opportunities for corruption; it also sets the regime for declaring income, assets and interests, defines the corruption offences and provides special means of obtaining evidence. Read this with the business registration service, the inspection and enforcement authority, the ombudsman and the public defender entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Câmara de Contas — a large contract needs the court's visto before it can take effect
trackers.desc: A large contract must pass the accounts chamber before it takes effect. The law governing the chamber of accounts of the higher administrative, tax and audit court subjects to prior review the contracts of any nature entered into by the entities under its jurisdiction which exceed five million United States dollars, together with the final drafts of such contracts. For a community facing a large project, that means there is a stage after the award and before the contract can operate, and whether the visto has been granted is a precise question with a documentary answer rather than a matter of impression. The chamber publishes who it intends to audit. Its annual action plans, published on the courts' own site, record that preparatory analysis is carried out of all the acts and contracts submitted for prior review, and name the entities to be audited for a given financial year, among them public enterprises such as the national electricity utility and the national pharmaceuticals institute. A community can therefore see whether the body behind its project is on the list before the audit happens. Control continues during and after execution. The chamber's support service is organised into units covering the opinion on the general state account, prior and concomitant control, successive control, internal verification of accounts, and consultancy and planning. Concomitant control is the stage at which a project already under way can be examined, which matters because most objections arrive after the paperwork is finished. The threshold has moved before, and can move again. The law which set the five million figure records that, six months into the exercise of prior review, the public administration was not yet prepared to comply with all the procedures required for submitting acts and contracts for the visto, and that delays were occurring both in submitting files and in completing them at the chamber's direction. Check the current threshold before relying on it. Read this with the anti-corruption commission, the business registration service, the inspection and enforcement authority and the ombudsman entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Environmental licensing — a licence that lapses if unused, decisions that must be reasoned, and a second institution holding copies
trackers.desc: A licence lapses if the work does not start. The environmental licensing decree provides that projects holding a licence must begin implementation within two years where the project is classified in the higher impact category, and within one year where it falls in the middle category, counted from the date of notification of approval. Where a licence was granted years ago and nothing has been built, the first question is therefore whether it is still alive at all, and that question has an answer based on two dates rather than on anybody's opinion. Every decision must be in writing and reasoned. The same decree states that all decisions provided for in it are taken in writing and duly substantiated. A decision communicated without reasons is not merely unhelpful; it fails a requirement of the instrument that authorises it, and a reasoned decision is the document an objector can actually attack, point by point. Time limits can be extended, but only so far. The superior environmental authority may, by reasoned dispatch, authorise the extension of any period laid down in the law, for a duration never greater than double the original period. An indefinite delay in a licensing procedure is therefore not lawful, and the cap is the sentence to quote when a file has been sitting for a year. The authority, its fees, and the second institution that holds copies. The licensing procedure was created by decree-law in 2011 and amended in 2022, and is administered by the national environmental licensing authority; a government decree of 2025 fixes the fees payable, which vary according to the category of the project — reflecting the potential scale of environmental impact — and according to the stage of the procedure, on a polluter-pays basis. The decree also requires the environmental authority to keep the regulator for the project's own sector informed, sending it copies of the notifications issued during the licensing procedure, and allows that sector regulator to request meetings about the timetable. A second institution therefore holds the same paperwork, which is sometimes the easier place to ask. Read this with the anti-corruption commission, the land registration entry, the ombudsman and the chamber of accounts entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Registration and discipline of private lawyers — the register that makes a lawyer a lawyer, and how few there are outside the capital
trackers.desc: The title is reserved to those on a register. The statute governing the exercise of private advocacy provides that practising as a lawyer and using the title are reserved to persons registered in that capacity at the legal training centre, pending the creation and entry into function of a bar order. The practical instruction that follows is simple and worth acting on before any money changes hands: ask for the registration, and check it. Paying someone who is not on that register is one of the commonest ways a community's money disappears without a case ever being filed. A council manages and disciplines the profession. The same law records that although it was considered premature to create a full bar order, a management and discipline council for advocacy was established to carry out those functions for the profession, and the statute also governs the status and the professional training of lawyers, with a provision requiring the government to promote periodic studies toward eventually creating the order. Complaints about a lawyer's conduct therefore have a named destination. The scarcity is documented, and it should shape strategy. A government-published review records two hundred and ninety-three lawyers registered with that council as at July 2022, of whom forty-three per cent were foreign and overwhelmingly Portuguese, with the great majority based in the capital and one enclave district reported to have only three private lawyers; the same review notes that the register also counts lawyers who have appeared in the country only occasionally, for a single case. Plan for travel, for delay, and for counsel who does not live anywhere near the land in dispute. Foreign counsel is permitted, and free representation is already recorded elsewhere in this file. Published accounts record that the 2008 law, as amended in 2013, allows foreign lawyers to practise in the country, with cooperation arrangements between the council and foreign bar bodies to supply information about lawyers wishing to do so. Read this with the public defender entry, which records free representation in any court, with the land network's legal aid members, and with the first registration and anti-corruption entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Tara bandu marine closures — the route a community uses to close its own waters, and the Timorese organisations that help
trackers.desc: A community can close its own waters, and on one island it has been done thirteen times. Published accounts record thirteen marine managed areas established across the island through tara bandu, the customary code, with the first declared at one village in 2016 as a no-take zone. The code is described as a communal agreement restricting or prohibiting practices harmful to natural resources, which in the marine context empowers communities to enforce locally agreed rules on fishing practices and zoning. This is the closest thing recorded anywhere in this file to a community protecting an area by its own decision rather than by petitioning for a designation. The declaration is a documented event, with instruments attached. The inauguration at one village in June 2025 involved the agriculture and fisheries ministry, the island's administrative authority, a local foundation and the marine protected area management unit, and included the signing of the tara bandu regulations, the symbolic handover of buoys and the provision of zone markers, alongside the customary ritual and the hanging of animal horns marking the community's commitment. Signed regulations, marked zones and physical buoys are what turn a declaration into something that can be pointed at and enforced. On the mainland the same route produced a five-year closure. Communities at one coastal area declared a tara bandu zone extending one kilometre from the coast, closed to all fisheries activity for five years and managed by three named communities, with published accounts citing the environmental basic law of 2012 as the supporting instrument. A closure with a distance, a duration and named managing villages is a far more defensible thing than a general commitment to conservation. The organisations are named, and they are Timorese. An island-based community organisation — independent, non-profit, non-political, non-denominational and registered with the country's NGO forum, formed in 2000 by island community leaders to secure community ownership and control of key community assets, and running a community eco-lodge from 2001 — assisted the government in establishing one of these marine areas and worked with community members to set its rules. A second Timorese conservation organisation provides technical expertise and organises community planting events including mangrove restoration. The useful request to either is for the text of the regulations from a village that has already completed the process. Read this with the national land network, the first registration route, the ombudsman and the environmental licensing entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Community radio — sixteen stations across all thirteen districts, and the near-only medium outside the capital
trackers.desc: Outside the capital, community radio is close to the only medium there is. Published research on the media sector records seventeen community radio stations of which all but two are based outside the capital, and states that in those places they remain the near-exclusive form of media specifically targeting the needs of local audiences; the remaining private stations are all based in and broadcast to the capital. For a village trying to reach the people in its own municipality — rather than an audience in the capital or abroad — that is the channel that exists. An association represents them, and it trains their journalists. The community radio association, established in 2001 as a grassroots membership body, describes itself as representing and supporting community radio stations with sixteen member stations covering all thirteen districts including the capital, and has been an active member of the world community radio body since 2004; published research puts fifteen of the seventeen stations in its membership, with two further stations established with government support in 2023 on an island and in an inland post. Its own news pages record it running journalism training for community radio journalists drawn from several municipalities, including training in online media, and workshops with humanitarian agencies on radio programming to reduce disaster risk. Language is the reason it matters. The association's own account notes that alongside the two official languages there are dozens of dialects spoken across the districts, that the spoken word is how most people get their information, and that the oral tradition goes back centuries — which makes radio the practical instrument for knowledge sharing. A notice in a national newspaper does not reach a hamlet that discusses things in a language the newspaper is not printed in. What the stations are, and their weakness. Under the association's constitution ordinary members are community radio stations operating on a not-for-profit basis, subscribing to its objectives and code of practice and holding a broadcasting licence, and members cannot be political parties, religious groups or entities seeking profit from broadcasting. The published research identifies economic sustainability as the sector's biggest challenge, with many smaller operations dependent on volunteer labour — so approach with material ready to broadcast rather than with a request for investigation. Read this with the national land network, the public defender, the community marine closures and the environmental licensing entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Expropriation law in Tetum and Portuguese — arbitration for the money, court for the public purpose, and land before cash
trackers.desc: The statute is published in Tetum alongside Portuguese. The expropriation law of April 2017 was published in the official gazette, and the ministry of justice publishes a bilingual translation of it on the gazette's own site. A community can therefore read the law in the language it actually argues in, rather than working from a lawyer's paraphrase of a Portuguese text — which is rare enough across the countries in this file to be worth naming as the first fact about this entry. Two different objections go to two different places. The law gives affected parties the possibility of resorting to arbitration, with appeal to the court, where there is disagreement about the amount of compensation; and direct recourse to the court where they consider that the concept of public utility has not been made out. Deciding which objection is being made therefore decides where it is filed: a dispute about the figure and a dispute about whether the taking is lawful at all are not the same case, and running them together is how both get weakened. Replacement property comes before cash. While the law establishes criteria and principles for the valuation, primacy was given to compensation through the handing over of alternative immovable property, expressly as a way of avoiding the loss of the means of subsistence of the affected populations. Asking for land rather than only for money is therefore asking for what the statute itself prefers, which is a stronger position than asking for a favour. Who declares it, and the threshold to test. The declaration of public utility is a matter for the Council of Ministers, and the regime applies where the State, pursuing an end of public utility and faced with the absence of other viable alternative solutions, takes to itself immovable property held in private ownership. The phrase about the absence of other viable alternatives is the one to test first: if an alternative alignment, site or design exists and was not properly considered, that goes to the declaration itself rather than to the size of the cheque. Read this with the first registration route under the land law, the public defender, the national land network and the environmental licensing entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: National system of protected areas — community-status protected areas exist in law, and forty-six areas were classified automatically
trackers.desc: Community-status protected areas exist in the statute. The decree-law on the national system of protected areas, approved in Council of Ministers in February 2016 and revoking the transitional regulation of 2000, provides for a national nature protection system made up of terrestrial and marine protected areas of public, private and community status. That third category is the one a suku can aim at: it means a community-held area can be inside the national system rather than outside it, and it sits directly alongside the customary marine closures already recorded for this country. The decree also allows transboundary protected areas to be established under international law. Forty-six areas were classified automatically. The same decree recognises the existence of forty-six protected areas at the time it was made and classifies them automatically as protected areas. The first question for any project, therefore, is not whether the ground could be protected but whether it already sits inside one of those forty-six — a question with a documentary answer that predates any current dispute. Five years to finalise the plan, which is an opening rather than a delay. The executive was given a period of five years to finalise the national plan for the creation and management of the system. A plan still being written is a plan that can still be written into, and a community with a boundary it wants recognised is better placed while the plan is open than after it closes. The framework duties behind it, and the collaborative management requirement. The environmental framework law obliges the State to define and implement a biodiversity conservation strategy securing in situ and ex situ protection of populations, species, habitats and ecosystems, the reproduction of threatened species, the rehabilitation and restoration of degraded habitats and ecosystems, and the creation and maintenance of a national system of protected areas that guarantees the ecological coherence of the territory and the continuity of species and ecosystems. Donor documentation for a national protected area network project records that it aimed to build the understanding and capacity of local communities to manage their own resources in accordance with the country's collaborative management requirement, and to manage corridors outside protected areas as well as inside them. Read this with the customary marine closures, the environmental licensing decisions, the national land network and the human rights and justice ombudsman entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Laboratório Nacional da Saúde and the public health institute — the country's own laboratory capacity, and what it says about its own limits
trackers.desc: The country's public laboratory capacity sits in the health ministry. The national health laboratory states that the ministry of health, through it, is responsible for ensuring the provision of efficient and reliable quality health laboratory services to all citizens. It is the national reference point for laboratory analysis, and it is the first place to ask when samples need to be analysed by an institution rather than by a project's own consultants. Separately, the national public health institute carries the research and training side, including field epidemiology training run with international partners — relevant where a community's concern is a pattern of illness rather than a single sample. It is candid about its own constraints, and that candour is useful. The laboratory's own account records that, like most developing countries, the country faces difficulties in meeting expected standards because of challenges in human resources, infrastructure and financial resources. Read that as practical guidance rather than discouragement: ask at the outset which specific analyses can be run in country, on what equipment, and within what turnaround, before designing a sampling programme around results the laboratory may not be resourced to produce. Where an analysis cannot be run locally, the accredited laboratories recorded for neighbouring countries in this file are the fallback, and the question then becomes sample preservation and transport. What this does and does not give a community. It gives an institutional analysis, produced by a national body rather than commissioned by the developer, which is the distinction that matters when results are contested. It does not give an environmental laboratory in the sense used elsewhere in this file: air, noise, vibration and stack emissions are not health laboratory work, and nothing in this country's published material shows a body offering them. That gap is worth stating plainly rather than papering over. How to use it alongside the rest. Pair a laboratory result with the land law's first registration route, the community protection zones and the environmental licensing entries already recorded for this country: an analysis has more weight when it is filed into a procedure that must respond to it than when it is published on its own.

trackers.name: Buscar acórdãos and the jurisprudence portal — the courts' own search for decisions, and where constitutional rulings are published
trackers.desc: The courts run their own site with a decisions search. The court of appeal's portal states that a visitor can find information about the appeal court and the district courts, search decisions, and read publications of the audit chamber, and its navigation carries a search decisions function alongside sections for the four first instance judicial courts, legislation in force and older legislation, court editions and other publications. A separate jurisprudence portal run under the same domain states that it will make the jurisprudence of the country's courts available, describing itself as an easily accessible, searchable and updated database. Check both, because the newer portal is where the searchable collection is being built. The audit chamber's work is on the same site, and it is the part most likely to bite on a project. The portal carries the audit chamber's legislation and rules, plans, opinions, prior review, reports and financial responsibility sections. Prior review is the mechanism by which public contracts are examined before taking effect; for a community facing a state-funded project, the chamber's opinions and prior review decisions are documents about the contract itself rather than about the environment, and they are published here. Constitutional rulings are published in the official gazette. Decisions of the appeal court on preventive and successive review of constitutionality are published in the official journal, and an annotated constitution published on the courts' own site lists the jurisprudence citing each provision with the place of publication of each decision — which is a ready-made index for anyone trying to find whether a constitutional point has already been decided. How to use it. Search the decisions function for the subject and the statute; check the annotated constitution's citation lists for constitutional questions; and read the audit chamber material where public money or a public contract is involved. Read this with the land law first registration entry, the public defender, the private lawyers' register and the national laboratory entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Tara bandu — the customary prohibition that has been used to create protected areas, and the ceremony that brings it into force
trackers.desc: The strongest instrument a community here holds over its own land is customary, not statutory. Published accounts record that tara bandu is the customary law governing relations between people and between people and natural resources in this country; that the words mean hanging and prohibition; and that the rules vary between ethnic groups and places. They are used by communities to manage extraction — fishing and hunting among them — and to carry conservation initiatives. For a community facing a project, this is an instrument it can invoke itself rather than apply for. It has been used to create protected areas, then extended onto land. The same account records that after marine protected areas and locally managed marine areas were successfully implemented through tara bandu rules on one island, community members, non-governmental organisations and the government went on to implement water conservation and permaculture projects to improve land conservation and food security. The sequence matters: the customary rule established the protected status, and the projects followed it. The ceremony is the operative act, and who attends it is the point. The rules are brought into force through an official ceremony attended by funders, police, policymakers, local authorities and the traditional authority. That attendance list is what converts a village decision into something the police and the administration have witnessed and can be held to — which is precisely what a community needs when a developer later disputes that any restriction exists. Record the ceremony, its date and its attendees. There is money for it. A small grants programme operating in this country since 2012 and launched formally in 2013, hosted by a development agency's country office and reaching ten municipalities including the enclave, states that it funds non-governmental and community-based organisations to assist community leaders and members to establish tara bandu ceremonies to protect natural resources and community property, alongside reforestation of critical community land, mangrove rehabilitation and agroforestry. Published calls record grants in the range of tens of thousands of dollars to groups registered in their suco, with an experience requirement that usually means a newly formed group applies through an established one. Read this with the community protected area status, the national land network, the public defender and the courts portal entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: ANM and ANP — who names the aldeia in a mining permit, the environmental licence category, and the consultation notices for drilling
trackers.desc: The minerals authority publishes permit awards down to the aldeia. Its own announcement of awards records four companies receiving mineral permits and three receiving environmental licences, and names each site by aldeia, suco, administrative post and municipality — for example three permits to one company across three municipalities, and single permits with environmental licences to others. It records that the companies complied with the mineral permit procedures set out under the mining code of 2021, and that they are expected to conduct activities in adherence to the approved mining plans. For a community, that means the existence of a permit over its own aldeia is publicly checkable by name, and the approved mining plan is a document to request. Environmental licences for mining come with a category, and the category is published. The petroleum and minerals authority's media releases record the issue of Category B environmental licences to local companies for sand and gravel quarry activity, following a decision of the higher environmental authority for the petroleum and mineral sector and publication of that decision in the official journal, citing named articles of the environmental licensing decree. Two facts follow: the category determines the procedure, and the decision appears in the gazette, so the date and reference are findable. Petroleum operations run consultations, and the notices are published. The petroleum authority's site carries public consultation notices on draft environmental impact statements and environmental management plans for specific wells under named production sharing contracts, alongside contract signings, licensing rounds with numbered blocks onshore and offshore, an interactive map, petroleum revenue pages and extractive industries transparency reporting. Watch that page for the consultation on a project near you, and note the contract identifier — it is how the documents are indexed. Know which authority you are dealing with. The authority was created under a 2016 decree-law amending the 2008 legislation, regulating petroleum and mining onshore and offshore; a 2023 decree-law made a further amendment, and a separate national minerals authority now handles minerals while the petroleum authority handles petroleum. Published practitioner material records a 2023 public tender over dozens of concession areas for metallic minerals, gemstones, industrial minerals, radioactive minerals, rare earths and coal, with prospecting licences awarded over thirteen mining areas to four companies that November. Read this with the environmental licensing entry, the land network, the protected areas and the audit court entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Direção Nacional do Património Cultural — the body that registers, inventories and classifies, and the uma lulik inventory run through the municipal secretariats
trackers.desc: One national directorate registers, inventories and classifies cultural property, and its competences are published. The ministry's pages record that the national cultural heritage directorate is the service responsible for carrying out measures for preservation of the country's cultural heritage, and that it is competent to manage, preserve and disseminate oral history and the architectural, archaeological and ethnographic heritage; to register and inventory the country's cultural heritage; to classify it; to manage the system of applications for authorisation for scientific research; and to carry out the inventory, study and classification of the movable and immovable property that makes up that heritage. Registration and classification are separate steps, and a community can ask for both by name for a site in its area. Sacred houses are inventoried, and communities can start the process themselves. Published ethnographic research on heritage policy records two parallel routes at the state culture body: one in which communities apply to it for financial support for their houses, and one in which government agents identify houses at risk. It records that municipal secretariats identify sacred houses considered representative from the point of view of local community history, or houses at risk of architectural destruction through weather damage or deterioration over time; that experts are then designated with specific forms to carry out the inventory; and that inventories are archived physically and entered into the body's database, of which there are two, one digital and one physical. The municipal secretariat is therefore the nearer door, and the inventory form is the document a community wants completed for its house. Know what is not yet in force. The same research records that the framework law on cultural heritage was still under discussion while a tourism policy framework had already been approved, and that responsibility for culture moved between ministries, with heritage reframed from an element of national unity towards a development and tourism discourse. It also records the critique that state and cooperation interest has concentrated on cultural practices that can be turned into aesthetic attractions, including the restoration and construction of sacred houses. A community should therefore expect an inventory and a classification process rather than a statutory protection regime of the kind recorded elsewhere in this file — and should read this alongside the customary prohibition entry, which is the instrument that actually restrains use on the ground here. Read this with the tara bandu entries, the protected areas system, the land network and the environmental licensing entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Planos de ordenamento do território — the national plan, the municipal plans, the consultative commissions and the public discussion moments the law requires
trackers.desc: There is now a national territorial plan, and it names what it protects.
