The national territorial planning plan, published in volumes by the planning directorate, records that its orientations are received by ordinary legislation, in particular the 2017 territorial planning law; that it addresses coastal areas, the margins of lagoons and rivers, agricultural areas, forest areas and specific ecosystems; that a municipal plan defines the strategic and programmatic framework for management and use of the municipality's territory based on the local development strategy, with a second, operational instrument; and that the framework sets the rules on who prepares and approves plans and on the forms of citizen participation, the moments of public discussion and the forms of publicity. Those three phrases are what to quote when asking when the discussion will be held. Municipal plans exist, and they were reviewed by consultative commissions. A council of ministers record states that municipal territorial planning plans for two named municipalities establish the territorial development strategy and the municipal policy for planning and urbanism, and define the rules for occupation, use and transformation of the soil and the criteria for executing the plans, ensuring programmed management of the municipal territory by the local administrative bodies, in respect of legislation in force and of local uses and customs; and records that those plans received a favourable opinion from the consultative commissions that accompanied their preparation, all formalities required by the 2021 decree-law approving the territorial planning instruments having been met. Local uses and customs are named in the plan's own purpose — read that alongside the customary prohibition entries already in this file. What the plan's soil classes actually decide. Ministry planning material records that the fundamental distinction is between classes of soil, and that the plan establishes concrete rules for occupation, use and transformation covering agricultural spaces, forest spaces, spaces for exploitation of natural resources and built spaces, distinguishing land already urbanised from land intended for future urbanisation, and requiring in particular the protection and enhancement of natural, cultural and landscape heritage. Ask which class your land is in, and what the plan says may be done there. The national plan's own principles are quotable. Reporting of its approval records that it applies to the whole national territory including the autonomous region and the named islands, an area of 14,919 square kilometres, and is governed by the principles of participation, subsidiarity, prevention, precaution, equity or social solidarity, and environmental and social efficiency. Read this with the environmental licensing entry, the protected areas system, the land network and the expropriation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Water abstraction and the regulator — every well needs a licence, water is state patrimony, and the sanctions regime is not yet in force
trackers.desc: All water is state patrimony, and every abstraction needs a licence. A published interview with the national water utility records that all natural resources, at the surface or below ground, including water resources, constitute patrimony of the State regulated by the government; that a directorate general under the utility acts as the water regulator responsible for managing and controlling the use of water resources; and that all abstraction activities, including drilling wells, must comply with the regulations and be authorised by official licence. A community losing its spring or watching a project sink boreholes can therefore ask a single question: what licence authorises this abstraction. The enforcement gap is stated by the regulator itself. The same interview records that unauthorised drilling continues in large numbers, by day and by night, making monitoring difficult; that the directorate general has made this its focus for the year, reinforcing application of the rules; and — candidly — that the utility can only apply sanctions once the corresponding legal instrument is approved and in force, with all sanctions applied according to law. It also records that the utility does not at present register citizens wishing to drill wells, with that responsibility to fall fully under the authority in future. Ask what is in force today rather than assuming a penalty exists. The water and sanitation directorate's stated duties are the ones to hold it to. The organic diploma published in the official journal records that the directorate general is charged with ensuring a universal public water supply service in conditions of safety and hygiene; planning and adopting strategies concerted with other public bodies to guarantee access to drinking water for all citizens; drafting laws and regulations including technical standards on water quality, sanitation and the treatment of waste and industrial water and solid waste for the protection of public health and the environment; and licensing and supervising activities in the water sector, including preventing illegal connections to public networks. The gaps are documented, and so is the pending law. Reporting records that a legal adviser for water and sanitation regulation submitted a decree-law on water resources management to the council of ministers twice without success, describing water as renewable but limited; and records national figures for the share of the population without adequate sanitation facilities and without drinking water. A minister has also urged attention to preserving water resources from the springs onwards. Read this with the environmental licensing entry, the national laboratory, the tara bandu entries and the territorial planning entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Fisheries law — the minister may declare protected zones in national waters, artisanal licences are decided nationally, and a vessel that kills marine life owes the State compensation
trackers.desc: Protected zones in national waters can be declared to let fish stocks recover. The 2004 decree-law on the general bases of fisheries and aquaculture management, published in the official journal, provides that the minister may by ministerial diploma declare certain zones of national waters to be protected zones, in order to preserve or favour the recovery of fishery resources, with the regime for managing and exploiting resources in those zones set by regulation; and that the minister determines by ministerial diploma the fishing zones where fishing is to be permitted. A coastal community whose fishery is collapsing has a named instrument to ask for, and it can be paired with the customary marine closure entry already recorded in this bucket. Artisanal and non-commercial licences are decided by a named official. The same decree-law provides that the grant, suspension or revocation of artisanal fishing licences, and non-commercial licences, fall to the National Director of Fisheries and Aquaculture; that any related fishing operation requires a licence and is subject to the same provisions with the necessary adaptations; and it sets additional requirements for national commercial vessels, including registration with the maritime authority and the fishing vessel register, an allocated catch quota for the fishery or area applied for, and being actually equipped for the operations the licence covers. Asking who holds which class of licence is therefore answerable from one office. Foreign vessels are framed by agreements, with a cooperation duty attached. The decree-law provides that licences to foreign vessels in national maritime waters must primarily be framed by international access agreements or contracts with foreign fishing associations, and that such agreements must include the contracting state's or organisation's obligation to cooperate with national authorities in planning and conducting marine scientific research, making available all statistics and scientific data collected. That data obligation is worth naming when a foreign fleet is working offshore. Damage to marine life carries compensation to the State. The same law provides that, without prejudice to fines and other penalties, a fishing vessel or any other vessel that causes damage to or the death of marine biological resources — by oil spill or otherwise — incurs an obligation to compensate the State. Related instruments include the 2004 general fisheries regulation and a 2005 decree-law amending the fee provisions. Read this with the tara bandu marine closures, the protected areas system, the environmental licensing and the water abstraction entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Environmental Basic Law — published quality standards for water, sea, air and soil, an order to cease and restore, and the light and visual pollution provisions
trackers.desc: The State must issue and publish environmental quality standards for four named components. The environmental basic law, published in the official journal, provides that the State shall issue and publish environmental quality standards for water, the sea, air, and soil and subsoil, and that the law defines the mechanisms for inspecting compliance with environmental quality and emission standards with a view to integrated pollution control. Where a project's discharges or dust are at issue, those published standards are what a measurement is compared against, and the inspection mechanism is named in the same law. Inspectors can order the harmful activity stopped and the site restored. The law provides that where a violation of environmental legislation is found, the authorities may issue general directions for compliance, order the offender to cease the harmful activity, to clean up or rehabilitate the site affected by environmental damage, or issue any other orders appropriate to restore the state existing before the act that caused the harm; and that any attempt to interfere with environmental inspection activities, the provision of false information, or failure to comply with those directions and orders is subject to administrative or criminal sanction. Restoration to the prior state is the remedy to ask for by name. Light and visual pollution are covered, which is unusual. The law provides that any fixed or intermittent light which by its size, characteristics or location may disturb or adversely affect public health, quiet, human wellbeing, or environmental components — above all threatened or endangered species — must be kept within the limits set by the environmental quality and emission standards; and that the State is responsible for creating and maintaining the means to control visual pollution resulting from economic activities, in particular advertising and other activities with harmful effects on the landscape. A floodlit site next to a nesting beach is therefore addressable. Waste, chemicals and strategic assessment sit in the same law. It provides that the import of dangerous chemicals is subject to the State's prior informed consent, contains a section on waste including solid waste management with a duty on each citizen as to deposit of solid waste, and requires assessment for the agriculture, forestry, fisheries, energy, industry, transport, waste and water management, telecommunications, tourism, spatial planning and land use sectors. Read this with the environmental licensing entry, the territorial planning entry, the water abstraction entry and the fisheries protected zones entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Forest law and the national forest policy — a general forest regime binding public and private alike, watershed conservation priority areas already identified, and community forest management instruments
trackers.desc: There is a general forest law, and it binds everyone in the national territory. A published summary records that the 2017 general forest regime defines the fundamental principles and rules on the management, protection, conservation and sustainable use of forest resources and river basins, within a rational and integrated administration, so as to meet the needs of the communities who use the forests for their livelihood and prosperity, and that it applies to all persons of public or private law, natural or legal, throughout the national territory. Where a project proposes clearing on land a community uses, that statement of purpose and scope is the starting text. Priority watershed conservation areas have already been identified. The national forest policy records that the priority areas for river basin conservation were identified in the national forest conservation plan of 2013, and sets out the policy instruments: instruments for management of forests and river basins for sustainable management by the communities; instruments for use of forest products to add value and improve their sustainability; and instruments of knowledge and information providing research and extension support to communities in forest management. Asking whether a catchment is inside that identified set is a question with a documented answer. The policy's own targets and measures name what communities are owed. The policy records strategies to promote ecologically realistic afforestation through new plantations, reforestation and recovery — including enrichment planting and restriction of access to mountainous zones — and natural regeneration, to optimise the productivity of natural forest in watersheds and the coastal fringe; and a target to meet half of national timber demand from local plantations by 2040 through technical, marketing and management advisory services to rural communities on nursery management, supply of seeds of different tree species and tools, clear identification of beneficiaries, and training of local authorities in forest and agroforestry methods. Those are commitments a community can ask to have delivered. The reasons given are the ones to quote back. The policy records that well-planned plantations contribute economically, socially and environmentally, conserving biological diversity, contributing to food security, maintaining the quality of water resources and producing low-cost renewable energy, and that the benefits of afforestation and reforestation are particularly high in watersheds. Read this with the protected areas system, the environmental licensing entry, the water abstraction licence and the tara bandu entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The national park and the marine protected area network — fifteen terrestrial areas already designated for protection under the transitional regulation, named marine sites, and the conservation body that helped communities build the first network
trackers.desc: Fifteen terrestrial areas are already designated for protection, and the list includes coastal swamps and beaches. Official tourism material records that beyond the national park the government has indicated interest in protecting further significant areas by implementing the transitional administration's regulation on protected areas, and that the fifteen terrestrial areas designated for protection include significant mountain peaks, forest remnants, coastal swamps, several beaches and a named island, treasured for historical, cultural and environmental reasons. Where a project touches a coastal swamp or a beach, whether it is inside that set is the first question. Marine protected areas are named site by site, with one still being finalised. The same material records that five marine protected areas have been identified, with four named sites already designated and a fifth being finalised; a regional atlas records seven marine protected area sites identified within the national park and names them, records the country reporting it will launch small marine protected areas in three major areas, and records the threats identified as including erosion and sedimentation, particularly affecting mangroves and riparian vegetation. That threat list is the language a downstream community can borrow. The park itself is one instrument covering land and sea. Published material records the national park declared in 2007, covering some 1,236 square kilometres from forested mountain ranges to a marine area, including a named lake, a named island and 556 square kilometres of the coral triangle; records it linking named important bird areas; and records over two hundred bird species and five species of sea turtle resident. Part of it had been a natural conservation reserve before independence. A conservation organisation works across every protected area, and helped build the first network. That organisation records that its first project site was the national park and that, at the government's invitation, it expanded to all of the country's protected areas, both nationally and community managed, marine and terrestrial; and that it worked with the communities of a named island to establish the nation's first marine protected area network. For a community wanting its own waters closed, that is a body with the relevant experience. Read this with the tara bandu marine closures, the protected areas system, the fisheries law and the environmental licensing entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: FONGTIL — the NGO umbrella with a published member register by municipality, fourteen thematic networks, and a directory platform that profiles each organisation
trackers.desc: The umbrella publishes its member list, split into local, national and international bodies. The forum's own site carries an NGO member page and a separate local and national NGO listing, alongside its press releases, its submission to an international human rights review, and a national extractive industries transparency report; its contact page gives a street address in the capital, two telephone numbers and an email address. Where a community needs an organisation that already works in its own municipality, the member list is the place to start rather than a search engine. The membership is large and organised into networks. Published material records the forum as founded in 1998 as a non-profit, non-sectarian and non-partisan body of member organisations across the municipalities — local, national and international — with one account recording 380 members across thirteen districts and twenty-four national networks, and another recording it as an umbrella for 270 organisations and fourteen networks. The thematic networks are the useful part: an organisation working on land, environment or extractives sits inside one, which is faster than approaching members one by one. Its stated mission is advocacy for people facing injustice, and monitoring government. Published material records the mission as working with member organisations to promote and advocate in all sectors for the wellbeing and interests of all citizens; work towards ensuring people are free from all forms of injustice, including poverty, exploitation and discrimination, and have the opportunity to participate openly and freely in political and democratic decision-making; and support and strengthen the sector to be an effective voice, especially for the most vulnerable; and records it as an independent organisation that monitors government while partnering state institutions. A directory platform profiles the organisations themselves. Published material records a platform managed by the forum, with external technical support and donor funding, carrying organisation profiles; and records the forum launching an online learning platform to strengthen information exchange, coordination, capacity building and advocacy among local organisations, covering financial management, crowdsourcing, outreach, research and advocacy tools. Read this with the land network, the environmental foundation, the community radio and the legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The census and the statistics institute — population down to suco and aldeia, the pre-census geocoding of every dwelling, and the surveys published alongside it
trackers.desc: The census reports down to the lowest administrative unit, and the geography is set out. The statistics institute records that the census delivers benchmark information at all administrative levels down to the lowest administrative unit, the suco. Its main report records the census geography as fourteen municipalities including the exclave and the island, sixty-seven administrative posts, four hundred and fifty-two sucos and two thousand two hundred and thirty-one aldeias, and records a table of population by municipality, administrative post, suco and urban or rural location. Where a project's affected population is disputed, that is the unit a community actually lives in and the table that carries it. Every dwelling was geocoded before enumeration. The report records pre-census mapping as including field data collection with tablets synchronised with a central server, aimed at identifying and geocoding dwellings; and records the questionnaire application as integrating a digital map that allowed field workers to navigate their assigned areas, strongly reducing omissions and double counts. It records aldeias used as enumeration areas when holding stated ranges of housing units, with larger ones split and smaller ones grouped. The 2022 count and the method behind it are stated. The institute records the usual resident population at the census moment, the midnight of 5 to 6 September 2022, as 1,341,737, with a stated share enumerated in private households; the report records the change to a de jure enumeration, counting people at their place of usual residence, as producing more relevant information for planning and better capturing family composition and migration, and records digital questionnaires as reducing process errors. Knowing the count is de jure matters when a project's figures rest on who was present rather than who lives there. The institute publishes a wider series, and its own legal basis. Its site lists national accounts, annual trade statistics, a business activity survey, crime statistics, a fish consumption survey, a demographic and health survey and the monthly consumer price index; published description records the institute created in 2023 by a named decree-law as successor to the former statistics directorate, responsible for compiling and disseminating data on the people, society, economy and environment and the national censuses. Read this with the land network, the suku development programme, the protected areas system and the forest policy entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The tara bandu policy brief and the organisation behind it — published guidance on running a customary agreement so it is genuinely community-owned, and what the ceremony can be made to cover
trackers.desc: There is published guidance on how these customary agreements should be run, from a domestic organisation and a foundation. The policy brief records tara bandu as a traditional custom that enforces peace and reconciliation through the power of public agreement to define social norms and practices acceptable to a given community; records its increasing prevalence as local and international organisations support it in communities as a means of strengthening natural resource management systems and addressing conflict; and considers the factors that influence how effectively the practice can be used. Its authors record themselves as ready to work with organisations supporting these processes to ensure they are both genuinely owned by communities and consistent with the relevant standards, and call for further research including by the justice ministry to review the various approaches to ceremonies that have taken place across the country. Community ownership is the test the brief itself sets. What the agreement can cover is documented, and it reaches land use. Published research records the ceremony as anchoring communities in defining participatory land use plans, including agreements on property boundaries, rules of engagement, and interdictions and sanctions, describing it as a customary right with state recognition, generally applied at the scale of the smallest administrative division and for several years at a time, aimed at management of natural resources with a focus on forests. Other material records rules restricting access to and use of natural resources and spaces, giving as an example a district where the ceremony prohibits the cutting down of trees to prevent flooding, and records that the justice ministry has sought to recognise the usage and enforcement of customary law. The ceremony's participants are named, which is what makes it enforceable locally. Published material records rules varying by ethnic group and location, with implementation through an official ceremony attended by funders, police, policymakers, local authorities and the traditional authority; and records a lake-area agreement established by consensus between three named village councils, with community members conducting visual observations to set the timing for opening harvesting, and village leaders informed to reconsider opening it where there is a significant decline in the lake's resources. Read this with the customary organisation entry, the community conservation account, the land network and the forest policy entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The land network and the legal aid organisations — a national network that helped write the land law, a paralegal body that trains communities and takes complex land cases, and a registered legal social enterprise
trackers.desc: A national land network exists, and its members helped write the current land law. Published description records the network as a long-standing national civil society network advocating for just and sustainable land rights for all Timorese people, and records its members, working together with community representatives, making a compelling contribution to the development of the 2017 land law. A community arguing about land is arguing under a statute that organisations it can join helped shape. One member is a paralegal organisation that takes complex land cases. The same description records a legal aid and paralegal organisation that provides training for communities on legal issues, provides legal aid for communities facing complex land issues, and undertakes analysis and advocacy relating to land laws and policies; and records it as closely involved in the network's research on land registration, which highlighted the negative impacts of the land registration process on women's rights. Training first, then representation, is the sequence a village usually needs. A registered legal social enterprise offers specialist work alongside them. A legal practice records itself as a partnership company in the form of a social venture, registered in the country as a limited company with its registration number published, offering legal consulting specialising in human rights, gender equality, children's rights, socio-economic rights, access to justice and rule of law, including enforcement and justiciability of socio-economic and cultural rights and services supporting those more vulnerable. Its stated vision is to empower individuals, groups and communities and give them instruments to demand accountability for human rights violations. Other bodies sit around them. Published description records a regional justice organisation working with local partners and providing technical assistance to the national victims' association and to state institutions including the human rights and justice ombudsman, and records it as a member of the network for land, to ensure rights are considered in the drafting of new laws and policies. Read this with the customary agreement guidance, the land network entry, the non-governmental forum and the census entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The shared organisation platform and the project monitors — a directory of more than a hundred organisations with profiles, and the monitoring body whose focal points check roads, clinics and schools
trackers.desc: There is a shared platform listing the organisations working here, with profiles you can open. The platform records itself as a multi-sector programme bringing more than 100 organisations together to enhance the collective impact of projects, using a collaborative information management system that allows organisations to better coordinate their efforts. It records itself as managed by the national non-governmental forum — the forum already recorded in this bucket — with technical support from a named firm and stated donor funding, and it publishes profile pages for organisations including government ministries. It records having started as a pilot in a named municipality in 2016 and later pivoting to strengthen the forum's multi-sector response, and records holding a resource library and a tool for spreading official messages among partners, while supporting the government's monitoring and evaluation efforts. For a community trying to find who is already working in its municipality, a platform of profiles beats asking around. Project monitoring by citizens has its own organisation. Published material records a monitoring body established on 20 June 2005 by activists committed to a participative and accountable development process, whose staff together with focal points conduct monitoring on projects such as roads, clinics, schools and veterans' houses, as well as on the preparation and expenditure of the general state budget and transparency in the oil and gas sector, describing this as its strategy toward economic justice. Focal points checking roads and clinics is exactly the model a community can copy for a project on its own land. The analytical institute beside them keeps its distance from funders. Published description records the development monitoring institute — already recorded here — as publishing in Tetum and English and as not accepting grants from donors who may have a significant interest in the country, naming the international financial institutions, major aid donors, the government, political parties and companies operating there among those it does not take money from. Read this with the non-governmental forum, the land network, the customary agreement guidance and the census entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Fundasaun Mahein — a civil society organisation doing advocacy, monitoring and research on security and defence, publishing in Tetum, and writing on land lost to a state megaproject
trackers.desc: A community in a dispute with security forces or a state project has a domestic watchdog that publishes in the language people read. The organisation records itself as a civil society organisation that carries out advocacy, monitoring and research on security and defence matters — policy, legislation and the budget of the security and defence institutions in the country. Its output is published in Tetum, which matters where legal texts are usually Portuguese. It has written directly about a megaproject's cost to the coast. Its published commentary records that although the national strategic development plan discusses agriculture, small industry and tourism, its foundation is a named coastal petroleum project and the onshore petroleum industry; records the argument that petroleum activity on that coast could damage other sectors because it takes much agricultural land, damages the environment and diverts government resources; and records that the security and wellbeing of many people on the south coast have already been negatively affected through loss of land and daily economy, and through social conflict arising because people have had to move to new places with insufficient support for the community. It records the project as the government's largest and most ambitious plan while noting that many other state projects are not based on realistic plans, do not consider community needs, and do not analyse real conditions in the country. That is a domestic organisation putting displacement and inadequate resettlement support on the public record. Its research reaches how disputes are actually settled. A published report examines women's roles in community-level conflict resolution and peacebuilding, drawn from qualitative interviews with women actively involved in dispute management in two named municipalities, focusing on informal and often unrecognised practices; it records that women are repeatedly called on to mediate disputes, particularly within families, while also working to prevent conflict by resolving its underlying causes, and that formal authority concentrates among men while women's contribution sits inside family and community structures. Read this with the land network, the ombudsman, the anti-corruption commission and the community radio entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Permatil and Planting Water — spring restoration with swales, trenches and small dams, over 700 springs recorded flowing again, and youth trained to run projects in neighbouring communities
trackers.desc: Dry springs have been brought back, and the techniques are named. The organisation records that through its work over 700 water springs are flowing again, benefiting thousands of communities, with impacts running from mountainous inland regions through the river systems to coastal towns, estuaries and beyond to the reefs, including a reduction in flooding and landslides, the planting of tens of thousands of ecologically appropriate tree species, and natural ecosystem recovery after only one to two years. Published material records the method as catching, storing and filtering wet season rain into the ground using swales, trenches, small dams, reforestation, burn reduction and animal exclusion techniques, with 500-plus projects completed since 2016 — work done with government, non-governmental organisations and communities. For a community whose water failed after upstream clearance, this is a repair method with a count behind it. The training is designed to spread without the organisation. Published description records the organisation working with local government authorities, community leaders, women's groups and disability groups, targeting 50 or more communities per year, and records that youth are trained to lead their own initiatives and teach in neighbouring communities, with a youth movement now a national association, so that communities are capable of enlarging their catchment systems independently and sharing it with neighbouring communities. It records the organisation's other work as training future trainers — including non-governmental and government staff, community leaders and local farmers — in water and soil conservation, agro-ecology, agroforestry, aquaculture and organic farming, and establishing a national farmers' food sovereignty network. The manuals are published and cheap. It records producing illustrated readers, films, posters and a permaculture guidebook in 2008, and a tropical permaculture guidebook in 2018 accessible online on a pay-what-you-can basis; and records a schools programme with over 240 school gardens and more than 41,000 students. Published material records the water work tied to customary agreements in which community members commit to protecting their water sources and reducing water wastage. Read this with the customary agreement guidance, the land network, the community conservation account and the organisation platform entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Asosiasaun HAK — free legal services and community legal education, an assessment of 23 of 25 neighbourhoods before designing the training, and the women's organisation and monitoring programme beside it
trackers.desc: A legal organisation exists that was built to give free services to people harmed, and its training is designed from an assessment rather than assumed. Its own programme update records that one of its priorities was training community leaders in human rights, law and legal procedures, and that to develop a training programme that corresponds to the real problems of communities and the needs of the village chiefs and community leaders, it conducted an assessment of 23 of the 25 neighbourhoods in the capital over a stated week, looking into community knowledge. Assessing first, then designing the training, is the practice worth copying. Its founding purpose and its scale are on record. Published description records the founder establishing it in 1996 to provide free legal services to human rights victims, serving as director and, for a time, the group's only lawyer, defending prominent political prisoners and ordinary people alike; and records the organisation methodically documenting massacres, extrajudicial killings, tortures, rapes and arbitrary arrests — 339 cases in its first year alone — becoming the single authoritative source about such abuses. Published description records it as a non-governmental organisation based in the capital focusing on promoting and protecting human rights in civil society and state institutions, established in August 1996 by Timorese and Indonesian activists. The risk attached to this work is documented, and so is one refusal. A published appeal records the organisation's executive director reporting repeated police calls about the organisation's involvement in organising a peaceful demonstration, with his safety at risk; records that on the day, two members of the defence force visited the office and requested to use the space as a security base, and that he refused to allow them to use it; and records a soldier demanding a staff member remove a t-shirt carrying a political slogan. Two neighbouring organisations are named with what they run. Published description records a women's communication forum founded in 1997 by Timorese women activists, which supports survivors of gender-based violence, runs community education and has established two women's shelters and a transit house in named towns; and records a judicial system monitoring programme whose director began as a volunteer at the legal organisation. Read this with the ombudsman, the land network, the security watchdog and the organisation platform entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Suco councils and aldeia chiefs — an elected village council with women's, youth and elder seats, hamlet delegates chosen village by village, and the chain a land dispute actually travels
trackers.desc: Every village has an elected council, and its seats are allocated by category. A government release records local elections held across 442 villages and 2,225 hamlets, in which voters in each hamlet elected a female and a male delegate to represent their hamlet on the village council, their hamlet chief and the village chief; other published description records the council including one chief for each hamlet, two women's representatives, two youth representatives — one man and one woman — and one community elder, and records a council meeting to designate the traditional authorities, the word masters, and elect one male and one female youth representative. It records 728,363 voters registered and 2,071 candidates for village chief, with 319 female candidates standing across all 12 municipalities and the special zone, and terms of six and later seven years. For a community facing a project, the council is a body it elects and can be held to. The chain a dispute travels is documented, and it starts below the council. Published research records that in practice the institutional figures for resolving conflicts at community level are the head of family and their word master, the hamlet chief, the village chief, the elder and other members of the village council, the sub-district administrator and the police, with the church sometimes mediating; and records that use of land and other natural resources is a common source of conflict in development projects, with the village chief, hamlet chiefs and village word masters commonly mediating land disputes. It records the law giving the village leader responsibility for favouring the settlement of minor disputes involving two or more villages. The limits are recorded by the people inside it. Published research records that the 2009 reforms gave villagers the right to directly elect the chief and council, but had uneven effects: in some villages elections generated wider participation in decision-making; in others participation narrowed to the chief's family or electors. A council member is quoted that in our structure, the biggest power is with the village chief and then the word master. Read this with the customary agreement guidance, the land network, the free legal services organisation and the organisation platform entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The public defenders' office and its access-to-justice clinics — the only lawyers most municipalities have, a district defender's office with a published address, and the travel problem stated by the government itself
trackers.desc: Outside the capital, the public defender is often the only lawyer available. A published assessment records that, in a country like this with hardly any presence of private lawyers outside the capital, the role of the public defenders' office is central, while noting diverging views on the need for such an institution. It records the office as overburdened, and records the government's own statement that the four existing district courts are too far away from the country's diverse and widely dispersed population centres, that the road and transport network in these areas is very poor, that it is common for people to spend hours travelling just a few dozen kilometres, especially during the rainy season, and that these journeys entail excessive loss of working time and income, representing a very high cost for a large part of the population, with hearings repeatedly postponed due to the absence of the parties. For a rural community, the distance to a court is itself the barrier, and it is the state that says so. The office is old, and a district office has a published address. Published description records the public defenders' office as created by a numbered regulation of 5 September 2001, and records the building housing the district defender's office of the capital and the national public defenders' office at a named avenue and suburb. It records access to justice clinics created under a long-running technical cooperation project with another country's public defenders, intended to bring the office's work closer to people. The rights institution has regional offices too. Published description records the national human rights institution as established under a constitutional section in May 2002, opening in 2006, with a dual mandate covering human rights and good governance, activities including monitoring and conducting investigations in relation to human rights issues or abuses, and four regional offices in named towns besides the capital. Read this with the free legal services organisation, the suco councils, the ombudsman and the land network entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Municipal legal aid organisations — a national women's and children's service with offices in four municipalities, area-based legal aid bodies named one by one, and the count of private lawyers in the country
trackers.desc: The legal aid organisations working outside the capital are named one by one, with their geographic focus. A published research report records that legal aid outside the public defender's office is provided mostly by non-profit organisations, naming five bodies including a community education foundation, an enclave foundation and a justice and peace commission in a named eastern town, and records that most of these organisations carry out a broad range of legal work but focus on a specific geographical area or areas, the exception being the women and children's service, which works throughout the country in the specific area of assisting women and children, particularly victims of gender-based violence. It records these organisations as historically highly or completely dependent on donor funding, with such funding declining over time. For a community outside the capital, the practical question is which organisation covers its own municipality, and that report answers it. The scarcity of lawyers is quantified. The same report records around 180 private lawyers qualified to practise in the country, the majority of them foreign citizens, and records public defenders as based in the four municipal capitals that house district courts. Knowing there are fewer than two hundred lawyers in the country, most of them foreign, explains why the municipal offices of a handful of organisations matter so much. The women's and children's service has offices and a caseload. Published description records it as an independent and impartial not-for-profit legal aid organisation governed by the needs of women and children, which became independent in December 2012 after being a transitional unit of a monitoring programme, and which at one date had 27 staff and four offices in named municipalities, providing assistance across the country's 13 districts. Published reporting records it in one period assisting more than 260 new clients while continuing to support over 2,000 existing clients, and records a digital case system built with its teams so that legal teams in all municipalities can update and monitor cases in real time, bilingual and working on computers and smartphones. Read this with the public defenders and clinics, the free legal services organisation, the suco councils and the land network entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Municipal land and property directorates and the national cadastre — district teams collecting claims alongside community leaders, the civil society network watching the titling, and the four courts behind it all
trackers.desc: Land claims are collected under a published ministerial regulation, and the office that does it works at district level. Published description records the land, property and cadastral services office as the institution for dispute management and resolution, institutional support, consolidation of the land claims process including support to the determination of disputed claims to ownership, a system of communal land rights administration, and the establishment of a system of land use management; and records that the justice ministry rejected an omnibus land legislation approach and in 2008 issued a numbered ministerial regulation on cadastre, which outlines the systems and procedures for collecting land claims. A government release records certificates of land ownership being issued in a named district, with the district directorate collaborating with community leaders and the authorities to carry out the work, and the district administrator stating that the allocation of certificates does not end here and the process will continue until everyone gets their own. For a community, the claim is collected in its own district, with its own leaders present. A civil society land network watches the titling and says what it wants. Published description records that a national cadastre system was introduced in 2013 and a land legislation package in 2017 which legislated equal rights for women and men to own land, the recognition and protection of ancestral land rights, and the protection of communities from eviction; and records that a civil society land rights network convened a press conference calling for the cadastre process to be fully transparent, because a lack of transparency has raised genuine concerns about its legality and its effects on communities, with titles due to be awarded from a stated date. The formal system's size is the constraint to plan around. The same description records that the reach and influence of the formal justice system remains limited, with just four courts in the country, and records the primary reasons for land conflicts as family or inheritance disputes, expropriation of land by the government, and multiple claims on land parcels, with customary conflict resolution mechanisms having prevailed. Read this with the municipal legal aid organisations, the public defenders and clinics, the suco councils and the customary agreement guidance entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Municipal authorities and administrative post administrations — the tier between the village and the ministry, post administrators recruited on merit, a 30 per cent gender quota for leadership posts, and a candid published assessment
trackers.desc: The tier between the village and the ministry has a published statute and merit-recruited administrators. The decree-law establishing the statute of municipal administrations and municipal authorities records that administrations of administrative posts shall be headed by administrative post administrators, recruited through merit-based selection processes, as with the other holders of management and leadership positions in the municipal administrations and municipal authorities; and records that, to promote gender equality in filling management and leadership posts in local administration, a quota of at least 30 per cent is set for filling those positions. It records a consultative role of giving the municipal authority the advice that proves useful and timely for the progressive improvement of the provision of public goods and services at local level and for the promotion of development. For a community, that is the office between its suco and the capital, with a named head recruited on merit. The constitutional basis for a local tier is published. Published legal analysis records the constitution as establishing that local power is constituted by legal persons of territory endowed with representative bodies, with the objective of organising citizen participation in the solution of the problems of their own community, with the organisation, competence, functioning and composition of local power bodies defined by law; and records the constitutional requirement that public administration be structured so as to avoid bureaucratisation, bring services closer to the populations and ensure the participation of those concerned in its effective management. The candid assessment is published too. Published commentary records that central and municipal governments still do not share the same perception in describing their authority; that the space for participation that ought to be widely provided to the community has not been implemented consistently; and that in practice people remain concentrated on the central government for public services, treating it as the only alternative. Read this with the suco councils and hamlet chiefs, the village development programme, the municipal legal aid organisations and the land directorates entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Transparency International Zimbabwe (TI Z)
trackers.desc: Transparency International's Zimbabwe chapter (accredited since 1996). Knowledge-driven anti-corruption CSO — legal aid, community journalism and trial observation, and monitoring of policy and legislation, with focus areas including land and mining corruption.

trackers.name: Urgent Action Fund–Africa (rapid response grants)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a pan-African feminist rapid-response fund with reach across all 54 African countries — small grants released quickly for unanticipated, time-critical situations rather than planned programme work, covering safety and protection needs when defenders are threatened and short windows for advocacy after an unexpected event. WHO IT SUITS: women's rights organisations, feminist collectives and movements in which women or gender-diverse people are the primary decision-makers. It does NOT fund individuals, and the action must be strategic, genuinely unanticipated, and completable in under three months. HOW IT DIFFERS: this is emergency money for a moment, not a budget for a campaign — decisions are fast and grants are modest.

trackers.name: PRAZ
trackers.desc: National public-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Zimbabwe, and for how much.

trackers.name: Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC)
trackers.desc: Johannesburg-based regional NGO that advances human rights, the rule of law and access to justice in Zimbabwe through strategic litigation, criminal-justice reform and capacity-strengthening of local lawyers and courts. SALC RESOURCES A LAWYER — IT DOES NOT REPLACE ONE. It provides technical and monetary support to local and regional lawyers and organisations litigating human rights and rule of law cases, working primarily through strategic litigation and capacity-strengthening support to lawyers and grassroots organisations. So the ask is not ‘please take my case’ but ‘please back my lawyer’ — come with a local lawyer or local organisation. It also trains human rights lawyers and facilitates networks across the region, so it is a route to finding counsel too. THE SECOND FORUM MOST PEOPLE MISS: SALC supports litigation in South African courts that advances human rights in the southern African region — so where your own courts are slow, captured or hostile, there may be another venue, and SALC is the body that supports using it. NAME THE RIGHT CLUSTER WHEN YOU APPROACH: its themes are criminal justice, civil and political rights, socio-economic rights, international criminal justice, business and human rights and equality rights — ‘environment’ is not one of them, so frame a land-defence case as business and human rights or socio-economic rights. Established 2005 in Johannesburg out of the International Bar Association and OSISA. It has also run open calls for small organisational development grants to emerging CBOs in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe — periodic, so watch for them.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights (ZLHR)
trackers.desc: Harare-based membership organisation of lawyers upholding the rule of law, separation of powers and the unimpeded administration of justice in Zimbabwe through strategic and anti-impunity litigation, monitoring of judicial intimidation and public-interest advocacy.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe Anti-Corruption Commission (ZACC)
trackers.desc: National anti-corruption body of Zimbabwe — investigates graft, financial crime and abuse of public office.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe — Registrar of Companies (DCIP / ZimConnect e-Services)
trackers.desc: National corporate registry; the Registrar of Companies under the Deeds, Companies & Intellectual Property (DCIP) office registers PLCs, PBCs & other entities under the Companies and Other Business Entities Act [24:31], via the official ZimConnect government e-services portal, Zimbabwe. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: ZimLII
trackers.desc: Zimbabwe Legal Information Institute: free judgments and legislation. · Find here: free Zimbabwean judgments and legislation (ZimLII / Laws.Africa).

trackers.name: SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement
trackers.desc: A REGIONAL TREATY WHOSE DEFINITIONS DO REAL WORK. The SADC Protocol on Wildlife Conservation and Law Enforcement (1999, in force 2003) defines ‘taking’ as hunting, killing, injuring, capturing, harassing, collecting, picking, uprooting, digging up, cutting, destruction and removal of any wildlife species. So clearing vegetation for a development is ‘taking’ under this definition, not merely site preparation — that reframing is the most useful thing here. It defines community based wildlife management as management by a community which has the right to manage the wildlife AND to receive the benefits from that management, giving a benefit-sharing argument a treaty source; and ‘conservation’ to include rehabilitation and restoration, so restoration sits inside the defined term. THE CROSS-BORDER HOOK: States Parties must cooperate to manage shared wildlife resources as well as any transfrontier effects of activities within their jurisdiction or control — a mine, dam or plantation whose effects cross a border engages a treaty duty on the state that authorised it. Article 4 objectives include enforcing wildlife laws within, between and among States Parties and facilitating community-based natural resources management. CHECK YOUR STATE HAS RATIFIED — the Protocol is legally binding only for countries that have signed and ratified it, and this entry does not assert that your state has. ON TFCAs: they encompass protected areas as well as multiple resource use areas, so they are not exclusion zones; a TFCA practitioners network founded September 2013 has membership open to all stakeholder groups. And SADC's own 2023–2033 TFCA programme names the marginalisation of communities living in and around protected areas as a problem it exists to address — quotable against the body that wrote it.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association — public interest lawyers who litigate for communities against mining, with a rights-violation hotline
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: a public interest environmental law organisation that publishes a hotline for people whose environmental, economic, social or cultural rights have been violated or are about to be — +263 777 195 006 and +263 719 556 893. Formed in 2000 and constituted as a trust in 2001, it does impact litigation, not only advocacy — it puts its own lawyers on cases for communities rather than referring them elsewhere. Its programmes are organised around mining and extractives, land and natural resources, responsible investment and business, and local service delivery, which is the right shape for a community facing a concession rather than a factory. It also does conflict resolution and civic education, and it convenes and trains — so a community that is not yet in a dispute can get its people trained before one starts. WHO IT SUITS: its published strength is extractives — mining, lithium, minerals, and access to information about investment contracts, including Chinese investment contracts, and it has run work on community development agreements and on mediation mechanisms for the mining industry. If your fight is a mine, a quarry or a concession, this is the strongest single door in Zimbabwe. It is a smaller organisation than the national scale of the problem, so treat the hotline as a triage line rather than a guarantee of representation. Offices at 26B Seke Road, Hatfield, Harare; info@zela.org; +263 8677 010060. CAVEAT: no published intake criteria, means test or case-selection policy was found — unlike South Africa's law clinic, ZELA does not say in advance who qualifies, so make the first call short and factual: what is proposed, where, who is behind it, what stage it has reached. WHICH DESK TO ASK FOR: ZELA was formed in 2000 and legally constituted as a Trust in November 2001, and runs five programmes — Extractive Industries and Mining; Climate Change and Energy; Local Service Delivery; Land and Natural Resources; and Responsible Investments. Naming the programme when you approach an organisation this size gets you to a lawyer who already knows your sector. Its stated methods are public interest environmental litigation, investigative and evidence-based research, advocacy, legal education, COMMUNITY ORGANISING AND MOBILISING, institutional strengthening and CONFLICT RESOLUTION — so it will mediate as well as litigate, which matters where a case would take years. THE INSTRUMENT TO ASK ABOUT IF A MINE IS NEAR YOU: ZELA has analysed COMMUNITY SHARE OWNERSHIP TRUSTS (CSOTs) — the Zimbabwean vehicle through which a mining company is expected to place a shareholding or payment in trust for the host community — alongside the indigenisation legislation and the minerals revenue transparency initiative. Ask whether a CSOT exists for your district, who its trustees are, what the company actually paid in, and where that money went; a trust that exists on paper and pays nothing is a common outcome. ZELA holds observer status with the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, so a case that exhausts domestic remedies has a route onward, and it is based in Harare.

trackers.name: CAMPFIRE Association — the route by which a Zimbabwean district holds legal authority over its own wildlife, and the money that comes with it
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY, AND WHY IT IS ALSO A WAY OF HOLDING LAND: under the Communal Areas Management Programme for Indigenous Resources, rural district councils are granted Appropriate Authority — legal devolution of the rights to manage, use and benefit from wildlife — and, acting for the communities on communal land, sell safari operators access to that wildlife. Land that earns is land that is defended. The association reports the programme operating in 58 districts, with 23 rural district councils contributing to it, covering about 50,000 km² or roughly 12.7 per cent of the country, and touching 2.4 million people in an estimated 800,000 households; income comes principally from levies on 33 hunting safari operators and eight photographic operators. The first two councils received Appropriate Authority status in 1988. WHAT TO DO WITH THIS IF YOUR AREA IS UNDER PRESSURE: find out whether your district council holds Appropriate Authority, and if it does not, whether it has applied — a district with devolved authority over its wildlife has a revenue interest in refusing a land use that destroys habitat, and that converts a conservation argument into a council budget argument. The association works with the parks and wildlife authority and the local government ministry. THE ARGUMENT AGAINST IT, WHICH YOU SHOULD KNOW BEFORE RELYING ON IT: authority was devolved only to district councils, not to wards or villages, and independent studies of southern lowveld districts found the direct household benefits small — with councils criticised for excessive retention of the revenue generated — though households valued the infrastructure built with it. WHO IT SUITS: communal-area communities in wildlife districts, and ward councillors who want the district's own money argument on their side. CAVEATS: this is a national programme association working with government, not an advocacy or legal body — for litigation Zimbabwe's entry for the Zimbabwe Environmental Law Association is the one to use. Revenue depends on safari hunting, which is exposed to import bans and market shifts, and no intake route for a community approach was published.

trackers.name: Zimbabwe Homeless People's Federation and Dialogue on Shelter — savings collectives that turned into a fund, then into land and 5,000 built houses
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Zimbabwe Homeless People's Federation (ZHPF), constituted in December 1998 as a national network of women-based savings and credit collectives of the urban poor (men are not excluded), with Dialogue on Shelter for the Homeless in Zimbabwe Trust, registered April 1998, as its support NGO. It began among families in the holding camps people were dumped in after mass evictions from informal settlements. THE SEQUENCE IS WHAT MAKES THIS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER FEDERATION ENTRIES IN THIS FILE: savings first, then a collectively held Urban Poor Fund (Gungano), then negotiation with councils, then land allocated to the federation itself and houses built on it. Reported delivery is roughly 5,000 housing units — including 512 at Victoria Falls, 233 at Crowborough in Harare and 150 at Kariba — with reach reported at more than 12,000 families across 73 of Zimbabwe's 92 councils. The Harare Slum Upgrading Programme, 2010–2016, was co-led by the federation, Dialogue on Shelter and Harare City Council, piloted at Dzivarasekwa Extension, where the council contributed exemption of approval fees, equipment and technical supervision alongside community contributions. Enumerations and settlement profiles were produced by residents — Dzivarasekwa, Mbare, Chinotimba — and used to show how long people had actually lived where they lived. Money you saved collectively is the only money in this file that buys land on your own terms. WHO IT SUITS: Zimbabwean urban households facing eviction, living in holding camps or unserviced settlements, or wanting a route to serviced land and title through a savings collective. CAVEATS: this is a slow route — progress has been minimal against the scale of need, regularisation is politically sensitive, and settlements have been tolerated or evicted according to shifting political allegiances; large projects here depended on foreign foundation grants. It builds housing; it does not litigate — for that, Zimbabwe's ZELA entry.

trackers.name: Legal Resources Foundation — free lawyers and paralegals in 25 offices across 9 of Zimbabwe's 10 provinces, and legal pamphlets in Shona and Ndebele
trackers.desc: WHERE TO GET FREE LEGAL HELP: the Legal Resources Foundation (LRF), which provides legal education and legal services so that disadvantaged people, particularly women, can assert their rights. THE COVERAGE IS THE POINT, and it is the widest recorded anywhere in this file: underprivileged people get FREE ADVICE AND HELP FROM LAWYERS AND PARALEGALS IN 25 OFFICES ACROSS 9 OF ZIMBABWE'S 10 PROVINCES, organised as provincial centres with district offices under them — a provincial centre manager coordinating four district offices is the documented pattern. Its practitioners list COMMUNITY AND CUSTOMARY LAND RIGHTS and ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE among their working areas, alongside inheritance, marriage and gender-based violence. THE PUBLICATIONS UNIT IS THE SECOND REASON IT IS HERE: LRF produces practical information on around 28 legal topics — including wills, the Declaration of Rights and birth certificates — in ENGLISH, SHONA AND NDEBELE, distributed through workshops, offices, partner networks and places people already go, such as HOSPITALS AND POLICE STATIONS; it also publishes law reports and textbooks for the profession. Putting plain-language rights pamphlets in the hospital waiting room reaches people who will never enter a law office — the same logic as Malawi siting its legal aid desks inside the agriculture building. Offices in Harare at 5th Floor Blue Ridge, Eastgate, Sam Nujoma Street/Robert Mugabe Road, and 16 Oxford Road, Avondale. It also trains community leaders, teachers and prison officers as multipliers. Alongside it, Zimbabwe's justice ministry runs a Legal Aid Directorate providing advice and representation to indigents in civil and criminal litigation, and the Midlands State University Legal Aid Clinic offers free civil litigation and consultations subject to a means test. WHO IT SUITS: Zimbabweans anywhere outside the capital who need free legal advice, including on customary land and inheritance. CAVEATS: LRF'S OWN SITE DID NOT RESOLVE TO A VERIFIED PAGE — this entry points at a directory record documenting it; it is a generalist legal aid and education body, not an environmental litigator. For mining and environmental cases, Zimbabwe's ZELA entry; for wildlife devolution, CAMPFIRE.

trackers.name: AZTREC, Masvingo — a grassroots conservation body made up of chiefs, spirit mediums, war veterans and villagers, which elects ordinary members as chairperson, plus the Zimbabwe environmental NGO directory
trackers.desc: THE ORGANISATION MADE OF CHIEFS AND SPIRIT MEDIUMS — which matters because in Zimbabwe traditional authority holds real standing over land, and this file had no route through it: the ASSOCIATION OF ZIMBABWE TRADITIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL CONSERVATIONISTS (AZTREC), BASED IN MASVINGO PROVINCE in southern Zimbabwe, A POWERFUL GRASSROOTS ENVIRONMENTAL FORCE COMPOSED OF INDIGENOUS PEOPLE, TRIBAL CHIEFS, SPIRIT MEDIUMS AND CONSERVATIONISTS, whose founding came out of the liberation struggle and a second struggle described as THE LIBERATION OF CREATION. ITS PHILOSOPHY IS GROUNDED IN THE REVITALISATION OF INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE AND CULTURAL TRADITIONS, AND ITS ACTIVITIES RANGE FROM IMPROVING THE SITUATION OF WOMEN IN RURAL SOCIETY TO ADVOCATING SUSTAINABLE MANAGEMENT OF NATURAL RESOURCES; its main objective is recorded as REVIVING CULTURAL NORMS AND VALUES, PARTICULARLY TRADITIONAL FARMING PRACTICES, WHILE PROMOTING ENVIRONMENTAL CONSERVATION AND RESPECT FOR MOTHER EARTH. An organisation whose members include the chiefs and the spirit mediums is one that can convene the people whose word settles a land question in a Zimbabwean village. Bring your case to the traditional authority THROUGH a body they already belong to, rather than approaching them cold. AND ITS MEMBERSHIP IS OPEN IN A WAY THAT MATTERS: AZTREC INCLUDED SPIRIT MEDIUMS, CHIEFS, WAR VETERANS AND ORDINARY PEOPLE — one member records that she was approached at her WOMEN'S CLUB, chosen to represent it in the organisation, attended the meetings and workshops, AND WAS EVENTUALLY ELECTED AS CHAIRPERSON OF THE ORGANISATION. A rural women's club member became chairperson of the whole association. That is what an open membership structure actually produces — ask whether your women's club or village group can be represented, because representation is the route to the chair. WHERE TO FIND THE REST: A PUBLISHED DIRECTORY OF ENVIRONMENTAL NGOs OPERATING ACROSS ZIMBABWE (ecohubmap.com) lists organisations by country, naming among others AN ALL-FEMALE ANTI-POACHING UNIT working through community-based conservation strategies, and the GO GREEN ASSOCIATION OF ZIMBABWE, which empowers communities to engage in environmental stewardship. A country directory is the cheapest first step — search it for your province before writing to anyone in Harare. AND ON THE LEGAL SIDE, WORTH KNOWING WHAT IS COMING: ZELA'S EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR SAT ON A PANEL ON THE ESTABLISHMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL COURTS, at a regional dialogue attended by Zimbabwe, Kenya, South Africa and Senegal, on strengthening environmental law for thriving communities — with SPECIALISED ENVIRONMENTAL COURTS OR TRIBUNALS named as one of the ways of doing it. ZELA also COORDINATES THE PUBLISH WHAT YOU PAY COALITION and has chaired the ALTERNATIVE MINING INDABA and the KIMBERLEY PROCESS CIVIL SOCIETY COALITION, and trains media practitioners on profiling environmental human rights defenders. An organisation that chairs the Alternative Mining Indaba can put a community's case in front of the whole regional mining sector once a year. WHO IT SUITS: Zimbabwean rural communities, women's clubs, and anyone whose land question runs through a chief. CAVEATS: PARTS OF THIS RECORD ARE HISTORICAL — confirm AZTREC's current activity. For public interest environmental litigation, Zimbabwe's ZELA entry; for the CAMPFIRE route to a share of wildlife revenue, the CAMPFIRE Association entry; for land through savings schemes, the Homeless People's Federation entry; for free lawyers and paralegals, the Legal Resources Foundation entry.

trackers.name: ZERO Regional Environment Organisation, Harare — a 1987 land organisation naming the landless and resettled among its constituencies, plus ZELA's trust deed number, street address and research arm
trackers.desc: THE ORGANISATION FOR PEOPLE WHO WERE MOVED: ZERO REGIONAL ENVIRONMENT ORGANIZATION IS A NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANISATION ESTABLISHED IN 1987, AT 158 FIFE AVENUE, GREENWOOD PARK, PO BOX 5338, HARARE, aimed at MAKING STRATEGIC CONTRIBUTIONS TOWARDS EQUITABLE DISTRIBUTION AND EFFECTIVE MANAGEMENT OF LAND AND LAND-BASED RESOURCES WITHIN SOUTHERN AFRICA — with the more specific goal TO INFORM THE PROCESS OF FORMULATING AND IMPLEMENTING LAND POLICIES THAT ARE SENSITIVE TO THE NEEDS OF DISADVANTAGED RURAL COMMUNITIES, PAYING PARTICULAR ATTENTION TO WOMEN. ITS NAMED CONSTITUENCIES ARE THE POINT: RURAL COMMUNITIES, RURAL WOMEN, AGRICULTURE WORKERS, FARMERS, FISHERS, FOREST USERS AND DWELLERS, INDIGENOUS PEOPLES AND ETHNIC MINORITIES, THE LANDLESS, PEASANTS AND RESETTLED PEOPLE. The LANDLESS and the RESETTLED are named as constituencies in their own right. Almost nothing else in this file speaks to people who have ALREADY lost land rather than people trying to keep it — if your community was moved and is still without secure tenure where it was put, that is the organisation whose stated constituency you are. HOW IT WORKS, AND THE FIRST TWO ARE WHAT A COMMUNITY CAN USE: APPLIED RESEARCH; PARTICIPATORY POLICY ADVOCACY; CAPACITY BUILDING; INFORMATION SHARING AND NETWORKING; AND BUILDING COLLABORATION AND PARTNERSHIPS AMONG VARIOUS STAKEHOLDERS. Participatory policy advocacy means the community is in the advocacy, not represented by it. Ask ZERO what participation means in practice before you agree to be researched. THE STANDARD IT WORKS TO, WORTH QUOTING BACK AT ANY EVICTION: RESPECT, PROTECT AND STRENGTHEN THE LAND RIGHTS OF WOMEN AND MEN LIVING IN POVERTY, ENSURING THAT NO ONE IS DEPRIVED OF THE USE AND CONTROL OF THE LAND ON WHICH THEIR WELL-BEING AND HUMAN DIGNITY DEPEND, INCLUDING THROUGH EVICTION, EXPULSION OR EXCLUSION, AND WITH COMPULSORY CHANGES TO TENURE UNDERTAKEN ONLY IN LINE WITH INTERNATIONAL LAW AND STANDARDS ON HUMAN RIGHTS — AND ENABLE THE ROLE OF LOCAL LAND USERS IN TERRITORIAL AND ECOSYSTEM MANAGEMENT, RECOGNISING THAT STEWARDSHIP IS BEST ACHIEVED THROUGH PARTICIPATORY DECISION-MAKING AND MANAGEMENT AT THE TERRITORIAL LEVEL. Eviction, expulsion AND exclusion are named as three separate ways of being deprived. Exclusion is the quiet one — you keep the title and lose the access — and it is the form most projects in this file actually take. AND THE INCORPORATION DETAIL FOR THE COUNTRY'S ENVIRONMENTAL LAW GROUP, WHICH IS THE TEMPLATE FOR HOLDING ASSETS: ZELA WAS FORMED IN 2000 AND LEGALLY CONSTITUTED AS A TRUST IN NOVEMBER 2001 UNDER NOTARIAL DEED OF TRUST MA1669/2001, at 26B SEKE ROAD, HATFIELD, HARARE, telephone (+263) 08677010060, email published. A notarial deed of trust with its number printed is the Zimbabwean vehicle for an organisation that must outlive its founders and hold property. If your association needs to own anything, that is the form to ask a lawyer about — and ZELA's own deed number is the worked example. ZELA UNDERTAKES RESEARCH THROUGH ITS OWN ARM, THE AFRICA INSTITUTE OF ENVIRONMENTAL LAW, WHOSE MANDATE IS TO GENERATE CREDIBLE, ANALYTICAL AND EVIDENCE-BASED INFORMATION, and its methods include CONFLICT RESOLUTION alongside impact litigation and civic education; it has published guidance under a project on STRENGTHENING COMMUNITY LAND RIGHTS AND RESPONSES TO INVOLUNTARY DISPLACEMENTS CAUSED BY DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS IN ZIMBABWE, HIGHLIGHTING CRITICAL AREAS TO BE ACCOUNTED FOR BEFORE INTRODUCING LARGE SCALE DEVELOPMENTAL PROJECTS, and has analysed COMMUNITY SHARE OWNERSHIP SCHEMES. A published guide on what to account for BEFORE a large project arrives is the document to get hold of while you still have time. Ask ZELA for it by name, and ask the Institute what its research shows about the company approaching you. WHO IT SUITS: Zimbabwean resettled and landless communities, rural women, and any association that needs to hold property. CAVEATS: A RESEARCH AND ADVOCACY BODY AND A PUBLIC INTEREST LAW GROUP. For chiefs and spirit mediums in one association, Zimbabwe's AZTREC entry; for the CAMPFIRE route to wildlife revenue, the CAMPFIRE Association entry; for land through savings schemes, the Homeless People's Federation entry; for free lawyers and paralegals, the Legal Resources Foundation entry.

trackers.name: The Urban Poor Fund International — capital for national community funds in nine African countries, held so communities negotiate with government and banks from a position of liquidity — and the Gungano loan fund still running after two decades
trackers.desc: MONEY THE COMMUNITY CONTROLS BEFORE IT NEGOTIATES — and the fund states the reasoning itself: THE URBAN POOR FUND INTERNATIONAL IS THE FINANCE FACILITY OF THE SLUM DWELLERS NETWORK AND PROVIDES CAPITAL TO NATIONAL URBAN POOR FUNDS AFFILIATED TO IT — FOUNDED ON THE PROPOSITION THAT THE POOR ARE CENTRAL ACTORS IN URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND ARE BEST ABLE TO DECIDE AND CO-MANAGE THEIR OWN IMPROVEMENT PROGRAMMES, BECAUSE GIVING THE POOR DIRECT CONTROL OF CAPITAL ENABLES THEM TO NEGOTIATE WITH FORMAL BODIES SUCH AS GOVERNMENT AND BANKS. DIRECT CONTROL OF CAPITAL as the point of the fund, not the outcome of it. A community that already holds money is negotiating; a community waiting for money is petitioning. That is the whole argument, and this file has watched it play out from the other side in every entry where a project arrived with financing and a village arrived with none. THE BRIDGING FUNCTION, STATED PLAINLY AND WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU SIGN ANY GOVERNMENT DEAL: WHEN FEDERATIONS STRIKE DEALS AT THE NATIONAL LEVEL, IT CAN TAKE TIME TO RECEIVE FUNDS FROM GOVERNMENT, OR CERTAIN REGULATIONS MAY HOLD UP PROJECT IMPLEMENTATION — THE FUND CAN HELP BRIDGE THIS GAP, STRENGTHENING THE HAND OF THE FEDERATIONS IN THESE NEGOTIATIONS, AND THE AUTONOMY OF AFFILIATES IS ENHANCED BY ITS LIQUIDITY. The government agrees, and then the money takes a year. Every community that has won something in this file has met that delay, and it is where agreements quietly die. A bridging fund is the specific answer: it lets you start while the state catches up, which also means the state cannot use the delay against you. WHERE IT REACHES IN AFRICA: SINCE ITS INCEPTION IN 2007 IT HAS PROVIDED GRANTS AND LOANS TO NAMIBIA, SOUTH AFRICA, ZIMBABWE, MALAWI AND ZAMBIA IN SOUTHERN AFRICA; KENYA, UGANDA AND TANZANIA IN EAST AFRICA; AND GHANA IN WEST AFRICA. Nine African countries with a national community fund already capitalised. Before founding anything, ask whether your country has one — and if it does, ask what it lends for and at what rate. THE ZIMBABWEAN EXAMPLE, STILL RUNNING: A GUNGANO URBAN POOR LOAN FUND WAS CREATED IN 1999 BY THE NATIONAL HOMELESS PEOPLE'S FEDERATION AND IS STILL HELPING TO UPGRADE INFORMAL SETTLEMENTS OVER TWO DECADES ON — SUPPORTED BY A NAMED LOCAL SHELTER TRUST, BY HARARE CITY FUNDS, AND BY A LIST OF INTERNATIONAL FUNDERS. HARARE CITY FUNDS is the detail to notice: the municipality itself put money into a fund the residents run. That is a further step beyond an MOU — not the city building for you, the city lending to the fund you control. Twenty-five years and still lending is the durability test, and this one passed it. THE SOUTH AFRICAN FUND'S OWN DESCRIPTION IS THE MODEL TO COPY: IT IS NOT A HOUSING DELIVERY AGENCY — IT SUPPORTS SUSTAINABLE USES OF BROADER ASSET MOBILISATION, BLENDING LOANS, SAVINGS, AND SOCIAL CAPITAL, AND LINKING ALL THIS TO THE STATE HOUSING SUBSIDY SYSTEM — AND IT IS DESCRIBED AS A PIONEER IN TENURE SECURITY, INCREMENTAL HOUSING DEVELOPMENT, HOUSING FINANCE INNOVATION AND THE CREATIVE UTILISATION OF POLICY AND SUBSIDY INSTRUMENTS BY BUILDING PRAGMATIC PARTNERSHIPS WITH GOVERNMENT. Linking the community's own savings TO the state subsidy rather than replacing it. The subsidy already exists in most countries and most poor households cannot reach it; a community fund that knows the subsidy rules becomes the bridge. And its name means GRASS — roughly, the grassroots fund.
