trackers.name: Accountability Counsel - free support for communities complaining to the accountability offices of banks financing a harmful project, taking cases ONLY WHERE THE COMMUNITY ASKS, plus a searchable global complaints database and a resource guide
trackers.desc: IT ONLY TAKES CASES WHERE THE COMMUNITY ASKS FIRST, AND IT SAYS WHY. It states: TO ENSURE THAT WE DO NOT REPLICATE THE POWER DYNAMIC WE SEEK TO UPEND AND ARE A TRUSTED, WANTED PARTNER IN COMMUNITIES, WE ONLY TAKE CASES IN WHICH COMMUNITIES REQUEST OUR SUPPORT; assistance BEGINS WITH A REQUEST FOR SUPPORT FROM THE COMMUNITY ITSELF OR A LOCAL CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANIZATION, and NEARLY ALL CASES COME TO US THROUGH REFERRALS THROUGH CIVIL SOCIETY NETWORKS, OFTEN WITH ONLY ONE OR TWO DEGREES OF SEPARATION; it asks that a case INVOLVE A TRUSTWORTHY LOCAL PARTNER WITH WHOM WE CAN CLOSELY COLLABORATE, and weighs THE LIKELIHOOD OF A COMPLAINT LEADING TO A POSITIVE RESULT AT THE COMMUNITY LEVEL and of CREATING SYSTEMIC CHANGE AT THE INSTITUTIONAL LEVEL. Ask through an organisation that already knows you. One or two degrees of separation is the stated norm, so the introduction matters more than the application. WHAT IT DOES: it ASSIST[S] COMMUNITIES TO DEFEND THEIR RIGHTS THROUGH COMPLAINTS TO ACCOUNTABILITY OFFICES TIED TO PROJECTS THAT CAUSE HARM, specialising in NON-JUDICIAL COMPLAINT OFFICES ESTABLISHED TO RECEIVE COMMUNITY COMPLAINTS; its case work RANGES FROM INTENSIVE AND COMPREHENSIVE ASSISTANCE TO LOCAL COMMUNITIES AND THEIR PARTNERS THROUGHOUT A COMPLAINT PROCESS, TO PROVIDING MORE TARGETED SUPPORT WITH DAILY CASE WORK CONDUCTED PRIMARILY BY LOCAL PARTNERS, and it CONDUCT[S] TRAININGS IN LOCAL COMMUNITIES ABOUT ALL OPTIONS FOR ADDRESSING HUMAN RIGHTS AND ENVIRONMENTAL ABUSES ASSOCIATED WITH INTERNATIONALLY FINANCED PROJECTS. A complaint to a bank's own accountability office runs alongside any court case rather than replacing it. Ask for the training even if you never file: it maps every route available against a financed project. WHAT IT HAS ACHIEVED, INCLUDING IN THIS REGION: recorded results include supporting communities TO PREVENT ABUSES IN MEXICO and elsewhere, TO COMPEL REDESIGN OF A PROJECT in one country and TO REACH HISTORIC AGREEMENTS in others including one Caribbean state; its impact includes REDESIGNED PROJECTS THAT NOW REFLECT COMMUNITY NEEDS, HARM STOPPED AND PREVENTED TO DEFEND WATER RESOURCES, AND AGREEMENTS RESULTING IN COMPENSATION. Redesign, prevention and compensation are the realistic outcomes. A complaint of this kind rarely cancels a project outright, and knowing that before starting keeps a community's expectations intact. THE DATABASE AND GUIDE ANYONE CAN USE: it runs THE WORLD'S MOST COMPREHENSIVE COMMUNITY COMPLAINT DATABASE — SEARCH BY REGION, SECTOR, INSTITUTION, TYPE OF HARM, and a comparison of accountability policies ACROSS SIXTEEN INSTITUTIONS; its resource guide contains INFORMATION ABOUT TOOLS FOR REDRESSING HUMAN RIGHTS AND ENVIRONMENTAL VIOLATIONS BY INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS, EXPORT PROMOTION AGENCIES, AND PRIVATE CORPORATE ACTORS, intended TO ASSIST COMMUNITY LEADERS, LAWYERS, NGOs, AND INDIVIDUALS IN DETERMINING WHAT RIGHTS THEY HAVE AND HOW TO FILE A COMPLAINT, and it also covers INFORMATION DISCLOSURE RULES at those institutions. Search the database for your sector before writing anything. Someone has complained about a comparable project and the outcome tells you what to ask for. WHICH OFFICES EXIST, AND WHERE THE GAPS ARE: the offices it works with include those of the regional development bank for this continent, the world bank's public and private arms, a climate fund, a development programme's compliance unit and one national development bank's ombudsperson; it records that THERE ARE MANY COMMUNITIES THAT LACK AN AVAILABLE ACCOUNTABILITY OPTION BECAUSE NO SUCH ACCOUNTABILITY OFFICE EXISTS AT THE INSTITUTION(S) FINANCING A PROJECT, and works to open avenues where investment has none, INCLUDING IMPACT INVESTMENT, PRIVATE EQUITY, AND FINANCING FROM CHINESE INSTITUTIONS; its advocacy removed a requirement that complainants cite specific policy violations, since PREVIOUSLY A COMPLAINT COULD BE REJECTED IF IT DID NOT CONTAIN THIS TECHNICAL INFORMATION. Identify the financier before assuming there is a complaint office. Where the money is private equity or a Chinese lender there may be none, and that absence is itself worth publicising.

trackers.name: Caribbean Natural Resources Institute (CANARI) - a regional technical institute with staff in four countries that COACHES community organisations to write proposals and then manages the grants, and sells participatory forest, site planning and protected area management services
trackers.desc: IT COACHES COMMUNITY ORGANISATIONS TO WRITE THE PROPOSAL, THEN ADMINISTERS THE GRANT — 68 ORGANISATIONS AND 77 GRANTS IN EIGHT COUNTRIES IN ONE PROGRAMME. Its record states that it SUPPORTED 68 CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS TO IMPLEMENT 77 GRANTS IN EIGHT COUNTRIES, and that ONCE A PROJECT CONCEPT WAS APPROVED, it COACHED CSOs TO HELP THEM DEVELOP PROPOSALS THAT WERE WELL ALIGNED TO the funder's STRATEGY, MET LOCAL NEEDS AND HELPED FULFIL THE INDIVIDUAL CSO'S MANDATES; the same programme leveraged AT LEAST US$2 MILLION IN ADDITIONAL FUNDING. Among its listed services is MANAGEMENT OF GRANT PROGRAMMES. Coaching on the proposal, not just a form to fill in. For a small island organisation with no grant writer, that coaching is worth more than the grant. WHAT IT IS AND WHERE ITS PEOPLE ARE: it is A REGIONAL, NON-PROFIT TECHNICAL INSTITUTE WITH MORE THAN 30 YEARS OF DEDICATED EXPERIENCE ACROSS THE COUNTRIES AND TERRITORIES OF THE CARIBBEAN REGION, headquartered in one island capital with staff based in three further countries; it CHAMPION[S] LOCALLY LED APPROACHES TO USING AND MANAGING NATURAL RESOURCES THAT PUT THE NEEDS OF COMMUNITIES FIRST, ESPECIALLY THOSE WHICH ARE OFTEN OVERLOOKED, and promotes CARIBBEAN SOLUTIONS FOR CARIBBEAN CHALLENGES, RECOGNISING THAT THE REGION'S UNIQUE ISSUES REQUIRE HOMEGROWN RESPONSES. Staff living in four countries, not a distant headquarters. For the small islands, where most entries in this file point to bodies far away, this is the regional organisation that is actually present. THE TECHNICAL SERVICES IT SELLS OR PROVIDES: named areas include DEVELOPMENT OF TOOLKITS AND TRAINING IN FACILITATING PARTICIPATORY APPROACHES, PARTICIPATORY FOREST POLICY DEVELOPMENT, SITE PLANNING AND COMMUNITY FORESTRY, PARTICIPATORY PROTECTED AREA POLICY DEVELOPMENT, PLANNING AND MANAGEMENT, CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONAL CAPACITY BUILDING, SUPPORTING DEVELOPMENT OF SUSTAINABLE COMMUNITY SMALL AND MICRO-ENTERPRISES and DEVELOPMENT OF COMMUNICATION STRATEGIES AND PRODUCTS such as case studies and policy briefs. Site planning and protected area management planning are services you can commission. Where a community has been told to produce a management plan it cannot write, this is who writes it with them. WHAT THE MICRO-GRANTS LOOK LIKE: one programme assisted SIX CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS WITH TECHNICAL SUPPORT AND MICRO-GRANTS TO SCALE UP ECOSYSTEM-BASED SOLUTIONS... IN SIX HIGH-RISK COMMUNITIES across three island states, covering HILLSIDE, RIVERBANK, MANGROVE, AND COASTAL VEGETATION RESTORATION; a recent advocacy facility awarded grants RANGING FROM $1,500 TO $8,000 to six organisations for work from recognising women in agriculture and fisheries to DOCUMENTING THE IMPACTS OF HURRICANES and advocating equitable resilience. Fifteen hundred dollars is a real grant here. Hillside and riverbank restoration is exactly the work a community does after a development has destabilised a slope. WHAT IT HAS BUILT WITH OTHERS: it convenes a regional climate justice alliance, implements a forest sector project IN PARTNERSHIP WITH two named national organisations in one island, and has run a project to STRENGTHEN THE TECHNICAL AND FINANCIAL CAPACITY OF SELECTED CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS and to improve understanding of THE INSTITUTIONAL REQUIREMENTS FOR EFFECTIVE CIVIL SOCIETY PARTICIPATION IN NATURAL RESOURCE GOVERNANCE; earlier work included SAFEGUARD[ING] WATERSHEDS THROUGH TARGETED PAYMENTS and participatory forest management across seven islands. It works through national member organisations. Find which one in your island already partners with it, and approach through them.

trackers.name: Mongabay Latam and the regional environmental journalists' network - a newsroom of 90+ journalists across 14 countries with a published contact for story tips, satellite and data investigations that have INFORMED JUDICIAL AND POLICE ACTION, and an honest account of the risk to sources
trackers.desc: A REGIONAL NEWSROOM OF MORE THAN NINETY ENVIRONMENTAL JOURNALISTS, AND A PUBLISHED EMAIL FOR TAKING A STORY TO THEM. A network of environmental journalists across the region records MORE THAN 120 SERIES AND INVESTIGATIONS IN THE LAST EIGHT YEARS THAT HAVE INCLUDED JOURNALISTS AND MEDIA OF 14 COUNTRIES OF THE REGION; the regional newsroom behind it publishes a contact address for anyone who NEEDS HELP WITH A STORY and asks writers to CONSULT THE PAGE THAT EXPLAINS THE CONDITIONS FOR COLLABORATIONS first. Its reporting draws on INDIGENOUS LEADERS, LOCAL SCIENTISTS, PARK RANGERS, FISHERS, FARMERS AND ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENDERS as SOURCES AND PRINCIPAL ACTORS. An editor's email address, and community sources treated as principal actors rather than colour. Read the collaboration conditions before writing, then send the documents, not the outrage. WHY COVERAGE CHANGES A LAND FIGHT: the newsroom has built 20-PLUS DATABASES CONTAINING CRITICAL INFORMATION ON MINING, DRUG TRAFFICKING, FINES IMPOSED ON FOSSIL FUEL AND PALM OIL COMPANIES, CASES OF ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENDER KILLINGS THAT HAVE GONE UNPUNISHED OR THAT HAVE BEEN PROSECUTED, GEOLOCATED ENVIRONMENTAL LIABILITIES LIKE CONTAMINATED SITES LEFT BEHIND BY THE OIL INDUSTRY, and records that THE FINDINGS HAVE BEEN USED TO INFORM JUDICIAL AND POLICE ACTION; one series analysed MORE THAN 724,000 satellite DEFORESTATION ALERTS... TO DOCUMENT ILLEGAL DEFORESTATION OF INDIGENOUS LANDS in four countries, and a satellite analysis of two protected areas in one country counted alerts inside each before A TEAM OF JOURNALISTS TRAVELLED TO THESE AREAS. Their analysis has fed judicial and police action. A published investigation is not only pressure — it can be the document a prosecutor opens a file on. WHAT THE JOURNALISTS BRING THAT A COMMUNITY USUALLY CANNOT BUY: collaborators have acquired experience in INVESTIGATION, SATELLITE ANALYSIS, DATA JOURNALISM, MULTIMEDIA PRODUCTION AND CROSS-BORDER WORK, and for allied outlets these collaborations HAVE OPENED ACCESS TO SPECIALISED COVERAGE THAT, IN MANY CASES, WOULD BE COSTLY TO PRODUCE ON THEIR OWN; the strongest reporting came from JOURNALISTS WHO KNEW THE LOCAL STORY AND COULD RECOGNISE WHEN A SPECIFIC CONFLICT FORMED PART OF A BROADER PATTERN. Show the editor how your case fits a pattern across several places. A single village dispute is a local story; the same company or the same permit failing in five places is a regional investigation. THE HONEST RISK, IN THEIR OWN WORDS: the network records AN ESCALATION OF VIOLENCE THAT GROWS AT GREAT SPEED AND THAT INCREASINGLY PUTS AT RISK OUR SECURITY AND THAT OF OUR SOURCES, ESPECIALLY THOSE OF INDIGENOUS AND COMMUNITY LEADERS, alongside THE LEGAL ONSLAUGHT FROM POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC POWER TO THREATEN JOURNALISTS WHO REVEAL UNCOMFORTABLE TRUTHS. Sources are named in print unless you agree otherwise in advance. Decide who speaks and under what protection before the first interview, and read this alongside the protection funds filed for defenders. THE WIDER STRUCTURE BEHIND IT: the regional newsroom operates as part of a global environmental news organisation producing content IN FOUR LANGUAGES WITH 500 CORRESPONDENTS IN 50 COUNTRIES, largely as a non-profit, and it seeks A NETWORK OF COLLABORATORS; the regional journalists' network was formed because OUR COUNTRIES HAVE THE SAME ENVIRONMENTAL PROBLEMS WITH DIFFERENT NUANCES AND, LIVING IN A GLOBALISED WORLD, IMPUNITY CANNOT be treated as local. Ask which correspondent covers your country. A local journalist inside a regional network can place a story that a national outlet would drop under pressure.

trackers.name: COICA - the Amazon basin indigenous coordination representing 511 peoples through named national organisations in nine countries, whose first statutory objective is to DEFEND TERRITORIAL CLAIMS, and which covers peoples in voluntary isolation
trackers.desc: ONE COORDINATION SPEAKS FOR 511 INDIGENOUS PEOPLES ACROSS NINE AMAZON COUNTRIES, THROUGH A NAMED NATIONAL ORGANISATION IN EACH. It describes itself as AN INDIGENOUS ORGANISATION OF INTERNATIONAL CONVERGENCE THAT ACTS IN REPRESENTATION OF 511 INDIGENOUS PEOPLES, OF WHICH APPROXIMATELY 66 ARE INDIGENOUS PEOPLES IN VOLUNTARY ISOLATION AND INITIAL CONTACT, ARTICULATED THROUGH POLITICAL-ORGANISATIONAL BASE ORGANISATIONS, PRESENT IN THE 9 AMAZON COUNTRIES; those members are named individually for Peru, Brazil, Venezuela, Bolivia, Ecuador, Guyana, Colombia, Suriname and French Guiana. Founded in 1984 at a first congress, it has been domiciled in one Andean capital since 1993. Nine national indigenous organisations, each named and reachable. Your national member is the body that already sits in ministries and courts on territorial matters, and it has affiliates at regional and community level below it. WHAT ITS STATUTES COMMIT IT TO: its objectives are TO PROMOTE, DEVELOP AND DRIVE THE MECHANISMS FOR THE INTERACTION OF THE PEOPLES AND INDIGENOUS ORGANISATIONS that are its members, and TO DEFEND THE TERRITORIAL CLAIMS, THE FREE DETERMINATION OF THE INDIGENOUS PEOPLES, THE HUMAN RIGHTS OF THEIR MEMBERS AND OTHER RIGHTS AND INTERESTS; its mission is THE PROMOTION, PROTECTION AND SECURITY OF THE INDIGENOUS PEOPLES AND TERRITORIES THROUGH THE DEFENCE OF THEIR FORMS OF LIFE, PRINCIPLES AND SOCIAL, SPIRITUAL AND CULTURAL VALUES. Defending territorial claims is the first stated objective, not a programme it might add. A dispute over the boundary of a titled or untitled territory is the core of what this structure exists for. THE PEOPLES IT SPECIFICALLY COVERS THAT OTHERS DO NOT: some sixty-six of the peoples it represents are IN VOLUNTARY ISOLATION AND INITIAL CONTACT. Where a project's footprint may touch a people in isolation, that is a distinct legal and ethical regime and this coordination and its national members hold the evidence and the standing on it. HOW THE MEMBERSHIP HAS CHANGED, WHICH MATTERS WHEN YOU WRITE: the recorded history shows members added and substituted over time — a Brazilian organisation replacing an earlier body, a Colombian Amazon organisation replacing a national indigenous organisation in 1995, and a regional Venezuelan organisation replacing a national council in 2005 — and the figure of president was replaced by a general coordinator. Check which organisation currently holds the seat for your country before writing. Older directories still list bodies that were replaced twenty years ago. THE SCALE AND THE STANDING: it is described as THE LARGEST INDIGENOUS ORGANISATION IN THE WORLD, recorded a population of nearly 2.8 million people across its member organisations, holds membership of an international conservation union, and built its own communication system including a magazine and a portal PROGRAMMED FOR THE 4 LANGUAGES and a mail system to SUPPORT THE DEMANDS OF ALL THE MEMBER ORGANISATIONS. Membership of the international conservation union gives it a seat where protected areas are decided. Where a state proposes a park over a territory, that is a table your national member can reach. THE HONEST NOTE ON ROUTE: the coordination works through its national members and their affiliates rather than with individual communities directly. Go to your national member first, and to its regional affiliate before that. A request arriving at the continental office without the national organisation behind it will be sent back down the chain.

trackers.name: Afro-descendant territorial mapping viewer and the Central American Black Organization - a free regional cartographic tool built with Afro-descendant representatives showing lands and territories, alongside the cross-border network of national Garifuna, Creole and Black organisations
trackers.desc: THERE IS NOW A FREE CARTOGRAPHIC VIEWER SHOWING AFRO-DESCENDANT PRESENCE, LANDS AND TERRITORIES ACROSS LATIN AMERICA. A joint investigation TO IDENTIFY THE PRESENCE, THE LANDS AND TERRITORIES OF THE AFRO-DESCENDANT PEOPLE IN LATIN AMERICA produced, FOR THE FIRST TIME, A FREELY ACCESSIBLE CARTOGRAPHIC VIEWER that BRINGS TOGETHER DECISIVE DATA IN THE REGION ON THE TERRITORIAL PRESENCE AND THE SIGNIFICANT RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THESE TERRITORIES AND AREAS OF GREAT IMPORTANCE FOR CONSERVATION AND TERRESTRIAL AND OCEANIC CLIMATE STABILITY; it COMBINES MORE THAN 100 STATE, PRIVATE AND ORGANISATIONAL SOURCES and has been CONTRASTED AND ENRICHED WITH CARTOGRAPHIC INFORMATION BUILT WITH REPRESENTATIVES OF THE AFRO-DESCENDANT PEOPLE IN THE COUNTRIES OF THE STUDY, covering AFRO-DESCENDANT, BLACK, MAROON, GARIFUNA AND CREOLE PEOPLES. A map built with Afro-descendant representatives rather than about them, and free to open. Where a community's occupation of land is denied in an official file, that viewer is a published source it can cite. WHY IT MATTERS FOR A LAND CLAIM: it is THE FIRST TIME THERE IS A TOOL THAT MAKES VISIBLE POPULATION, TERRITORIAL AND ECOSYSTEM DATA AT REGIONAL SCALE, and it was built to show the overlap between those territories and areas critical for conservation and climate. Overlap with a conservation priority area is an argument a ministry understands. Print the map layer showing your territory inside such an area and attach it to the submission. THE REGIONAL ORGANISATION BEHIND AFRO-CENTRAL AMERICAN CLAIMS: a Black Central American organisation WAS BORN IN DANGRIGA, BELIZE, ON AUGUST 25, 1995, WITH THE PURPOSE OF ESTABLISHING A CROSS-BORDER ORGANIZATION CAPABLE OF MAKING VISIBLE AND STRENGTHENING THE SOCIAL, POLITICAL, ECONOMIC, CULTURAL, ENVIRONMENTAL AND ORGANIZATIONAL LIFE OF THE AFRO-CENTRAL AMERICAN COMMUNITIES and those in the diaspora, and is described as THE ONLY ORGANIZATION OF ITS KIND, holding annual assemblies since its foundation; it STRENGTHENS THE POPULATION'S INSTITUTIONAL DEVELOPMENT THROUGH THE ESTABLISHMENT OF COORDINATION MECHANISMS AND INTER-INSTITUTIONAL SUPPORT. A cross-border body for Garifuna, Creole and Black communities from Belize to Panama. Where the same people are split by a national border, that is the organisation that can carry a claim on both sides. WHAT ITS MEMBER ORGANISATIONS ARE, BY COUNTRY: recorded members include national Garifuna and Creole councils and an educational foundation in one country, Black organisations and a Black women's organisation in another, a community and ethnic development organisation in a third, a Garifuna organisation and a coast development association in a fourth, a Caribbean project association and an Afro-Costa Rican women's centre in a fifth, and an Afro-Panamanian response body, an Afro-Panamanian women's network and an ethnic museum association in a sixth, plus diaspora organisations. Each is a real, named organisation in a named country. Find the one nearest you rather than writing to the regional body first. WHAT ITS ASSEMBLIES HAVE WORKED ON: recorded agendas include MAPPING AND INVENTORY OF RESOURCES IN THE AFRO-CENTRAL AMERICAN COMMUNITIES, land tenure, participation of Afro communities in the local economy, and guaranteeing AT THE HIGHEST LEVEL THE PARTICIPATION OF THE AFRO-CENTRAL AMERICAN COMMUNITIES AND POPULATIONS WITHIN THE MESOAMERICAN BIOLOGICAL CORRIDOR INITIATIVE; one assembly recorded a DECLARATION OF DENUNCIATION BEFORE THE INTER-AMERICAN COMMISSION ON HUMAN RIGHTS. It has taken a denunciation to the inter-American commission before. Ask the national member how that was done and what it produced. THE HONEST CURRENCY WARNING: much of the accessible documentation of this network's membership and assemblies dates from the 2000s, though it remains listed as a member of a contemporary regional alliance and holds recent assemblies. Verify who currently leads it and which organisations are still members before relying on the list. The national members are the durable part; the regional office is not always reachable.

trackers.name: International Land Coalition, Latin America and the Caribbean - a regional platform of 61 member organisations across 20+ countries supporting MORE THAN 30 NATIONAL LAND COALITIONS, with a defender-protection commitment signed by every member and an independent land governance index
trackers.desc: MORE THAN THIRTY NATIONAL LAND COALITIONS EXIST, AND THEY ARE BROAD PLATFORMS THAT A LOCAL ORGANISATION CAN JOIN. The coalition SUPPORTS MORE THAN 30 NATIONAL LAND COALITIONS, described as BROAD PLATFORMS OF MEMBERS AND ALLIES THAT WORK IN FAVOUR OF land rights; its regional platform BRINGS TOGETHER 61 MEMBER ORGANISATIONS OF LOCAL, NATIONAL AND REGIONAL CIVIL SOCIETY OF DIVERSE PROFILES: GRASSROOTS ORGANISATIONS (SMALL PRODUCERS, PEASANTS, INDIGENOUS), WOMEN'S ORGANISATIONS AND/OR THOSE FOCUSED ON THIS SECTOR, NGOs, RESEARCH OR ACADEMIC CENTRES, AND ORGANISATIONS SPECIALISED IN KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT, drawn from MORE THAN 20 COUNTRIES, within a global membership of nearly three hundred in eighty-one countries. A grassroots organisation sits in the same platform as the research centres and the NGOs. Ask whether your country has a national coalition: that is the room where land conflicts get compared and carried upward. THE TWO COMMITMENTS EVERY MEMBER SIGNS: ALL THE MEMBERS OF THE coalition SIGN TWO IMPORTANT COMMITMENTS THAT PROTECT AND EMPOWER BOTH WOMEN AND LAND DEFENDERS WITHIN OUR NETWORK. Defender protection is a membership condition, not an optional programme. If members of your community are threatened, that commitment is something you can invoke by name. THE DATA TOOL THAT MEASURES YOUR GOVERNMENT: the coalition runs a land governance index whose data officer records that it REVEALS WORRYING TRENDS IN LAND GOVERNANCE and shows THE GAPS IN THE MONITORING THAT GOVERNMENTS CARRY OUT ON LAND GOVERNANCE, AND HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE WAY IN WHICH WOMEN AND INDIGENOUS PEOPLES, AMONG OTHER ACTORS, EXPERIENCE THAT GOVERNANCE; recorded country findings include one Caribbean island where THE INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES HAVE LITTLE ROOM FOR MANOEUVRE TO DECIDE ON THE IMPLEMENTATION OF PROJECTS THAT AFFECT THEIR TERRITORIES, SINCE PRIOR CONSULTATION IS APPLIED DEFICIENTLY, one Central American country where only 3.18% OF A BUDGET OF USD 184 MILLION reached family farming while THE CRISIS FACED BY LAND DEFENDERS... IS PERPETUATED BY THE STATE IN ALLIANCE WITH THE CORPORATIONS WITH INTEREST IN THEIR TERRITORIES, and another with AN ALARMING DISPOSSESSION OF LANDS OF INDIGENOUS PEOPLES AND AFRO-DESCENDANT COMMUNITIES, BECAUSE OF THE EXPANSION OF THE AGRICULTURAL FRONTIER. An independent index that contradicts the government's own monitoring, country by country. Quote your country's score back at the ministry that claims consultation works. THE LAND DEAL DATABASE AND ITS REGIONAL FOCAL POINT: a global land acquisitions observatory names a regional focal point organisation for Latin America and coordinates national pilot land observatories in several countries with the coalition. If a large land acquisition has been announced near you, check whether it is already recorded there — and if it is not, the focal point is who records it. WHAT ITS OWN ANALYSIS SAYS ABOUT THIS REGION: land IS AT THE CENTRE OF DIVERSE CONFLICTS IN THE REGION, WHERE THE HIGHEST NUMBER OF ATTACKS AGAINST THE PEOPLE WHO DEFEND IT IS RECORDED, LINKED IN GREAT MEASURE TO THE EXTRACTIVE INDUSTRIES; the coalition works THROUGH THE PROMOTION OF REGIONAL PLATFORMS AND NATIONAL COALITIONS... SO THAT THE WOMEN, MEN AND COMMUNITIES WHO LIVE ON AND FROM THE LAND HAVE DECISION-MAKING POWER OVER THEIR LANDS AND TERRITORIES. The region with the most attacks on land defenders is the one you are in. Read this entry with the protection funds and the pro bono routes already filed.

trackers.name: Rainforest Foundation US - land titling accelerated with regional government agrarian offices (75,000 acres for 20 communities in months), 400+ trained and financed community patrollers monitoring 19.6M acres, and support to strengthen organisations' capacity to manage funds
trackers.desc: WHAT HISTORICALLY TOOK YEARS WAS DONE IN MONTHS: TWENTY COMMUNITIES TITLED 75,000 ACRES IN ONE INITIATIVE. The foundation records that, working IN CLOSE PARTNERSHIP with a national indigenous federation and a regional government agrarian directorate, it WAS ABLE TO SIGNIFICANTLY ACCELERATE THE TITLING PROCESS, MEANING WHAT HISTORICALLY TOOK YEARS WAS ACCOMPLISHED IN JUST MONTHS; through that initiative 20 COMMUNITIES... SECURED LEGAL TITLES IN RECORD TIME FOR 75,000 ACRES OF THEIR ANCESTRAL LANDS, and in another year SIXTEEN INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES it supported RECEIVED LEGAL TITLE TO THEIR ANCESTRAL LANDS; separately it supported titling initiatives AIMING TO SECURE LAND TENURE FOR MORE THAN 11M ACRES ACROSS three countries and advanced tenure security for NEARLY 300,000 ACRES with two peoples in another. Titling accelerated by working with the regional government office that issues the titles, not around it. That is the partnership shape to copy. THE MODEL, STEP BY STEP: its PROVEN LAND-TITLING MODEL is that COMMUNITIES MAP THEIR ANCESTRAL BOUNDARIES, STRENGTHEN THEIR GOVERNANCE, AND USE REAL-TIME MONITORING TOOLS... TO DETECT THREATS; INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES, GRASSROOTS ORGANISATIONS, FEDERATIONS, REGIONAL GOVERNMENTS and the foundation HAVE JOINED FORCES TO MAP AND TITLE INDIGENOUS PEOPLES' LANDS. Mapping, governance and monitoring are done together rather than in sequence. A community that starts mapping while its governance documents are weak will stall at the titling office. THE MONITORING PROGRAMME AND ITS SCALE: it has TRAINED AND FINANCED OVER 400 COMMUNITY-BASED PATROLLERS TO MONITOR AND PROTECT 19.6 MILLION ACRES OF THEIR LANDS ACROSS four countries, using a programme in which INDIGENOUS FOREST MONITORS USE SMARTPHONES, SATELLITE IMAGERY, AND DRONES TO DETECT THREATS AND PREVENT DEFORESTATION against ILLEGAL LOGGING, MINING, AND CRIMINAL ACTIVITY; an earlier year recorded 307 COMMUNITY-BASED FOREST PATROLLERS ACROSS 129 COMMUNITIES. In one country it supports AROUND 114 INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES, FIVE INDIGENOUS FEDERATIONS, AND ONE REGIONAL INDIGENOUS PEOPLES' ORGANISATION to run it. Patrollers are trained and paid. Community monitoring fails when it depends on volunteers, and this programme treats it as work. THE MONEY IT MOVES TO COMMUNITIES: it UNLOCKED OVER $10.5 MILLION IN FUNDING FROM AROUND THE WORLD TO FUEL INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES' FOREST PROTECTION WORK in one year, and supports partners to STRENGTHEN ORGANIZATIONAL GOVERNANCE AND THEIR CAPACITY TO MANAGE FUNDS AND PROJECTS FOR THE COMMUNITY'S BENEFIT; its forward plan is to STRENGTHEN 67 INDIGENOUS AND LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS AND INCREASE THEIR ACCESS TO FUNDING. Capacity to manage funds is what unlocks direct financing. Ask for that support before asking for a grant, because the audit trail is what most community organisations lack. WHO IT WORKS THROUGH, AND THE DEFENDER RISK: its named partners include a Central American regional forest peoples alliance, a national umbrella organisation of one large country's indigenous peoples, a district council representing one people, and two national congresses representing peoples inside and outside a comarca; it records that THE AMAZON IS THE MOST DANGEROUS REGION IN THE WORLD FOR ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENDERS and collaborates with a national federation TO IMPLEMENT PREVENTIVE MEASURES, ENABLING COMMUNITIES TO BE BETTER PREPARED AGAINST THESE THREATS. It works through representative organisations, not with communities directly. Approach through your federation or council — and note that it also plans titling for communities next to territories reserved for peoples in voluntary isolation, to build a protection corridor.

trackers.name: The Global Alliance of Territorial Communities and its Shandia platform - direct funding channelled to territorial organisations' own financial mechanisms, with FISCAL SPONSORSHIP and financial capacity support where an organisation cannot yet receive funds, plus named community-led funds already re-granting
trackers.desc: IF A COMMUNITY ORGANISATION HAS NO WAY TO RECEIVE INTERNATIONAL MONEY, THIS PLATFORM SAYS IT WILL FIND IT A FISCAL SPONSOR. Its published design states that regional and national component funding WILL BE CHANNELLED TO alliance member organisations, that those members WILL DETERMINE HOW REGIONAL/NATIONAL FUNDS WILL BE USED, CHANNELLED AND ADMINISTERED, USING THEIR OWN REGIONAL/NATIONAL FINANCIAL MECHANISMS, and that IF A REGIONAL/NATIONAL indigenous or local community ORGANISATION REQUIRES A FISCAL SPONSOR, THEY WILL BE SUPPORTED IN THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE FUNDS, AND PROVIDED CAPACITY BUILDING SUPPORT ON FINANCIAL management. The commonest reason a community group is refused international funding is that it cannot receive or account for the money. This platform treats that as the thing to fix rather than a reason to refuse. WHAT THE PLATFORM IS FOR: it is OUR COMMON PLATFORM TO PROMOTE AND FACILITATE DIRECT, PREDICTABLE, EFFECTIVE, AND SUSTAINABLE FUNDING FOR INDIGENOUS PEOPLES AND LOCAL COMMUNITIES THROUGH THE ESTABLISHMENT OF DIRECT REGIONAL AND NATIONAL FUNDING MECHANISMS, CAPACITY-BUILDING, EXCHANGE OF EXPERIENCES, AND ENHANCED DIALOGUE WITH DONORS; for the communities behind it, DIRECT FINANCING IS MORE THAN JUST MONETARY SUPPORT — IT IS A VITAL TOOL FOR SECURING OUR FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS... TO LIVE ON OUR LANDS, EXERCISE FREE, PRIOR, AND INFORMED CONSENT, PRESERVE AND ADAPT OUR TRADITIONAL KNOWLEDGE, AND LIVE FREE FROM VIOLENCE. Direct means the money does not pass through an intermediary NGO that takes the overhead and the decisions. Ask any donor offering to fund your community whether it can pay through one of these mechanisms. THE FUNDS THAT ALREADY EXIST UNDER IT: named community-led mechanisms include a Mesoamerican territorial fund, an Amazonian fund led by the Brazilian Amazon indigenous coordination, a fund launched by the national Brazilian indigenous articulation DEVELOPED THROUGH A COLLABORATIVE PROCESS LED BY a national forum of indigenous leaders and a fund working group, REFLECT[ING] A STRONG COMMITMENT TO DEMOCRATIC AND TRADITIONAL GOVERNANCE PRACTICES, a quilombola fund, a fund led by a movement of babassu coconut breaker women, and further funds in Asia that have BEGUN RE-GRANTING IN SIX COUNTRIES, FOCUSING ON INDIGENOUS WOMEN, YOUTH, AND PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES and working to REACH REMOTE COMMUNITIES, SIMPLIFY GRANT ACCESS, BUILD CAPACITY. Several of these funds re-grant to communities in their own region. Ask which one covers your country and whether it has an open window — they are separate from the alliance itself. WHO THE ALLIANCE IS: A COALITION OF INDIGENOUS AND LOCAL COMMUNITY ORGANIZATIONS FROM MESOAMERICA, AMAZONIA, AFRICA AND ASIA, PROTECTING MORE THAN 958 MILLION HECTARES OF TROPICAL FORESTS and representing 35 MILLION PEOPLE FROM FOREST TERRITORIES IN 24 COUNTRIES, made up of five named networks including the Amazon basin coordination, the Mesoamerican forest peoples alliance and the national Brazilian indigenous articulation; the Mesoamerican alliance's own members are listed by name, from national forestry alliances to named indigenous nations and general congresses. Your national organisation is probably already inside this structure through one of the five networks. Trace the chain upward before assuming you need a new relationship. THE EXCHANGES IT RUNS BETWEEN TERRITORIES: recorded exchanges include Brazilian community funds invited to Mesoamerica to bring their experience to the grassroots of the alliance there, and a delegation from eight African countries meeting Brazilian community fund experts for nine days in indigenous communities; one review recorded honestly that grassroots organisations in that African network STILL HAVE LIMITED, THOUGH GROWING, CAPACITY TO REQUEST AND MANAGE RESOURCES FROM INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION. That honesty is useful. If your organisation cannot yet manage an international grant, say so and ask for the capacity support first — it is a stated part of the offer, not a disqualification.

trackers.name: Business & Human Rights Resource Centre - invites companies to answer a community's allegation and PUBLISHES THE NON-RESPONSE on the company's own page, with regional researchers, investor escalation and published policy and benchmark data on 10,000+ companies
trackers.desc: A COMPANY'S REFUSAL TO ANSWER A COMMUNITY'S ALLEGATION IS ITSELF PUBLISHED, ON ITS OWN PAGE. The centre INVITE[S] COMPANIES TO RESPOND TO ALLEGATIONS OF MISCONDUCT AND PUBLISH[ES] THEIR COMMENTS, doing so WHEN WE FIND NO EVIDENCE THAT THEY HAVE OTHERWISE RESPONDED TO THE CONCERNS; the process ENCOURAGES COMPANIES TO PUBLICLY ADDRESS HUMAN RIGHTS CONCERNS, AND PROVIDES THE PUBLIC WITH BOTH THE ALLEGATIONS AND THE COMPANY'S COMMENTS. It states plainly: WE INDICATE RESPONSE RATES IN THE COMPANY SECTIONS OF THE SITE, and IF A COMPANY IS LISTED AS HAVING FAILED TO RESPOND TO A PARTICULAR ALLEGATION, BUT IT HAS IN FACT ISSUED A RESPONSE... PLEASE LET US KNOW. A permanent public record that the company was asked and said nothing. For a developer that presents itself as responsible to lenders and buyers, that line on its own page is a cost. THE SCALE AND WHO DOES THE ASKING: it collects evidence on MORE THAN 10,000 COMPANIES IN MORE THAN 180 COUNTRIES and takes up ALLEGED ABUSE QUICKLY AND DIRECTLY WITH COMPANIES, INVITING THEM TO RESPOND TO SPECIFIC ALLEGATIONS (OVER 1,500 PER YEAR); a network of regional researchers BUILD LONG TERM RELATIONSHIPS WITH HUMAN RIGHTS ADVOCATES ON THE GROUND, BRINGING UNDERSTANDING OF THE DYNAMICS IN THE COUNTRIES THEY COVER, and WHERE THERE IS AN ALLEGATION OF CORPORATE HUMAN RIGHTS ABUSE THAT HAS NO PUBLIC RESPONSE, THEY REACH OUT TO THE COMPANY. Its site runs in several languages including Spanish and Portuguese. There is a researcher for your region who already knows the local advocates. Send the documented allegation to them rather than to a general address. WHAT IT DOES BEYOND PUBLISHING: its recorded practice is that DIALOGUES CAN EXTEND FURTHER AND OCCASIONALLY WE TAKE AN ACTIVE ROLE IN SUPPORTING COMMUNITIES AND NGOs; in one recorded case concerning an imprisoned indigenous leader who HAD LED THE OPPOSITION TO A PROPOSED... MINE IN HIS COMMUNITY'S TERRITORY, it POSTED THE ALLEGATIONS ON OUR WEBSITE AND SOUGHT RESPONSES FROM TWO COMPANIES WHO DID NOT RESPOND, AND ASSISTED THE LOCAL VILLAGERS IN SUBMITTING THE CASE TO THE UN SPECIAL REPRESENTATIVE ON HUMAN RIGHTS DEFENDERS, then CONTACTED PUBLIC INVESTORS... AND INVITED THEM TO COMMENT, of whom two responded and ONE COMMITTED TO RAISING THE ISSUE WITH ITS CLIENTS WHO ARE INVESTED in the company. Going up the chain to the investors is the step that moves a company. Identify who holds the shares or the loan before you send the allegation, and ask that they be invited to comment too. THE HONEST NUMBERS: the centre records a response rate averaging 43% on one page and 60% on another, and its own field acknowledges criticism about WEAK AND TANGENTIAL COMPANY RESPONSES and about the LACK OF REMEDY AND THE INEQUITY IN ARMS FOR THOSE AFFECTED BY ABUSE; a published analysis notes that A COMPANY RESPONSE TO A CRITICAL CIVIL SOCIETY REPORT IS NOT NECESSARILY A POSITIVE SIGN. Roughly half of companies answer, and an answer is not a remedy. Treat this as a public record and a pressure point, not as a complaint procedure that decides anything. WHAT IT ALSO PUBLISHES ON EACH COMPANY: company pages carry news, allegations, KEY DATA POINTS BASED ON CORPORATE POLICIES, AND SCORES FROM PROMINENT CIVIL SOCIETY BENCHMARKS, and its stated goals include a SAFE AND ENABLING ENVIRONMENT IN WHICH COMMUNITIES AND WORKERS CAN ADVOCATE FOR THEIR RIGHTS AND INTERESTS, INCLUDING THROUGH FREE AND FAIR NEGOTIATIONS. Read the company's page before your first meeting with it. Its own published policies and benchmark scores are the standard you can hold it to at the table.

trackers.name: Environmental Defenders Office — Pasifika Program
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific region, whose Pasifika-led programme works on extractive industries, forestry, marine protection and climate across Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Vanuatu and Tuvalu. WHO IT SUITS: an in-country organisation rather than an individual — EDO works predominantly through partner organisations (CELCOR in PNG, the Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit and the Solomon Islands Environmental Law Association, the Fiji Environmental Law Association and the Vanuatu Environmental Law Association), supplying strategic legal capacity, co-authored law-reform papers and litigation support. Approach your national environmental law association first; its free advice hotline is for Australia only. YOUR NATIONAL PARTNER IS the Vanuatu Environmental Law Association. EDO is an Australian organisation based in Sydney, and its Pasifika Program is Pasifika-led — including diaspora Pasifika lawyers with cultural and spiritual links to the region — working predominantly through partner organisations. So the partner is the front door and EDO is the legal capacity behind it. Focus areas: climate change, threats to marine environments, forestry and mining. EDO is an accredited community legal service with a community advice hotline, the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific, and records a historic Solomon Islands bauxite mine case. REACH IS LIMITED AND STATED: EDO names PNG, Solomon Islands, Fiji and Vanuatu, plus Tuvalu — it does not cover the other Pacific states, so do not assume regional coverage.

trackers.name: Vanuatu Environmental Law Association (VELA)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: an association of ni-Vanuatu lawyers formed to protect Vanuatu's environment through the legal system, and one of the Environmental Defenders Office's named Pacific partners — the EDO channels strategic legal capacity and law-reform work through it rather than acting directly in Vanuatu. It has been a Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund grantee for organisational strengthening and has run community legal-awareness work alongside the Fiji and Solomon Islands associations. WHO IT SUITS: a Vanuatu community or custom landowning group facing a development, logging or coastal decision — this is a small association of practising professionals, not a staffed legal-aid office, so expect referral to a member lawyer rather than intake. Domain unverified: reachable through the partner list on the Environmental Defenders Office's own site (edo.org.au/our-work), and named by Vanuatu's Department of Environmental Protection and Conservation at environment.gov.vu. VELA has no website of its own; the link is the Pacific Islands Climate Action Network member directory, which lists it as a non-government, not-for-profit public interest environmental law organisation. It is also a named Pacific partner of the Australian Environmental Defenders Office, which delivers joint legal work with its partners — so an approach through EDO is a second route in.

trackers.name: Vanuatu Environmental Advocacy Network (VEAN)
trackers.desc: The Vanuatu Environmental Advocacy Network — a national network of environmental civil-society organisations, named by Vanuatu's Department of Environmental Protection and Conservation as a Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund grantee receiving support to strengthen its capacity for biodiversity work. For activists: the non-legal counterpart to the Vanuatu Environmental Law Association, and the likelier first call for finding out who else is already working on a site. Domain unverified: named on the Vanuatu government's own environment department site, environment.gov.vu. No website or directory listing could be verified for VEAN, so none is given rather than guessing one. It is active: the Vanuatu Department of Environmental Protection and Conservation records VEAN and VELA as recipients of CEPF small grants administered by IUCN Oceania, to strengthen their organisations for biodiversity work. USE IT: reach VEAN through the Department, through IUCN Oceania's CEPF programme, or through VELA.

trackers.name: SPREP — three conventions, and 26 members is not 12 parties
trackers.desc: THE REGIONAL BODY FOR PACIFIC ENVIRONMENT, AND IT IS SECRETARIAT TO THREE CONVENTIONS. SPREP is an independent intergovernmental organisation, autonomous since the Agreement Establishing SPREP was signed at Apia on 16 June 1993, with the Article 2 purpose of providing assistance to protect and improve the environment and ensure sustainable development for present and future generations. It has 26 members — 14 Pacific island countries, 7 territories and 5 metropolitan states — and is headquartered in Apia, Samoa. ESTABLISH WHICH CONVENTION FITS YOUR ISSUE: the Noumea Convention (1986, in force 1990), described by UNEP as the only comprehensive multilateral umbrella agreement for protection of natural resources and environment in the region; the Waigani Convention on hazardous and radioactive waste imports; and the Apia Convention on nature conservation. THE NOUMEA CONVENTION IS UNDER ACTIVE REVIEW — WHICH IS AN OPENING: a 2021 Review produced recommendations now being implemented through a Noumea Workplan and Budget whose stated aim is to elevate the work of the Convention and enhance awareness and implementation, with a Communications Plan and a Finance Strategy named as critical. BUT CHECK WHETHER YOUR STATE IS A PARTY: SPREP has 26 members while the Noumea Convention has only 12 contracting parties — membership and party status are different things, and this entry does not assert the latter. GOVERNANCE POINT WORTH KNOWING: the SPREP Meeting is the plenary decision-making body; the Executive Board (established 2015) is subordinate to it and has no power to make decisions requiring input of all Members — so a decision affecting all members must go to the Meeting. IF YOUR ISSUE IS SEABED MINING: UNEP records deep sea mining as an emerging contentious issue the region is dealing with — the regional body has already named it. SPREP is also developing a portal for protected areas managers. THERE IS A SPREP PRESENCE IN YOUR COUNTRY: beyond Apia, host country agreements exist with the Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, the Marshall Islands, Solomon Islands and Vanuatu — so you need not approach Samoa first.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — citizens may apply
trackers.desc: AN INDIVIDUAL CAN APPLY, AND THE FIRST DOCUMENT IS SHORT. The Pacific Development and Conservation Trust, administered through the New Zealand government's Community Matters service with requests assessed by Advisory Trustees, states that ‘citizens or organisations’ from eligible Pacific places may request funding — so no incorporated body is required, which removes the commonest barrier recorded across this map. THE PROCESS IS TWO-STAGE: submit an Expression of Interest; only successful applicants are invited to submit a full project application. Do not prepare a full proposal before the EOI is accepted — wasted work, and expensive wasted work where drafting means travelling. Applications must be on the current form with all sections completed, submitted online where connection allows. READ THE PUBLISHED GRANT RECORD BEFORE DRAFTING: the Trust publishes records of grants by round — 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 (two rounds), 2023/24 and 2024/25 — showing what the Trustees have actually funded, at what size and in which countries. That is better evidence of what will succeed than any guidance note. UNDP SUPPORT HERE IS COUNTRY-LEVEL: UNDP's Pacific Office provides country support to this state, so an in-country office is a realistic second route alongside the Trust.

trackers.name: SPREP EIA and SEA guidelines — intervene at scoping, not after
trackers.desc: SCOPING IS WHERE STAKEHOLDER CONCERNS BECOME TERMS OF REFERENCE — and the guidelines say so themselves. Assessments must be individually customised to the aspects most relevant to stakeholders, and ‘customisation usually occurs during the scoping phase and results in the preparation of terms of reference’. Intervene at scoping and the assessment is required to examine your issue; intervene later and you are commenting on an assessment that was never asked to look. SPREP's Strengthening Environmental Impact Assessment: Guidelines for Pacific Island Countries and Territories (60pp, English and French) is the regional practice standard, SPREP having been mandated on EIA capacity since the 1990s. KNOW WHICH INSTRUMENT YOUR FIGHT NEEDS: EIA assesses a project; the companion Strategic Environmental Assessment guidelines (developed 2018–2020) assess a policy, plan or programme and are addressed to environment agencies, national planning offices, development control agencies, municipal authorities and provincial administrations — so if the problem is a tourism plan or a zoning programme rather than one hotel, SEA is the instrument and the municipal or provincial authority is the addressee. There is also a sector guideline for coastal tourism development, made with the South Pacific Tourism Organisation. THE HONEST PART, FROM A REGULATOR'S OWN ACCOUNT: Vanuatu's Principal EIA Officer publicly described her department's challenges as lack of staff, lack of political support, weaknesses in public consultation, and low capacity in monitoring and enforcement. Expect to supply evidence the agency cannot gather itself, and expect post-consent monitoring to be weak unless someone outside government does it — it is also a citable admission when arguing that a condition needs an independent monitoring mechanism attached. CHECK YOUR OWN ENVIRONMENT ACT FIRST: many Pacific countries have EIA mandated under their Environment Acts and EIA Regulations, and these guidelines support the implementation of current legal requirements rather than replacing them — the practice standard, not the obligation. SPREP runs in-country EIA training workshops, and the Pacific Environment Portal carries regional and national data.

trackers.name: Waigani Convention — radioactive waste, and 200 miles not 12
trackers.desc: IT REACHES WHERE BASEL CANNOT — and for island states that is the whole point. The Waigani Convention is modelled on Basel and is the regional implementation of the hazardous waste regime, but differs in two decisive ways: it also covers radioactive wastes, and its territorial coverage includes each Party's Exclusive Economic Zone — 200 nautical miles — rather than stopping at the 12 nautical mile territorial sea as Basel does. That makes it the instrument for dumping, transhipment and seabed disposal cases Basel cannot touch. It is annex-driven: obligations extend to all wastes in Annex I or those possessing the listed characteristics — check Annex I first; if the substance is listed the obligations attach automatically, and if not, the argument runs through the hazard characteristics instead. It is closely tied to the London Convention on dumping at sea. THE BODY TO CONTACT: the Pacific Regional Centre for the Waigani and Basel Conventions, based at SPREP in Samoa, which has developed a model law implementing all four waste conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Waigani) with a worked Tonga project — so where a national statute is missing or fragmented, the model already exists and a government can be pointed at it. AND A CONSULTATION WINDOW IS OPEN NOW: Cleaner Pacific 2025, the regional waste and pollution strategy built with 21 member countries around four goals and 15 strategic actions, is being replaced — the successor CP2036 was endorsed at the 31st SPREP Meeting (September 2023) with consultation in Suva, 21–22 July 2025. Priorities for the next decade are being set now. Ask whether your country has a national waste and pollution policy written against the regional strategy — it is the document your government is measured against. Delivery vehicles include PacWaste Plus (EUR 16.5 million, 72 months, EU-funded, across eight waste streams). THE HONEST LIMIT, FROM SPREP'S OWN REVIEW: Australia's reporting capability far exceeds that of most Pacific island countries, relying on weighbridge data requiring infrastructure that is not available — so do not assume an absence of data means an absence of a problem, and community-gathered data may be the best evidence there is. Watch the Clean Pacific Roundtable and CIRCLE EXPO, held alternately for an annual meeting of countries, industry and civil society — named as a participant category, not an observer.

trackers.name: Right to information — what your country actually has
trackers.desc: ASK EVEN WHERE THERE IS NO STATUTE — UNESCO's 2022 report on SDG 16.10.2 records that even Pacific states without access-to-information laws have an environment ‘generally favourable to the public's exercising of their right to information’. The absence of a law is not, on the region's own evidence, a reason to expect refusal. AND THERE IS A COMMITMENT TO CITE WHERE NO LAW EXISTS: the Boe Declaration on Regional Security (2018) Action Plan includes the adoption and implementation of constitutional, statutory and/or policy guarantees for public access to information as a measure for success — a government that signed Boe has already agreed that access to information is a measure of its own success. The Pacific Plan 2005 and the UN Pacific Strategy urge the same. The underlying right sits in article 19 of the ICCPR and of the Universal Declaration. REGIONAL POSITION: only four Pacific island countries have adopted RTI laws — Cook Islands (2008), Palau (2014), Vanuatu (2016) and Fiji (2018) — with several others drafting. A SOURCING WARNING FROM VANUATU'S OWN RTI UNIT, which applies region-wide: its site carries the notice ‘beware of fake websites pretending to be official’ — verify the domain before submitting anything containing your identity and your concern. IN VANUATU — THE STRONGEST IN THE REGION: the Right to Information Act No. 13 of 2016, assented 20 December 2016 and commenced 6 February 2017, requires all government agencies to release information and establishes a complaints mechanism where they do not, overseen by an Information Commissioner serving three years with the Judicial Service Commission involved in appointment. THE PROVISION TO USE AGAINST A DEVELOPER: for trade secrets protected by law, disclosure may be allowed if the public interest in disclosure outweighs any possible harm or injury — a public-interest override of commercial confidentiality.

trackers.name: DEPC Vanuatu — four divisions, and three documents to ask for
trackers.desc: KNOW WHICH OF THE FOUR DIVISIONS YOU NEED — it saves a week. The Department of Environmental Protection and Conservation (DEPC), established in legislation by the Environmental Protection and Conservation Act [CAP 283], runs a Legislation Division, a Biodiversity and Conservation Division, an Environmental Planning and Impact Assessment (EIA) Division and an Environmental Protection Division. Contact: Ministry compound, Nambatu, PMB 9063, Port Vila, (678) 25302 or 33430 — and there is a provincial presence at the Sanma Provincial Government Council, Luganville, which matters in an archipelago of about 80 islands: if you are on Santo, Sanma is closer than Port Vila. THREE DOCUMENTS TO ASK FOR BY NAME. The EIA Division, implementing Part 3 of the Act, undertakes Preliminary Environmental Assessments — the screening document, where a project is decided to need or not need a full EIA. Ask whether a PEA was done and ask to see it. Its officers visit project sites — a factual record made by the regulator, and the moment to ensure they see what you see. And it organises review of EIA reports and Environmental Management and Monitoring Plans by an EIA Review Committee, preparing that Committee's minutes — so minutes of the body that reviewed the report exist, are written by the department, and can be requested. THE EMMP IS WHERE MONITORING GETS WRITTEN IN: this map records Vanuatu's own Principal EIA Officer describing low capacity in monitoring and enforcement, so an independent monitoring obligation has to be in that plan or it will not happen. ON THE ACQUISITION SIDE: working with communities to establish Community Conservation Areas is a named function of the department, not a favour — the department is the counterparty. The Nguna-Pele Marine Protected Area — sixteen communities across two islands organised as one indigenous NGO, winner of the 2008 UNDP Equator Prize and the first of its kind in Vanuatu — is the worked precedent. AND A WARNING FROM THE DEPARTMENT ITSELF: ‘beware of fake websites pretending to be official — official Vanuatu Government sites end with .gov.vu’.

trackers.name: ELAW — free attorneys and scientists who will critique the developer's EIA
trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. ELAW is a global alliance of attorneys, scientists and other advocates, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries, that provides legal and scientific support to grassroots advocates to challenge destructive projects. FOUR CONCRETE FORMS OF HELP: legal support to local public interest lawyers; scientific support, including critiquing environmental assessments; economic insights on projects; and security expertise — ‘ELAW helps environmental lawyers improve their security so they can work without fear. When our partners are targeted, we act quickly to help defend and protect them.’ That last one is a named function, not an aspiration, and ELAW co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous and Environmental Defenders. HOW TO USE IT — THROUGH A LAWYER, NOT AS A CLIENT: ELAW works through more than 300 public interest advocates in its network, and its stated strategy is ‘locating strong lawyers who are committed to protecting the environment in their home countries’. You can approach ELAW directly, but the leverage is greatest when a local advocate is the conduit — that is how the network is built. It has hosted nearly 300 advocates from more than 65 countries as Fellows and provided support on thousands of cases; several partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize. Focus areas include biodiversity, fossil fuels — expressly assisting advocates in contesting fossil fuel development projects — plastic pollution, and work with coastal communities. It publishes guidebooks, including one to give communities sufficient understanding to challenge oil and gas projects, and clause-level summaries of national EIA law — so its site is also a route to learning exactly what your own EIA law requires. ASK WHETHER ELAW HAS A PARTNER IN YOUR COUNTRY: the network is described as spanning 70 to 80 countries but the member list is not published country by country, so this entry does not assert a presence in yours.

trackers.name: Nakau — income instead of logging, with the land staying with the clans
trackers.desc: WHERE LAND IS UNDER CUSTOMARY OWNERSHIP AND CANNOT BE BOUGHT, THIS IS THE EQUIVALENT OF BUYING IT: an income stream that makes keeping the forest worth more than felling it, with ownership staying with the landholders. Nakau works with Indigenous customary landowners across the Pacific, within local governance systems, expressly to ensure all projects are owned by the customary landholders — which is the difference between this and a concession. Its delivery partner across Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and PNG is Live & Learn. THE CASE THAT PROVES IT AGAINST AN ACTIVE LOGGING THREAT: at Drawa on Vanua Levu, logging coupes were already mapped and clearing had started when eight mataqali united to form the Drawa Block Forest Community Cooperative — a reversal at the last moment, and the vehicle was a cooperative formed by eight clans together. It now protects close to 4,000 hectares, is verified under Plan Vivo Climate, and won the International Energy Globe Award. WHERE THE MONEY WENT MATTERS MORE THAN THE HECTARES: credit income funded water and sanitation across five villages and supported women-led enterprises, honey, agroforestry, ecotourism and youth initiatives — the argument to put to neighbours who fear protection means poverty. ASK TO BE CONNECTED TO A WORKING PROJECT: Babatana, Drawa and Loru are verified and producing credits, not proposed. Others include Yato on Makira (10,000 hectares, with timber concessions still encroaching as recently as early 2025), East Rennell with 11 tribes, and 1,000+ hectares on New Georgia. NOW THE TWO REAL RISKS, BECAUSE THE RESEARCH RECORDS THEM: such agreements may create social unease by emphasising the disparity in wealth and power between rural landowners and environmental NGOs and donors, or cause within-community tensions through elite capture; and in one Manus case covering 83 clans in 19 villages and over 20,000 hectares, carbon financing had not yet started flowing. So the money may not arrive, and the benefits may be captured by a few — settle the benefit-sharing arrangement BEFORE any distribution, as that project did. Named backers include the EU, Ekos, MFAT, WWF-Australia and the Solomon Islands Threshold Program; Nakau and Live & Learn publish a toolkit for project coordinators.

trackers.name: In-depth Solomons
trackers.desc: In-depth Solomons — Non-profit investigative newsroom in the Solomon Islands (OCCRP member centre) exposing corruption, unexplained wealth of leaders, and abuses in logging and mining. — Independent watchdog of officials and public power.

trackers.name: Environmental Defenders Office — Pasifika Program
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific region, whose Pasifika-led programme works on extractive industries, forestry, marine protection and climate across Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Vanuatu and Tuvalu. WHO IT SUITS: an in-country organisation rather than an individual — EDO works predominantly through partner organisations (CELCOR in PNG, the Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit and the Solomon Islands Environmental Law Association, the Fiji Environmental Law Association and the Vanuatu Environmental Law Association), supplying strategic legal capacity, co-authored law-reform papers and litigation support. Approach your national environmental law association first; its free advice hotline is for Australia only. YOUR NATIONAL PARTNER IS the Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit and the Solomon Islands Environmental Law Association — note that a unit named for landowner advocacy is the most precisely relevant body this map has found in the Pacific. EDO is an Australian organisation based in Sydney, and its Pasifika Program is Pasifika-led — including diaspora Pasifika lawyers with cultural and spiritual links to the region — working predominantly through partner organisations. So the partner is the front door and EDO is the legal capacity behind it. Focus areas: climate change, threats to marine environments, forestry and mining. EDO is an accredited community legal service with a community advice hotline, the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific, and records a historic Solomon Islands bauxite mine case. REACH IS LIMITED AND STATED: EDO names PNG, Solomon Islands, Fiji and Vanuatu, plus Tuvalu — it does not cover the other Pacific states, so do not assume regional coverage.

trackers.name: Public Solicitor's Office — Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit (LALSU)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit inside the Public Solicitor's Office — a constitutional office under section 92 giving FREE legal aid, advice and representation to Solomon Islanders. LALSU is the unit dedicated to logging, mining and customary land matters: it educates customary landowners on their rights under environmental and resource law, brings strategic environmental litigation, and works on resource-law reform. Around 80% of Solomon Islands land is customarily owned, and the licensing process gives landowners several points at which they can refuse or have their land excluded. WHO IT SUITS: any Solomon Islander in need — eligibility is means-tested and weighs the nature of the problem, age and disability. PSO lawyers never charge; if one asks you for money, report it to the Public Solicitor.

trackers.name: Solomon Islands Environmental Law Association (SIELA)
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the Solomon Islands' national environmental law association, established in 2009 and re-launched in 2014 as a non-profit, working to improve access to justice for customary landowners by building the capacity of professionals to provide environmental-law services, and running community legal-awareness workshops. It is one of the Environmental Defenders Office's named Pacific partners, alongside the Public Solicitor's landowner unit. WHO IT SUITS: customary landowners and community groups facing logging or mining licensing — SIELA is a professional network rather than a firm, so it is the route to a lawyer and to plain-language explanation of the law, not a service that will take your case itself. Domain unverified: reachable through the partner list on the Environmental Defenders Office's own site, edo.org.au/our-work. SIELA has no website of its own; the link is the Environmental Defenders Office partner page, which names it alongside the Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit and runs joint legal work in the Pacific, including a Solomon Islands bauxite mine case. Established 2009 and relaunched in 2014 as a non-profit, SIELA runs community legal-awareness workshops on the Environment Act 1998, Fisheries Management Act 2015, Mines and Minerals Act 1990, Forest and Timber Utilization Act and Protected Areas Act 2010. USE IT: it specifically helps conservation groups use the Protected Areas Act 2010 to establish Protected Areas — a repeatable route for a community that wants its land formally protected.

trackers.name: Solomon Islands — Ministry of Finance & Treasury (MoFT)
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares & manages the annual recurrent budget and advises on monetary, budget & fiscal policy, Solomon Islands. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in the Solomon Islands.

trackers.desc: Free case law and legislation for Solomon Islands via the Pacific Islands Legal Information Institute. · Find here: free Solomon Islands legislation and court decisions, hosted by PacLII.

trackers.desc: National — Registry of Companies, Solomon Islands, public 24/7. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.desc: THE REGIONAL BODY FOR PACIFIC ENVIRONMENT, AND IT IS SECRETARIAT TO THREE CONVENTIONS. SPREP is an independent intergovernmental organisation, autonomous since the Agreement Establishing SPREP was signed at Apia on 16 June 1993, with the Article 2 purpose of providing assistance to protect and improve the environment and ensure sustainable development for present and future generations. It has 26 members — 14 Pacific island countries, 7 territories and 5 metropolitan states — and is headquartered in Apia, Samoa. ESTABLISH WHICH CONVENTION FITS YOUR ISSUE: the Noumea Convention (1986, in force 1990), described by UNEP as the only comprehensive multilateral umbrella agreement for protection of natural resources and environment in the region; the Waigani Convention on hazardous and radioactive waste imports; and the Apia Convention on nature conservation. THE NOUMEA CONVENTION IS UNDER ACTIVE REVIEW — WHICH IS AN OPENING: a 2021 Review produced recommendations now being implemented through a Noumea Workplan and Budget whose stated aim is to elevate the work of the Convention and enhance awareness and implementation, with a Communications Plan and a Finance Strategy named as critical. BUT CHECK WHETHER YOUR STATE IS A PARTY: SPREP has 26 members while the Noumea Convention has only 12 contracting parties — membership and party status are different things, and this entry does not assert the latter. GOVERNANCE POINT WORTH KNOWING: the SPREP Meeting is the plenary decision-making body; the Executive Board (established 2015) is subordinate to it and has no power to make decisions requiring input of all Members — so a decision affecting all members must go to the Meeting. IF YOUR ISSUE IS SEABED MINING: UNEP records deep sea mining as an emerging contentious issue the region is dealing with — the regional body has already named it. SPREP is also developing a portal for protected areas managers. THERE IS A SPREP PRESENCE IN YOUR COUNTRY: beyond Apia, host country agreements exist with the Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, the Marshall Islands, Solomon Islands and Vanuatu — so you need not approach Samoa first.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — citizens may apply
trackers.desc: AN INDIVIDUAL CAN APPLY, AND THE FIRST DOCUMENT IS SHORT. The Pacific Development and Conservation Trust, administered through the New Zealand government's Community Matters service with requests assessed by Advisory Trustees, states that ‘citizens or organisations’ from eligible Pacific places may request funding — so no incorporated body is required, which removes the commonest barrier recorded across this map. THE PROCESS IS TWO-STAGE: submit an Expression of Interest; only successful applicants are invited to submit a full project application. Do not prepare a full proposal before the EOI is accepted — wasted work, and expensive wasted work where drafting means travelling. Applications must be on the current form with all sections completed, submitted online where connection allows. READ THE PUBLISHED GRANT RECORD BEFORE DRAFTING: the Trust publishes records of grants by round — 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 (two rounds), 2023/24 and 2024/25 — showing what the Trustees have actually funded, at what size and in which countries. That is better evidence of what will succeed than any guidance note. UNDP SUPPORT HERE IS COUNTRY-LEVEL: UNDP's Pacific Office provides country support to this state, so an in-country office is a realistic second route alongside the Trust.

trackers.name: SPREP EIA and SEA guidelines — intervene at scoping, not after
trackers.desc: SCOPING IS WHERE STAKEHOLDER CONCERNS BECOME TERMS OF REFERENCE — and the guidelines say so themselves. Assessments must be individually customised to the aspects most relevant to stakeholders, and ‘customisation usually occurs during the scoping phase and results in the preparation of terms of reference’. Intervene at scoping and the assessment is required to examine your issue; intervene later and you are commenting on an assessment that was never asked to look. SPREP's Strengthening Environmental Impact Assessment: Guidelines for Pacific Island Countries and Territories (60pp, English and French) is the regional practice standard, SPREP having been mandated on EIA capacity since the 1990s. KNOW WHICH INSTRUMENT YOUR FIGHT NEEDS: EIA assesses a project; the companion Strategic Environmental Assessment guidelines (developed 2018–2020) assess a policy, plan or programme and are addressed to environment agencies, national planning offices, development control agencies, municipal authorities and provincial administrations — so if the problem is a tourism plan or a zoning programme rather than one hotel, SEA is the instrument and the municipal or provincial authority is the addressee. There is also a sector guideline for coastal tourism development, made with the South Pacific Tourism Organisation. THE HONEST PART, FROM A REGULATOR'S OWN ACCOUNT: Vanuatu's Principal EIA Officer publicly described her department's challenges as lack of staff, lack of political support, weaknesses in public consultation, and low capacity in monitoring and enforcement. Expect to supply evidence the agency cannot gather itself, and expect post-consent monitoring to be weak unless someone outside government does it — it is also a citable admission when arguing that a condition needs an independent monitoring mechanism attached. CHECK YOUR OWN ENVIRONMENT ACT FIRST: many Pacific countries have EIA mandated under their Environment Acts and EIA Regulations, and these guidelines support the implementation of current legal requirements rather than replacing them — the practice standard, not the obligation. SPREP runs in-country EIA training workshops, and the Pacific Environment Portal carries regional and national data.

trackers.name: Waigani Convention — radioactive waste, and 200 miles not 12
trackers.desc: IT REACHES WHERE BASEL CANNOT — and for island states that is the whole point. The Waigani Convention is modelled on Basel and is the regional implementation of the hazardous waste regime, but differs in two decisive ways: it also covers radioactive wastes, and its territorial coverage includes each Party's Exclusive Economic Zone — 200 nautical miles — rather than stopping at the 12 nautical mile territorial sea as Basel does. That makes it the instrument for dumping, transhipment and seabed disposal cases Basel cannot touch. It is annex-driven: obligations extend to all wastes in Annex I or those possessing the listed characteristics — check Annex I first; if the substance is listed the obligations attach automatically, and if not, the argument runs through the hazard characteristics instead. It is closely tied to the London Convention on dumping at sea. THE BODY TO CONTACT: the Pacific Regional Centre for the Waigani and Basel Conventions, based at SPREP in Samoa, which has developed a model law implementing all four waste conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Waigani) with a worked Tonga project — so where a national statute is missing or fragmented, the model already exists and a government can be pointed at it. AND A CONSULTATION WINDOW IS OPEN NOW: Cleaner Pacific 2025, the regional waste and pollution strategy built with 21 member countries around four goals and 15 strategic actions, is being replaced — the successor CP2036 was endorsed at the 31st SPREP Meeting (September 2023) with consultation in Suva, 21–22 July 2025. Priorities for the next decade are being set now. Ask whether your country has a national waste and pollution policy written against the regional strategy — it is the document your government is measured against. Delivery vehicles include PacWaste Plus (EUR 16.5 million, 72 months, EU-funded, across eight waste streams). THE HONEST LIMIT, FROM SPREP'S OWN REVIEW: Australia's reporting capability far exceeds that of most Pacific island countries, relying on weighbridge data requiring infrastructure that is not available — so do not assume an absence of data means an absence of a problem, and community-gathered data may be the best evidence there is. Watch the Clean Pacific Roundtable and CIRCLE EXPO, held alternately for an annual meeting of countries, industry and civil society — named as a participant category, not an observer.

trackers.name: Right to information — what your country actually has
trackers.desc: ASK EVEN WHERE THERE IS NO STATUTE — UNESCO's 2022 report on SDG 16.10.2 records that even Pacific states without access-to-information laws have an environment ‘generally favourable to the public's exercising of their right to information’. The absence of a law is not, on the region's own evidence, a reason to expect refusal. AND THERE IS A COMMITMENT TO CITE WHERE NO LAW EXISTS: the Boe Declaration on Regional Security (2018) Action Plan includes the adoption and implementation of constitutional, statutory and/or policy guarantees for public access to information as a measure for success — a government that signed Boe has already agreed that access to information is a measure of its own success. The Pacific Plan 2005 and the UN Pacific Strategy urge the same. The underlying right sits in article 19 of the ICCPR and of the Universal Declaration. REGIONAL POSITION: only four Pacific island countries have adopted RTI laws — Cook Islands (2008), Palau (2014), Vanuatu (2016) and Fiji (2018) — with several others drafting. A SOURCING WARNING FROM VANUATU'S OWN RTI UNIT, which applies region-wide: its site carries the notice ‘beware of fake websites pretending to be official’ — verify the domain before submitting anything containing your identity and your concern. IN SOLOMON ISLANDS: a draft FOI policy and law is reported to be in the final stages of review — the closest to adoption of the drafting group.

trackers.name: Environment & Conservation Division — three Acts, one desk, consultation open
trackers.desc: ONE SMALL DIVISION HOLDS DEVELOPMENT CONTROL, WILDLIFE AND PROTECTED AREAS TOGETHER — so a single approach can raise a species point, a protected-area point and a permit point at the same desk. The Environment and Conservation Division, established 1985 by Cabinet directive and given legal status under section 5 of the Environment Act 1998, administers three Acts — the Environment Act 1998 (development control, EIA and pollution control), the Wildlife Protection and Management Act 1998 with its 2008 Regulations (birds, reptiles, amphibians, mammals, insects, plants and marine organisms, and CITES compliance), and the Protected Areas Act 2010 — ‘despite its relatively small size’, in its own words, which also means it is stretched. A CONSULTATION IS OPEN ON THE STATUTE ITSELF: the Division records that it is reviewing the Environment (Amendment) Act 1998 and is now inviting submissions on the proposed amendments as part of a public consultation. A consultation on the Act is rarer and more valuable than one on a project — the amendments will govern every future development. Check whether the window is still open. CHECK THE PUBLISHED EIA CATEGORIES, AND NOTICE ONE IN PARTICULAR: under the Act and the Environment Regulation 2008 they include food industries; non-metallic industries — expressly lime production, brick and tile manufacture, extraction of minerals and mining, EXTRACTION OF AGGREGATES, STONES AND SHINGLES, radioactive-related industries and cement; and leather, paper, textile and wood industries. River and beach aggregate extraction is among the commonest and least-regulated causes of land and coastal loss in the Pacific — and it is expressly on the EIA list here. The statutory purpose of EIA includes predicting and avoiding, minimising or offsetting adverse significant environmental, SOCIAL and other relevant effects — social effects are inside the purpose, not an add-on. ON WASTE: the Waste Management and Pollution Control Strategy 2017–2026 was endorsed by Cabinet in November 2017 after validation workshops in 2015 and 2016 that included NGOs alongside line ministries and the private sector — a precedent to cite when asking to be included in the next one. It is on the Ministry site and the Solomon Islands Environment Data Portal. MECDM is in Honiara with four divisions.

trackers.name: ELAW — free attorneys and scientists who will critique the developer's EIA
trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. ELAW is a global alliance of attorneys, scientists and other advocates, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries, that provides legal and scientific support to grassroots advocates to challenge destructive projects. FOUR CONCRETE FORMS OF HELP: legal support to local public interest lawyers; scientific support, including critiquing environmental assessments; economic insights on projects; and security expertise — ‘ELAW helps environmental lawyers improve their security so they can work without fear. When our partners are targeted, we act quickly to help defend and protect them.’ That last one is a named function, not an aspiration, and ELAW co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous and Environmental Defenders. HOW TO USE IT — THROUGH A LAWYER, NOT AS A CLIENT: ELAW works through more than 300 public interest advocates in its network, and its stated strategy is ‘locating strong lawyers who are committed to protecting the environment in their home countries’. You can approach ELAW directly, but the leverage is greatest when a local advocate is the conduit — that is how the network is built. It has hosted nearly 300 advocates from more than 65 countries as Fellows and provided support on thousands of cases; several partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize. Focus areas include biodiversity, fossil fuels — expressly assisting advocates in contesting fossil fuel development projects — plastic pollution, and work with coastal communities. It publishes guidebooks, including one to give communities sufficient understanding to challenge oil and gas projects, and clause-level summaries of national EIA law — so its site is also a route to learning exactly what your own EIA law requires. ASK WHETHER ELAW HAS A PARTNER IN YOUR COUNTRY: the network is described as spanning 70 to 80 countries but the member list is not published country by country, so this entry does not assert a presence in yours.

trackers.name: Nakau — income instead of logging, with the land staying with the clans
trackers.desc: WHERE LAND IS UNDER CUSTOMARY OWNERSHIP AND CANNOT BE BOUGHT, THIS IS THE EQUIVALENT OF BUYING IT: an income stream that makes keeping the forest worth more than felling it, with ownership staying with the landholders. Nakau works with Indigenous customary landowners across the Pacific, within local governance systems, expressly to ensure all projects are owned by the customary landholders — which is the difference between this and a concession. Its delivery partner across Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and PNG is Live & Learn. THE CASE THAT PROVES IT AGAINST AN ACTIVE LOGGING THREAT: at Drawa on Vanua Levu, logging coupes were already mapped and clearing had started when eight mataqali united to form the Drawa Block Forest Community Cooperative — a reversal at the last moment, and the vehicle was a cooperative formed by eight clans together. It now protects close to 4,000 hectares, is verified under Plan Vivo Climate, and won the International Energy Globe Award. WHERE THE MONEY WENT MATTERS MORE THAN THE HECTARES: credit income funded water and sanitation across five villages and supported women-led enterprises, honey, agroforestry, ecotourism and youth initiatives — the argument to put to neighbours who fear protection means poverty. ASK TO BE CONNECTED TO A WORKING PROJECT: Babatana, Drawa and Loru are verified and producing credits, not proposed. Others include Yato on Makira (10,000 hectares, with timber concessions still encroaching as recently as early 2025), East Rennell with 11 tribes, and 1,000+ hectares on New Georgia.
