Within seven working days of issuing the conclusion on the content of a denunciation and the decision dealing with the violation, the resolver must make the conclusion public, and the authority imposing discipline or an administrative penalty must publicise the handling decision. A denunciation that succeeds therefore produces a public document rather than a private outcome, which is rare among the complaint routes recorded in this file. The person you name is told, and quickly. Within five working days of the decision to accept a denunciation, the resolver must notify the person who made it and must notify the person denounced of its content; where the conditions for acceptance are not met, the denouncer must be informed immediately of the reason. Acceptance itself requires that the content give a basis for identifying the violator and the violating act. Knowing that the subject will be told within days is essential before deciding whether to file under your own name or to seek protection first. Protection is a chapter of the law, not a practice. The act contains provisions on who is protected and the scope of protection, the rights and obligations of the protected person, and the bodies competent to apply protective measures, and its principles require that resolving a denunciation ensure the safety of the person who made it. Denunciations may be made in writing or presented directly at the competent body; those showing signs of a crime are handled under criminal procedure law, and measures to stop the violation may be applied. Read this with the land data provision procedure, the access to information law, the commune-level duties and the accredited laboratory entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Kiểm toán nhà nước — the audit report is posted at the audited office, and binds it
trackers.desc: The report must be made public, and one form of publication is posting it at the audited office itself. Under the state audit law an audit report, once issued, is published except for content classified as a state secret, and the auditor general organises that publication through one or more forms: a press conference, publication in the official gazette and the mass media, posting on the audit body's website and in its publications, and posting at the headquarters of the audited unit. A community can therefore read the finding on the wall of the office that was audited, which is the shortest distance between an audit and the people it concerns. The report binds the audited unit. Published accounts of the law record that an audit report, after issue and publication, is compulsory for the audited unit as regards the violations it identifies in the management and use of public finance and public assets, serves as a basis for the legislature, the government and other bodies in their own work, and is the basis on which the audited unit may exercise its right to complain. The report is therefore an instrument rather than an opinion. Implementation is checked, and the check is published too. The audit body requires the audited unit to report in writing on the implementation of audit conclusions and recommendations, organises checks on implementation at the unit and at related bodies, and prepares a report on the results, which — with the annual summary report of audit results — is published after being reported to the National Assembly. The question of whether a recommendation was actually carried out therefore has a published answer. Files go to the investigators where crime is indicated. The auditor general transfers files to the investigation agencies, the people's procuracy and other competent state bodies for consideration and handling of matters showing signs of crime or of violations of law by agencies, organisations or individuals discovered through audit activity. Read this with the denunciation law, the land data provision procedure, the access to information law and the accredited laboratory entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The bar federation and the provincial bar associations — where to find a lawyer, and who supervises them
trackers.desc: Every province has a bar association, and the federation is the body above them. The federation is described on its own pages as the unified national professional organisation of the bar associations and lawyers of the country, representing, gathering and supporting its members and protecting their lawful rights; bar associations had already been established in almost every province and city before the federation itself was founded in 2009 under a government decision approving a national lawyers' organisation. For a household looking for counsel, the provincial bar association is the address to start from — a named institution in the provincial capital rather than a search engine result. The code of professional ethics is the supervision instrument. The federation's stated responsibilities include building and maintaining the ethical standards and professional rules of lawyers, ensuring the independence and the quality of legal services, and exercising self-management of the profession. Published training material records that the federation, the bar associations and law practice organisations use that code to supervise their member lawyers, to commend good practice and to correct conduct that falls short. Where a lawyer takes a fee and does nothing, or turns out to be acting for the other side as well, the body that supervises them has a name and a written standard. The charter is the document to cite. The federation's charter regulates the organisation and operation of the federation and of the provincial and city bar associations, and sets out the rights and obligations of members and the relationship between the federation and its members. Asking a bar association to act on a complaint is asking it to do something its own charter provides for. Read the structural fact with it. The federation's own description states that it operates under the leadership of the Communist Party and is a member of the Fatherland Front, and its site publishes legal knowledge sections by field, including land law, administrative law, investment and tax. This is a professional route, not a campaigning one: it will help a household find and hold to account a lawyer, and it is not the place to take a campaign. Read this with the state legal aid register, the land data provision procedure, the denunciation law and the access to information entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The annual list of eligible valuation enterprises and valuers — and the companion list of those that failed the conditions
trackers.desc: The state publishes who may value property, once a year. The finance ministry issues an annual notice, dated at the end of December and taking effect from the first of January, publishing the list of price valuers eligible to practise at valuation enterprises. Reported counts from those notices run to two hundred and seventy-eight eligible enterprises for 2024, two hundred and seventy-five for 2025 and two hundred and seventy-seven for 2026, each notice carrying its own number and date. Before accepting a valuation or commissioning one, the individual who signed it and the firm they work for can both be checked against the current year's list — which is a different and stronger act than asking whether they are qualified. The same notice names the firms that failed. Each notice carries a second appendix listing the valuation enterprises and branches that do not meet the conditions for carrying on valuation services for that year, and the law provides that an enterprise failing to meet the conditions for three consecutive months is suspended from the business of valuation. A firm appearing in that second appendix is a documented fact, and it is worth producing where that firm's certificate is the basis of a compensation offer or an asset figure. A valuation certificate carries legal weight. Published descriptions record that the certificates issued by these enterprises have legal validity for transactions involving the value of assets, and that the enterprises hold ministry-issued certificates of eligibility to trade in valuation services, with both enterprises and individual valuers obliged to comply with the price law and its guidance and with the terms recorded on that certificate. That cuts both ways: it makes an independently commissioned valuation usable, and it makes the other side's certificate checkable. How to use it. Check the individual valuer and the enterprise separately against the current notice; record the notice number and its date; and if the enterprise appears in the second appendix, or the individual does not appear in the first, put that in writing to whichever body is relying on the report. Read this with the bar federation, the state legal aid register, the land data provision procedure and the denunciation law entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Ban Giám sát đầu tư của cộng đồng — a statutory community board that can demand the compensation, resettlement and waste plans
trackers.desc: A board is formed for each project, with at least five members. Under the grassroots democracy legislation of 2022 and its implementing decree, the commune-level Fatherland Front committee decides the establishment of a community investment supervision board for each public investment programme or project, each public-private partnership project, and each programme or project funded by the capital and labour of the residential community or by direct sponsorship to the commune. The board must have at least five members, and the Front committee organises a supplementary election where places fall vacant. This is a seat created for each project rather than a standing body somebody else already occupies. The information right is the substance. The board may require the programme owner or the investor to answer and to supply, for the purpose of supervision: the investment decision; information about the investor and the project management board with a contact address; the progress and the investment plan; the area of land occupied and the land use; the detailed site plan and the architectural design; the compensation, site clearance and resettlement plan; and the waste treatment and environmental protection plan. For programmes funded by community capital and labour, by the commune budget or by direct sponsorship, the owner must additionally supply technical processes and standards, the types and norms of materials, and the acceptance results and final settlement of the works. That is a documented right to the very papers most communities in this file spend months trying to obtain. What it supervises, and where its chair sits. Its duties include monitoring whether the investment policy and decision conform to the planning and investment plans for the commune, and whether the investor complies with the law on land boundary markers and land use, the detailed site plan, the architectural and construction plans, waste treatment, environmental protection, compensation, site clearance and resettlement, and the investment plan; it follows implementation and progress, and whether information is being disclosed publicly during the investment. The head of the board is invited to attend meetings of the commune people's council, people's committee and Front committee that concern the programmes and projects it supervises. Obligations on the other side, and the limits. State management agencies, programme owners, investors and project management boards are required to create favourable conditions for the board to perform its tasks. The board works collectively and decides by majority, must be objective, public, transparent, timely and rigorous, and must not obstruct or affect the implementation of the programme or project. Read this with the bar federation, the state legal aid register, the land data provision procedure and the annual valuation enterprise lists already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Xếp hạng di tích — the owner or manager applies, and the protection zone drawn on the map is what restricts building
trackers.desc: The owner or manager applies, and the contents of the dossier are published. The circular governing scientific dossiers for the ranking of historical-cultural relics and scenic landscapes lists what a dossier must contain: an application for ranking from the organisation or individual that owns the relic or is assigned to manage it; the relic's record; a location map with directions; technical drawings including an overall site plan at one in five hundred and plans, elevations, sections, structures and typical carved details at one in fifty; a set of descriptive colour photographs; an inventory of the objects and antiquities at the site; rubbings and translations of steles, couplets and other classical or foreign-language inscriptions; the minutes and map delimiting the protection zones; and a submission sheet. A village that manages a communal house, a shrine or a landscape can be the applicant in its own name. The zoning map is the heart of it. The map delimiting the protection zones is drawn on an extract of the local cadastral map, with the boundary around protection zone one shown in red and the boundary around zone two in blue; where the protected area does not follow whole parcels, or lies where no cadastral map exists or across large or complex terrain, the necessary coordinates must be given. That line is what later restricts building, so it is the part to get drawn accurately and widely rather than the prose around it. The minutes need a row of confirmations, and a missing zone must be explained in writing. The zoning minutes must carry confirmations from the commune people's committee, the district culture and information office, the district natural resources and environment office, the district people's committee, the body preparing the dossier, the provincial culture department, the provincial natural resources department, and for national and special national dossiers the provincial people's committee. Where it is determined that a relic has no zone two, the provincial department director must provide a written explanation attached to the zone one minutes — so an absent buffer is a decision somebody has to justify on paper. The level decides who signs, and what protection then means. The provincial department director submits to the provincial people's committee chairman for provincial ranking; the provincial chairman submits to the minister for national ranking; the minister submits to the prime minister for special national ranking. Published guidance records that building within the protection zones is restricted: works directly serving the protection and promotion of the relic require the written consent of the authority competent to rank it, with works in zone two of a provincial relic requiring the provincial chairman's written agreement; and the protection zones must be marked on the ground with durable boundary markers in visible positions, the provincial chairman being responsible for organising the marking. Read this with the community investment supervision board, the forest allocation route, the land data provision procedure and the information access entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Tư vấn, phản biện và giám định xã hội — a provincial union that can convene an independent expert council to critique a project
trackers.desc: There is a body in each province whose assigned task is critiquing projects. The union of science and technology associations was given the task of advisory review, social critique and social appraisal by prime ministerial decision in 2014, replacing an earlier decision of 2002, and provincial people's committees have issued their own decisions naming the provincial union as the focal point for that work in their territory. The activity is described in its own materials as social, independent, objective and not for profit, the responsibility of the scientific and technological intelligentsia to supply scientific grounds to policy-making. For a community facing a project it is the nearest thing in this country to an expert body that can be pointed at a specific scheme. The procedure and the money are both set out. Published accounts of how a provincial union works record that, once the people's committee assigns it a particular scheme or project, it invites experts and scientists, issues a decision establishing an independent critique council, budgets the cost, draws up the critique outline, studies the dossier of the project to be reviewed, holds a workshop to gather contributions, and compiles and reports the result. The budget is set in the annual estimate under a finance ministry circular covering preparation — building the outline, studying the file — the holding of workshops and expert consultations, and the summing up. A community is therefore asking for something that already has a procedure and a line of funding behind it. The track record is on large infrastructure. Published accounts record participation in comment and critique on major national schemes including two large hydropower projects and flood planning for the delta, as well as education, health and environmental policy. The limits are stated plainly, and they decide the tactics. A provincial union's own published assessment records that critique of programmes and projects is entirely voluntary, so the request for it comes from the project side; that there is no legal provision making independent advisory review, critique and social appraisal compulsory before major decisions on planning, investment and development; and that the result is advisory, for the decision-maker to study and consider, with no obligation to follow it. It also records shortages of lead experts and uneven awareness among agencies. The practical move follows from those limits: rather than asking the union directly, ask the provincial people's committee to assign it the project, because assignment is what starts the procedure and releases the budget. Read this with the community investment supervision board, the forest allocation route, the state legal aid register and the information access entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Bồi thường, hỗ trợ, tái định cư — resettlement must be arranged before the land is taken, and the plan is posted for fifteen days first
trackers.desc: Resettlement must be arranged before the land is recovered. Under the land legislation of 2024, the approval of the resettlement plan and the actual arrangement of resettlement must be completed before recovery of the land is carried out — a change from the previous position, under which it was enough to have finished building the houses or the infrastructure of the resettlement area. The same article states the governing principles: compensation, support and resettlement are to be carried out democratically, objectively, fairly, openly, transparently, promptly and in accordance with law. Where a recovery decision is nonetheless made before resettlement has been arranged, the provincial people's committee is to regulate temporary accommodation, its duration and its cost — so a household moved out before resettlement exists is entitled to something, and the provincial rule is the document to ask for. Fifteen days of public posting before the plan is approved. The body tasked with compensation and resettlement must notify the person whose residential land is being recovered, and the owner of housing who must move, of the expected resettlement arrangement, and must post it publicly for at least fifteen days — at the commune people's committee office, at the common activity location of the residential area where the land is being recovered, and at the resettlement site where people are already living — before the competent authority approves the plan. Those three posting locations are checkable facts: a plan approved without them has skipped a statutory step. Thirty days to pay, and a penalty for paying late. Within thirty days from the date the decision approving the compensation, support and resettlement plan takes effect, the body carrying out compensation must pay the person whose land is recovered and the owners of assets; where payment is late, an additional sum is payable when the compensation is settled. Unfulfilled financial obligations on the land are deducted from the compensation and returned to the state budget, so a household with outstanding land dues should expect a net figure rather than a gross one. Where the price comes from, and what to check. The land price used for compensation, and the price used for land at the resettlement site, are taken from the land price table together with the adjustment coefficient set by resolution, with the authority determining a price where the location is not in the table; and the law lists the cases in which no compensation for land is payable at all. Because both the table and the coefficient are periodically re-issued, check which version applied at the date of the decision. Read this with the community investment supervision board, the land data provision procedure, the annual list of eligible valuation enterprises and the state legal aid register entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Giấy chứng nhận for a residential community — a certificate over the communal house, shrine or clan land, on a commune confirmation
trackers.desc: A residential community can hold the certificate itself. Under the land legislation of 2024, a residential community currently using land on which stand a communal house, temple, shrine, hermitage, clan worship house or other belief structure — and pagodas outside the separate provision for religious organisations, together with agricultural land falling under the article on community agricultural land — is granted the certificate of land use rights and ownership of assets attached to the land, provided the land is not in dispute and there is written confirmation from the commune people's committee that it is land used in common by the residential community. The community is the holder; this is not a certificate in the name of an individual or a clan head. The commune confirmation is the document that carries it. Two conditions do the work: no dispute over the land, and the commune-level written confirmation of common community use. Both are obtainable before any project is announced, and both are far harder to obtain once a dispute has begun — which is the argument for applying while the ground is quiet. For a village whose burial ground, communal house or festival land has no paperwork, this is the route by which it acquires some. Two dates that remove the levy. The same article provides that households and individuals using land stably who hold one of the listed documents made before 15 October 1993 receive the certificate without paying the land use levy; and those holding documents from a state agricultural or forestry enterprise allocating land for housing, or housing combined with agricultural or forestry production, before 1 July 2004 likewise receive it without the levy. Where old paperwork exists, its date decides whether money is owed. Land wrongly allocated is not automatically lost. A further article deals with land allocated by a body without proper authority: for allocations made between 1 July 2014 and the start of 2025 a certificate may still issue where the commune people's committee confirms there is no dispute, the use conforms to the land use plan and the user has documents proving payment; outside that case, land allocated or leased without authority from 1 July 2014 onward does not receive a certificate. Read this with the forest allocation to a residential community, the community investment supervision board, the land data provision procedure and the heritage ranking entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Luật Báo chí — a press agency can compel an official answer within thirty days, and must explain why it will not publish you
trackers.desc: The press law gives an editor a lever that a citizen does not have directly. Under the press legislation of 2016, the head of a press agency has the right to require the competent agency, organisation or individual to answer an issue that a citizen has raised in the press; and within thirty days of receiving that request, they are responsible for answering in the press. For a community whose letters to an authority go unanswered, that is the practical value of getting an issue published: the answer becomes a legal obligation with a deadline attached, owed publicly rather than privately. The press agency also owes duties to the person who writes in. Press agencies are required to publish citizens' petitions, criticism, news, articles, photographs and other journalistic works, where these accord with the agency's charter and purposes and do not contain the categories of prohibited content the law lists; and where the material is not published, the agency must reply and state the reason if asked. Press agencies must also answer, or ask the competent body or person to answer in writing or in the press, the petitions, complaints and denunciations that citizens send them. A submission to a newsroom is therefore not only an appeal to its news judgement — it carries a duty to respond. Know the refusal grounds before you are met with one. The same law lets authorities decline to give information to the press where it is a state secret, a Party secret, personal privacy or another legally protected secret; where it concerns a case under investigation or not yet tried; where a matter is under inspection with no conclusion issued, or is in the course of complaint or denunciation resolution, or is a dispute between state bodies without an official conclusion that may not yet be published; or where policies and projects are still in draft and not cleared for release. Several of those grounds are time-limited rather than permanent: a refusal because an inspection is ongoing is an answer that expires when the conclusion issues. Corrections have their own clock. Where a correction or apology is required, electronic newspapers must publish it as soon as the concluding document is received or the error is discovered, and periodicals appearing less often than monthly must reply in writing immediately and publish in the next issue. Read this with the denunciation procedure, the access to information law, the community investment supervision board and the state legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Quỹ Bảo vệ và Phát triển rừng — payment for forest environmental services, paid per hectare to households and village communities
trackers.desc: Holding forest is paid work here, and the money comes from the users downstream. A national forest protection and development fund under the agriculture ministry, with provincial funds beneath it, administers payment for forest environmental services — a policy this country was the first in the region to institutionalise nationally, in 2010. Reported figures record the national fund targeting collection of 2,800 billion đồng in a single year with 70 per cent to be disbursed to forest owners, expressly including households, individuals and village communities, sustaining coverage of 6.7 million hectares — some 45 per cent of the country's forest — and earlier protection contracts covering more than 5.8 million hectares. For a community deciding whether it can afford to keep forest standing instead of converting or selling, this is the fund that pays them to keep it. The rate depends on which catchment you are in, and the differences are large. Reporting to the national assembly records provisional unit prices in one province ranging from over 200,000 đồng per hectare per year in the catchments of certain hydropower plants to under 100,000 in others, and as little as 46,000 in one — with contracted protection rates also differing markedly between places, prompting comparisons of entitlement between contracted households. Ask which catchment your forest falls in and what the current unit price for it is, because that single fact decides the value of the arrangement. Two documented failure points to check for. The same reporting records that funds have had persistent difficulty collecting arrears from hydropower plants, so that ordinary payments collected through electricity and water bills have not always reached the fund and the forest protection groups supplying the service; and that in one province hundreds of eligible forest owners had not opened accounts and hundreds more did not yet meet payment conditions, leaving billions of đồng held undistributed. If payment has not arrived, the question is whether it was collected, whether you are recorded as eligible, and whether an account is open. The rules changed recently. A 2024 decree clarified who must pay, adding industrial production facilities using water from the source, and broadened what organisational forest owners may spend receipts on; a separate decree pilots transfer of emission reduction results, with a regional emission reductions payment agreement funded at tens of millions of dollars. Read this with the community land use certificate, the compensation and resettlement rule and the published judgments entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Nghị định 93 — an individual may raise money publicly, with a written notice to the commune, a separate bank account and published accounts
trackers.desc: An individual can lawfully appeal for money here, provided the steps are followed. The 2021 decree on mobilising, receiving, distributing and using voluntary contributions — for overcoming difficulties caused by natural disasters, epidemics and incidents, and for supporting patients with critical illness — sets out what an individual must do. They must announce through the media the purpose, scope, method and form of the appeal, the receiving account for money and the receiving location for goods, and the committed distribution period; and they must send that same information in writing to the commune-level people's committee where they reside, using the notice form issued with the decree. The commune keeps that notice and supplies the information on request to contributors, recipients and inspecting authorities. A separate account for each appeal. The individual must open a dedicated account at a commercial bank for each appeal to receive and manage all the money contributed, arrange a suitable place to receive and safeguard contributions in kind during the receiving period, and issue receipts for cash and goods where the contributor asks. They must keep a book recording in full the results of receipt and distribution by beneficiary and area, including conditional contributions and specific addresses where given. The end of the receiving period is a hard stop. The decree provides that no further contributions may be received after the committed receiving period ends, and that the individual must notify the bank where the account was opened to stop receiving contributions. That single rule prevents the most common complaint against community appeals: money still arriving after the purpose has been met. Disclosure is on a published timetable. Guidance on the decree records that the document calling for contributions is disclosed immediately after issue; the time, place and method of receiving are disclosed one to three days before receiving begins; the total mobilised and received is disclosed no later than fifteen days after the receiving period ends; and the written result is sent to the commune people's committee where the individual resides to be posted publicly at its office for thirty days. The individual must also coordinate with the people's committee where support is delivered, and provide information to competent authorities on request. Read this with the forest environmental services fund, the community land use certificate, the press law duties and the published judgments entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Trung tâm tư vấn pháp luật — free legal advice through the association you already belong to, and law schools can run one too
trackers.desc: Membership of an association is the route to a free lawyer here. A provincial justice department's analysis of the legal advice decree records that legal advice centres provide advice free of charge to the members and affiliates of their parent organisation, and that the state encourages them to advise poor people and those entitled to preferential policies without charge. The activity is defined as social in character and not for profit. For a farming household or a village group, the practical question is therefore which association it already belongs to — a farmers' union, a women's union, a professional or trade association — because that membership carries an advice entitlement. Who may establish a centre, and where it may reach. Socio-political organisations, socio-political-professional organisations and social-professional organisations at provincial and district level may establish a centre within their locality; training institutions and specialised legal research institutions may establish one within the province where they are based. Centres belonging to central or sectoral level organisations, and to law schools and research institutions, may open branches nationwide, while a provincial-level organisation's centre may open branches within its own province. The name must contain the words for legal advice centre and show the parent organisation's name. That means a law faculty in the provincial capital is a legitimate place to ask. The centre operates from the date of its registration certificate. A centre may operate from the day the operating registration certificate is issued, with the justice ministry prescribing the form of that certificate and of the legal adviser's card — so a community can ask to see both before relying on advice. Published commentary records that establishment requires meeting conditions on premises and personnel. How centres are funded, which tells you what to expect. Funding comes from the parent organisation's regular operating budget for centres established by socio-political organisations; from state legal aid funds where the centre has registered to take part in legal aid; from fees charged to those outside the free categories; and from support and donations by domestic and foreign individuals and organisations. A centre registered for legal aid is the one to look for if you are outside the membership. Read this with the state legal aid entry, the bar federation, the community land use certificate and the published judgments entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Giấy phép khai thác khoáng sản — which authority licenses what, the provincial lists including revoked and expired permits, and the vessel registrations behind sand mining
trackers.desc: Two authorities license minerals, and knowing which one holds your file is the first step. The geology agency's published answer records that under the minerals legislation the competent authority at central level is the natural resources and environment ministry and at local level the provincial people's committee; that the ministry issues survey, exploration and extraction licences; and that extraction and processing licences for ordinary construction materials and peat are issued to domestic organisations, including for areas straddling provincial boundaries, after the ministry has issued the exploration licence and approved the exploration results. Sand, gravel and quarry stone fall under ordinary construction materials, which is why most such licences are provincial. Provinces publish lists, including the ones that have ended. Provincial departments publish mineral licence catalogues, among them lists of extraction licences that have been revoked by decision, and notices of the licensing situation naming a company whose licence, already extended twice, has expired. A licence that has expired or been revoked but whose site is still being worked is the clearest complaint a community can make, and the list is where the expiry is proved. Sand mining is licensed vessel by vessel. A city department's published notice records, for named companies, each registered vessel with its bucket capacity in cubic metres, its extraction capacity in cubic metres per day, the registration confirmation number and date, and the date to which extraction is permitted — and records that one company had two of its four registered vessels actually operating under the licence. It also records suspension of filling-sand extraction on a named river stretch by a numbered departmental notice. Vessel identifiers, daily capacities and end dates are all things a riverside community can check against what is on the water. What the file must contain before a licence issues. A published provincial instruction records that an application to extract or process minerals must include an extraction and processing project and an environmental impact assessment appraised and approved as required; that the licence must conform to the approved planning; that enterprises must comply strictly with the environmental restoration deposit obligation and with mine closure after extraction ends; and that the list of mineral deposits in the area is to be supplied to districts and cities for local management and protection. Ask the district for that list. Where the procedure is published. Provincial resources departments publish the licensing procedure with the office that receives the file, the receipt with a stated return date, and the counter where the result is collected. Read this with the forest environmental services fund, the published judgments, the legal advice centres and the individual fundraising decree entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Bảo vệ người tố cáo — protection covers your family too, the name is stripped from the file, and there is a written application form
trackers.desc: The protection extends to the denouncer's family, by name. A provincial justice department's explanation of the 2018 denunciation legislation records that protection of a denouncer means protecting the confidentiality of their information and protecting the work position, employment, life, health, property, honour and dignity of the denouncer and of their spouse, natural father, natural mother, adoptive father, adoptive mother, natural children and adopted children. That list is the answer to the first fear a person has before reporting an illegal quarry or a forged land file. The trigger is threat or retaliation, and the decision can be taken without waiting for you to ask. Published explanations record that where there are grounds that the work position, employment, life, health, property, honour or dignity of the denouncer or those family members is being infringed or is at immediate risk, or that they are being victimised or discriminated against because of the denunciation, the person handling the denunciation or another competent body decides on its own initiative or at the denouncer's request to apply necessary protection measures; and that people's committees at all levels, trade unions at all levels and other bodies must coordinate in carrying that protection out. Three named classes of measure, in three named articles. Published summaries record measures to protect information, to protect work position and employment, and to protect life, health, property, honour and dignity, set out in three consecutive articles. Information protection includes removing the name, address, handwriting and other personal details from the denunciation and its attached documents and managing them under confidentiality rules when the content is sent for verification, and asking related bodies to take necessary steps to keep the information secret. Employment protection includes suspending or annulling part or all of an adverse decision, requiring an employer to end the violation and restore the position, income and other lawful benefits, and considering a transfer to other work with the person's consent to avoid victimisation. Life and property protection includes moving the person to a safe place, assigning personnel, means and equipment to protect them where necessary, and applying measures to stop or deal with acts or threats. Applying is a written act with prescribed contents. Published material records that an application for protection states the date of the request, the name and address of the denouncer, the name and address of the person to be protected, the reason and content of the request, and the signature or fingerprint of the denouncer; and that a protected person must comply with the protecting body's requirements, keep the protection arrangements confidential and report promptly any problems arising during the protection period. Read this with the individual fundraising decree, the mineral licence lists, the legal advice centres and the published judgments entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Luật Di sản văn hóa — the project owner must halt work on finding relics, zone I stays untouched, and work outside the zones can still need cultural appraisal
trackers.desc: The duty to stop falls on the project owner, not on the community. The cultural heritage legislation provides that where, in the course of renovation or construction, it appears there may be a relic site or relics, antiquities or national treasures, the project owner must temporarily halt construction and promptly notify the competent state cultural authority; and published guidance records that on receiving such notice the authority must take timely measures so as to keep the construction schedule. A resident who sees pottery, bones or foundations coming out of a trench therefore has a specific duty to point to, owed by the developer. Two protection zones, with different rules. Zone I comprises the relic and the area determined as the original constituent elements, and must be preserved in its original state as to ground plan and space; zone II surrounds or adjoins zone I, protects the landscape and ecological environment, and is where works serving conservation and enhancement may be built. Construction in zone II requires written consent — from the provincial people's committee chairman for a provincial-level relic and from the culture minister for national and special national relics — and must not affect the original constituent elements, the natural landscape or the ecological environment. The implementing decree records how zone I is drawn for each kind of relic, including that for an archaeological site the whole area where relics, terrain and landscape directly related to the living environment of those who created it were found must be kept in its original state, and that for a scenic landscape the integrity of natural scenery, terrain and other geographical features containing biodiversity or an unusual ecosystem must be preserved. Ask which zone a project sits in, and who signed the consent. Even outside the zones there can be an appraisal requirement. Published guidance records that when approving a renovation or construction project located outside the protection zones, if it is considered capable of adversely affecting the natural landscape and ecological environment of the relic, a written appraisal opinion of the competent cultural authority is required. That is the provision for a project next door rather than on top. The enforcement precedent exists. Press reporting records a city culture department requiring suspension of construction and of all related activities for works inside relic grounds, restoration of the original ground and space, and stricter monitoring of building and restoration within relics; and another culture department recommending immediate dismantling of unlawful works inside zone I and the area adjoining it at a royal tomb, technical measures to restore the site, and formal review of the responsibility of the bodies and individuals involved. Read this with the denouncer protection, the mineral licence lists, the legal advice centres and the published judgments entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Cây Di sản Việt Nam — a community proposes, the owner registers, and a national association recognises; the age, height and girth criteria
trackers.desc: The community proposes the tree and the owner registers it — that is how the scheme is described. Published accounts record that the selection and honouring of heritage trees was initiated by the national nature and environment protection association in 2010; that a heritage tree is a large woody tree, naturally grown or planted, living more than one hundred years if planted and more than two hundred years if naturally grown, with one or more values of landscape, environment, science, culture or history; and that such a tree is proposed by the community, registered by the tree's owner, recognised by the association and conserved as well as possible. That sequence is the practical route, and it starts with the neighbours rather than with an authority. The criteria are published, and there is a third category for trees that fall short. Reporting of the association's heritage tree council records the criteria as: for naturally grown trees, living over two hundred years, large and majestic, with values of biodiversity and environment, culture and history; for planted trees, the same but over one hundred years; and for other trees, those close to meeting either standard but of special scientific, biodiversity, historical, cultural or aesthetic value. A tree that misses the age test can still qualify on significance. The measurements, and how they are taken. Reporting of the council chair's account records minimum dimensions for naturally grown trees — for woody trees a height of at least twenty-five metres and trunk girth of at least six metres; for banyan and related Ficus species a height of at least fifteen metres and a main trunk girth of at least six metres, or at least ten metres counting the aerial roots — and records that a tree must have a lawful manager or owner. Published guidance records that girth is measured at 1.3 metres above the ground for a single-trunk tree, twenty centimetres above the buttress where a tree has buttress roots, and around the aerial roots as well for banyan and related species. Measure it the way the criteria say. What the dossier looks like in practice, and the honest limit. Reporting of one recognition records a site management board working with the ward people's committee to conduct a field survey and prepare the registration dossier for the association and its heritage tree council to appraise, with the certificate later presented at a public ceremony and the trees recorded as strictly protected by the neighbourhood community. Other reporting records a recognised tree that declined and died despite local efforts, and notes calls for specific binding regulations to conserve heritage trees — so treat recognition as standing and attention rather than a legal bar on felling. Read this with the cultural heritage protection zones, the forest environmental services payments, the individual fundraising decree and the denouncer protection entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Tham vấn cộng đồng in the environmental assessment — who counts as directly affected, the fifteen-day online consultation window, and the village posting and meeting the project owner must hold
trackers.desc: The residential community is written into the law as a subject of environmental protection. An environment agency's account of the 2020 legislation records that the residential community is prescribed as a subject in environmental protection work, with strengthened disclosure of information and consultation, an enhanced role in supervision and critique, and its rights and interests assured when it takes part; and records that the law sets out clearly the responsibility to consult, who is consulted, the main content of consultation and its forms, and that the result of consulting the residential community and related organisations is important information for the project owner to study in devising measures to reduce the project's environmental impact and to complete the assessment report. That last sentence is the one to quote where a consultation result has plainly changed nothing in the report. Who counts as directly affected is defined, and it is wider than the land take. Published legal material records the directly affected as including the community and individuals living, producing or doing business in the area of land, water surface, land with water surface or sea area occupied for the project; the community and individuals within the direct impact range of the project's wastewater, emissions, dust, noise, solid waste and hazardous waste; and others affected by the project's activities. A household outside the boundary but inside the dust or noise footprint is therefore a consultee by definition. Two forms of consultation, with dates attached. The same material records that before submitting the report for appraisal, the project owner sends the consultation content to the unit managing the appraising authority's website; that unit must post it within five days of the request; the consultation runs for fifteen days; and at the end the unit must send the consultation result to the project owner — excluding state and business secrets. It records the second form as a meeting: the project owner, together with the commune people's committee where the project is located, posts the assessment report at the committee's office and notifies the community. Someone who cannot attend the meeting can still read the report and comment online. Disclosure continues after approval, and an online channel exists. Published material records the law requiring publication of the appraisal approval decision, publication by the project owner of the approved assessment report, and of the content of the environmental licence application, excluding secrets, for the opinions of interested parties; and records an online system to receive, handle and answer reflections, petitions and consultations from organisations, individuals and residential communities. Read this with the community investment supervision board, the pollution hotlines, the information access law and the denunciation law entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: VNSDI — the national spatial data portal, the administrative map reissued after the 2025 merger of provinces, and the mapping authority that holds the national base data
trackers.desc: There is a national spatial data portal, and it is the official source for boundaries after the administrative merger. Published description records the portal as the Vietnam national spatial data infrastructure, managed by the survey, mapping and geographic information department, an online platform aggregating and providing geospatial data, maps and related information for state management, scientific research and socio-economic development; and records it providing the administrative map system updated to the current thirty-four provinces and cities, at scales from the national base map to detailed provincial maps, with data grouped into named layer sets including the administrative map, provincial boundary data and hosted online services for integration. Where a boundary changed in the 2025 reorganisation, this is where the current line is. The department issued the new administrative map as the base document for local correction. Reporting records the department as having provided the new administrative map of the thirty-four provinces and cities as the source data for localities to correct and update commune boundaries accurately, describing it as the official and unified base document on which localities continue to update and supplement commune-level boundary detail according to actual management; and records the department preparing to complete a national administrative map at a stated small scale to be provided free to ministries, localities and the public online. A community whose commune boundary is disputed can therefore name the base document the correction must start from. The portal's stated services are the practical part. Reporting of its development records it operating as an electronic means allowing access to national geospatial data and providing related information and services, the services being sharing, converting, analysing, integrating, looking up and downloading framework data and sector data. Published description records online lookup and analysis tools among its functions. The department also publishes the rules and the fees. The department's own site carries the surveying and mapping legislation and its instruments, including a circular amending an earlier one, a national technical regulation on the process for producing the national topographic map, and new provisions on charging fees for the use of surveying and mapping information and data, and records the administrative procedures in the surveying and mapping field as standardised by a published ministerial decision. Read this with the land data provision entry, the community investment supervision board, the assessment consultation and the judgment publication entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The land and forest network and the alliance behind it — organisations that train communities to gather evidence for customary forest land claims, and the seventeen articles they got into the Forestry Law
trackers.desc: An alliance of domestic organisations works with communities on customary forest land, and says what it changed. A member institute records an alliance of named science and technology organisations with more than thirty years working with ethnic minority communities, contributing to keeping and maintaining indigenous knowledge to enrich biodiversity and secure ecological and cultural livelihood sovereignty based on the community economy; and records that through the alliance's research and consultation input, seventeen articles were accepted into the numbered 2017 Forestry Law. A community citing those provisions is citing text these organisations helped write. Communities can be trained to collect the evidence a claim needs. A member organisation's programme page records four commitments: continuing to support communities in the land and forest network through research and training in how to collect the evidence needed to advocate for customary forest land rights; developing cooperation with partners in the country and the region to jointly address problems arising from large-scale development programmes in the river basin; promoting exchange of experience in implementing the forestry legislation between communities, and between community representatives and policy makers, state officials, civil society and community organisations; and using evidence to support the state in developing and implementing land and forest laws in the direction of respecting the traditional rights of ethnic minority communities. The gap they work in is documented. A rural development centre records that issue of land use right certificates for forest land to communities remains slow and problematic, with incomplete statistics separating forest allocated to communities but without a certificate, forest with a certificate, and forest the community recognises as its own; and records that communities participating in forest management without being granted ownership — including forests managed traditionally under the customary law of ethnic minorities — creates difficulties and risks forest loss and degradation. Field practice shows what a supported model contains. A development centre records a community-based forest management model built with a resource management centre and the district forest protection unit, in its first year supporting a forest patrol plan, a forest management convention, and rules for using a livelihood fund, with funding for livelihood models, and records participating communities sharing their own indigenous patrol knowledge. Read this with the forest allocation entry, the forest environmental services payment, the communal certificate and the consultation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: FORLAND — a nine-member forest and land alliance formed from two networks, its named member organisations, and its record of work on land recovered from state farms and forestry enterprises
trackers.desc: A named alliance of domestic organisations works on forest and land, and its members are listed. The alliance records itself as a network connecting organisations and individuals working in the forestry field, formed in 2012 to contribute to building and improving policies for better management and development of forest resources and to improve the livelihoods of communities whose livelihoods are tied to land and forest. It records itself as the merger of a central-region land rights network of local organisations and a forest-land network, to create diversity and increase collective strength, and as cooperating with the press and media to influence policy makers' decisions. It lists nine core member organisations by name, including centres for rural development, resource management research and consultancy, indigenous knowledge research, a people and nature centre, and a rural development and poverty reduction fund. A community looking for help can approach the nearest member rather than a network in the abstract. Its advocacy targets the land held by state farms and forestry enterprises. The alliance records continuing advocacy on ethnic minority communities' access to land arising from the recovery of land from state agricultural and forestry enterprises, active participation in building the 2017 forestry legislation, and participation in supporting the drafting of the decrees under it. Where a community's claim is against a state enterprise's holding, that is the body already working on it. Earlier project work names the specific problems. Published material records the alliance in 2014 running four issue-based projects with a stated total budget, led by named members: promoting policy advocacy and review of land recovery, review of agricultural and forestry enterprises, and resolving shortcomings in land and forest allocation; community consultation and policy advocacy on the forest protection and development legislation; and mainstreaming gender in that legislation and its subordinate documents. A separate national organisations' network on forest law enforcement and trade is recorded as having grown in membership and standing, treated as an important partner to be consulted in those processes, with member organisations' research, communication and advocacy capacity raised. Read this with the alliance and evidence-training entry, the forest allocation, the community forest agreements and the consultation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: CSRD — a Huế centre that sets up village research groups to document what a hydropower dam changed, runs gender impact assessments at named dams, and publishes the results
trackers.desc: Villages here have been organised into their own research groups to record what a dam did to them. The centre records that in 2013 and 2014 it supported five communities in two named provinces to establish five indigenous knowledge research groups, and encouraged them to carry out research on the changes in their lives and local environment caused by hydropower. A community that can produce its own documented account of change is in a different position from one that can only object. The centre records its purpose as raising the capacity and resilience of communities to adapt and respond to industrial development, climate change, hydropower construction, agricultural development and gender inequality, working through four main activities beginning with field research on problems from the community level, keeping information updated at every stage of a project, and creating change and awareness through training courses and advocacy. It has run impact assessments at named dams, including on gender. It records a pilot gender impact assessment at two named hydropower schemes on tributaries of a shared river system, with study areas being communities affected by three numbered dams, and records group discussions held with people from a dam resettlement area in a named hamlet and with affected communities in named villages, distinguishing patrilineal and matrilineal communities. It records the assessment as a learning process aimed at maximising the participation of different stakeholders rather than only a final product, ending with recommendations on the assessment toolkit itself. Its water governance work built livelihood models with villages. The centre records a water resource governance project from 2016 under which it established four community livelihood models in three named hamlets and a commune across three districts of a highland province, and records that province's river tributaries as holding the richest natural aquatic resources of that river system in the region. It publishes its street address in a named city, explains what a donation buys — a training course, a solar water heater, a household biogas digester — and records earlier work assessing a foreign agency's empowerment principles. Read this with the forest and land alliance, the evidence-training entry, the consultation requirement and the community forest entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: SRD — a registered science and technology centre working in 42 provinces, with water user associations formed in named villages and a forest law enforcement and governance programme
trackers.desc: A domestic centre works with rural communities across most of the country, and publishes what it has delivered. The centre records its projects as focusing on sustainable agriculture and livelihoods; climate change and disaster risk reduction; forest law enforcement, governance and trade; support for people with disabilities; gender equality and child protection; the free trade agreement with the European Union; and research and advocacy in related fields, with interventions supporting communities in poverty reduction, environmental protection, climate adaptation and mitigation, and raising people's governance capacity so they can better manage their own development. It records having carried out, over fifteen years, 88 projects including 14 small projects, with total funding of 14.6 million dollars, across 42 provinces and cities, and records mobilising around 20 million euros over nineteen years, with roughly 350,000 direct and 400,000 indirect beneficiaries. It describes its aim as becoming a pioneering science and technology organisation in sustainable development, climate change and renewable energy, and supporting poor people from strengthening grassroots community capacity to national policy recommendations. Water user associations are the concrete output a community can copy. Its programme pages record a project assessing water supply and demand and training on rational water management and use in 16 project villages, which established 16 water user associations with 454 participants and began forming local rules on water use, protection and the collection of water use fees; and record eight forums on the role of forests. It records the project running from January 2021 to December 2023, led by the centre with the district people's committee, the crop production and plant protection sub-department and the provincial forest protection sub-department, aiming at mitigating climate impacts through community forest management and getting adaptation measures integrated into policies with the necessary budget allocated by the state. It also works through existing local bodies. Its records include environmental awareness sessions organised jointly with a diocesan social charity committee in a named province, focused on water and air pollution in a named town and a craft village commune, with suggestions for limiting pollution. Read this with the forest and land alliance, the community research centre, the forest allocation and the consultation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: MCD — a registered science and technology non-profit for coastal communities, training core groups in co-management of fisheries resources, and consulting communities on the rules that govern them
trackers.desc: Coastal communities have a registered domestic organisation whose licence number is published. The centre records itself as a non-public science and technology organisation operating not for profit in marine environmental conservation and sustainable coastal development, licensed by the science and technology ministry under a stated registration number since 2003, and a member of a national marine science and technology association and the national union of science and technology associations — the union already recorded in this bucket. Published description records it as a Vietnamese non-governmental organisation with experience in more than ten coastal provinces and close to 70 projects, working through two main programmes — marine resource and environmental management, and sustainable livelihoods, fisheries management and community development. Its practical work is building the community side of co-management. Its own records describe training to raise the capacity of core groups implementing co-management in protecting fisheries resources, covering knowledge and skills in managing and protecting those resources in the central coastal region, with group work on drawing up local plans to manage and protect fisheries resources; and record a district agriculture official stating that the training supported the local core group and that, based on the annual plan, the parties would organise the community and support funding from the local budget. Getting the local budget named as the funding source is the step that makes a community arrangement last. It also brings communities into the drafting of the rules. Its listings record local and community consultation on draft legal documents guiding implementation of the 2017 fisheries legislation, and sharing of experience in devolving rights to communities to manage, protect, exploit and develop sea areas containing coral reefs; record a community conference on co-management in protecting fisheries resources in a named commune; and record training for shrimp cooperatives on market mapping and livelihood initiatives. Its team is described as covering resource and environmental management, community development, marine biology, economics, law, communications, training and social science, and its office room, floor, building and telephone are published. Read this with the fisheries co-management provisions, the community research centre, the forest and land alliance and the rural development centre entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: CIRD and the university community centre — provincial advisers who walked two named hamlets through forest allocation with the district people's committee, and a Huế centre that builds fisher chapters at lagoon level
trackers.desc: A district people's committee and an advisory centre took one hamlet all the way to a land certificate, and the province published it. The provincial portal records that on 30 July 2014 the district people's committee, in coordination with a named research centre, held a closing ceremony for forest allocation tied to forest land allocation, and handed over the land use right certificate for forest land to the residential community of a named hamlet in a named commune; and records that through close participation and coordination between the local authority, the centre's advisory staff and the agencies preparing the land dossier, the programme was carried out according to the correct order and procedures. For a hamlet wanting title to the forest it already uses, that is the exact combination — district committee, technical adviser, dossier agency — that produced a certificate. It was the second such model, and the first is named too. Published reporting records the centre's deputy director stating that this was the second model after forest land allocation to the residential community of a named ethnic group in another named commune, carried out successfully by the centre in coordination with the district people's committee, and strongly supported by the people; and records that from then the hamlet's people are truly the owners of the named forest. Published material records the centre as belonging to the national union of science and technology associations, with staff assigned to research indigenous knowledge and assist a named ethnic community in a named village and commune. A university centre does the same work on the lagoon. A university department records a community research and development centre whose activities include building the network of fisher association chapters on a named lagoon system from 2002 to 2009, community-based coastal resource management research, planning a wetland conservation area at a named river mouth, and a pilot model devolving fishing rights; and records its services as including consultancy and technical services for rural, agricultural and forestry development programmes and training to raise the capacity of communities, management staff, local officials, and fisher association staff and members for building community organisations and co-managing natural resources. Read this with the coastal co-management centre, the community research centre, the forest and land alliance and the rural development centre entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The commune People's Inspection Board — members elected at hamlet meetings, one seat per hamlet, power to demand rectification from the commune chairman, and quarterly reporting
trackers.desc: Every commune has an inspection board whose members are elected in the hamlets, not appointed. Published material records that members of the commune-level people's inspection board are elected at a meeting of the residential community, that the board consists of members elected from the hamlets and residential groups in the commune, and that the number of members corresponds to the number of hamlets and residential groups but is not fewer than five, with the commune fatherland front committee deciding the exact number on the principle that every hamlet and residential group has a representative on the board. One seat per hamlet, filled at a village meeting, is as close to a resident's own seat as this system offers. Its powers are aimed at the commune's own officials. Published material records the board's tasks as checking the implementation of decisions the people have discussed and decided; supervising the implementation of policy and law, and of the law on grassroots democracy, by the commune-level local authority, its cadres and civil servants and part-time workers in the commune and in the hamlets and residential groups; and recommending that the competent body or person handle the matter under the law when signs of legal violation are found, and supervising the implementation of that recommendation. It records the board recommending to the chairman of the commune people's committee, commune cadres and civil servants, hamlet heads and residential group leaders that they remedy limitations and shortcomings found through inspection and supervision, and notifying the results of inspection, supervision and verification in writing to whoever raised the matter. Its term, its standards and its reporting are all fixed. Published material records the board's term as following that of the hamlet heads and residential group leaders in the same area, and records the member standard as good moral character, prestige in the residential community, sufficient health, understanding of policy and law, and voluntary participation. It records the board reporting to the commune fatherland front committee on results quarterly, six-monthly, annually, for the term, and irregularly on request or when something arises, and records that if a member no longer holds confidence, the hamlet that elected them is asked to consider removing them. Read this with the community investment supervision board, the commune forest allocation advisers, the coastal co-management centre and the rural development centre entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Provincial state legal aid centres and their branches — free lawyers for named categories including ethnic minority residents of disadvantaged areas, mobile sessions in communes, and village heads as the referral route
trackers.desc: Each province has a state legal aid centre, and it travels to the communes. One provincial department records its centre, after more than twenty years, as having organised more than 1,500 mobile legal aid sessions in communes, wards and townships for tens of thousands of people; more than 800 sessions combining legal aid with legal dissemination in remote, upland and ethnic minority communes and communes with special difficulties under poverty reduction policy; more than 10,000 cases advised and assisted at the office and on mobile trips; and 2,365 cases in which it represented, defended or protected the rights of eligible people. Mobile sessions in a commune are the version of legal aid that reaches a village without a bus fare. Who qualifies is listed, and land disputes are the worked example. Published guidance records eligible categories including ethnic minority people residing in areas with especially difficult socio-economic conditions, people in near-poor households, and others; and records that a woman in that category pays no fee of any kind, receives explanation and advice on the land dispute, guidance on writing the application and preparing the file, and, where necessary, a lawyer or legal aid officer assigned to represent and protect her rights in dealings with the authorities or at court, continuing until the case ends. The referral route runs through people a village already knows. The same guidance records that a person may go to the provincial state legal aid centre where they live, a branch of the centre in the region if there is one, or contact the women's union, the commune people's committee, the village or hamlet head, or people trained as legal collaborators. Filing is a written request, and the state pays. Published guidance records that a requester submits a legal aid request file to the provincial centre, a branch, or a participating organisation, which enters it in the acceptance and case-monitoring register; and records that the beneficiary pays no fee, the cost of the person providing legal aid being borne by the state, with rights including being informed of the right to legal aid and the procedure, and requiring confidentiality about the content of the case. Read this with the commune inspection board, the community supervision board, the commune forest allocation advisers and the coastal co-management centre entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: District land registration branch offices — where a household asks for a cadastral map extract, the commune office as an alternative counter, the five-working-day survey deadline, and the written refusal rule
trackers.desc: A household can ask for a cadastral map extract at its own district branch, and one province publishes where. A provincial department records the competent bodies as the provincial land registration office and the district branches of that office, and records where to file: for four named districts and the provincial city, at the district or city receiving and returning results counter; for the remaining districts, at the district branch of the land registration office, with organisations able to file also at surveying bodies in the province, and receiving hours given by the morning session. Published guidance adds that an extract may be requested at the land registration office, its district branch, or the commune people's committee. For a household whose boundary is in doubt, three counters are named, one of them in the commune. What the extract is, and is not, is stated plainly. Published legal guidance records that the extract is not a legal document proving the land user's right to use the land; it only provides information and characteristics of a particular parcel, and is evidence in cases resolving land-related disputes, listing its uses as land registration; applying for a land use right certificate; re-issue of a certificate; a basis for resolving land disputes; on the request of a person applying for land allocation or lease; and applying to change land use purpose. Knowing the extract is evidence rather than title stops a family relying on the wrong document. The deadline for a fresh survey and the refusal rule are both fixed. Published material records that where a registration file has no cadastral survey sheet, the district land management body requests the branch office, which must check and approve the survey sheet, or carry out the survey, within not more than five working days of receiving the request, the land user paying the cost as prescribed. The national public service portal records that the office must extract the parcel or area as requested and pass the result to the receiving and returning counter for delivery to the land user, and that where data is refused, a written reply stating the reason must be given — with refusal grounds listed, including requests whose content is not clear and specific, and forms lacking the signature, name and specific address of the individual requesting. Read this with the commune inspection board, the provincial legal aid centres, the commune forest allocation advisers and the community supervision board entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The district compensation and resettlement council — a seat for representatives of the people whose land is taken, 30 days' public posting at the commune office, and a minuted meeting that counts the votes against
trackers.desc: The draft compensation plan must be posted publicly, and then discussed at a meeting whose minutes record the opposition. A city legal information service records that the implementing body posts the compensation, support and resettlement plan publicly at the commune people's committee headquarters and at the communal activity location of the residential area where the land is to be recovered, and that immediately after the posting period ends, opinions on the plan are collected by holding a direct meeting with the people in the area, with those unable to attend for a legitimate reason sending opinions in writing. It records that the collection of opinions must be recorded in minutes stating the number of opinions agreeing, the number disagreeing and the number of other opinions on the plan, together with the receipt and explanation of comments, certified by a representative of the commune people's committee and by representatives of the people whose land is recovered.
