Its goals include strengthening the ability of communities and community organisations — named ahead of government agencies — to conserve biodiversity, and supporting conservation of priority natural biodiversity resource areas. THE REGIONAL PRECEDENT IS LARGE: the Micronesia Challenge has aided in strengthening or establishing over 150 protected areas, so comparable local examples exist. Also active and named in the partnership records: OneReef, Island Conservation, RARE, the Pacific Marine Resources Institute, and PIMPAC, which shares community and government approaches to enforcement of marine managed areas. Micronesians in Island Conservation is a peer network of the national societies with a member-nominated steering committee, offering members peers, mentors and experts, with MCT funding its annual retreats. IN MICRONESIA THE ORGANISATIONS ARE STATE-BY-STATE, NOT NATIONAL — approach the one for your state: the Conservation Society of Pohnpei, the Kosrae Conservation and Safety Organization, and the Chuuk Conservation Society are each named in the published partnership records.

trackers.name: Palau Conservation Society (PCS)
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: Palau's first environmental NGO, founded in 1994 during a period of rapid development and still the country's leading conservation organisation — community-based, a BirdLife partner, working across marine and terrestrial ecosystems from Koror. It supports STATES in preparing Protected Areas Network site plans and protected-area management plans, with the stated aim of building each state's own capacity rather than managing on its behalf, and runs a Private Lands Initiative extending conservation onto land outside the state system. USE IT: if your state or village wants a conservation area recognised and managed, PCS is the body that helps write and run the plan. It implements national policy rather than opposing it, and says openly that what it can take on is limited by staff and funding.

trackers.name: Palau Protected Areas Network Fund (PAN Fund)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: the independent non-profit that acts as financial trustee for Palau's Protected Areas Network, holding and disbursing money raised from donations and from the arrival fee paid by visitors. Areas enter the network at the initiative of state governments, traditional leaders and individuals who have protected land or reef inside their own boundaries; the Fund then supports the running of those sites, including enforcement coordination and conservation training. WHO IT SUITS: states, traditional leaders and landholders whose area is a PAN site or could become one. This is money for managing a designated protected area, not a grant for campaigning against a project. HOW IT DIFFERS: it is financed by a visitor arrival fee rather than by donor cycles, which makes it far steadier than most conservation money in the region.

trackers.name: Micronesia Conservation Trust (MCT)
trackers.desc: WHERE TO RAISE MONEY: a conservation trust fund based in Kolonia, Pohnpei, running small-grant programmes across the five Micronesia Challenge jurisdictions and accredited as an entity of the Green Climate Fund. Its stated impact areas include coastal fisheries management plans and actions, forest stewardship, expansion and improvement of Protected Areas Networks, watershed and forest management for climate resilience, invasive species control, and livelihoods tied to conservation. WHO IT SUITS: legally recognised not-for-profits in those jurisdictions — NGOs, associations, schools and universities, church groups, women's groups, youth groups, research bodies — and, importantly, communities themselves: a chartered community can apply directly, and an unchartered one can too if its legitimacy is corroborated in writing by a state or municipal government. HOW IT DIFFERS: it gives priority to projects implementing an EXISTING management plan or Local Early Action Plan over projects that would write a new one, so an already-adopted plan is worth more here than a good idea. Money moves by periodic calls for proposals, not on a rolling basis.

trackers.name: Office of the Public Auditor
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Palau, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Palau — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; manages expenditures, revenues & financing and supports the national budget process, Republic of Palau. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Palau.

trackers.name: Palau — Bureau of Revenue & Taxation (Business Registration)
trackers.desc: National business registry; Palau has no separate companies registrar — all commercial entities must register with the Bureau of Revenue & Taxation (Ministry of Finance) and obtain a business license; foreign investment via the Foreign Investment Board. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: EQPB — earthmoving is regulated in its own right
trackers.desc: A SEPARATE, CHECKABLE PERMIT FOR CLEARING LAND. The Environmental Quality Protection Act, Title 24 of the Palau National Code Annotated (1981), created the Environmental Quality Protection Board, a semi-autonomous agency of the executive branch. Title 24 authorises it to promulgate and enforce regulations on 9 named topics, and the first is EARTHMOVING — alongside marine and fresh water quality, wastewater, solid waste, pesticides, public water supply, environmental impact statements, air pollution and ozone-depleting substances. Site clearance and grading is regulated in its own right, not merely as a component of an EIS — so an earthmoving permit is a separate document to ask for. EQPB issues permits for activities that may affect the environment, including industrial operations, land development and waste disposal. CONTACT: P.O. Box 8086, Bureau of Public Works Building, Koror 96940; tel (680) 488-1639 or 488-3600; fax (680) 488-2963; palaueqpb@gmail.com — recorded as the agency publishes it. The separate Bureau of Environment holds regulatory oversight and enforcement, aiming at a protected areas network defined by science and traditional knowledge.

trackers.name: PAN Act — designation runs upward, and joining unlocks the money
trackers.desc: THE STRUCTURE IS THE REVERSE OF MOST IN THIS MAP. Under the Protected Areas Network Act 2003, state governments, traditional leaders and individuals independently protect areas within their own boundaries, and the national government supports those efforts — designation runs upward. ALL SITES THAT JOIN THE PAN ARE ELIGIBLE TO APPLY FOR PAN FUNDS, used by each site to manage its own resources — so for an existing local protected area the question is whether it has joined, not whether it qualifies. Note that 35 MPAs exist but not all are part of the network. THE MONEY COMES FROM VISITORS: the green fee supports local communities with US$1.8 million annually — a long-running, directly transferable design. WHAT SITES DO: management plans and monitoring protocols built on biological, ecological, socio-economic, cultural and historical gap analyses, baseline data collected in parallel, record-keeping, and enforcement mechanisms including prosecution of illegal fishing or poaching. A DOCUMENTED OUTCOME WORTH CITING: it created jobs so that people returned to their villages, reducing urban drift — reverse migration as a conservation result. THE CUSTOMARY INSTRUMENT: chiefs of Ngarchelong and Kayangel jointly declared the first modern-day bul, a moratorium on fishing in their traditional grounds to protect spawning aggregations — a joint declaration by two communities' chiefs is the precedent for a shared resource. The 2015 National Marine Sanctuary Act closes 80 percent of the EEZ to commercial and extractive activity.

trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: Samoa Conservation Society (Fa’asao Samoa)
trackers.desc: A Samoan NGO established in 2013, working with communities, government and NGO partners on the threats to Samoa's biodiversity and natural heritage — invasive species, over-harvesting, habitat degradation, pollution and climate change — through research, awareness raising and practical conservation carried out with communities. WHO TO ENLIST: SCS if you have a site or a species to protect rather than a project to fight. It states plainly that if you or your group want to run a project protecting Samoa's native species and habitats it wants to hear from you, which is an unusually open door for a country with few options. You CAN'T expect a campaigner or a litigator: it works collaboratively with government, and its strength is research, partnership and practical action rather than opposition.

trackers.name: Samoa — Audit Office (Controller & Auditor General)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution; independent public-sector auditor reporting to Parliament and promoting public-administration accountability, Samoa.

trackers.name: Online Samoa Company Registry
trackers.desc: National — Samoa company register (MCIL), searchable free. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Samoa — Ministry of Finance
trackers.desc: National budget authority; prepares the national budget and publishes fiscal & budget documents, Samoa. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Samoa.

trackers.name: PacLII – Samoa
trackers.desc: Free case law and legislation for Samoa via the Pacific Islands Legal Information Institute. · Find here: free Samoa legislation and court decisions, hosted by PacLII.

trackers.name: The fono makes village law — and which chief controls your land
trackers.desc: IN SAMOA THE DECISION-MAKER FOR VILLAGE LAND IS THE VILLAGE COUNCIL. Under the Village Fono Act 1990, councils hold authority over village law and order and are given additional powers over the development and usage of village land for the betterment of the village, exercised in accordance with the traditional custom and usage of that village. Fono can impose fines, work or banishment, and appoint sub-committees for local matters as they see fit. So a conservation measure adopted by the fono is not a request to government — it is village law with sanctions, and a sub-committee can be created to run it. IDENTIFY YOUR LAND CATEGORY FIRST: customary land divides into village, plantation and settlement land — all village land is controlled by the village chiefs; residential and plantation land by the family chiefs. Get this wrong and you are negotiating with people who do not control the land. Matai are the chiefs, heads of extended families (aiga), in two kinds — tulafale (orator) and ali'i (high chief). FOR A COASTAL VILLAGE: under customary law the waters adjacent to a village were part of the land controlled by that village, and no-take zones were declared by imposing tabu, with fines in money or pigs — the customary precedent for a village-declared marine closure.

trackers.name: Land classification is a lever — and village by-laws may become justiciable
trackers.desc: TWO THINGS TO CHECK BEFORE ACTING. 1. THE CLASSIFICATION OF YOUR LAND IS ITSELF A LEVER. The Land, Surveys and Environment Act 1989 provides for establishing national parks and other protected areas, and classifies land as farm, urban, or commercial/industrial — with alienation, disposal or reservation determined on the basis of those classifications. So the classification decides what can lawfully happen to the land, and is worth establishing early. MNRE's functions include advising the Minister on all aspects of environmental management and ensuring and promoting conservation of Samoa's natural resources. 2. A CHANGE TO WATCH IN THE COURTS. The Land and Titles Court arbitrates disputes over customary land and matai titles — and under the 2020 reform package (Land and Titles Bill, Constitution Amendment Bill and Judicature Bill) it gains added powers to adjudicate on village laws passed by village councils, with its own appeal structure separate from the Supreme Court. If village laws become justiciable in a separate court, a fono conservation by-law becomes both more enforceable and more challengeable — check the current position before relying on either. ALSO: the Internal Affairs Division of the Ministry of Women, Community and Social Development oversees village authority. TARGET TO CITE: protected areas covered 5 percent of land in 2010; the government aims for 15 percent.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — citizens may apply
trackers.desc: AN INDIVIDUAL CAN APPLY, AND THE FIRST DOCUMENT IS SHORT. The Pacific Development and Conservation Trust, administered through the New Zealand government's Community Matters service with requests assessed by Advisory Trustees, states that ‘citizens or organisations’ from eligible Pacific places may request funding — so an individual can apply, which is rare and matters where no registered body exists. Eligible places include Kiribati, Tonga, Samoa, Cook Islands, Niue, Nauru, Tuvalu, Fiji, Palau, PNG, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Tokelau, the Marshall Islands, FSM, and the French and US Pacific territories. THE PROCESS IS TWO-STAGE: submit an Expression of Interest, which the Trustees consider; successful applicants are then invited to submit a full project application. Do not prepare a full proposal before the EOI is accepted. Applications must be on the current form with all sections completed, submitted online where connection allows. THE MOST USEFUL THING BEFORE YOU DRAFT: the Trust publishes records of grants by round — 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 (two rounds), 2023/24 and 2024/25. Read the published record of what the Trustees have actually funded, at what size and in which countries — that is better evidence than any guidance note. ONE DISTINCTION THAT AFFECTS HOW YOU REACH UNDP HERE: UNDP's Pacific Office provides country support to ten states — FSM, Fiji, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Nauru, Palau, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu — but only regional support to five, including Samoa, Cook Islands, Niue, PNG and Tokelau. Check which applies to you before expecting an in-country office.

trackers.name: ICCA Registry and Protected Planet — and registration is not a precondition
trackers.desc: CHECK WHETHER YOUR SITE IS ALREADY IN A REGISTRY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — it may carry a designation nobody locally mentioned. The World Database on Protected and Conserved Areas at protectedplanet.net is a joint UNEP and IUCN product managed by UNEP-WCMC, drawing on almost 500 data providers in 245 countries, updated monthly and downloadable; it underpins the UN List of Protected Areas. THE OECM ROUTE IS THE ONE MOST COMMUNITIES MISS: a site qualifies as an other effective area-based conservation measure if it delivers sustained, positive conservation outcomes EVEN THOUGH IT MAY BE MANAGED PRIMARILY FOR OTHER REASONS — so a grazing commons, a sacred site or a watershed managed for water supply can qualify without being managed primarily for conservation. Land that is worked rather than preserved is not excluded. But note the exclusivity: a site can be a protected area or an OECM — it is not possible to meet both, so ask which is being proposed. THE ICCA REGISTRY IS THE ONE COMMUNITIES FILL IN THEMSELVES: at iccaregistry.org, communities themselves provide data, case studies, maps, photos and stories, and its operators state it is meant to be used to enhance advocacy and recognition — not merely as an inventory. Documenting a territory there creates a citable, third-party-hosted record. THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS MOST: UNEP-WCMC states these territories must be recognised and respected ‘whether or not they have been reported to the ICCA Registry’ — registration is NOT a precondition of rights, and anyone arguing a claim is weaker for being unregistered is arguing against the registry operator's own position. AND USE THE SCALE FIGURE CAREFULLY: over 1,500 sites are reported under indigenous and community governance — just 1 percent of all recorded sites, with UNEP-WCMC adding that no one knows how many ICCAs exist globally. That 1 percent measures how little has been recorded, not how little communities conserve. Filter Protected Planet by governance type to find such sites; UNEP-WCMC's manual Global Databases to Support ICCAs gives guidance on contributing data.

trackers.name: SPREP EIA and SEA guidelines — intervene at scoping, not after
trackers.desc: SCOPING IS WHERE STAKEHOLDER CONCERNS BECOME TERMS OF REFERENCE — and the guidelines say so themselves. Assessments must be individually customised to the aspects most relevant to stakeholders, and ‘customisation usually occurs during the scoping phase and results in the preparation of terms of reference’. Intervene at scoping and the assessment is required to examine your issue; intervene later and you are commenting on an assessment that was never asked to look. SPREP's Strengthening Environmental Impact Assessment: Guidelines for Pacific Island Countries and Territories (60pp, English and French) is the regional practice standard, SPREP having been mandated on EIA capacity since the 1990s. KNOW WHICH INSTRUMENT YOUR FIGHT NEEDS: EIA assesses a project; the companion Strategic Environmental Assessment guidelines (developed 2018–2020) assess a policy, plan or programme and are addressed to environment agencies, national planning offices, development control agencies, municipal authorities and provincial administrations — so if the problem is a tourism plan or a zoning programme rather than one hotel, SEA is the instrument and the municipal or provincial authority is the addressee. There is also a sector guideline for coastal tourism development, made with the South Pacific Tourism Organisation. THE HONEST PART, FROM A REGULATOR'S OWN ACCOUNT: Vanuatu's Principal EIA Officer publicly described her department's challenges as lack of staff, lack of political support, weaknesses in public consultation, and low capacity in monitoring and enforcement. Expect to supply evidence the agency cannot gather itself, and expect post-consent monitoring to be weak unless someone outside government does it — it is also a citable admission when arguing that a condition needs an independent monitoring mechanism attached. CHECK YOUR OWN ENVIRONMENT ACT FIRST: many Pacific countries have EIA mandated under their Environment Acts and EIA Regulations, and these guidelines support the implementation of current legal requirements rather than replacing them — the practice standard, not the obligation. SPREP runs in-country EIA training workshops, and the Pacific Environment Portal carries regional and national data.

trackers.name: Waigani Convention — radioactive waste, and 200 miles not 12
trackers.desc: IT REACHES WHERE BASEL CANNOT — and for island states that is the whole point. The Waigani Convention is modelled on Basel and is the regional implementation of the hazardous waste regime, but differs in two decisive ways: it also covers radioactive wastes, and its territorial coverage includes each Party's Exclusive Economic Zone — 200 nautical miles — rather than stopping at the 12 nautical mile territorial sea as Basel does. It is annex-driven: obligations extend to all wastes in Annex I or those possessing the listed characteristics — check Annex I first; if the substance is listed the obligations attach automatically, and if not, the argument runs through the hazard characteristics instead. It is closely tied to the London Convention on dumping at sea. THE BODY TO CONTACT: the Pacific Regional Centre for the Waigani and Basel Conventions, based at SPREP in Samoa, which has developed a model law implementing all four waste conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Waigani) with a worked Tonga project — so where a national statute is missing or fragmented, the model already exists and a government can be pointed at it. AND A CONSULTATION WINDOW IS OPEN NOW: Cleaner Pacific 2025, the regional waste and pollution strategy built with 21 member countries around four goals and 15 strategic actions, is being replaced — the successor CP2036 was endorsed at the 31st SPREP Meeting (September 2023) with consultation in Suva, 21–22 July 2025. Priorities for the next decade are being set now. Ask whether your country has a national waste and pollution policy written against the regional strategy — it is the document your government is measured against. Delivery vehicles include PacWaste Plus (EUR 16.5 million, 72 months, EU-funded, across eight waste streams). THE HONEST LIMIT, FROM SPREP'S OWN REVIEW: Australia's reporting capability far exceeds that of most Pacific island countries, relying on weighbridge data requiring infrastructure that is not available — so do not assume an absence of data means an absence of a problem, and community-gathered data may be the best evidence there is. Watch the Clean Pacific Roundtable and CIRCLE EXPO, held alternately for an annual meeting of countries, industry and civil society — named as a participant category, not an observer.

trackers.name: Right to information — what your country actually has
trackers.desc: ASK EVEN WHERE THERE IS NO STATUTE — UNESCO's 2022 report on SDG 16.10.2 records that even Pacific states without access-to-information laws have an environment ‘generally favourable to the public's exercising of their right to information’. The absence of a law is not, on the region's own evidence, a reason to expect refusal. AND THERE IS A COMMITMENT TO CITE WHERE NO LAW EXISTS: the Boe Declaration on Regional Security (2018) Action Plan includes the adoption and implementation of constitutional, statutory and/or policy guarantees for public access to information as a measure for success — a government that signed Boe has already agreed that access to information is a measure of its own success. The Pacific Plan 2005 and the UN Pacific Strategy urge the same. The underlying right sits in article 19 of the ICCPR and of the Universal Declaration. REGIONAL POSITION: only four Pacific island countries have adopted RTI laws — Cook Islands (2008), Palau (2014), Vanuatu (2016) and Fiji (2018) — with several others drafting. A SOURCING WARNING FROM VANUATU'S OWN RTI UNIT, which applies region-wide: its site carries the notice ‘beware of fake websites pretending to be official’ — verify the domain before submitting anything containing your identity and your concern. IN SAMOA: work toward a freedom of information act is reported, with UNESCO technical assistance through the India-UN Development Partnership Fund and the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology leading.

trackers.name: ELAW — free attorneys and scientists who will critique the developer's EIA
trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. ELAW is a global alliance of attorneys, scientists and other advocates, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries, that provides legal and scientific support to grassroots advocates to challenge destructive projects. FOUR CONCRETE FORMS OF HELP: legal support to local public interest lawyers; scientific support, including critiquing environmental assessments; economic insights on projects; and security expertise — ‘ELAW helps environmental lawyers improve their security so they can work without fear. When our partners are targeted, we act quickly to help defend and protect them.’ That last one is a named function, not an aspiration, and ELAW co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous and Environmental Defenders. HOW TO USE IT — THROUGH A LAWYER, NOT AS A CLIENT: ELAW works through more than 300 public interest advocates in its network, and its stated strategy is ‘locating strong lawyers who are committed to protecting the environment in their home countries’. You can approach ELAW directly, but the leverage is greatest when a local advocate is the conduit — that is how the network is built. It has hosted nearly 300 advocates from more than 65 countries as Fellows and provided support on thousands of cases; several partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize. Focus areas include biodiversity, fossil fuels — expressly assisting advocates in contesting fossil fuel development projects — plastic pollution, and work with coastal communities. It publishes guidebooks, including one to give communities sufficient understanding to challenge oil and gas projects, and clause-level summaries of national EIA law — so its site is also a route to learning exactly what your own EIA law requires. ASK WHETHER ELAW HAS A PARTNER IN YOUR COUNTRY: the network is described as spanning 70 to 80 countries but the member list is not published country by country, so this entry does not assert a presence in yours.

trackers.name: Samoa Conservation Society — and a national carbon programme already running
trackers.desc: THE VEHICLE ALREADY EXISTS HERE AND DOES NOT HAVE TO BE BUILT: in 2016 the Samoa Conservation Society (Fa'asao Samoa) began a pilot programme with the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment on offsetting carbon emissions by planting trees in O Le Pupu-Pu'e National Park, expanded in 2017 into a national carbon offsetting programme — so where a community wants an alternative income for forest land, there is a domestic NGO-and-ministry programme to join. Established 2013 to promote conservation of Samoa's biological diversity and natural heritage, it is BirdLife International's newest Pacific partner, with James Atherton as president since 2020 and Tofilau Tepa Suaesi as founding president. Its first campaign was to save the manumea, Samoa's critically endangered national bird, leading an international campaign in 2017 with Auckland Zoo and the Ministry — evidence it can convene government and overseas institutions behind a local cause. It also works on forest restoration. ALSO PRESENT: Conservation International has worked in Samoa since 2006.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — individuals can apply
trackers.desc: INDIVIDUALS CAN APPLY, NOT JUST ORGANISATIONS — the third fund in this file with that feature, and consistently the thing local groups do not realise. New Zealand's Pacific Development and Conservation Trust distributes up to $250,000 a year in grants to groups and individuals for conservation, cultural heritage, development and goodwill, prioritising community projects including those involving representative, endangered, threatened or unique habitats and species. Cook Islands, Niue, Nauru, Tuvalu and Samoa are all expressly on its eligible list, alongside every other Pacific state and territory. TWO OF ITS FUNDING CRITERIA ARE UNUSUALLY USEFUL: it funds projects that ‘improve legal access to facilities or resources necessary for social, cultural and economic sufficiency’ — broad enough to cover securing a community's access to land and water, which is not how most conservation funds are written — and projects that develop local capacities, particularly for indigenous ecological knowledge development. So documenting customary knowledge of a threatened site is itself a fundable project, and that documentation is often exactly the evidence an objection needs. The Trust is committed to communities working in partnership with iwi, hapū, aiga and local indigenous people — a proposal led by a customary group is what it is looking for, not an exception it tolerates. Apply via New Zealand's communitymatters service. THE OTHER REGIONAL FUNDER, WITH ITS LIMITS STATED: the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund invested in the Polynesia-Micronesia hotspot — backed by AFD, Conservation International, the EU, the GEF, Japan, the MacArthur Foundation and the World Bank, run through CI's team in Apia with SPREP support — funding over 90 projects in 13 countries, including 58 community-based projects. That five-year programme ran 2008–2013 and this entry does NOT assert an open window — check CEPF directly. A RESULT WORTH CITING: in Fiji the National Trust of Fiji, Pacific Invasives Initiative, BirdLife and the local community eradicated goats and rats on Monuriki, creating a haven for the Critically Endangered Fiji crested iguana. AND A FIGURE THAT STRENGTHENS ANY APPLICATION FROM HERE: only 21 percent of the region's original vegetation remains pristine, across a hotspot of 4,500 islands whose total land area is about the size of Switzerland.

trackers.name: Tonga Registry Services
trackers.desc: National — Business Entities Registry, Kingdom of Tonga, searchable free. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Tonga — Office of the Auditor General (TOAG)
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution; scrutinises public spending under the Legislative Assembly via financial, performance & compliance audits, Kingdom of Tonga.

trackers.name: Tonga — Ministry of Finance & National Planning
trackers.desc: National budget authority (Treasury); delivers the Government budget and manages expenditure & financial management, Kingdom of Tonga. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Tonga.

trackers.name: PacLII – Tonga
trackers.desc: Free case law and legislation for Tonga via the Pacific Islands Legal Information Institute. · Find here: free Tonga legislation and court decisions, hosted by PacLII.

trackers.name: All land belongs to the King — find whose estate your site is on
trackers.desc: THE TENURE POSITION RULES OUT MOST ROUTES IN THIS MAP. Since at least 1852 all land in Tonga has legally belonged to the King, who may grant nobles and matapule hereditary estates. The types are royal estates, royal family estates, hereditary estates (nobles) and government estates under the Minister of Lands, who is also Registrar General of Lands. Land may be leased but not sold, for terms not exceeding 99 years — so there is no purchase route and the land trust model cannot operate here. ESTABLISH WHOSE ESTATE YOUR SITE SITS ON BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: the estate-holder, not a municipality, is your counterparty, and for government estates it is the Minister of Lands. Every Tongan male aged 16 and over is entitled to a town allotment (max 1,618.7 m²) and a tax allotment of 8.25 acres, hereditary in the male line; allocated land can be reacquired by the King with Privy Council consent, with compensation for improvements possibly payable. TWO COASTAL LEVERS: the Land Act 1936 controls development in the littoral zone, defining foreshore to include all areas within 15–24 metres of the high water mark — a defined strip to measure against any coastal proposal — and the Resource and Environmental Planning Act requires an EIA before consideration is given to a development application, not merely before approval.

trackers.name: Special Management Areas — rule-making power follows designation
trackers.desc: THE CONDITION IS THE WHOLE POINT. Under the Fisheries Management Act 2002, Special Management Areas are designated by the Ministry of Fisheries to be managed by coastal communities, with a coastal community management committee — and communities can set their own management rules ONLY if they have been designated as an SMA. Rule-making power follows designation, so the designation is not a formality to chase afterwards; it is the thing that confers authority. The Fisheries (Coastal Communities) Regulations 2009 set the boundaries and establish the committee, which helps draft and enforce the management plan, and measures may include closed seasons, closed areas, gear standards, species size limits and prohibited methods. THE HISTORY EXPLAINS WHY THIS MATTERS: under the earlier Fisheries Act 1989 the Minister could declare reserved fishing areas after consulting local committees — but those committees were consultative and advisory only, with no management or co-management role, and earlier 1980s attempts including the first fishers' association and giant clam sanctuaries were short-lived. Advisory committees did not last; SMAs with rule-making power expanded rapidly. Tonga now has 13 marine managed areas — 6 locally managed SMAs alongside government MPAs — plus many community conservation areas. PRESSURE RECORDED: coastal lowlands and mangroves allocated for residential use, mangrove loss a named priority, and remaining natural forest under 4,000 hectares.

trackers.name: VEPA — a national society with a local board, not a branch office
trackers.desc: Incorporated as a national society in the Kingdom of Tonga in January 2010 and governed by a local board — not a branch office of an overseas organisation. The Vava'u Environmental Protection Association works across three areas: biodiversity and conservation, resource development, and education, with a large focus on ecosystem-based adaptation through community conservation projects. Its projects cover conservation and rehabilitation of marine and terrestrial species and ecosystems, climate adaptation and waste management; it works closely with the Government of Tonga and hosts the Marine Mammal Stranding and Entanglement Response Team, trained by SPREP, NOAA and the IWC. Also named in regional records: the Tonga National Youth Congress. IF YOU NEED A DIFFERENT ORGANISATION, TWO DIRECTORIES WILL FIND YOU ONE: PIANGO publishes a member directory of national umbrella NGOs across 25 Pacific countries, with named contacts and addresses — an umbrella body is the fastest route to the right local organisation when you do not know who to call. PICAN lists members including the Anglican Church of Melanesia (nine dioceses across Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia) — a community-level network with reach no NGO in the region matches — and Vanuatu's Campaign for Justice, whose stated mission is to actively confront and expose those who obstruct natural justice with impunity. Live & Learn runs Climate Resilient Islands with rural communities in Fiji, Tonga, Vanuatu, Tuvalu, Solomon Islands, PNG and Samoa, with outcome areas including nature-based land management, and publishes filterable case studies and fact sheets. AND A FUNDING MODEL PACIFIC NGOs HAVE STUDIED: at Mida Creek in Kenya, 22 organisations share resources and finances around one protected area, funding guided eco-tours and alternative livelihoods such as beekeeping to relieve harvesting pressure — pooling finances around a single site is a funding model, not just a partnership.

trackers.name: Nakau — income instead of logging, with the land staying with the clans
trackers.desc: WHERE LAND IS UNDER CUSTOMARY OWNERSHIP AND CANNOT BE BOUGHT, THIS IS THE EQUIVALENT OF BUYING IT: an income stream that makes keeping the forest worth more than felling it, with ownership staying with the landholders. Nakau works with Indigenous customary landowners across the Pacific, within local governance systems, expressly to ensure all projects are owned by the customary landholders — which is the difference between this and a concession. Its delivery partner across Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and PNG is Live & Learn. THE CASE THAT PROVES IT AGAINST AN ACTIVE LOGGING THREAT: at Drawa on Vanua Levu, logging coupes were already mapped and clearing had started when eight mataqali united to form the Drawa Block Forest Community Cooperative — a reversal at the last moment, and the vehicle was a cooperative formed by eight clans together. It now protects close to 4,000 hectares, is verified under Plan Vivo Climate, and won the International Energy Globe Award. WHERE THE MONEY WENT MATTERS MORE THAN THE HECTARES: credit income funded water and sanitation across five villages and supported women-led enterprises, honey, agroforestry, ecotourism and youth initiatives — the argument to put to neighbours who fear protection means poverty. ASK TO BE CONNECTED TO A WORKING PROJECT: Babatana, Drawa and Loru are verified and producing credits, not proposed. Others include Yato on Makira (10,000 hectares, with timber concessions still encroaching as recently as early 2025), East Rennell with 11 tribes, and 1,000+ hectares on New Georgia. NOW THE TWO REAL RISKS, BECAUSE THE RESEARCH RECORDS THEM: such agreements may create social unease by emphasising the disparity in wealth and power between rural landowners and environmental NGOs and donors, or cause within-community tensions through elite capture; and in one Manus case covering 83 clans in 19 villages and over 20,000 hectares, carbon financing had not yet started flowing. So the money may not arrive, and the benefits may be captured by a few — settle the benefit-sharing arrangement BEFORE any distribution, as that project did. Named backers include the EU, Ekos, MFAT, WWF-Australia and the Solomon Islands Threshold Program; Nakau and Live & Learn publish a toolkit for project coordinators.

trackers.name: Environmental Defenders Office — Pasifika Program
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific region, whose Pasifika-led programme works on extractive industries, forestry, marine protection and climate across Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Vanuatu and Tuvalu. WHO IT SUITS: an in-country organisation rather than an individual — EDO works predominantly through partner organisations (CELCOR in PNG, the Landowners Advocacy and Legal Support Unit and the Solomon Islands Environmental Law Association, the Fiji Environmental Law Association and the Vanuatu Environmental Law Association), supplying strategic legal capacity, co-authored law-reform papers and litigation support. Approach your national environmental law association first; its free advice hotline is for Australia only. YOUR NATIONAL PARTNER: Tuvalu is within EDO's stated geographical reach, but no named national partner organisation appears on EDO's own pages — unlike PNG, Solomon Islands, Fiji and Vanuatu, which each have one. Approach EDO's International Program directly rather than looking for a local association that may not exist. EDO IS AUSTRALIAN (Sydney), and its Pasifika Program is Pasifika-led, including diaspora lawyers with cultural links to the region; it works predominantly through partner organisations. Focus: climate change, threats to marine environments, forestry and mining. It is an accredited community legal service with a community advice hotline, and the largest environmental legal centre in the Australia-Pacific.

trackers.name: Tuvalu — Ministry of Finance & Economic Development
trackers.desc: National budget authority; the Planning, Budget & Aid Coordination Dept prepares the national budget and a Citizen’s Budget Guide, Tuvalu. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Tuvalu.

trackers.name: Tuvalu — Office of the Auditor General
trackers.desc: National public-finance watchdog; the constitutional Office of the Auditor General (ss.171–172) independently audits the public accounts & government activities and reports to Parliament through the Speaker, publishing whole-of-government financial statements & audit reports, Tuvalu.

trackers.name: SPREP — three conventions, and 26 members is not 12 parties
trackers.desc: THE REGIONAL BODY FOR PACIFIC ENVIRONMENT, AND IT IS SECRETARIAT TO THREE CONVENTIONS. SPREP is an independent intergovernmental organisation, autonomous since the Agreement Establishing SPREP was signed at Apia on 16 June 1993, with the Article 2 purpose of providing assistance to protect and improve the environment and ensure sustainable development for present and future generations. It has 26 members — 14 Pacific island countries, 7 territories and 5 metropolitan states — and is headquartered in Apia, Samoa. ESTABLISH WHICH CONVENTION FITS YOUR ISSUE: the Noumea Convention (1986, in force 1990), described by UNEP as the only comprehensive multilateral umbrella agreement for protection of natural resources and environment in the region; the Waigani Convention on hazardous and radioactive waste imports; and the Apia Convention on nature conservation. THE NOUMEA CONVENTION IS UNDER ACTIVE REVIEW — WHICH IS AN OPENING: a 2021 Review produced recommendations now being implemented through a Noumea Workplan and Budget whose stated aim is to elevate the work of the Convention and enhance awareness and implementation, with a Communications Plan and a Finance Strategy named as critical. BUT CHECK WHETHER YOUR STATE IS A PARTY: SPREP has 26 members while the Noumea Convention has only 12 contracting parties — membership and party status are different things, and this entry does not assert the latter. GOVERNANCE POINT WORTH KNOWING: the SPREP Meeting is the plenary decision-making body; the Executive Board (established 2015) is subordinate to it and has no power to make decisions requiring input of all Members — so a decision affecting all members must go to the Meeting. IF YOUR ISSUE IS SEABED MINING: UNEP records deep sea mining as an emerging contentious issue the region is dealing with — the regional body has already named it. SPREP is also developing a portal for protected areas managers.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — citizens may apply
trackers.desc: AN INDIVIDUAL CAN APPLY, AND THE FIRST DOCUMENT IS SHORT. The Pacific Development and Conservation Trust, administered through the New Zealand government's Community Matters service with requests assessed by Advisory Trustees, states that ‘citizens or organisations’ from eligible Pacific places may request funding — so no incorporated body is required, which removes the commonest barrier recorded across this map. THE PROCESS IS TWO-STAGE: submit an Expression of Interest; only successful applicants are invited to submit a full project application. Do not prepare a full proposal before the EOI is accepted — wasted work, and expensive wasted work where drafting means travelling. Applications must be on the current form with all sections completed, submitted online where connection allows. READ THE PUBLISHED GRANT RECORD BEFORE DRAFTING: the Trust publishes records of grants by round — 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 (two rounds), 2023/24 and 2024/25 — showing what the Trustees have actually funded, at what size and in which countries. That is better evidence of what will succeed than any guidance note. UNDP SUPPORT HERE IS COUNTRY-LEVEL: UNDP's Pacific Office provides country support to this state, so an in-country office is a realistic second route alongside the Trust.

trackers.name: SPREP EIA and SEA guidelines — intervene at scoping, not after
trackers.desc: SCOPING IS WHERE STAKEHOLDER CONCERNS BECOME TERMS OF REFERENCE — and the guidelines say so themselves. Assessments must be individually customised to the aspects most relevant to stakeholders, and ‘customisation usually occurs during the scoping phase and results in the preparation of terms of reference’. Intervene at scoping and the assessment is required to examine your issue; intervene later and you are commenting on an assessment that was never asked to look. SPREP's Strengthening Environmental Impact Assessment: Guidelines for Pacific Island Countries and Territories (60pp, English and French) is the regional practice standard, SPREP having been mandated on EIA capacity since the 1990s. KNOW WHICH INSTRUMENT YOUR FIGHT NEEDS: EIA assesses a project; the companion Strategic Environmental Assessment guidelines (developed 2018–2020) assess a policy, plan or programme and are addressed to environment agencies, national planning offices, development control agencies, municipal authorities and provincial administrations — so if the problem is a tourism plan or a zoning programme rather than one hotel, SEA is the instrument and the municipal or provincial authority is the addressee. There is also a sector guideline for coastal tourism development, made with the South Pacific Tourism Organisation. THE HONEST PART, FROM A REGULATOR'S OWN ACCOUNT: Vanuatu's Principal EIA Officer publicly described her department's challenges as lack of staff, lack of political support, weaknesses in public consultation, and low capacity in monitoring and enforcement. Expect to supply evidence the agency cannot gather itself, and expect post-consent monitoring to be weak unless someone outside government does it — it is also a citable admission when arguing that a condition needs an independent monitoring mechanism attached. CHECK YOUR OWN ENVIRONMENT ACT FIRST: many Pacific countries have EIA mandated under their Environment Acts and EIA Regulations, and these guidelines support the implementation of current legal requirements rather than replacing them — the practice standard, not the obligation. SPREP runs in-country EIA training workshops, and the Pacific Environment Portal carries regional and national data.

trackers.name: Waigani Convention — radioactive waste, and 200 miles not 12
trackers.desc: IT REACHES WHERE BASEL CANNOT — and for island states that is the whole point. The Waigani Convention is modelled on Basel and is the regional implementation of the hazardous waste regime, but differs in two decisive ways: it also covers radioactive wastes, and its territorial coverage includes each Party's Exclusive Economic Zone — 200 nautical miles — rather than stopping at the 12 nautical mile territorial sea as Basel does. That makes it the instrument for dumping, transhipment and seabed disposal cases Basel cannot touch. It is annex-driven: obligations extend to all wastes in Annex I or those possessing the listed characteristics — check Annex I first; if the substance is listed the obligations attach automatically, and if not, the argument runs through the hazard characteristics instead. It is closely tied to the London Convention on dumping at sea. THE BODY TO CONTACT: the Pacific Regional Centre for the Waigani and Basel Conventions, based at SPREP in Samoa, which has developed a model law implementing all four waste conventions (Basel, Rotterdam, Stockholm, Waigani) with a worked Tonga project — so where a national statute is missing or fragmented, the model already exists and a government can be pointed at it. AND A CONSULTATION WINDOW IS OPEN NOW: Cleaner Pacific 2025, the regional waste and pollution strategy built with 21 member countries around four goals and 15 strategic actions, is being replaced — the successor CP2036 was endorsed at the 31st SPREP Meeting (September 2023) with consultation in Suva, 21–22 July 2025. Priorities for the next decade are being set now. Ask whether your country has a national waste and pollution policy written against the regional strategy — it is the document your government is measured against. Delivery vehicles include PacWaste Plus (EUR 16.5 million, 72 months, EU-funded, across eight waste streams). THE HONEST LIMIT, FROM SPREP'S OWN REVIEW: Australia's reporting capability far exceeds that of most Pacific island countries, relying on weighbridge data requiring infrastructure that is not available — so do not assume an absence of data means an absence of a problem, and community-gathered data may be the best evidence there is. Watch the Clean Pacific Roundtable and CIRCLE EXPO, held alternately for an annual meeting of countries, industry and civil society — named as a participant category, not an observer.

trackers.name: Right to information — what your country actually has
trackers.desc: ASK EVEN WHERE THERE IS NO STATUTE — UNESCO's 2022 report on SDG 16.10.2 records that even Pacific states without access-to-information laws have an environment ‘generally favourable to the public's exercising of their right to information’. The absence of a law is not, on the region's own evidence, a reason to expect refusal. AND THERE IS A COMMITMENT TO CITE WHERE NO LAW EXISTS: the Boe Declaration on Regional Security (2018) Action Plan includes the adoption and implementation of constitutional, statutory and/or policy guarantees for public access to information as a measure for success — a government that signed Boe has already agreed that access to information is a measure of its own success. The Pacific Plan 2005 and the UN Pacific Strategy urge the same. The underlying right sits in article 19 of the ICCPR and of the Universal Declaration. REGIONAL POSITION: only four Pacific island countries have adopted RTI laws — Cook Islands (2008), Palau (2014), Vanuatu (2016) and Fiji (2018) — with several others drafting. A SOURCING WARNING FROM VANUATU'S OWN RTI UNIT, which applies region-wide: its site carries the notice ‘beware of fake websites pretending to be official’ — verify the domain before submitting anything containing your identity and your concern. IN TUVALU: no RTI law is recorded — it appears on a published list of Pacific countries without one. Recorded as an honest absence; rely on the Boe commitment above.

trackers.name: ELAW — free attorneys and scientists who will critique the developer's EIA
trackers.desc: IT WILL READ THE DEVELOPER'S EIA AND TELL YOU WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT — which is the thing a community cannot produce alone and usually cannot afford. ELAW is a global alliance of attorneys, scientists and other advocates, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries, that provides legal and scientific support to grassroots advocates to challenge destructive projects. FOUR CONCRETE FORMS OF HELP: legal support to local public interest lawyers; scientific support, including critiquing environmental assessments; economic insights on projects; and security expertise — ‘ELAW helps environmental lawyers improve their security so they can work without fear. When our partners are targeted, we act quickly to help defend and protect them.’ That last one is a named function, not an aspiration, and ELAW co-founded the Alliance for Land, Indigenous and Environmental Defenders. HOW TO USE IT — THROUGH A LAWYER, NOT AS A CLIENT: ELAW works through more than 300 public interest advocates in its network, and its stated strategy is ‘locating strong lawyers who are committed to protecting the environment in their home countries’. You can approach ELAW directly, but the leverage is greatest when a local advocate is the conduit — that is how the network is built. It has hosted nearly 300 advocates from more than 65 countries as Fellows and provided support on thousands of cases; several partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize. Focus areas include biodiversity, fossil fuels — expressly assisting advocates in contesting fossil fuel development projects — plastic pollution, and work with coastal communities. It publishes guidebooks, including one to give communities sufficient understanding to challenge oil and gas projects, and clause-level summaries of national EIA law — so its site is also a route to learning exactly what your own EIA law requires. ASK WHETHER ELAW HAS A PARTNER IN YOUR COUNTRY: the network is described as spanning 70 to 80 countries but the member list is not published country by country, so this entry does not assert a presence in yours.

trackers.name: Pacific Development and Conservation Trust — individuals can apply
trackers.desc: INDIVIDUALS CAN APPLY, NOT JUST ORGANISATIONS — the third fund in this file with that feature, and consistently the thing local groups do not realise. New Zealand's Pacific Development and Conservation Trust distributes up to $250,000 a year in grants to groups and individuals for conservation, cultural heritage, development and goodwill, prioritising community projects including those involving representative, endangered, threatened or unique habitats and species. Cook Islands, Niue, Nauru, Tuvalu and Samoa are all expressly on its eligible list, alongside every other Pacific state and territory. TWO OF ITS FUNDING CRITERIA ARE UNUSUALLY USEFUL: it funds projects that ‘improve legal access to facilities or resources necessary for social, cultural and economic sufficiency’ — broad enough to cover securing a community's access to land and water, which is not how most conservation funds are written — and projects that develop local capacities, particularly for indigenous ecological knowledge development. So documenting customary knowledge of a threatened site is itself a fundable project, and that documentation is often exactly the evidence an objection needs. The Trust is committed to communities working in partnership with iwi, hapū, aiga and local indigenous people — a proposal led by a customary group is what it is looking for, not an exception it tolerates. Apply via New Zealand's communitymatters service. THE OTHER REGIONAL FUNDER, WITH ITS LIMITS STATED: the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund invested in the Polynesia-Micronesia hotspot — backed by AFD, Conservation International, the EU, the GEF, Japan, the MacArthur Foundation and the World Bank, run through CI's team in Apia with SPREP support — funding over 90 projects in 13 countries, including 58 community-based projects. That five-year programme ran 2008–2013 and this entry does NOT assert an open window — check CEPF directly. A RESULT WORTH CITING: in Fiji the National Trust of Fiji, Pacific Invasives Initiative, BirdLife and the local community eradicated goats and rats on Monuriki, creating a haven for the Critically Endangered Fiji crested iguana. AND A FIGURE THAT STRENGTHENS ANY APPLICATION FROM HERE: only 21 percent of the region's original vegetation remains pristine, across a hotspot of 4,500 islands whose total land area is about the size of Switzerland.

trackers.name: Bahrain Open Data Portal
trackers.desc: National — official government open data / budget portal. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Bahrain.

trackers.name: Ministry of Justice (Bahrain)
trackers.desc: Ministry of Justice, Islamic Affairs and Awqaf: court services and Court of Cassation information. · Find here: Bahrain's Ministry of Justice, Islamic Affairs and Awqaf — courts and legal services.

trackers.name: National Audit Office
trackers.desc: National — supreme audit institution of Bahrain. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in Bahrain.

trackers.name: National Audit Office
trackers.desc: Supreme audit institution of Bahrain, auditing government accounts and the use of public money. HOW THIS DIFFERS: an audit body reports AFTER money is spent — use it to find documented waste, irregularity and misspending already uncovered, not live tenders; for who is winning contracts now use the procurement portal, and for aggregate budget totals the statistical office.

trackers.name: Personal Data Protection Authority (PDPA)
trackers.desc: Personal Data Protection Authority (PDPA) — Bahrain’s national data-protection / information authority, overseeing how public bodies handle personal data and enforcing access and privacy rights. — Holds to account: officials handling public information & personal data — find rulings, guidance and complaint channels.

trackers.name: Sijilat Commercial Registration
trackers.desc: National company / corporate registry. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Tender Board
trackers.desc: National public-procurement portal. Here you can trace which firms win government contracts and tenders in Bahrain, and for how much.

trackers.name: Kuwait Regional Convention (ROPME) — and its Judicial Commission
trackers.desc: THE ONE BINDING ENVIRONMENTAL INSTRUMENT COVERING ALL EIGHT GULF STATES. The Kuwait Regional Convention for Cooperation on the Protection of the Marine Environment from Pollution was signed 24 April 1978 and entered into force 1 July 1979 — 30 articles, described as the basic legal instrument binding the eight States of the Region. ALL EIGHT ARE FULL PARTIES: ROPME records ‘no signatories without ratification, acceptance, approval or accession’, so unlike some regional instruments there is no signed-but-unratified state to argue about. ARTICLE II fixes the Sea Area by coordinates, from Ras Dharbat Ali (16°39'N, 53°3'30"E) to Ras Al Fasteh (25°04'N, 61°25'E) — a treaty boundary you can check a project location against. Use the term ‘ROPME Sea Area’: it was coined by the Plenipotentiaries to achieve unanimity, cooperating in spite of existing geopolitical boundaries, and it is the name all eight accepted. THE ORGAN MOST PEOPLE DO NOT KNOW EXISTS: alongside the Council and Secretariat, ROPME has a Judicial Commission, established March 1989, of 6 nationals of Member States highly qualified in international law. In a region with almost no environmental litigation route, a standing judicial commission under a ratified convention is the most significant legal fact available — though this entry does not assert that individuals may petition it; establish who may seise it first. AN EVIDENCE SOURCE THAT NEEDS NO SITE ACCESS: ROPME's scientific bodies include a Remote Sensing Unit, alongside RIIS and MEMAC. WHICH PROTOCOL FITS YOUR ISSUE: oil-spill emergency response; land-based sources of pollution — the limb for a coastal development, discharge or reclamation; and transboundary movement of hazardous wastes. Development is named as a stressor in ROPME's own statement of purpose. At stake: over 20 species of dolphin and whale, all five subtropical turtle species, and more than 1,000 fish species, most endemic.

trackers.name: MBZ Species Conservation Fund — frame it as species work, not climate
trackers.desc: DO NOT DRESS A SPECIES PROJECT UP AS A CLIMATE PROJECT HERE — which is the opposite of the advice that fits almost every other fund in this map. The MBZ Fund was established on the basis that direct species conservation has lost out to wider concerns such as climate change, sustainability and poverty alleviation, and is now seen as a by-product of larger issues, leaving underfunded field biologists and wardens. It exists to correct that displacement, so frame the work as direct, field-based species conservation. A philanthropic endowment announced at the World Conservation Congress in Barcelona, October 2008, taking applications since March 2009; managing director Razan Khalifa Al Mubarak, also President of IUCN. By end-2010 it had disbursed just over US$5 million to about 380 projects in almost 100 countries; awards run up to US$25,000. TWO UNUSUAL ELIGIBILITY POINTS: it covers all animal, plant AND FUNGI species — fungi are named, which almost no other fund in this map does — and its focus includes data-deficient species, so you need not prove the species is threatened; where the problem is that nobody knows, that is itself a qualifying category. Individual conservationists may apply, and priority goes to projects supporting young conservationists. Funding is for direct conservation impact rather than administrative costs. HOW IT RUNS: three rounds a year, March, June and October; the Fund forwards recommendations to an independent body, so its staff are not the final decision-makers; and late submissions are automatically moved to the next round — missing a deadline costs a cycle, not the application. Apply online in English; the form requires a budget, references and permits, so have your permissions in order before applying. READ THE PROJECTS DATABASE FIRST — searchable by species, IUCN classification, continent and year, it shows what has been funded for comparable species in comparable places. NOTE: THIS FUND IS GLOBAL, NOT REGIONAL — it is recorded here because this country holds no other funding entry, not because Gulf applicants receive any preference.

trackers.name: Rufford Small Grants — Bahrain is named eligible, individuals can apply, and there is no deadline
trackers.desc: THIS IS THE FIRST RESOURCE RECORDED FOR BAHRAIN IN THIS MAP, AND IT IS OPEN TO A PERSON RATHER THAN AN ORGANISATION — which matters here more than anywhere, because searching this country produced no environmental organisation with a verifiable presence at all. Bahrain appears by name on the foundation's own eligibility page. THREE FEATURES SET IT APART FROM EVERY OTHER FUND IN THIS FILE. There are no deadlines — applications can be submitted at any time of year. Applicants are individuals and small groups, not necessarily registered bodies, with the focus on people early in a conservation career, current or recent MSc and PhD students in particular, though others may apply against the published criteria; undergraduates are not funded. And the eligibility test for species work is exact enough to check yourself before writing a word: the foundation considers work on any species NOT listed as Least Concern globally on the IUCN Red List, and also species not yet assessed but thought to be globally threatened. Look your species up first. Projects may equally focus on threatened habitats, human-wildlife conflict or community education rather than on a species at all. THE MONEY IS STAGED AND THE STAIRCASE IS THE POINT: a first grant up to £7,000, then a second, then a Booster and finally a Completion Grant, with the range running to about £18,000. Each stage requires the previous project to have been completed with updates and a final report, which are published on your own page on the foundation's site. That public record is itself an asset for a community group with no track record. THE CONSTRAINTS TO PLAN AROUND: one application in any twelve-month period, a twelve-month wait after a rejection before reapplying, and the foundation expects to provide between half and all of a project's cost — where it is not the only funder it requires evidence of the co-funding. It will not fund pure research with no obvious conservation benefit, nor expeditions the applicant must fundraise to join. The foundation is UK-registered; its global operation belongs elsewhere in this map and only its application to this country is recorded here.

trackers.name: Accountability Counsel — Bahrain is a named dark spot, and this is the body that files the complaint for you
trackers.desc: BAHRAIN IS NAMED IN THIS ORGANISATION'S RESEARCH AS AN ACCOUNTABILITY DARK SPOT — no community complaint has ever been submitted from the country to any development bank's accountability office. The organisation's own view is that this reflects inability or unwillingness to use the mechanism rather than an absence of harm. WHAT IT DOES: at the request of communities it assists people in using accountability offices to defend their rights and remedy harm caused by internationally financed projects, with support ranging from multi-year accompaniment through a complaint to a limited review of key documents. It is expert in the mechanisms of the World Bank Group, regional development banks, export credit agencies and OECD National Contact Points, and it trains communities on the options available while partnering with local lawyers so that the international complaint runs alongside a domestic strategy. ITS FREE PUBLIC DATABASE HOLDS EVERY COMMUNITY COMPLAINT EVER FILED TO EVERY ACCOUNTABILITY OFFICE, which lets you see how similar projects and the same lenders have been challenged elsewhere before you commit to anything. ESTABLISH THE FINANCING FIRST: whether an accountability office is available depends entirely on which institution is providing the money. Founded 2009 and having worked with communities in fifty countries. THIS MATTERS PARTICULARLY HERE BECAUSE BAHRAIN HAS BEEN ESTABLISHED ACROSS THREE ROUNDS OF THIS WORK AS HAVING NO INDEPENDENT ENVIRONMENTAL ORGANISATION AT ALL. Its other two entries in this map are a foreign grant portal and an intergovernmental heritage centre that serves states rather than communities. This is the first entry for Bahrain of a body that will act for a community on request.

trackers.name: Inclusive Development International — free tools to trace a project's financiers, and researchers who will do it on request
trackers.desc: THE FREE TOOLS ARE THE PLACE TO START BECAUSE THEY COST NOTHING AND NEED NOBODY'S PERMISSION: a shareholder tracker and a development bank investment tracker that map the investment chain behind a project and identify its investors and financiers. This organisation built them because the subscription financial databases its own researchers use are unaffordable for the communities that need them most. BEYOND THE TOOLS, IT TAKES REQUESTS FROM COMMUNITY ADVOCATES to research and map who is behind a project — banks, investors, insurers, development finance institutions, brands — using company reports, import data and shipping manifests, and returns a summary together with an analysis of pressure points and advocacy options. In high-potential cases it will help execute strategies; otherwise it refers to partners. THIS COMPLETES THE SEQUENCE FOR BAHRAIN. This file records that no community complaint has ever reached a lender's accountability office from this country, and that Bahrain has no independent environmental organisation. Identifying the financier is the step that turns those facts into a possible case. THE LIMIT: no work by this organisation in Bahrain or anywhere in this region could be established — its documented casework is in Southeast Asia, Africa and the Americas. The service is open to requests without a stated geographic restriction, so it is untested here. The tools, however, are usable by anyone immediately.

trackers.name: University of Bahrain, College of Science — published critiques of the country's own impact assessments
trackers.desc: ACADEMICS HERE HAVE PUBLISHED AN EVALUATION OF BAHRAIN'S ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT SYSTEM, AND A SEPARATE EVALUATION OF THE QUALITY OF THE ECOLOGICAL INPUT IN ITS EIA REPORTS. If scholars have documented in print that the assessments are weak, that is a citable objection to the assessment in front of you — far stronger than asserting it yourself, and this file has recorded across several countries that attacking the assessment is what actually works. THEY HAVE ALSO PUBLISHED THE CUMULATIVE IMPACTS OF RECLAMATION AND DREDGING ON MARINE ECOLOGY AND LAND USE, ASSESSED BY READING THE RECENT ASSESSMENT REPORTS TOGETHER and mapped with geographic information covering 1963 to 2008 — finding reclamation running at around 21 square kilometres a year over one decade, and adding some 118 square kilometres, about 17.7 per cent, to the national land area since the 1960s. Cumulative analysis is exactly what a project split into separate applications is designed to avoid, as this file recorded in Kazakhstan and Turkiye; here the cumulative work already exists for a whole country. AND THERE IS DIRECT EXPERIMENTAL EVIDENCE OF WHAT RECLAMATION DOES: organisms taken from a PROPOSED reclamation site were buried in the laboratory under sediment from the designated borrow area, and 41.8 per cent survived. An experiment using the actual site and the actual fill is the most specific harm evidence in this payload. THE HISTORICAL BASELINE EXISTS TOO: a satellite study mapped 312 sites and produced seventeen maps of marine habitats and coastal ecology INCLUDING AREAS RECOMMENDED FOR PROTECTION, with an accompanying volume, and a repeat survey was planned a decade later to measure change. Ask for both surveys; two dates make an argument that one cannot. Published work also covers seagrass beds and the fauna depending on them, and names the pressures precisely — reclamation, dredging, industrial effluents, domestic discharges and brine from desalination plants. Heavy metals have been measured in fish, oysters, snails and sediments, and a state marine monitoring programme has tracked priority metal contaminants since 2007. IT IS CURRENTLY RUNNING A MANGROVE ECOSYSTEM STUDY IN PARTNERSHIP WITH A UNITED NATIONS AGENCY, covering vegetation cover, biomass and carbon stock, water quality, soil and sediment properties, AND A SOCIO-ECONOMIC STUDY — with students placed in the fieldwork teams. THE LIMITS: a state university, working here alongside the national environment council, which is the regulator, and a bank. It will not campaign, and the route in is a named researcher and the published record rather than a request for help. Contact details for individual academics appear on the university domain in their published papers, which is the practical way to reach the person who wrote the study you need.

trackers.name: MBZ Species Conservation Fund — up to $25,000 to a person, for survey work and data gathering
trackers.desc: IT PAYS INDIVIDUALS AND COMMUNITIES, NOT ONLY ORGANISATIONS — which is what makes it usable here, since this file could verify no independent Bahraini environmental organisation and the country's other entries are foreign bodies, state portals and a university. THE MOST USEFUL THING IT FUNDS IS SURVEY WORK AND DATA GATHERING IN THE FIELD, alongside direct action, recovery management and training. That matters in a country where this payload has recorded reclamation adding roughly a sixth of the national land area and academics publishing on the weakness of the impact assessments — what is missing in such a dispute is usually current, site-specific evidence of what lives there, and this fund pays for exactly that. A grant of up to twenty-five thousand dollars to one person to survey a threatened species on a threatened site is a proportionate and achievable ask. IT WILL COVER STIPENDS, PER DIEMS AND PROJECT LIVING COSTS as part of the fieldwork, but not an organisation's overheads — the reverse of most funders, and suited to someone working without an institution. IT PREFERS SPECIES THAT ARE THREATENED BUT DO NOT NORMALLY RECEIVE ATTENTION, including plants, fungi and invertebrates — so intertidal and coastal invertebrates, the very organisms this country's published reclamation research concerns, are squarely within its interest. Maximum twenty-five thousand dollars, applications above that rejected; three review rounds a year through its own online system; continuation grants for completed and properly reported projects; grantee case studies published on its site, which are worth reading for this country before applying. THE LIMIT: it funds species conservation, not objection — and no casework of its own here could be established.

trackers.name: Professional Fishermen's Society — the people who lose the ground when the sea is filled in
trackers.desc: ITS OWN PRESIDENT DESCRIBES WHAT THESE SOCIETIES DO, AND IT IS EXACTLY WHAT A COMMUNITY LOSING GROUND NEEDS: CONVEYING THE FISHERMEN'S VOICE TO OFFICIAL BODIES, DEMANDING THEIR RIGHTS, AND PARTICIPATING IN FORMULATING POLICIES relating to fish wealth. In a country where this file could previously record no independent domestic organisation at all, a vocational society that speaks to ministries on behalf of its members is the closest thing to a body that represents people against a scheme. AND IT SPEAKS TO THE RIGHT HARM. Its secretary appeared on a national newspaper's programme on THE FISHING PROFESSION COLLAPSING BECAUSE OF SAND SUCTION IN THE COUNTRY'S SEA, describing environmental protection policies as neither serious nor strict and the marine and fish wealth of the country and the wider Gulf as deteriorating. This file recorded the science of that separately — published research on the cumulative impacts of reclamation and dredging, reclamation adding roughly a sixth of the national land area, and a burial experiment using sediment from a real borrow area in which fewer than half the organisms survived. The fishermen are the human side of that evidence, and a case that joins the two is far stronger than either alone. ITS POLICY ASKS SHOW WHERE IT WILL ENGAGE: stocking government artificial reef sites with juvenile fish, siting those reefs near the coastal areas where ARTIFICIAL ISLANDS HAVE BEEN CREATED, deterrent laws protecting juveniles, and shifting the closed season from the spawning period to the nursery period so that breeding females remain. A community objecting to reclamation can attach itself to demands a recognised body is already making. NOW THE WARNING, AND IT COMES FROM THE SAME PRESIDENT: SEVERAL SUCH SOCIETIES EXIST, AND HE SAYS THEIR STRENGTH IS MEASURED NOT BY THEIR NUMBER BUT BY CLOSENESS TO FISHERMEN, SINCERITY OF REPRESENTATION AND EFFECTIVENESS IN DEFENDING THEM — adding that what matters is which are accredited and trusted BY THE FISHING COMMUNITY ITSELF. Ask fishermen at the landing site which society actually represents them before relying on any of them. THE REGIONAL POINT IS WORTH CARRYING: the same collapse is described across the Gulf, and the society was asked publicly whether it would raise the matter REGIONALLY with neighbouring states where the profession still operates more freely. THE LIMITS: it is a vocational society working within fisheries policy, not an objector or a law practice, and nothing found shows it opposing a specific development. Its address here is its own public account rather than a website, though a domain under the same name appears to exist — verify it.SOMETHING CHANGED FOR THIS FLEET IN JUNE 2026, AND IT WAS NOT RECORDED HERE: A BAHRAINI FISHERMAN LAW CAME INTO FORCE ON THE FOURTH OF JUNE REQUIRING A BAHRAINI FISHERMAN TO BE ABOARD A FISHING VESSEL WHEN COMMERCIAL SEA FISHING IS PRACTISED. THE PART THAT MATTERS TO THE SMALL BOATS IS THE ONE ABOUT PAPER: AS A FIGURE QUOTED IN THE PRESS PUT IT, THE LAW OBLIGES HOLDERS NOT TO RENT OUT LICENCES, PUTTING AN END TO SUB-LEASING PRACTICES, WHILE CONTRIBUTING TO TRAINING BAHRAINI FISHERMEN AND GIVING THEM THE FULL OPPORTUNITY TO WORK AT SEA AND PROTECT THEIR LIVELIHOOD. RENTED LICENCES ARE HOW A FISHERY GETS WORKED BY PEOPLE WITH NO STAKE IN IT WHILE THE NOMINAL HOLDER COLLECTS A FEE. FROM JUNE 2026 THE SOCIETY HAS SOMETHING TO POINT AT WHEN IT REPORTS ONE. ITS MEMBERS WERE ALREADY USING THEIR VOICE THIS SEASON: WITH THE RETURN OF THE SHRIMP SEASON IN AUGUST 2026 THEY PUBLICLY DEMANDED THE RENEWAL OF THEIR LICENCES AND TIGHTER MONITORING OF VIOLATORS - AT A MOMENT WHEN A MARKET SURVEY FOUND LIMITED SUPPLIES OF LOCAL SHRIMP AT FOUR TO FIVE DINARS A KILO AGAINST IMPORTED GULF SHRIMP AT ABOUT SIX KILOS FOR TEN DINARS. LOCAL CATCH AT FIVE DINARS A KILO BESIDE IMPORTED AT UNDER TWO IS THE ECONOMICS THAT EMPTIES THE WATER FASTER THAN ANY REGULATION — AND IT IS THE FIGURE TO PUT IN FRONT OF ANY OFFICIAL WHO SAYS THE FISHERY IS HEALTHY.

trackers.name: Bahrain Women's Association — its environmental programme is accredited to the UN environment programme
trackers.desc: IT IS A DOMESTIC MEMBERSHIP ASSOCIATION, AND ITS ENVIRONMENTAL PROGRAMME HOLDS ACCREDITATION STATUS FROM THE UNITED NATIONS ENVIRONMENT PROGRAMME. That accreditation is unusual for a national association of this size, and it matters practically: a body with standing at a United Nations programme can carry a concern into forums a community cannot reach, and its statements are harder to dismiss at home. THIS COUNTRY'S LISTING IN THIS MAP HAS BEEN A FISHERMEN'S SOCIETY, A UNIVERSITY AND STATE PORTALS. This is the second independent domestic organisation recorded here, and the first that a resident might join on the basis of who they are rather than what they do for a living. ITS ENVIRONMENTAL CITIZENSHIP PROGRAMME IS FRAMED AS RAISING AWARENESS OF HUMAN IMPACT AND OF THE CONSEQUENCES OF OUR ACTIONS, and it argues environmental protection as an individual and shared responsibility arising from self-motivation rather than instruction — the language of a body building a constituency, which is what a community needs alongside it. IT IS PRESENT INTERNATIONALLY: a member and environmental activist of the association took part in the global climate summit at the twenty-ninth session of the climate convention's conference of parties. A named person who has been in that room is a route out of a purely local argument. WHY THIS PARTICULAR BODY IS WORTH APPROACHING ON LAND QUESTIONS: this file has documented across the region that women are excluded from land decisions and stripped of claims by customary inheritance practice — recorded in Iraq, Palestine, Israel and Kyrgyzstan, and named in the land-rights pledges signed by bodies in Yemen and Kyrgyzstan. A women's association with an environmental mandate sits exactly at that intersection, and no other entry for this country does. THE LIMITS ARE PLAIN. Environment is one programme among several for this association, not its core purpose. Its stated method is awareness and citizenship rather than objection, and nothing found shows it opposing a development scheme, challenging a permit or taking a case. Use it to reach women in affected communities, to have a documented environmental concern raised by an accredited body, and for a route into international climate forums; take an objection to the free legal aid routes and the international accountability bodies recorded separately for this country.THREE DETAILS OF THAT ACCREDITATION WERE NOT RECORDED HERE, AND EACH CHANGES HOW TO USE IT. FIRST, WHAT IT ENTITLES THE HOLDER TO DO: ACCREDITED CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANISATIONS MAY ATTEND THE MEETINGS OF THE UN ENVIRONMENT ASSEMBLY AND OF ITS SUBSIDIARY BODIES.
