The law on lawyers as published carries provisions on participation in criminal and civil proceedings and the rights and duties of lawyers in each, on legal consultancy, on legal aid, on legal service charges, on the expenses of lawyers appointed by the people's court, on the preservation of client confidentiality, on respect for lawyer ethics and on the independence of lawyers, together with articles establishing the bar association, its organisational structure, its members, their rights and duties, and how membership expires. When a lawyer takes a fee and does nothing, or turns out to be acting for the other side, those are the article numbers to cite, and the association is the body they are cited to. The bar association runs legal aid clinics, and they are provincial. Published accounts record clinics operating in the capital and in Champasak, a further clinic opened at the provincial bar association office in Vientiane Province, and five more planned at provincial level in Savannakhet, Salavan, Luang Prabang, Oudomxay and Xayabouly, with the services described as advice, documentation and court representation. Representation is the part that matters: most free clinics recorded elsewhere in this file give advice and stop there. The pool of lawyers is small, and that shapes strategy. Published accounts note that there are a limited number of independent lawyers in the country. Approach early rather than at the deadline, expect capacity limits, and confirm whether the clinic in your province has actually opened before travelling to it — a planned clinic and an operating one are different things, and the published lists mix the two. Read it beside the ministry's own service, and note one limit. This file already records the ministry's legal aid service and the statutory definition behind it; the association route is the professional one, with the statute's ethics, fee and independence provisions standing behind it. Published accounts also record that a lawyer seeking to represent a foreign citizen in a criminal matter may need prior permission from the ministry of justice — worth knowing where outside supporters are involved in a dispute. Read this with the ministry legal aid, the land information network, the assembly petition line and the compensation decree entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Lao Biodiversity Association — a registered domestic association working on village co-management agreements
trackers.desc: A registered domestic association, not a foreign project. Published profiles record the association as founded in 2003 under the national union of science and engineering associations and officially registered with the ministry of home affairs in 2011, operating as a non-profit association with some thirty-three members of varied qualifications, most contributing their time as needed. Its stated mission is to promote community-based livelihoods linked with active, participatory biodiversity and natural resource conservation through cooperation and partnership with all stakeholders, and it provides technical support for conservation while implementing state strategies and action plans. In this country, a locally registered association is the kind of partner a village can be seen working with without the association itself becoming the problem. The route it works on is the village co-management agreement. Published accounts of a co-management scale-up programme record it as one of the organisations that carried a model developed in a national protected area out to village forests, through training modules, district-level workshops and local capacity building, with the wider programme producing twenty-one officially approved village co-management agreements covering more than two hundred thousand hectares of village forest. An approved co-management agreement is the strongest piece of paper a village here can hold over the forest it uses. It works in named provinces, and on the ground. Its co-management work is recorded in Phongsaly and in Xepone; a project running from 2024 to 2027 with other partners and the provincial agriculture and forestry office covers twelve villages across districts of Khammouane province with six hundred farming families as beneficiaries, and includes environmental education sessions, training in cultivation and sustainable forest management, the establishment of nine village plant nurseries and work on the law regulating illegal wildlife trade. How to approach it, and what it is not. A director's name, email address and mobile number are published through a regional network directory. It provides technical support and implements projects alongside government offices: it does not litigate, does not represent villagers in a dispute, and works within state policy rather than against it. The useful requests are for the co-management training module and for the names of villages in the same province that already hold an approved agreement. Read this with the ministry legal aid, the bar association clinics, the land information network and the compensation decree entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Village mediation units and the land dispute ladder — where a dispute must start, and the offices above it
trackers.desc: Small disputes must start at the village unit. The civil procedure law provides that small disputes, or disputes not of high value — family disputes, disputes over the possession of animals, rights of way and others — must be settled by the village mediation unit; that if the parties cannot reach a settlement the district justice office must educate them, encourage reconciliation and mediate again, based on the regulations of the village mediation unit and the district office; and that only then may the dispute be brought to a court, where the judicial tribunal may mediate between the parties once more. Where a dispute involves a high amount, the parties may either request that mediation or submit a claim to a court directly. Knowing which of those two categories a dispute falls into decides where it has to start. The land ladder has its own first rung. Published accounts of land governance record that administrative land disputes — use of land without authorisation, use not in line with its purpose, failure to use land, failure to pay taxes or fees, and boundary disputes — go first to the district office of natural resources and environment as the authority tasked with addressing them, then to the provincial department, and then to the People's Court, with resolution possible by compromise or mediation, by arbitration, or by lodging a complaint with the court. Taking a boundary dispute straight to a court skips the office that is supposed to deal with it first. The system carries most of the country's disputes. Ministry data reported for 2017 records three thousand nine hundred cases registered by village dispute resolution committees, of which only four hundred and fifty-three — under twelve per cent — could not be resolved and were referred to a court; mediation exists in some form in every village and follows procedures adopted from traditional dispute resolution, which makes it more familiar than court proceedings. Mediated agreements are enforceable through the courts, so an agreement reached at village level is not merely a handshake. The gap worth knowing before starting. Published analysis records that the legal framework does not fully match the complexity of tenure: shifting cultivation is not recognised in existing law, so land cared for in that way in mountainous regions cannot be formally registered, and conflicts continue where parties fail to recognise customary land rights, including rights that have been formally registered. Where a claim rests on customary use, expect the registration gap to be the fight itself. Read this with the village co-management agreements, the bar association clinics, the land information network and the compensation decree entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: National heritage registration — natural heritage has a local level, village managements have duties, and impact assessment was added in 2021
trackers.desc: Natural heritage has a local level, and it is reached by registration. The national heritage law divides natural national heritage into four levels — local, national, regional and world — with national-level natural heritage defined as areas of outstanding national value including from the point of view of aesthetic scenery. The State administers the national heritage centrally and uniformly by registering it and dividing responsibility for its administration among sectors and local administrations, and the amended law carries a specific article on the registration of natural national heritage. A village that wants a waterfall, a cave, a grove or a stretch of river recognised therefore starts at the local level rather than reaching for national or world listing, and the operative act is registration. Village managements have stated rights and duties. The amended law sets out, in consecutive articles, the rights and duties of the information, culture and tourism offices at district or municipal level, the rights and duties of the village managements, and the rights and duties of other concerned agencies; it also allows local heritage committees, and provincial world heritage offices where national heritage has been adopted as world heritage, to be established where necessary. A village body with a named role in the statute is in a different position from one asking to be heard, and the article number is worth quoting when asking a district office to act. Every resident carries a duty to protect. The law provides that Lao citizens, foreign residents and stateless persons residing in the country have the obligation to participate in the protection, conservation, restoration and rehabilitation of the national heritage, and that foreigners and tourists entering the country carry the same obligation. A duty framed on everyone is a basis for an individual villager to intervene without first needing a special standing. Heritage impact assessment was added in 2021. Published accounts record that the heritage law was revised in 2021 to include heritage impact assessment provisions, that a heritage department leads the work, that an inter-ministerial process was convened to strengthen those assessments, and that training on planning and undertaking impact assessments in heritage contexts has been developed with international guidance translated into Lao. Asking whether a heritage impact assessment has been carried out — separately from any environmental assessment — is therefore a live question rather than a theoretical one. Read this with the village mediation ladder and the district natural resources office, the village co-management agreements, the bar association clinics and the land information entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Impact assessment participation — village-level meetings at review stage, a named public involvement guideline, and the certificate to ask for
trackers.desc: Village-level meetings must be held at the review stage. Under the impact assessment decree, investment projects are sorted into those requiring a preliminary assessment, for projects expected to cause less or non-severe impacts, and those requiring a comprehensive assessment, for projects expected to cause large or severe impacts. During the preparation of the assessment the project owner must convene dissemination meetings about the development plan, the environmental impacts and the benefits of the project; and during the review stage, village and provincial level meetings must be held, with affected community members among those permitted to attend. The decree also places a joint responsibility on the bodies in charge of investment and on the project developer to ensure the participation of the people who are, or will be, affected — so participation is their duty to organise, not the village's favour to request. There is a named guideline, and a named compensation decree. The environment department is recorded as the lead agency for developing, disseminating and monitoring compliance with the national environmental and social legislation, which includes the impact assessment decree, the compensation and resettlement decree as amended in 2016, and a public involvement guideline of 2012. Asking whether the public involvement guideline was followed, by name and year, is sharper than asking whether consultation happened, because it points at a document with contents that can be checked. The limits are documented, and they matter. A published legal review records that when the ministry reviews the proposed scope of the assessment it must consult other concerned ministries but is not required to seek public review or input; that the decree is not clear whether members of the public may express their views at the dissemination meetings; and that it is likewise unclear whether the project proponent or ministry officials must solicit or consider public views at the review meetings. Knowing that in advance changes what a community brings to a meeting: a written submission, delivered and receipted, does not depend on being invited to speak. Ask for the certificate, and check which decree is current. The process ends with an environmental compliance certificate issued once the ministry is satisfied with the assessment report and the management and monitoring plans, carrying specific conditions and an expiry date before which it must be renewed. That certificate, its conditions and its expiry are the documents to request. Note also that a further assessment decree was issued in 2022, so the operative text should be checked before any deadline is relied on. Read this with the village mediation units and the district natural resources office, the resettlement committee entry, the national heritage registration route and the environment protection fund entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Communal land titling — what land qualifies, the four neighbours who testify, and the clause that blocks a concession
trackers.desc: Collectively titled land cannot be allocated for a concession. Published analysis of the communal titling framework records that land held under a collective title cannot be sold, transferred, leased or allocated for a concession. For a village whose grazing land, use forest or spirit forest is the sort of ground that concessions are granted over, that restriction is the protection: the title works less as ownership than as a bar on the transaction a company would need. What counts as eligible land is listed. A ministerial direction of 2014 sets out the land eligible for a communal title: village use forests, communal tree plantation areas, agricultural land, ponds, grazing land, cemeteries and ceremonial grounds, sacred or spiritual forests, and land reserved for future use and allocation. Communal titles may be issued to one village or to several where a larger area is managed jointly. A village preparing a claim should map against that list, because a category on it is far easier to register than one that has to be argued into existence. Village testimony is part of the proof. The adjudication rules used for registration provide for recognition of land rights on the testimony of the village chief together with at least four neighbouring landowners. That is a documentary requirement a community can assemble itself, and it is worth assembling before an application rather than after a dispute has started. Two limits, stated plainly. First, titling cannot take place in protection forest or conservation forest areas, so in practice it reaches production forest, village use forest and uncategorised forest — a village inside a conservation forest is on a different route. Second, published assessments describe the model as delegated management rather than ownership: although the collective title is issued to the co-operative, collective organisation, community or ethnic group, the land is managed by the government, which continues to claim ownership on the community's behalf, and the rights conveyed are to protect, use, take the fruits of and inherit the land, not to transfer it. Where it has been done, and who does the work. The first community land titles were issued in January 2013 to five villages resettled for a hydropower project, and titling is carried out by the land administration department under the natural resources ministry through its provincial and district offices. Read this with the land information network, the resettlement committee entry, the village mediation ladder and the national heritage registration entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: An accredited independent environmental laboratory — water, air, soil, sediment, noise and vibration, tested against the national standards
trackers.desc: There is an independent laboratory in the country that will run environmental analyses. The laboratory describes itself as an independent environmental laboratory service provider, accredited to the international testing and calibration standard, offering a range of environmental analyses covering water, air, sediment and soil, together with noise and vibration testing, carried out according to the Lao national environmental standards. That last point is the one that matters most: results expressed against the same national standards a project is assessed and permitted under can be set directly beside the proponent's own monitoring returns, rather than being dismissed as a different measurement of a different thing. Noise and vibration are on the list, not only pollutants. For communities next to quarries, crushers, piling rigs or haul roads, vibration and noise are usually the first and most continuous harm, and they are the hardest to evidence without instruments. A laboratory offering both alongside water, air and soil analysis means one commission can cover the range of complaints a village actually has. What to establish before commissioning. Ask for the current scope of accreditation — accreditation is granted for specific tests and matrices, not for a laboratory as a whole, so the question is whether the particular analysis you need is inside it. Ask how samples must be taken, preserved and transported for the result to be defensible, since a correctly analysed sample that was badly taken proves nothing. And ask whether the laboratory also works for project proponents in the same sector, which is not a disqualification but is something to know before relying on the report in a dispute. Where the results go. Read this with the assessment participation entries recorded for this country: the village-level meetings at review stage and the named public involvement guideline are the points at which independent measurements have somewhere to be filed, and the provincial monitoring bodies are where a discrepancy against a proponent's returns can be raised. Read it also with the communal land titling and heritage entries already recorded here.

trackers.name: Getting a story out when there is no domestic independent press — what closed, what remains, and the risk of being the source
trackers.desc: Start from the honest position: there is effectively no independent domestic press. The press freedom organisation's country assessment records that the ruling party suppresses all forms of free collective expression, and that the country's newspapers, television networks and radio stations are required to follow the party line set by the propaganda and training board. Journalists interviewed by external broadcasters have described reporting only what authorities approve, including where they know it to be untrue, and being unable to report official corruption or anything the government treats as a security matter. A community here should plan on the assumption that a domestic outlet cannot carry a story critical of a licensed project, and should design around that rather than be surprised by it. The external service that carried these stories has closed. The broadcaster whose Lao service reported for twenty-seven years on governance, human rights and environmental problems — including dam construction on the Mekong and the plight of migrant workers — terminated that service in 2025 after its funding was cut, having already suspended shortwave transmission. Its English-language regional desk continues to publish, and press freedom organisations documented the closure and called for the service to be restored. Anyone relying on old advice to take a story to that service needs to know it is gone; check what remains before making contact. What is left is regional and diaspora reporting, and it is thinner. Regional Mekong-focused platforms carry environmental and dam coverage and state that they are moving from aggregation towards original reporting on environmental challenges, policy and community resilience. International wire services and regional outlets cover major projects. In practice this means a story travels outward first and returns as external coverage, rather than starting in the domestic press. The risk sits with the source, and it is documented. A woman was jailed for five years in 2019 for posting videos criticising the government's response to flooding, and a presidential decree of 2015 required foreign journalists to submit reporting to the foreign ministry before publication. Anyone considering speaking to an outside outlet should treat anonymity, secure contact and the consequences for named individuals as the first questions, not the last. Read this with the village mediation ladder, the assessment participation guideline, the communal land titling and the independent laboratory entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: No published judgments — but one statutory precedent rule, the value threshold that fixes your court, and the language right
trackers.desc: Judgments are not published, and case law is not a source of law — with one exception written into the statute. Published legal research guidance records that this is a civil law country in which jurisprudence is not recognised as a source of law and is not part of the legal system, and that court judgments are not publicly published. But the courts legislation provides that a judgment of the People's Supreme Court on a matter not defined, or not clearly defined, by the laws shall be considered a court precedent which the people's courts must comply with until the matter is regulated by a law. Where a question genuinely is not covered by statute, that is the one kind of decision worth asking about. The value of the claim decides which court hears it. The civil procedure law provides that district and municipal courts have jurisdiction over civil cases with a value below a threshold stated in kip, with provincial and city courts taking civil, family and juvenile cases outside that jurisdiction as well as commercial cases; and that where there is a dispute about which court has jurisdiction, the court that received the request submits it to the People's Supreme Court for a final decision. Knowing the threshold before filing prevents a case being started in the wrong place and lost to a jurisdiction argument. Two provisions worth knowing before a hearing. The same law provides that proceedings must be conducted in the national language and that persons involved who do not know it have the right to use their own or another language through translators — which matters directly for ethnic minority communities. It also provides that tribunals sit as three judges deciding by majority, that deliberations are secret, and that judges are independent and comply with the laws only. Where the authoritative text lives. The official gazette, launched under the law-making legislation, is where laws are published, and in civil law systems the gazette is often the sole authoritative source until codes are updated. Guidance also records open collections of major laws in translation, including a set of official translations produced with a development agency. Read this with the ministry legal aid service, the provincial bar legal aid, the communal land title and the accredited laboratory entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Decree on Associations 238 — seven days to declare domestic funds, foreign ministry approval for foreign ones, and who the decree does not cover
trackers.desc: Money received has to be declared, and the clock is seven days. Analyses of the 2017 associations decree record that an association receiving funds from citizens, legal entities or organisations of this country must notify the relevant authorities in writing within seven days of receipt; and that an association wanting to receive funds or assets from foreign individuals, legal entities or organisations must obtain approval from the foreign affairs ministry, which holds exclusive authority to inspect, certify and consider acceptance of foreign funds and assets, with no procedure set out to challenge a refusal. Sector guidance on one class of association records the same shape: declare domestic funds and their sources to the supervising ministry, and for overseas funds declare and obtain foreign ministry approval, that ministry consulting home affairs — with six-monthly updates to local authorities on the association's status, operations and income and expenditure, and funds required to be used towards the association's objects. Registration is decided by one ministry, without an appeal route. The home affairs ministry is recorded as the sole authority approving registration applications, with no appeal process set out where an application is denied, and with ministries and provincial, district and village authorities responsible for supervising, monitoring and inspecting associations including their activities, members, funds and annual reports. Published assessments record that the decree includes measures criminalising unregistered associations and allowing prosecution of their members, and that membership is reserved for citizens. Know which bodies the decree does not cover. The decree applies specifically to incorporated associations and has no effect on the mass organisations, friendship associations, religious organisations, funds and foundations listed in it, which are subject to separate rules — as are unincorporated organisations and associations of foreign residents. A community exploring how to hold money should establish which of those categories fits before applying under this decree. Non-profit is defined, and it defines the accounts. The decree defines non-profit-seeking as properties and revenues obtained from an association's activities, after deduction of administrative costs, not being distributed but applied towards the objectives in its charter — which is the standard the books will be read against. Read this with the ministry legal aid service, the communal land titling, the accredited laboratory and the precedent rule entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Legal aid clinics — the bar association's clinic, the women's legal education association's clinics, and what legal aid covers
trackers.desc: Legal aid here is not limited to criminal cases, and land is named. A foundation working with the justice ministry records that legal aid covers provision of information explaining what the law says, legal consultation on how the law applies to a situation, assistance preparing legal documents such as a contract or a will, and representation during litigation or in a specific case; and that it can be used not only in criminal matters but in cases about land, inheritance, divorce, child custody, loans and other agreements. It records eligibility as covering trafficking victims, children in need of special protection, women and children victims of violence, people living with disabilities, and disadvantaged and impoverished people — so the test is the person's circumstances rather than the subject of the dispute. The bar association runs a legal aid clinic. An embassy announcement records that the bar association opened its first legal aid clinic at its provincial office, providing advice, documentation and court representation, in support of the legal aid decree's objective of increasing access to justice, with the justice minister and the provincial vice governor present. That is a route to a practising lawyer rather than to an official. A women's legal education association runs community clinics and trains village paralegals. Press reporting records that the association for the development of women and legal education established the first community legal aid clinic in the country in 2015 and later set up two more in the capital, offering the full range from advice to assistance with documents to lawyer representation in litigation, and that it trains volunteer village paralegals to give frontline assistance and act as a bridge between village communities and the clinics. Academic work records these clinics as complementing the government's own legal aid offices at district and provincial level, established under the legal aid decree in 2019, and records village dispute resolution committees formalised by a 2016 prime ministerial decision. Three mediation routes, and no administrative court. Published descriptions of the system record mediation at the village unit, an economic dispute resolution office under the justice ministry, and mediation by judges at the courts — and record that the country has neither a constitutional nor an administrative court. That last fact shapes strategy: a dispute with an authority has no dedicated forum, so the documentary and mediation routes carry more weight here than elsewhere in this file. Read this with the ministry legal aid entry, the communal land titling, the accredited laboratory and the precedent rule entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Water and Water Resources Law — the natural right of way downstream, the three scales of use and who approves each, and the protected zone power
trackers.desc: Water must be allowed to follow its natural course, and blocking it makes you liable. The water and water resources law provides for a right of way in water: water must be allowed to follow its natural course, and land owners must allow the natural flow of water to proceed downstream unhindered — with the owner who creates an obstruction responsible for all resultant loss to upstream or downstream land owners. Where a project has bunded, diverted or filled a watercourse, that provision names both the wrong and who bears the loss. The law also gives a permit holder a legal right of way to convey water, including waste water, by pipe or trench across another's land provided no harm is caused, with appropriate measures and compensation for damage that arises. Three scales of use, and the approving body rises with the scale. The law records that individuals, communities and organisations have the right to use water and water resources for family domestic or business purposes, classified into small, medium and large scale rights of use; that the right must follow the water sources allocation plan; and that small scale use requires no approval, while medium and large scale use requires approval, registration and an agreement — with an earlier translation recording approval by local administrative authorities, the government and the national assembly at the respective scales. Establish which scale a project claims, because that decides who signed for it. Protected zones can be added where damage is serious. The law provides that the government shall determine protected and reserved areas to preserve water resources, and that where it is seen that there is serious damage to water volume and quality, or a risk of spreading disease, the government shall determine an additional protected area; it also carries provisions on reforestation in protected zones and on waste water discharge standards. That is a route to ask for protection after harm has begun, not only before. What the 2017 revision added. Published summaries record the amended law as thirteen parts and ninety-eight articles, with new provisions on water rights and use including waste water discharge permits, wetlands and water resource protection, groundwater management and river basin management, expanded terms for the three scales of use, articles on environmental flows for hydropower and provisions on irrigation use, with basin-level strategic planning resting with the environment ministry. They also list the related statutes — on minerals, water supply, fisheries, irrigation, chemicals, aquatic animals and wildlife, meteorology and hydrology, and disaster management. Read this with the Mekong consultation window, the accredited laboratory, the village forest allocation and the assessment participation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Fish conservation zones — a village can close a deep pool year-round, the district governor's signature makes it official, and the fisheries committee hears disputes first
trackers.desc: A conservation zone is defined as a deep-water area that a village's own regulations can govern. The 2009 fisheries law defines a conservation zone as deep water areas either in bodies of water or along the rivers, as determined by fisheries management committees or administered under village fisheries regulations, which the relevant department has designated as a year-round prohibited zone to serve as habitats and safe breeding areas for aquatic fauna; defines bodies of water for fisheries to include permanent or seasonal, natural or man-made waters including rice fields used for aquaculture; and defines destructive fishing gear as equipment such as poison, explosives, electrical devices, chemicals and noise-making devices. A village that wants its pool closed is asking for a category the law already names. Two signatures make a zone official. A status report prepared for a conservation fund records that these zones are a form of co-management, responsibility being shared between local communities and government officials, usually from the district agriculture and forestry office; and that to be recognised as official the zone's regulations must be signed by the village committee and approved and signed by the relevant district governor's office, with officially recognised zones making up the majority of those inventoried, alongside unofficial ones established and managed at community level without government approval. That is the paperwork path, and it is short. Disputes start at the water body's own committee. The law provides that disputes over fisheries administration — fishing in prohibited areas, use of prohibited tools, non-payment of fees or taxes — shall be resolved by the management committee for fisheries of that body of water, with a right to take the matter to a higher organisation if either party is dissatisfied, and to the court in accordance with law. The law also empowers the authorities to consider or order the suspension or cancellation of fisheries operations. The zones exist on the ground, with measurements. A published guidebook records examples including a series of three zones along a fourteen kilometre stretch of the Mekong, the northernmost 135 metres wide by 2.2 kilometres long with an average depth of about 26 metres, and zones on named streams established with international organisations from 2008; national reporting records continuing use of electrofishing, explosives and small-mesh gear, and low community awareness of fishing law, as the problems the zones are meant to answer. Read this with the village forest allocation, the water resources law, the Mekong consultation window and the village mediation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Wildlife and Aquatic Law — the three species categories, the duty to survey habitats and conservation zones with local people taking part, and the village-level management role
trackers.desc: Habitats and conservation zones are to be identified by survey, with local people taking part. The 2007 wildlife and aquatic legislation provides for organisations and local authorities to conduct a survey to identify the habitats, conservation zones and feeding zones for wildlife and aquatic species, by participatory inclusion of local people, in issuing regulations and guidelines under their responsibility; and for classification and listing of species by reference to population situation and trend — endangered, rare and threatened species and their habitats. Where a project would take a feeding ground or a breeding area, that survey and the zones it identifies are the documents to ask for. Three categories, and the first is a prohibition list. The law divides wildlife and aquatic life into a prohibition category, a management and control category, and a common or general category, and states that species listed in the categories are endangered and that the habitat of those species needs to be protected. It prohibits catching aquatic species and hunting wildlife of the prohibition category — naming rare and near-extinct animals including the dolphin, elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, saola, bear, gaur and kouprey — and prohibits fishing and hunting tools and methods outside the regulations. Published analysis records the prohibition category as species at risk of extinction and of high value, whose use is prohibited. Protection covers the habitat, not only the animal. The law provides that protection means preserving the prohibited, managed and general categories in sustainable abundance, and is the protection of the animals' habitats, preservation reservoirs and species conservation zones without any devastation, with measures taken against destruction from human and natural causes. That wording is what links a species listing to the ground a project wants. The village is given a management role. The law provides for gathering people within the village to carry out management, conservation, protection and development of wildlife and aquatic species, with guidance and monitoring of implementation. A published legislative review records a ministerial instruction directing provincial agriculture and forestry offices to strengthen patrols at provincial, district and village boundaries, and prohibiting at any time hunting and trading in listed category one and two species, and hunting them during the spawning season between stated months. Read this with the fish conservation zones, the village forest allocation, the water resources law and the Mekong consultation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Protected area levels, categories and zones — the village-level protected area, the totally protected and controlled use zones, and the co-management plan a village signs
trackers.desc: Protected areas exist at four levels, and one of them is the village. A conservation organisation that advised the forestry department on drafting records that the new protected area decree, replacing the 2015 decree, clarifies the levels of protected areas — national, provincial, district and village — six categories aligned with international standards, and the zones within them: totally protected zone, controlled use zone and buffer zone, which allow better control of the activities authorised in each; and records that it was drafted after analysing the shortcomings of the 2015 decree and the challenges practitioners met in the field, with consultation involving the justice ministry and the prime minister's office. A village can therefore ask for a protected area at its own level, not only for a say in a national one. The zone rules are specific, and the corridor is the strictest for outside works. Published material records the earlier zoning regulation as dividing national protected areas into core, managed and corridor zones, prohibiting hunting of all wildlife and aquatic animals in the core zone, prohibiting trade in wildlife and requiring guns to be registered; and records that in linking zones or corridors, which connect protected areas to one another or to other forest, no hunting, tree cutting or other damaging activities are allowed, while in controlled use zones villagers may use resources with restrictions on logging, collecting certain products and hunting. Establishing which zone a proposed clearing falls in is the first question. Co-management plans are written documents naming places, rules and penalties. A published co-management plan for one protected area records the zone boundaries by named place, records that people can access the zone for collecting non-timber forest products, trapping small animals and using other natural resources sustainably, with firearms forbidden except for official purposes and patrolling, and any transgression fined according to the protected area regulations; records named species that may not be hunted anywhere in the area because they are nationally protected category one species; and records the conservation division visiting villages monthly or at least quarterly, the military and police assisting with patrols and arrests, and the district reconciliation unit responsible for ensuring fair benefit sharing according to the relevant agreements. Ask for that plan by name. Read this with the wildlife and aquatic law, the fish conservation zones, the village forest allocation and the water resources law entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: State land leases and concessions — the approval level that rises with the area, the duty to inspect and reclaim illegally granted state land, and the public land database the 2019 law created
trackers.desc: Who approved a concession depends on how big it is, and the largest need the national assembly's standing committee. The state land lease and concession decree provides for approval by the land management authority at each level, with an area over ten thousand hectares requiring authorisation by the national assembly standing committee on the government's proposal, and records that a concession must be given out in suburban and rural areas only. The investment legislation records provincial assemblies empowered to approve conversion of one hundred hectares or less of degraded forest land that cannot self-rehabilitate, and conversion of completely deforested land between stated hectare limits per business operation, on the provincial administration's request. Establishing the area is therefore how you establish who signed, and whether they could. Illegally granted state land must be inspected and reclaimed. The land law provides that the state shall inspect and reclaim state land that has been illegally granted and revoke land use rights illegally granted by an organisation; and that where land certification documents have been illegally issued by ministries or provincial administrative authorities, the government will cancel those documents on the proposal of the responsible body. Published reporting records the government inspection authority revealing unauthorised land concessions. The 2019 law added a bidding requirement and a database the public may search. Published legal analysis records the 2019 land law replacing the 2003 law, no longer discriminating by nationality on lease and concession length, with leases and concessions of state land now up to fifty years depending on the nature, size and specifics of the project, and now required to undergo a bidding process, though with little detail on how; and records that the law provides for a new computerised national land ownership database which can be accessed by the general public for a small fee. Concessions have a floor, and the categories matter. Published country material records that concessions cannot be granted for less than five years while leases have no minimum duration, that leases tend to be smaller and shorter in practice, and that the 2019 law categorises land use purposes including conservation, covering protected areas governed by state authorities, and development, covering agricultural and industrial zones — with prohibitions on certain activities by land users but no specific penalties attached. Read this with the communal land titling, the resettlement decree, the land information network and the village mediation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The national development information platform and the open data hub — government data navigable and downloadable by province, district and village, with a manual explaining the map tools
trackers.desc: A government platform publishes data down to village level, and a manual explains how to use it. A published description records the national development information initiative as a government initiative to improve access to key data and information for development planning and well-informed decision-making, hosting social, economic, environmental and agricultural information and allowing users to navigate, visualise, combine and download the data at different levels of spatial disaggregation. The platform's own user manual sets out the map viewer's tools in plain steps — searching for a place name by province or district, reading the coordinates of the cursor or of a clicked point in degrees or degrees-minutes-seconds, measuring the length of a drawn segment in chosen units, selecting parts of a vector layer, and searching datasets. Measuring a distance and reading a coordinate off an official layer is what turns a community's claim into a figure. The data behind it reaches village level and is mirrored on an open hub. An open data hub records a dataset sourced from that platform containing detailed and disaggregated information on demographic and socio-economic characteristics of the population and households at village, district and province level; and records other Lao datasets alongside it, including the road network from the open street map database at a stated date, crop statistics aggregated by province, urban area polygons above a stated population, ethno-linguistic distribution by village, district and province, and the administrative boundaries for country, province and district as shapefiles. The same boundary set is published on a humanitarian data exchange as a gazetteer spreadsheet, shapefiles, a geodatabase and metafile archives. The hub states plainly what it is and is not. Its dataset pages record its own materials as published under an open licence, and state that it is neither a commercial research service nor a domain managed by any governmental or inter-governmental agency, but a private non-profit open data group, posting information only after a careful vetting and verification process. Read this with the land concessions entry, the land information network, the communal land titling and the protected area zones entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The civil society support directory and the capacity organisations — a listed set of providers with addresses, an association that works with unregistered groups too, and small grants for community-level environmental projects
trackers.desc: There is a published directory of capacity development providers, with contact details. A civil society portal lists providers for non-profit associations and community organisations, each with a street address, telephone and email, and describes what each offers — one provider recording work with international and local organisations in project proposal writing and other capacity development activities; another, a non-profit started by five former staff of the country's first civil society organisation, working on community development balancing social, environmental and economic development; another recording gender workshops, training of trainers for development work, social research and survey projects, design and construction of irrigation projects, a workshop on integrated water resource management and training on rural development project management, and its official registration as a non-profit association under the 2009 decree on associations. Finding someone to write the proposal is often the first obstacle, and this is a list of people who do it. One association works with unregistered groups as well. A capacity development association records itself as non-political, non-profit and non-religious, with activities open to all civil society organisations working in all development sectors, whether registered or unregistered, providing a supportive environment to develop capabilities and share experience; and states its mission as enhancing capability so that groups can mobilise funds from various sources and implement their project activities. That openness to unregistered groups is the operative fact in a country where registration is the barrier. Small grants for community-level environmental projects are documented. A development agency's programme records supporting organisations to strengthen communication, knowledge sharing and advocacy competencies and offering small grants to implement community-level projects within the thematic areas of environmental protection, gender equality and social inclusion; and records parallel work with provincial assemblies to enhance their capacity to conduct public engagement using public hearings, hotlines and petitions — the same channels recorded elsewhere in this bucket. It names a village-level disaster association working through participatory planning with local authorities, farmers and government officials. The constraints are recorded too. Published commentary records donor support concentrated on capacity building in the capital, little space for policy advocacy, critical analysis or reporting of field conditions prohibited, collaboration between international organisations and national associations forbidden in some cases, and international organisations facing extensive approval processes. Read this with the associations decree, the environment protection fund, the biodiversity association and the legal aid entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The community legal aid clinics — the first non-government clinic and what it has handled, seventeen bar association clinics in named provinces, and village paralegals drawn from the villages themselves
trackers.desc: Seventeen legal aid clinics exist, and the provinces they sit in are named. A published release records a grant to the bar association to operate seventeen legal aid clinics opened with donor support, and lists their locations as the capital and seven named provinces; it records the clinics as having provided citizens with free legal aid services, and records the partnership as involving the bar association and the justice ministry. Knowing which provinces have a clinic is what turns a national programme into an address. A non-government clinic came first, and its caseload is counted. Published reporting records an association establishing the first community legal aid clinic in the country in 2015, offering free legal services, and records that with donor support since 2019 its legal clinics have served over 300 clients, 261 of them women; it records the association as working to raise awareness of law, empower women within communities, and train village authorities, village mediation units and law enforcement officers. Published academic material records that association's clinics as complementing the general legal aid offices of the justice ministry at district and provincial level. Village paralegals are drawn from the villages. Published reporting records a programme run with the bar association and the justice ministry providing poor and rural populations with greater access to legal aid through paralegals made up of volunteers from local villages, and records the issues brought to clinics as ranging from compensation and land disputes to inheritance disputes — with the same reporting noting candidly that only a few clinics had then been set up to support tens of thousands of citizens. The formal framework behind them is dated. Published material records a 2016 prime ministerial decision on village dispute resolution committees, formalising village mediation services, and a 2018 legal aid decree to expand legal aid offices across the country, with government-run offices established from 2019; and records that village mediation remains a preferred way to resolve local disputes while formal mechanisms are sometimes necessary to protect an individual's full rights under the law. Read this with the legal aid decree, the legal support fund, the civil society providers and the consultation entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The mass organisations as a channel — a front with committee members in every village, a women's union sitting on village mediation committees, and what published accounts say each covers
trackers.desc: Where independent organisations are scarce, the state-linked mass organisations reach every village, and a community can use them. A published submission by the national front records it as a coalition organisation, a voluntary union of political, socio-political and social organisations and individuals representing all classes, social strata, ethnic groups, religions, constituted at four administrative levels — central, provincial, district and village — and gives committee member counts at each level, including 31,981 village-level committee members at the stated date. It records its duties as including enhancing unity and concord among all ethnic people and handling ethnic affairs and religious affairs, records the country as composed of 49 ethnic groups with equal rights before the law, and records state measures including funds for poverty reduction, road and network expansion, stable residence and employment, and reduction of scattered settlements and shifting cultivation. That last line is worth knowing: resettlement is stated policy, not an accident of a project. The women's union has a seat in village dispute resolution. A published submission records the women's union as a mass and social organisation of women at all strata throughout the country, part of the state system, and records that at village level it forms part of village mediation committees, ensuring women are represented; it records the union disseminating and monitoring implementation of the women's development legislation through workshops, handbooks, and broadcasting in three named languages. Where the mediation committee is the first forum for a land dispute, knowing who sits on it matters. The published limits are as useful as the reach. The front's own submission records shortcomings: education of ethnic people on citizens' rights and obligations and on human rights has been limited, plans of action lack detail, many localities have not held meetings of tribal and clan heads, and activities of social strata and organisations are limited to major townships with many places neglecting the matter. Published analysis records the four officially sanctioned mass organisations by name and records party cells existing within them. Read this with the village mediation units, the associations decree, the civil society providers and the assembly hotline entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Village Focus International — boundary mapping and land use planning with villages, a resource centre and legal guidebooks on land rights, and a national land network of more than seventy organisations
trackers.desc: Boundary mapping with villages is offered here as a service, and the first village to use it is named. The organisation records a boundary mapping and land use planning process, naming a village in a named district and province among the first to take part. It records why: the vast majority of families depend on land for food and income, villagers' land is increasingly sought after by government and private enterprises for mining, hydropower, commercial farming and other industries, and many villagers are unaware of their rights, most land lacks clear ownership, and existing land regulations are poorly enforced — so households may lose tenure over the land they live on. That is an unusually blunt statement of the problem from an organisation working inside the country. It publishes materials communities can actually use, and runs a resource centre. It records producing and distributing an annual land rights calendar, twelve videos addressing common land issues, educational posters and legal guidebooks, and creating a resource centre to equip people to research land issues and learn about their land rights. It records a capacity building and legal awareness project on land and natural resources whose training is designed to enable and encourage recipients to replicate it in their communities, with a team of trainers skilled at fostering real dialogue between diverse stakeholders, and quotes an assessment that its biggest success is making complex articles and provisions of the country's laws and regulations understandable to laypersons. It negotiates on the village side of a deal, and it is Lao-staffed. It records fostering relationships and facilitating negotiations between the government, the private sector and villages to ensure communities are informed in business deals affecting their land, organising land rights events reaching more than 12,000 participants, and creating a national land network of more than seventy organisations including civil society, government and the private sector. Published description records it as the first international organisation founded in the country, in 2000, having worked in more than 300 remote and vulnerable villages, with around fifty local staff, nearly all Lao, and publishes its street address, post box, telephone and email. Read this with the concessions data, the civil society providers, the legal aid clinics and the mass organisations entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Village Co-Management Committees and the associations that facilitate them — village regulations with harvesting fees and fines paid into a village fund, fish conservation zones, and a members' network with a stated fee
trackers.desc: Villages here have set their own resource rules, with the money going into a village fund. Published material records that entire communities have established regulations and village co-management committees, facilitated by a named association, to control and manage a valuable forest product sustainably; and records the terms: the village allows appropriate harvesting by outside villagers for a fee of 1.5 dollars, and the village authority levies a 350 dollar fine for improper forest harvesting, with that money put into the village fund and used for village administration, especially for the committee's patrolling. A fee, a fine and a fund that pays the patrol is a complete local system, and it is written down. Fish conservation zones are the water equivalent, and their limits are stated. Published research records fish sanctuaries as a type of aquatic protected area common throughout the country, with the best known established by villagers, but with government support, in a named district; records them as important places of concentration for various fish species, benefiting relatively sedentary species but also highly migratory ones; and records plainly that they are not panaceas for solving all the fisheries problems in the country or the river basin, but represent important management tools that should not be overlooked. It records that the key to their successful implementation appears to be local support. The facilitating associations are named, and one network publishes its membership terms. Published description records the facilitating body as a non-profit established in 1999 working primarily in the southern provinces, whose mission includes assisting people in developing their own potential in an ecologically sensitive and socially just manner and whose vision is that rural communities have control over their resources and are able to make informed decisions. A gender development association records ten member organisations working at grassroots level, each contributing to operational costs through an annual membership fee of 300 dollars, and names among its partners a rural mobilisation association working in five named provinces. A civil society portal records a community knowledge support association working to promote natural resources management for sustainability and cherish biodiversity based on indigenous knowledge. Read this with the village land mapping organisation, the civil society providers, the concessions data and the mass organisations entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Rural Development Agency and the training centre it came from — a Lao non-profit with a published address and phone, environmental education and community study services, and an eco-school teaching land law
trackers.desc: A Lao non-profit publishes what it does, where it is and how to call it. The agency records itself as a Lao-based non-profit social enterprise founded in 2009, tracing its origin to a participatory development training centre and beginning as an eco-forest learning centre educating young people and the general public on ecology before becoming the agency in 2015. It records its mission as facilitating holistic capacity strengthening and quality provision of services in environmental education, nutrition, youth empowerment and community study, and records extensive experience and networks working with young people, communities, local authorities and village functionalities. Its published listing gives its village, district and city address, an email and a telephone number. Its programme areas name what a village can ask for. That listing records four areas: environmental education and climate change adaptation, focusing on environmental education awareness, combating illegal wildlife trade and promoting forest conservation; nutrition and water, sanitation and hygiene, including community-led total sanitation; youth, women and network, promoting green job opportunities and income generation, volunteerism, leadership and partnerships; and monitoring, evaluation and active learning, including community studies and serving as a knowledge station. It records a three-year aim of strengthening youth and women in 20 communities, and records holding its own finance, human resource, procurement, code of conduct and child safeguarding policies — the governance documents a village group can ask any partner to show. Its predecessor's work shows what such bodies deliver in villages. Published material records the training centre as a not-for-profit Lao organisation registered under a named ministry department and as an indigenous, all-Lao organisation; records it running a national training on climate change and forest carbon for 20 students who then interviewed villagers; and records a hydropower operator approaching a health ministry centre and the training centre to launch a community-led sanitation project in a named village, working with the schools and the women's union. A separate organisation records running an eco-school in a named village whose curriculum combines sustainable agriculture, green business, community leadership, environmental and social studies, organisational governance, land law, health and appropriate technology. Read this with the village co-management committees, the village land mapping organisation, the civil society providers and the legal aid clinics entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Lao CSO platform's member directory and a registered rural research association — how non-profit associations are licensed here, and one that sat in the timber negotiations
trackers.desc: There is a member directory of registered Lao non-profit associations, with addresses. A civil society platform publishes member profiles giving house number, unit, village and district, and records one member as an independent, non-political Lao not-for-profit association which is locally managed, providing training, action research and resources for community development. For a community trying to find a domestic organisation rather than a foreign project, a members' list with addresses is the practical starting point. How an association gets licensed is set out in that profile. It records the association operating from April 2004 under the umbrella of the union of science and engineering associations as a training centre; records that a 2009 decree for the regulation and operation of Lao non-profit associations authorised the public administration and civil service authority, with line ministries, to register and monitor all non-profit associations; and records that the association received its licence from the home affairs ministry on 6 September 2012 to operate as a registered non-profit association. Umbrella first, licence later, is the route a new Lao group will most likely have to follow. Its work reached a trade negotiation, and the outcome is stated. Published material records the association's director as a former hydropower student and private-sector engineer who became an environmental impact assessment consultant for civil society organisations, and records the association as one that helps to improve forest governance and social inclusion by providing training and conducting research. It records him saying the government is listening more closely to civil society organisations and communities than in the past and that such organisations play an important role in ensuring the voices of local communities are included in policy discussions; and records that because of changes to the forestry legislation in 2019, timber from a village forest can now be used for commercial purposes to support villagers' livelihoods, an issue discussed in the timber trade talks. It records that 70 per cent of the population lives in rural areas and more than 80 per cent live in or next to forests. Read this with the village land mapping organisation, the civil society providers, the co-management committees and the concessions data entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The Lao Farmer Association and its provincial networks — 220-plus farmer organisations across 17 provinces and 52 districts, member groups listed with village addresses and phone numbers, and its own debt case studies
trackers.desc: Member farmer groups are listed with their village address, a named contact and a phone number. A published directory records member organisations such as a farmer association for sustainable agriculture production at a named village in a named district and province, with a named contact, a telephone number, 142 members and rice, coffee and organic vegetables as its commodities; an organic farmer association of a named district with 223 members; an agriculture cooperative with 35 members; and a zone farmer association with 25 members. A village-level group with a phone number is the unit a neighbouring village can actually copy or join. The association above them is district and province wide, and it says so. Published description records it as a nationwide network bringing together over 220 farmer organisations across 17 provinces and 52 districts, collectively representing more than 50,000 smallholder farmers, established on 20 January 2014 as a farmers' network, formed by farmers, governed by farmers, and existing for the benefit of farmers, and officially registered as an association in 2024; earlier accounts give 173 farmer organisations from 16 provinces and 31 organisations from 10 provinces with more than 4,000 members. It records its aims as strengthening cooperation to make farming sustainable, productive, resilient and environmentally friendly, and influencing agricultural policies at local, provincial and national levels. Its own publications name the trap that costs farmers their land. Its site lists case studies on farmer indebtedness in sugarcane in a named district, cassava in a named district and pig production in the capital, alongside material on herbicide use in the uplands and on provincial network meetings. An organisation that publishes debt case studies by crop and district is naming the mechanism by which smallholders lose land, in its own members' words. It publishes its village, district and capital address with a map link, describing the office as next to a named bank near the village authority office. Read this with the village co-management committees, the village land mapping organisation, the CSO platform directory and the civil society providers entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: District natural resources offices and village mediation — the district office as first authority in a land dispute, the one-door registration counter with a thirty-day objection period, and the village head's certificate
trackers.desc: The district office is named as the first authority for an administrative land dispute. Published description records that administrative disputes can arise from use of land without authorisation, use not in line with its purpose, failure to use land, failure to pay taxes or fees, and land boundary disputes, and that the district office of natural resources and environment is the first level of authority tasked with addressing the issue, the next level being the provincial department, then the people's court. It records the routes for resolving them as compromise or mediation, arbitration, a complaint to the court, or international settlement. Knowing the district office comes before the court saves a community a wasted filing. Registration happens at a one-door counter, and objections have a fixed window. Published legislation records that land title registration shall be performed at the one door service unit of the district office of natural resources and environment; that the notification period is thirty days from the day the notification is issued, after which, if there are no objections or the objection has been addressed, the competent authority proceeds; and that the district office coordinates with village administrative authorities to establish the land record for each land parcel, with the register signed and sealed by the head of the district office. Thirty days from notification is the deadline a neighbour must watch. Village bodies come first, and one document is worth having. Published description records that village authority is responsible for mediating disputes including disputes over land and land related resources, and where the village level cannot solve the problem the case may be transferred to higher levels; and lists the avenues as mediation before the village mediation committee, district justice offices or district court; judicial resolution through the district or provincial people's courts; administrative resolution; and the complaints division of the national assembly. It records that the village head may issue a village head's certificate on land ownership, which is not valid on its own but may be used by local authorities to resolve disputes or by a family as additional proof when applying to the state. Read this with the village co-management committees, the village land mapping organisation, the concessions data and the CSO platform directory entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: District agriculture and forestry offices — the district unit that trains villages through demarcation, mapping and management planning, the village forestry committee it signs with, and its own staffing limits
trackers.desc: The office that walks a village through forest management sits in the district. A published guideline records that at district level it is the forestry unit within the district agriculture and forestry office that provides direct implementation support to the villages, with the provincial office above it, and records that villagers need to be trained and assisted by district agriculture and forestry and district natural resources staff on all steps of village forest management, starting with the demarcation of all forest areas, participatory forest resource assessment or forest inventory, the preparation of the village forest map, and the elaboration of the long-term village forest management plan and the annual work plan, with regular training and advice on forest management techniques. For a village that wants its forest recognised, that is the named office and the named sequence. The agreement is signed by the village committee and the district office together. A published model agreement records signature blocks for the village administration chairperson and the village forestry committee head on one side, and the district office head, the provincial office head and a vice governor on the other; records the district office as required to provide training to the village forestry committees on organisational, technical and entrepreneurial aspects of sustainable forest management, formulate management and annual operation plans with the committees' participation, and conduct operations with their participation; and records a duty to check that activities are carried out according to the rules, the approved management plan and the approved operations plan and, in case of violations, impose the pertinent fines and penalties. The management plan's required contents are listed. Published material records that the plan is developed by the village administration and forestry unit with technical support from the district forestry office, based on the land use plan and the village forestry agreement, and should define existing customary rights; basic principles for sustainable management, preservation and utilisation; rights and duties of the parties involved; and the principles of benefit sharing. The office's limits are documented too. Published research records the district office as faced with staff shortages, with limited opportunities for formal training and generally limited capacity to pursue participatory resource management planning. Read this with the district natural resources offices, the village co-management committees, the village land mapping organisation and the farmer association entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Village funds and savings groups — thousands of village-level banks that lend without collateral, a network support organisation covering 40 to 140 villages, and the excess-funds problem that limits them
trackers.desc: Two kinds of village-level financial institution exist, and both lend to their own members. Published research records village-level savings groups as semi-formal rural financial institutions formed to collect savings from member villagers and lend them back to needy members, with profits distributed as dividend, initiated in the late 1990s by the women's union with a foreign non-governmental and a governmental partner; and records village banks, organised since 2009 as a joint venture between a development agency and the central bank, as having a mechanism for the transfer of excess funds to outside borrowers. It records that where successfully established, these groups have become a major source of credit for villagers. For a community that needs money before it needs a lawyer, the fund is inside the village. The scale and the terms are published. A published roadmap records village funds, also called village banks, as the primary informal organisations offering financial services, estimated at 4,000 to 6,000, accepting deposits and many also offering credit to members, present in most villages and officially promoted by government. Published description records one programme reaching 553 village banks in 23 districts, 84 per cent operating profitably, supervised through network support organisations licensed as microfinance institutions, each supporting 40 to 140 village banks and managing liquidity between them. A village fund story records members contributing a monthly amount within a stated floor and ceiling, and lending at one per cent compound interest for education or healthcare and two per cent for business, lower than the bank's rate and without the need for collateral. The limits are recorded as clearly as the reach. The research records the problem of excess funds as a major constraint on sustainable development, with transfer to outside borrowers through federations at higher administrative levels technically possible but limited in practice. Another account records earlier village banks as often not working sustainably and performing poorly, and records a fund keeping about one million kip on hand for emergencies, with anyone able to join but only those over 18 able to borrow. Read this with the district agriculture and forestry offices, the farmer association, the village co-management committees and the CSO platform directory entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: The village as the only elected tier — a chief with an express duty to protect natural resources, an elected seven-person body that examines village problems first, and minutes that must be signed and distributed
trackers.desc: The village is the only level of local government that is elected. A published country profile records that local administration is divided into provincial level, districts and villages, that each has its own budget, and that villages are the only elected local government level; and records the 2015 local administration legislation as defining the scope of rights and duties of local administration. For a community, that makes the village office the one local authority its own vote reaches. The chief's duties expressly include protecting natural resources. The constitution records that village chiefs have the responsibility to organise the implementation of the laws and regulations, and take the lead in socio-economic development, protection of natural resources and environment, and maintaining security and public order, educating local people with a view to maintaining harmony and making them the key actors to take the lead in developing their villages. A duty to protect natural resources, written into the office itself, is a hook a village can use on its own chief. An elected body of about seven people examines problems before anything goes further. Published research records that, on the model of the traditional council of elders, each village elects a body of about seven persons which becomes a preliminary body to examine and make judgments on village problems, whose elected members tend to include not only respected elders but also young and educated residents; and records that if people are not satisfied with that body's decision, the case can revert to the elders' council or go on to the district court. Other description records villages as governed by an administrative committee headed by a village president with others responsible for economic and population records, agriculture, women's affairs and youth affairs. Meetings must be minuted and the minutes distributed. The local administration legislation records that in each meeting minutes shall be recorded, approved and signed by the chairman, then distributed to the participants and concerned parties for implementation, with a resolution of the meeting where there is a decision on important issues.
