Published accounts of the monitoring describe trained community members analysing the contracts for infrastructure projects and assessing the quality of the work, visiting sites regularly to meet the site engineer, checking the quality and the projected cost of materials, and then raising what they find with the contractor, at community feedback meetings and provincial assemblies, and through sectoral monitoring groups containing representatives of the relevant ministries, the media and civil society organisations. A monitor holding the contract while standing on the site is a fundamentally different kind of witness from a complainant writing a letter afterwards. The scale, and the reported results. Its own account records around ninety staff and some seven hundred volunteers, a head office in the capital and programmatic presence across a dozen provinces at various times, with work in others through local partners. Published evaluation figures record that the proportion of problems identified in monitored infrastructure projects which were subsequently resolved rose from about a fifth in 2010 to roughly nine in ten by 2019, and that access to information for monitors rose to complete over a similar period. Those figures are from before 2021 and should be read as what the method achieved, not as a promise of what it achieves now. There is a handbook, and it is written to be used anywhere. A community-based monitoring handbook drawing on nearly two decades of practice is published, organised to take a reader from the approach through to implementation, and covering schools, health centres, infrastructure projects, trial courts and extractive industries. For communities in any country in this file, that handbook is the transferable part of this entry. Read it with the community development council, the procurement portal, the mining transparency portal and the supreme audit office entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Independent media in exile — what can be published inside, and what it costs to report
trackers.desc: Read the risk before anything else. The executive director of one exiled newsroom has stated publicly that journalists arrested merely for working for a media outlet operating from outside the country have been tortured, that some are imprisoned, and that there are cases of journalists being disappeared; reporters working inside for that outlet keep their identities secret even from one another, including from colleagues in the same town. Published accounts record that certain subjects are off limits — the oppression of women, corruption, security incidents and executions — and that crossing those lines risks summonses by the intelligence services, physical violence, confiscation of equipment and arbitrary detention. A journalists' body recorded at least a hundred and fifty violations of media freedom and journalists' rights in twelve months and named five journalists held in detention. This entry records who exists and what the conditions are; it is not a recommendation to contact anyone. The rules that define what a domestic outlet may print. Eleven journalism rules issued a month after the change of power prohibited coverage deemed contrary to Islam or to Afghan culture or insulting to public officials, and more than twenty further regulations followed, including strict pre-broadcast censorship, prohibitions on criticising laws and policies, a ban on live political broadcasts, and a requirement that programme topics and invited experts be approved in advance — with television stations told in September 2024 that guests could be drawn only from a list of sixty-eight pre-approved experts. Anything a domestic outlet publishes has passed through that filter, which is worth remembering before treating its silence as evidence. The exile sector is substantial but shrinking. Sector tracking records forty independent exiled outlets, some founded in exile after 2021 and others relocated, reaching millions inside the country; sixteen of them drew fifteen and a half million video views in a single month of 2025. But eleven became dormant within a year, publishing rarely or ceasing entirely, partly because of shrinking donor support, with at least one large outlet reducing operations after aid cuts, and social media reach down markedly year on year. Check that an outlet is still publishing before relying on it. How the reporting actually gets out. One exiled newsroom, founded in 2007 as a daily newspaper and now publishing online from abroad, is described as relying on collaborators operating covertly inside the country; its website is prohibited domestically, and its stories circulate inside through social media or for readers who have a virtual private network. Material meant to reach people inside the country therefore has to survive a website ban, which shapes what form it should take. Read this with the community development councils, the mining transparency portal, the community monitoring handbook and the supreme audit office entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Historical and cultural property law — a stop-work duty on the project, and suspension where a site is endangered
trackers.desc: The standing caution for this country applies throughout. The legislation described here dates from 2004 and this research did not verify how, or whether, it is administered now. What follows is a record of what the statute says, not an assurance that invoking it is safe or effective. There is a stop-work duty, and it sits on the project rather than on the community. The law provides that whenever municipalities, urban or residential building corporations, irrigation projects or any other government or private corporation come across historical and cultural properties while undertaking construction, expansion or improvement works, they are bound to stop their work and to inform the institute of archaeology. The obligation is therefore on the contractor and the authority, which changes what a community needs to do: record what was found, photograph it in place, note the date, and record who was informed and when, rather than trying to obtain an order. Where a site is endangered, the project is suspended. The law goes further and provides that in the case that construction work endangers an archaeological property or its site, the project is suspended until a definitive solution is found for their protection. Suspension until a solution is found is a stronger formula than a duty to consult, and it is the sentence to quote in a written notification. Registration, modification and what counts as heritage. Any modification of the structure of a registered monument of historic and artistic value is prohibited without the authorisation of the responsible ministry, which is to make arrangements for the protection of such monuments. The law's definition covers movable and immovable artefacts of historical, scientific, artistic or cultural value that are at least a hundred years old, together with items less than a hundred years old which are determined to be preservable and valuable, that determination being made by an archaeology committee and taking effect on ministry approval. The penalties, and the reporting clock. A person who deliberately destroys or damages historical and cultural property is liable, in addition to paying compensation, to imprisonment of between one month and ten years; and a person who fails to inform the relevant authorities of the discovery of a cultural property within the fixed period is liable to imprisonment of one to three months. Both cut both ways: they are a reason for a contractor to stop, and a reason for a finder to report promptly. Read this with the community development councils, the mining transparency portal, the community monitoring handbook and the supreme audit office entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Protected areas — a landscape with villages inside it can be declared, and the system plan already lists candidates
trackers.desc: The standing caution for this country applies throughout. The declarations and arrangements recorded here date from between 2009 and 2019, and this research did not verify which of them are administered now or by whom. What follows records what was declared and how, not an assurance that the arrangements survive. A landscape with people living in it can be declared, and was. The environmental protection agency declared the country's third protected area over a valley of more than seven hundred square kilometres in the central highlands, an area in which more than five thousand people live, adjacent to a world heritage site; it was established as a landscape conservation area and described in official reporting as a community conservation site, with community-based natural resource management projects running in more than twenty communities that form the gateway to it. The precedent matters more than the place: protection here was not conditioned on emptying the land of its inhabitants. Two national parks, one of them co-managed with communities. The first national park, a chain of lakes separated by natural dams in the same province, was declared in 2009 and 2010 with fourteen surrounding villages engaged in its management and livelihoods work; the second, declared in 2014, covered an entire district of just over a million hectares in the far north-east, and published accounts record that it was to be co-managed by government and local communities, with livelihoods related to the park and improved services for one of the most isolated regions in the country. A wetland sanctuary near the capital is also protected. Official reporting records that the four protected areas are guided by specific management plans, and that classification and official recognition make the implementation of conservation strategies mandatory. The system plan already names the candidates. Published research records a national protected area system plan that took fourteen previously proposed protected areas and sorted them into three types according to the data available for each and the expected time to establishment, with the first group expected to be gazetted soonest and the others needing further work to determine whether they remained viable. A community whose landscape appears on that list is arguing for the completion of an existing plan rather than for a new idea, and a further plateau area was proposed for addition to the network in 2018. What to ask for. The declaration instrument, the management plan for the area, and the record of which villages sit inside or at the gateway to it are the three documents that decide what a protected status actually means on the ground. Read this with the environmental agency's appeal right, the elected community council governing the first national park, the community development councils and the habitat and natural resource programme entries already recorded for this country.

trackers.name: Occupancy certificates for informal settlements — a document against eviction, issued jointly to spouses, with the caution that applies to everything here
trackers.desc: Read the caution first. Everything below describes a programme built and running before August 2021, documented by the United Nations agency that provided the technical assistance. Whether certificates are still being issued, honoured or reissued under the present authorities is not something this entry can verify, and the surviving value may lie in the records already created rather than in new applications. Treat it as a description of what exists on paper and of what a household may already hold. What the certificate does. The programme recognised and regularised the forms of tenure that exist outside the formal register in informal urban settlements, and the agency's own account states the effect plainly: the certificate guarantees residents the right to stay in their homes without the threat of eviction. The legal framework came into place with a regulation approved in December 2017 and a decree on the registration of properties in urban informal settlements that entered into force in February 2018, the first five hundred certificates being issued in Herat days later, after a pilot handover in the capital in 2016. On state land, the certificate is issued to both spouses. Published programme documentation records that occupancy certificates for properties on state land are issued jointly to heads of households and their spouses. In a country where women were recorded as owning or controlling four per cent of urban land, a jointly issued document is a materially different instrument from one in a single name, and a household holding one should keep both names on any copy it retains. The survey records are the underlying asset. Municipalities surveyed and registered properties across twelve cities — more than 830,000 by late 2020 — with a target of issuing certificates to a large share of informal settlement properties. A survey of 270,000 properties in the capital found that only fifteen per cent held a formal deed, forty-one per cent held an informal or customary document and forty-four per cent held nothing at all: the survey entry may therefore be the only record of occupation a household has. A digital registry holding the parcel records and allowing a certificate's authenticity to be checked independently was handed to the government at the end of 2020. Read this with the cadastral and land record entries, the legal aid route, the human rights complaint channel and the protected area entries already recorded for this country, each of which carries the same caution.

trackers.name: The Official Gazette — the one authoritative publication of laws, distributed to every court, with the post-2021 caution
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry recorded for this country. The former constitution and the legislation of the former government were dissolved after August 2021 while the judicial structure was retained with modifications, and supreme court appointments are now made by the supreme leader. Everything below is recorded because it remains the way legal texts are published and because older law is still the reference point for land and property questions, not as an assurance that any of it will be applied. Take advice on personal risk before approaching any institution. The gazette is the authoritative publication, and it reaches the courts themselves. The justice ministry states that the official gazettes contain official government announcements that must be communicated publicly, including laws and other principal documents; that everything in them is published in both official languages; and that they are distributed to all government offices, courts and universities across the country and sold to the public. Published accounts add that the ministry is responsible for issuing the gazette monthly, with extraordinary issues where the government considers it necessary, and that the ministry was named as official concessionaire of the gazette by a numbered gazette issue in 1998. For a community, the point is that the text distributed to the court is the gazette text: a printout from anywhere else is a copy of it, not the source. Court decisions were required to state their reasoning. A judiciary profile records that under the former system court proceedings were open to the public unless the judge found this contrary to the interests of the parties, public order or public etiquette, and that judgments were announced publicly and included the legal basis for the decision and the reasoning process. That is the standard to ask for when a decision is delivered without explanation. Two structural points that survive. The courts organisation legislation provided that a case is decided at first instance by three judges, with fewer only where three are unavailable, and by three judges on appeal; and that a court may not refuse to issue an order in a case before it, with cases lacking a clear legal provision handled under named constitutional articles. Read this with the occupancy certificates entry, the land records and the legal aid entries already recorded for this country, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Registering to hold money — the economy ministry is the single registration point, the 2022 procedure, and the reporting cycle
trackers.desc: Caution first, and it is heavier than in any other entry in this file. Published assessments record that in early 2026 new registration and reporting requirements were imposed on all organisations, with approval from the economy ministry required before conducting any activities and all staff vetted by the authorities' intelligence service, and that several major international organisations withdrew entirely. Anyone considering registering should treat staff vetting and disclosure of members as the central risk, and take advice before filing anything. One ministry registers, and the framework is layered. The directorate responsible states that the non-governmental organisations law regulates the activities of domestic and foreign organisations, describes such organisations as non-profit bodies established by volunteer, like-minded people working regardless of material interest for social and cultural activities of public utility, and records that the ministry's coordination directorate has been the only place of registration in the country, with four organisations selected as coordination bodies. Published legal notes record that a procedure on controlling and regulating the activities of domestic and international organisations was announced in April 2022 and is treated as the primary framework, with the earlier organisations law applied where the procedure is silent, and that domestic registration licences run three years and must be extended. The association form has effectively lapsed. The same notes record that operating licences of bodies registered as associations have not been renewed since 2021 and that, because registration certificates last three years, there are no longer legally operating associations — leaving the organisation form as the recognised vehicle. A community weighing how to hold donations should know that before choosing a form. Reporting runs twice a year plus an annual return. Coordination body guidance records two semi-annual reports and one annual report to the ministry, with the same forms for domestic and international organisations; a first form applicable to all registered organisations and a second only to foreign organisations that give grants to others, the latter requiring only the amounts under each cost category, signed and stamped by the head of the organisation. Narrative and financial annual reports are expected for the stated fiscal period. Read this with the occupancy certificates, the land records and the gazette entries already recorded for this country, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Land acquisition and compensation — payment before vacation, remnant plots, and the constitutional rule that acquisition needs a court decision
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: the constitution and legislation of the former government were dissolved after August 2021, so what follows describes the framework as enacted and as it is still the reference point for property questions, not an assurance it will be applied. The acquisition law states its own purposes, and they are usable words. A published record of the land acquisition law of 2017 lists its purposes: allowing fair acquisition of individuals' properties; regulating methods of determining the properties acquired; allowing implementation of the urban master plan and other public interest projects; determining standards for appraisal of fair compensation for properties under acquisition; allowing transfer of government properties for public interest projects; resettlement of owners of acquired properties in major national projects; compensation to the owner and all other people affected by the expropriation process; and increasing the positive impact of expropriation on people. Compensation to all other people affected — not only the titled owner — is the phrase to quote. Payment comes before vacation, and structures are covered explicitly. An assessment of the 2017 acquisition law read with the land management law of the same year records as positive provisions the obligation to pay compensation to affected persons prior to compulsory vacation of properties, transparent stipulation of how residential, farm and business premises and structures will be compensated, and assisted relocation where whole communities are affected. Those three are the entitlements to ask about by name. The remnant plot rule, and the market-value standard. Analysis of the expropriation framework records that compensation is at fair value based on current market rates, and that where acquisition of a plot or part of it would prevent the owner using the rest or hamper its use, the whole property is to be acquired. A household left with an unusable strip can therefore demand the whole plot be taken and paid for. The constitutional rule behind it. The same analysis records the constitutional provision that no one's property shall be confiscated without the order of the law and the decision of an authoritative court, and that acquisition of private property is permitted only for public interests and in exchange for prior and just compensation. Where the administration now sits. Practitioner material records that the land authority merged into the ministry responsible for urban development and land in December 2018, together with the finance ministry's state properties directorate, and that occupancy certificates began issuing to informal urban residential areas in eight cities. Read this with the land authority entry, the occupancy certificates, the gazette and the huquq offices entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The 2007 Environment Law guide — integrated pollution control, the permitting system, and the agency's stated air and water management functions
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: this describes the framework as enacted and published, not an assurance of present enforcement. A published guide walks through the environment legislation section by section. A guide to the 2007 environment law, produced with the United Nations environment programme and the national agency and circulated through UN human rights channels, records that the agency has issued or was developing regulations under the law across named sectoral areas including environmental impact assessment, integrated pollution control, protected areas management and ozone depleting substances; and that the law creates the framework for an assessment permitting system whose detail sits in the assessment regulations and national policy, to be read together with the relevant section of the law. For a community without a lawyer, a section-by-section guide in plain terms is the most useful single document about this statute. The agency's functions include pollution control and permitting. Published descriptions record that the agency, established in 2005 with the law promulgated in early 2007, is the environmental policy-making and regulatory institution with the role of regulating, coordinating, monitoring and enforcing environmental law, and that its functions include providing environmental management services in environmental impact assessment, air and water quality management, waste management, pollution control and the permitting of related activities. They also record that at central and provincial level it develops national policy and regulation, coordinates between line ministries, collects and manages environmental data and information, develops environmental standards, monitors environmental indicators and coordinates licensing — with an overall coordination role retained even where another ministry holds a sector such as underground resources. The provincial office is the nearer address. The record of what the agency has acted on is itself useful. Published material records the agency identifying substandard fuels, emissions from old vehicles and pollutants from brick kilns as key sources, with hundreds of brick kilns and industrial activities contributing, and records the agency closing a number of polluting restaurants and non-compliant brick production companies. Reporting records the agency and the health ministry attributing thousands of deaths a year to air pollution and the agency advising the use of masks at rush hours, and records agency officials describing seizure of green areas for building. Where a kiln or a workshop is the problem, there is precedent for closure. Named partners. The guide records other national institutions as key partners, including universities and the independent human rights commission — the latter already recorded in this file as a complaints route. Read this with the environmental agency entry, the water testing standard, the land authority and the gazette entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The 2004 artefacts preservation law — the hundred-year test, the committee that values newer objects, and the institute that decides what counts
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: the law described here was enacted under the former government and enforcement now is unverified. It is recorded because a site or an object found during construction is one of the few things that can stop work, and because the definitions are published in full. The statute is available in translation, in full. The law on the preservation of the country's historical and cultural artefacts, published in the official gazette in 2004 in nine chapters and eighty-five articles, provides that all historical and cultural artefacts belong to the public and are a manifestation of their role in preserving such artefacts for all humanity. A community does not have to work from summaries: the articles themselves are readable. The hundred-year test, and the exception that matters. The law defines historical and cultural artefacts as all movable and immovable objects of historical, scientific, artistic or cultural value that are at least one hundred years old, and also objects less than a hundred years old that have cultural, scientific and artistic value and are determined to be preservable and valuable. The value of that second class is determined by an archaeology committee and becomes valid after approval by the information and culture ministry. A shrine, a graveyard or a structure younger than a century is therefore not automatically outside the law — but it needs a committee determination. Who decides, and what is prohibited. Trade records describe the institute for archaeological studies and historical monuments, under the information and culture ministry, as the body that decides whether an item is historical and cultural heritage, and record that a named article of the law prohibits the export of the country's cultural and historical relics. Name that institute when asking for a determination. Two further duties are recorded outside this statute. Published analysis records the constitutional provision that both government and people are responsible for protecting cultural heritage, and that all artefacts on the country's soil, known or unknown, are government property so that transfer without permission is theft; and records that the penal code makes a range of acts unlawful, including failing to notify officials of new heritage discoveries and damaging sites. A duty to notify is also a lever: it obliges whoever is digging to report what they hit. The same analysis states plainly that whether these laws are now enforced is unclear. Read this with the environment law guide, the land acquisition entry, the occupancy certificates and the gazette entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Forest and pasture law — forest management associations, the pastures inside village boundaries that may not be sold, and the grazing restriction
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: these laws were enacted before August 2021 and their present administration is unverified. Village pastures inside the village boundary are protected from sale, and that distinction is the useful one. Published research records that the law on pasture and grazing land of 2000, the rangeland law and the forest law of 2012 form the legal framework for management and protection of natural vegetation; and that the 2000 law differentiates between specific pastures located within village boundaries, which are protected from sale, lease or agricultural conversion, and barren communal pastures outside village limits, which may be sold or leased with approval but may not be converted to agriculture. A community facing an allocation of its grazing land should establish first which side of the village boundary the land falls on. It also records that the framework restricts goat and camel grazing in forested areas to prevent degradation. Forest management associations are the vehicle, and there is an alternative registration route. The same research records forest management associations as the community-based vehicle under the forest law, with a parallel rangeland-based framework for areas where trees are small or a minor part of the landscape; it records that rangeland associations were hampered by the absence of an enacted rangeland law giving them formal status; and it records a district community conservation and forestry association that was not registered with the agriculture ministry but operated as a civil society organisation registered with the justice ministry, supporting sustainable natural resource use with technical support, environmental education and outreach across forty-four villages to address biodiversity and watershed concerns threatened by grazing. Where one registration door is closed, that is the documented example of another. The environment law makes conservation planning obligatory. The environmental legislation provides that planning for sustainable use, rehabilitation and conservation of biological diversity, forests, rangeland and other natural resources, prevention and control of pollution, and conservation and rehabilitation of the environment from adverse effects shall be an obligatory element of all national and local land use plans and natural resource management plans developed by all relevant ministries and national institutions; and that the environmental agency, with the finance ministry, relevant institutions and provincial, district and village councils, shall develop economic incentives for protection and disincentives for activities that do not encourage sustainable use. Know the contradictions before relying on any one statute. A land governance assessment records the expropriation law of 2000, the survey and cadastre law of 1988, the pastures law of 2000, the forest law of 2012, the municipal law, the mineral law of 2015 and the land management law of 2008 as the relevant instruments, and records that these laws sometimes contradict each other on the classification of state, public and private land, with unclear boundary delimitation and conflicting definitions of property including between the state and communities. Read this with the land authority, the water user associations, the protected areas and the community development council entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Building permits and restricted areas — the municipality's own urban law page, the published violations graph, and the duty to designate no-build zones
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: the framework described here is being administered by the authorities in power since 2021, and enforcement is unverified. The capital's municipality publishes its urban laws, its city plans and a graph of construction violations. The municipality's urban laws and regulations page sits alongside its city plans page, its tender listings, its municipal databases and a published graph of construction violations in the city. For a neighbourhood watching an unauthorised building rise, the existence of a violations record is the first thing to ask about, because it means violations are counted somewhere. Permission is the rule, and building outside its terms is a stop-work ground. Press reporting quoting the municipality's spokesperson records that high-rise construction in the city is allowed only by obtaining a permit from the municipality; that those building without a licence, or with a licence but against the provisions of the licence, will have their activities stopped; and that permission for tall buildings depends on the area and the connecting road. The same reporting records residents complaining about the cost of municipal service charges and about a requirement of up to thirty per cent green area in many areas — a figure worth knowing when a developer says none is required. The permit chain has documents a neighbour can ask about. Reporting of a later directive records that applicants must present a property deed compliant with religious law, tax documents and transaction records, along with confirmation from a local mosque imam, before a municipality grants a construction permit; that security forces are instructed not to obstruct citizens during the process; and that land authorities were told to submit land maps to municipalities within one month. Municipalities must identify where building is restricted. The same directive requires municipalities to identify and designate areas where construction is restricted, including flood-prone zones, historical sites, and locations unsuitable under urban planning regulations, with particular emphasis on major cities. Asking whether a site falls inside a designated restricted area is therefore a question the municipality is under instruction to be able to answer. Published research records that a 2021 regulation on issuing building permits and preventing illegal construction functions as the zoning rule, followed by a procedure for issuing permits in planned and unplanned areas. Read this with the land authority, the occupancy certificates, the environmental agency and the heritage entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Air quality standards and the pollution reporting channels — national limits to measure against, weekly published data, and a hotline that was used to report violations
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: the arrangements described were in place before August 2021 and their present operation is unverified. There are national air quality standards, and measured pollution has been compared against them. Published research records that the environmental agency operated air quality equipment in the capital, taking data from numbered districts, and sets out the common air quality parameters and the national air quality standard in a published table; other research records recorded particulate levels several times the national standard, and records that the agency's own sites do not represent the average for the whole city. Those published figures are what a community's own measurement can be set beside. The reporting channels were named and public. Reporting records that the agency began publishing air quality data on its website weekly, ran a public campaign on the issue, and set up a messaging-app hotline for residents to report violations; that it moved against specific sources including tower block furnaces and by closing businesses; and that the issue was debated in the lower house of parliament. A high committee for the prevention of air pollution was convened at cabinet level. The named sources are the ones a complaint can identify. Reporting records the agency's concern with quarrying firms crushing rock around the capital and the city's several hundred artisanal brick furnaces, kilns that run year-round burning coal, wood and car tyres, with emissions thought to include sulphur oxides, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, particulate matter including black carbon and compounds from burning those fuels; and records that the agency criticised public and private institutions for failing to implement measures to minimise pollution. Published research records the agency closing named numbers of polluting restaurants and non-compliant brick production companies. The legal base is the environment law already recorded in this bucket. Published accounts record that the agency is the country's environmental policy-making and regulatory institution, its role being to regulate, coordinate, monitor and enforce environmental laws, with the law setting frameworks for natural resource conservation and biodiversity, drinking water, pollution control and environmental education, and providing tools for enforcement. Read this with the 2007 environment law guide, the water testing entry, the building permit entry and the forest and pasture entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The protected species list and the wildlife committee — thirty-three species banned from hunting or harvest, five-yearly re-evaluation, and a national park co-managed with fourteen communities
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: the arrangements described date from before August 2021 and their present operation is unverified. A list exists, and being on it bans hunting or harvest. Published reporting records that the environmental agency released the country's first list of protected species, banned from hunting or harvest, comprising thirty-three species — twenty mammals, seven birds, four plants, one amphibian and one insect — including the snow leopard, wolf, brown bear, goitered gazelle, markhor, saker falcon, the Paghman salamander and the Himalayan elm tree. It records that before the listing it would have been lawful for any person to kill an endangered species such as the snow leopard. Where a project's assessment records a listed species on site, that listing is the sentence to quote. A named committee did the listing, and the list is reviewed. The same reporting records that the agency, with a conservation organisation, the agriculture ministry and the university, created a wildlife executive committee to carry out the listing process, evaluating species against expert information; that the agency is responsible for managing protected species including writing recovery plans for species designated as threatened; and that species are re-evaluated every five years to determine whether populations have recovered enough for removal from the list. Asking for a species to be assessed is therefore a request to a body with a stated method. The first national park is co-managed with the communities around it. Reporting records the creation of the country's first national park, protecting a landscape of six lakes separated by natural dams, and that it is co-managed by the government and a committee consisting of all fourteen communities living around the park; and records a second national park declared in 2014 in a north-eastern district. Other published material records rangers trained to monitor wildlife and enforce laws against poaching, conservation education in schools across that region, predator-proof livestock corrals and a livestock insurance scheme compensating shepherds, and work with more than fifty communities to monitor and manage their own wildlife and resources. What the protected area system amounts to. Published description records the agency as the lead authority, with a small number of formally gazetted national parks and wildlife reserves, further proposed sites, and community-managed conservancies, with roughly two per cent of the land area under formal national protection. Read this with the air quality entry, the forest and pasture law, the environment law guide and the building permit entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The Kabul wetland declaration — a two-hundred-hectare marsh inside the capital declared a protected area, one of the city's two water sources, and the record of how it was encroached before and since
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: the declaration and the accounts below date from 2017 or earlier unless stated, and present enforcement is unverified. A wetland inside the capital was declared a protected area, and its water supply value was part of the case. Published reporting records a wetland of around two hundred hectares squeezed between the capital's housing and the surrounding mountains announced in 2017 as the country's newest protected area; that it is an internationally important staging area on a named flyway, providing food and resting for thousands of storks, egrets, pelicans and flamingos, with an agency head estimating three to four hundred species passing through; and that, together with a named reservoir, it is one of the capital's two water sources, a marsh some eight metres deep at its centre. Pairing the habitat argument with the drinking water argument is exactly how that case was made. The history shows what an unformalised protection is worth. An assessment records that the wetland was declared a waterfowl reserve in the 1930s and supported tens of thousands of ducks in the 1960s, but that protection was never formalised, game wardens were ineffective, canals were dug to divert water, and the land was encroached for housing and seized by military commanders — with the same pattern repeated elsewhere in the country. It records other named waterfowl and flamingo sanctuaries found completely dry, and states that long-term sustainability requires coordinated management of water extraction from dams, rivers and wells, and prevention of contamination from waste dumps, sewers and chemicals. The threats and the local work are both named. Reporting records the lake threatened by water drawn off for irrigation and city supply, by new housing including sizeable concrete properties put up by powerful land grabbers and mud homes built by returning refugees, and by rubbish; records a local youth environmental organisation tasked with organising waste collection and working with the shoreline villagers, its director describing how residents were persuaded; and records later reporting that part of the lake's land was illegally seized and birds secretly hunted. Read this with the protected areas entry, the protected species list, the water testing entry and the air quality entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The assessment regulations — a certificate of compliance no project may proceed without, four points where the public may state opinions, and the recorded public hearing the agency cannot decide without
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: the framework described predates August 2021 and its present operation is unverified. Nothing in the listed categories may proceed without a certificate of compliance. A published summary records that the assessment regulations, made under the environment law, run to twelve regulations with three schedules; that they apply to the activities listed in categories one and two of the first schedule, or others determined by the environmental agency; that the agency is the sole authorised body to issue a certificate of compliance for those activities; and that before applying, the applicant must conduct a screening process and complete a screening report consistent with international best practice. Establishing which category a project falls in is the first question, and the schedule is where the answer is. The public may state opinions at four separate stages. Published legal description records that members of the public may express their opinion on a proposed project, plan, policy or activity at the preliminary assessment or screening phase; that individuals affected may express opinions at the preliminary assessment stage, the impact statement stage, the final record of opinion stage and the comprehensive mitigation plan stage; and — the operative sentence — that the agency may not reach a decision until the proponent has demonstrated that it has convened and recorded the proceedings of a public hearing. A hearing that was never convened, or never recorded, is therefore a defect in the decision itself. The assessment must consider doing nothing at all. The same description records that the assessment must include the likely environmental impacts and benefits of alternative means of carrying out the activity, including the preferred means and the alternative of not undertaking the activity at all. The permit lapses if unused, and the documents are named. Published material records that a permit lapses where the proponent fails to undertake the activity within three years of the date it was granted; that the process produces a screening report, an impact statement, a comprehensive mitigation plan, a review document and the certificate of compliance; that the agency distributes a notice of public disclosure before taking the screening decision; and that a board of experts reviews and assesses the applications and documents submitted, with the agency able to request further information or refuse the certificate with written reasons. Read this with the environment law guide, the protected areas entry, the air quality entry and the building permit entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The statistical yearbook and the population estimate — a numbered annual series compiled from ministries, district-level population figures published yearly, and the geospatial directorate inside the same authority
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: the institution has continued publishing since August 2021, but its independence and the collection behind its figures are unverified. The yearbook is a numbered annual series, and it says where its numbers come from. An edition of the statistical yearbook records that the data and statistical information have been collected from ministries, government organisations and the private sector, covering population, agriculture, education, health, national accounts, consumer price index, energy, construction, mines and energy, services, foreign trade, finance and foreign aid, for use by planners and data users; that edition is numbered as the forty-first issue. It records the national population estimate for its year, split by sex, and urban, rural and nomadic populations separately. Where a project's justification rests on a population or an economic figure, that is the compendium to check it against — and its tables name which ministry supplied what. Population is published to district level, and updated every year. Published citations record the authority issuing an estimated population of the country for each year, in a document paginated by province and district, with district totals cited to specific pages — one district's estimate cited at page thirteen of the 2025 edition, another at page seventy-six. A community disputing a project's claimed catchment has a district figure with a page reference behind it. The authority's own structure includes the mapping function. Published description records the authority formed in 1972, extended to provincial offices through the 1970s, conducting the first nationwide census from 1975 and completing it in 1979, and resuming surveys and data collection after 2002; and records that in 2018 a deputy director general office for geospatial information management and an office for management and development of information systems were added to its structure. Published material records the geodesy and cartography department and the land authority having been merged into the urban development ministry — the department already recorded in this bucket. It records the authority as maintaining branches in every province. Read this with the geodesy and cartography entry, the habitat and natural resource programmes, the mining portal and the gazette entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The conservation organisation behind the national parks — work in more than fifty-five communities, trained community rangers, and the co-management committee of all fourteen villages around the first park
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: this work is recorded from before August 2021 and its present continuation is unverified. The organisation worked through communities, and the numbers are recorded. Published material records a conservation society supported to work in more than fifty-five communities across the country, training local people to monitor and sustainably manage their wildlife and other resources; records that one output was the country's first national park, now co-managed by the government and a committee consisting of all fourteen communities living around the park; and quotes the society's deputy Asia director that about eighty per cent of the country's people depend directly on natural resources for their survival. A community asking to co-manage the land beside it has a fourteen-village committee as precedent. Rangers were trained locally, and their work is described. The same material records fifty-nine rangers trained, monitoring not only the cat but also named wild sheep and ibex while enforcing laws against poaching, with conservation education in every school of the region, and records the construction of predator-proof livestock corrals and a livestock insurance programme compensating shepherds. Published project material records training community rangers to patrol and report poaching as a complement to strengthening the capacities of police, judiciary and customs. The second park was declared over an entire district, with residents kept inside it. Published reporting records the declaration of an entire district as the country's second national park, just over one million hectares, to be co-managed by the government and local communities, providing livelihoods related to the park and improved services; published description records residents allowed under an agreement with the government to remain and involved in park management, many employed as rangers and other personnel, and records the park managed by a park office with a warden and rangers. The mapping behind the designations is recorded. Published material records the organisation using geographic information systems to develop sustainable resource management plans, map habitats, and map biologically significant wetlands and important bird habitats including proposed protected areas, and to analyse change, classify forest cover and demonstrate forest degradation in a named forest complex — with policy makers agreeing to implement conservation plans at three major sites when presented with the findings. Read this with the protected areas entry, the park's community council, the wetland declaration and the species list entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: ACBAR — the NGO coordination body with 230-plus members, provincial managers based in member offices in four cities, and a resource library of laws and practice for organisations
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: conditions change and this body's own pages are the current source. A coordination body exists that can point to the organisations working in a given province. It records itself as a trusted, neutral intermediary with over thirty years of experience and a membership of more than 230 national and international organisations, whose convening role runs through coordination meetings, advisory bodies, and donor and policy forums at national and sub-national level, reducing duplication and enabling information sharing among organisations, donors, agencies and other stakeholders. Published description records it created in August 1988, its secretariat in the capital since 2002, and four provincial managers based in members' offices in four named cities; and records a general assembly in which all members are represented as the highest decision-making body, meeting twice a year. For a community trying to find who works near it, provincial managers inside member offices are the nearest thing to a local index. It publishes and maintains data on who does what where. Its own pages record an information and coordination department that disseminates information to members and outside stakeholders, including mapping of members' activities, listing of the different aid sector working groups, and circulating fundraising calls from donors; record a website resource library gathering publications, laws and good practices related to non-governmental organisations in the country; and record that it maintains a field-level activity database of its members, revised annually, generating data and analysis on organisations working in the country. That database is the answer to who is present in a district. It trains organisations and lobbies for them. Its pages record a training department offering professional development training for the staff of national non-governmental organisations, and published description records core functions as coordination, information, advocacy and policy — lobbying on behalf of members with government, donors and other stakeholders to promote and enable the activities of organisations — and capacity building through training and mentoring. Read this with the community development councils, the habitat programmes, the conservation organisation and the registration entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The bar association in exile — human rights complaint forms for citizens and for defence lawyers, its recognised international status, and the record of how lawyer licensing was taken over
trackers.desc: Caution first, and it is the point of this entry: the professional body that used to license lawyers here now operates in exile, and licensing inside the country has been taken over. A complaint route exists that does not run through the authorities inside the country. The association in exile publishes, among its quick links, a human rights complaint form for defence lawyers and a separate human rights complaint form for citizens, and a donation route. It records its mission as the promotion and protection of the rule of law, social justice, human rights litigation, and providing legal services for citizens, holding that every citizen has the right to access justice and legal representation, with disputes resolved through highly qualified defence attorneys practising independently, free from discrimination or external interference. For someone whose case cannot safely be raised locally, a complaint form held outside the country is the difference between a record and nothing. Its status is externally recognised, which matters for anyone weighing whether to use it. Published material records that in May 2024 the international bar association's council voted unanimously to welcome the association back in its current format as an entity in exile, and records its president and a leadership council member stating that the extension of membership showed they are not alone. The takeover of licensing is documented, which is what a community needs to understand before looking for a lawyer. Published reporting records the justice ministry announcing that all defence lawyers, and those holding a licence from the bar association, should come to the ministry to obtain a licence, moving regulatory authority from the association to the ministry, with no information given on whether the advocates legislation or licensing procedures would change; and notes the ministry already held a legal aid directorate meant to provide assistance to people who cannot afford a lawyer. Published description records the association established under the 2007 advocates legislation, with duties including ensuring legal aid in criminal, civil and commercial matters, ensuring free legal services for indigent suspects and accused persons, monitoring advocates' professional activities, and providing public legal awareness programmes. Read this with the legal aid directorate, the coordination body, the media in exile and the gazette entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Afghanistan Analysts Network — an independent research organisation registered in two countries with both registration numbers published, peer-reviewed special reports, and everything free to read
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: conditions change and the organisation's own site is the current source. An independent research organisation publishes on land, water and governance, and all of it is free. Published description records it as an independent non-profit policy research organisation founded in 2009, aiming to bring together the knowledge, experience and drive of a large number of experts to better inform policy and increase understanding of Afghan realities, committed to analysis that is independent, of high quality and research-based, and summing up its stance as impartial, but not indifferent. It records that its publications include in-depth thematic reports, shorter policy briefings, quick discussion papers and dispatches from the field, and that all of its research and analysis is publicly available on its website. For a community or a lawyer needing documented background on how land, water or a district is actually governed, free published field research is the resource that is hardest to replace. Its registration is public in two jurisdictions, which is the check on who is behind it. The same description records it registered in Germany as an association with its registration number given, and as a non-profit research organisation at the ministry of economy in the capital under a stated registration number and date, with a structure of three co-directors and founders, a core team of analysts and researchers based in the capital, and a network of contributors with long-standing expertise in politics, governance, rule of law, human rights, security and regional affairs, and a permanent office in the capital. Its method and its review process are described, which matters when a report is used as evidence. A source-description service records its thematic focus as including economy, environment and development alongside political and human rights subjects; records that its reports are based on extensive desk and field research and that its special reports are all externally peer-reviewed; and records that publications may draw on qualitative interviews and focus group discussions with informants including government officials, tribal elders and other community members and civil society representatives, with the backgrounds of its analysts published. Read this with the coordination body, the bar association in exile, the media in exile and the statistics entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Housing, land and property legal assistance — information sessions, one-to-one counselling and representation across named provinces, and a published property law guide
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: coverage and access change, so confirm the provinces and the office before travelling. Housing, land and property is one of four named service areas, and the three levels of help are distinguished. A published services listing records the programme as offering information sessions, counselling and legal representation, focused on four areas — legal identity and civil documentation; housing, land and property rights; access to benefits; and employment law rights. It records group sessions giving detailed information on legal rights so participants can make informed decisions and take appropriate actions to claim their rights, and records one-time individual counselling sessions to support people in resolving problems or asserting their rights independently. Knowing that the first tier is a session, the second a single counselling appointment and the third full representation tells a household where to start. The organisation states where it works and what its legal programme is for. Its own pages record that its legal assistance programmes aim to enable people affected by displacement to claim and exercise their rights and to find lasting solutions, and to prevent displacement for those at risk; record that it is recognised for expertise in housing, land and property rights and in legal identity; and list its areas of operation in this country as a capital country office and eleven named provinces. Its own evaluation publishes the outcome rates, including the weaker one. A published evaluation records a survey of 281 former clients — 134 counselling cases and 147 legal assistance cases — and records that 88 per cent of counselling cases had a durable solution, meaning the problem was solved and has not recurred, against 71 per cent of legal assistance cases, noting the lower figure perhaps reflects the additional complexity of those cases. It publishes a guide to property law in the country, produced with a refugee agency. Read this with the land registry, the coordination body, the bar association in exile and the community development councils entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The rights commission reconstituted in exile as a monitoring organisation — its original complaint mandate, what happened to it, and where documentation now goes
trackers.desc: Caution first: the domestic commission was dissolved, and what exists now is an exile monitoring organisation. The original mandate is worth knowing because it names what a citizen was entitled to. Published description records the commission as a national human rights institution established under an international agreement, a decree and a constitutional article, with the constitution providing that every individual shall complain to this commission about the violation of personal human rights, and that the commission shall refer human rights violations of individuals to legal authorities and assist them in defence of their rights; and records among its listed functions collecting documents, evidence and testimonies of witnesses on cases of human rights violations. It records a board of nine commissioners appointed for five-year terms. What happened to it is on record, and so is its own answer. A source-description service records that after August 2021 the commission lost its ability to operate on the ground, its offices closed and its programmes suspended, with staff contracts not renewed, and that it was dissolved by the de facto government in May 2022; and records the commission's response that the decisions of a government which lacks national legitimacy and international recognition and is not based on the people's will cannot lead to the elimination of the commission, vowing to continue its work in collaboration with national and international institutions. It records the commission continuing to publish statements and reports since. Where the work went is named. Published description records the commission partly reconstituted in exile as a named non-governmental organisation to monitor human rights violations in the country, under its former chairwoman. Published comment records an international official describing the loss as retrograde and stressing the importance of re-establishing an independent human rights mechanism that can receive complaints from the public. For a community documenting land loss or forced displacement, the practical point is that the receiving body is now outside the country. Read this with the bar association in exile, the media in exile, the analysts' network and the land legal assistance entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Village shuras and district community councils — what replaced the abolished development councils, the district tier above them, and what the loss of women members did to village decisions
trackers.desc: Caution first, and it is the substance here: the elected village development councils recorded earlier in this bucket were abolished in May 2024, and aid coordination was directed to religious councils instead. The older village bodies persisted and are what remains. Published research records a longstanding tradition of grassroots, collective decision-making and problem-solving bodies called shuras or village councils that long predate the development councils, and records that the already existing local shura with a traditional leadership of elders, respected community members and religious leaders often continued in parallel with the development council. For anyone working at village level now, the traditional council is the body still standing. The district tier is named, which matters when a village needs to act beyond its own boundary. The same research records the structure as having been developed further with district community councils, with representation from all the village councils and structured to coordinate their activities, under a charter programme introduced in 2016 that included urban areas and aimed to combine and coordinate efforts between the different ministries. It records a gradual weakening of the government-established councils and raises whether all of the facilitating partners were sufficiently qualified for the task of establishing and guiding them, which produced large differences between their capacities and skills. The women's seats were the first thing lost, and villagers said what that cost. Published research records that very few shuras had managed to keep their female members, though both national programmes had mandated the equal participation of women, and records that more than half of interviewees rued this loss, if only for practical reasons, such as the shura's inability to ascertain and address issues concerning women in the community. It records that the letter abolishing the councils indicated future delivery of aid would have to be coordinated with ulema councils, and that organisations which had premised their work on the development councils may now face problems. Read this with the development councils entry, the water user associations and mirabs, the protected area community council and the coordination body entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Municipal nahia offices and the city information request form — the district offices that issue building licences and collect taxes, gozar assemblies at neighbourhood level, and a published route to demand information
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: administration has changed since 2021, so treat this as the structure to ask about. A city municipality publishes a form for demanding information, and names the law behind it. The capital's municipality records that, in accordance with the provisions of the access to information law, it remains accountable to its citizens and, in coordination with the access to information oversight commission, is prepared to provide information regarding its services, and that citizens who wish to obtain various types of information about the city and municipal services may submit their inquiries using the information request form and receive a formal response. A published form with a named oversight commission behind it is the cheapest first step against a municipal decision. The district offices are where building licences are issued. Published description records the capital as administratively divided into five zones and 22 municipal districts, with the municipality's structure comprising 17 departments under the mayor, and records that the city districts collect certain taxes and issue building licences. It records other provincial cities as similarly divided — two named cities with 15 districts each — with their own mayors and municipal websites. Knowing that the licence comes from the district office, not the ministry, tells a neighbourhood where to look for the file. A neighbourhood tier below the district is documented. A published programme description records activities including citywide property survey, registration and house numbering; strengthening municipal finance and revenue collection especially of district offices; and establishing representative neighbourhood assemblies to foster improved municipal-citizen relations in land management and service delivery, alongside neighbourhood-level infrastructure and block grant projects. The municipality's own land programme is named. The municipality records planning and implementing a land readjustment and urban redevelopment programme with a foreign agency's cooperation, stating it is carried out through public participation, urban planning and design processes, and adaptation of these projects in accordance with the country's applicable laws. Read this with the tenure security entry, the urban laws page, the land authority and the shuras entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: District and provincial land offices — settlement commissions at provincial capitals, the amlak and the municipal property office in each city district, and the share of transactions that never touch them
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: institutions and staffing have changed since 2021, so treat this as the structure to ask about. Land administration runs through provincial and district offices, and their functions are listed. Published description records the land authority as vested with state-owned land inventory; state land registration through the land rights identification process; land registration through the cadastral survey process; land transfers and exchanges; leasing land to the private sector; and resolving disputes involving state and public lands; records it as keeping records with respect to all land, both public and state, including maps, surveys, ownership records and land transactions; and records it engaging in state land management at the provincial and district levels through settlement commissions set up at provincial capitals. The municipal side has its own office in every city district. Published research records that land the government classifies as municipal land is under the administrative jurisdiction of a municipality, and that a municipal property office is located in each municipal district, under the district presidents in larger cities or the mayor directly, holding maps as the district land offices do, which maintain books containing lists of land parcels and their owners. Knowing there is a property office in your own city district, with maps and parcel books, is the difference between a rumour about ownership and a record. The honest share of transactions is published, and it is small. The same research records that the proportion of transactions occurring through the courts, the land authority, municipalities and finance offices is relatively small — around 10 per cent in rural areas and maybe reaching 30 per cent of all transactions in some urban areas, with most people documenting transfers through customary deeds or other private documents witnessed by local respected figures; and proposes bringing customary deeds into a district or village recording office with verification, supervision and archival backup provided by provincial offices. Published research records dispute cases being collected at the district or provincial level and forwarded to the national body, and records a pilot that created a registration book for cases brought to the dispute resolution department and for land registration arising from a community dispute resolution process, with training delivered to two named provincial offices. Read this with the municipal district offices, the land legal assistance, the village shuras and the land registry entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: District primary courts and the councils people use instead — a court in each district and an appeal court in each province, the value threshold that makes a decision final, and the recorded shift to shuras and jirgas for land
trackers.desc: Caution first: the judiciary changed hands in 2021, so this records the structure and what current reporting says about its use. The formal structure put a court in every district. A judicial profile records the judiciary as having included a supreme court in the capital, one appellate court in each of the 34 provinces, one primary court in each district, military courts, and specialised courts with jurisdiction over anti-corruption, juvenile justice, violence against women, usurpation of government land and narcotics; and records provincial courts grouped into eight judicial zones, each led by a rotating team of one justice and two advisory judges changing every six months, with the zone's appellate chief judge remaining as deputy. It records that court proceedings were open to the public unless the judge found this against the interests of parties, public order or public etiquette, and that judgments were announced publicly and included the legal basis and the reasoning. The district court's composition and its finality threshold are published. The published courts legislation records that the district primary court shall consist of a chief and two members, and where members are not available cases shall be decided by fewer than three; and records a decision as final when both parties agree upon it; when the time for appealing has expired; when the disputed property is worth up to 100,000 afghanis; when a cash fine of 50,000 afghanis is ordered; and in other situations set forth in law. A property value threshold that ends the case at district level is worth knowing before filing. Current reporting records where land disputes actually go. A country guidance body records that land disputes are handled through informal dispute resolution mechanisms or de facto courts; that many disputes are resolved informally both because litigants prefer those mechanisms and because judges refer disputes to them; and that given the absence of a clear legal framework for housing, land and property administration since 2021 and ambiguity in enforcement, many individuals turn to informal methods including community councils. It records land disputes as common because of fragmented registration, large population movements, rapid urbanisation, protracted conflict and weak rule of law, and as able to escalate and become violent. Read this with the district and provincial land offices, the village shuras, the municipal district offices and the land legal assistance entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: The property law guide written for judges and practitioners — the document that sets out how competing claims are weighed, judges as land administrators, and the thresholds at which a decision becomes final
trackers.desc: Caution first, as with every entry for this country: the guide predates 2021 and current practice is unverified. A published guide sets out how a judge is meant to weigh competing land claims, and an advocate can read the same book. The guide records the role of judges as covering both arbitrating disputes, either between private individuals or between individuals and the state, and acting as officers of land administration, which requires an understanding of the country's Sharia-based civil law, the statutory law and the overall strategy of the central government towards land and property rights. It records the basic role as upholding national law, including international law where it has been incorporated into domestic legislation, and presiding independently and impartially over the administration of justice; and records that in weighing the merits of competing claims in civil cases, judges must refer only to the established facts, the merits of each party's position and the relevant law. A guide written to instruct the decision-maker is the most useful thing a community's representative can hold. It names the specialist forum for property disputes. The guide records a special property disputes resolution court among the bodies dealing with land, alongside its treatment of state law comprising supreme constitutional law and statutory law. The finality thresholds are published in the courts legislation. The courts legislation records a decision as final when both parties agree upon the issued decision of the court; when the time for appealing has expired; when the disputed property is worth up to 100,000 afghanis; when the order is for a cash fine of 50,000 afghanis; and in other situations set forth in law. Knowing that a dispute below a stated value ends at first instance tells a household whether an appeal exists at all. It also records a directorate for documents and deeds registration, headed by a person appointed from among judges holding judicial authority. Read this with the district primary courts, the district and provincial land offices, the housing land and property legal assistance and the village shuras entries already recorded here, each carrying the same caution.

trackers.name: Supreme Court of Uzbekistan
trackers.desc: Official Supreme Court portal (built with USAID/UNDP support) offering case information, reports of decisions and hearing broadcasts. · Find here: the portal and judgments of the Supreme Court of Uzbekistan.

trackers.name: Open Judgment Data (data.egov.uz)
trackers.desc: Uzbekistan's official open-data portal dataset of court judgments (de-identified), separate from the Supreme Court site. · Find here: Uzbekistan's official open-data dataset of de-identified court judgments.

trackers.name: Open Data Uzbekistan
trackers.desc: National — official government open data / budget portal. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this is the broad budget/open-data hub for how money is allocated overall — for the specific firms winning tenders use the procurement portal, and for findings of misspending use the supreme audit institution. Here you can trace how the public budget is allocated and spent in UZB.

trackers.name: Uzbekistan — Unified Interactive Government Services Portal (State Registration)
trackers.desc: National company registry; legal entities register via the Unified Portal (State Registration Center, Ministry of Justice) with online name reservation & status records, Uzbekistan. — Holds to account: state firms & government-linked companies — find their registration, directors and filings.

trackers.name: Statistics Agency of Uzbekistan
trackers.desc: Uzbekistan's national statistical office, publishing official national accounts and government-finance statistics — government revenue, expenditure, deficit and public debt. HOW THIS DIFFERS: this gives AGGREGATE national totals, not project-level detail — use it for the big picture, not to see who won a specific contract (use the procurement portal) or what one project cost.
