trackers.name: Montserrat National Trust - accepts donated and bequeathed land (Director, by letter)
trackers.desc: THE TRUST'S OWN OBJECTIVES INCLUDE ACQUIRING PROPERTIES FOR THE ISLAND'S BENEFIT AND TAKING FUNDING BY SUBSCRIPTION, DONATION, BEQUEST AND GRANT - BUT THERE IS NO PURCHASE FUND AND NO PUBLISHED ACQUISITION CRITERIA. The evidenced route is a gift, not a sale: in 2021 the Piper family donated four parcels of roughly 13 acres at Friths for biodiversity protection and habitat restoration, and the offer was made in a letter to the Director, after which the family were entered as Benefactor Members. That is the working channel - a written approach to the Director, not an application. Contact info@montserratnationaltrust.ms, +1 664 491-3086. WHAT WEAKENS THIS: the Trust describes itself as thriving on volunteers, and its published projects page still leads on the Centre Hills Project launched in 2005 - so treat capacity, not willingness, as the constraint, and expect to bring the survey and the legal work yourself. If your land is in or adjoining the Centre Hills - the island's main remaining forest since the 1995 volcanic crisis and the source of its water supply - say so, because that is the area the Trust is already resourced around.

trackers.name: Adopt A Home For Wildlife (Montserrat National Trust with UKOTCF) - management agreements over land you do not own
trackers.desc: THIS IS THE ONE ROUTE ON THE ISLAND THAT PUTS A THIRD PARTY IN CHARGE OF LAND WITHOUT ANY TRANSFER OF TITLE. An adopter is defined by the project as a person, group or business that has agreed - with the project and with the landholder, where the adopter is not the landholder - to take on responsibility for managing a site so it is protected long term. Run by the Montserrat National Trust with the UK Overseas Territories Conservation Forum, part-funded by the UK Government's Darwin Plus, and launched on 29 October 2022 with the Ministry of Agriculture. The pilot worked with several landowners; the documented result is invasive Casuarina cleared from much of the Belham Valley while native coastal-defence and shade species were deliberately kept. THE CAVEAT THAT MATTERS: the material on the Trust's own site dates from the 2022 launch and pilot, and no later status is published there - confirm the project is still running before you build a plan around it. Project team: info@montserratnationaltrust.ms, +1 664 491-3086.

trackers.name: Planning & Building Control — and when DEFA cannot decide its own application
trackers.desc: TWO THINGS HERE THAT CHANGE WHERE YOU SEND AN OBJECTION. FIRST, THE DECIDER AND THE POLICY-WRITER ARE IN DIFFERENT DEPARTMENTS: Planning & Building Control sits in the Department of Environment, Food and Agriculture (DEFA), but the Planning Policy Team sits in the Cabinet Office and prepares the Isle of Man Strategic Plan and Area Plans. To object to an application write to DEFA; to change the policy it is judged against, write to the Cabinet Office. SECOND, WHEN THE REGULATOR IS THE APPLICANT: where an application is made by DEFA itself, or is one in which the Department is deemed to have a vested interest, it will not be determined by DEFA — after 21 days it is referred to the Council of Ministers, with representations conveyed to the Office of the Chief Secretary, Cabinet Office. A built-in conflict-of-interest route with a different decision-maker is rare — check for it on any application involving a government body. AND WRITE THE FIRST PARAGRAPH DELIBERATELY: published guidance says that to give weight to a representation and to enable assessment for ‘interested person’ status, you are encouraged to clearly indicate the relationship between your land or buildings and the land that is the subject of the application. State your spatial relationship to the site explicitly — it governs both the weight given and whether you qualify as an interested person, which matters for later appeal rights. Governing statute: Town and Country Planning Act 1999. Counter: First Floor, Murray House, Mount Havelock, Douglas IM1 2SF; +44 1624 685950; planning@gov.im — counter open Monday, Tuesday and Friday only, but staff reachable by phone and email Monday–Thursday to 5pm.

trackers.name: Manx National Heritage — a statutory body holding 3,000 acres in trust
trackers.desc: A STATUTORY BODY THAT HOLDS LAND IN TRUST IS AN ACQUISITION ROUTE, NOT ONLY A MUSEUM OPERATOR. Founded 1951 and formally still the Manx Museum and National Trust, MNH is the island's statutory heritage agency and a registered Manx charity (no. 603) governed by a board of trustees. It manages over 3,000 acres of coastline and landscape and holds property, archives and collections in trust for the Manx nation — the same model this map records for the National Trusts of Saint Lucia, Grenada, the Bahamas and Anguilla. THE LIST WORTH ASKING FOR: DEFA designates structures of special architectural or historical interest — over 250 registered, and 275 more identified as having potential for listing. A structure already identified but not yet registered is a far stronger objection basis than an unassessed one, so ask for that list by name. There are also 21 conservation areas, which protect the relationships of enclosures and open spaces rather than individual buildings alone — useful where the harm is to a setting rather than a structure. MNH land was initially excluded from the register but no longer is. DEFA separately maintains the Manx National Glens, and the island holds a UNESCO Biosphere designation.

trackers.name: Manx Wildlife Trust — four sites acquired in 2026 alone
trackers.desc: AN ORGANISATION THAT BOUGHT FOUR SITES IN A SINGLE YEAR IS ACTIVELY IN THE MARKET — approach it with a site, not a suggestion. The Manx Wildlife Trust, founded 1973 and the island's leading nature conservation charity, manages 37 nature reserves totalling about 1,103 hectares, roughly 2% of the Isle of Man — and it publishes acquisition dates per reserve. Ballanoa, Close y Corvalley, Close y Vaillee and an extension at Close Umpson were all acquired in 2026; Creggans (19 ha) in 2025; Creg y Cowin (44 ha) and Billown in 2023. A QUARRY INSIDE A WILDLIFE TRUST RESERVE IS A PRECEDENT WORTH CITING where a community is told a worked site cannot be conserved: Billown includes Rosehill Quarry ASSI. Several reserves already carry statutory designations — Close Sartfield and Close Umpson are part of the Ballaugh Curraghs ASSI and Ramsar site, Cronk y Bing is an ASSI, and Creggans sits in the Isle of Man Hills Important Bird and Biodiversity Area. AND IT WORKS WITH THE OTHER HOLDER: the Calf of Man (262 ha) is owned by Manx National Trust and co-managed with MWT — this map records Manx National Heritage separately, and the two act together. Note: MWT's own domain was not verified in this round — search for it directly and check the address ends in a Manx or charity domain before sending anything.

trackers.name: Practice Note 8 — Guernsey publishes what will be DISREGARDED
trackers.desc: ALMOST NO JURISDICTION IN THIS MAP PUBLISHES THE EXCLUSION LIST. Most tell you what you may argue; Guernsey publishes what is NOT a material planning consideration, in Practice Note 8, ‘Supporting or objecting to a planning application: making a valid representation’ (v3, January 2022). Among the matters named as not normally planning considerations is the status of property under other legislation, with the Housing Control Laws given as the example. READ IT BEFORE YOU DRAFT: an objection built on an excluded ground is not weighed and not refuted — it is simply disregarded, and you never learn why. Getting the exclusion list is worth more than another paragraph of argument. HOW TO FILE: comment is called making a representation and must go to the Planning Service in writing; the closing date appears under each application once the site notification has been issued, and the public consultation period is 21 days. THE TRAP: applications are removed from the live page once that period ends, after which details remain searchable but not including plans — download the drawings while the application is live, because afterwards you can see that it exists but not what it proposed. The note records its own limits: it is the Authority's interpretation, not exhaustive, and not a substitute for the legislation, whose text is at the Greffe and guernseylegalresources.gg. Governing law: the Land Planning and Development (Guernsey) Law, 2005.

trackers.name: Development & Planning Authority — and how to get elected members to decide
trackers.desc: THERE IS A PUBLISHED TEST FOR WHO DECIDES YOUR CASE. The DPA maintains schemes of delegation so that only the most contentious, high profile or atypical applications are referred to the elected members — so if you want politicians rather than officers to decide, those three words are the argument to make. It determines applications of all kinds, including protected buildings and scheduled sites, and administers tree protection orders and functions relating to sites of special significance and conservation areas. AN UNUSUAL SEPARATION WORTH CITING ELSEWHERE: its constitution provides that neither the President nor any member may also be President or a member of the Policy & Resources Committee or of the Committee for the Environment & Infrastructure — the people who decide planning are statutorily barred from also sitting on the island's resources and environment committees. COMPLAINTS GO SOMEWHERE ELSE AGAIN: the formal Customer Complaint Procedure is administered by the Office of the Committee for the Environment & Infrastructure, not the DPA, and recurring issues are reviewed with amendments to policies and guidance recommended. A separate Planning Panel, an independent statutory body established April 2009 under the 2005 Law, also determines applications. AND THE PLAN IS THE BIGGER TARGET: the Island Development Plan is periodically reviewed, and a recent round drew 276 submissions containing about 500 individual representations, with concern recorded over allocation of green field sites for housing and over areas of biodiversity importance. The DPA publishes responses to initial representations and then invites further ones, with public hearings on local planning briefs — a second chance to answer after seeing how the Authority replied to the first round.

trackers.name: La Société Guernesiaise — it changed its constitution so it could hold land
trackers.desc: IT REWROTE ITS OWN CONSTITUTION TO BE ABLE TO BUY LAND. In the early 1970s La Société Guernesiaise recognised that because of increasing development many rare habitats were under threat, and ‘accordingly changed its constitution to enable it to hold land as nature reserves’. Some reserves are owned outright; some are LEASED TO IT FOR NOMINAL RENTS — and that lease is the route for an owner who will not sell and will not gift: title stays with the owner, control passes to the conservation body. IT IS BUYING NOW: a recent round secured three more fields — two at Rue des Vicheries extending the Bridget Ozanne Orchid fields, one purchased and one donated by a family who asked that it be protected in their mother's memory, and a third bought at Pleinmont for ground-nesting birds including the skylark — though only after an ecological assessment. A field donated in someone's memory is a real and underused route. AND IT WILL SUPPLY YOUR EVIDENCE: its botany section surveyed one landholding and found 116 species, a few dozen more than in 2019, including the many-stalked spike rush, so rare its identity needed confirmation by a UK specialist — while an adjoining field ploughed and reseeded was visibly less diverse. A species survey with a neighbouring field as the control is exactly what an objection needs, and the botany section will do it. THE OTHER HOLDER: the National Trust of Guernsey (founded 1960), whose president has said it welcomes approaches from landowners who want to protect their holdings in perpetuity — an open invitation, stated publicly. It has received gifted land at Chouet and Creve Coeur. AND INDIVIDUALS CAN DO THIS TOO: one resident assembled 5.5 acres over decades — holding first refusal on one field for 32 years — expressly to prevent building. First refusal is the instrument.

trackers.name: LDCA — 14 days, or 28 if EIA is required, and the meeting is open
trackers.desc: ESTABLISH IMMEDIATELY WHETHER THE APPLICATION NEEDS AN EIA, BECAUSE IT DOUBLES YOUR WINDOW. Members of the public have 14 days to make a written representation — but on major applications requiring Environmental Impact Assessment the consultation period is 28 days. Fourteen days is very short; if the developer has avoided EIA you have half the time. ASK FOR THE ENVIRONMENTAL CHECKLIST FOR SCREENING OPINION BY NAME — it appears in the LDCA's published record and it is where the decision on whether EIA is required gets made. THE DECIDER IS UNUSUAL: the Land Development Control Authority's members are appointed by the Governor but are independent of the Government, it meets on the first Thursday of each month, and the meetings are open — diarise it; attendance is a right, not a favour. Applications are determined under the Land Planning and Development Control Ordinance and the Land Development Control Plan, ‘unless material planning and environmental consideration indicate otherwise’ — the plan is the default but environmental considerations can displace it, and that phrase is the opening an objection needs. Applications are viewable at Essex House in office hours, advertised in the local papers, with site notices and a weekly list. The Land Planning and Building Control Division sits in the Environment, Natural Resources and Planning portfolio; tel 22270.

trackers.name: St Helena National Trust — a statutory trust, and a £10 stake in the land
trackers.desc: TEN POUNDS IS THE LOWEST DOCUMENTED ENTRY POINT INTO LAND PROTECTION IN THIS FILE — and the money is not the point. Sponsored tree planting at just £10 per tree supports the Millennium Forest, and what it builds is a constituency: as one participant put it, the striking thing is the people's sense of ownership — parents and grandparents can take their children there and say, I planted this tree. A campaign that lets every household buy a stake for £10 creates a constituency no developer can buy out — and this was done on degraded wasteland nobody wanted. The forest covers 19 hectares of a 225-hectare National Conservation Area on a highly eroded site with little original soil; it began at the initiative of the local community, over 250 hectares has been set aside for restoration, over 10,000 gumwood trees planted since 2002, and it won the JNCC Blue Turtle Award in 2010. THE TRUST IS STATUTORY, WHICH CHANGES ITS WEIGHT: established under the St Helena National Trust Ordinance 2001 (amended 2008, 2017, 2019), its objects expressly include to preserve, maintain, manage, protect and AUGMENT, and to tender advice on land and buildings of national interest — a body whose land role is written into statute is harder for a government to ignore, and asking for its advice is asking it to do its statutory job. A SUCCESSION PRECEDENT: management of the forest was transferred to the Trust under a development plan — a worked route for moving a community project into permanent institutional care. AND FRAME RESTORATION AS WATER, NOT WILDLIFE: the Cloud Forest Project — with the St Helena Government, RSPB and Connect St Helena — justifies re-vegetating key areas of mist capture to secure the island's water security, alongside biodiversity and ecotourism, education and conservation training. On a dry island that is the strongest argument available. Monitoring shows the endemic spiky yellow woodlouse moving into newly restored areas — evidence that restoration worked, which is what a sceptical planner asks for. Funders across its work include the Darwin Initiative, Fauna & Flora International, OTEP/DfID and JNCC. Also on island: the St Helena Nature Conservation Group (since 1993), which way-marked the Postbox Walks — a documented route network is evidence of established public access and use.

trackers.name: Planning & Building Committee — past agendas give you the winning wording
trackers.desc: IN A JURISDICTION THIS SMALL THE SAME COMMITTEE APPLIES THE SAME POLICIES REPEATEDLY — SO THE PUBLISHED REFUSAL WORDING TELLS YOU WHAT WORKS. The Planning and Building Committee publishes its agendas with the full text of objections and the reasons for refusal. Recorded reasons include that a proposal ‘by virtue of its size would appear harmfully dominant and out of scale amongst the dwellings that define the character of this part of the Conservation Area’, and that a change of use ‘would result in a net loss of housing from the Stanley housing stock, contravening wider government objectives’. Those are tested phrases, not inventions — read past agendas before drafting. AND COPY THE METHOD FROM THE RECORDED OBJECTIONS: one objector cited the site's position within Zone 2 of the Development Plan, where only residential development should be supported, and named policies SP4 and TP12; another corrected the applicant's own drawing, stating the access point was smaller than shown. Cite the zone and the policy number, and check the applicant's plan against the ground. Governing documents: the Falkland Islands Development Plan 2015 and the Stanley Town Plan 2015–2030, which operates a zone system. The service covers Stanley, Camp and the Islands, administers the historic buildings system, and assists the Historic Buildings Committee. Officers invite contact before, during and after a formal application. Applications are also posted to a government Facebook page — a real notification channel at this scale, but not a substitute for the formal register.
