A Fellowships Fund supports nationals of the Territories. THE AWARD RATE IS THE ARGUMENT FOR APPLYING: since January 2024 alone, Darwin Plus has supported nearly 130 projects worth over £20 million across fourteen small territories — this is not a lottery-odds fund. THE MOST TRANSFERABLE PRECEDENT: Bermuda's Microforest Restoration Initiative received £50,000 — the full Local ceiling — a small-scale habitat restoration project on a small island, funded to the cap. Deep-sea research at the Bermuda Institute of Ocean Sciences received £316,829. HOW TO FRAME IT: the fund delivers the UK Overseas Territories Biodiversity Strategy, which emphasises protecting globally significant and unique species, ecosystem resilience, invasive non-native species and building local capacity, and says it aligns investment with locally identified priorities — so write the application as a locally identified priority and as habitat or species protection, in the strategy's own words. The territories hold over 90% of the UK's globally unique species. Where a territory has no permanent population, an applicant must demonstrate a long-term meaningful connection to it.

trackers.name: Falklands Conservation — owns 20 islands, and nine reserves are privately owned
trackers.desc: NINE OF THE NINETEEN NATIONAL NATURE RESERVES ARE PRIVATELY OWNED — which means designation here does not require the state to buy the land, and that is the single most useful fact for a landowner under pressure to sell. Of the 19 reserves designated under the Conservation of Wildlife and Nature Ordinance 1999 (covering 354 km², under 3% of the territory), eight are government-owned, two belong to conservation groups and nine are private. AND A CONSULTATION IS OPEN NOW: the Falkland Islands Government has proposed 10 new National Nature Reserves and the expansion of 5 existing ones, to safeguard land and habitats in perpetuity and build an ecologically connected network. The proposed sites include land owned by private landowners — and those landowners have given their full support. Private owners volunteering their own land for statutory designation is the precedent to put in front of a reluctant neighbour: it happened here, publicly. Views go in by online survey, with a drop-in at the Malvina House Hotel, Stanley — check whether the window is still open. THE ALLY ITSELF OWNS LAND: Falklands Conservation is owner of 20 islands and islets and a mainland reserve, about 3,220 hectares, including a National Nature Reserve (The Twins), parts of three Key Biodiversity Areas, three Important Bird Areas and two Important Plant Areas — with six islands probably almost pristine, never grazed, stocked or invaded by non-native mammals. It is the largest membership charity in the Islands (since 1979), an IUCN member and the BirdLife partner. THE MERGER IS A SUCCESSION MODEL WORTH COPYING: the New Island Conservation Trust, founded 1995 by one conservationist, merged into Falklands Conservation on 1 July 2020, which now holds the island — when a small single-site trust cannot carry on, merging into a larger charity keeps the land protected instead of returning it to the market. WHAT IT OFFERS YOU DIRECTLY: its priorities include ensuring best practice for offshore and onshore developments and habitat restoration, and it reports landowners already seeking advice and help in restoring their land — though it says candidly the Islands lack a strong and forward-thinking national policy on ecological restoration. Its New Island Restoration Programme states that crucial funding is still required.

trackers.name: Turks and Caicos National Trust - manages entrusted sites; no acquisition programme evidenced
trackers.desc: MANAGED, NOT VESTED - AND THAT DISTINCTION DECIDES WHETHER THIS BODY CAN HELP YOU. The Trust describes itself as managing national parks and maintaining the country's significant historical sites; nothing on its own domain evidences a land-purchase fund, an acquisition programme or a route for offering it a threatened parcel. Established 1992 as a membership organisation; office at Unit 50, Salt Mills Plaza, 363 Grace Bay Road, Grace Bay, Providenciales. Approach it as a body that can be asked to take a site into management and to speak to Government about designation - not as a buyer. TWO TRAPS ON THE WAY IN. First, there are two domains: turksandcaicosnationaltrust.com carries current content, while nationaltrust.tc is the address cited in older references - confirm which is answering before you send anything. Second, the current site's own Who We Are page still contains Lorem ipsum placeholder text and describes an XX-member council, so its published governance and membership detail cannot be relied on; ring the office and get it confirmed by a person. Recorded here as the island's only heritage and parks body of this kind, with those limits stated rather than dressed up.

trackers.name: Access to Land network — find the farmland-buying body in your country
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a European federation of civic organisations that secure farmland for agroecological farming, founded in 2012 by Terre de Liens, Regionalwert AG, Xarxa, the Soil Association, AIAB, Viva Sol and Terre-en-vue. It now runs to eighteen members in thirteen countries and is still expanding into Scandinavia, eastern and southern Europe. WHY IT IS IN THIS FILE: it is the shortest route to finding out whether a body that buys farmland exists in your country, and its members page carries a profile of each one with what it does and how it is financed. Named members include Terre de Liens in France, Terre-en-vue in Wallonia, De Landgenoten in Flanders, Kulturland eG and Regionalwert AG in Germany, the Soil Association and Shared Assets and the Biodynamic Land Trust and the Real Farming Trust in Britain, Eco Ruralis in Romania, Nadace Pro půdu in Czechia, AIAB in Italy, Terra Franca in Portugal, Xarxa de Custòdia del Territori and the Catalan nature conservation network in Spain, Rurbans, and Viva Sol in Lithuania. The Scottish Farm Land Trust and the German Netzwerk Flächensicherung, a platform of seven organisations founded in 2018, also appear in its orbit. USE IT AS A DIRECTORY, NOT AN ALLY: it does not buy land or take cases. It tells you who does, in your country, and its published comparisons of how each member is financed are the fastest way to work out which model could be copied where no such body exists yet.

trackers.name: Eurosite — click your country and see who manages the land
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the European network of natural site managers, founded in 1989, bringing together non-governmental and governmental organisations and individuals from the Atlantic islands to the Black Sea and from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean. Secretariat at Hart van Brabantlaan 12-14, 5038 JL Tilburg, Netherlands. WHY IT IS WORTH A COMMUNITY'S TIME: its network page carries an interactive map — click a country and it lists the members based there, with a full list below the map. That is the fastest way to find out who actually holds and manages nature land in a given country, which is the question this whole file exists to answer and which is otherwise a week of searching in a language you may not read. Its members are the bodies that do day-to-day site management and land conservation, which is exactly the category a community needs and exactly the one that is hardest to find from outside. WHAT IT IS NOT: a directory, not an ally. It does not buy land, fund anyone or take cases. Use it to identify the organisation, then approach that organisation directly. Note also that its membership deliberately mixes governmental with non-governmental bodies, so a name on the map may be a state agency rather than an independent one — check which before you write.

trackers.name: International National Trusts Organisation — find the body that takes buildings and land in your country
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the worldwide federation of National Trusts and equivalent heritage bodies, formally established in December 2007 in New Delhi and registered as a non-profit in England and Wales. Over 100 member organisations across more than 80 nations and territories, covering built and natural, tangible and intangible heritage — from the National Trust for Scotland to the Bahamas National Trust, and from Australia to Malta, Taiwan to Zimbabwe. Its members page lets you find the one for your country. WHY IT MATTERS FOR STOPPING SOMETHING: national trusts are the category of organisation that takes ownership of buildings and land permanently and will not sell them, which is precisely the ally a community needs when a mill, a farmstead, a chapel or a landscape is threatened. This file already holds several of them one at a time — An Taisce in Ireland, Din l-Art Ħelwa in Malta — without recording that they belong to a global family with a member in most countries. If you do not know whether your country has one, this is where you look first. AND ONE THING IT DOES ITSELF: its TAP INTO small grants scheme funds partnerships between member organisations, covering travel and collaboration costs so expertise can move between trusts. That is not money for a community directly, but it is the route by which a small or new trust in one country can bring in someone who has already handled your kind of case in another. USE IT AS A DIRECTORY: it does not buy property, fund campaigns or take cases. Its members do. Note also that a national trust's remit is heritage rather than development control — some will object to a scheme, many will only take on a property, and you should ask which at the outset.

trackers.name: European Community Foundation Initiative — find the grant-maker in your own district
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the umbrella initiative for community foundations in Europe, launched January 2016 and hosted by the German Association of Foundations. It maps 829 active community foundations across 28 European countries, and it runs two tools a community can use directly: an Atlas to explore them by location, and a country-by-country Directory, both stated to be regularly updated. Twenty-five new foundations were established in the last year across ten countries, including the first ever in Austria and Albania, with sixteen more in development. WHY THIS ANSWERS THE COMMONEST GAP: a community foundation is a grant-maker rooted in one geographic area, mobilising local money for local purposes, and they range from neighbourhood bodies run by volunteers to professionally staffed institutions. Across this region the missing resource is almost never a lawyer and almost always money — and most countries have dozens of these, unlisted anywhere a campaigner would look. If you need a few thousand euros for a survey, a valuation, a deposit or a hall, the nearest community foundation is a likelier answer than any national body. IT ALSO PUBLISHES COUNTRY GUIDES: its knowledge centre carries dedicated guides to community foundations in Romania, Italy, the United Kingdom and Germany, and a directory of the national support organisations — 32 foundation associations and networks operating at national level — which is who to ask if your country's foundations are not individually listed. USE IT AS A DIRECTORY: ECFI itself makes no grants. It tells you which local foundations exist. And note what a community foundation is not: it is a general local grant-maker, not an environmental funder, so frame the application around the community rather than the habitat.

trackers.name: European Community Land Trust Network — the model that takes land off the market permanently
trackers.desc: WHAT A CLT IS, AND WHY IT BELONGS IN A FILE ABOUT STOPPING PROJECTS: a community land trust is a non-profit, democratic, community-led organisation that acquires land and holds it in trust permanently. The land is separated from what stands on it and is never returned to the market, which is the same result a conservation trust achieves and a different route to it — through a body the residents themselves control rather than a national organisation they petition. Where no conservation buyer exists in a country, this is the model a community can build itself. THE SCALE, WHICH IS LARGER THAN MOST PEOPLE REALISE: the network was launched in June 2023, based in Brussels, and links more than 300 CLTs; the wider European sector has grown from 33 in 2017 to over 500, and reports more than 31,500 homes delivered and €145.7 million in funding secured. Members span countries including the UK, Ireland, Belgium, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy, Portugal and Germany, with emerging groups in Poland, Slovenia, Croatia, Hungary, Greece, Montenegro and Sweden. Founding members include London CLT, CLT Brussels, Stadtbodenstiftung Berlin, South of Scotland Community Housing, CLT H-Buurt Amsterdam, Self Organised Architecture Ireland, OFS Métropole Lilloise, CLT Leuven, CLT Gent, habitatge.social Barcelona, Habicoop, Cohabitac and the CLT Network of England and Wales. WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES FOR YOU: it supports the formation of new CLTs, which is the offer that matters. A community facing a site being sold can be told how to become the buyer. Its partners are named too, and the pattern is worth copying — local governments donating land or granting long leases, social housing providers co-financing, developers allocating sites. BE CLEAR ABOUT THE FIT: this sector is about housing affordability, not habitat. A CLT will take on land and buildings and steward other assets that serve a local community, but a case argued as conservation will not fit. Argue it as land taken permanently out of speculation for local people, which is what it is.

trackers.name: International Land Conservation Network — a world map of private land conservation groups
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a global network hosted at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, formally launched at its first congress in Berlin in October 2015 with 90 participants from 27 countries, connecting civic and private organisations that protect and steward land and water. It works on six continents across five areas: conservation finance, conservation law and policy, organisation and governance, land stewardship and management, and large landscape conservation. THE PART TO USE: it publishes a network map of civic and private land conservation groups around the world, and it invites anyone to add an organisation or a location to it by emailing ilcn@lincolninst.edu. Two things follow. A community anywhere can look up whether a private land conservation body exists near it — and where the map is thin, that thinness is itself information rather than proof of absence. READ THE CAVEAT IT PUTS ON ITS OWN MAP, BECAUSE IT MATTERS: the locations shown come from a global census carried out in mid-2015 and do not necessarily indicate any affiliation with the network. So treat it as a decade-old snapshot to be confirmed, not a current directory — and since it takes additions by email, a community that finds an active local body missing can put it on the map for everyone who looks next. WHY IT COMPLEMENTS THE OTHER DIRECTORIES IN THIS FILE: Access to Land covers farmland buyers in Europe, Eurosite covers site managers in Europe, INTO covers heritage trusts. This one is global and covers privately protected areas as a category — the Americas, Africa, Asia and Oceania included. It is also the parent idea behind the European land conservation initiative, so the two are connected rather than competing. It does not buy land, fund anyone or take cases; its resource library and recorded webinars are aimed at practitioners rather than campaigners.

trackers.name: International Land Coalition — 300 land-rights organisations in 81 countries
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the largest coalition working on land rights in the world — almost 300 member organisations across 81 countries, representing over 70 million land users: farmers, pastoralists, Indigenous Peoples, women and youth. Founded in Brussels in 1995, hosted by IFAD at Via Paolo di Dono 44, 00142 Rome, with a global secretariat and regional coordination units for Africa, Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean; Europe, the Middle East and North Africa are handled from the secretariat itself. WHY A COMMUNITY WOULD USE IT: its network pages are the route to finding a land-rights organisation in a country where nothing else in this file reaches, and its membership is the opposite kind of body from the conservation trusts elsewhere here — peoples' organisations and farmers' unions rather than nature charities. Where a project threatens people's access to land rather than a habitat, these are the organisations that work on it. It also maintains a database of documented good practices in land governance drawn from its members, which is where to look for a community elsewhere that has already faced your situation. THE PLEDGE WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: every ILC member signs two commitments, one protecting and empowering women within the network and one protecting land defenders. If your fight has put people at risk, that is a stated obligation you can hold a member organisation to, and it is unusual for a network to make membership conditional on it. WHAT IT IS NOT: a directory, not an ally. It does not buy land, fund communities directly or take cases; its members might. It is also a coalition that includes intergovernmental organisations alongside civil society, so check what kind of body you have found before you rely on it.

trackers.name: BirdLife Europe and Central Asia — 48 national partners owning 320,000 hectares
trackers.desc: WHY THIS IS A LAND DIRECTORY, NOT A BIRD CHARITY: BirdLife Europe and Central Asia is a partnership of 48 national conservation organisations present in 47 countries including every EU member state, and together with its national partners it owns or manages more than 6,000 nature sites totalling around 320,000 hectares. Each partner represents one country. So for almost anywhere in this region there is a national organisation that already holds land, and its partner page names it. HOW A COMMUNITY USES IT: find the partner for your country, then ask the question that matters — do you own or manage reserves, and would you take on this site. Partners vary enormously in what they do: Natuurpunt and Natagora between them own or manage over 400 reserves covering 17,147 hectares in Belgium, with local branches doing the acquisition and monitoring work; the Dutch partner works largely through advocacy, legal action and restoration projects with other reserve managers rather than owning; the Italian partner runs species protection, habitat conservation and litigation for stricter application of Italian and EU wildlife law. Ask which kind you have reached before you plan around it. THE BRANCH POINT AGAIN: Belgium's partners work through more than 150 local branches and antennas, and the Belgian page says plainly that volunteer work and regional government support are essential for acquiring, managing and monitoring the reserves. As with the Austrian, Hungarian and Irish entries in this file, the useful unit is the local branch and not the national office. USE IT AS A DIRECTORY: BirdLife itself does not buy land or take cases; the Brussels team works on EU policy. Its value here is that it is the single largest roster of national organisations that actually hold land in this region, and it is organised one partner per country.

trackers.name: Rewilding Europe Capital — loans and repayable grants up to €100,000
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the financing division of Rewilding Europe, providing commercial loans since 2014 to businesses in and around its rewilding landscapes, and now also repayable grants, with an upper limit of €100,000. Two conditions: the recipient must deliver rewilding impact, and must have a repayment mechanism in place or under development. Prospective enterprises are invited to make contact at any time. WHY IT IS IN A FILE ABOUT STOPPING PROJECTS: a loan from it enabled the Finland-based Snowchange Cooperative to buy the 110-hectare Linnunsuo wetland in 2017. That is the whole argument — this is money that can be borrowed to buy a specific piece of ground, by a community enterprise rather than a conservation charity, and repaid from what the land then does. For a community with a willing seller, a business idea and no capital, almost nothing else in this file offers that. WHERE IT REACHES: in and around Rewilding Europe's landscapes — eleven areas from the Danube Delta to the Scottish Highlands, including the Velebit Mountains in Croatia, the Oder Delta, the Central Apennines and the Greater Côa. Ukraine is explicitly among the countries where the mechanism operates. Croatia and Ukraine are both countries where repeated searches for a conservation land buyer found none, so this is a route into two of the emptiest buckets in the region. BE HONEST ABOUT WHAT IT WANTS: it funds enterprise, not campaigns. The pitch has to be a business that generates income and repays — nature tourism, sustainable products, grazing — and that delivers measurable rewilding impact. If your case is purely to stop something with no enterprise behind it, this is the wrong door.

trackers.name: Civil Society Fund (EEA and Norway Grants) — NGO-run grant operators in 15 countries
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the civil society strand of the EEA and Norway Grants, funded by Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway, with €327 million allocated across 15 countries: Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Greece, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia. Those are, almost exactly, the countries this file has found hardest to fill. WHY IT IS A RESOURCE AND NOT A SCHEME: in each country the money is managed by an independent Fund Operator drawn from civil society itself, contracted to run the calls and answer to national needs — not by a ministry. The operators are named organisations you can ring. In Hungary the lead is the Ökotárs Hungarian Environmental Partnership Foundation, already in this file as a grant-maker in its own right. In Slovenia it is CNVOS with the Legal and Information Centre Maribor and DRPD Novo mesto. In Cyprus it is a consortium of the NGO Support Centre and GrantXpert Consulting. Poland's operator is likewise a consortium of NGOs chosen directly by the donor states, handling €83.5 million. SCALE AND SHAPE: Slovenia's previous round allocated €2.5 million across four open calls, with medium projects up to €60,000. Hungary's current fund is close to €23 million. The stated objective is a resilient civil society protecting democracy, the rule of law and human rights, and building the long-term capacity of civil society organisations — so a local group's own durability is a fundable purpose here, which is rare. WHAT TO WATCH: the rounds run in cycles and there are gaps between them; Poland's fourth-edition calls were expected to begin in the first half of 2026 after programme agreements were signed. Find your country's Fund Operator and ask when the next call opens rather than assuming one is live. Donor-country organisations cannot apply but can be project partners, which is a route to an outside collaborator if you want one.

trackers.name: Prespa Ohrid Nature Trust (PONT) — long-term money for Balkan parks and local NGOs
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a transboundary conservation trust fund, registered as a foundation in Germany and established in 2015, covering the mountainous cross-border protected areas of Albania, North Macedonia and Greece and the corridors between them — the Wider Prespa and Ohrid areas, the Korab-Shara region, the Albanian Alps and north-western Greece. It describes itself as the only conservation trust fund working in the Balkans. Contact via the Nature Trust Alliance, Friedrich-Ebert-Anlage 36, 60325 Frankfurt am Main. WHO CAN APPLY, WHICH IS THE POINT: it runs two grant programmes — one co-financing the operational costs of protected areas, and one, the Environmental Actors programme, for qualified NGOs, municipalities and research institutes in the region working on conservation, community improvement and citizen participation in conservation. It has run open calls for proposals, and at one count held 24 ongoing grants, 7 to protected area authorities and 17 to environmental actors. WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT FROM OTHER FUNDERS IN THIS FILE: an external evaluation records that it is one of very few institutions that will fund operating costs, that it works directly on transboundary cooperation rather than through bilateral arrangements, and that it has financed studies at short notice which donors' procurement processes would have delayed. For a small organisation the ability to fund salaries and running costs, and to pay for a study quickly, is worth more than a larger project grant. Its grants also fund staff directly — one municipality used a PONT grant to employ a biologist and a chemist for monitoring. THE CASE IN ITS OWN REGION WORTH KNOWING: Galicica National Park in North Macedonia built its management plan through a stakeholder council with every village in and around the park involved in the zonation — and the government later tried to alter that plan to create a ski resort and access road, threatening the World Heritage status of the Lake Ohrid region. A management plan made with the villages is the thing that made the alteration contestable.

trackers.name: LIFE ENPLC — 18 private land conservation organisations in 11 countries
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: European Networks for Private Land Conservation, a network of landowners and conservationists protecting and restoring private land, funded by the EU LIFE programme and successor to the earlier ELCN and L.I.F.E. projects. It brings together 18 organisations from 11 European countries — Belgium, Czechia, Estonia, France, Germany, Italy, Latvia, Portugal, Romania, Spain and the Netherlands — with the aim of establishing durable governance structures for private land conservation in Europe. WHY THE COUNTRY LIST MATTERS: Estonia and Latvia are on it. Both are places where repeated searches in this file found no conservation land buyer, and Latvia is the thinnest bucket in the whole region. If organisations in those countries are partners in a private land conservation network, they are the closest thing to the missing acquirer, and this is where they are named. Romania, Czechia, Portugal and Spain are also on it, and the file's entries for those countries can be checked against the partner list. WHAT THE NETWORK IS FOR: engaging private landowners who are willing to put at least part of their land into conservation. Its own diagnosis is worth knowing before you approach a landowner — a survey of European private land conservation practitioners found the majority perceive a lack of adequate legal tools for engaging private owners in voluntary conservation, and the network has studied conservation easements as a way to close that gap. If an owner is willing but there seems to be no instrument, that is a known European problem and these are the people working on it. IT IS ALSO WHERE THE MONEY ADVICE IS: the network has run sessions specifically on using EU LIFE funding for private land conservation, aimed at landowners and at conservationists working with them. USE IT AS A DIRECTORY, AND NOTE THE STRUCTURE: this is a project rather than a permanent institution, and its work has been folded into Eurosite, which launched a working group on nature finance and land stewardship in November 2025. Eurosite is already in this file. Treat ENPLC as the partner list and Eurosite as the standing body.

trackers.name: European Landowners' Organization — the other side of the table, and it has a network
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: a non-profit federation representing the interests of owners and managers of rural land and rural businesses across Europe, founded 1972, secretariat in Brussels, a network of more than fifty member associations whose national constituents represent millions of landowners. It is an IUCN member. Alongside it sits Friends of the Countryside, a support group of over 600 private landowners, rural managers and entrepreneurs from 27 countries, founded 1997. WHY A COMMUNITY TRYING TO STOP SOMETHING SHOULD KNOW ABOUT IT: this is the organised voice of the people who own the land, and it has formally partnered with the conservation sector. With Eurosite it established the Conservation Landowners Coalition, a standing European partnership between landowners and conservationists, created out of the LIFE ENPLC project and intended to outlast it. If the obstacle in your case is that the owner will not engage with conservation arguments, there is now a body that exists precisely to make that conversation normal, and the owner's own federation is a founder of it. IT ALSO RUNS A LABEL: the Wildlife Estates label promotes collaboration between private and public actors to demonstrate that a land manager's practice aligns with biodiversity conservation principles, working through national delegations that engage NGOs, administrative bodies, universities and independent scientists. An owner who wants recognition rather than restriction has something to be offered. AND BE CLEAR-EYED ABOUT IT: this is a landowners' lobby, not a conservation organisation. It founded the Forum for the Future of Agriculture jointly with Syngenta, and Cargill is among the partners. Its interests will frequently be opposed to a community trying to stop a rural development. Use it for what it is — the route to owners and a source of legitimacy for a conservation offer — and expect nothing else. OTHER NETWORKS IT LISTS THAT MATTER HERE: European Historic Houses, an umbrella of 27 national associations of privately owned historic houses; and Europa Nostra, founded 1963 and covering over 40 countries, the largest heritage network in Europe.

trackers.name: Europa Nostra — nominate your threatened site to the 7 Most Endangered
trackers.desc: WHAT IT OFFERS A COMMUNITY: Europa Nostra, founded 1963 and covering over 40 countries, runs a programme that takes a site threatened with demolition or unsuitable development and puts an international expert team, a technical and financial report, and a funded first step behind it. Launched January 2013 with the European Investment Bank Institute; 56 threatened monuments and sites from 31 countries listed so far. Each listed site is eligible for an EIB Heritage Grant of €10,000 towards an agreed early action, and teams from Europa Nostra and the EIB Institute then visit, meet the stakeholders and issue recommendations. The 2025 list included three sites threatened specifically by invasive new buildings and unsuitable development — Nyborg Castle, the Castle of Monemvasia and Victoria Tower Gardens in London. WHO CAN NOMINATE, WHICH IS THE PART TO PLAN AROUND: public and private organisations active in heritage registered in a Council of Europe member country, or individual members of such organisations resident in one. Every valid nomination needs at least two letters of support in English, at least one from a Europa Nostra member or associate organisation. So a local group cannot nominate alone — it needs a member organisation behind it, or it must join the network itself. Find the member in your country first; that is the gating step. WHAT TO PREPARE, ON ITS OWN ADVICE: identify the owner or custodian, the public authorities, local experts and community organisations, and start the dialogue early; tell stakeholders you intend to nominate and discuss collaboration; collect letters of support, preferably including the owner and the local or regional authority; and gather high-resolution photographs, video and material showing the site's significance, the current threat and its potential. It advises starting before the call opens, which runs on an annual cycle with a deadline around September or October. BOTH TANGIBLE AND INTANGIBLE HERITAGE QUALIFY, publicly or privately owned, and it explicitly welcomes sites endangered by neglect or underfunding as well as by climate hazards. Listing is not protection — it is a catalyst, an independent expert assessment and a small grant, and the entry says so.

trackers.name: Coastal & Marine Union (EUCC) — the coastal network, with 15 national branches
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: an association founded in 1989, based in Leiden, uniting scientists, environmentalists, site managers, planners and policy makers on coastal and marine management. Around 500 full members and 2,700 network members across 40 countries, with 15 national branches and offices in seven countries — the largest network of coastal practitioners in Europe, working across Europe, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea and neighbouring regions. It holds observer status in the OSPAR and HELCOM regional sea conventions. WHY IT FILLS A REAL GAP HERE: this file covers farmland buyers, nature site managers, heritage trusts, community land trusts and local grant-makers, and until now had nothing for coasts — where a great deal of development pressure sits. Find the national branch for your country: that is a body of coastal specialists who already know the planners and the site managers on your stretch. AND ONE BRANCH OWNS LAND: EUCC Poland owns around 1,000 hectares at the Polish part of the Szczecin Lagoon, within roughly 4,000 hectares of wetland, forest and lagoon waters protected there, the remainder belonging to the forestry and maritime offices and to private owners. That is a working example of a coastal branch as a landowner, and worth asking of the branch in your own country. WHAT IT PUBLISHES THAT A COMMUNITY CAN USE: it initiated the Coastal Wiki, an online encyclopaedia of coastal management, and the ENCORA network of coastal management networks; it publishes a quarterly magazine; and it runs QualityCoast, an award and certification programme — which is a lever where a coastal municipality cares about its reputation. WHAT IT IS NOT: a network of experts and a policy body, not a campaigning organisation and not a law firm. Its history is in developing integrated coastal zone management as a policy approach, so it is strong on evidence, standards and contacts and will not front a fight for you.

trackers.name: European Rivers Network — the river-defence network, and its dam campaigns
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a French-based network founded in 1994 out of the citizen movements that saved the Danube between Vienna and Budapest and the Loire from source to mouth, maintaining an informal information network across all the major river catchments of the continent. Its earlier incarnation, SOS Loire Vivante, won the Goldman Environmental Prize in 1992. It holds French state agréments, is recognised by the environment ministry, is a long-standing European Environmental Bureau member and a WWF freshwater partner, and it is co-founder of both the Dam Removal Europe platform and the Living Rivers Europe coalition. WHY IT BELONGS IN THIS FILE: hydropower is the single most recurring threat across the entries here — Bosnia, North Macedonia, Albania, Croatia and Slovenia all appear in this file with small hydro cases. ERN is the continental network behind those fights. It states that the finest rivers of the Balkans, from Slovenia to Greece, are threatened by more than 3,000 new dams in project, and it hosts the campaign material, including a handbook on the future of hydropower in the Balkans produced by a Bulgarian association. It also flags small hydropower specifically as an alarming expansion, and names high-risk micro-plant projects on wild rivers inside French national and regional parks. WHAT IT OFFERS A LOCAL GROUP: a label and network for the remaining wild rivers of Europe, which is a designation a community can seek for its own river; a directory of river organisations worldwide including basin-level platforms; and the Living Rivers Europe coalition, which opposes hydroelectric deployment in protected areas, sits in European Commission meetings and publishes the positions a national campaign can cite. Through Dam Removal Europe there is also a route for the opposite case — getting an existing barrier taken out. WHAT IT IS NOT: a campaigning and information network, not a funder, not a law firm and not a buyer. Ask it for the campaign material, the label, the contacts in your catchment, and the European-level position papers — then take those to the legal ally in your own country.

trackers.name: Yes to Life No to Mining — the network for communities facing a mine
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: a global solidarity network of and for Indigenous Peoples, impacted communities, local organisations and networks resisting mining, formed in 2012 and established as a network in 2014, now with over 60 member groups across borders. Coordination runs through Co-Coordinators and, importantly for a community, Regional Contact People — so there is a named person for your part of the world rather than a general inbox. General enquiries info@yestolifenotomining.org, membership membership@yestolifenotomining.org. WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES FOR A LOCAL GROUP: it exists to support its membership to resist unwanted, ecologically destructive mining operations by building international solidarity. In practice that means joint statements signed by members across continents, an Action Fund, published guides and case studies, a bi-monthly newsletter, and emblematic case work — its examples include a reopening mine at Rouyn-Noranda in Quebec and the Thacker Pass lithium mine in Nevada, where an international lithium working group's solidarity statement was co-signed by more than a dozen organisations. For a village facing a permit, a statement carrying signatures from Ecuador, Serbia and Ireland is a different object from a local petition. IT ALSO TRACKS THE DANGER TO THE PEOPLE INVOLVED, WHICH NOTHING ELSE IN THIS FILE DOES: it records that between 2012 and 2023 more than 2,100 land and environmental defenders were killed according to Global Witness, and that mining was the deadliest industry to resist, with 25 defenders killed after opposing mining operations in 2023 alone. It has published on the repression of civic freedoms and suppression of activists in Serbia. If a community faces intimidation as well as a permit, this is a network that treats that as part of the case. WHAT IT IS NOT: not a funder beyond a small action fund, not a law firm, not a buyer. It is solidarity, publicity, contacts and standing. Take a mining case here and the legal and technical work to the national allies already in this file — Turkey's environmental law network and Bosnia's centre both work mining and quarry cases.

trackers.name: CEE Bankwatch Network — go after the money behind the project
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: founded 1995 as a coalition of grassroots environmental and human rights groups, now 17 member organisations in 14 countries across central and eastern Europe and the Caucasus, headquartered in Prague with a Brussels office. It monitors the public finance institutions behind large projects — the European Investment Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank — and the spending of EU Cohesion, Recovery and Just Transition funds. Its declared subjects include dams and infrastructure, energy, mining and extractives, water and sanitation, and land rights. WHY THIS IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF ALLY: every other entry in this file goes at the permit, the land or the species. This one goes at the lender. A road, a dam, a mine or a power plant in this region is very often financed by an institution with its own environmental and social rules, its own complaints channel and its own reputation to protect — and a community that knows which bank is paying has a second front that the developer cannot close locally. Bankwatch states that it works with local communities on campaigns to stop or change harmful investment projects funded by international public finance, and that it makes sure those stories are told in Europe's power centres. ITS MEMBERS ARE THE NATIONAL DOOR, and several are already in this file or adjacent to it: Zelena akcija in Croatia, Hnutí DUHA in Czechia with dozens of local chapters, CEKOR in Serbia working on transport and biodiversity, Friends of the Earth CEPA in Slovakia, Za Zemiata in Bulgaria, the National Ecological Centre of Ukraine, and Bankwatch Romania. Find the member for your country and ask who financed the scheme. IT ALSO WORKS THE PARTICIPATION SIDE OF EU FUNDS: it publishes on transparency and public participation in EU cohesion spending, and argues that in many member states participation is reduced to a formal process with limited access to information for affected communities. If your project is EU co-financed, this is the organisation that knows what the managing authority is supposed to do. WHAT IT IS NOT: not a buyer, not a funder for communities, not a law firm. Research, monitoring, campaigning and access to European institutions.

trackers.name: European Platform Against Windfarms — a directory of 1,300 local groups already fighting
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a platform whose membership is more than 1,300 local, regional and national groups opposing wind development, listed individually by country and region — parish action groups in Offaly, village associations across Brittany and the Pays de la Loire, residents' groups in Norfolk and Suffolk, an interest group in Graubünden, a sustainable living platform in western Turkey, citizens' initiatives in Bavaria and Ostwestfalen, and groups in Finland and elsewhere. Any organisation can apply to join by emailing contact@epaw.org. WHY IT IS USEFUL EVEN IF YOU DISAGREE WITH IT: this is the only place I have found where a community facing a specific wind development can look up the group nearest to it that has already been through the same fight — often in the same region, sometimes against the same developer. That group will know the consultants, the arguments that worked, the procedural steps and the costs. The directory is the resource; the platform's own campaigning is separate. AND BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT IT IS: this is a campaigning platform opposed to wind energy as such, and some members describe themselves as campaigning against renewable energy generally. That is a political position many communities defending a landscape do not share and will not want to be associated with. Use the member list to find neighbours who have run the same case; decide separately whether to attach your name to the platform. Nothing about the directory requires you to adopt its position.

trackers.name: REScoop.eu — the route where the community owns the project instead
trackers.desc: THE OTHER ANSWER TO A WIND OR SOLAR SCHEME: the European federation of citizen energy cooperatives, whose case is that opposition is usually about ownership rather than about turbines. Its president puts it directly — local opposition to energy projects can be a major barrier, and energy communities are a way to build acceptance, because when people own the project and the profits stay in the community, support increases sharply, and the community is then able to choose where the turbines go. That siting power is the part that matters for a threatened field. THE NUMBERS TO PUT IN FRONT OF A COUNCIL: a ten-country YouGov study commissioned through this network found 86% of people across Europe would support new wind and solar near where they live, and 79% support governments giving more finance to community groups to generate their own energy, against 9% opposed — with support for community generation at 89% in Romania, 88% in Italy, 87% in Spain, 86% in Bulgaria and 84% in Poland and Greece. A community that is told it is standing in the way of the energy transition has an answer: it is not opposed to the turbines, it is opposed to somebody else siting them and taking the money. USE IT WITH THE REST OF THE FILE: this pairs with the community land trust network and the farmland cooperatives already here. All three are versions of the same move — the community becomes the owner rather than the objector.

trackers.name: Counter Balance — a support service for communities hit by publicly financed projects
trackers.desc: WHO THEY ARE: a European coalition of development and environmental NGOs formed in 2007 specifically to challenge the European Investment Bank, since widened to the EBRD, export credit agencies and national development finance institutions. Members: CEE Bankwatch Network for central and eastern Europe, les Amis de la Terre in France, urgewald in Germany, Re:Common in Italy, BothEnds in the Netherlands, ODG in Spain, and the Bretton Woods Project, The Corner House and Platform London in the UK. THE SENTENCE THAT PUTS IT IN THIS FILE: it states that it works in close cooperation and solidarity with affected communities and citizens around the world and is willing to act as a support service for them. Very few organisations of this size say that plainly. WHAT IT KNOWS THAT A COMMUNITY CANNOT FIND OUT ALONE: it tracks the EIB's Complaints Mechanism in detail, including the draft policy revisions, the deadlines, the new early-stage dispute tool between project companies and impacted communities — and its own warning that a better complaints policy means little if the department stays understaffed. If you intend to complain to a European public bank, this is who can tell you whether that mechanism currently works. AND THE STRUCTURAL FACT WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU START: it reports that in roughly one third of EIB projects the bank lends not to the project but to an intermediary — a bank, a venture fund, an equity fund — which then relends the money. So the public money behind a scheme may be two or three steps removed and invisible from the ground. A community that has been told no public bank is involved should not take that as settled. USE IT WITH THE NATIONAL MEMBER: Bankwatch and its member groups are already in this file for central and eastern Europe, and Counter Balance adds France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and the UK. Find the member for your country, and bring the project name and the developer. WHAT IT IS NOT: research, advocacy and access to European institutions. Not a funder, not a law firm, not a buyer.

trackers.name: Dam Removal Europe — submit your barrier and they will look for a sponsor
trackers.desc: WHAT IT OFFERS, IN ONE SENTENCE FROM ITS OWN PAGE: if none of the listed funding opportunities suits you, write to pao@fishmigration.org and submit your barrier proposal for funding — they will send a form, and they say they always try to find sponsors for new dam removal projects. Across 118 candidates that is one of very few organisations that invites a community to send it a specific site and then goes looking for the money. WHO IT IS: a coalition led by the World Fish Migration Foundation, including WWF, ERN, Rewilding Europe, Wetlands International, The Rivers Trust and The Nature Conservancy. Its south-east Europe project, running three years with Fauna & Flora, MedINA Greece, Wetlands International, ERN and WWF Netherlands, Slovakia and Adria, exists specifically to build a pipeline of removable barriers in the Balkans, where dam removal is not yet mainstream. Part of that project is explicitly about identifying and releasing other funding sources for removal. WHY THIS BELONGS BESIDE THE ANTI-DAM ENTRIES: this file already holds organisations that fight proposed dams in Bosnia, Albania, North Macedonia and Bulgaria. This is the other half — for the obsolete weir, culvert or mill dam already sitting in the river, which is often the thing actually degrading a site a community is trying to defend.

trackers.name: Open Rivers Programme — grants that pay to take a barrier out
trackers.desc: WHAT IT FUNDS: a charitable foundation registered in the Netherlands making grants across Europe for the removal of small dams and artificial river barriers, and for the preparatory work that gets there — barrier identification and prioritisation, feasibility studies, technical designs, and securing the permissions for removal. Grant categories range from small awards under €10,000 for preparatory phases to full-scale removals, and projects are generally expected to complete within twelve months. THE ARGUMENT IT HANDS A COMMUNITY: 68% of barriers in Europe are under two metres high, and these small culverts, fords and weirs cause the most fragmentation while being the least expensive to remove. Over a million barriers sit in European rivers. So the case for taking out the weir upstream of your site is cheap, evidenced and already funded by somebody. WHAT IT HAS DONE: it has supported the removal of 100 barriers; on the Vindel in Sweden, a Natura 2000 site and UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, removals reconnected 102 kilometres of river with 112 kilometres expected in total; in the Central Apennines five barriers came out of the Giovenco in November 2024, freeing 11 kilometres. READ THE ELIGIBILITY BEFORE YOU PLAN: applicants are expected to be organisations with an environmental focus and a track record in river or ecological restoration. Community groups are encouraged to take part as partners, but the managing authority states it will not accept unsolicited applications from them. So a community needs a constituted environmental partner to lead — which is exactly what Dam Removal Europe and the national river bodies in this file are for.

trackers.name: CASE — a map of lawyers who will defend you for free when a developer sues you
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS FOR: the Coalition Against SLAPPs in Europe, over 120 non-governmental organisations across Europe and beyond, formed against Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation — unfounded lawsuits brought by powerful litigants to silence critics and freeze public debate. Its work is built on three pillars: expose, help and advocate. THE PART TO USE, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS ENTRY EXISTS: it publishes a map of the lawyers, law firms, legal organisations and funds across Europe able to support SLAPP victims pro bono or at reduced fees, each having told CASE it is willing and able to take SLAPP work, with expertise across media law, intellectual property, criminal law, corporate law and fundamental rights, and with the map indicating which can advise and which can represent. A resident who has just been sued personally by a developer has, in one page, a list of people who will defend them without a fee. WHY THIS BELONGS IN A FILE ABOUT LAND: SLAPPs target activists and NGOs as well as journalists, and are typically brought to shut down discussion of corruption, government action, business practice and environmental concerns. This file has already recorded two: a Kosovar company suing one environmental activist for €100,000 and another for €10,000 after they documented river damage, cases Amnesty International classified as SLAPPs. CASE's own research across 35 countries found cases rising from 570 in 2022 to over 820 in 2023, most brought against individuals rather than organisations, with a median claim of about €15,150. THE LAW HAS CHANGED, AND IT IS NOT ENOUGH: an EU Anti-SLAPP Directive was adopted in 2024, and CASE's 2025 report with the Daphne Caruana Galizia Foundation finds abusive lawsuits still rising despite it. Treat the directive as useful and unfinished, and go to the map rather than assuming protection. WHAT IT IS NOT: a coalition and a referral map, not a law firm itself. Its members include press freedom, transparency and environmental organisations.

trackers.name: Common Lands Network — the commoners, who already hold rights over the ground
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a participatory network open to people, communities and organisations supporting commons and Territories of Life across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. It is the entry point to a category this file has almost entirely missed: the bodies that already hold collective use rights over land, as opposed to conservation charities that would like to. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR STOPPING A PROJECT: across the Alps and much of southern Europe there are common land organisations whose members are the residents themselves. In Italy the amministrazioni separate dei beni di uso civico hold land that legally belongs to the resident community of the municipality and grant user rights over pasture, meadow, fuelwood and other resources, managed by a committee of residents; in many cases only long-term residents — ten to twenty years — can access those rights, and the rights are recognised for households rather than individuals. In Germany the Gemeindealmen and Rechtlerwald are owned by the municipality while residents hold partial property rights — individual easements and servitudes — over the land's resources. Most such bodies in Switzerland and Austria are public-law institutions. THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: if the threatened ground carries civic use rights, the residents are not objectors, they are rights-holders, and there is usually an existing committee with standing and a legal personality. Find out whether your site sits under one before you form a new association. This is the strongest version of the question this file arrived at in batch 119 — what instrument attaches to this land, rather than who owns it. THE SOUTH-EAST EUROPEAN WARNING: research on Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro and Albania records that after the collapse of socialism privatisation proceeded rapidly, practically all communal forms of ownership were abolished, and the notion of commons is generally not directly regulated in the national legal frameworks — access to forest, pasture, foraging and allotment commons persists as social norm and informal arrangement rather than as enforceable right. In those countries a community's customary use is real and legally weak, and that gap is worth knowing before relying on it. WHAT IT IS NOT: a network and a research community, not a funder and not a law firm.

trackers.name: Arnika — Centre for Citizen Support: solves tens of citizen cases a year, and works abroad
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: a Czech non-profit uniting people striving for a better environment since 2001, with a dedicated programme — the Centre for Citizen Support, established 1996 — whose experts help solve tens of cases throughout the Czech Republic every year and which has long experience of promoting positive legislative change and of stopping attempts to narrow the space for public participation in decision-making. ITS METHOD, WHICH IS THE TEMPLATE: it relies on three components — public collaboration, expert opinions and justified requests, and media coverage of the problem. That is the Kruščica checklist stated as an operating model by a professional body: the community, the expert, the press. AND IT WORKS OUTSIDE ITS OWN COUNTRY, which is why this is filed as global rather than Czech: it states that it shares its know-how and protects the environment and environmental rights regardless of geographical location, and it participates in international projects protecting the environment and implementing the Aarhus Convention in Central and Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia. It found the women of Kruščica in Bosnia in 2017 and began supporting them. A community outside the Czech Republic can ask. IT DOCUMENTS WHEN A STATE BREAKS THE RULES: with the Bosnian organisation Eko Forum Zenica it published an alternative report on the application of the Aarhus Convention in Bosnia and Herzegovina, finding the convention violated by the authorities. An alternative report is a recognised route into the convention's compliance machinery, and this is a body that writes them with a local partner. ITS STANDING NETWORKS: member of the Green Circle association of Czech environmental NGOs, the European Environmental Bureau and the European ECO Forum, and it takes part in meetings of the parties to the Aarhus Convention.

trackers.name: Aarhus Centres — free basic legal advice on environmental rights, in 14 countries
trackers.desc: WHAT THEY ARE: a network founded by the OSCE to give members of the public practical resources to exercise their environmental rights, now over 60 Aarhus Centres operating in 14 countries across four regions — in South-Eastern Europe, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Serbia, and further centres in the Caucasus and Central Asia. The page above lists them by country with the activities each one covers. WHAT A COMMUNITY GETS, and this is the sentence that matters: they provide basic legal advice to citizens, citizen groups and civil society organisations on access to justice where their right to information and public participation has been violated. Free, and open to a group as well as an individual. They also provide information, organise public hearings and consultations, and facilitate dialogue. The matter can be local — pollution from a rubbish dump is the example given — or national. THE THREE PILLARS THEY WORK ON are the Aarhus Convention's: access to information, public participation in decision-making, and access to justice in environmental matters. Individual centres list their own activities, which include environmental impact assessment, environmental legislation, access to justice, extractive industries including mining, hazardous waste, water resources management and eco-journalism. Check what your nearest centre actually covers before you go. THEY ALSO WORK ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE COUNTER: they inform judges and advocates about the Convention and existing environmental law, and organise public hearings on projects, draft laws and policies. In regions where environmental legislation is still developing, they are described as key resource centres where citizens can inform themselves about the law relevant to their rights. TWO CAVEATS. Their form varies: Georgia's was transformed by its environment ministry into an independent state entity, so a centre may be governmental rather than independent — ask whose it is. And their host-government partnership means the work is, in the OSCE's own words, highly political. Bosnian Aarhus centres have nonetheless filed suit to protect a river.

trackers.name: ELCN — the private land conservation network, for owners willing to protect part of their land
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS FOR, and it is a category this file has been circling for 180 entries: the European Land Conservation Network was built to support private landowners — non-public bodies or individuals — who are willing to engage in conservation on at least part of their land. Not owners who want to sell. Owners who want to keep the land and protect some of it. WHY THAT MATTERS FOR A COMMUNITY: almost every acquisition entry in this file assumes a purchase. This one assumes the owner stays. Where a community's threatened ground belongs to a farmer or a family who would rather protect it than sell it, this is the network built around exactly that situation. WHERE IT LIVES NOW: the ELCN was established through a LIFE project running 2017 to 2022, coordinated by NABU in Berlin, and at the end of 2019 it was integrated into Eurosite, which changed its name to Eurosite — the European Land Conservation Network and now acts as its secretariat with responsibility for its long-term management and growth. So the by-country member map already filed here is the live door; this entry records what the private-land strand is and who it is for. THE LINEAGE, which tells you who else works on this: the idea of a European Landowners Alliance for Wildlands and Nature was presented in 2013 by Eurosite, Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera, DBU and The Wild Foundation among others; a call for a European Land Stewardship Network followed in 2014 at the closing conference of the LANDLIFE project in Barcelona; and in parallel the International Land Conservation Network was founded in September 2014 in Providence, Rhode Island, as the first global network of private land conservation practitioners. A community outside Europe has that global network to approach. IT HAS WORKING GROUPS: including one on Agriculture, Biodiversity and Climate, chaired from outside the secretariat with a published contact. Approach the working group whose subject matches your ground.

trackers.name: ELAW — will critique the environmental impact assessment and give evidence in court
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the Environmental Law Alliance Worldwide, founded 1989 in Eugene, Oregon by public interest lawyers from ten countries. Today more than 300 public interest advocates from around 80 to 85 countries work together through it, and in a single year advocates call on the network for assistance with more than 400 projects. WHAT ITS SCIENCE TEAM WILL ACTUALLY DO, and this is the reason to file it: critique environmental impact assessments; submit expert testimony to courts; help partners explain technical matters to communities; develop systems to monitor environmental conditions; recommend cleaner alternatives to proposed projects; and connect local scientists with local lawyers. Across 182 candidates, nothing else in this file offers to read the developer's EIA and tell you what is wrong with it. AND ITS LAW TEAM: high-quality legal support to help partners bring enforcement actions, critique proposed statutes, advance policies and replicate model laws, using a global vantage point to spot emerging legal issues and share resources. HOW THE MODEL WORKS, WHICH DETERMINES HOW YOU APPROACH IT: its strategy is finding strong lawyers committed to protecting the environment in their own countries and supporting them. ELAW backs the local advocate rather than arriving to run the case. So a community's route in is usually through a public interest lawyer in its own country who is, or can become, an ELAW partner — and that is how a small case gets access to an international science team at low cost. IT ALSO PROTECTS THE PEOPLE: alongside legal and scientific support it provides security and organisational expertise, and works to enhance the safety of environmental defenders facing threats. Fifth entry in this file to treat the personal risk to defenders as part of the work. IT PUBLISHES USABLE MATERIAL: including a guidebook aimed at giving public interest advocates and the communities they represent enough understanding to challenge unacceptable oil and gas projects. It has brought nearly 300 advocates to the United States as ELAW Fellows, and a number of its partners have won the Goldman Environmental Prize.

trackers.name: ProtectDefenders.eu — a 24/7 helpline and emergency grants, including for legal costs
trackers.desc: WHY THIS IS FILED: five jurisdictions in this file now show the risk landing on the person rather than the case — a 150,000 euro personal claim in Albania, SLAPPs in Kosovo, liquidations in Belarus, legislation against challengers in Romania, and moves against the right of action in Germany. Africa and Latin America had emergency defender funds in this file. Europe had a map of lawyers and no fund. This is the fund. WHAT IT IS: the European Union Human Rights Defenders Mechanism, fully EU-funded and managed by a consortium of international NGOs, with 30 million euros for 2022–2027. Since 2015 it reports having supported more than 85,000 individuals. WHAT IT ACTUALLY PROVIDES: emergency grants for relocation, legal assistance, medical care or security measures; temporary relocation programmes for individuals or families, within their own country or abroad; financial and technical support for local organisations facing pressure, covering capacity building, psychosocial support, security and advocacy training; and training in security, advocacy and psychosocial wellbeing. The list is described as non-exhaustive and an organisation may propose further measures. Legal assistance is named explicitly — this can pay to defend the personal suit. HOW TO REACH IT IN A CRISIS: protection officers are available 24/7, through a permanent emergency helpline run by Front Line Defenders that operates at any hour, with the option of being forwarded to someone speaking Arabic, English, French, Russian or Spanish. Urgent actions can include appeals to the relevant authorities, raising the case through the EU or individual government representatives, and practical help with temporary relocation or medical and legal expenses. PRACTICALITIES A COMMUNITY SHOULD KNOW BEFORE APPLYING: requests can be made for an individual or for an organisation, through separate routes; you may communicate officially in English, French, Spanish, Arabic or Russian, with other languages accommodated where possible; an emergency decision procedure exists for urgent cases, otherwise applications go to a monthly board. On relocation specifically: it is temporary, up to one year, does not facilitate permanent relocation or asylum, priority goes to relocation within the defender's own country or sub-region, and it cannot cover 100 per cent of relocation costs. Emergency support is delivered through partner programmes including Front Line Defenders, FIDH, OMCT, RSF and regional funds.

trackers.name: Aggregates Europe (UEPG) — the quarry industry's own body, and what it admits about permits
trackers.desc: THE OTHER SIDE OF THE TABLE, filed for the same reason as the European Landowners' Organization already in this file: a community facing a quarry has no European network of its own — I looked and did not find one — but the industry has this. Aggregates Europe is the European aggregates industry association, whose national member associations identify who quarries in your country and whose published positions tell you the arguments your developer will make. WHAT COUNTS AS AGGREGATES, so you know whether this is your fight: granular construction materials — sand, gravel, crushed rock, marine, recycled and manufactured — extracted from quarries and sand and gravel extraction sites, occasionally sea-dredged, or recycled from construction and demolition waste. THE ADMISSION WORTH KNOWING, from industry-side reporting rather than campaigners: community opposition, environmental regulations and lengthy permitting have slowed approval of new aggregate sites to a trickle in many Western countries, with under-resourced planning offices contributing to multi-year approval timelines. In Britain, demand for construction aggregates has outstripped newly permitted reserves for ten years running by industry survey. Objection to quarries demonstrably works, and the industry says so. AND THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT TO PREPARE FOR, also from that source: that blocking a local quarry means the same material is trucked in from farther away at higher overall environmental cost. Research on the Madrid region found quarries did move farther from demand areas — but concluded the main cause there was not citizen opposition but a combination of demographic factors and different land use restrictions. That study is the answer to the argument, and it comes from the extractive-industry literature. USE IT FOR: identifying the national association and therefore the operators, reading the industry's own sustainability and good-practice claims before a hearing, and quoting its permitting and reserve figures back.

trackers.name: The Commission's access-to-justice guidance — and what it admits blocks communities
trackers.desc: WHAT IS HERE: the European Commission's Aarhus page, carrying its Notice on access to justice in environmental matters, published 2026, which consolidates the evolving case law of the Court of Justice and gives a comprehensive overview of all pertinent case law. The same page carries a citizen's guide to access to justice. For a community whose lawyer needs the current EU position in one document, this is the official consolidation rather than a commentary. AND THE ADMISSION WORTH QUOTING, because it comes from the Commission and not from campaigners: the Notice addresses persistent disparities in the implementation of Aarhus obligations across Member States and responds to ongoing obstacles faced by individuals and environmental NGOs in gaining effective access to national courts, drawing on the 2019 and 2022 Environmental Implementation Reviews and a 2019 study, which identified persistent systemic challenges — excessive litigation costs, restrictive standing rules and procedural complexity. Those are the three obstacles this file has met country by country, named by the institution responsible for the law. THE THREE PILLARS TO CITE: the right to receive environmental information held by public authorities; the right to participate in decisions relating to the environment; and the right of recourse to a court to enforce rights to information and participation, or to challenge public decisions that contravene environmental law. The Convention is the only international legally binding instrument giving the public — individuals and their associations — broad and specific rights on environmental matters. ONE PRECEDENT WORTH KNOWING: in March 2021 the Aarhus Convention Compliance Committee found the EU itself in breach of Article 9(3) for failing to provide NGOs access to justice against Commission State aid decisions breaching environmental law. The compliance machinery has been used successfully against the EU, which tells you it is not decorative. Also note that the rules allowing access for members of the public beyond environmental NGOs apply from 29 April 2023.

trackers.name: IUCN NL Land Acquisition Fund — grants up to €85,000 to buy the land yourself
trackers.desc: WHAT IT DOES: the IUCN National Committee of the Netherlands runs a fund providing money to local NGOs and CSOs to acquire threatened nature, create reserves, and connect habitats for vulnerable and endangered species, with grants reported up to €85,000. It has run for 25 years and is supported by a growing number of private donors. THE MODEL, WHICH IS THE POINT: the fund does not own any land — it only provides the money, and the local NGO ends up owning and managing the purchased area. It works only with carefully selected local conservation NGOs with proven capacity in managing natural resources. For a community whose problem is a willing seller and no purchase price, that is the exact shape of help needed, and the land stays local. ELIGIBILITY, AND READ THIS FIRST: the applicant must be locally registered as a non-profit, NGO or CSO in Africa, Asia, Latin America or the Pacific; be directly responsible for preparing and implementing the project; and hold a bank account in the organisation's name where it is established or where the project runs. EUROPE AND NORTH AMERICA ARE NOT ELIGIBLE. This is filed as a GLOBAL entry for the regions that can use it — a European community should not spend time on it. WHAT MAKES A PROPOSAL WORK, in the fund's own words: proposals must contribute directly to tangible conservation outcomes and include local participation in the conservation and management of the area. Its own reasoning for the whole approach is worth quoting anywhere: in areas under high pressure, buying remnants of natural vegetation and creating private protected areas can have a massive impact, and with land prices exploding there is no time to wait for decisive action from politicians or decision makers. TIMING: applications have run to a 1 May deadline in recent years — check the current call.

trackers.name: CEPF Mediterranean small grants — the Balkan team is a phone call, not a form
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund's small grant programme in the Mediterranean Basin Biodiversity Hotspot — a joint initiative of the Agence Française de Développement, Conservation International, the European Union, Fondation Hans Wilsdorf, the Global Environment Facility, the governments of Canada and Japan, and the World Bank. Its stated goal is to mobilise and empower civil society — non-governmental organisations, Indigenous peoples and communities, universities and more — to protect the world's biodiversity hotspots. THE MONEY AND WHO CAN GET IT: recent calls have run at USD 15,000–40,000 and USD 20,000–50,000 per grant, with USD 540,000–600,000 available in a round, projects of minimum 12 months. Eligible countries have varied by call and have included Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia alongside Middle Eastern and North African states; an earlier round also covered Cabo Verde and others. Check the current call for the country list — it changes between rounds. The hotspot itself takes in parts of Spain and France, the Balkan states, Greece and Türkiye. AND HERE IS THE PART THAT MAKES IT USABLE: the programme is led by BirdLife International as regional implementation team, and in the Balkans BirdLife works with the Bird Protection and Study Society of Serbia (BPSSS) with support from DOPPS — BirdLife Slovenia. Both of those are already in this file as national entries. So a Balkan community's route into an international fund runs through two organisations it can telephone in its own region and, in Serbia's case, its own language. THE APPLICATION SHAPE: a Letter of Inquiry first, not a full proposal — the same concept-note principle recorded for Cyprus and Germany. Applicants are directed to the Ecosystem Profile's chapter on eligible activities under each Strategic Direction. SCALE, FOR CALIBRATION: CEPF has provided grants to organisations in 14 countries in this hotspot, with more than USD 23 million to Mediterranean civil society, and in one phase awarded 154 grants to local organisations, representing 89 per cent of the budget.

trackers.name: EIA — a confidential channel for reporting forest crime, and a public crime tracker
trackers.desc: THE CHANNEL, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THIS ENTRY: for over three decades EIA has worked with whistleblowers and other sources, and it publishes a route for anyone with credible information or knowledge of potential illegal activity or harmful practices connected to environmental injustices or related human rights impacts. Email with the subject line 'Confidential – Environmental Report', on a channel restricted to and monitored only by limited designated EIA leadership; or write to PO Box 53343, Washington DC 20009, addressed to 'EIA Designated Leadership' and marked Confidential. Reports are reviewed and where needed assessed with legal counsel. Phone +1 202 483 6621. WHY A EUROPEAN COMMUNITY SHOULD CARE: EIA tracked logs from ecologically significant forests to ten pellet mills and three power plants in Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia and Poland, finding about a third of wood shipments to those factories originated in protected areas. It also filed a complaint with the Austrian Federal Forest Office — the authority responsible for implementing the EU Timber Regulation in Austria — over Romanian timber, supported by Agent Green and Neuer Weg. This is the body that follows the material to where it is bought, and complains to the regulator there. AND THE PUBLIC TOOL: the Global Environmental Crime Tracker, a publicly accessible interactive dashboard visualising seizures, arrests and prosecution records collated from government reports, enforcement agency releases, court cases, academic papers, news media in several languages and partner NGOs. The timber dashboard shows the precise location of incidents. EIA says it hopes the expansion makes this easier for individuals, researchers and journalists to use. SCOPE, SO YOU KNOW IF YOUR CASE FITS: wildlife, timber, plastic waste and refrigerant gases; its forests work began in the late 1990s and targets illegal logging, illegal timber flows and the corruption facilitating forest crime, using international laws to press for action.

trackers.name: Kohesio — every EU-funded project in your region, with budget and beneficiary named
trackers.desc: WHAT IT IS: the European Commission's public database of projects financed by EU cohesion policy — discover EU projects in your region — searchable in every EU language and giving, per project, the start and end dates, the fund, the total budget, the EU financial contribution and its percentage, the programme and programming period, the managing authority, the beneficiary and the field of intervention. WHY A COMMUNITY SHOULD OPEN IT: the protected area near you has probably been the subject of an EU-funded project, and Kohesio names who received the money, how much, and what they undertook to do. Real examples in its records include implementation of active biodiversity conservation measures under a Natura 2000 site's management plan at 9,261,408.80 EUR with an 85 per cent EU contribution; monitoring of species and habitats of Community importance under the Habitats and Birds Directives at 20,915,216.90 EUR; preparation of care programmes for a national park and its protected zone; and drawing up management programmes for named protected landscape areas. THREE USES THAT FOLLOW: check whether the site you are defending is already inside a funded management plan — a scheme that damages it then contradicts a commitment the state took EU money for; find the beneficiary organisation, which is a body with staff, expertise and a duty to that site; and see what comparable work costs before you ask anyone to fund a study. AND IT SHOWS THE OTHER SIDE TOO: entries include tourist paths, lighting and infrastructure inside protected areas. The same database that documents protection also documents development funded in the name of it. PRACTICAL: search by region, beneficiary or theme; each project has a stable page you can cite in a submission.

trackers.name: Conservatoire du littoral — Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon office
trackers.desc: WHO TO ENLIST: France's coastal land agency, a public establishment created in 1975 whose whole function is buying threatened coastal ground and holding it permanently, operates in the archipelago and keeps a local office — 13 rue Albert-Briand, BP 4244, 97500 Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, tel. 05 08 41 19 80, spm@conservatoire-du-littoral.fr. The isthmus of Miquelon-Langlade is one of its sites, and the Office français de la biodiversité records that the Grand Barachois lagoon belongs to it. USE IT: the mechanics are what to know before a parcel reaches the market. It acquires parcel by parcel and signs three to four hundred deeds a year across France; roughly 70% of acquisitions are by agreement with the owner, 26% by pre-emption, meaning it can step in ahead of a buyer on a sale already under way, and 4% by expropriation. More than 40% of its annual budget goes on buying land, funded principally by the droit annuel de francisation des navires alongside European, water-agency, local authority and private contributions. It also does not keep the management: it owns the site and entrusts the running of it to a région, département, commune, intercommunalité, syndicat mixte or an association — so a local group can finish as the site's manager rather than its petitioner. THE LIMIT: the OFB records that the archipelago has no marine protected areas and no nature reserves at all, only two hunting and wildlife reserves which together with the Grand Barachois cover about 2,138 hectares, every hectare of it at sea. On land, Conservatoire ownership is close to the only durable protection instrument Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon has.
